As promised, I will update my review.  The issue with T1 NPCs not spawning appears to have been fixed.  I still do not recommend the game, as I feel there are still too many features missing for the $13 price tag.  However, if you like hacking sims and can get the game on sale it may be worth it.
As others have mentioned.  At the time of writing this (10/1/16), the game is basically a $13 chat client with some scrpting capability.  It's like a mediocre version of one of those text games you play while watching streamers on Twitch.
Even if you manage to overlook the sometimes buggy, semi-responsive terminal where players spend most of their time, the game still falls short.  The main game breaking issue that still pursists is the spawning (or lack there of) for T1 NPCs.  Which as far as I know, has yet to be acknowledged by the dev.  Translation, new players cannot level up and so cannot progress in the game. i.e. purchase upgrades, upload scripts, or do anything really (view other reviews for more details). They can however, join chat rooms.
I do feel this game has potential, but until this specific, obvious flaw is resolved, and exploiters punished or victims rewarded, I simply cannot recommend this game in good conscience.
I will update this review if anything changes.

This game is quite simply amazing. There are a few unique things that really make this game great because they have really thought about does and doesn't make good play experiences, and then made the game to make sure there are no bad experiences.
First example is the item system. There are no menus and no inventory. Every item is a physical object. You can only carry one at a time, you have phsyical slots on your back pack to attach them, and you physically seem them all taking up room. You can store things on rovers, spaceships, bases, or just throw them on the ground. It all involves physically moving every item in the world. No boring menus/investory to manipulate, no 'stacking'. It really makes the game immersive because you feel like you are part of a more 'real' world having to gather resources. Infact most of the game is based around how you will physically carry things back to your base (hence the need for trucks and rovers etc.).
Secondly the crafting is simple. The formulas are never more than one item, and they are shown to you at various crafting stations that you build (like 3D Printer, Vehicle Bay). So you don't have to go hunting for various things at the same time, and you always know what you need. It may sound overly simple, but its actually liberating because it makes mining and exploration more fun and goal driven.
Another amazing system is the idea of teathering. To get air (And power if needed) you need to tether to a supply. You can drop teathers every 10m or so. Its a vantastic idea because it not only serves as a good limiting mechanism for air/power, but it also doubles as a way to mark your path. Plus the tethers look quite simply amazing especially as you start to make tether lines to various mines etc.
The game also has a sort of module system in which you build things and attach them to each other in various ways. For example you can make a rover, then attach things to it like a seat, a storage shelf, solar panel for power, etc. Its all done extremely simply and intuitively, yet it allows amazing flexibility.
The world is very well chosen for scale. It currently has a solar system of about 5 planets and a moon. They planets are big, yet at the same time small (you can probably drive around one in 30minutes or so). The solar system really behaves like a real one, with planets orbiting the sun, and planets rotating for day night cycle.
Overall, I only review this on the current content. I don't care if its supposidly 'pre alpha'. There maybe on only about 10 hours of actual play, but it is great and makes you want to start again for new experiences several times over.

While still in Alpha the concept and a lot of game is there. Yes you can research and acquire everything relativley quickly (6-10 hours) the fun is the exploration aspect. You start out on a Terran planet. Basic materials are on the surface which is relativley flat and hostile free. Go into caves for more advanced resource and native research items. There are some hostile plants in caves that can kill you but that is about it. The terran planet is fun and the base building while very basic is fun. The magic came in when I went to another planet. I realized that going to another planet doesnt mean leaving your home planet behind. In fact its the opposite. You go to other planets and farm more resources. For example Arid planets have copper and aluminum on their surface unlike Terran which are in caves. Build a mining base and bring some of that sweet ore or refined metal back to your home planet.
The game is loads of fun, even better with friends. So excited to see what the devs do with this game. Already it has soooooo much promise. If you like Minecraft or wished No Man's Sky was what it actually advertized itself as get this game you will not be disappointed.

Very interesting game - not a new concept, but interesting all the same.  No, it isn't Minecraft and it isn't like Minecraft, but it would be nice to have some similar features down the road.  As it is, it is a very laid back open world exploration game that is lacking a bit in content.
No FPS issues at all, no issues on Windows 10 - the only issues I have appear to be with the bugs in this EA title.  The few bugs encountered are not game breaking as others have stated, just frustrating - I've had a vehicle and storage units launch themselves into space and overlapping items/vehicles/nodes under certain circumstances, but that''s it.  Usually it means rebuilding, but you learn from the mistakes and play smarter the next time - these bugs will probably be fixed...
I like that the tutorial is fairly short, unobtrusive, and doesn't hold your hand well into the game.  Yes, there are some frustrating moments as you try to figure out something after making a mistake, only to find you can't undo that mistake.  Also, there are some things that won't be easy to figure out at all, but Minecraft was similar in this respect and didn't suffer much because of that.  Note to the devs - ignore anyone whining about the lack of an in-depth tutorial.
I'd like to suggest they edit the store page - they mention "custom" vehicles and modules, when in fact there isn't much to customize.  You can add a few attachments to either, but customization implies that you can do more than simply select from a limited number of attachments that you'll HAVE to use in certain situations - and some can't be removed once placed on a vehicle.  You can't even pick where to place some of them on the vehicle and there are no options for customizing color or look.
I like to support EA titles and have been "burned" on numerous ones, but this one seems to be heading in the right direction for now and is completely enjoyable right now.  Consider this a tentative thunbs up...

We've been waiting for this game since it came out exclusively XBLA to arrive on PC and now we've been waiting even longter for it to finally remove GFWL. Now we got that, too!
ITSP is a Metroidvania-type game where you control a flying saucer through an... well, an insanely twisted shadow planet! You gain new abilities and have to backtrack to other locations where your new ability will come in handy. The visual aesthetics are comical yet not ridiculous, the sound design is quite intense. The game's cutscenes feature music by Dimmu Borgir, whereas the background music is more atmospheric yet not less fitting.
All in all a very engaging experience, some may consider it short, yet intense none the less. Recommended!
[CONCERNING FRAMERATE ISSUES]
Edit: I feel like I have to edit this review. The game is great in design and visual style! Yet, unfortunately, for some users there seems to be a problem, that the game just won't go above 30fps. Which is pretty cross, as the game is intended to run in 60fps and gets slower with the framerate. Thus, people who have the same problem as me will play through the game in HALF OF THE INTENDED GAMESPEED. For nVidia users, turning on maximum performance in power management mode works, for amd users, like me, however... nope? I'll remove this text, as soon as a fix has been found.
Edit 2: After having this issue for two years and almost forgetting about it, out of curiosity I checked how well ITSP would perform on the very same machine after I did the upgrade to Windows 10. I didn't change any of the hardware. I just looked into the game and WOW it's RUNNING LIKE HELL! Verified with Fraps - yupp. Solid 60fps now. :) I will let the first edit stay here for reference for others.
Verdict: Runs great - even better - on Windows 10. Still recommended!

There are balance issues with respect to food (you can combine slimes and make a slime that will eat what you can mass produce) but the marketplace changes daily, so some slimes will be better than others depending on prices. Once again, this game is early in development. While there are a lot of things you can do, about 4 hours worth before you hit endgame, there are many missing features that will be added in future patches (hopefully).
TL,DR: If you like cute and don't mind spending $20 on a currently 4 hr experience that will have you smiling more often than not, go for it. But it's missing some things.

This game took me by surprise!
It's a little precision-jump game that does a lot of thing right where others seem to fail...
It's got simple but very decent graphics, the music is sadly enough a limited tracklist of 2 songs but they're very very nice to hear and don't get boring very soon (and you can disable it) and last but not least; the controls of the 'ball' are just fenomenal. A lot of these 'jumping' games lack the buttersmooth AND tight control over the character at the same time ...
It's the reason why so many 'meatboy' clones fail; because they don't invest enough into the controls, and in meatboy there's put a lot of effort to get the controls just exactly like they are; buttersmooth and supertight at the same time.
This little game called BRIC is really worth your money as a little timekiller you play inbetween...  I wish the dev would only put a little bit more time into the game and finish of some options like having the game going fullscreen and giving us a resolution option which are now both fixed.  Also using a controller would be a nice option.
And if he has more music coming like the one that's already in the game; some more tracks are always welcome!
now, my conclusion is definitely that this game is worth your money as so it was mine. The complete randomness of the game is also done very well so you'll never play the exact same game twice, it's always different... Some extra devtime would be nice but it's not necessary to make this game great. Ow, and it's not as hard as "the impossible game" :)

War Thunder, World of Tanks and Heroes and Generals

textures, you can actually be inside houses, so
expect some snipers.

Tanks are my favourite, the controls are manual so you
have to turn the engine on, change gears and move
forward and backwards slowly.
Planes are good, you can use a joystick (I should buy one)..
IMO the best part is that all vehicles with more than 1 crew
can actually be played by more than 1 person, you can ask
people to join your tank/bomber crew, even friends!
So! What are you waiting for? Invite friends, the game
only is 1.8gb!

I like adventure games, and I buy a lot hoping to find the occasional gem. The Raven sadly fails in almost every way. It's surprisingly worse than the average discount game I pick up.
The trailer shows an interesting premise: a thief, out of retirement, striking again. Secret identities, crazy capers, danger and intrigue - it sounds almost like a Mission Impossible movie.
But while the idea is ok, it was ultimately turned into a plodding, dull game. The puzzles are obtuse and require massive amounts of backtracking. It can be hard to find the exact mouse position to move between screens, or do the exact thing the game expects you to. While most of the time you can move things slowly forward, there are quite a few places where it's easy to get stuck and feel frustrated.
The game has hints and ways of exposing clickable items, but they come at a cost: using them lowers your score. I wouldn't care if the score were just a number, but it actually dictates the unlockable bonus content and achievements you get. That means functions that might've helped move the game along become totally off limits. They might as well have not even included them.
The graphics are ok, but the animations are lacking. And a lot of the set pieces and backgrounds get re-used. It's lazy artwork.
The voice acting is possibly the worst I've ever heard in an adventure game. The biggest offender is whoever plays the main character. The character itself is beyond boring to the point of annoying, and the voice acting only serves to accentuate those traits. He says his lines like he has all the time in the world, only rarely showing emotion. The others might have some good moments, but overall they're not much better.
The story is disappointingly empty of any meaning. There's a plot, and there are twists, but since you won't care about any of the characters they all feel inconsequential. Despite all the reveals at the end it doesn't feel like you accomplished anything.
There's no real journey here. Moving from point A to point B simply isn't interesting without something at stake. Spend your time elsewhere.

Is the master criminal known as the Raven actually dead, or has he (or she!) returned to strike again? At first glance, this seems like your ordinary mystery/heist story in adventure game form. It starts off as an Agatha Christie homage aboard the Orient Express, and later an Agatha Christie homage on a boat to Cairo, but it turns into something so much better. For the first half of the game (which is in three separate chapters), you play as Constable Zellner, a Swiss policeman who loves mystery books and thus inserts himself into the mystery unravelling around him. He's basically the most likable character in the world, and is like your favorite old uncle who slips you a twenty and tells you not to tell your parents. You follow him through jewel heists and murders, investigating alongside the detective who supposedly killed the Raven years ago--or did he? Then, right at the story's climax halfway through, where normally you would get the big exposition dump about how it was all done, you instead actually jump to the start of the game and get to replay the story's events as thte thieves. You get to see all the weird unexplained details that you revealed as the constable and begin to understand what was really going on the whole time. There are twists and turns even when you know what was going to happen during the flashback playthrough, which keeps it interesting. It finishes with a pretty satisfying ending.
So, the good and the bad.
The good: EXCELLENT music, which is very cinematic. It might as well have been the score from Death on the Nile or any other good detective movie. GREAT characters. You interact with a small group of characters, with new ones added along the way, and you get to interact with them and slowly learn their stories. These aren't NPCs that you never learn their names or don't care about them . The voice acting is likewise EXCELLENT. The story is entertaining.
The bad: The animation is not great. A couple of the character models are plain creepy (one lady's smile is 90% teeth). Shadows are off frequently, not fantastic lip-syncing. The backgrounds and scenery are fantastic (in one scene, they even animated the little dust particles in a beam of light from a window) but the characters compared to it are awkward. The character motion is often annoying, as characters will move to a spot when you interact with an object and often get stuck and turn around or shimmy several times to try to get into a spot blocked by local geometry. It's frustrating to watch. Also, there is a "fast forward" function when you are going to a new area that is SUPPOSED to allow you to cut away from the chraracter walking to that area, but it didn't work 70% of the time, and I had to watch as these characters walked horribly slowly to the next scene. There is also a puzzle in Chapter 3 where there are 3 WRONG orders to put together some items, and only 1 right order. If you do the wrong order, the character simply won't do what you need them to, and there's no way to undo the steps you already did. I got stuck and had to redo the entire chapter from the beginning because the autosave didn't put me far enough back in the story to get around the glitch. Save often! Don't rely on autosave!
Overall, if you like Agatha Christie-like mysteries, jewel heists, great characters, point-and-click adventure games, or all of the above, you should definitely play this game. It's glitches and less-than-stelllar character models/animations are easily ignored for this story.

If you enjoy puzzle games then Plith is worth a try. Your goal is to connect the green and red gears in each stage together by placing additional gears of 3 different sizes. You have to place gears in the random order they are given to you which makes you adapt as you play each stage which keeps you on your toes. The game also does a nice job of adding new rules and mechanics when things start to get a little repetitive. These include placing gears in your way that you need to blow up,  time limits for puzzles, lightning that stuns you if your cursor touches it, and more.
The only issues I have with Plith are pretty minor. Throughout my time playing the game I experienced an occasional crash to my desktop (the game autosaves the level you are on so it wasn't much of an issue) and some lag upon completing levels. The graphics also leave a little bit to be desired but given it's an indie puzzle game I didn't really expect much. None of this affected my enjoyment of the game too much.
If you like puzzle games I'd recommend Plith, there's plenty of enjoyment to be had with it.

I pre-ordered and played No Man's Sky when it was released. One of my favorite games is Terraria and I love sandbox building games in general. ASTRONEER feels like a space version of Subnautica. I put 10 hours into ASTRONEER before writing this and am thoroughly impressed. The game plays like what I thought No Man's Sky would be like when it was released.
+ Explore different enviroments and planets
+ Can build bases on each planet
+ Can shape the enviroment any way you want, remove and add land
+ Coop works well despite being in pre-alpha
+ Weather that is "interactive" Kappa
+ Customize your gear and vehicles with gadgets to fit your play style and the planet's atmosphere
+ Surprisingly a lot of different gadgets to use even in pre-alpha
+ Helpful and easy to understand controls menu, hit escape and go to controls (sodapoppin missed this)
- Bugs, I never encountered any in my 10 hours of single player mode. I did watch sodapoppin's stream of coop and they ran into bugs. Expected of pre-alpha and Early Access.
- Still a lack of content, can probably play 15 hours and see pretty much every feature, it's still in pre-alpha though
- Loading games is surprisingly unintuitive, if you read this and want to continue your save, go to the far left and click the outline of a new pod
- Environment loads slow and it's the game since it happened on sodapoppin's $10,000 PC and my PC which is modestly cheaper than his
- No steam achievements, cloud saves, or trading cards yet

Depending on your patience with repeating content and how many friends you have to play with, you could probably put 15-20 hours into the pre-release. If you feel that is worth $19.99 for you, I definitely recommend purchasing it.

Don't let the graphics fool you.  I started playing this when it was released in June 2001 and I'm glad to see it finally released to a much larger audience.  The amount of detail, the variety of roles, equipment, tactics, vehicles, physics/damage model and the sheer number of players that are on the map at any given time is unsurpassed in this type of sub-genre.
Want to be a lone-wolf and roam the country looking for unsuspecting tank commanders who like to drive around with their hatches open and their heads exposed?  That tank is now immobilized by your superior tactics and a cheap bullet.  Want to be a part of a massive paratrooper drop? Then hop on a flight and hope a fighter doesn't find you first.  My point is that you may think this could be a pay-to-win model, but it's not.
You can have lots of fun and do some real damage with even the simplest of weapons.  Although I've been a paying subscriber, my favorite tactics are those that involve guerilla warfare.  "Kill em with a stick".  There is nothing more fun than beating the player with the biggest, most powerful weapon by using better tactics and a cheaper, less powerful weapon.
I can't even begin to tell you how many unique and fun experiences I've had playing this with hundreds of people from all over the world.  This game never died.  That's right, its been around since 2001, but was never been exposed to the masses on Steam until now.
There is a reason why the new team behind Cornered Rat Software is finally bringing it to Steam.  The gameplay has proven to be sustainable/fun and exposure to a successful game service model with a huge pool of potential players will surely extend its already long lifespan.
It is a social experience (If you want it to be) and a never-ending war on one map that saves your progress.  Don't worry about the graphics not being top-of-the-line like todays releases.  This will simply be overlooked after you discover whats really available under the hood and it also makes this game accessible to more gamers who won't need the latest, most expensive equipment to play.
Nobody thought Minecraft, CS-GO or PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds would be a hit because of their outdated looks.  It was their superior/addictive gameplay that pushed those titles to historical highs.  I hope the same happens to WW2 Online here on Steam.  It already has its longevity award.
Give this a try.  There is a big learning curve and you will be required to complete an initial training tutorial, but you will be glad you did later.  Read more about this games history here:

This game does have dated graphics, but for me that is a worthwhile trade off to have such a huge playable map.

ITSP feels sort of like a Metroid-lite twin-stick space shooter that features a blend of combat, puzzles, and exploration. While the game does combat quite nicely for the most part, it struggles in the other two areas. Puzzles are usually interesting yet don't provide much of a challenge. And despite the map being so massive, there's a lot of backtracking and perhaps too much linearity over the course of the campaign.
In spite of these issues, ITSP is still a fun experience. Its best accomplishment is creating a wonderful world that oozes atmosphere through its eerie ambient sounds and a colorful animation style that's used to create some beautiful, creepy and varied environments. There's a good variety of ship upgrades, although switching between them on a gamepad can be clunky. The main campaign is pretty short but I felt that was much more preferable to dragging on for too long. And while the puzzle-solving isn't a strong point, the combat portions of the game are fun thanks to the simplified controls and bizarre enemies/bosses.
While far from perfect, ITSP is a solid enough game to warrant a discounted purchase. A flawed yet atmospheric and beautiful space shooter that features huge and diverse locations and some solid twin-stick combat.

Are you looking for a Left 4 Dead style zombie apocalypse shoot em' up?
No More Room In Hell, or NMRIH is a zombie apocalypse survival horror.

- Resource management is a must, especially when playing on a larger map with a crew
- There are consequences for being a little too close with infected
- Health, movement, and other survival related parameters must be tended to
- Voice communication, especially in public lobbies is encouraged
What makes it good? If you're looking for a difficult survival oriented zombie apocalypse game that you can play for hours with friends on a Friday night, then you found it. Otherwise, stick to something like Left 4 Dead.

You don’t get to play one of the worst games ever made that often. This is one such game. The Deer is an educational game for children that aspires to teach players about the Ice Age. The focus is on the deer and its immediate surroundings. Like the mouse. And an oak tree. The game can be completed in less than 5 minutes. Using an abysmal control scheme, you guide the deer from the left to the right. There’s the aforementioned mouse, oak tree, a squirrel and a rhino. After about 5 meters, you come to a lake. Not a problem because deer don’t swim, they simply walk along the bottom of the lake. After about 4 meters of underwater walking, there’s nowhere else to go. Along those 9 meters of gameplay, you can click on three points of interest to play three mini-games. One is a memory game, the other is about recognizing deer food (deer don’t eat fries from McDonald’s – shock!), and I don’t even know what the hell was the third one about anymore.
I didn’t learn crap from this game. But the worst offending thing is the horrible grammar, especially considering that this is supposed to be an educational game. “Between the companions of The Deer, there were even the lazy dormouses.” “Did you know that the majestic oaks can live even 1000 years?” “Near the lake, lived even many frogs and toads.” Unless you want your kids to learn broken English, stay away. Absolute bullcrap. Apart from the illustrations, which are nice and which drew me to the game along with the premise, the only good thing was that I bought the game during launch for 11 cents (the developer has since increased the price to 99 cents). It has trading cards, so I actually made a profit.

Problems with this port:
- Occasionally stuttering framerate
- 8 direction movement
While there may be more issues, I only encountered these two in my playtime but I couldn't enjoy the game with these considered. The stuttering framerate is distracting and it really something that you can't deal with in a game based on speed and precision. I should note that I don't mean a BAD framerate, but frame STUTTER, meaning that certain frames are dropped entirely, or many frames in a row, making the game appear to be jerking. I have a GTX 760 in my test machine if that helps prove that the stuttering is not a hardware issue.
More importantly though, the control is problematic. While I used a gamepad to play this game, it does not simulate the proper 360 degree input of a joystick like the dreamcast and gamecube versions of the title, but rather emulates a keyboard. This means that it can only enter eight directions, much like the 8 most common directions labelled on a compass. Thus your 360 degrees of analog input is split into 8 45 degree parts that equate to a very specific direction. Unfortunately this makes Sonic feel very clumsy and often it makes it unplayable.
Regardless of your opinion of the original game, it's a lackluster port that gets some very crucial aspects of the game wrong.

I've always had a soft spot for the earliest signs of surrealist art styles in gaming. Featuring astounding camera angles and
, your action stages advance into areas such as an impressionist version of Twister and the trippiest casino on Dreamcast. One stunning moment is when a road leading out of station square is blocked by cop cars. Sonic cannot go past, but you see a man in a suit right nearby.  One can almost feel Sonic's emotional pain, wondering "What's it like, being white?"
You are supposed to be able to play co-op with one person controlling Sonic and one controlling Tails. Unfortunately, both players control Sonic. You can lead him in different directions, and in the end he is torn and confused, unable to go anywhere. The representation of young miles prower's simultaneous independence and loyalty speaks so well to his childhood and friendship, transcending even the thought provoking powerups, each more metaphysical than the last. Therefore, I would strongly recommend this far from perfect game for the enjoyable concepts it presents when played with a friend.

This is a tough review to write, because I've only played through the beginning of episode two, and I'm already 8 hours in. (See edit below: finished it after writing this review.)
With that said, the game has two major flaws for me.
1) It's buggy. I'm frequently stuck in spots walking infintely, or unable to open doors (the triggers vanish). I'm forced to reload a prior save to sort this out, but this causes me to lose progress. Save early, save often.
Also, manipulating the inspector is like watching Austin Powers maneuver the cart at the end of the first movie. You'll click on a location to exit a scene and watch the inspector go forward, back, forward, turn, forward, back, then forward again like he's lost his mind.
2) It's boring. As said, I'm 8 hours in, and I don't care one bit about any of the characters. They all seem lifeless and interchangeable with one exception - the kid. You spend a lot of time backtracking and listening to people talk about the boring details of their life. There are some attempts at red herrings but they all fall a bit flat.
One other minor complaint is the animation. I'm not expecting photo-realistic graphics or skeletal rigging here, but when the characters talk, their mouths flap open and closed like ventriloquist dummies. It's very disconcerting. The worst was watching the American lady talk on the outside of the ship in the first episode - just one big hinged jaw and a gigantic mouthful of teeth flapping at me.
The game does have some things going for it. It's one big Agatha Christie homage, so if that's your cup of tea, it may be enough to overcome some of the other aspects of the game.
I'd like to finish the game to see how the plot plays out, but since it took me just over 7 hours for the first episode, I don't have the patience to put in a potential 14 more hours. I feel like the game does not respect my time, which is enough for me to press abort.
Not recommended, unless you really really like Agatha Christie homages and don't mind being disinterested for hours on end while trying to steer the shopping cart that is the inspector.
Edit: I finished the game today, after I wrote this review. Fundamentally, my opinion has not changed but I do have a bit more to add.
First, the game is - as far as I can tell - not able to be completed if you're using a gamepad. There are two parts in episode 3 where you will not get the proper interaction spots when using a gamepad. The first happens when you're in the ship cell area trying to hook a rope onto a hook. The hook prompt will not appear and I was only able to progress by switching to keyboard play.
The second happens outside the museum. You get no prompt to enter the museum. Again, switching to keyboard lets you enter and continue on. At that point, I stopped trying to use the gamepad.
Furthermore, I did run into two more cases where the character got stuck walking infinitely. The first was again in the cell portion of the ship, the second was - surprise! - outside the entrance to the museum. For both cases, I had to quit the game and relaunch.
So again - pretty buggy and frustrating experience. I did feel that the game picked up some interest once you start playing as other characters, but that is somewhat deadened by having to go through the same environments all over again.

Alot of people love this game, so there's no real need to add another review to the thousands of others. However if this review does get read by someone, its worth it to add - less of a typical review but more so 2 personal ideas.
Note I 106% completed this game on ps4 as I prefer the dual shock 4. I have limited hours on the steam version, but its safe to say its exactly the same experience (except for the music - steam has better soundtrack, as well as different character unlockables).
-    First point (I think the most important) - this game essentially drew my attention back to the gaming industry.
-    Second point - This game is a gateway (it was for me) to other challenging games.
First point - my attention was raised, I researched games again, I read books about the industry's history, and proudly began to play games with more effort and generally just play more games in general (mostly platformers admitedly). I firmly attribute my love of Super meat boy towards my refound love of all gaming.
Prior to even attempting super meat boy, I didnt play platformers often - I had super mario land as a young kid and along with the crash bandicoot series I only really played these two franchises of platformers. I didn't complete them as a kid, I just enjoyed them enough. As I grew up, I would play gta, saints row, gran turismo, tekken... And then all but gave up gaming from mid high school through the end of university. Very casual, mainstream games. Very limited hours invested...
Then 3 years ago (approx) i found super meat boy...
Catch up to today and Ive bought old nintendo consoles, old playstations (the ones I didnt have or had sold) and went bananas and bought platformers galore. Whats more is I play them, and appreciate them. The jumping arc, the speed, momentum, the wall jump, weight, gravity, just the sheer joy in movement, the flow. I love it all, but it was only after meat boy that I paid attention to these dynamics in all games in general. I analyse the moveset in 2d games, 3d games, platformers, racers (sim and arcade), skating games, twin stick shooters, shooters, old arcade games. Anything that focuses on movement.
I attribute it all, my love for gaming as an adult, but espeically how they flow and feel, to Super meat boy.
Second point - this game made me, forced me, to play other games of revered difficulty. I used to suck as gaming. This was due to lack of interest and practise, not innate skill. Super meat boy WILL improve your play, it will make you more determined, and will force you to persevere. You, as I did, will return to earlier levels in the game and clear worlds with no deaths. I humbly learned what my limits were, then pushed them, and they grew. Yours will too. It will be work, but you'll love it. If you hate it, all the time, dont play platformers! Or maybe it just doesnt click. That's fine. But while you're raging away just recall how you can now fly through a previous devil of a 20 level world, and enjoyed doing so.. Leave the game. Tomorrow it will be there to fight.
So that essentially sums up my attitude towards this and other diffcult games, after playing super meat boy. I used to stop after a while and give up hard games. Ive now near 100% completed many games because I want to. I'm not a super gamer, I just love them.

Thanks for reading. Enjoy the game.

It starts easy, and then has a perfectly sensible difficulty curve for about ten levels.
After that, you're on your own.
The game is brutally difficult, and often punishing of even the most minute mistakes. This is exacerbated by a control set that is both incredibly precise and very loose simultaneously, giving you absolute control over your character, but also forcing you to watch him slip around the environment like he's covered in oil.
It's also certainly not lacking in content. With 20 levels per chapter and at least 5 (Or more, but that's spoilers) chapters, plus 'Dark World' versions (Which are the same map, but with the difficulty cranked up a couple notches (Which is saying something)), not to mention quite a few bonus stages and levels, there's more than enough content to keep even the most avid player going for ages, but since most gamers aren't going to make it past Chapter 2, it's a shame that they didn't include a few easier stages so that less capable players couldn't also get their money's worth.
In short, if you want a vast challenge, go ahead. If you want something a bit more relaxed, go elsewhere.

This is my opinion, don't get your sentience in a twist.
I want to like this game, I really do. The problem, currently at least, is what I can only chalk up as a lack of foresight on the developer's part, or perhaps the inevitable cruel intentions of others that is provided by the glory of anonymity on the Internet.
Don't get me wrong, Sean has a brilliant and amazing idea here. I really enjoy the idea of this game. The exeuction, however, seems to have been poor. Maybe he didn't consider how big of a market a game like this would please - or how big the market was for a game such as this. Either way, this breaks down to a few very key factors, which I'll list here:
1) Early-game systems (Classified as T1) are almost always in a Breached state. This means that no one else can access them, which effectively renders them useless for anyone else trying to get some cash (Classified as GC) in game. On one hand, I can understand why Sean put this in place and it's an entirely immersive design choice, in my opinion. On the other hand, mechanically, it inhibits people from progressing in a more peaceful (not attacking other players) manner.
There are a lot of T1 systems, of course, but this doesn't prevent players with automatic scripts that syphon GC from those systems from adding literally all of the T1 systems to their scripts. After all, the starting points for these scripts (let's take one, weyland.out) don't change. The accounts within them may change, and probably do, but the starting points themselves do not. This makes it very easy for someone to create a script that goes through and automatically fetches the individual nodes (accounts, such as abndnd_1vt453.ext14gs) within the systems to then draw the funds on those nodes to the script creator's personal account.
This is very powerful, certainly, and I do think this should be enthused. There are, however, better ways to handle it. An older (no longer operational) hacking simulator similar to ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ allowed almost the same level of scripting, but didn't implement it in such a way that other users couldn't access those hacked systems. This game is called HackWars; in HackWars, the developers created their own proprietary scripting language inside of the game (complete with its own API and Wiki) that allowed you to create some extraordinarily powerful scripts and do some real damage within the confines of the game. They designed it in such a way that it wouldn't necessarily allow someone to automatically farm and lock systems the way ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ does.
2) The game goes out of its way to be cryptic. Even when you do start hacking a system, there's no clean and clear way to determine what type of system you're hacking. To elaborate further on this, allow me to explain some mechanics of the game: Systems are secured by in-game products called Locks. These locks come with various complexities and intricacies - think along the lines of standard encryption methods today, but simplified as to not include absurd hashes. In the game, the few locks I came across were EZ_21, EZ_23, c001, and c003.
Cracking an EZ_21 lock is taught to you in the game through its initial tutorial, which is great. EZ_23 locks function similarly to EZ_21 locks, and are easy enough to determine with the knowledge gained from cracking EZ_21 locks, which I think is also a really great method of teaching someone your game.
However, there comes to be a certain problem with c001 and c003 locks. You aren't taught how these locks act, or what the constraints are of them. You have to figure this out yourself, or learn it from someone who did. On one hand, this is great, on another, it's bad. With c001 locks, you essentially guess a certain thing (I'm trying to avoid spoilers here) and can get it right pretty quickly if your knowledge on those things are already pretty ironclad (it is for most people). c003 locks add on to c001 locks by requiring a complement to the thing in a usual c001 lock. There's no way for you to determine what the complement could be to that thing, even if your knowledge on the thing is pretty extraordinary.
There's no guides that are prebuilt into the game after the tutorial (everything is playermade, which may or may not be the truth). On one hand, this is good because it fosters experimentation and trying what you think will work, but on another hand it's very bad. What makes this bad is that it leaves the door wide open for misinformation, or for people to flat out lie to each other so that they don't ever gain an advantage or even a footing in the game. Not only that, but the game directly tells you to trust no one, except "Trust", which is Sean the Developer. The game's emphasis on "trust no one" is so directly said that - if you're like me - you'll come out of the tutorial not believing anything anyone says, which just puts you even more in the dark.
3) Risk. The game makes a big emphasis on risk, and determining if doing something is "worth the risk" or not. That's made difficult to do, because as I described in my previous point, the game is cryptic. There's no way, going into a system, for you to determine if it's a risky hack or a run-of-the-mill easy-peasy system. There's no way to determine if something is "worth the risk", which completely destroys the game's very emphasis. I don't have much else more to add here, because it's simply a fault on the game in the mechnical sense.
4) There's no way to determine if a system is a player or a NPC. This is good and bad, as I said before. It's good because it adds some vibrancy to the game's world, with no way to tell if you're about to hack a poorly protected player, or a NPC. On that aspect, this is actually a great thing. On the more mechanical aspect, however, I consider it a poor design choice. What makes this a poor design choice is based on the person:- I don't like making people angry at me, and prefer cooperation over competition. By making it impossible to tell if I'm hacking a player or NPC, it's impossible for me to govern myself, to keep me from making some other real person angry at me. It's a teardown of an aspect of my agency, and I don't think that's good to have in a game such as this.
In conclusion, the game falls flat on a few key design choices, and fails to deliver on the basic principle of instruction. It does some good things right, but the good things are drastically overshadowed by the things it does wrong. They're overshadowed so much, actually, that I find it hard to find the good things about this game. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, it means that it's a good game needing major improvements/overhauls to be great.
My final score for ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ is a "sys.migrate out of this game". Thanks Sean, it's a solid experience, but it needs a lot of improvement.

There are a lot of problems with this game.
First and foremost, you should know that you probably will not be able to get a refund, because the single player "tutorial" alone takes more than 2 hours, and it's actually the best part of the game, so you will play through it. But once you're in the multiplayer, you may very well likely want to refund.
I am starting to feel like this game basically hacked me.
- once you're thrown into multiplayer, you're thrown into the deep end, and a lot of players are rightfully saying they have no idea what to do. 2-3 hours of tutorial shouldn't do that to you. Other players will help you, once you figure out what the hell is going on at all. In the tutorial, you're given a lot of what you need. Gold (GC) and scripts. In the multiplayer, you start with nothing, and it feels like you can do nothing.
- once you finally figure out you need to hack into npc scripts, you will also find that the lowest level scripts have already been hacked. There is supposed to be a "reset" every day at midnight UTC, but this seems haphazard - I have not yet seen this happen. Usually I'm at work at midnight UTC, but I've just had a day off and the scripts did not reset. Instead, there is just people trying to trick you into running malicious scripts. The malicious scripts may even be covered up to look like safe scripts.
This means every new player can't really play the game except to be tricked by people who already have high level scripts going on and know what they're doing.
The game is very javascript heavy, and while you will learn a few basics the multiplayer really relies on you being able to learn how to create your own user scripts. This is real javascript. The dev actually asks us to not break the game with it, despite a few safeguards built into the game. My point here isn't that the game is dangerous (beyond other users potentially being able to crash your game), but that the game can be very hard to learn to play. This is not like Hacknet at all. People recommend that you try a codecademy course on coding javascript, which many claim isn't hard. That's true, coding is quite easy, for some people. It is quite difficult for others, even with the little that the game tries to teach you.
I'd be seriously considering a refund right now if the tutorial hadn't screwed me over with how long it took. If only the game kept on with its single player campaign, or at least if the damn low level scripts would be available on the regular, that might have been its saving grace.

-- The npc's that newer players depend on after finishing the tutorial/campaign only respawn once every 24h.
This is way to long of a time with the amount of new players joining up at this time. This severly limits their game experience, in such a way that it shouldn't and won't be ignored by the dev. I hope so at least, because for the rest the game really has potential, if you enjoy hack-themed games & muds.
If you also enjoy coding (javascript) you will get something extra out of this game... and if dont but you always wanted to learn - here is your chance to dip your toe into the water.
But for now, with the t1 npcs being drained shortly after spawning, I can't recommend this game. I will edit this if the issue gets fixed in a reasonable time and ofcourse change the rating.

WWII Online is an old game. I played it first in 2005.
The question is, why should you play such an outdated game?
First, It is a MMOFPS. All the War Thunder and Heroes and Generals and other wannabe MMOs are basically 16x16ish games. Here you can play with thousands in massive battles on massive seamless map with persistent campaign. The only other game that can itself MMOFPS is Planetside II, with a much smaller map. There is no other game that attempted the same goal and I doubt any other game will. Period.
Second, there is no money / xp / golds, etc. There is only a rank - newbie can't take a Tiger tank because he would waste it in two minutes. You play long enough and you can drive / fly anything. No microtransactions, booster packs, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Third, you will join a great community of mature players.
Now, this is all great, but there is the other side...
The graphics is outdated. A lot. But this will be changed in the future, if you care.
This is not a game for casual players. The game is hugely teamplay oriented, rambo style will not get you far.
Be prepared to invest some time into learning the actual tactics with the given vehicle, before you have any success ... For example, you can shoot all your 30mm rounds from an AT gun into a tank and still do nothing to it - the armor plate might be too thick. You need to learn where to hit and under what angle. Every tank has its weaknesses. All this is based on the real stuff research.
If you do not recognize that and play it as a one man action, you are about to get into running / dying / waiting simulator.
Ok, even after all that, why should you give them your time and / or money?
If you support them, they will make the game up to date, even with new graphics (they considered UE4) and things like VOIP. The game had a long history and was having a slow death with limited updates and the playerbase decreasing. Now, there is new dev team in the house - they mean it and they can deliver.
The question for you is, what are you going to do about it?

At first, I couldn't really wrap my mind around this game. It shares a lot with No Man's Sky: endless mining just to get to the next planet. To be honest, the biggest differences I could make was that Astroneer starts out small, offers a gun that shapes terrain, and multiplayer. Sure, there are more differences than that, but to me, this game is very similar to No Man's Sky.
Then it hit me: this is No Man's Sky if they went the early access route.
Think about it. What if Peter Molyneux said this game would be early access instead of a complete game? What if the game sold for 20$ instead of the full 60$? I think this is why Astroneer feels better. Sure, I may not like it now, but updates promise a better game later.
I think this is why people will agree why Astroneer is better than No Man's Sky. Should you buy it right now? Maybe. Right now, there are a few notable bugs and it does feel a bit bland. For me, I'd say it certainly is a good buy.

This is an amazingly enthralling text-based mmo if you are into hacking sim types of things. The tutorial is frustrating at times, but very fufilling when you figure out the challenges. However, after the tutorial you are thrown into a WAN with little information and a vague direction on where to go next. It's up to you to either figure out how to write your own scripts (in js, really), or take your chances on public ones of differing security levels.
This is not a game where someone with a big exclamation mark over their head tells you what to do, you need to figure it out! I think this may lead to a lot of people (including myself, at first) to sit in the 0000 channel and just kind of stew, wondering what the hell you're supposed to do?
You're supposed to figure it out. That's the nature of "hacking". the resources are around, you need to find them and work out how to exploit them for your gain.
You may find a t1 harvester and get some GC that way, but did you buy this game to sit at a feeding trough? No, figure out a better way to collect that GC.
My first few days, I was frustrated, then I figured out t1 locs.
Somehow I got interested in figuring out what a t2 loc was, and through my own exploration and poking around (Hacking has two meanings, not just exploiting) figured out how to find those npcs. There was a lot of trial and error, and me even throwing a bung, but I eventually figured it out on my own with just a little google on the tough parts and that was
. I have also started writing my own scriptand made me feel like I actually accomplished something, even if its in a fictional game world.
This is actually an amazing game with a huge potential in the long-term, but its easy to get short-sighted (as I did at first too!) and just think this is a glorified chat program with a bunch of spammy scammers. The content is there, and PvP is a thing if you want to go after players, but there is no "manual" to read and the entire point of the game is trying to "figure it out", so if problem solving and unique thinking are your thing then this is the game for you!

Great concept, but way too little content.
The game starts in the "vLAN", a tutorial zone where you're alone with NPCs and some features are locked (like scripting), until you complete the main quest, which lasts for about 2 hours (there are some nice shortcuts and secrets to find, so it can last a little longer, but it gets repetitive quite fast).
After that, you're released into the wild, free to interact with other players.
However once you've reached this point, you've pretty much exhausted the content the game has to offer.
You don't get quests like in the tutorial anymore. You can interact with others players, but you can't really hack them directly (although you can try to trick people into running a script you made to send your their cash or upgrades).
The main game seems to revolve around hacking NPCs, but the process is currently *very* repetitive, and almost impossible for new players (all resources are usually acquired a few minutes/hours after spawn, which happens only once per day).
The ability to create and share scripts is interesting, but without a goal most scripts end up being either crackers to automate the few tasks required to hack NPCs, small games or scams... (And is not accessible to new players, as some resources are required to start, which cannot be acquired, as all NPCs are grinded by a few players as soon as they spawn).
Currently, it feels more like a BBS/IRC channel mixed-up with a few user-made tricks than a game.
Which is a shame, because hackmud has a lot of potential, and could be a great game if it offered players something to do...
I'll definitely keep an eye on hackmud though.

If for some reason you're reading this and not playing the game, let me tell you the pros and cons of buying this game.
Each character has their own style of gameplay centered around their abilities. Sonic, for example, will play differently than Knuckles or Amy.
The Good:
-This is the first appearance of Chao, and if you know anything about Chao, then you get why this is good. for those who don't know, Chao are raisable creatures who take on parts of animals given to them, and inherit stats from animals, birds will help your creation fly, while things like cheetahs will make them faster. All of this to win specific races.
-The levels, minus Big's and E-102's are built fairly well, and feel like they belong in a platforming game. Sonic's feel like a traditional Sonic game (for the most part) while other character's stages fit them just fine.
-Power ups are scattered around the main worlds, and while some are essential, like the light speed shoes, some just help make things easier, such as the crystal ring.
-This game proves that hub worlds can be used in a good way, with the environments being interesting, and having hidden special chao eggs to find, and secrets, such as power ups to gather.
Now For The Bad Things:
-Big the cat. Just...His gameplay is so bad it's basically a joke now.
-The story can be kind of hard to follow if you're trying to keep track of what is happening when, especially when characters split up.
-The EGG VIPER is cheap, and pretty glitchy, at least from my attempts. You'll fall through the floor when dodging that final attack, and not make it back to the platform if you spindash jump into the robot.
-Who thought the two Sky Chase acts were a good idea?
That's all, I'm going to leave the final decision to you, with all that I said, it's up to you if you wanna buy it or not.

I enjoyed myself in the few minutes that I played this game. I bought it for 11 cents on sale and it's a good price, but I'd be willing to pay up to 1 euro for this concept, even though it's short. It would be a great way for (young) kids to learn about life in earlier time periods on Earth, but it doesn't really teach them much. "The Raven: Legacy of A Master Thief", a point-and-click adventure game with a great story. The story is the best part of the game. Taking a page from the "Arsene Lupin" short stories, the game's main antagonist is 'The Raven', a mysterious gentleman thief. You play as Constable Zellner, a veteran Swedish police officer whom gets caught up in a grand adventure/mystery while escorting some very valuable cargo. I won't go any further as to avoid spoilers, but if you play this game for one reason it should be the story. Also, allow me to mention the soundtrack. I found it to be very charming and found myself humming the main theme far after I turned of the game.
The drawbacks to the game a few but glaring. The first being the camera angles, transtioning from one part of a room to another, that is not on screen, is frustrating. The second being the audio/video sync for the character models. Weather you play the game on it's lowest or highest setting the sound does not always sync properly and it takes you away from the immersion. Last, and certainly least, is the overall stiffness that the game has. I know it's a point and click game but the animations are just so lifeless and boring. If they patched these issues in an update I know it would be appreciated.
"The Raven: Legacy of A Master Thief" a game worth playing. My final thought is that this game is a good introduction to point-and-clicks and you should give it a try.

In the beginning, The Raven seems like a fantastic little adventure game. The characters are interesting, from the Hercule Poirot-like main character to the various passengers you'll interact with, including a genre-savvy mystery novelist who may as well be Agatha Christie (it's easy to tell where their inspirations came from), and the mystery and intrigue that the first episode builds up seems like it's going to be a great time. But then episode 2 strolls along, and the story ends about halfway through it - the entire rest of the game, including all of episode 3, is essentially a recap detailing the events from the perspective of two other characters. Everything after the middle of chapter 2 is just a downward spiral, both in the storytelling and in the actual game stability, with episode 3 being a rollercoaster of moments where you can get stuck in a walk cycle and have to force the game to close. The reveal of the villain isn't just uninteresting, it's practically insulting; at one point in the game, while talking to the mystery novelist, the main character is discussing her thoughts about the culprit and she replies "This isn't one of those cliche mystery novels where the culprit is someone who isn't introduced until the end - it's likely someone you already know well!", and yet that is exactly what happens. The game has little side-puzzles and optional things you can do throughout it, but none of them matter because despite being episodic the game doesn't actually link the episodes like most do; you have to start a new game and choose a new episode for each one. The Raven showed a lot of promise initially, but underneath its mask there wasn't a master thief, just disappointment and regret.

The puzzles were relatively easy, so they did not get in the way of the story development.
If you are looking for a challenge you might need to look elsewhere, but if your main interest is the story, you are in for a treat.
As for the gameplay itself, it is a fairly standard point-and-click adventure game. There is a built-in hint system and there is a button that highlights the clickable objects in the scene, although you can still breeze through the game without using them. There was some degree of pixel-hunting, but it was rarely excessively annoying.
The most frustrating aspects were the camera angles, since sometimes it was not clear where was I supposed to click to go to a neighbouring scene. Moreover, the character animations were far from smooth and there were lots of "jumps" in the animation. I got the impression that, near the end of the game, it got even worse, with a character being able to pass through another and characters getting stuck in front of objects only to jump instaneously to another location. I also thought the characters walked a bit too slowly for my taste. I don't know if these issues happened only for the Linux version (I am using a notebook with Ubuntu 14.04). Either way, it shows it either a lack of polish or a lack of care for Linux users.
Still, if point-and-click is your cup of tea and you favor story over puzzles, there is plenty to enjoy here.

I liked the first part, so it goes without saying that I waited for this. Was it worth the wait? Yes, probably. Is it flawless? Not by a long shot, no.
First, some positives. Music is very nice. CGs are pretty, in general. Backgrounds are pretty too. Graphics in general are very nice, although there are one or two odd ones. Branching is very decent, although I have some gripes with it. Story is at least half-decent, although I have some gripes with it as well.
So, my first gripe is the story lacks focus. A lot of stuff is crammed into the package, but it becomes a bit of a mess and hard to keep track of. There are, in total, three major story branches with a lot of more or less minor variations along the way. Two of those are particularly insufferable in that sense because they keep jumping around between two locations where separate groups of characters are each doing their own thing, with almost no intersection. What's worse, story in one of those locations is pretty much the same no matter what branch you're on (well, to be fair, it has some branching of it's own).
My second gripe is apparent lack of polish. I was playing on Linux, so YMMV, but I experienced a number of misplaced voice clips that, while usually at least match the character, don't match the text -- usually voice clip happens to be one screen ahead or behind the text. If nothing else, it's immersion-breaking. Also, there are some places (a couple rather lengthy) where voice acting is missing altogether, some of which are definitely bugs, other's I'm not too sure. Also, as I mentioned, some graphics look like sketches, and while this makes sense in most cases (quick-paced scenes, inserts, etc), in some cases it doesn't make any sense to me. Not sure if it's a creative direction I don't quite understand or some prerelease graphics left in by accident.
Last gripe, there's more than a bit deus ex machina in the story. I'll try to avoid major spoilers here, but some branches are worse than others in this regard. Still, there's fair amount of said dei overall. It was easy enough for me do distract myself from those, most of the time, but... using
as a plot device is in poor taste.
One more thing, which might not be apparent immediately. This is not a complete story, it's a single arc, more or less. So it's not "finished". Devs talk of "final chapter DLC", but to be honest, I couldn't imagine how everything could possibly be resolved in a single chapter, so fingers crossed they don't botch it.
So... it might seem like I'm being very negative. That wasn't really the point though. The VN is very good, leagues better than some ...other... VNs I've seen recently. It could've been better though. So don't expect a flawless masterpiece.
All in all, I find that current asking price is more or less justified. I hope bugs will be fixed at some point, but there's nothing game-breaking, so while distracting, those are not something to be too concerned about. And one can get a lot of enjoyment from this. Well... unless you're uncomfortable with LGBT, because there's
of that. All very sweet and believable, and not
in your face, but... well, yeah,
I liked it.

Back when Brilliant Shadows: Part One of the Book of Gray Magic was released, I wrote a long and glowing review with nothing but praises for the work. In other words, I loved it.
Now some years later (has it really been 2 years already?) we have the sequel, Pale Spectrum. I feel it was definitely worth the wait, and in fact there is far more game here than I expected.
You see, at 12 hours I have finally finished my initial playthrough of Pale Spectrum. Now, I knew it was going to be a longer title than Brilliant Shadows' ~3-4 hours playtime had been before I started Pale Spectrum, but I wasn't expecting 3-4 times as long! And that's just a single playthrough worth. There are far more varied branches offered to the player this time around. I get the feeling many more variances to the endings exist than were in the first entry as well, if I'm reading that progress map correctly anyway.
This must have been an incredible amount of work for the Ithaqua Labs dev team, the voice cast, everybody involved in the project really to basically create three times the game content in just 2 years.
Just like with my review of Part One, I really can't find anything to fault this game. In fact I am left with nothing but a feeling of being awestruck, impressed with the whole thing. It went so much further and reached so much higher than even the high expectations I had held for it. I am once again touched and moved by this experience. This is how you create something that endures.
If I may tangent for a moment, I feel like I am being offered the rare privilege to see something that is going to go on to be much larger and gain greater renown, like a proofreader of an up and coming famous author, or a private screening of a sure-fire hit movie. Suffice to say I am a happy kickstarter returning backer, happy that this Part Two came to exist and that I got to experience it.
Back to the matter at hand, before I began my play session of Pale Spectrum, I decided I had better refresh my memory with another run through Brilliant Shadows, so I did that first. Then I followed up with a quick jaunt through Embers of Magic to brush up on that backstory as well.
Doing my best to keep spoilers to a minumum for myself, I didn't dig too deeply for details on the new game (I like experiencing it firsthand.) I knew Pale Spectrum was going to be a longer game than Brilliant Shadows, and that Belinda was now the main character, and that there seemed to be more endings possible than the first game. That was about it. This raised some questions and concerns in my head.
Spoilers from Brilliant Shadows:
Thankfully though, my fears were put to rest early in the story, and those concerns were non-issues in reality. In fact, it went so much further than I expected it to that it was very pleasantly surprising how far each character's story was developed in Pale Spectrum. I was not expecting such depth or breadth of plot and character developments.
And that really sums up the charm of Pale Spectrum. It's everything that Brilliant Shadows established, except bigger, more expansive, more encompassing. There was so much more of the wonderful first entry's experience here to enjoy.
In just the writing alone for example, there was enough to make it at least 3 times the first game, and it was
too. Not just more text added for the sake of game length. Quality and quantity both. Lots of twists and turns, plenty of surprises, and frankly the story went in directions I never would have guessed, but that just made it all the more enjoyable to experience.
I can't even imagine how much more work the art must have been. Some of the background pieces, especially the landscapes, were unexpectedly breathtaking. And the sheer number of character art variations must have taken...well...years! It all comes together very well though in the end. I'm sure that doesn't do the work justice, but it is a very well done aspect to the game to put it succinctly, and is even more impressive than it was the first time around.
I really liked the recurring music themes from the first game. I think my outlook regarding the soundtrack in my review of the first game back then was a bit harsh in hindsight, but I will say folding in some of the pieces from the first game's soundtrack was a great idea. It helped with continuity and it did build some of that familiarity into the score and the experience while playing. The new pieces all fit right at home too and in my completely inexpert opinion felt even more expressive than before. Again, impressive work.
The voicework was undoubtedly a much larger undertaking this time around too, but it was once again an enjoyable addition. With many new faces, and a lot of returning favorites, it was great to hear the characters come to life again. I liked a lot of the new characters but I think my favorite of the new ones is Sword. I don't like picking favorites though, all of them were very well done and brought the life of a voice to an interesting and colorful cast. Thank you for your hard work voice actors and actresses in helping bring these games to us fans.
I can say Pale Spectrum is a triumphant success for all your hard work. You all have created something extraordinary. Knowing that the tale still has more to be told honestly boggles my mind. Pale Spectrum went so much further beyond what Brilliant Shadows and Embers of Magic started that it's hard to imagine there's yet even more of the tale to be told, and I mean that in the most supportive way possible. It was fantastic, and I think I'm somehow spoiled at the prospect of getting even more of this a few years down the road.
There were so many unexpected events in Pale Spectrum and I feel more strongly for the cast of characters now than ever before. They've all grown a lot and I'm looking forward to seeing what other surprise twists and turns await in their future tales. Until then I suppose I will have to get started on a second playthrough of Pale Spectrum, from the beginning of course. I get the feeling I have quite a few more variations of the story to experience, and I know I have at least one or two more entire story branches to uncover.
Thank you again Ithaqua Labs and supporting staff for all your hard work on bringing this wonderfully imaginative world to life. Give yourselves a well earned rest while you enjoy the aftermath of part two of your masterpiece-in-the-making, and just like with the first game, I'll be looking forward to the bright future of this wonderful series.

I have followed the borderlands empire since origination.  I have thoroughly enjoyed every game!  I only have 270 hours atm, but I have many more on XBOX console (All maxed heroes).
Borderlands is not you normal shooter.  True some other shooters out there have fictional storylines and some based on a small amount of truth, but borderlands takes those ideas and throws them into a comical world; with not just humor, but in art.  The Post-apocalyptic environments also grab that mad max "Road Warrior" movies series feel; which you might love as well.
BORDERLANDS 2 PROS:
1. Character customization
2. Unique Badass ranking that grants extra bonuses to all your created characters account-wide
3. Randomly Generated loot creates some unique builds
4. Questline that makes sense
5. Comedic animations, NPC quotes and physical antics
6. Unique Characters = all different looking and playstyle
7. Enjoyable music (Arguable)
8. Very rewarding Expansions (Season Pass)
9. Shift Codes on twitter weekly for free GOLDEN KEYS and sometimes other rewards
10. Each Borderlands prepares you for the next in the series
BORDERLANDS 2 CONS:
(Based on circle of circles opinions and asking random people)  Also all of the below are arguably not CONS, but what is more suggestions about what is missing...
1. MAPS (They are in vector graphics and there is no real way to tell elevation) for the players that have no idea where to go, may find them unhelpful and frustrating.
2. Only Single-player and up to 4-player co-op.  How about some team based arenas and/or some 10/15/20 player boss RAID battles with room queuing and possibly custom rules and setting manipulations = custom games
3. Does not have Weapon/Armor/Skins creations in-game or for PC: STEAM WORKSHOP or some other third-party handling programming
4. No Armor to change character's look past default, found or purchased skins
5. No Custom Worlds or any creator options
6. In-Game Music (Arguable)
All-in-all a great rounded out game with potential for so much more!  I will continue to purchase any and all up-and-coming titles.
SIDE NOTE:  I tried to write this review without any knowledge of Prequel so the review could be clean to the point.

--Review is not about server stability--
------------TL;DR AT BOTTOM------------
I had bought this game with an idea it would be similar to most other hacking sims, more along the lines of Hacker Experience. While this one took me by a slight surprise with it being more about coding than the others, which is fine.
I originally was really enjoying this game while in the tutorial, which really is a mini-singleplayer campaign. It was only after this ended that I started seeing the flaws in my opinion that the game had.
After the tutorial is over you get thrown out into the multiplayer, no idea what to do but if you have had my luck your chat will probably be getting spammed (we'll get to that in a bit)
slight how to start playing spoilers ahead- - - So eventually you'll realize that the beginner thing to do is to scavenge inactive ai account and take their money, which sounds alright however it gets repetitive real fast. You type a command "scripts.fullsec" and it brings a huge list of servers/locations up. It's a list of both NPC, and player servers with no way to tell which is which, which doesnt sound that bad but it starts bringing on the repetitiveness really early going down a huge list til you get to a NPC server. Now remember the spam in chat I mentioned? If you connect someones server they can run scripts. fullsec scripts can't do anything bad, but they can make you spam in the chat, spam players directly, and the sort. When I was in the chat it was hell, constant spams of ascii art, people clicking on spam servers, people namespoofing, namespoofing system messages, and one other thing, providing fake servers.
If you type "scripts.fullsec" it'll do what I mentioned above, show you the list of servers. However, if you type "script.fullsec" that can instantly take you to someones server and take your money you got from that monotonous finding npc servers and hacking them over and over.  I never went to them thankfully so I dont exactly know the extent of what they do. And it's not just script.fullsec. Every command in the game starts with word.word, and as far as I can tell a player server can be any combination that isn't taken. This includes chatting, shutting off the game, checking your system info, and anything. If someone decides to grab that server, a simple typo will mess you up. While not a big deal, I found it silly the way that works with checking my account balance or even viewing my system info, or turning off the game, is the same command scheme for joining what is possibly a dangerous server.
Now if that wasn't bad enough, the game also has an auto complete, where you type part of a word and it enters it. You quickly learn how useful this is in the tutorial when they give you a long server name and you just need to type a couple letters and hit tab. However, once in multiplayer it goes to hell as well, any time a player puts for instance, "script.fullsec" it will show up on your autocomplete list. And there is no way to get it off, or block them from coming. So what you are taught to be a great thing, is now, a timebomb. All this really just screws over anyone with a simple spelling mistake once, and a player for being new and not realizing this, a LOT more than it should.
So in the end I ended up having to leave chat with all the spam and autocomplete words, and was essentially forced out of communicating with anyone due to scripts people made, while some other people just try to find an NPC or do something of the sort with others name spoofing system messages. That didn't get rid of the autocomplete though I'm stuck with that forever, so it seemed the only proper choice there was to leave the chat as soon as you get out of the tutorial.
My last negative point is the text box itself, is horrible. I'm not sure if it was to go with the theme of a terminal, or if it was just done poorly, but in a game about typing stuff, it helps a ton to have a good area to type in, which this does not. Clicking stuff can be a minor annoyance, you get a notepad but can only copy one line at a time, theres a chat box but chat still comes up where you put all your code in and floods it with no way to change it. And its missing some basic hotkeys, most noticeable selecting a group of letters/words with highlighting them and deleting them, as well as ctrl+A or select all for windows.
With all that said I do have two positive points about the game
A. the tutorial, without spoiling anything it had a cheesy/slightly cringy story but it grew on me and I did like the stuff I was doing there, it had a good pace and was really fun and enjoyable
and B. Along with the spam servers, npcs, and whatever else you may find, there is ones that players have made, where its a script that does certain things for you for a fee.
TL;DR / Summary
1. The tutorial was great, it was more like a mini-singleplayer campaign and provides 1-2 hours of entertainment.
2. You seemingly can just code some basic javascript stuff which may be enjoyable
3. The box where you write EVERYTHING in , is one of the worst I see in a game.
4. a lot of beginner traps and the like
5. chat spam is through the room do to javascript spam scripts.
6. really monotonous gameplay. (even compared to other hacking games)

TL;DR ::
If you're looking for a children game, just find another. It's not worth the buck (pun intended).
PROS :
- cute graphics
- soothing music
- (not quite useful) informations about the pleistocene epoch
- Steam trading card (the only reason I bought this game on discount)
CONS :
- too short
- only 3 mini games
- only several minutes play time (I played several hours just to receive the trading card drops)
- poorly executed
============================================================
FULL REVIEW ::
Did you know that majestic oaks can live even 1000 years?
I don't.
And this game tells me that stuff along with other things about the pleistocene epoch.
The concept is quite good; making children learn something using interactive media like this. Cute graphics, soothing music, and simple gameplay. That's perfect, right?
NOPE.
It's poorly executed. You can only go right, left, and find "hidden" informations about the pleistocene epoch in the background. There are 3 mini games that you can play once and you won't play it again.
1. Memory : Match similar images from a set of images. Once you've completed it there's no message or anything. You just press back button and that's it. Try replay it and you'll find the same images position from previous game. They didn't even bother randomizing it. :(
2. Snack and Lunches : Choose 5 foods that deers ate. If you choose wrong it will display X on the image, otherwise it will display a checkmark. You can choose all the foods. There's no message on completing the game, just like the previous game. Well, at least you get to know what deers ate.
3. Paleopuzzle : There are scattered bones and a silhouette of a deer. Place the correct bones into the deer. If you place it correctly the bones will auto-snap into the right position. And just like the other games, it has no message when you've completed the puzzle.
Yes, that's the whole game. I'm not trying to undermine the developer's effort in developing this game, but I've made a better "game" for my history subject in high school within only several days. At least make the deer's journey longer, add more minigames, and make it more interesting.
I bought it on 90% discount at around $0.1 so I won't complain too much. But this game doesn't deserve its full price.
