A nifty little metroidvania-like with some awesome art direction and far better mouse+keyboard support than I would expect from a game that started on the 360. The controls are SMOOTH.
The gameplay is mostly focused on environmental puzzles. Combat can be hectic but all save points heal you to full and they are frequent enough that you don't really have to worry that much about getting hit outside of boss battles. It's quite strictly linear- don't expect to sequence break or do levels out of order. Nevertheless you can and should backtrack to collect upgrades that were blocked off before.
They really got the atmosphere right, too.  It feels like you are a tiny tresspasser on a violently hostile, starkly alien planet, completely alone and carefully blazing a trail into the heart of the beast to strike where it is most vulnerable.
I only have one real complaint- it seemed a little short. I wouldn't have minded a couple more areas.

I need to emphasize the bosses in this game, wherein half the challenge and fun is figuring out what to do. If you like puzzles, arcade shooting, Metroidvania-style exploration, and beautiful landscapes, get this game. Its one of the best I've played this year.

Spoiler Alert:

Disclaimer: I know the creators of this game and was a primary tester for the game. I did however purchase the game myself via Kickstarter with no special discount.
As mentioned I have been testing this game throughout its development and am very familiar with the game at this point. I have gone through just about every ending/each path through the game and can safely say there should be something for everyone. I would say that if I went through the game for the first time and completed the game with a real ending (Yes there are fail/dead-end paths, choose carefully!) it would take maybe about 8-10 hours depending on which ending and how often you cut off voice lines to go faster.
If I had to sum up the game in a couple sentences I would say: This is a fantasy game that covers a lot of topics including: Personal growth, Love, Identity, Loss, War, Grief, Failure, and more. The game’s scope is massive and tackles a lot of hard but interesting topics while being punctuated with fun.
•	Fully voice acted: Almost everything is voice acted, narration is not (which I actually prefer). All of the voices are amazing.
•	Branching paths: When I said there are multiple endings that is true, but it is more like multiple story paths as there are vast differences between them. Yes, there is some overlap but each run will have a lot of new scenes and mysteries to discover. To be clear there are not just 1 or 2 of these but many.
•	Different stories: Within each branch there are multiple characters each with their own agenda/plot.
•	Humor: The game has a lot of well written jokes that help break up the periods of heavier plot. In addition to the jokes themselves some of the lines are delivered by the voice actors in such a way you can’t help but laugh.
•	Characters: Every character is extremely well written, even in the testing group everyone had a variety of favorite characters.
•	Art: Everything is beautiful. Lots of amazing peices of art ranging from comic style action strips to heavily painted cinematic-esque scenes. There are tons of characters and backgrounds that you will come across. Some of which are tied to certain paths to ensure there is always something new as mentioned above.
•	Hand-crafted world: The entire world and magic system is deep and nuanced, not all mysteries are covered in every path in the game and some ideas were merely hinted at setting up for future games.
It would not be much of a review if I didn’t list some things like this.
•	Humor: While for me this is a huge plus I understand some readers may want a fully serious game. While this game IS serious there is still a lot of humor thrown in. I could imagine some readers may not like this.
•	This is a Sequel: You will be able to follow the plot just fine without playing the first but this still is a sequel and that may be of fputting to some people and it is worth mentioning here.
•	Not a Dating Sim: I noticed that sometimes people confuse visual novels for dating sims sometimes. This is not a dating sim. There are choices you can make regarding going out and dating a few people in the game but that is not a core defining feature of it.
I hope this spoiler-free highlight of the game should give you a good idea of whether or not you would like the game. I personally feel it it worth your time to play this game.

If Agatha Christie would have written a heist thriller, it would have probably been a lot like The Raven: an interesting whodunit wrapped in an exciting jewel thievery, all presented as a three-part, solid point ‘n’ click adventure game with a clear, comfortable interface.
Playing through The Raven: Legacy of a Master Thief is like sitting down to watch ‘Murder on the Orient Express’ (the ’74 one), which miraculously transforms into ‘The Italian Job’ (again, the original).
The story even starts on the Orient Express, where we meet our first protagonist, Constable Zellner, an obvious Poirot homage (we even meet this world’s Agatha Christie). He eventually manages to get mixed up in an investigation against the Raven: master thief who plans to steal two Egyptian jewels.
From this point on, we are treated to both a classic English style whodunit murder mystery on-board a cruise ship (a smaller homage to ‘Death on the Nile’), and a heist thriller where many people are not who they seem, and several well-crafted plans are at work at the same time, directly opposing each other. This is also the point where the story introduces the other protagonists, a young burglar couple.
Not only the plot is great, but the characters as well. All of them have detailed, often tragic backstories, just like the best Christie novels. And they are played by talented English actors.
Since the story tries to imitate Ms. Christie’s work, the puzzles are also straightforward and realistic, aided by a simple interface. Don’t expect an easy game though, because progress usually requires carefully examining every possibility before the game lets the player choose the correct one. The characters cannot run and many tasks are divided into dozens of small steps, yet the pacing is so good that the game never feels boring, and the 12-15 hours of play time just flies by pretty fast.
The game would be lovely if it wouldn't for the unusable controls. And it looks like one of those games which will never receive a bug fix update.

I've had a love hate relationship with this game, heck even before I brought it I developed the most petty issue I've ever had with a game, that being the addition on the abbreivation DmC to the title (Presumably as a way to differentiate it from the original), the combination of an abbreviation being pointless if you then state the full title anyway (With the exception of if you are creating an abbreviation for multiple uses later on, such as in an essay), combined with the fact that the abbreviation is capitalized differently to the title it states afterwards makes me physically unable to read the title as anything other than "Devil may Cry: Devil May Cry"
Anyway, once I actually brought the game i developed issues other than my pathetic pet peeve; the storyline is about as generic as can be and the new Dante is extremely unlikable, I don't mean in the intentional 'rough and gruff' sense, more in the 'I want to punch him in the mouth' sense.
That said the gameplay is a lot of fun and although some may take issue with how your powerset is very different to the previous DMC games this isn't something I have a problem with, on the contrary I not only found the new powers fun to use but also felt it made the reboot more worth while, giving you something unique instead of just completely rehashing the old games with a new story. Due to these conflicting points, I probably wouldn't have given this game a positive or negative review if I hadn't have played the Vergil's Downfall DLC, which was an entirely negative experience.
The whole thing feels like it was rushed in development; I experienced several clipping issues which is the last thing you need in fast-paced combat, the diffculty setting you select does not line up well with the base game since the enemies will be of the same difficulty and quantity as at the end of the base game, despite the fact you start out as weak as Dante did. The combat feels a lot more focused on button mashing than skill when compared to the base game, and finally it is absolutely tiny in scale. There's 6 missions but don't go thinking those 6 missions of the same scale as the missions in the base game, no, these are 6 extremely tiny missions all of which are samey even by hack and slash standards, in fact the last mission is just the first mission again with your new powers. Perhaps the scale would have been bareable if the full scope of your powers had been unlocked quicker, but as it happens you'll be half way through before you even unlock both angel and demon mode, and you'll only unlock your equivilent to Devil Trigger (Vergil's Doppleganger ability) on the literal last mission of the DLC. Considering that DMC 4 had two playable characters in the base game (Even if it did involve backtracking through some previous missions), the fact that your adventures with a second playable character in this game's paid DLC happens to be so pathetically short lived is hard to swallow. Finally, it ends on a cliff-hanger for a sequel, and if the recent leaks are to be believed, that sequel is being dropped for a continuation of the original series with Devil May Cry 5.
Overall it may be the most disappointing story DLC I've ever played, since it 'untied' a bunch of loose ends the main game had just finished tying and replaces that with a wanting for more both in terms of gameplay and story, only for the developers to lose their nerve and decide to appease the fans of the original series rather than sticking to their guns and contuning on with their new incarnation.
I understand that choosing to write this review as negative based off the DLC may seem unfair, but I must stress once again that I was already on the fence about this game, the DLC just happened to push me over the edge.

Borderlands 2 is a big game. The sprawling cooperative shooter has arrived, delivering long hours of shooting, looting, and butt jokes. Well, almost intact. Game design changes, like changing the enemy death animations, do a good job of cutting corners while preserving the core action. Technical shortcomings, however, leave little doubt that this is the lesser version of Gearbox's great sequel. Dialogue and sound effects frequently sound flat and occasionally disappear, while the frame rate often slows down in combat and makes the chaotic action feel unwieldy.
Combat in Borderlands 2 is naturally a bit floaty and loose, largely due to way player movement and enemy behavior are paced. As a result, it can accommodate the small degree of control imprecision added by the touchscreens and be none the worse for it. Likewise, the smaller range of motion of the analog sticks may cause some making the PC/console transition to balk a bit, and indeed, aiming can initially feel ungainly if you're used to the game on other platforms. After you adjust the aim sensitivity and spend some time wandering the wastelands, however, the mercenary satisfactions of long-range headshots and up-close bullet barrages are well within reach.

I played this game to absolute DEATH back when I had a Dreamcast many years ago, and I still think this is easily one of the best Sonic games. But that just may be me basking in nostalgia. Unfortunately, this game hasn't aged all that well.
The story is nothing really to write home about but here I am. A god of destruction, aptly named "Chaos" is getting it's hands on the Chaos emeralds, turning him into a more powerful creature, with the help off Eggman of course. And it's up to you as the player to stop him! Pretty straight forward
Let's start off with the gameplay itself. It's your original Sonic game but remade onto a 3D plane, granted this already has been done before but this time SEGA acutally got it right. You get to enjoy the game not only from Sonic's perspective but from the perspective from other charaters such as Tails and Knuckles. Their stories are different obviously and occasionally do cross with one another. Even if you DO get sick from just "GOTTA GO FAST" then you can enjoy gameplay with Knuckles where you get to the monotonous chore of searching for Emeral shards in various levels that you visited as Sonic or run from a robt who's trying to capture you as Amy. Each character provides a lot of variety to this old game.
The Graphics...are well...dated. But what can you expect from a game that as originally designed for the dreamcast so everything kinda looks like stretched lego figurines. The animation is alright, facial expressions can get pretty spooky at times where the character would should a face of shock and it would be a step by step revealing of their face contorting to show the emotion.
The levels are still just as enjoyable and varied for an old game. You've got one level where you running along a beach to save Tails and the next you're in a Casino trying to collect rings to build a high enough pile to get a Chaos emerald. Each level makes you feel like you're playing MORE than just a Sonic game. And to top it all off, you have a Hub world where you can run around and talk to other citizens that really have nothing to contribute to the game than just to breathe life into the world. As you run around like the rainbow colored animal you are, you can find permanent powerups that will assist you in the levels.
In the end, I recommend giving this game a try if you've never played but yet want to see where Sonic really hit home in a 3D game. Or you just want to relive some nostalgia from the good ol days when Sega wasn't continually destroying itself with each game they release

This is a classic game originally released on the Dreamcast (which I still own). This was released when Sonic was still one of the biggest franchises in gaming and marked his first trip into the world of 3D. This is a true classic game.

Sonic Adventure is one of my personal pavorites.  A likable cast, awesome music, a fun overworld to explore, and so much more.  The stories of all six characters do over lap, but beat all six stories, and you unlock the seventh and final story as Super Sonic. One of Sonic's best games in my opinion and it's still replayable for me to this day and I got it for the Dreamcast when it first came out and I got it for the Game Cube as well.

Sonic Adventure is definitely one of the top picks from the era of experimental 3D. This one runs at a great framerate and recent updates have brought us a higher resolution. Amy is actually an active character and while I don't like her role, I appreciate that she's playable in this one. Chaos are fun to play with. the backstory with the echidnas is great, I would have loved to see Tikal in more games with a higher relevance like in the comics.
As Sonic's first leap into 3D, it's not half bad but SA is extremely dated now. you'd have to have either a hardcore desire to go through these games or blinding nostalgia. The dialogue is an embarrassment. There is no conflict riding up to the climax beyond "OOPS I DROPPED THE CHAOS EMERALD." There is also a lot of unpolished factors to this game, like the music restarting whenever a new option is selected.
The fact that this is a piece of gaming history, but you could honestly probably get a copy of this for Gamecube for the same or less on Craigslist. Still, I highly appreciate the addition of achievements and the convenience of a digital copy. I think it's worth the $8.00 USD it's listed as for those reasons alone, but it also sees frequent sales between 60-75% off.
Steam overlay works great, achievements added, no part of this port really suffers besides small updates that don't remain faithful to the original, and other bundled games being taken out. I appreciate this port, and despite its flaws I love the game.

I don't often write reviews, much less to recommend people not to buy a game but Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief is a game that annoyed me enough to take the time to write a negative review.
It has a lot, and I mean a lot of technical issues. It's playable but you will encounter many critical bugs, such as being unable to transition between places because the KB+M control scheme doesn't work properly. You can end up stuck in one scene if you go back an area, unable to return. Animations are very jerky, with many characters looking like ugly puppets when they talk. Movement is slow, tedious and your character sometimes gets stuck into movement or going the other way around than the direction where you clicked. I had to swap to a gamepad control scheme a few times to transition between some areas and then go back to KB+M, because it's even worse than KB+M. For some reason, my game stopped adding new saves after 7 pages of it, which meant I had to manually erase old saves. Naturally, the game doesn't inform you of this upper limit, you get to find out the hard way it stopped recording your saves. And Alt+Tab can crash your game or leave it in a state where the only thing you can see is a dark screen.
Next are some gameplay annoyances, some of which are unforgivable for a mystery adventure game. Your character has to walk to switch areas, instead of the standard double click for an instant area switch. When you click something, you can't cancel your movement midway. And since your character moves like a slowpoke, it's pretty irritating. Want to highlight what objects you can click? That'll cost you points, which you can accumulate by solving mysteries and advancing the story.  Oh, and it only highlights for like 1-2 seconds. So you better have eagle eyes and a good visual memory because otherwise, you just wasted those points for nothing.
Finally, the only somewhat redeeming element of this game is its story. Sadly, while it starts strong, with your main character being a constable that seems to be based on Poirot. The quality of the story goes down the drain in the second and third chapters, as you switch to new characters, which are considerably worse and then you have to go back through the same story, except with a different POV. It felt like a chore. If I wasn't a perfectionist, I would have given up on this game during chapter 2. Also, it breaks a huge mystery rule, but I'll refrain from saying which because it would spoil the disappointing twist they had at the end.
Recap: Don't waste your money on this, there are much better options out there when it comes to mystery adventure games.

Played this on the Dreamcast when it first came out and blew my mind- the graphics, so "futuristic" (it was actually ahead of the curve at the time)  I own this game on the NGC as well, but for the price, it was worth downloading for PC.
The game is clunky, voice acting is terrible (except for Robotnic) and it has LOTS of camera problems and bugs- but for a game originally released 16 years ago, this is forgivable- however, things like music mixing during cut-scenes and the added in Cream and upgraded Chao's flickering like mad with polygons exploding, this stuff is unforgivable and further adds to Sonic Team's reputation of lacking polish.
Look past the flaws and its a fun nostalgic game, Sonic missions are the best with some speed sections that actually work  (unlike Sonic 06), the music, although cheese-tastic, is upbeat and fun, and its always a treat listening to Eggman repeating "get a load of this" and "all systems full power" 10 times a second.
If you enjoyed or even remembered this game from your past, I would download it, If you are the new generation of gamer I would probably avoid it, unless you are willing to put up with its flaws and limitations, it sure does make you respect today's hardware and game engines.
Honestly, this game is more enjoyable than half of what the Sonic franchise has had to offer in a over a decade.

I never played this game when it came out, so as somebody with no nostalgia for it I have to say it has aged quite poorly.
Characters like Sonic, Tails and Knuckles never feel nice to control. They have way too little inertia and just sort of fling themselves across the screen at the slightest tap of the control stick. Like, say you have Sonic running full tilt in the right lane of a city highway, and you see a line of rings coming up in the left lane. It's nearly impossible to change lanes; when you press left Sonic will either immediately make a 90 degree turn and plow into the guardrail, or, if you're lucky, he'll only make a 70 degree turn, still plowing into the guardrail but at least sort of maintaining forward momentum.
The hub worlds that connect the levels are pointlessly large and very boring. There are a bunch of little character arcs with the NPCs that play out as you go through the game, but these are all dull as dishwater, and while there are little character upgrades and hidden tokens scattered throughout, they aren't very hard to find, and when you do find them they don't particularly improve your character. It feels like that stuff was just included because other 3d games were doing similar things, but they never put in the time or effort to make those bits seem meaningful. It's also often very hard to understand where the game wants you to go next.
That said, I enjoy the level design, and while they'd be a lot better if you could actually control things, they have a lot of neat set-pieces and are still kind of fun to run through and explore. It's a game that's constantly on the cusp of being really great. I keep thinking to myself "This would be super fun if the controls and camera actually worked, if there were more hidden secrets in the overworld and better NPCs." But that's a lot of problems, isn't it?
Basically, the central formula of the game is good, but the execution is lackluster at best and at a lot of points it's bad even for the time it was released, let alone 15 years later.
If you have Sonic nostalgia and you want to pick this up you won't end up hating it or yourself, but it's such a flawed game that I don't think it could really survive without that nostalgia.

Let me get the negative out of the way first: this game requires Games for Windows Live. However, if that hasn't scared you off, read on. ITSP is a fairly unique puzzle/shooter hybrid in the classic "Metroidvania" style (explore a sprawling 2D map using progressively earned abilities, backtracking to progress further, etc). So what sets this apart from similar games? Firstly, it has a very unique 'shadowy' art style that is pretty cool. And second, instead of being a character-based platformer, it's a spaceship-based twin-stick shooter with heavy puzzle elements. If that sounds interesting or up your alley, I would say don't hesitate to check this out. The only downsides to the experience are that the game is pretty short (~7 hours for the single-player, but it also has a multiplayer mode) and it is not particularly difficult (you will certainly die on occasion, but checkpoints are plentiful). It's not an all-time classic, but it's definitely a cool low-key experience. Check it out!

So, I've now beaten the game on normal difficulty, clocking at 12.6 hours and 2420 deaths, for what is apparently, "40% total progress". If you find it on sale for $1 as I did, it's a must have, and if it's still 15$, then it's still, in my opinion, the best platformer on steam. There's a free flash "Meat Boy", so go try that if you're unsure you'd like the style of platformer.
For the specifics of why it's great:
Over a hundred manually-created levels, including 5 bosses, and more difficult varients for every (non-boss) level, which you unlock by beating the speed challenge on the default level. If that wasn't enough, there's steam workshop with an infinite potential of player-created levels, too.
The game only lagged on the last level for me, and even then it was only noticable for a tiny part of the level, and never caused me to die directly.
Character variety: There's something like ten characters to choose from, each having different style of movement and unique appearance.
And the game just looks great. As the screenshots show, there's a variety of mini-levels and several large chapters that have their own appearance, so you'll get a lot of visual variety.
As a whole, the game is very solid, although I will confess that it caused me to invoke the damnation of god against a boy made of meat and a fetus in a jar. Prepare for rage, prepare for death, and prepare to get the girl, and you'll be ready for Super Meat Boy.

Possibly the best game I've ever played in my entire life, a Platform that can reach the same levels of quality of Super Mario Bros 3 and Super Mario World, and that's saying something!
Super Meat Boy is a fast paced platformer where you'll have to complete hundreds of short, ultra-difficult levels with no ability other than being able to run and wall-jump. It's plafrotming to its finest as it relies on it level design alone without any other move or special ability to use, that's why the levels really need to be spot-on for the game to be enjoyable, and they are!
All the stages are incredibly creative and different from eachother, also the "blocky" graphics with the simple color palette manages to give an incredibly retro feel to the game, the stellar sountrack is also pretty memorable and you'll probably start humming the stages' tunes if they'll ever come to your mind.
If you like Platform games Super Meat Boy is a must-have, give the game's really high difficulty it's not a game suited for beginners; while you may be stuck for hours on a single stage being able to complete a world's level in any order helps you in not getting frustrated, also the feeling of beating a level that made you go crazy is just AMAZING!
So what are you waiting for? Go play this game right now! You won't regret it!

This is one of those games that starts off as just kind of fun, but not great, then really picks up steam about halfway through and ends amazingly. If you haven't managed to get past the first chapter, I highly suggest you try and push through it. The story is fantastic, with some extremely memorable characters and a wonderful intervweaving of complicated events.
However, there is one major problem you should be aware of: the controls are
If you're not the sort who has patience for battling through difficult controls, you won't be able to appreciate this game. You also may not be able to play it without a controller. At all.
There are several scenes where clicking to go go the next screen simply does not work. It absolutely will not work. The only way I've managed to make it work is by plugging in a controller and using that to move the character. And that only works... intermittently. It's only a few specific screens that have this problem, but they recur often enough to be incredibly annoying. Plus, you can't even simply play with a controller the whole time, because there are
screens in which you can't select certain items without using the mouse. So I basically had to play the whole game switching back and forth from the mouse and controller. Moving with a controller is also very awkward and often just doesn't work.
I have a lot of patience, so this wasn't enough to ruin the game for me. I'm all about story and character, so if that's what you love about these sorts of games, I highly reccommend it to you. But if you are easily frustrated by bad controls or put more weight into gameplay than character and story, then I'd suggest you pass.

This is an excellent game, if a bit on the short side. The presentation is fantastic, with a great soundtrack (by Dimmu Borgir, of all people, though you wouldn't know it) and  a strong artistic style. If you want to, you can marathon through it in a single sitting, though I took my time over a couple days so I could enjoy it longer. It's got a great balance of puzzle and exploration elements, and if you like Metroidvania style exploration, you should definitely pick it up. It doesn't have the same enemy density as a Metroidvania game, and sometimes it's a better tactical decision to run than fight. The boss fights are clever, making good use of the weapons available to you at the time, neither too easy nor frustratingly difficult, offering a balanced challenge. The only thing I found slightly frustrating was steering rockets, but after a few tries, it became easier. A definite must-have if you enjoy puzzle exploration games.

"Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet" marks Michel Gagné's first foray into the world of video games and hopefully it won't be his last. Not only does the game possess Gagné's distinct visual style (giving it a gorgeous, colorful, and abstract look) but "Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet" also employs "Metroidvania" style gameplay, providing it with an old-school air of exploration. If there is one flaw it would most likely be the game's length (it's a little on short side) but that shouldn't deter you: "Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet" is definitely worth visiting.

Such a visually impressive game, with lots of gadgets to toy with and lots to unlock along the way. The map exploration is similar to Metroid and you can't help but feel like this little UFO up against all odds. The game felt short but the multiplayer modes extend the re-playability. Worth your time if you're looking for a unique action-adventure game.

Unfortunately, I discovered that it reminds me too much of my actual job, and that's not what I needed. I was hoping for a game that felt a bit more like other similar "games", and hackmud is a bit too far a departure from that.
In addition, the tutorial was pretty infurating and incredibly vague. Ambiguity is the enemy in the real world, so I struggle when a game designed after the real world has a tutorial full of ambiguity.
It does have full Javascript support, which is pretty cool for a game, but based solely on the fact that this game reminds me of actual work, I can't recommend it.
That being said, I would give it a definite recommend for anyone who isn't actually in the information security industry (and probably who isn't a programmer). Great ideas, just kind of missed the mark for me.

Adventure games are and have always been my favourite genre.  So when I stumble across a gem like 'The Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief' I wonder why on earth I haven't heard of it before now.
I have no technical experience in making computer games.  I am purely a game player - the consumer.
I am playing this game on a pretty powerful rig with a 29" Widescreen Monitor.
This is a review of the Steam Version of the game.
Here's what I think:
The story is written in the style of an Agatha Christie novel with the obligatory twists and turns that just draw you further and further in.  In fact, it pays homage to probably her most famous work, 'Death on the Nile' with a touch of 'Murder on the Orient Express'.  Personally, I've never been good at whodunnits whether in book form or in the movies so no surprise then that I was guessing all the way to the end.  On the other hand I think this just goes to show the strength of writing.
The characters were well imagined and fleshed out.  They were likeable and made you care abut what happened to them.  The villains were over the top which reminded you that although you were in the middle of an intense confrontation it was just a game.  The tone of the game was well balanced.  Whilst being, in essence, a crime adventure there were lots of lighter moments and the characters were not without humour.
With the opening animated sequence and intro you just know that this game was a labour of love and not just a money spinner.  I think, as with any media format, that the first 3-5 minutes either hook you or sink it.  Well, this definitely left me wanting more.
The game's makers got the period spot on visually.  It was like wandering back into the 1950's.  The scenes are beautifully hand drawn and are rich in colour and detail.  The characters' costumes were well designed.  The only issue I had with the visual side were the characters' teeth.  This may have been a limitation of the software they were using as they looked far from natural.  Check out Lady Westmacott's companion.  Her teeth were scary looking!
There were some issues with continuity.  For example,
I also had a few instances of graphical artfacts appeaing in certain scenes.  This suggests some kind of compatibility issue with my graphics card but as I've had no issue with other games the jury is out on this one.  Either way, it didn't affect the game in any serious way or my enjoyment.
The score was orchestral and would give any hollywood blockbuster a run for it's money.  It was evocative, upping the tempo when playing an action sequence whilst dropping the tone when someone was relating some sad event.
Sadly, for some inexplicable reason, there is no music playing when the credits roll.  I can only assume that this is a pretty big oversight as who would commission an orchestra to score their game and then leave it out completely when the credits roll?!
As I've said in other reviews, poor voice acting can turn a great game into a very average game if not worse.  It's 50% of your connection to the story, assuming that the visuals make up the other half.  Well, in this game they nailed it.  The voices were so natural that I barely had reason to even notice them in the same way as if you were watching a movie.  The voices matched the characters that were speaking, accents and all.  The warmth of Constable Zellner would be hard to beat.  I'm so pleased that the makers went for quality here.
This element let the game down significantly.  Although the interactive items within a scene were limited, the number of pixels that allows a user to activate the 'Item Label' was so small that finding some items was next to impossible and led to the much derised 'pixel hunting'.
Moving from one scene to another or one room to another was just horrible.  This is a fundamental part of any game.  If a player can't progress to the next scene then it defeats the object of being a game.  In my mind, this was probably the most unforgiveable flaw.  How this got past all the beta testing beats me.  To move from one scene to the next involves some 'pixel hunting' and some patience.  The flaw wasn't consistent throughout the game as the flaw was more pronounced in some areas than it was in others.
It's a shame that Chapter 3 sees you controlling 2 additional characters.  After controlling Constable Zellner, the main protagonist, for 2 chapters it takes the game in an unusual direction.  The reason for doing this, amongst other reasons, is to avoid the typical 'Last Scene' in most Agatha Christie novels (at least in all the TV adaptations I've ever watched) of one long boring speech on how the crime was committed and then exposing the villain.  As I said, it's a shame that you have to switch characters but the makers made an interesting choice here and I think it works well.
An additional plus point was the balance between dialogue and puzzles, not too much of either.  Also, the puzzles were logical and of the right level of difficulty.
This Steam version generously offers some bonus features on completion of the game.  However, the most appealing feature for me, the soundtrack (not the score), didn't work.  You can highlight the track you want to hear but nothing happens.  So much for bonus features.  In my opinion it's really simple.......... don't offer what you can't deliver!
From about the mid way point of the game I encountered some serious bugs which caused the game to crash.  These involved the controlled character disappearing or getting stuck in a spinning cycle.
From my initial contact with them, the development team do seem interested in logging these bugs and have offered some basic support.
*Classic Whodunnit Story
*Great Depth
*Interesting Characters
*Logical Puzzles
*Natural Voice Acting
*Orchestral Score
*Poor Gameplay Mechanics
*Navigating Rooms
*Bonus Material
Despite having some issues with the gameplay, I really enjoyed my time playing with these characters in the rich environments of the 1950's.  The story is engrossing and like any good novel will have you playing it again to pick up on the details you missed the first time round.  It very much depends on how much the gameplay issues impact on your first play through.
If you're an adventure gamer I can happily recommend this title but patience is definitely a requirement.  Patience is well rewarded with this game so go ahead and and give it a try.

Super Meat Boy is a hardcore platformer that does everything right. Everything? Well, almost. The game crashes once in a while, and for me the audio crashes almost everytime I play it. The animations are outdated and the gameplay, even though it's mostly solid, can feel slipery sometimes. Also, you can't remap the controls on a keyboard. The game advertises how controllers are better and all. While this might be true for some games, this one has only TWO buttons! It wouldn't be that much of an issue to play with a keyboard if I could change the controls (that are by default shift for running and space for jumping), which is the bare minimum when you release a game on PC (I still beat it with a keyboard, yay me!).
Anyway, I'm a passionate platformer player, and apart from what I mentionned, I found this game highly enjoyable. The level design is amazing. It keeps reinventing itself by using the same components in new ways (something McMillen talked about in Indie Game: The Movie). The difficulty increases at a perfect rate. I thought it would be incredibly hard from the start, or soon enough, but no, it increases perfectly so that a veteran like me don't get bored, but that anyone can progress quite quickly to the third or fourth world.
It's refreshing to have a platformer that challenges me, and it makes it even more rewarding to finish it.
It was short (4hrs), but I enjoyed every minute of it. Get it if it goes on sale.

A poor man's Aquaria on a prince's budget.
It's jarring to play such a beautifully made game, in my absolute favorite genre, and everything around me tells tells me it's wonderful... but for some reason it sucks.
The game is too forgiving from moment to moment, so much so that this scary planet actually tries to feed you health right within sight of your weird magical filling stations. Then you get locked into a boss fight with a single trial-and-error solution. If this is an homage to Metroid, it's an homage to the wrong part of Metroid.
The game is full of what seem like puzzles but aren't, and what seems like exploration but isn't. Nice touches squandered on room-by-room level design, and a scanner device that always tells you exactly what to do. A nice music system which is used for only one thing, and good sound marred by the constant whirr of your saucer engine.
None of these problems are absolutely damning, but together they sink what should have been a phenomenal game.
This is the result of if the atmosphere, world design, and player progression of Super Metroid - with a touch of linearity from Metroid Fusion - made a baby with Aquaria's control aesthetics.

A good exploration arcade puzzle scroller, if you're into that kind of things. Comes with 2 multiplayer modes for extended fun.

Sonic Adventure DX for PC is just so, amazingly... ok. It just trys to be something absolutly huge for the franchise, mixing dramatic storytelling with the rush of Sonic gameplay, and yeah, at the time and on the right hardware, this was revolutionary. Its just plain awful today.
The advancements in PC gaming make the attempts for story telling, and the technology used for this effect just laughable. Seriously, the developers of the PC version must have LOW expectations. Your first playthrough of this game (all campaigns) will be memorable for years to come, but not in a good way.  Why?
Because this PC port is complete♥♥♥♥♥ Missing button presses was a frequent problem through my experience, no matter how many different keyboards and computers I played on. (tested on 5, btw) For example, During the final boss fight of Amy's campaign, during phase 3, I game-overed 3 times from full lives because of the missed presses. In the fight, you have to jump over an obstacle. In my experience, Amy jumped probably 3/4 of the time. Eventually I got so badly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the game, I borrowed a second USB keyboard just to double my button presses.
This problem was only present in the Boss fights. There is literally no reason for this.
Why do I say thats its OK then? Well, Sonic Adventure DX is on the fence on being Good or Bad. The cornyness of the cinematics makes it funny and good, but only seconds later, a glitch where you are thrown uncontrolably off a stage by a pickup, losing a life and possibly game-overing you makes it bad. This effect (and unfortunatly glitch) happens frequently.
If you are curious, wait untill it's like $1 in a sale before you buy. Just the hours alone and ONLY the hours alone playing this game would justify that price. If you are on the fence, just don't.
Here's hoping Sonic Adventure 2 isn't this broken.

This game is really fun to play, but of course with every game it has it's flaws that make it a bit less enjoyable than what people would've hoped for. Don't get me wrong, this game has some really nice graphics and interesting maps but sometimes can get a bit boring and repetitive if you play it longer sessions.
Let's start off by talking about some of the good things about this game that really make it what it is. The game play is decent and the objective is simple enough to understand. Keep the generator on and wait for a helicopter to come and rescue you while you defend yourself against zombies. It has a nice way of keeping the game too easy or too hard with the threat level that you can choose from, Low, Medium or High. Starting off you will probably want to start with low just to get used to the game. But where this game falls apart is the controls. You start off without any indication of what each button does or what. I mean it took me a minute or two to figure out, but it would've been nice for even just a screen at the start of the game to show what buttons do what. There is also no story at all to why you are where you are and how you got in this situation in the first place. It would've been nice for at least a little story to go with the game. The community itself is dead, don't even bother trying to find people in a public server because I doubt you will anymore. I would suggest playing this game with friends who already own it or if you're really desperate then buy a 4-pack so that you can play this game with your other friends. The enemies on this game are zombies and ghosts. When I first started up this game it came up with kill the ghost or you will be cursed. I was confused as I hadn't even had time to adjust myself to what the controls were. I would've liked a explanation to what you had to do to kill the ghost at the start when it explains how to win (keep generator on until the helicopter arrives) which would've made it a little less stressful. The game can also get a little repetitive as this isn't much variation to each of the levels which there are only 6 of. The ranking system whoever is nicely presented and well made. You unlock guns by levelling up then use the money you have got form the missions to buy them. It works really well with this sort of game. It's a great way to pass the time either if you're playing alone or with some of your friends. Although I would've liked the choice of First-Person mode instead of over the should Third-Person mode. There might've been a way to change but I couldn't figure it out because of there being no control menu or screen telling me.
This game has a smooth Frame even for not so good laptop like mine, but the walking animation for me is a bit weird. I would walk forward a step or two and the character would slide along and then do the walking animation half a second after. This really didn't look very good as the graphics in this game where really nicely presented and well polished. The map design was well implemented for the game play.
There isn't really that much to say about Music and Sound in this game because there isn't much to talk about. There's some nice music at the starting menu, but once you enter a level there is no background music. There are just some generic sounds that you would expect from a game like this and that's it. Nothing really that unique about the sounds or music in this game.
All in all a alright game, as long as you have some
to play this game with then you will be okay. The public multilayer servers are dead, don't even try to find people to play with on this game. Graphics are nicely presented but walking animation is a bit weird at times. Nothing really unique or special about the sounds or music in this game. Would recommend to people who want to play this game with their friends.

Now the biggest issue is the Interface... I ATTEMPTED the controller option but that was joke, Frankesntien is more agile and responsive than the lead. However if you can navigate through these issues, its a decent adventure game and WAY worth it if its on sale for 50% or more. The puzzle are mostly logical save a few (one involving a door) and its not to hard to avoid the "looking up a walkthrough" method online.

It doesn't take a significant amount of time to realize just what kind of narrative The Deer is trying to establish.

The Deer, taken at surface value, is an educational game oriented towards young children, going over the evolution of the deer as we know it, but it's far more than what it claims to be.

At it's core, The Deer is a gripping experience that asks the age old question of human existance and what it truly means to be alive. It is executed perfectly, never once taking control away from the player- an important detail that greatly aids us in understanding the central idea behind the game.

The game is thoroughly nihilistic in it's thoughts, questioning much (if not all!) of what we, as a species, consider important.

I'll be spoiling the majority of the game, so if you wish to have a blind playthrough, don't read following section. It's currently on sale (Dec 4-10) for only 11 cents, and it's an absolute must have. Even without the sale it's only 19 cents, so you really don't have a reason to miss out on this gem. I highly recommend this game to anyone that's looking for a game with purpose and meaning.
EDIT: Price has been raised, still worth it.

-----------SPOILER-----------

The game opens on a somber notice. Melancholy guitar plucks away in the background as a painting of our protagonist standing by a pool of water fades from full color to oversaturation, representing the passage of time. Summer becomes winter, winter becomes summer. Again and again the transition plays back and forth, all the while our protagonist is silently staring at the water, observing their own reflection.

This symbolises self-doubt and self-questioning. Our protagonist is unsure on how to continue with their life, coming back day after day and observing their reflection- their own self image and past. They quietly judge themselves, trying to correct their course in life as best as they can, mourning their losses and repenting over their wrongs. This continues day after day, our protagonist practically petrified in place, weighed down by their past actions and regrets.

The tragic part, however, is that they have no reflection. I'll leave that open to interpretation as many things can be derived from this one small detail, far too many to list in a single steam review, so let's simply continue


As we press play, the screen fades to black from left to right, which is an important detail. As everyone knows, when you play Mario, you go right. When you play Megaman, you go right. Right is the only and "correct" direction that you can go, any attempts to swim against the current are promptly shut down. This aggressive fade from left to right forces our character to move forward; to forget about their past (the left) and to boldly march forth into the future (the right.)

As the fade dissipates, we see our protagonist standing in a forest. For the first time since we've seen them, they appear happy and content with their situation. Relaxed, optimistic music plays in the background, birds sing their songs and the local wildlife goes about their preparation for winter. However, the trained eye will notice white outlines around some of the artwork, as though the surroundings were cut and pasted to form the scene, as though it was deliberately engineered to appear pleasant and happy.

The forest is an illusion; a mirage constructed by the psyche of our protagonist as they desperately try to block out reality. It's their own personal dreamland. They aren't -actually- happy. They want to be, but whatever was left in the past prevents them from doing so. This is when the player gains control over the character.

The controls are simple. A and D moves the character left and right. The mouse can be used to inspect and interact with the scenery. Please do recall, this is all still brilliantly disguised as an educational game targeted towards young children.

Our character starts below a tree with the label "Memory" on it, with a play button below it. When clicked, the screen once again fades from left to right and we're greeted with the age old game of memory, in which we have 12 face-down cards we have to match with eachother. It's a trivial task for anyone with developed mental capacity, but what's strange about this section is that once we match all cards together, nothing happens.

Our efforts, like our protagonist's, were for naught. Not a victory jingle, or any sound for that matter, is heard. Our only option is to go back to the forest by clicking the -left- button.

Our character wants to go back. They wish to undo their wrongs.

When we click the button, we get an uncharacteristic fade to black from right to left. Our character is ready to go back. But the fade is different now. A large black rectangle blocks the left part of our screen, symbolically preventing us and the protagonist from looking "back". The important detail here is that we were exiting the minigame -memory-. This is a metaphor for Alzheimer disease. Our character wishes to go back and repent, but, tragically, cannot remember what exactly they wish to go back and fix.


We're back in our character's false forest. When attempting to move there is a slight bit of delay. This is our character hesitating to make a move, wanting to stay where they are but wanting to make a change at the same time.

The longer we hold down a direction, the more difficult it becomes to start moving in the other one. People may view this as shoddy programming, but in truth this is intentional. As our idea gains more sway in our mind and we begin to dedicate more and more of our energy to it. It becomes increasingly harder to let go and we refuse to approach it from another angle.

Our character is tunnel-visioned on one solution, unhealthily so.

If we attempt to go left we are, unsurprisingly, blocked off by an inconspicuous tree. What's important to note is that the further left you move, the denser the forest becomes, blocking more and more light, symbolising our character's dark and twisted past. Seeing this, they wish to move forward, but due to what was mentioned just earlier, it takes them a long while before they gather their resolve.

The protagonist is forced to move forward. There is no other solution.

As our character moves onward, the passage of time becomes more and more apparent. The forest begins shedding it's leaves and the ground is covered in snow. It's getting colder and colder. It represents the response our character received in their darkest hour from those that he cared and loved; the cold shoulder.

Shortly after we encounter our second minigame in which we have to help our protagonist make provisions for the winter. We select from a list of 12 (in truth 13) foods. Logically speaking, it's the player's objective to select the five foods that are fitting for a deer. In truth, however, it isn't. Like the previous minigame, this one doesn't reward you for completing it. Whether or not the player chooses correctly, incorrectly or not at all is irrelevant.

This is our character's current mindstate. They do not care whether they succeed or fail.

The only option, like previously, is the back button. Our character wants to go back. It's the only thing they care about, but they know the way back is blocked off and that the damage has already been done.

The protagonist and in turn we, the player, are forced to move forward.

We are railroaded in one direction. We cannot deviate, our path is clear-cut and unavoidable. Our protagonist is not fatalistic, they are simply powerless or without will to change their life. The "choice" of movement we are given isn't truly a choice, but a veil that gives us meaning, one that, when broken down, removes our false sense of purpose...

This was a fun game when I fisrt started playing it.  Being able to customize my character to whatever I wanted and having almost the same for the car was nice also.  The graphics were OK, and the amount of guns, clothing, and veheicles to choose from was moderate.
Gameplay itself was decent.
It was fun exploring the area and going after the criminals and getting paid for it.   Most missions were fun to do and most of the time I did have a good team.  After awhile however, the missions dd tend get repetative.  Especially if the player is solo and searching for a mission/group.  Many times I had gone with a team of 4 against a team of 2.  Other times it was an equal match but the player levels were unbalanced.  Whether or not I failed, the same mission would usually pop up after the next or right after that.  Also, it's awesome when a player is doing great on a mission then all of a sudden becomes a High Value Target and everyone is alerted to that HVT.  Now, that player that was doing great has around 20 players hunting their♥♥♥♥♥for a bounty.   Usually they were killed within 15 seconds.
I'm honestly a bit mixed on the gun/car lasting only a few days.  Guns I can understand, even the paid ones to *try* and balance the game.  But I hated paying a lot for a car that would be gone in a few days.  It would take awhile to get enough money to ..I guess one could say to "rent" a vehicle since payment was little and I started to be matched against higher levels.  The money I was saving then had to be used for a better weapon if  I wanted even a chance at killing some.  Even the default gun players receive at the start is fairly balanced.  I've killed many with it.  But it doesn't compare to a sniper rifle that is a one hit kill.
Most players kept to their self.  Others were chatting on the global chat which was mostly friendly.  The rest were of course people trolling.  I only had trouble with a few and the rare person that laged like hell.  (or hacked)
What I played was fun...
...Till I was killed 22 times trying to get to a mission objective and being blown up by someone on the opposing team with a RPG.  No matter where my team and I went, there was always somebody waiting in a corner, or at the objective.  I did get to run over the person once though!  Why stay for 22 deaths?  I don't like to rage quit.
Since then I would drive around waiting to see some action pass by.  Then when a group went by I would follow them to the objective then take the cars they stole from the civies and impound them for cash.  Which was pretty good if they stole a high performance veheicle.  Especially armored trucks.  Oh, and the vehicle wasn't damaged too bad.
- I can't say I fully enjoyed the game since I died *alot* from people who used real currency to purchase their guns.  However, because of that, I can't fully recommend the game.  I could over look the matchmaking (since CoD did that alot to me) and the missions.  But it doesn't work in the end.  Think this qualifies as a "Great concept, poor execution" kind of game for me.

Super Meat Boy is a hardcore platformer that does everything right. Everything? Well, almost. The game crashes once in a while, and for me the audio crashes almost everytime I play it. The animations are outdated and the gameplay, even though it's mostly solid, can feel slipery sometimes. Also, you can't remap the controls on a keyboard. The game advertises how controllers are better and all. While this might be true for some games, this one has only TWO buttons! It wouldn't be that much of an issue to play with a keyboard if I could change the controls (that are by default shift for running and space for jumping), which is the bare minimum when you release a game on PC (I still beat it with a keyboard, yay me!).
Anyway, I'm a passionate platformer player, and apart from what I mentionned, I found this game highly enjoyable. The level design is amazing. It keeps reinventing itself by using the same components in new ways (something McMillen talked about in Indie Game: The Movie). The difficulty increases at a perfect rate. I thought it would be incredibly hard from the start, or soon enough, but no, it increases perfectly so that a veteran like me don't get bored, but that anyone can progress quite quickly to the third or fourth world.
It's refreshing to have a platformer that challenges me, and it makes it even more rewarding to finish it.

Foreign Legion : Multi Massacre is a game that shows a lot of potential.
Being released in 2012 by Sakari Games as a sequel to Foreign Legion : Buckets of Blood.
The community of this game is long gone seeing as how you will 99.9% of the time not see a single match up and running, but if you have a few friends that have this game then you will enjoy your time.
Like I said this game shows a lot of potential, but it seemed to have gone to waste at some point during development and feels as though it was rushed out. Reusing the music from the first game.
As of its current state it seems to be stuck in its Halloween update and has been abandoned by the developer for a long time now. There are many glaring issues with the game such as the camera, some gamemodes being completely broken (Deathmatch on Pipeline can not end.), and also just having repetitive gameplay.
Surprisingly I find myself playing this game more often than I should and it is an absolute blast for me. Unlike the opinions of many other people I really hope they do make another Foreign Legion and I really hope they take on the potential of being a whacky casual third person shooter.
I would honestly give this game a 6/10 for the fact that it's a dead game when it comes to it's community, it's a buggy mess at times, and it just as so many issues that shouldn't exist even during the time of it's original release in 2012.
But during sales especially during the time of this review of being less than a dollar and the 4-pack being less than 2 dollars I find it worth it. Grab a few friends and have mindless fun for a few hours here and there.
TL:DR
-Game shows a lot of potential
-Dead community and lots of issues
-Great time waster
Personal Score : 6/10

Slime Rancher is a game munch in the vain of farming Simulator if your cows could suddenly turn into rampaging cannibals that completely ruin your entire lifestock and crop if your not fully prepared and educated enough about the games mechanics. If you were able to get threw that sentence without laughing too hard, you'll find the game has an infectious cuteness to it thats quite endearing to a younger audience, while also having mechanics that require you to think and plan propperly in order to become a sucsessful Slime Rancher.
If farming was the end all for the game, the game would simply be sub par, but the game also further grasps your attention by also incorperating a large and fully explorable sandbox world where you are expected to gather more advanced slime types, discover treasures, mysteries, and new dangers, all in the prospect of greater reward.
However as of the 0.2.4 releace, the game is quite unfinished and the sandbox elements are limited, though diverse enough to keep ones attention for a few hours. After roughly 3-4 hours, a more experenced gamer will quickly run out of much to do with the game, but that does not undermine the fact that Slime Rancher still possesses a great deal of potential. It is definitely a game to keep an eye on as further releaces come about, and particuarly to get when the full releace is expected to come out in fall of 2016. As it is now, its not a waste of money to pick it up now, but a potential investment of something good that is to come.

The Raven was dead - or at least to begin with.
The career of the world famous "Gentleman Master Thief" came to an abrupt and unexpected end thanks to the intervention of a young, up and coming police officer by the name of LeGrand, and a several storey drop from the roof of a building that he was robbing at the time.
Flash forward a few years though, to 1964 and questions over his possible demise begin to be raised following an explosive heist at the British Museum, leading to the theft of one of the priceless jewelled "Eyes Of The Sphinx".  Has the Raven returned from the dead, or is this just the work of a copycat?  And why has his modus operandi changed to include violence, something which he had previously avoided?
Inspector LeGrand, feted for his part in the apparent termination of the Raven previously, is put in charge of both the case and also of guarding the other Eye Of The Sphinx during its long and perilous trip from London to Cairo, where it is to be displayed, via The Orient Express and luxury ocean liner.  However, you do not play as Inspector LeGrand, or even his eager sidekick from Scotland Yard.  No, instead you are Constable Anton Jakob Zellner - an elderly, balding overweight Swiss policeman whose presence on board the Orient Express is the bare minumum of assistance that the Swiss government could provide and who hitherto has never done anything more exciting than walk the same beat every day of his working life - an extremely unlikely hero at first glance and which does make for a bit of a slow start to the game, with plenty of talking and very little action.
It is not until about 20 minutes in that you come across a character called Lady Westmacott, the expy of a certain other real life massively successful classic British crime author and you begin to  understand that you find yourself in a lovingly constructed homage to the works of Agatha Christie.  Constable Zellner is a huge fan of her work and it soon becomes apparent that he shares several traits with that of her most famous fictional detective "Monsieur Partout".  He has a logical mind and a keen eye for human behaviour, and it is this that helps him get under the skins of his fellow passengers, one or more of whom may be a great deal more than they appear.
In contrast with the obsessed Inspector LeGrand, he is convinced that this Raven is nothing more than a copycat and in his own quiet way is just as determined to bring him to justice.  He is also aware that this adventure may be his last chance to accomplish something worthwhile in his life, as retirement is looming and he is in poor health anyway.  "If I don't do anything exciting I might have a few more years to live?" he asks, before dropping his heart tablets in the ocean while preparing to disobey orders and sneak onboard the SS Lydia to search for a stowaway.  His adventures will end up taking him all the way to the catacombs of Cairo, while along the way he will save a young boy from a runaway train, survive being bombed, chloroformed, drugged and concussed (not necessarily in that order), solve the locked room murder of a Baroness on the high seas - which enabled me to live out my dream of gathering a group of suspects together before outlining my deductions - before finally unmasking the Raven.
However the game then abruptly switches narrative, changing its viewpoint to that of not one, but two different characters whose plots run parallel to that of the good Constables, overlapping with it at crucial junctures.  The trouble was that by then I was really enjoying my time spent in the comfortable and soothing presence of Constable Zellner that this change of viewpoint was initially disappointing and, although it did explain more fully several key events, the game did lose some of its idiosynchratic charm in the process.  One thing it did do well though is to shed new light on some of the games wide and varied cast.  For example a character that is pretty much a one dimensional comic relief type in Zellner's playthrough is revealed as being old, tired and unwell and very much aware that his presence onboard ship is neither needed or particularly wanted by the crew he is supposedly in charge of, and another unsympathetic character confesses that they realise just how hollow their life is, that they are estranged from their family and that they keep their father's pistol on hand for when they want to end it all.  All the separate plot strands then meet together for the climax leading to a twist ending that, while containing at least one giant plothole and relying a little too much on coincidence, was for me perfectly satisfying.
As for the gameplay, one thing I did like was the puzzles.  While some of them may be a little obscure and it is worth mentioning that some of them require you clicking on an object twice as your protagonist may miss details the first time, they are for the most part logical and usually involve common objects that you would expect to find in the immediate surroundings.  So while there is nothing here as brain melting as something you might find in the Sam And Max series for example, this can have the side effect of making proceedings a little too simple, there will be very few instances where you will be genuinely stuck.  The score, provided by the Brandenburg State Orchestra is wonderfully filmic and, while the visuals can be workmanlike, the vocals are absolutely spot on, with the characters sounding exactly how you would imagine them to.
Now to the bugs.  A quick scan of both the forums and other reviews of this game can soon unearth some real horror stories and to be fair all the glitches should have been sorted out months ago.  I don't know if I was lucky or if the patches have done their job, but apart from difficulty moving from one screen to another in various spots and one instance where I clicked to perform an action and was then stuck in a loop of a character wandering round in circles until I force closed the game down I managed to get through ok.  It is still worth saving regularly though, just to be on the safe side!
In conclusion then, a game with a few rough edges, but the strength of the writing and of the characters make it well worth your time.  If it was an Agatha Christie novel, it wouldn't be a blockbuster like Murder On The Orient Express, but one of her lesser known yet solid efforts like A Mysterious Affair At Styles, perfect for a rainy afternoon's escapist fun.

I initially bought this game at full price due to the positive early reviews (which were mostly based on the first chapter).
Unfortunately, the game is severely broken for many users and the developers have done little to fix these issues since the game's release. These are not only minor bugs or annoyances, but critical game breaking issues.
I usually love these types of adventure games, but in this case, I have been unable to progress beyond the first chapter (disregard the deceptive amount of hours on record; I have left the game running in the background on several occasions while running errands, sleeping or looking for solutions to the problems I've encountered). It is unlikely that I will get a refund as I bought the game long before Steam's refund policies were changed. Instead, I want to warn future potential buyers of the problems they may encounter.
Take a look at the forum posts below:
Bug thread (13 pages so far):
Save games disappearing (this is my biggest issue at the moment, as you can see by my posts to the below threads):
Linux/Mac issues (there are too many of these threads to list them all):
Etc.
More examples can be found on the game's discussion page and I recommend reading through it. These issues have NOT been fixed, despite the game having been out for two years now.
This leaves the game unplayable for many people; whether you are going to be one of these people depends on your luck and on your operating system. Mac and Linux users seem to have the most issues. As the game is listed as being compatible on these operating systems, this is inexcusable.
As for the game itself (or the little I have been able to experience of it), the story is an obvious homage to Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot. The first chapter starts off slow, but quickly builds up suspense once the titular "Raven" makes an appearance. I have heard that the second and third chapters are a bit of a let down compared to the first chapter's conclusion. The puzzles are alright, but nothing memorable comes to mind. They mainly seem to revolve around using the right object in the right location. I didn't encounter any logic puzzles or truly creative solutions. There is some pixel hunting involved, which I found annoying in the initial train sequence (although it is possible to reveal hot spots in the game by using up "points", this locks certain achievements from being accomplished). The animation and movement in the game is frankly awful, but I was able to ignore it for the most part. It does not really compare well to contemporary medium-high budget games, and as such the standard asking price is a tad steep. I would write more about the game itself, but my save games were erased three times in a row and I have given up on making any progress beyond this chapter.

Basically, if you play on Mac or Linux: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
If you play on Windows... buy at your own risk. The first chapter seems decent enough; I can't personally comment on the final two chapters, but many reviews online seem to paint them in a rather mediocre light. Even if you do not encounter the technical issues that apply to Mac or Linux users, the game is still rife with random bugs which can impede your progress. I'd wait for a sale, or hope that the developers finally take notice of these issues and release a patch.

I fondly remember the time when the bandwagon (myself included) hated this game before it released. And while yes, if you've been a veteran of the franchise for a long time, this might seem rather unnecessary, it's actually quite decent. Since there's no way this game could ever replace the original series, think of this as a fun little spinoff from a more western cultural perspective. Developed by British Based Ninja Theory, DMC tells the origin story of an alternate universe dante who struggles with a meaningless, angry and hedonistic lifestyle until he is awakened by a dark truth regarding his origins and the oppressed city of signal, controlled by the demon mundus. If you're new to the series, at least google the original franchise first, and if you're a veteran, take it for what it is, a fun little spinoff in an alternate universe. It's a very, very fun game with interesting political commentary, suprising depth and storytelling and a fresh take on a very old franchise.

Upon purchasing this game I was understandably expecting a lampooning of SJW culture, but I'm not sure WHAT I got in all honesty. While it's certainly self-deprecating towards the phenomenon of "social justice warriors", it does ultimately seem more intent on portraying all "politically incorrect" people as drooling, ignorant "trolls". So the self-deprecation effort comes off a tad tokenistic, at best...
The actual gameplay, in any case, is where things fall down the most. For each character class of SJW that you play - paladin, mage, cleric, or rogue - you get four different possible ways to "defend" each of your "troll" opponent's attacks. These are amusing enough, and include writing a logical but long-winded rebuttal of their claim which erodes their Patience, or simply insulting them with a high-damage attack which in turn wreaks havoc on your own Reputation score.
Regrettably, though, it seems your chances of victory depend mostly on unpredictable RNG. This said, I did find one appalling exploit where the paladin could continually "block" the opponent's attack, which seemed to all-but guarantee a boost to one of my two attributes every single time...so you may as well just spam that one until you're topped up and ready to take 'em down from a position of power (I did appreciate the joke of "no need to dignify with a response" as the paladin's justification here, though; anyone who's battled in real-life forums will surely have heard THAT one before).
Had it been a more genuinely balanced parody at the expense of BOTH sides of the debate, as it claims to be on the Store page, then I may have found this game more endearing. (A choice to play as either SJW or "troll" may have helped herein, as might have renaming the "troll" to something less one-sided; let's face it, BOTH sides are arguably "trolls", to some extent.) As it is, it doesn't especially work as either insightful satire OR an otherwise compelling strategy game, as aside from the above-mentioned exploit I didn't find much "strategy" to employ. Perhaps if I'd given the game a bit more time and patience I might have discovered more strategic potential, but the whole thing lost my interest so quickly that I honestly didn't give it that chance.
One thing I will say in the developer's defence: the landscape has changed a LOT in the few years since this was released, so anything aiming to be this topical can't possibly have the desired impact when there's little or no mention of such recent buzzwords as cisgendering, transphobia, Islamaphobia, mansplaining, toxic masculinity, cultural appropriation...hell, this game even pre-dates the Trump-for-president era! So one can't help but wonder if this game might have more teeth if it were remade or updated to include such contemporary concerns.
As it is, this game is definitely more bark than bite, and is unlikely to offend or inspire anyone on either side of the "political" fence, especially in the year 2017. You might as well just go on Facebook now and start up a "debate" with the eejit of your choice: you'll probably find more fun in doing so. Any enjoyment you get out of this game will be short-lived at best, so it's definitely not worth eight dollars of your hard-earned, evil, exploitative capitalist cash (that's sarcasm at the end there, btw).
Verdict: 4.5/10.

The premise of the game is fun and it has been an enjoyable experience at times, but that being said the game has a few issues which just prevent from being able to enjoy it fully.
First stability; in my case my game crashed in the short time I played. While a little bit of instability is expected I am still not sure how my prison save disappeared in the process. I was able to recover most of my process from an autosave so this is based a make or break issue.
Second tutorial: The campaign in this game is in my opinion kind of dull and is enough that I did not finish it. I actually for a few things had to lookup how to preform the action they wanted me to. In another instance the task did not register so I had to restart the tutorial stage.
Third, bugs: Every game is expected to have a few bugs, but that being said there is a limit to what can be tolerated. In my case I had one bug where I had so many people trying to pass through an area it was not possible to resolve. Other issues with things such as coloring coding on hot water do not function properly. Other issues such as doctors not healing prisoners next to them. There is no way to control (that I could see) what ingredients are sent to what kitchen either.
Fourth, escape AI: The AI used for escaping by the prisoners is incredibly simple to fool; for example I had an enclosed area between two buildings that prisoners would always tunnel into. Honestly escapes became a chore of removing the tunnel dug and were completely resolved with dog patrols.
Fifth, too many prisoners: The flow of prisoners into your prison is somewhat maddening for example 30-40 prisoners each makes the idea of building a new cell for each impossible while dormatories present plenty of issues for rehabilitation in the long term. You will be expanding facilities you built repeatedly and spamming previous structures.
It's strengths? The systems in the game are frequently very well developed and micromanaging is actually enjoyable. Riots are actually a lot of fun to calm. The risk tiers of min, normal, and max add a great deal of depth to securing the prison. Balancing initial cost, profit, and security will make you think.
I don't know how much more I will play this game, but it does fill that strange niche of a high-risk planning game (if you liked Simcity I recommend) so I can see myself coming back for a new prison every so often...
...my recommendation do not buy this unless it is on sale; I paid $12 for my copy and honestly that's about what is worth in my opinion due to the bugs and issues present.
