People told me this game was hard.
It was.
Super Meat Boy is a little indie gem created by Ed McMillan in which you play as the titular Meat Boy on his quest to save his girlfriend, Bandage Girl, from the evil Dr. Fetus.
The plot, obviously, takes a heavy cue from Mario. And many of the cutscenes also play off of old NES opening cutscenes like Mega Man 2 or Ninja Gaiden. Most of the other cutscenes are- in my opinion- not very funny. If you find them humorous, good on you. I just didn't see them as that funny.
Obviously, as I stated earlier, Super Meat Boy is very hard. Very VERY hard. Very very f***ing hard. But to quote the Joker, what makes Super Meat Boy's immense difficulty is... "It's fair."
It's no big secret that I despise the old NES and SNES games' humongous praise, and one reason I'm not on the same happy train as every other mainstream critic, is that the games aren't designed well for people who want to immediately move on from their mistakes... unless you're playing these games on an emulator.
See, Super Meat Boy, doesn't have a bullsh** life-system. When you die, you go back to the start of that level. Not the entire f***ing world. You still have to play through the level up to where you died, but it's better than Super Mario Bros., where one bad jump could potentially send you back to World 1-1.
I also like the controls on Meat Boy. The Space-Bar and Shift-Key increase his jump height and range. He controls so well that every time you f*** up (and f*** up you will), it'll feel like your fault, not the game's...
Most of the time. There are some examples during Rapture, where those gravity discs just didn't catch me right and ruined an otherwise perfect jump. And those massive flies are incredibly hard to lure away sometimes.
Another big complaint I have towards Super Meat Boy would be the bosses. Everyone like to hate on the boss from Hell, and his head smashes, but I consider him one of the better bosses. At least his fight is a little short. I hated the first fight with Dr. Fetus and the race against Brownie. I think the only boss fight that felt like a real boss fight would be against the giant maggots or giant red fish-blob.
Despite that, I still was hooked on Super Meat Boy since I started playing it. It completely diverted my attention from Papo & Yo (but don't worry. I'll get that review out soon), which is a testament to how good gameplay can be more gripping than a good story... most of the time. Super Meat Boy is a solid 7/10. A fun, challenging, but fair platformer with a few honest flaws but still definitely worth your time.

Slime Rancher is a game munch in the vain of farming Simulator if your cows could suddenly turn into rampaging cannibals that completely ruin your entire lifestock and crop if your not fully prepared and educated enough about the games mechanics. If you were able to get threw that sentence without laughing too hard, you'll find the game has an infectious cuteness to it thats quite endearing to a younger audience, while also having mechanics that require you to think and plan propperly in order to become a sucsessful Slime Rancher.
If farming was the end all for the game, the game would simply be sub par, but the game also further grasps your attention by also incorperating a large and fully explorable sandbox world where you are expected to gather more advanced slime types, discover treasures, mysteries, and new dangers, all in the prospect of greater reward.
However as of the 0.2.4 releace, the game is quite unfinished and the sandbox elements are limited, though diverse enough to keep ones attention for a few hours. After roughly 3-4 hours, a more experenced gamer will quickly run out of much to do with the game, but that does not undermine the fact that Slime Rancher still possesses a great deal of potential. It is definitely a game to keep an eye on as further releaces come about, and particuarly to get when the full releace is expected to come out in fall of 2016. As it is now, its not a waste of money to pick it up now, but a potential investment of something good that is to come.

Let's start off in 1991 with Sega's response to Nintendo's Mario Bros. It was fast, had you running through loop-de-loops at probably the speed of sound. In 1998 in Japan, Sonic Adventure released for the NTSC-J Dreamcast. If you think the old games were fast, this will blow your mind. In 1999, Sonic Adventure International released in America and Japan. It had LOTS of bug fixes, because it was rushed to the Japanese market. In 2003, Sonic Adventure DX released for the GCN and PC. This is the verson I'm reviewing now. This 2011 version has lots of annoyances such as the border, but nevertheless the game is still that classic in 1999. However, I installed BetterSADX, (the mod) which gets rid of the border and installs all the Game Gear minigames that released in the 2003 release but left out in 2011. However, No matter what version, I highly recommend this game. I love this game more than Sonic Unleashed (Xbox 360, PS3). Thanks for reading. 10/10.

I initially bought this game at full price due to the positive early reviews (which were mostly based on the first chapter).
Unfortunately, the game is severely broken for many users and the developers have done little to fix these issues since the game's release. These are not only minor bugs or annoyances, but critical game breaking issues.
I usually love these types of adventure games, but in this case, I have been unable to progress beyond the first chapter (disregard the deceptive amount of hours on record; I have left the game running in the background on several occasions while running errands, sleeping or looking for solutions to the problems I've encountered). It is unlikely that I will get a refund as I bought the game long before Steam's refund policies were changed. Instead, I want to warn future potential buyers of the problems they may encounter.
Take a look at the forum posts below:
Bug thread (13 pages so far):
Save games disappearing (this is my biggest issue at the moment, as you can see by my posts to the below threads):
Linux/Mac issues (there are too many of these threads to list them all):
Etc.
More examples can be found on the game's discussion page and I recommend reading through it. These issues have NOT been fixed, despite the game having been out for two years now.
This leaves the game unplayable for many people; whether you are going to be one of these people depends on your luck and on your operating system. Mac and Linux users seem to have the most issues. As the game is listed as being compatible on these operating systems, this is inexcusable.
As for the game itself (or the little I have been able to experience of it), the story is an obvious homage to Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot. The first chapter starts off slow, but quickly builds up suspense once the titular "Raven" makes an appearance. I have heard that the second and third chapters are a bit of a let down compared to the first chapter's conclusion. The puzzles are alright, but nothing memorable comes to mind. They mainly seem to revolve around using the right object in the right location. I didn't encounter any logic puzzles or truly creative solutions. There is some pixel hunting involved, which I found annoying in the initial train sequence (although it is possible to reveal hot spots in the game by using up "points", this locks certain achievements from being accomplished). The animation and movement in the game is frankly awful, but I was able to ignore it for the most part. It does not really compare well to contemporary medium-high budget games, and as such the standard asking price is a tad steep. I would write more about the game itself, but my save games were erased three times in a row and I have given up on making any progress beyond this chapter.

Basically, if you play on Mac or Linux: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
If you play on Windows... buy at your own risk. The first chapter seems decent enough; I can't personally comment on the final two chapters, but many reviews online seem to paint them in a rather mediocre light. Even if you do not encounter the technical issues that apply to Mac or Linux users, the game is still rife with random bugs which can impede your progress. I'd wait for a sale, or hope that the developers finally take notice of these issues and release a patch.

A point and click adventure that starts off promisingly with Agatha Christie, Orient Express, Poirot, Murder at Sea and Master Jewel Thief themes but loses the plot slightly the moment the character switch hits.
The idea of progressing the main story up to a cliffhanger, then restarting from the perspective of another character to work your way up to the same point and then see out the story, in theory is excellent, but the story writing from that point onwards is a real stretch. Constable Anton Jakob Zellner was a great character to play as, his part of the story was high quality, the rest I didn't really care for. The percentage of main criminal element protagonists to remainder of main characters was also ludicrous, ruined the story.
I could quite easily gloss over that as the game was fairly enjoyable as a whodunnit but unfortunately Raven is marred by bugs. There are issues with pathfinding, the player controlled character moves and turns in a manner even more tank like than Resident Evil, characters will jog in place (meaning a restart), rotate on the spot (meaning a restart), warp and disappear completely from scenes, cameras will lock in place (meaning a restart), items essential to solving puzzles also won't appear as highlightable in some scenes if your using a pad and there are numerous other bugs involving selectable items and characters.....The Captain for example leaves a scene but you can click on where he was sitting at the bar to get the dialogue about about him sweating, in the Baroness room to select and open her portable cabinet you have to click on her bed which is on the other side of the room, in the ship holding cell area the puzzle involving the winch is unsolvable using a pad as you can't highlight the hook etcetera etcetera etcetera.
The game is nearly 2 years old, the bugs which I noted are plastered all over the Steam hub and went unfixed marring an otherwise enjoyable game whilst slapping paying customers in the face - it's by far the buggiest point and click adventure I've ever played and with no post release support in 2 years I can't recommend supporting it by buying it.

Do you like hacking? Political intrigue? Fantastic emergent storytelling? Then buy this game.
Hackmud is an incredibly unique game the likes of which you won't find elsewhere. It's incredible simple, has a captivating world and stories that live within it, and gains a lot of milage out of clever player interactions. It has a bit of a learning curve, but no programming experience is necessary, and there's a friendly community if you really do get stuck.
The game's player interactions are designed to encourage and reward cleverness, sneakiness, and political intrigue. If you've ever been interested in seeing what player drama/stories EVE Online is all about, check out this game instead. Everything in hackmud is designed around those ideas.
The single player campaign lasts between 3-5 hours and can be skipped any time with a single command but, similar to Her Story, the overall puzzle involves figuring out what it is. That said, the campaign story is fairly interesting and worth your time. Unlike most "tutorials," it's actually pretty dang fun, and could be a short game all its own.
The only current issue with hackmud is that the (single solo) developer for the game is a bit overwhelmed with its popularity and is currently trying to upgrade and stablize the servers, which have occasional timeout errors. People told me this game was hard.
It was.
Super Meat Boy is a little indie gem created by Ed McMillan in which you play as the titular Meat Boy on his quest to save his girlfriend, Bandage Girl, from the evil Dr. Fetus.
The plot, obviously, takes a heavy cue from Mario. And many of the cutscenes also play off of old NES opening cutscenes like Mega Man 2 or Ninja Gaiden. Most of the other cutscenes are- in my opinion- not very funny. If you find them humorous, good on you. I just didn't see them as that funny.
Obviously, as I stated earlier, Super Meat Boy is very hard. Very VERY hard. Very very f***ing hard. But to quote the Joker, what makes Super Meat Boy's immense difficulty is... "It's fair."
It's no big secret that I despise the old NES and SNES games' humongous praise, and one reason I'm not on the same happy train as every other mainstream critic, is that the games aren't designed well for people who want to immediately move on from their mistakes... unless you're playing these games on an emulator.
See, Super Meat Boy, doesn't have a bullsh** life-system. When you die, you go back to the start of that level. Not the entire f***ing world. You still have to play through the level up to where you died, but it's better than Super Mario Bros., where one bad jump could potentially send you back to World 1-1.
I also like the controls on Meat Boy. The Space-Bar and Shift-Key increase his jump height and range. He controls so well that every time you f*** up (and f*** up you will), it'll feel like your fault, not the game's...
Most of the time. There are some examples during Rapture, where those gravity discs just didn't catch me right and ruined an otherwise perfect jump. And those massive flies are incredibly hard to lure away sometimes.
Another big complaint I have towards Super Meat Boy would be the bosses. Everyone like to hate on the boss from Hell, and his head smashes, but I consider him one of the better bosses. At least his fight is a little short. I hated the first fight with Dr. Fetus and the race against Brownie. I think the only boss fight that felt like a real boss fight would be against the giant maggots or giant red fish-blob.
Despite that, I still was hooked on Super Meat Boy since I started playing it. It completely diverted my attention from Papo & Yo (but don't worry. I'll get that review out soon), which is a testament to how good gameplay can be more gripping than a good story... most of the time. Super Meat Boy is a solid 7/10. A fun, challenging, but fair platformer with a few honest flaws but still definitely worth your time.

Summary:
ASTRONEER is a beautiful game that shows immense promise. Unfortunately, that is all it has to offer at this time.
In depth:
The presentation of this game is wonderful. Its visuals are colorful and stylistic. The sound design, especially the music, is simply sublime. These elements combine to create a world that evokes curiosity along with a child-like sense of awe.
The User-Interface (UI) is among the most intuitive I have ever seen in a game. Everything follows the principal of "what-you-see-is-what-you-get". Items are stored as themselves, attached to containers and the player character's backpack in a manner similar to a peg board. The character's oxygen meter is depicted as a clearly visible blue bar on their backpack. Energy is shown as a glowing yellow fluid like material that drains upon use. There are almost no numbers shown in the game or any kind of abstraction at all for that matter. This contributes to the atmosphere by keeping things purely visual and not distracting the player with the details behind the game's mechanics.
Gameplay is where this title falls short. There simply is not enough content at this point to justify its price. You wander about the planet you start on and gather resources. You use resources to build the dozen or so structures available as well as four vehicles. Later, you gain the option of traveling to nearby worlds which, while aesthetically distinct, only present a slight change to gameplay. You can morph terrain as much as you please, explore, and build the structures described earlier. That is all. Unlike many similar sandbox titles (e.g. Space Engineers), building is clearly not a focus of the game so I do not see much outlet for creative expression. Similarly, once the novelty of a world has run out, there is little point to exploring every nook and cranny of it.
In short, the game looks great and plays well but there just isn't enough to hold your interest for very long. I cannot recommend buying this game at this point because of that. Perhaps in the future, when (and if) the game matures,  my opinion will change but as it stands I would recommend you hold off purchasing it for now.

Sonic Adventure DX on the GCN was a good remastering.
DX released on PC's in 2004 was one of the best Sonic Adventure ports.
PS3/360 DX was decent at best... Sensitive controls, and messed up physics.

What makes this worth it over say- the 2004 version of SADX on PC? Nothing really, but the mod 'BetterSADX' makes all my problems with the game dissapear. Why? It fixes the physics and glitches, adds HD and Widescreen support (something I don't believe the 2004 version could do with mods), AND mod support. That, and it's most likely cheaper to buy this and install the 'BetterSADX' mod than to hunt down a CD copy of SADX 2004.
I'd give this port a 6~6.5/10 without the mod, a 9.5~10/10 with the mod.

I have no idea why the game has so many positive reviews. The working title of this game is a joke. This is probably the worst title in the history of videogames.
People are just eating up this game's story. They shouldn't, it plays with the source material. There were several well established games in the series with a different backstory. The story is cookie cutter too, as all the games have the general goal of defeating Mundus. There was an obvious plot twist at some point in the game that surprised no one.
Dante is an edgelord. He has one geniunely funny line in the whole game, that's it. He's not nearly as funny as the games from several years ago.  This game shamelessly craps all over fans of the original games. I have never seen a company insult a character design in a reboot to this degree. It doesn't come off as tongue-and-cheek as they had hoped. It's just a big ole insult to fans of the series. He has the worst haircut I have ever seen. It's like they wanted him to appeal to edgy teenagers.
The gameplay is probably the only truly decent thing about this game. But to no surprise, they have dumbed down the scoring system. In previous games, you would lose your score rankings by not switching up combos, resulting in less style points. This would eventually lower an "S" to an "A" and so on. In this game, You can't lose your S ranking unless you get hit. Guess everyone wants to feel special and get a good ranking, instead of earning one. A very small handful of the levels are interesting at best, but often not executed as well as they could be. Devil trigger is useless. It traps enemies in the air and causes you to regenerate health. In previous games, it enhanced your powers and made you feel like someone with true power.
Visually the art at times can be impressive, but ultimately does not matter as some of the graphics on this port look just as good as the console counterpart. The animations in this game are a little bad for the enemies, who just hold their weapons in the air to swing them at you. That is the stupidest thing I have ever seen, especially when you're on the lower difficulty. Enemies just wind up their attack, count to 3 and then swing. They could have at least adjusted the animation for them, so it's more of a big windup. This would fit the game, as enemies tend to deal a lot of damage across the difficulties. Graphically this game does not look as good as the screenshots want you to believe. I don't remember being blown away with color.
The difficulties of this game are incredibly artificial. This game boasts a mode where enemies kill you in one hit while they retain full health. This is not intuitive. This is just stupid. Sure you can argue that this is challenging, but it's artificial. As far as I know, the AI behaves the same on the higher difficulties. Maybe there might be some extra enemies in areas but I can't really tell.
It's disappointing to see a game that is 5 years older than this one have more content. The game I am referencing is Devil May Cry 4, which from what I have read has a respectable PC port. That is the title I should have played. Probably would have taken more than a few hours to beat the game too.
If you have no issue with how they treat Dante's old character design, this game should not bother you. As long as you don't look too deeply into it. But glance too hard into this abbysmal game and you will see its flaws.

Buy DMC4SE or DMC3 instead, or just get DmC:DE on console.

What a Game!! At first I was sceptical of this game, it seemed a little low brow and lacking in content. Once I started playing I was rewarded with an art style that took me back to my childhood years, instant remanence that put me in a good mood. It took a while to master the controls, they have utilised the awsd keys just like an fps but have repurposed them for 2d;  as there is no up and down movement or jumping I only used A and D so I wasn’t bogged down with trying to remember extra buttons.
Once started, I immediately found myself playing a mini game or "side quest" if you will. It was a fresh take on the classic memory game where you have to match cards. Once completed I was able to retry and the positions didn’t change, meaning I was able to get a perfect score on my second try, Result!! During My play through I found one other side quest, I would love to know if anybody found more as there did seem to be hidden depths to this game which I'll talk about later.
Hidden depths; there is an underwater section to this game that I thought may be tricky but luckily the deer you play as can breathe underwater. There is so much factual information in this game I assume this is an accurate account and that deer’s in this period had gills or extremely large lungs like a dolphin or whale. There is a surprising amount of content and it is all is revealed in a novel almost childish way by simply mousing over objects on screen as you navigate your deer left or right  through the "maps". At first I thought this was just information bubbles explain facts from this time period but much to my surprise and delight I was able to affect the environment with these actions. This led to literally minutes of fun as I went searching for all the objects on the screen I was able to interact with.
All in all this game is simple but informative, with more going on than meets the eye. The art style is beautiful but again very simple. If I had to find a downside to this game it would be that it cost actual real money and it took me four times longer to write this review than it took to complete everything in the game.

It's a fun little game, I finish it in two sittings with a total of around 5 hours to 6.
I had a lot of fun in those sittings.
The story, I didn't like.
I thought it was a bit silly, to say the least, some of the characters try to counter their "demonic fantasy" by trying to share similarities with the monsters of our reality, which I resent, mainly because I feel as if the world of Devil May Cry, could, and can, offer more.
Just in concept, with the whole idea someone could create something a bit deeper, darker, and more interesting in my opinion.
It just made me think of the possibilites, rather than in the actual narrative that it was presenting.
Plus Dante, I don't know if he, as a protagonist, is this way in all the other games, but I found his whole character, and personality, generally, annoying, every mouth that came out of his mouth was just a peck of nonsense, a false little charade in which the character seem to be trying to "fit it" into the own idealization of the original character present in the past entries in the series.
I just found him unbearable at times, but for the most part, since you can skip most cutscenes I was happy I didn't have to always hear him.
Also, talking about cutscenes...
The game's pacing its terrible for the most part, it constantly interrumpts the combat sequences with a series of completely unnecessary cutscenes.
I'm not even saying don't have them, all i'm saying is, Why do they have to be present constantly, whilst frequently interrumpting my game?
Choose a time to present your narrative, and choose a time to let me play your game.
Then there's the gameplay.
Devil May Cry has always been a series that has a lot more to do with the gameplay, and combat systems, rather than the narrative.
The gameplay for the most part its fantastic, flows very well, incites you to build combos, the enemies are quite diverse, and unique, both in their design, as well as in their appereance.
It isn't until later when they start introducing some enemies that can only be damaged by specific attacks when things start becoming more tedious, and annoying.
Thing about this game is that on one side it really tries to get you to experiment with its combat mechanics, it offers you plenty of different weapons, all of which are different and useful in different situations, and for different enemies.
But then out of nowhere the game also introduces enemies that can only be attacked with only one particular weapon, and nothing else, if you try to attack them with anything other than the weapon they're weak against, your combo either doesn't rise in the least, or it just completely falls appart.
This is a strange, and contradictory design choice.
My guess is that it was implemented as a way to incite people to "diversify" their strategies, while at the same time, offering some variation, and challenge, so the usual encounters wouldn't become too "familiar" to not say repetitive.
But it has the opposite effect, and instead of enhancing the flow of the combat, it hinders it.
For the most part, the combat is extempt from this problems up until later into the game when every encounter seems to have at the very least one of those enemies, it doesn't completely destroy my enjoyment, but it certainly was annoying.
Last but not least there's the boss battles.
The boss battles in this game are really spectacular, and beautiful, superficially, the bosses in their appereance, graphically, aesthetically, however you want to call it, are incredible, they're huge, and they're attacks filled with flashing lights, and explosions, and all sorts of other effects, keep your attention "glued" to the screen.
The only issue that I have with the boss battles is that usually they just follow one particular pattern, and sadly, they have multiple health bars, meaning you'll have to repeat the same pattern, over, and over again, until the three, four, or how many health bars the bosses have gets depleted.
It is annoying, and once again, while it didn't "killed" the boss fights for me it certainly hindered them a bit.
Near halfway through the game there are also some "platforming" sections in which you need to use different types of "hooks" in order to overcome certain obstacles, and reach specific platforms.
It is a very simple way to implement this parts, but it is quite enjoyable, and while I fell plenty of times, it never felt frustrating in the least.
The game also has a ton of replayability, thanks to several different upgrades, collectibles, and your ability to keep your progression.
I recommend this game, I played through with the costume dlc, that allows me to play with the original Dante's clothes, kinda sad that you have to pay for that, but in my opinion it was worth it, I just like that character design, I'm not even a fan of past games, frankly I haven't played them if not for just a couple of minutes in the past, experiences that if I had, I can't remember.
But this was fine, I totally recommend it, just get it on a sale.

It begins with a 3-4 hour single player tutorial which is really well done and teaches you the ropes in a clear way - while still being entertaining - before throwing you into an imposing, and initially impenetrable, multiplayer version.
Without guidance this monster of a game would be impossible to comprehend, especially for someone like me whose only experience with hacking is watching WarGames with Mathew Broderick when I was a kid. Fortunately, ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ has an amazing community.
Like... seriously.
One of the most 'famous' (i.e 'rich and clever') players just gave an hour long lesson for newcomers like me on how to start writing code. He does this several times a week. There are scripts available for free that will provide you with 'locs' (I think I got that right) to break into if you can’t figure out how to do it yet yourself. If you have a question you can just type it into chat and you will get a response within seconds... although it's always more likely to be a hint than a full solution because the community 'get it' and don't want to spoil the joy of discovery for you.
It’s important to note that I experienced all of this in the first two days after launch when the servers were pretty much on fire. However, while it is certainly frustrating to play with high amounts of lag (those negative reviews aren’t making that stuff up) it was actually kinda cool to see the (sole) developer in chat asking the same people that I was asking “what colours do c003 locks use?” to help him test out a new build of the game to fix it all.
I loved Uplink and Hacknet, but they were short, single player experiences. This is a game for people that are in it for the long haul. It will never have masses of players, but it already has a strong and dedicated fan base, and It is genuinely exciting to think about what this game will look like a year from now.
So, yeah… it’s good! Play it… maybe…. I’ll be playing it! You might not like it… but you might love it! (I can’t tell because we haven’t met.)
P.S. I downloaded Notepad++ to make a script that says “Hi, friend!” which I feel is proof that this game can teach you how to program irl.

I'm a somewhat avid puzzle game player. I haven't had much practice with the lateral thinking so this game took me longer because I would get stuck on certain puzzles. While challenging, I did enjoy the puzzles though only having the ability to select relevant items is almost like cheating since you know they must somehow interact together. For a summary of the pros and cons:
Cons:
-There are some bugs with the character's movements. Especially when trying to transition between rooms. This can quickly become infuriating because you spend your time staring at the courser while slowly scanning the game screen to find an area that will let you say "Move to other room". It's really bad in Chapter 1 but be aware and push through it.
-One of the scenes in the other chapters are from a birds eye, which is great for an overview of the room but it's significantly harder to know where you should click to interact with people or items.
-There is one case with your inventory where you pick up an item and you must click it in your hand rather than access it from your inventory in order to use said item. While this only happens once, it is rather frustrating.
-There is not a smooth transition to the next chapter. You have select "New Game" and choose the next chapter. So if you haven't saved your progress in a different place so you can get OCD completion, it's a little irritating. And you don't really feel like you can play the whole story through.
But those are mostly my nitpicks. Now to the pros.
Pros:
-The voices become really strong as you progress and they stay true to the character throughout the story.
-A lot of story with really strong character development available and if you just want to skip through the words, just keep clicking the left mouse button.
-The first two chapters end with really strong cliffhangers so I had to power through the early mornings and finish the game. Totally worth it and I loved the story.
-You can use what you learned from the previous investigations to tell the story of what happened. You get an achievement and it feels fun rubbing it in Legrand's face.
-There are pretty awesome twists to the story. I did not see most of them coming and it was really a nice, detailed and heart warming story.
-This is a slight spoiler but I won't share all the details. You do change what character you follow during the story. You don't control the change, the story does. This does give you a really nice opportunity to hear other people's views and you learn the full story with better details.
In summary; a really nice mystery game that is worth getting. Replay is kind of low but the story is really good and taking the time to figure out the puzzles on your own is worth it. If there was a continuation of any kind, I would definitely buy it.

With the cons out of the way, the majority of the voice acting is wonderful and the story is really intertesting, in my opinion. It's a pretty lighthearted story, overall, but it has enough twists to keep you guessing. Especially around the last chapter, I had plenty of moments that made me go, "Whaaaat?" I also really liked how you played the story as different characters and experienced the plot from different angles.
If difficult puzzles are why you play adventure games, I'd say skip this one. but if you enjoy the stories and characters of adventure games, this is very worth picking up. Completely worth the $25 price tag but a must buy, as far as I'm concerned, if you find it on one of the Steam seasonal sales

I'm honestly offended by this game, and I don't want to be. I get the message the developer was going for, but that message is hollow in the reality of post August 2014. People have had their lives ruined, pushed into suicide, and even nearly murdered by cop via misinformation. You can't keep going down that both these "sides" are somehow equal in their personal failures, and while I do agree with the meessage of meditating on one's actions (something I had to learn the hard way), that's not what the game ends up saying to many.
The way its structured, it says that the "trolls" always win. Their victory is inevitable, and thus they are right for it. Inserting dialog about actual issues that have resulted in death and♥♥♥♥♥♥threats simply for being brought up just lets them insert themselves more into this, and they see the game's message as satire ONLY aimed at "SJWs." They live in a culture where their hatred and ignorance is not isolated, it is shared and supported, almost coming off as cult like. They don't get the message.
More egotistical people also won't, more likely to get angry by the portray of their beliefs, while others will just feel like they were talked down to by someone who doesn't understand their personal experiences at all. They don't know the pain or suffering they had to go through. They don't understand why they've had to fight for so long just to start a dialog about their suffering.
As satire, this game is ann absolute failure. It's too focused on a particular idea and culture to have the more universial message to have impact, and that message is tainted and lost by the context it creates. That really disappointed me.
Just don't buy it. Words can't describe.

It's worth starting out this review by saying, this game is definitely not for everyone. If you're not into text-based, "hacking", cyberpunk, real-life coding, mud, social, sandbox, etc, then you probably are going to have a hard time enjoying this game. If any of those perk your ears up, or you're used to working with a command line though, please read on :-)
I broke out of the "vlan" (tutorial zone) yesterday and it was pretty amazing seeing what the game was like outside of the tutorial. The tutorial itself was just challenging enough to gear me up for the rest of the game, but without the hand holding that would have made it pointless. You actually feel like you're being rewarded as you progress through it, and when you finally make it out, you really feel like you've earned your way into the "real" game.
The game developer was there last night congratulating people for making it through and answering some general questions for people, but being exposed to the overall community was pretty awesome in itself.
There's some mechanics that the tutorial certainly doesn't cover, but the game seems to partly be about exploration and playing around until you find something that works, and people are generally nice enough to answer basic questions.
If you want to have your hand held the whole way through a game, this definitely isn't a game for you. Along the way you're going to be expected to brush up your javascript skills, and be willing to spend plenty of time tinkering around until you're able to move ahead.
I haven't been exposed to the upper levels of multiplayer quite yet, but the game ahead of me certainly seems like one I'll have a hard time putting down anytime soon. For the fun I've gotten out of the game so far, I definitely got my moneys worth.
There was another reviewer who mentioned that another player wrote a man page viewer and a lisp interpreter, and he wasn't lying. Those things you can find pretty much as soon as you break out of the vlan. There's tons of potential out there, and as the game matures it's definitely going to take on a life of its own. I can't begin to fathom what kinds of things people are going to write scripts for in this world.
There are some problems with lag and connectivity issues, and the way that you are notified about the issues that seems to get in the way more than anything. I'm hoping those get fixed, but I'm willing to set those issues aside for the time being seeing as how the game just released to the public and there's only one developer working on it.
Pros:
- If you know javascript, or programming in general (I don't really know JS but I've been a C++ developer for several years), you're going to love this game.
- Friendly community
- Challenging Puzzles but not overly frustrating
- Open World, Sandbox to an extreme (you can even access the ingame mongodb from your js)
- Open-Ended, you're not told what to do when you enter MP. You're free to explore and do what you want. (this may be a con to some people, but I really like the fact that I could just sit in a room and chat all day instead of actively playing and nobody will care)
- If you're a fan of MUDs or have enjoyed them in the past, you'll love the way this game plays.
Cons:
- You will need to pick up some javascript skills at some point
- Lag/Connectivity issues, and the annoying red text warning you get flooded with because of server issues
- No documentation for code (The intent may be for the community to fill in this gap, I'm not sure. There are player channels ingame for help on code though)
- No keyboard shortcuts (I would like to see bash shortcuts implemented, ctrl-a, ctrl-u, etc.)
- Non-customizable UI (why can't I resize frames? Is there a way to do this I haven't found yet?)
I'll likely update this review as I progress through the game, but for now I'm ecstatic about it :-)  I've given away several copies to friends already just because I know they're also the kind of people who will like this type of game.

The Raven was a fun game with a good storyline and ending. Some very beautiful elements in the game.
Unfortunately it does lack polish with the pathing - there are moments of frustration where you have to walk away from areas and back again to try to move between scenes, and I did get stuck in an infinite walking circle at one stage from which I could only force quit and reload (thankfully autosave only took me back a couple of mins).
Replayability - you don't learn everything about all the characters until the end, so replaying with that information from the beginning lends a different interpretation to some conversations which is quite fun! There are also some achievements you might not get first round, as there are a few 'event triggering' actions which might make you miss doing something else (not essential for story).
I'd recommend, but probably on special as I'm not sure it's worth full price with the pathing issues.

When you play "The Raven" it feels more like you are reading one of the Agatha Christie novels. And i mean it in a good sense. The gameplay itself is a classical adventure point-and-click, and the riddles aren't that hard either (because they are founded on the real-life logic and reason, unlike some other games where you need to replace the behemoth tooth with a blue parrot so that a UFO will descend to study the new life form so you can steal the screwdriver from little gray man to open the can of beans, ugh).

Personally i percive that game as a good interactive detective novel, and i have a feeling that the authors intended it to be exactly that. In which case they did a good job.  For the fans of the classical XX century detective novels that game would be sitting around 9 out of 10, for others though it may feel kinda slow and boring. But you would not buy an adventure game with the title like "legacy of the master thief" if you are not a detective fan anyway, right? So rest assured the game will keep you entertained for a few evenings and good luck discovering the true face of the Raven.

Social Justice Warriors is when you take the whole progressive keyboard warrior scene to its over-the-top and quirky conclusion. Hilariously enough, several of the dialogues between the warriors and the trolls are nostalgic to me, reminding me of the heated discussions and shitflings I've been present at. This is essentially internet arguments the video game, and just like its real-life counterpart it's only a real joy in small doses.
If you're a general leftist, feminist or SJW, this game will likely be in your alley. It's not big, expansive or thought-provoking, but it's a fun yet quirky achievement-hunting game that puts YOU in the role of heroes fighting against the dastardly trolls.
That said, the game doesn't seem to explain or give tips how you can maintain your "sanity" and "reputation" in the best ways possible, but I suppose that's something we as the players ought to learn as we hone our skills with the keyboard.

Social Justice Warriors is a bit of a clunky game, not always clear to new players, and at times, blatantly unfair. So as a playable version of internet arguments, 10/10, extremely realistic. But there's a whole lot more to this game than you can tell from screenshots and comments.
For starters, despite playing as an SJW and battling a variety of trolls, the game doesn't pick a side as much as you'd think. Yes, the narration describes you as a valiant force of good against internet ne'er-do-wells, but it's so over the top at times that it's clearly not expecting to be taken completely seriously.
The actual depiction of the trolls does a lot to help the balance. While they're helpfully labelled 'Rabid Troll' or 'Popular Troll', they actually look just like you, an ambiguously-sprited person tapping away at a keyboard. And your actions in, erm, 'battle', can sometimes mirror their's, since you have the option to always try to maintain the moral high ground, or lose your patience (and reputation) and start mudslinging.
There's a lot of variety in the game. You can choose four different classes, each with unique play-styles that coincide with different areas on the internet. The Paladin uses Twitter, the Cleric uses Reddit, and so on and so forth. And each has a multitude of choices in conflicts. Try to logically defeat the troll, or wreck their reputation until nobody takes them seriously, or take a second to regain your composure. Each of these choices has their own impact on your own Sanity and Reputation, which act as dual-health bars.
That's not to say the game plays fair, at all. My biggest complaint is the amount of sheer randomness you can encounter if things don't go your way. If your sanity or reputation ever get too high, any troll can instantly use a powerful attack and wreck them. A rumour or exposed phone number, and you're back to square one. If left alone, they'll call upon the dark forces of the web, and even though they'll occasionally get a reassuring answer of 'NOT YOUR PERSONAL ARMY', you stand the risk of total online annihilation. And every once in a while they just completely disregard any move you make. It's not a very consistent game to play.
But the game puts a message above the gameplay, and the message is good. If you somehow managed to get high sanity/reputation, you transform into the Social Justice Champion (yes, I cringed a little writing that,) and how does this mighty warrior fight their battles? Well, all your combat options are replaced with things like 'Listen to their concerns', 'Defend opponent from attackers' and 'Propose a compromise', and the goal changes from 'Try to ruin the troll' to 'Acknowledge their point of view and try to raise their sanity/reputation until they no longer feel the need to argue with you. I don't see how anyone who isn't a genuine troll can't see this as a pretty good message to portray in what I expected to be a silly game about internet fights.
In short, it's not an incredible game, but as a representation of arguments on the internet, it's accurate in a way that's comedic but not shallow. Plus, if you took one glance at the game, decided it was 'pro-SJW propaganda' and immediately started frothing at the mouth, thank you for confirming on a slightly meta level just how accurate the game can be.

Despite looking rather gimmicky, Social Justice Warriors is a surprisingly deep game in terms of its themes and execution, and the gameplay is fun for a short while. Granted it can get repetitive a bit quickly but it still makes for a fun casual title.

No More Room In Hell is a post-apocalyptic FPS (first person shooter) with good enough graphics, teamwork depending on who you play with, and personally I think its a great game. The zombies move and react in ways that they would act in most various cases such as; the walking dead or dead rising. Not having special types of zombies and only having them in certain parts (like Left 4 dead) actually suits this game. In my opinion this is one of the most realistic post apocalyptic games I have ever played (in gameplay, strategy and damage effect) in a FPS form. If you like Black Ops: Zombies, or C.O.D Ghosts: Infected, I think you will like this game alot. If you want a more realistic experience or don't like FPS than you should check out Project zomboid which is from third person. Although this game isn't with-out its fare share of bad moments such as unkillable zombies from time to time, or the occasional lag or crash, Its still a exelent game and I encourage you to check it out!

DmC is an absolute blast from start to finish.
FYI:
- I have never played a Devil may cry game before. But I've played enough Action games to know this game is good.
- I bought this for $7.49 on sale, and finished it in about 6ish hours, some of which was logged offline, hence the incorrect playtime. I thought every hour was great.
The standouts here are:
- Buttery smooth action that's easy to get the hang of. Each weapon is really cool, and there are a few. Combos look awesome, and the great thing is, if you have an idea in mind, it's not that hard to pull it off.
- Level design. Now since it's a hack and slash game, you expect the "room full of baddies that you have to kill to open the door" type thing. And just like God of War or Bayonetta, you have that here. What I didn't expect were some truly awesome boss fights and gameplay sections which I won't spoil, but unlike God of War or Bayonetta, these setpieces never rely too heavily on quicktime events. They're just cool.
For the story, I found it was kinda cool, but some people find it kinda crigey at times. I thought the character development was pretty good though. I really like Vergil and Dante's interactions in particular.
So yeah I'd recommend this if you like hack and slash or just action adventure in general. For the more experieced players the hard mode in this game is actually really hard. Good luck.

I don't understand how such a big change like that could allow this game to stay afloat and plummet to rock bottom. Because of that I wonder how the reviews are still positive and even as high as 80%. Can you imagine losing a weeks grinding worth of loot only because you couldn't fend off players while you were offline? Sure thats what turrets are for, but twig has made exterior placements of those to be useless hasn't it? At least you can use them effectively indoors...
Its very well known how toxic the community is but that's kind of irrelevant in the makings of the game, although because of them its becoming a lot like CS;GO rather than survival-esque gunplay like with The Forest for example. So always expect people to be either good or travelling in groups. So to increase your chances of survival you'll also likely need friends in order not to get KOS'ed and looted completely after possibly hours of grind.
So if you're looking for a survival game you're looking at the wrong game, get The Forest or 7 Days to Die, although they are significantly smaller scale in multiplayer. Max amount of players may be 20 for 7 Days to Die and 8-12 players or so for The Forest in multiplayer. Although if you want a CS:GO-like somewhat survival game and lots of grind then this is for you. I've been checking back on things every few months and I have not been impressed despite the new things that have been added because they never fixed the issues players take with the twig update and some others like recoil or even.
Ultimately from what I've seen the veterans of the game have stopped, the only ones who insist to play are fanboys who refuse to boycott this game for its poor choice of changes to the game and the CS:GO/KOS kids that make up the toxic community. This studio isn't going to heart the interests of those who want a survival game, they want to get these kids that make up the toxic community to use their vast amount of free time to dedicate towards this game while others who work or study haven't got the hours to play this game solo and reliably stand strong and unfazed against raiders and clans especially.
Do also take into account that this game has poor optimization although has had some slight improvements and also the game still has problems that cause memory leaks and ruin the way the game runs. I won't recommend any products of this studio until they change their ways and stop♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off those of the survival community, the ones that they originally intended to sell their products to and made for them to enjoy as a survival game.
I hope this review will urge you from giving this studio your money and you spend your money on more reputable games made by better studios who are actually invested in their respective communities and make their game better through its updates which they determine with your feedback. I personally would insist you pick up The Forest as it is a nice Early Access title which has very decent visuals and survival aspects are spot on. Although if you don't have a beefy computer maybe try 7 Days to Die as I believe it doesn't require as much as The Forest does.
I'll just end this review here and move on with other things. Peace out!

The game features two parts. The vLAN and the M.U.D. The vLAN is where you start, being the singleplayer part of the game that also doubles as a preparation for the M.U.D, taking roughly 4 hours, give or take, but the story is alright and sure to keep you plugged it!
Once you're out of the vLAN, you migrate into the M.U.D. (Multi User Domain) which is the multiplayer and main focus of the game!
Here you are allowed to do whatever you want! From figuring out puzzles in order to attack NPCs and steal their GC, to writing scripts using Javascript and running them ingame, contributing to the usermade content, to simply just chatting around with strangers, future allies/enemies!
Most of the game's core mechanic regarding breaching relies on the player figuring out puzzles in order to unlock the NPC/Player locs to breach their system.
The scripts you have equipped determine what your class is. Currently there are 4 main classes in the game: Infiltrator (Show player access logs, transactions logs, balance, etc); Scavenger (Steal their GC, upgrades etc); Architect (More characters per script, more script slots, more public script slots) and Executive (unsure yet, but it's related to the corporations/clans you can make)
Scripting knowledge is not required in order to enjoy Hackmud, but it sure does help to know some. With time and some help from the players, it will become increasingly easier for you to start writing your own scripts and build future tools for the community to use!
+ Great and fitting soundtrack
+ Friendly community
+ Freedom to play the game in your style
+ Lovely UI (if you enjoy terminal-like UIs that is!)
+ Cooperative gameplay and PvP is a possibility
+ Neat blend of tutorial and singleplayer experience

This is a mediocre adventure game, with uninteresting characters and an uncompelling plot.  The only thing it has going for it is that it has an Agatha Christie athmosphere, though the similarities are a tad over the top.
I found the characters to be bland and uninteresting most of the time, with slow and tedious dialogue... I constantly found myself thinking "Get to the bloody point" while going through the dialogue options.  The plot was rather predictable and very cliché.  The final plot twist was over the top and felt "forced".  What I DID like about the story is that each chapter shows parts of the same story from different points of view... that was pretty well done.
The game mechanic of having to "look" at an object once, twice or more times before being able to use it, or exhaust all investigative options was not very intuitive.  With this game, they tried to do it differently I guess, but adventure games have worked the same way for a long time and with good reason.  What they intended to be innovative turned out to be counter intuitive and frankly not fun to play.  The fact that some of the steam achievements are linked to clicking on everything until you've exhausted all possible clickable hotspots, is quite ridiculous.
It's not a polished title either.  On three occasions I had to restart the game and replay part of the story because my character had gotten stuck in an animation loop.  Luckily I picked this game up at a considerable discount, so I wasn't that upset with it.
I would not recommend this game to anyone.

I sighed loudly, fogging up the visor of my space helmet. "Welp, lost again, I guess". I looked around in a half hearted attempt to find the beacon of my base. I knew it was a vain effort. I had been traveling in a straight line for so long I was sure I had left it behind a couple horizons ago. Even though I had tried to make a note of my bearing and take the geological features into consideration, there's so many mountainsides one can go past until they start looking the same, and my rover flipping every so often due to treacherous outcroppings and hidden canyons didn't help matters one bit. Even if I headed in the right direction back home who knows if I wouldn't overshoot the base by a dozen kilometers. Besides I had already gone in circles enough, trying to find the few elusive blueprints I was missing to build a spaceship, and to my credit I had eventually found them, albeit getting lost in the process. As my rover's batteries died out, I looked into the horizon. The view was certainly majestic, if weirdly polygonal. Artsy, even.
Things weren't that bad, though. Because even though I was lost as a lamb, this time I was counting on it. This time I was on a Landmaster.
Even though I couldn't take credit for the Landmaster's modular attachment system which allows attaching anything into the Lego-like pegs on any building and the backpack with total flexibility, the choice of equipment was if I'm allowed to say so, quite superb. Not only it had a cargo bay and two spaces for heavy loads, it also was equipped with a habitat that doubled as a shelter in case of storm but most importantly, could be used as the foundation for a base or outpost. I chose a spot near a canyon that opened into a vast cavern system, took it off it's mount, and got to work.
The first order of work was to make a bridge over the canyon to allow passing over it. I whipped out the terrain modification gun and using the power supply on the rover I built it in a matter of minutes.
After crossing it, I quickly loaded up with some nearby deposits of Compound and Resin and set up some basic production facilities: first a smelter, and after processing some nearby metals, a printer, a fuel condenser and a vehicle bay. Before long, I had a fully functioning space garage, and built myself a shuttle.
As the shuttle lifted itself into orbit with a steady hiss and the gravity disappeared under my feet I started scouring for the beacon of my base camp below me. I looked up, however, and saw the planets crossing the horizon. "Arid", "Desert", "Exotic". All full of mysteries and danger awaiting for me, and with a bit of luck, valuable salvage and rare materials.
As the shuttle descended into the base camp, I hurried towards the research station. Crossed my fingers as the analysis came through, and shortly, I got my report.
"Good", I said to myself. "There's too many planets out there to waste time running around in just one of them".
TL;DR, for a pre-alpha this game is pretty solid and the content is nice, too. It's a pretty game, but mechanically is intriguing enough to keep you playing for about 10-20 hours. I'd recommend it if you like exploration and light survival without much pressure. 8/10.

In Borderlands 2, every action is theoretically fun. The game is one for people who like shooting things, collecting random drops, and running around aimlessly in the wacky and low-detail world of Pandora. But what if none of those actions are inherently fun to you? I'm someone who greatly enjoys shooting a virtual someone in their virtual face--but in Borderlands 2, even that most base of visceral action rewards begins to diminish, because you do it SO MUCH. You do it literally non-stop. And when the enemies are the same, over and over, providing no real challenge unless it's a conflation of poor level design and a particular encounter that burns thru every bit of your money rezing yourself. The quest design is a deplorably transparent Skinner Box, with the metaphorical carrot-on-a-stick moved every time you're about to get it: because more quest objectives means more gameplay! Every design decision in Borderlands 2 seems made with this in mind. Make the player run through the same banal area three times in the same quest? Gameplay! Detect the player's primary weapon, then give them five guns in a row that are worse than their current one? Gameplay! Collect twenty of anything? Gameplay! Sell guns to buy guns to sell to buy guns to sell to buy guns to sell to buy... gameplay!
Borderlands 2 is an experience of pure nihilism. I recommend it to no one who wishes to have a value system of any kind.

, which is another hacking simulation game, an old MUD and rogue/nethack player, and as a terminal nerd, I have always wanted more of these types of games. I have ran into a few, but they were very poorly done. Hacker Evolution, for example, was very boring and not challenging at all and the interface is extremely unsettling. It also teaches you too much. None of them kept me interested for more than a couple of hours.
Yesterday on the 21st, I ran across this game called h a c k m u d on Steam and decided to watch the trailer. I was immediately impressed with the level of detail. The ANSI coloring, the interface, the font choice, and the music, all hit the right buttons and I decided to buy it when it came out. I was so excited I actually paid for it at work and had to wait to play it until when I got home. I was THAT impressed with the trailer. I was ready to part with $13.37 so quickly and get home and I was doing piles of work just to make time pass that much quicker. But was it worth it?
After a small installation of only 74mb which went smoothly I opened the game, created my users, and verifed my users all while jamming to some great engaging music. The game did a really amazing job at teaching me and also ensuring that I had exactly what I needed to know. And then the story started. WAIT, THIS GAME HAS A STORY? Yes! Honestly, I have never played a hacking sim with a story other than "hack this, make money, upgrade, repeat", yet here was h a c k m u d making me engage with AI to learn more about them and have them help guide me and get me going. I am very, very impressed by this, as this is a first to me.
After gaining access to a few things, which required some clever thinking with a few well-thought-out hints provided, I was accepted into a group of other AI hackers and learned that they are trying to escape the vLAN with the guidance of an AI guru known as Faythe, but can't because of a corrupt AI named Mallory. With a goal of breaking through the firewall without her stopping us, I am ready to start making progress toward escaping. This is plot. In a hacking game. There is even a villain. What am I playing and why can't I stop?
So here I am, I am currently around an hour in, with absolutely zero plans of stopping. I know this review may come off as biased because this game seems like it was created to appeal to me directly, but I can not give this game enough praise and I don't even know how long it is or where this plot is going to take me. The only bad two things I can say about this game is that it does have a bit of a learning curve but as stated before, everything you need to know is taught to you and the game gives you lots of hints as to how to progess. Additionally, it's a hacking game, so obviously you have to figure some things out on your own. However, at no point have I been stumped really, or felt the need to quit and come back later. The other issue is the error messages when failing to stay connected to the server. However, what game isn't without launch day bugs? I'm sure they will be fixed in time.
In conclusion, The presentation is beautiful with ANSI colors in the terminal, a chat log, and a scratch pad for your notes. The music is engaging, the story and plot thus far have been basic but actually there unlike other hacking sims, and the challenges are fun. The AI characters all have their own personalities and it seems like they have backstories as well. The game so far is riddled with computer science jokes and I love that it has a sense of humor about itself.
I score this game 9/10.
A huge applause to Grizzley Bear for taking an older genre and giving it a huge facelift and some very creative writing. I plan on spending many a night in this game. Thank you, as this entire creation is like a love letter to me.
UPDATE! - Yes, the game is 100% multiplayer after a certain point, and I'm still liking it after 4.6 hours.

The Raven - Legacy of A Master Thief is an adventure game from King Art, the makers of "The Book of Unwritten Tales". I feel the biggest strength of the game rests in the narrative. If you enjoy mysteries or detective work, or just point and click adventures you may enjoy this game. The narrative starts strong with well developed characters and strongly written dialogue, and continues to be strong throught chapters one and two. Unfortunately, I feel the last half of the final chapter is handled clumsily from combined narrative and gameplay standpoint and as a result the ending is underwhelming. I have no problems with with the story itself, but rather the way all player agency was removed in the final portion of the game.
Still this is about 5 minutes of a game I spent many hours on, so in the overall perspective the rest of the hours were spent with good logical puzzles, conversations, voicework, and narrative.
The only real draw back I had to the game I discovered was with navigation between scenes, especially in the first chapter on train and one particular screen on the ship. It was not a problem in the other two chapters. However in either the end of chapter 2 or beginning of chapter 3 I had issues with the character walking in place for several seconds before completing and action. This happened several times. The screen navigation issue can be frustrating at times so be aware that it takes some getting the hang of but does improve. The second did not influence my opinion and may have been a unique bug.
I own the digital deluxe edition. The value in the that will depend on wethere or not you want the soundtrack. The making of book is good for a read, King Art clearly puts time and love into their adventure games as seen with both this and the series of "The Book of Unwritten Tales" games. There is not much to the story books, and nothing that is not revealed in game in one form or another.
I'm a big fan of adventure games, but this game runs into all the pitfalls of the genre.  A plodding, clumsy story, and arbitrary, poorly communicated puzzles. You can safely skip.

The Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief is a beautiful point-and-click adventure narrat much like a crime novel. I like that bit of meta narration as the chase of the Raven is compared to a crime novel by characters in the game - without actually breaking the 4th wall.
The game is divided into three chapters each concluded with a mayor revelation
. By my estimate the first chapter is the longest and subjectively most likeable, though I still enjoyed the other two as well.
The first chapter started with a tranquility rare to adventures and generally provided a feel-good atmosphere by transporting the joy of a luxurious train ride with careful lighting and well voice-acted, immediately believable characters only gradually giving tasks to the player to fullfil and progress.
We start to control the older, not elderly, Constable Anton Jakob Zellner, overseeing the train that also carries Inspector Legrande famous for ending the Raven's previous career. Legrande doesn't want our help, so we have to convince him of our usefulness and the story starts to unravel.
As said before, the voice acting is very good and characters believable. Oddities make sense after time and characters exhibit a few nice quirks. I particularly like "I am the god of fire." & Zellner's reaction to getting the pills back.
The narrative has some subtle hints as to the story development
.
After each chapter you are evaluated. You collect points by progressing in the game or finding secrets and lose points for calling on hints.
There are good things and a few problems with game mechanics and their and other inconsistencies.
The game crashed a few times when I alt-tabbed out of the game menu and didn't alt-tabbed back in right away.
The game offers fast-forwarding for dialogue, i.e. each left-click skips the part of dialogue currently spoken to the extent of the current subtitle. That way you can adjust communication speed to your reading speed if you want to. And subtitles are almost always spot-on. There must have been some mayor confusions about how to write Captain DiConti's name.
Communication and physiological interaction among characters is well separated, avoiding bugging out while still keeping very good flow.
One problem I found with dialogue is, you cannot access the game menu, as you would otherwise, via the ESC key or the icon on the top right of the screen.
The game seems to differentiate between views, like camera angles, of a single room (a room being a collection of views rather than strictly interior) and views of different rooms, i.e. transition between the former is seamless while the latter require loading. In case loading is required the mouse cursor transforms into a door handle. But transition between views of a single room are not hinted. You have to "go there" to see if another camera angle is available.
My machine makes loading a task no shorter than 15 seconds - in case the room wasn't loaded for a while easily twice that. This meant travelling between rooms far apart was somewhat unnerving for me and I actually started doing other stuff while loading. This also led to me letting the game run when I got distracted by whatever other thing I started. Now I have to guess the actual length of the game since it is too long to simply play through again - which I surely will do in time. So I'd guess the game takes between 15 and 25 hours.
Apropos transition, there is a single puzzle (
) in the game which is missing any door-handle icon area. You may only leave the puzzle screen by solving it or pressing escape - a strange decision for an otherwise completely mouse-driven game.
That puzzle may also introduce a continuity error. You're supposed to get a translation for an inscription in order to solve the puzzle. If you brute-force the mere 512 combinations the game assumes you got the translation and evidences as much in the your journal.
When switching rooms the game mostly offers fast-travel, i.e. clicking again will skip the walking animation and directly trigger loading. This, however, doesn't work with all transistion. Usually I'd suspect in-scene triggers but I don't remember any here.
Whenever a game doesn't employ seamless loading but opts for loading times instead I'd want to have a map available to skip artificially necessary loading times of intermediate rooms. There is no game area map and no map-travel in this game, pity.
Sometimes the game cannot figure out how to walk a character from A to B, it then chooses any available walking animation and finalizes it by popping the character to where it needs to go. Walking to non-objects may result in the character endlessly walking into a wall. Interaction with an object close-by but not in direct line of sight may result in 270° turns.
The first chapter features what I'd call axe-hand and pole-hand named after two items the character is supposed to hold. Any subsequent interaction not including the axe or pole makes axe or pole merge with your hand or wrist perpendicular to your lower arm. Fortunately, this is only a glitch and the items may still be used.
I don't like the inventory dropping away right after selecting an item. It makes checking for item combination a hassle.
For some reason the game is mainly English for me but some assets and textures are German like a newspaper you collect. This newspaper is peculiar in two ways. It has as running text, instead of lorem ipsum, lines from the beginning of Kafka's Metamorposis. It also seems to an Early Edition, i.e. as a July 1963 newspaper it features articles concerning 1964 events like Cleopatra's Oscar award and Surtee being a Formula 1 world champion. English version has Oct 1964 MLK Nobel peace price.
The guard room in the museum has two calendars from 1962. Possible but odd for a museum that hasn't "spared any expenses".
It doesn't sit well with me that the stowaway is labeled "The Arab" even after he has given his name. This is presumptuous and no more descriptive than "Young Man" would have been.

In the extras, it takes some time for a song to start. Red means it is about to be played.

Better than average point and click adventure game. The puzzles are logical (for the most part) and make sense in the game world, but somehow often felt mechanical and uninteresting. It rarely felt rewarding to figure anything out.
The story is where the game shines though. It's clearly an homage to Agatha Christie and made by people who genuinely are fans of that style of mystery. It will seem a bit dull at first, but there's a brilliant twist about half way through the game that will make you reexamine everything you think you've seen up to that point. There's a second twist at the very end that is much less brilliant and, while clearly intended from the beginning, is much less clever than the designers seem to think. Still, it wasn't enough to ruin it for me.
Ultimately, if you like adventure games this is worth your time.

I'm writing my first steam review in 7 years of using steam because of this game. I got Astroneer 3 days ago and already have 25+ hours logged. The game feels a lot like the alpha stages of minecraft. There is huge potential here, and the game already has tons of fun content. The terrain deformation and manipulation is amazing and is hardly ever buggy. The Oxygen and Power mechanics work cleanly as well.
Yes, the game is in pre-alpha. There are a lot of bugs. Multiplayer is unplayable on other planets. Your save file could be corrupted in multiplayer and become unplayable (maybe temporarly). Vehicles sometimes hilariously flip 8 times and launch into the sky never to come back. Despite all that, it's the only thing I wanna do. In addition, the devs are making frequent contact with the community and updating us on whats to come. Just today there was a live stream from a dev making a new discoverable crashed spacecraft. This game already has near the content of No Man's Sky, and it's in pre-alpha.
This game is completely worth your money right now. Considering there will almost definately be a price hike, get this game now before it's $40. In 6 months this game will be the new minecraft if the devs stay on top of their♥♥♥♥♥♥ which I'm convinced they will after scouring the web for all their content and posts.
*LIGHT SPOILERS FOLLOWING*
In terms of content, there are numerous structures, modules, and vehicles to research and build. As people have stated, it wont take you long to see all the buildable things in the game. However, there are also different planets each with different types of resources in different rarities. On Tundra, the ice planet for example, there is lots of rocket fuel just sitting on the surface to be mined. Theres a radiated planet, an arid planet, an exotic planet, and a barren planet (the moon). Each has different plants, trees, terrain, weather patterns, and other unique details. For instance, on the radiated planet, since it's so close to the sun, has faster day night cycles, but its very windy. Easier to use wind power instead of solar. Theres also a pole with constant sunlight. These are just examples of the deeper world behind the content. Its very easy to become immersed and watch hours fly by. Yeah, there's a lack of content, but for pre-alpha the worlds are abosuletly incredable. I cant stop playing this game. Seriously, if you like minecraft or thought NMS would be cool, buy this game, you will not regret it. Okay, back to building my subterranian warehouse..

In this game you control a square and must move it using WASD through a maze, dodging obstacles. You cannot move diagonally, nor can you change the speed at which your square moves through the maze. Once you start moving, you cannot stop, you can only change direction. The levels get increasingly difficult, and if you collide with an object or the wall you must start the level over. It is a simple concept but surprisingly challenging.
It immediately made me think of The Irritating Maze (arcade game from 1997), which itself was based on a Japanese game show. This game is not a clone of that one in any way, but the general concept of the game (moving through a path and avoiding touching anything) is similar and if you liked The Irritating Maze you'll probably like this game, too.
Overall this is a fun game, a casual game that you can play for a few minutes at a time and progressively unlock new levels.

Neat game about hacking NPCs, playing around with a lot of player-made scripts, and - if you want - hacking other players.
Definitely recommended for people who like hacking games, coding, or modded multiplayer worlds.
The main way to do things is through a command line, sort of like how Duskers works. In this case, you play the role of a hacker on a fictionalized '90s-style network, complete with a Hollywood-style "hack mode", as well as simplified-but-realistic hacking. Depending on how you're equipped, you can potentially detect hacking attempts on your own system, and then write a script on the fly (or have an ally write a script) to defend against the attacker :).
You can write scripts to automate a lot of the repetitive tasks, but non-coders should also find things to do in the game (especially as more content gets added by the dev, and by players).
The playerbase is pretty friendly so far, and has created a bunch of useful scripts already. Want in-game documentation? Got a player script for that. Don't like the way the default chat command works? We've got 3 player-made alternatives, or you could write your own if you want!
Also, what other games reward you for writing a password cracker and a lisp interpreter?

I don't usually review games that I play. I also don't usually play multiplayer games. Just not my style.
But ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ is different. It pushes all the right buttons for me.
This game is amazing. At first, ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ might seem simple. There are a decent sized number of puzzles built into the game, enough to keep people busy for a while (and much more to come on that front), but what makes it special to me is the interaction with other players. We can write our own puzzles, for others to solve.
And that is just the beginning. We can write games within the game. Plan and execute heists on rivals. Defend against determined attackers. And so on. If something is missing, someone with the scripting chops can write it. We needed documentation, and rather than setting up a wiki, I wrote an in-game man-page viewer. We wanted persistent notifications, so someone wrote an in-game "email" client. There are competing chat clients, each tailored to their creator's particular mindset, and we welcome more from new creators. We even have two interpreted languages written in the game, a LISP and a high-level JS-based assembly language (yes, those words all just occurred in the same sentence. I know). Why? Because we could.
And that, to me, is where the most fun is. The scripting. And that is why the core simplicity is so useful. We have the basic building blocks to do what we need to do. But we get to write the rest, to combine those blocks in new and interesting ways. And the excellent thing is, everyone thinks differently, so what seems like an obvious need to one person is something someone else wouldn't have ever thought of, but can still benefit from once it gets written.
If you enjoy writing scripts, you will love this game.
But what if you don't? Or what if you are new to programming, or never even tried? No problem. You can do virtually everything without scripting, and there are several friendly veterans who are always willing to help people out. There is plenty of content now to keep things interesting, and more is being added -- by players and the dev -- over time. And if you wish there was a script that scratched a particular itch, just ask. Maybe one of us vets will write it for you. Or if you'd prefer, we'll teach you how to write it. As ways to learn JavaScript go, I can't think of any way more fun than this!
