For those of you unfamiliar with this type of game what happens is you send troops down a lane and the enemy send them up the lane. Reach the other side and you typically win. There are about a hundred of these games so if you've heard this all before you probabaly know what to expect.

This game mixes that formula up because the closer you get to the enemy base the more damage you automatically inflict, this means that wiping out every enemy is more important than wiping out enemy units that can snipe at range. Its actually a good idea in all honesty as it prevents stalemates and defensive builds because you get hurt no matter what.
Oddly however this particular game doesn't seem popular and I can see why. When you have a unit with a range of 3 and it has made the trek across the screen, that range is useless and it adds little to speeding up your enemies demise due to the game mechanics. Its unintuitive for beginners and if you have played these lane games before then its even more unintuitive.
I say give it a try and see if its for you. Its certainly different from other lane games of its type and I did genuinely have fun playing this game but it doesn't have lasting appeal for me and its hard to pin down why that was.
With a friend its intense and frantic fun however against the AI it leaves something to be desired. Against randoms? I couldn't find any to fight! Hopefully you will fare better. No one aspect ruins the game and I do therefore recommend it but bring a friend along is my tip.

One of the best Sonic Games of all time. I played this when the Dreamcast originally was released here in the United Kingdom and was the first game I ever owned for it. I immersed myself within the game immediately, playing it all day, everyday and whenever I could. When I couldn't? I played it in my mind until I could be reunited with it.
Even after all these years, going back to this game has blessed me with the realisation of how enjoyable it was and still is. The game is simple and fast to beat, but everything else a long side the main missions is what makes it a truly epic game. If you truly love playing this game, everything you once knew comes back to you instantly, I don't think there was anything I had forgotten about this game, and there are not many games that give you that experience, proving how enjoyable and entertaining it is.
The soundtrack is the most memorable part of the game and is by far one of the best sound tracks of any game every released in my opinion. If you haven't heard of CRUSH 40 go give them a listen, however I reckon most Sonic fans know who they are and how amazing their work is. Sure there are some bugs here and there that were in the Dreamcast and Gamecube versions but it's a small price for how nostalgic and great this game is and was for it's time.
All characters have good and cross-weaving storylines that inevitably come together at the end to defeat the 'Ultimate Evil', ignorantly created by the infamous Dr.Eggman.
On the side there is cart racing, and the amazing Chao gardens. Chao are little baby creatures that live peacefully with humans and can morph and gain stats in strength, run, flight etc...and can then be put into Chao races. Once you've completed the game and done what you can, you'll probably find yourself here a lot, as the Chao are just literally the best god damn things ever.
If you haven't played Sonic Adventure/SADX, then I suggest you should. It is by far one of the best games of the Sonic Franchise.

I'm in two minds about The Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief. The first episode and a half you follow Anton Zellner, an aging Swiss Police Officer trying to impress the Super Detective Legrand by helping him catch the Master Thief Raven. Zellner is a very pleasant character to follow (a welcome deviation from the usual 20 something point and click character), the voice acting is well-done, the music and settings very nice (some odd glitches here and there, but nothing major).
The puzzles are very simplistic, but mostly make sense. Since the storyline and the characters were interesting, I did not really care that the puzzles were so easy. An easy going game with a nice story I thought.
In the middle of the second episode you switch character and from there onwards the game loses steam. You play the same story, but from a different perspective. Unfortunately, this new perspective brings very little flavour to the story, and the simple puzzles suddenly seemed very tedious without any real story progression. Throw in a few “use the item two times for it to work even though the character gives no indication that would be the case” just to add to the frustration.
By the end I was bored by the game... but I persevered because I did want to know how the story ended. Rarely have I been so disappointed. The ending is just… so bad… so so bad. I really don’t think they could have managed to come up with a worse one without involving dinosaurs or robot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
So in conclusion; I really enjoyed the first one and a half episodes of The Raven and that’s why I’m still recommending it (if you can get it in a sale). But frankly, if you start getting bored after starting on the other half of the game, just quit. It doesn’t get better and the end is not worth playing the rest. Personally it makes me wary of episodic games in general. Well-presented, witty and of considerable length, The Raven: Legacy of a Master Thief is definitely worth playing for fans of the Sierra/Lucasarts style adventure game.
There's not a whole lot to explain here: Like just about every point-and-click adventure, gameplay involves a lot of pointing and clicking, waiting as something happens, and then pointing and clicking some more. There are some light puzzles, none of which I found very complicated (old hands at these types of games will have no trouble breezing through it), and a bit of mid-game twisty-turny stuff that I wasn't expecting, but otherwise there aren't a great deal of surprises here. Still, the story is what counts in an adventure game, and this one -- mostly a tribute to the works of Agatha Christie -- is pretty decent. I'm fairly gullible, so the few twists that popped up genuinely surprised me, which was nice, as was the ending. I'll never write The Raven down on a list of the greatest adventure games or anything, but it was worth my time.

To anyone who played Sonic Adventure on Dreamcast, this is the game you are looking for. There have been a number of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ remakes on the game cube, but now you can have the original beautiful sonic with sandbox play. It is a bit liear and the storyline jumps around a bit, but I'm pretty sure they were trying to divide it between the characters. At any rate, this is a brilliant game, and it's fun.

The real question you should be asking yourself before you purchase this game: Has it aged well?
The answer: NO.
To be honest, I first played Sonic Adventure on the gamecube. No dreamcast here, I didn't even know the game was a thing until I bought it on the gamecube and thought it was awful. Only after playing through half of it originally did I learn it was actually an older game ported and ""remastered"" for the gamecube, and then I excused it for some of it's faults. But in 201X, there's really no reason at all to play this game unless you are either a die hard fan of sonic/sonic adventure or you want to see a historical game showcasing where sonic started to go wrong.
What is wrong with this game?
-Awful Camera: The game's camera is bipolar and will sometimes be really nice to you and show you everything you need to see or jitter around and clip through the ground essentially putting your life in the hands of the level design
-Level Design: Speaking of level design, it's bad. There are multiple paths to get where you want to go which is nice, but there are so many instances of the game giving you massive speed boosts only to stop you 5 feet later, or worse- kill you. It seems like the developers couldn't decide if they wanted you to go fast like traditional sonic games, or to make a slow platforming adventure.
-Controls: Slippery and too fast. See level design. Play the Egg Carrier stage as sonic and cry as the controls rapidly change as the camera goes all over the place.
-Big the Cat Stages: Even people who love this game can't defend these.
Despite all this, not all is bad. Some of the levels are legitimately cool, I enjoyed the beach, casino, and temple levels very much. The ring dash is satisfying, and with upgrades, isn't annoying to use. Some characters here are really interesting, and while the robot isn't all that fun to play it's interesting to see a mech that has a machine gun in a sonic game.
TL;DR: Don't bother buying unless you're buying it for like 1 dollar or you're a huge fan of the game

I nominated this game in the steam awards for the "Beyond Description" award because truly, it's hard to describe rust.
I once had a friend try it and I learnt how confusing it must be for a new person to try it.
In Rust your ultimate goal is to survive, but how you do that is up to you.
You can build the biggest baddest base to try and directly confront any oppositions.
Or maybe you could hunker up in a small base you hid deep in a forest and hide from any enemies.
Maybe you're a hoarder and want the best loot possible so nobody dares to attack you.
You could live life peacefully as a community person, wandering the wasteland naked, speaking to any fellow survivors in the hopes your head remains afterwards.
And when the strategy you chose inevitably fails, you learn from your mistakes and start your experience anew, trying a new strategy or expanding on your last.
My point is, Rust is a game about learning and mastering and that's just my way of saying how much i love this game
Graphics | 8/10 | Graphics look great up close but the lod distance max isn't very high
- Note, optimization in this game is quite poor and the server you choose also impacts it differently
Gameplay | 10/10 | Diverse experiences, easy to get into, hard to master, Fun combat that requires skill AND fortune
- Note, every update changes gameplay in some form making it hard to review.
Replayability | 10/10 | With devellopers constantly tweaking, adding and fixing things in the game you can't help but start your experience anew.
Final Verdict:  9.5/10 Fun for people who enjoy difficult to master games.

If you're a fan of rewarding experiences due to challenging levels and intense game play, then pick this title up.  I cannot sing enough praises of this game.  I absolutely love this game.  There is a love/hate relationship though...as in; I hate how frustrated I get playing it, but I'll be damned if it isn't spot on.
Controls: Tight controls that are worth every ounce of effort put into them.  Think you're jumping too high?  Probably are from holding the button/key too long. (I hope you're not using a keyboard!)
Graphics: Throw back graphics that due the game justice as it isn't a "find this on the screen" type objective.  The graphics work.
Sound: GREAT MUSIC!  Holy crap the music  never gets old, and the sound effects are great...even when your meat goes "squish*
Overall: I'd have to stem a rating of about 9.5/10.  I can't say it's perfect, but damn if it isn't close.  I've bought this game 6 times (twice for myself - 360 and Steam, and 4 copies for friends.) that is how much I enjoy the crap out of this game.
You WILL be challenged, and you CAN get through the levels through patience and skill.  Timing is key, and how high you jump is also a factor.  For even more variation of play, play with a friend and hot seat levels you get stuck on. You'll see how they are trying to get through the levels and how you might try something different.  There isn't always just 1 single way to get through a level (at least early on...later levels there are  much less options for completion)
Go get this game!

Most of the cons were just nitpicks but as a huge DMC fan, it's a big deal. Get this on a sale or something. I'll keep raging at DMC 4.

The first half of this game was good. Chapter 1 was excellent. You started to learn aboout the characters and a real mystery was being developed. It was one of the funnest adventure games I've ever played, until about the middle of Chapter 2. I don't want to spoil it, but there is a massive cliffhanger that completely stops the story's progression and makes you play everything again from the villain's perspective for the rest of the chapter. This isn't such a bad thing, in fact it was pretty interesting, but playing as Constable Zellner for 1.5 out of 3 chapters so far and then playing as some other character for the next half of the chapter severed me from the game's flow. Also, the story didn't go any further because of the sudden stop when being Constable Zellner. As this new character I had to explore the same areas that I already did with Zellner, which was a little boring. Then, in Chapter 3, you continue playing as yet another character in addition to the second character for the rest of the game. It was very dissapointing that I could no longer be the character I started with. I was just re-exploring areas I already explored, which was quite boring. That cliffhanger from the middle of chapter 2 that seemed like it was the middle of the story, nothing ever progressed past that point. Once the point was got to, there was a horrible ending that completely contradicts a lot of the things that you've done before and a lot of the conversations you had. I am not going to spoil it, but the ending ruined the game.

I enjoyed that he was over the hill, going to seed and losing his hair.  Reminded me of Miss Marple series where due to outward appearances the hero is often underestimated and overlooked.   The landscape graphics were well done, some shots on the ship were really lovely.  The puzzles were simple but as I said, it wasnt necessary to have complex puzzles due to the story and attachment you make with the lead investigator.
all in all well done and would recommend this to any adventure gamer familiar with this style of game, fps and adrenalin addicts will not enjoy this slow thinking game

The multiplayer component of Batman: Arkham Origins is no longer operational. The multiplayer was removed on PC but not on console. The price of the PC version has not been lowered to reflect this.
The game itself was a cash grab. An inferior reworking of Arkham City developed without the Involvement of any members of the original Batman team.
Support for the game was dropped very quicky after launch and a patch was never issued to fix these problems.
The framework underlying the combat had to be redone from scratch and the result is that it just feels
, at least to most Arkham City veterans. Basic strikes feel more like beatdowns, enemies will float across the screen to hit you, animations that should be interuptable aren't, enemies will hit you even if you punch them first etc.

There are only a few new gadgets and they are all less useful than the ones they replace. The remote claw could have been great but you were too limited as to where you could use it. Shock gloves turned any combat encounter into mashing the strike button, same goes for the puzzles you use them to solve. Glue grenades are reskined freeze grenades.

There are 3 brand new districts added to the map but they are pointless and uninspired, its as if they're just there to add size.The new areas are separated from the rest of the city by a bridge that is as big as a district itself. You must grapnel across this bridge constantly throughout Arkham Origins. you do it in the exact same way each time. The city was reworked so that now there are inaccessable rooftops and ledges that look like they should be grapnel points but aren't. These tall, inaccessable buildings block your path forcing you to go around them. They clutter the landscape and are visually unremarkabe and indistinct from one another.
Previously I would have said "if you finnish Arkham City and you
want more, play Arkham Origins". but now we have Arkham knight and I'm left wondering what role Origins ever served... so, just play Arkham Knight instead.

Yesterday marked the 3rd time I finish the game. I bought it way back in 2013 for the XBOX 360 when it came out. I beat it, then beat new game plus, and then died at the very, very, very last fight in nightmare mode (I believe that's how it's called but it's where you have to beat the game without dying a single time). It was devastating. I never touched the game again. Then we come back to 2017, year where I built my PC and bought the 4 Arkham games (Asylum, City, Knight, and, of course, Origins) because I wanted to play them again.
The game is still more enjoyable with a controller instead of using the keyboard. I also forgot how good the story was, even though I have some complains on a certain character. I just don't like that he always has to be there, all the time. Let me make it clear, I absolutely love this character, but with Batman's villain repertoire, there are so many good villains that are not him that they could have focused but oh no, it's always coming back to him... those who have finished the game know who I am talking about.
Visually, it's not good. Let's face it, Arkham City came out a couple of year before and has better colors, better lightning, more contrast. This one is mainly... blue, and a blurry blue for that. That can be easily corrected with a mod at Nexus Mods so it's not that big of a deal.
The game didn't glitch on me more than once in my +20 hrs of playing it on PC and controls are good so I would say that today, the port is stable and playable.
Overall, it is a great game to play but get it get it when it's on sale, I wouldn't pay $20 for it today.

Overall though, can't recommend unless it's on sale.

I saw "No More Room In Hell" and thought of just another Left 4 Dead clone, I was surely wrong. This game is focused more on defense of an area rather then blazing through hordes of zombies. To me, the game felt a bit slow paced due to the fact of the zombies only stumbling forward rather then running. While the game does encourage you to conserve ammo, I believe it is a bit too strict. If you were to use melee, you only have a choice of a few effective weapons that other survivors most likely already have and will not give up. If melee combat was worth it, the ammo conservation would not be too bad. The gameplay itself isnt too bad, You can do everything you normally could in Left 4 Dead plus a bit more. This includes barricading your location, breaking locks, opening safes with secret codes, and a few others. I personally give this game a 6/10. The melee combat needs improvement, the AI and characters alike can be faster and weapons/ ammo should be spread evenly and plentifully if searched for.

I really enjoyed The Raven: Legacy of a Master Thief, despite some moderate issues gameplay-wise.
First off, this is very much an old school point and click game. For the most part, the player is never in any real danger. That said, it felt really natural playing as Constable Zellner, a sort of wannabe detective who gets involved in a jewel heist case.
The voice acting is quite good in the game, though there's not a huge cast. Across the game’s three chapters, you'll be running into a lot of the same characters and unravelling their personal stories. It was nice hearing varied accents from different characters for a transcontinental trip and while I may not be the best judge of European accents, I felt that the actor portrayals of the characters were some of the best I've heard in recent gameplay. Each actor's performance felt believable and appropriate. Zellner, the rich girl, and the Austrian violinist really stood out to me.
Another positive I can say about the game’s dialogue is that despite the dialogue choices themselves being mostly scripted, I never felt left out of the loop as the player. Any follow up questions I thought up based on something in a conversation, were available to talk about further. I never really had a moment where I was screaming at Zellner for not asking an obvious question.
Puzzle-wise, the game is pretty solid as well. Most of the puzzles involve standard point and click mechanics such as find this, use that, combine this, etc. What sets the puzzles in The Raven apart from other similar games was that they felt very logical and satisfying. Analyzing crime scenes and overcoming obstacles played out in a creative, but sensible way: Need to open a locked car door? Find a wire and jimmy the lock.
I did hit road blocks in a few puzzles for what seemed like unfair reasons. In one instance, I probably spent close to an hour trying to progress because I hadn't click something three times, revealing that I might want to use a specific item. Another time, I got stuck because of a translation issue for one of the puzzle items. Thankfully, these issues were not a huge issue and may have been avoided if I wasn’t playing past midnight.
The puzzles felt best in the game when they required a complex multi-step solution or when the puzzles used a mini-game style solution. I would really like to seen King Art focus on these kinds of puzzles in the future as they were highly memorable.
On the negative end, the game's presentation can feel rushed at times, with pathfinding completely failing at certain points in the game, requiring a restart of the program. Thankfully, there is a decent autosave feature so I never lost much progress, and I only ran into the issue a handful of times.
As far as plot goes, the game was a slight disappointment but still very enjoyable. The first chapter is fairly lengthy and really well done. The second chapter has some strange pacing and cuts away at a dramatic point to restart the game from the thief perspective. The third chapter is almost as good as the first, but felt a little rushed in terms of length and plot twists. The ending to chapter three was enjoyable, but felt a little thrown together, but I honestly feel that way about a lot of crime shows and books as well. Some things simply need to be explained away, rather than making sense I suppose. Overall though, the characters were really well done and it was a fun making the journey with them.
Journeying with Constable Zellner was very amusing and made me feel like I was caught up in an old detective story such as Tintin and the like.
The Raven may not be for everybody, but those who are able to overlook some presentation issues and a slow pace, will find a great story and enjoyable puzzles and dialogue.

Arkham Origins isn't all that great of a game, especially in the Arkham series. Rocksteady's games have been solid, Arkham City was probably among the best games I've ever played, and having Origins as the follow-up was pretty disappointing. Origins is kinda there to fill you in on the beginning of Batman's career, but the story it tries to tell just drags on and is very predictable, mainly due to having played Asylum and City. Character development is actually pretty good, as is the voice acting, but gameplay for the most part feels like a copy paste of Arkham City, as there is barely anything new introduced in Origins. Sure, Warner Bros pretty much nailed the combat system from Rocksteady, but what I mean is that there's absolutely no innovation, they didn't bother fixing details that previous titles got wrong. Gameplay can feel cheap, the map size is pretty big but feels relatively empty and lonely (Gotham is basically a ghost town for some reason), and so much about this game feels repetitive. Boss battles are so long and grindy and have you repeat the same three actions over and over and over x50. The Riddler collectibles have been made even more boring to find, as well as the inclusion of a couple other collectibles that are near impossible to find on your own.
Basically, Warner Bros has created many great characters, they did justice to Batman and the young Joker, but I don't think they wrote the story to their full potential. Skipping this title won't have you missing out on much. If you're planning on playing the whole series, go in order of release, not chronologically.

Famous Japan's action-adventure game, hack and slash "Devil May Cry" series is created, designed by Hideki Kamiya and developed by Capcom Production Studio. Which first release in PS2, PS3 and Xbox 360 on 2001, 2003 continue with Microsoft Window on 2005. Meanwhile, on 2015, the release of Devil May Cry 4@ Special Edition was made incorporation with several productions such as "Ninja Theory", "Valve Corporation" and "Capcom Studio" themselves. However this time, DmC Devil May Cry was fully handed and developed by Ninja Theory.
Yeah I know. Since Devil May Cry is a game developed by Japan. Many may think the latest game also developed by Capcom. But no, it not. However this game still an amazing art of works. It great and even has a decent story.
DmC stories tell Dante's Origin story or past, as he battles with his long-lost brother Vergil to save humanity from Mundus, king of the First Devil May Cry.
There are many weapons that can be use by Dante throughout the game. Players also can play Vergil's character on "Vergil Downfall" but this include as DLC.
Finally, playing this game, the clear differences between this game and other DMC series is the angelic power and demonic power that both obtain by Dante.

While the story was almost the weakest of the DMC titles (DMC2 can burn in a fire) it manages to remain engaging enough to want to finish the game.
Pros
+Gameplay A+ solid and fun.
+Graphics are unique and beautifully rendered
+Interesting and varied enemies/mechanics
+They didn't ruin Dante
+Decent length title
Cons
-With the previous entry in the series, I expected much more from the story
-Stage design, while varied, was uninteresting in its layout
-Traditional DMC humor missing
-Lack of replayability
Truly the fun combat carried the game for me the most. This game is totally fun and definitely worth it. Just dont get your hopes up for an incredibly interesting or engaging story.

I will start by adressing the elephant in the room.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is not only a great experience that everyone can enjoy, but also a masterpiece in its own right. With such a large and active fanbase, the game grew with the help of its community: mods, multiplayer, new skins, trucks, etc., besides the huge amount of content it has been given from the developers. Official content is still being added to the game to the current day, be it in the form of patches, expansions or bug fixes. This makes my first point: buying ETS2 is a smart investment, since the developers truly care about the game and continue to update it and listen to their fanbase. I can make a quick prediction and say that ETS2 will still have updates or expansions coming out for at least a year or two more after the writing of this review.
ETS2 is a truck driving simulator, but not only that. It places you into the position of the manager of an entire international delivery company. The goal of the game, even though most players will just say it's to relax or to have fun (which is also true), is actually to expand your company, hire more drivers, buy more trucks, more garages and obtain the monopoly for deliveries in Europe. The game takes this simple concept and manages to add an astonishing complexity to it (at first sight only, because after the first 20 hours or less in-game, you'll realize that the gameplay is actually simple and enjoyable). As the manager, you can also make deliveries yourself, which is how you will get your company up and running before you have the money to hire drivers to do that for you. You will start by doing quick jobs for various employers, with a truck given by them for the specific delivery, and your first objective is to buy your own truck so you can start taking jobs from the freight market, which get you more income. Once you get your own truck, it's all yours: you need to take good care of it, repairing it, refuelling it, being careful not to get fined for your actions on the road, and so on. From that point onward it is your job to build a strong and succesful business. As you do more deliveries and manage to get more experience (both literally, for leveling up, and figuratively, because you will learn the mechanics of the game better and better), you will earn skill points with each level up. There are a variety of skills to choose from, including getting better pay for different types of jobs (fragile cargo, urgent deliveries, ADR deliveries, valuable cargo), less consumption of fuel, or being able to deliver cargo across longer distances. Your employees also have skills, a feature that on its own opens lots of possibilities for company management.
If the information here or on the store page doesn't quite answer all of your questions, I'll tell you that there is also a demo for this game available to download on Steam so you can try the game out.
Before I start explaining the mechanics of the game, please take note that I'm not a truck driver and have never driven a truck before, so excuse me if I don't have all of my facts straight. From my 90 hours of playing the game at the time of writing this review, I'd say that the driving in this game is absolutely beautiful. First of all, the complexity of the mechanics is fully customizable, so everyone from the newest player to the veteran trucker are able to enjoy the game. The driving is relaxing, be it day or night, rain or sun, highway or forest road, because it doesn't require that much focusing, but only as much as to not pass the speed limit, to avoid other people in traffic and to not come tumbling off the road. That gives you time to enjoy the wonderful scenes you'll pass by, which I'll be talking about in the next section. On-board the truck you have every switch you need, meaning headlights, wipers, the horns (air, regular, light), the handbrake, the toggle for high beams, for the beacon and the turning signals. It has everything you would want and need from a proper simulator of real life driving, so don't expect a truck racing game. The only thing that is a tiny bit more difficult is the parking, but there's also a solution for that. The parking is skippable in every delivery, while denying you a small amount of experience. But as you gather more knowledge and start learning what's what, parking should immediately become a breeze after a few hours of gameplay.
Also, going a little off-topic, you also have a radio. You can upload your own playlist of music into the game and listen to it while on the road. Genius.
, I say.
Do not go into the game expecting it to look like it was made with Unreal Engine 32. The game came out a good amount of time ago (I'd even go as far as to call it a classic now, heh), and I can say it still looks decent to this day. The in-game world still is wonderful if you're willing to sit for a bit and think about how old the game is. Even if it doesn't have the latest graphics, ETS2 doesn't fail to impress, making up for raw graphical power in great world design. The landscapes in the game are beautiful, and the vehicle models still manage to look good and blend into the environment perfectly, giving the game a really special ambiance and relaxing potential. It is easy to get immersed into the massive world and if you're not careful you can lose hours driving your virtual truck around (as it happens to me quite often).
But if I were honest, the question here is how good you
make it look. As I have said before, the game has such an active community, and modders are no exception. There are a variety of graphic mods to choose from both in the Steam Workshop and outside of it that do a wonderful job at enhancing your visual experience, making the game not only graphically impressing, but also making you want to get into the photo mode and snap some shots of your journey through ETS2's Europe.
The short answer would be yes, absolutely. But the answer worthy of this review is that I just spent so many hours into this game, in which everything you basically do, if we were to dumb it down to an extreme level, is drive around and turn left or right at some points, and I can't even explain why exactly. ETS2 just has a mesmerizing atmosphere to it, making the game beautiful in its own way, and being one of the most relaxing games I have and will ever play. Other simulators can't even get near its level (except American Truck Simulator, made by the same developers and based on the same concept), because for me, ETS2 will always have that
, that *something* which always makes me come back to it and do yet another delivery, over and over again. In other words, everything about the game is enjoyable, from the relaxing driving to the sweet feeling of getting another truck or further customzing your current one, to the trance induced by the exquisite feeling of being alone with the road, and for that, Euro Truck Simulator 2 wil always and forever have a special place in my heart.
If you are looking for a relaxing driving experience with various customization options, a variety of trucks, perfect world design, mesmerizing atmosphere and most of all, a detailed company management gameplay component, then I am sure you will not regret buying this game. If you need further convincing, please do download the demo (which is available on Steam).

Hey Gamers,
I want to take a moment and review this game.
So to give you an idea, I have played it all. From Pox Nora to Heartstone. I like Turn Based Strategy, not Real Time Strategy. I like to think of my next move, then respond to my opponents actions.
In this game, this is exactly the case.
The game is like a WW2 style fantasy. I personaly at first didn't like the style, I like my knights, space knights and dragons, but this game wins in the playstyle. The idea is to draw a hand of cards and place units on a battle field. The objective is to destroy the other base by moving troops closer to their base. The closer you get, the more health their base will lose. Mixed in with this, you can attack your opponents units, and his/hers yours. You also get spells and buffs. It gets really tactical, and a game can last from 2 min to 30 min. Every game plays differently because every game is tactically different. A guy with great cards can lose. And a newbie can have a 8-0 streak. It all depends on how much you catch on, learn and adapt.
Yes of course you can pay and buy cards, but that doesn't mean you get a perfect deck. You can still lose if you screw up.
You start with a deck. Every pvp win gets you 100 gold. 450 to buy the cheapest deck. The game has acheivements that give you 100-500 gold. and daily missions can get you 100 to 900 gold. So if you play for fun, you can get a pack easy.
I paid 20 bucks and got 15 packs, and honestly? It got me more into trying different decks, but I am by no means OP.
The game has every day developers online asking the players what we think. what would be better and when you have a problem, they answer you within a minute. I mean ok, the game is a little new, but don't you like the idea of a developer listening to your opinion?
The community is friendly and I made a few friends just talking about other video games or replaying somone because he had a hard start or wanted to see how I played to get better. So the community is mature to say the least.
I know the videogame market is totally saturated and most people don't know which game to download anymore, but I really suggest you give this game a try if you want to play somthing different.

The short answer is that I liked the game. The long answer follows.
It is a point a click adventure that is divided on three chapters. You get to play different characters along the whole game, although I liked the first one the best: Constable Zellner. He reminds me of Detective Culombo. He keeps talking to all suspects, and at the end he gets to know who the guilty is. Although there is no bad decission on the game to make, the player is asked to give out the answers to various crimes. That keeps the game afresh in that you know you might give the wrong answer, even if that does not change the overall story a bit.
The game is slow paced, as with many other point and click games. Even in situations where the player character should be stressed, you can take all the time you want. There is the odd puzzle here and there, and some of the interface might have been done better. At some stage there is a door with washed out glyphs and no clear indication where the right position should be. There is no logical puzzle, like a sliding puzzle. Some people have complained about a single room where it was not obvious how to get outside.
There was one conversation puzzle I did not like, and that is because how far fetched it was. You are given four hints to four artists that should be related to four animals. If somebody asks you about A. Dürer, you probably would then link him to hares. However, the logical explanation given by the game is that Dürer draw some self-portraits, and that one of the most important ones is hanged in Madrid. Madrid then has in the city coat of arms a bear, so it is a bear then. A similar treatment is given to Picasso and Michelangelo. Thankfully, this puzzle is relatively short.
Chapter 3 has showed me some strange artifacts related to the technical side of the game. Pathfinding was not working all the times but the game recovered by moving the character to his or her final destination. Audio effects were also applied wrong and there was this scene where a character was not on the place she should be (player character walks over she!). However, I did not find any serious bug.
There are some things that could have been done better. Let me start with the hint system. You are given thousand adventure points at given plot points. You can then spend hundred points for a hint, many times for things you already did. You can also spend ten points in order to locate all objects you can interact in the room. The problem is that they are made only obvious by a magnifying glass. This hint would not be a problem if the magnifying glass would be more visible and did not disappear so fast. Other games have a more noticeable icon, or at least a bright color that is easy to spot.
The other thing that would need to have been reviewed is the game save system. Both autosave and your manual saves can send you to one or two actions on the past. It is usually not a problem, but it is not expected. I had no corrupted game save or anything like that.
So, in a nutshell, I liked the story far way more than the interface or some of the puzzles.

This game is one great piece of art. The graphic quality is outstanding for the genre, and the visual style perfect for the ambience the game wanted to set. A good adventure game with it's flaws. I found that the well known nordic and Adventure comapny finally put some action into its latest games moving to a mix of Agatha Christie and Homes style gaming.
The games art is good, it's done in a Tin Tin and semi cartoon/ comic style art style, yet real enough not to make you think your actually watching a cartoon; think of games like tourchlight or diablo to get the clay plastic type style of graphics, which I don't really like, but seems many do....so leans more to a novel from the 60s feel, which I guess is the idea of the presentation of the game.
Gameplay is good, has a few pacing issues but moves along alright, puzzles are real enough if fairly simple, don't expect some obscure puzzles that may no sense to the world or having you figure out the direction of statues, which is good but doesn't work your brain much  are basic at best. Sound is ok, i found the the first play area, the train is a bit to loud even when turning  up the voice actors voices. Detail is realistic, what you pick up is what you see, so your not "pocketing" huge items that somehow go into some magic bag that is held in suspension like a star trek transporter, its nice to see the person wearing major objects that wouldn't fit in a picket, eg you expect a wallet to be in the pocket but how can a AXE fit your your pocket, thus in the game it's something you wear.
Story reminds me of Agetha Christie games mixed with secret files Siberia and Lost Horizons, and actually provides stimulating situations without feeling overley static. The notebook updates as you go along and has details of the people, places, and events as they happen, with nice artwork done as if you sketched it, so talking with NPCS about other NPCS will update the details on the other person so you can check out the information, which moves the story along.
Game help comes at a cost of point lost, which tells you how your score is, showing you interactions in classic mode deducts points, the same way asking for hint in objectives book does as well, at a higher cost.
Downers, sadly I do have something negitive to report, the design of the game left out the ability to change scenes well, transitioning scenes via mouse click, most adventure games allow you to change locations by move along  via edge of the monitor , sadly in this game doesn't do that, it changes scenes as you walk to the edge of the screen, which leads to frustration if you play in classic mode, you can select to play with a gamepad that solves this issues as your stick controls the main figure, so you wont be stuck in area transitions, but that comes at a cost of showing you all the interactive parts of the screen, which takes the fun out of hunting for objects since everything is  highlighted. I know they did this because it was released on consoles, but they should have made the right stick the free curser instead of just a object selector, takes the fun out of it, its the same reason I play these type of games eg: Sherlock Homes with the mouse, because I dont want to be told where all the objects are, so thus you either retry to move to areas or you accept being told what to do. A few path finding bugs had me reloading because the person would get stuck walking and break the game.
All and all it was still fun to play, be prepared for a few furstrating click frustrations that are bound to get one or two people stuck thinking there is no further map to progress to when the main lead wont move to the  next area, but the story is decent and the game is entertaining.
Also keep saves as you only have chapter select, so found myself playing half the game to get a trophy I missed out on which is bugged so be warned.

I gave this game a shot when I saw it was on sale. As a person who likes the idea of adventure games, mainly the emphasis on storytelling, I'll be honest and say I am by no means a pro of the genre. Often I find point-and-clicks exhausting and puzzles too farfetched to get any kind of enjoyment out of finding the solution. You won't really have those sorts of problems with this game. The puzzles are not at all challenging, often times with characters flat out telling you what to do with what just by inspecting an item, and many of the solutions can be arrived at by exhausting all your dialogue options. For me, the lack of difficulty was somewhat disappointing, but I appreciate that I was able to keep the plot moving without getting stuck every couple of puzzles or so.
The story itself is entertaining for a majority of the game, a burglary mystery with some murder thrown in, and I enjoyed the fact that you were able to see the sequence of events from multiple character perspectives. The playable characters were likable enough and you are also joined by a cast of quirky side characters who, for the most part, stay with you throughout the playthrough. Sadly, several are rather underutilized. Probably left in just to keep you guessing 'whodunit?' however unlikely their culpability seems. Worst of all, the ending was utterly disappointing for me, so the conclusion may leave you with a sour taste in your mouth.
I really enjoyed most of the game as it has a lot going for it: a charming art style, good music, superb voice acting, and interesting characters but all that gets dragged down by a plot that falls a bit flat in the end. The gameplay itself can be a bit buggy with awkward character animations, but I only had to reload one time, so I hardly noticed. I wouldn't steer anyone away from this game, just don't expect anything too remarkable. Perhaps wait for it to go on sale.

I think as far as Sonic in 3D goes, the first Sonic Adventure got a lot of things right that games after it failed to grasp -- yes, even in the presence of 4 fishing stages. If you've come to think of Sonic in 3D as running quikcly across narrow paths crossing the abyss, you should at least go back over this game. Levels in this game have more variety in their structure, such as Ice Cap's  death-pit-free climb through a circular cave, or the almost Mario 64-like ascent up the Pleasure Castle of Twinkle Park. Part of the reason the levels work as well as they do is that every character has a slightly different way to play. For example: Knuckles' stages are all more open-ended and tend toward larger open spaces, while Tails' stages tend to be more straightforward runs of the faster segments' in Sonic's game. While people who are fans of Sonic mainly from Sonic 3 [& Knuckles] might find these changes in gameplay disappointing, I think they help keep the levels fresh. Since Sonic himself goes through nearly every stage and area on his own (including most of the open areas of Knuckles' game!), it makes completionism a bit less of a grind (although the less said about Big's missions, the better).
That all said, the camera is pretty bad, even now -- and it's probably the reason that the 3D Sonic games after this one tended toward less ambitious level design. This last playthrough I noticed an astounding amount of clipping; I assume this is an issue with the updated version, since while previous versions of the game (i.e., the Dreamcast or 2004 PC versions) didn't have this issue. This is still probably the definitive version of the game. Most of the important graphical effects are here, it runs at a stable 60 FPS on a modern gaming laptop, switching focus doesn't kill the game, and it can run at high-definition resolutions (in a forced 4:3 ratio, admittedly -- but the previous PC release only supported widescreen by cutting off the top and bottom of the screen). The game was rushed a bit to get it out in 1998 before Christmas so the Dreamcast had a killer app, and all versions of the game since (including the bugfixed Dreamcast releases put out for other regions, called the "International Edition" in Japan) have struggled to get a stable game out of it, and even in this recently-patched version many well-documented bugs are still hanging around. On the other hand, it's still probably a more stable game than Donkey Kong 64 -- and supports a wider variety of play interests than "wander around a big map collecting stuff".
Another minor frustration is the lack of cutscenes. While for Sonic's story that doesn't matter much (Sonic's story is defined mostly by the characters around him and he doesn't really develop as a character during it), the other characters all get to be a bit more complex and actually develop as indivduals over the course of the game. Gamma's quest of self-awareness, for example, has a surprisingly tragic end to it for a game about a fast talking blue hedgehog; it's not on the level of a game like Super Mario Galaxy, but it definitely had a lot of thought and heart put into it.
That's basically my summary of the game -- an ambitious but flawed game that definitely had heart in it, before sequel fatigue and shrinking budgets caused the level design to be formulaic and a bit on the bland side. If I were to recommend a 3D Sonic game other than Generations, this would be it.
You'd still do well to check out the Dreamcast release, however, as a few flashy graphical effects courtesy of the console's hardware shading never made it into any of the ports -- Sky Deck in particular has far more dramatic and foreboding lighting and shadows, looking a bit dead in comparison in the DX version. A shame, but these effects are rarely enough to spoil the game; the stable framerate and generally much nicer-looking textures more than make up for it most of the time. (And I suppose a patch to get the proper graphical effect in Sky Deck is not out of the question.)

DmC: Damn (good) music (and) Combat, this is the game other games of its type want to be like. It also has one seriously annoying platforming section and several not very fun bosses, but I hate those things and watched the final boss cutscenes on youtube. The lack of manual saves together with the platforming, my lack of skill with it and other console centric stuff made me less eager to explore, which is something I usually do, as a completionist.
Anyway, the bottom line is that the combat is fun enough to motivate me to get past all the not-fun sections. It's everything I was looking for in the Darksiders games and I actually put off playing DmC, because I didn't enjoy those games as much as I thought I would. I've never been that good at triggering combos in the heat of action, so I usually just went with a few basic moves that I could pull off without trouble. Not very fun, but better than being frustrated at failing again and again when there are so many other "features" in these games that also annoy me.
DmC, however, let's you fight against weaker enemies right until the very last levels, so you can practice new combos against easy opponents and has great controls. This is a game I want to return to just to experience the great melee combat again and that's quite rare.

Long and boring Vietnamese version:
The Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief is a point-n-click adventure game developed by KINGArt (who also made The Book of Unwritten Tales). Player plays as constable Anton Jakob Zellner and follows him on the adventure to reveal the identity of "The Raven", the notorious burglar who successfully stole the ancient "Eyes of the Sphinx". The story isn't so special, but the game managed to tell it through three characters' perspective which is a little bit different and unique. It does have some funny moments and the voice acting is excellent. Some characters are likeable, like Zellner, Patricia, the old lady or the kid; some are designed just to make you want to punch them in the face, like Legrand (uuuugh, I hate that ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) or the piano artist. IMO the story keeps getting better as the game progresses because of plot twist and unexpected moments. It's not so violent or mind-♥♥♥♥ed, but The Raven has its own unique and memorable story (the final twist is illogical, but I can live with it).
I have a love/hate passion with The Raven's gameplay. First, it has old-school point-n-click style with puzzles and some minigames, puzzles are not too hard, but they're enjoyable, minigames keep the game from being repetitive with some fun challenges like lockpicking or playing shuffleboard (Matt is a MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING HAX0R, he's OP as ♥♥♥♥, you'll owe him A LOT of ice creams). However, the game suffers from many technical issues, sometimes the game doesn't allow you to move your character out of a room because it's not shown on the screen, you have to lower the resolution to see it. Camera system is another problem, it only stands still in many angles and rarely follows your character as they move around, environments in the game are sometimes limited, so you will have a hard time moving your character because you'll have no idea where they're heading to.
Graphics are not so impressive, but it isn't bad either, but there are 2 things that irritate me a lot, first, we have the WORST FACIAL EXPRESSION EVER in a video game, I honestly can't tell if Legrand is smiling while subtitle's showing "ha ha ha", female characters don't look good except Patricia. Second, I expected to see more beautiful landscapes and locations, because the story takes place in Paris, I love Paris, I want to see the Eiffel Tower, the Seine river, the Pont des Arts bridge, the Tuileries Garden and the Place Charles de Gaulle,... Do they appear in the game ? Nope. Instead you'll only see a cruise ship, a train and a museum, yay, I'd rather watch "A Monster in Paris" again... Good thing is the soundtrack is great, I'd recommend paying $2 more for the digital deluxe edition, the soundtrack alone is worth it.
The Raven - Legacy of a Master Thief is a good adventure game, recommended for anyone who's looking for a different kind of adventure rather than Daedalic and Telltale's games. For $7.5 it's a steal. 7/10.

I wasn’t excited to play DmC, but I finished the campaign with half a mind to buy the rest of the franchise.
The majority of Hack N’ Slash games are often slapped with the labels of poor story and monotonous mechanics. By appealing to fans of fighting games, the latter is meant to account for the former through overwhelming the player with upgrades and weapon selection. Though DmC doesn’t have the biggest collection of these things, it more than makes up for it with a wildly amusing story and progressive combat mechanics that make every fight as engaging as the last.
With one of the producers having games from the Phoenix Wright series under his belt, I expected nothing less than an unpredictable and overly-dramatic performance. Needless to say, I got what I played for. Dialogue was a mix of overtly eloquent when it needed to be and cringily brash, which fit the characters of the story in their mainly short interactions. This may come off as pretentious, but it just worked really well in terms of how high action the combat and cutscenes appeared. While it played to the notions of how over-the-top it can be, they owned it shamelessly with watchable cutscenes that amazed on the motion capture end of things. The story itself had a basic structure of good versus evil, though it was the characters and overt themes (mind control, consumption, and that kinda stuff) that helped me embrace the rediculousness of it. The game is far from story rich, but the people you meet as Dante and the visually stunning places you’ll go are enough to give the combat a worthwhile purpose.
As you progress throughout the game, you’re given new weapons and abilities. Each weapon or unlockable attack adds another level of depth that makes racking up combos that much more fun. These games are naturally confusing at first, as you’re thrown into the basic movements, then combos, then certain weapons and more combos that you have to mix up with other weapons in the interest of getting more style points. But stick with it - it ultimately comes down to muscle memory, but the variety in enemies and weapons are enough to keep it interesting. It was also nice to see a natural sense of progression from beginning to end.
Some minor nitpicks are that levels do have a tendency to drag. They’re also segmented in a way that can kill the flow of the story. I would have liked to have seen a bit more variety in weapons and enemies, but I’d still have my preferences and mow them all down the same. The soundtrack is phenomenal, and they went out of their way to make it fit the grungy demonic nature of the game.
If you’ve been burned by the boring nature of Hack N’ Slash games, it will definitely restore your faith in the genre. It’s a reboot, too, so you won’t feel like you’re missing anything but the mechanics from previous games. I think playing this game once will be enough on normal for those new to the genre, though gluttons for punishment might want to try the more unforgiving nature of the other difficulties in new game plus. The DLC isn’t a must-get, though many vouch for some of the cool combos that Vergil can pull off.
All in all, if you like the genre and know the franchise, there’s a good chance it’s in your library. If you’re looking to switch up games from the genre’s you’re used to playing, this will be a fun title to pick up in a bundle or on sale that you’ll play from start to finish.
P.S: If you have a controller of anykind, use it. It just makes playing the game that much easier.

This is a game I have a history with. As a Kid I loved it. As a "Cynical Teen" I believed "It didn't hold up very well when I replayed it because the game isn't as good." Then I just basically decided to shut the heck up and rate it based on how fun it is now and not how it was or how it will be.
Gameplay:
This introduced the 3D gameplay of Sonic so you can expect it to be a bit buggy. And yes. It's a bit buggy sometimes but you know it was Sega's first attempt so you can forgive them slightly. There's 6 characters and they all play differently so i'll be rating their gameplays seperately.
Sonic: He plays just like you'd think he would. He has the spin dash and the jump like in the genesis days, but in this game he got a few new powers. He can home into an enemy by jumping twice (Akin to the Flame Shield in Sonic 3) he also has the light speed dash and attack where he can dash through a set of rings and later enemies.
His stages are action packed get to the End. (also if you replay stages a second person can play as Tails like in Sonic 2/3 ^_^. It doesn't help much but it's a nice touch). Almost perfect gameplay. I'm not saying perfect as there's room to improve.
9/10
Tails: He's like Sonic except he doesn't get the Homing Attack or the Light Speed Dash/Attack, but he can fly instead and hit robots with his tails.
Tails' stages are races against Sonic (typically) and you can beat Sonic because there are shortcuts placed that Sonic can't get to. My only gripes with this are.
1. Sonic rubberbands. (meaning the farther you are ahead the faster he goes. he even teleports sometimes.)
2. They are shorter versions of Sonic's stages.
I give it an 8/10
Knuckles: Knuckles plays completley differently. He retains his glide and climb abilties but gains the ability to dig and punch,
His gameplay is spent searching for the emerald shards. There are 3 in every level and you have to find them all.
This version of treasure hunting is REALLY fun. (SA2 ruins it a bit).
I give it an 8/10
Amy: Now this is Amy's first time being playable in the main series.(and the last that I know of until
:C poor amy).
She plays differently to the other characters in that she hits enemies with her hammer and runs away from a badnik named Zero the whole time. (No I don't find this "sexist" because Amy actually fuels the plot and her being kidnapped isn't because "Shes a dainty girl" it's because she fuels the plot.)
Amy gets a small amount of stages so it doesn't drag on too long.
I give her a 7/10
E-102 Gamma:
He pl-... HEY GET OUT OF MY PC! "HES A ROBOT ZOMG HE DOESN'T PLAY LIKE SONIC 0/10 SUX"... anyways yes he doesn't play like any other sonic character to date but IT'S NOT BAD! It's a fun gameplay style and it's different. (I'll go over why I love gamma more in the story section) He shoots enemies to gain time because THE TIMER COUNTS DOWN AND NOT UP! And if it gets to 0 you will die. He plays through missions.
I give him an 8/10
Big:
I don't hate Big. I think his gameplay is out of place but I don't hate him. He fishes. Thats all I have to say.
6/10 (for being out of place.)
Gameplay total: 7.5/10
Story:
Each character has a different story but I'll lump a few sets together because they are related.
Sonic/Tails: They have a story about fighting [s]Dr. Robotnik[/s] Dr. Eggman and they usually stay together.
Knuckles: He's usually on his own finding the emerald shards. Dr. Eggman managed to trick him again.
Amy/E-102 Gamma: Not gonna spoil it but they have an interaction that is great.
Big: He's usually on his own fishing and trying to find his frog Froggy but he finds a few other people along the way.
Rating: 8/10 (if Gamma's story wasn't here it would be an 7/10)
Music:
9/10. Just listen to this soundtrack on Youtube.
Final Score:

This card game is based off another free to play card game of a similar name, March of War.  This game is very well made and well balanced, with the developers actively working to enhance the game, and spending plenty of tiem in the chat talking to the players and taking suggestions.  Unlike some other card games, the only luck is in the unavoidable draw of the cards and cards obtained from packs, the rest is all skill.  An easy PvE mode allows you to get a simple understanding of the game before moving onto PvP.  Currently there are 0 items which require you to spend money.  Everything can be obtained for free.
The concept of March of War is 6 super factions composed of numerous countries are in an eternal alternate WW2 battle to rule the world, using different technologies and weapons unique to each faction.  In Face Off, 2 factions are already incorporated with a third coming up, hopefully for August 2015.  Your choice of factionoverns which cards can be incorporated into your deck.  Additionally decks can be made with completely different strategies, such as focusing on units that buff your other soldiers, or on creating a defense using shield abilities aswell as advancing across the field.  Most card games are fairly simple, but this game allows for in depth strategy with a variety of different unit abilities, and over 200 cartds already in the game.
Sadly the game is not perfect, but what game is?  Purchasing packs of cards can require lots of grinding and may yield frusturatingly poor results, and the game does not yet have a large player base, so PvP can get a bit slow at times.  Fortunately daily objectives and login bonuses are in place to make grinding easier and the game will expand for more players to join PvP, and further updates will improve the game even more.
Overall this is an excellent card game, the first one I've played that has been addictive and fun.  Besides, the game is free, nothing bad can happen if you download it, so give it a try.

This is a very nice CCG with a tactical element that sets it apart from Hearthstone, despite the many similarities otherwise. But for this review, I'll assume you're not familiar with that game or CCGs.
Basically, there are two aspects to Hearhstone: the deckbuilding, and the battles. During deckbuilding, you put together combinations of 30 cards that you will be dealt randomly during the battles. Since you get an increasing amount of resources (called MP) with each turn, you have to make sure you have cards to fit every stage of the battle. You also need to consider how the cards work with each other, and preferably have an overall strategy which your deck will focus on, with contingencies for any setbacks during the battle.
Deckbuilding is where you spend the game's various currencies: gold (earned from daily objectives), gems (bought with real money or gained from referrals) and/or tickets (from destroying cards you don't want). You buy card packs containing a random selection (with gems you can be more specific which faction you'd like out of the 2, soon to be 3 factions), or you craft the cards directly using tickets. The cards come in varying rarity levels, from iron to gold. The rarity level theoretically doesn't mean how powerful the card is, but the rarer ones often have special qualities to set them apart, while sacrificing other aspects. I don't have the experience to know whether the rare golden cards are overpowered or not, but I have had a good time and many wins so far as a free player.
The turn-based battles (always 1vs1) take place on a board where units try to encroach on the enemy's side. The longer they stay in the center or even in the enemy's home, they more damage they do until the enemy's HQ is broken. Different units can attack in different directions and at different ranges, and there are various special abilities. I find the battles really fun and even though the turns tend to be long, they give you plenty to think about even during the opponent's turn. It's never boring as long as you're alertly coming up with plans and contingencies. The board is a little small and I would have liked it to be one more tile wide for more flanking opportunities, but at the same time, the closeness of the spawns to the center of the field makes it absolutely possible to recover from being overrun, or even luring a greedy enemy into an ambush with foresight and luck. The attack directions and the command cards (many of them airstrikes) can keep every match from turning into a slugfest. Despite the narrow front, Breakthroughs are very feasible and rewarding.
There is PVE against bots but progression is hampered there and the devs have said that PVP is the current focus. Still, you can practice as much as you want against the half-decent AI, get some coins, and you can also test fighting against your own deck in a mirror match.
All in all, I'm really enjoying it. Maybe it's the tactical aspect or the awesome setting, maybe the current lack of crazy big spenders plopping down legendaries with mad synergies when you don't even have a rare (looking at you, Hearthstone), but it's the only CCG so far that I've had a consistently good time with.

I don't really remember why I bought Euro Truck Simulator 2. I have never been a fan of simulators but it just happened. Probably I want to see how it is to drive a long vechicle, while I prefer European trucks over American ones. The price and visual part of the game convinced me to buy it.
Graphically, production is not highest quality within today's standards, however it is nice, trucks are detailed and well done (tekstures, reflexes etc.) and there are many picturesque landscapes over the Europe's fields n' roads. Menu is transparent enough and eye candy, what I like in every game. Audio is just adequate. Engines sounds may be better, so do ambient sounds, but they are generally okay.
Game include 7, licensed brands: Scania, DAF, Iveco, Renault, Volvo, MAN, Mercedes, most of them deliver 2 possible models. Handling is good, you could even set such things as braking strenghth and trailer stability factor, it default settings don't meet your requirements. And the truck customization is huge. Starting from setting up your seat, FOV to equiping the car with many accesories, so interior as outise ones. You can literally build your own looking truck using custom paintjobs, accesories, wheel paints etc. but...
... more than half of it is a part of paid DLCs. But wait, I wouldn't point it as a bad thing. It is fun to do, and the prices of such DLCs are quite low (1 to 3 Euro mostly) and they introduce fun things into the game that allow you to paint truck to suit your taste. And they are not obligatory, for me just nice gadget to have and a nod for developers.
What is worth to add, there are thousands of free mods which can be downloaded from over the Internet or (limited amount but still growing up) via Steam worksop. They can modify every aspect of the game and installation is really reasy - using build-in game mod manager. Just several clicks and you are done. I can't tell much about free mods, because I have used only a couple, I prefer original content over fan-made, sometimes unstable mods.
On the other side, I have the feeling that the game has been made heavier for the PC through all those DLC and updates. It is not graphically demanding like some well looking titles, but it requires quite good computer. Mine is low-end right now, but I run for example DiRT Rally at capped 50 frames per second at medium setting and ETS2 is running much worse. In cities or in traffic I got about 20 fps, sometimes it even drop below while on really low settings. And I do not know what is the reason, beacuse while American Truck Simulator is based on the same engine it worths so much better for me.
In conclusion, it is definitely game not for everyone. For some people it may be boring, as long whole gaming joy is just about driving and delivering goods. Sometimes it is boring even for me, because game just deliver driving on straight, flat roads. There is lack of difficult, narrow mountain roads, and only experience with the Alps you will have is driving through tunels. Of course there are some up and down parts of map but there are definitely too short and in too small amount. But it is the best truck driving simulator on the market. If you are looking for one, take this and you won't be disappointed. Just sit down, brew a cup of tea, turn on ingame Internet radio and take a journey over European highways in 40 ton truck.

Tl;Dr "[...] though I loved it, I only recommend buying it at this stage if you want to contribute to it's development, or if you would be really into a relatively simple game about taking care of some cute slimebros."
Slime Rancher is the game I've always wanted. Of course, currently, as it's not close to release, it's unfinished. But I am able to far overlook the flaws that it has by keeping the mindset that one day it will be fully realized.
The slimes are perfectly cute and still animated to look like what they are. The world in general has a feel that is not trying to emulate real life, but is striving to keep it's own cartoony and bright feel, and I think that is great.
The market system is also a nice addition. The world thus far is well designed and each area feels unique, including the two ranch expansions, which I thought were great in their own right. The Jetpack also allows for so much exploration of the negative possibility space, and I love it. I don't think invisible walls would ruin it, but I definitely love being able to explore places that I probably wouldn't normally.
The issues I have with it are due to it's unfinished nature, but I'll list them anyway.
Firstly, I think the game could easily be called unbalanced. It definitely makes one particular set of slimes much stronger than any other set, but it definitely doesn't /force/ you to minmax.
Secondly, the Slime Trade seems kind of useless. Most times, the trade gives you signifigantly less than you have to put in.
Finally, I kinda had a little bit of a problem with the vacuum attempting to suck in literally everything but what I actually wanted. Most times I'd just end up with a slime stuck to the end of it and the item I was attempting to nab rolling off of a cliff.
Like I said earlier, most of the problems I have with the game, perhaps some I didn't mention(?) will be fixed as it is developed. And even though I loved it, I only recommend buying it at this stage if you want to contribute to it's development, or if you would be really into a relatively simple game about taking care of some cute slimebros.

No More Room in Hell truely captures the atmosphere of what I personally believe a zombie apocalypse to be. It shows us everything from Romero inspired maps and zombies to the minimal HUD and lack of supplies you'd expect in a real horror survial game, almost everything has been put into consideration.
Cost is obviously not an issue with this standalone as it comes with the pleasing price of FREE. The only thing you really need to worry about when downloading this game is memory and processing speed but if you have an average to good quality computer there's no reason you shouldn't download this.
Admittedly there are bugs and glitches, plus as the game is running on the nearly outdated source engine, you can expect average to good graphics with similar gameplay mechanics. Also as it's a strictly multiplayer experience, it can be prone to lag and problems with connecting to servers. But there's nothing a little tweaking can't fix. And most of the time you're just too caught up in surviving to notice.
The Verdict? No More Room in Hell offers players a great experience that many horror survival games fail to do, it's a fun and rewarding game. Given the right funding and equipment, this game could be the greatest zombie survival game ever. A must play for any fan of the FPS survival horror genre.
Rating: 9/10

Having only played Devil may Cry 4 before, I am by no means a DmC expert. Regardless, I found that DmC Devil may Cry stayed true to its predecessors in its core gameplay, but also introduced elements that make it a unique addition to the DmC series.
- The combat in DmC is excellent. Mistakes are solely your fault. With all the weapons and abilities in your arsenal the number of combos you can string together is practically limitless. Watching an expert play is jaw-droppingly impressive.
- Loved the inclusion of angel and demon weapons and their specific interactions with certain demons and the environment.
- DmC does a great job of discouraging button mashing by including a good variety of demons, so that you adjust your fighting style to suit your enemies. It also encourages the use of different combinations to further boost your combat score; repetitive attacks will lead to lower style points.
- The story is oriented around young Dante. I enjoyed this prequel as I never fully understood the relationship between Dante and his twin (Virgil). I also believe the story was designed to be a social criticism of sorts, which I appreciate. Though be warned, a large portion of the game consists of story/cutscenes (which are skippable on second playthroughs, thankfully).
-
- DmC is one of those games that you can get sickeningly good at. The high difficulty bar made me feel mediocre as a gamer. I played DmC on Nephilim (the normal ‘hard’ difficulty) and found it quite challenging. Yet there are 4 difficulty settings above that. I cannot even imagine how difficult the Hell and Hell setting is.
- Usually I believe that I am fairly good at finding hidden content. DmC proved me wrong. I did not even find half the lost souls, keys, and doors on my own, and believe me, I tried. Most hidden content are quite well hidden or requires you to replay levels once you acquired specific weapons.
- I enjoyed the scoring system for two reasons: [1] it shows where you can improve and what you missed in each level. [2] Since this is a single player game the scoring system serves as a medium for players to compete amongst each other.
- During escape sequences I sometimes found the pathing unclear, but never to the point of frustration. In fact, I liked that they included these segments as it provided some downtime from all the fighting without necessarily reducing the excitement.
- There are some segments where you are basically forced to walk from one point to the other. It was neither game play nor cutscene and it didn’t add much to the game. I would have preferred if they just made a cutscene out of it.
- Though fun and exciting, I did not find the boss fights to be particularly difficult. I found that the hardest part with the bosses was figuring out what to do (not all bosses are immediately vulnerable to your attacks). For the most part, I struggled more with fighting certain demons.
- One of the criteria you are scored upon finishing a level is the time taken to complete the level. I found it somewhat unfair that cutscenes do not pause the timer.
I had a lot of fun playing DmC Devil may Cry. It is just satisfying to shred demons to bits while your combo counter and combat score steadily increase. Even on my mediocre difficulty setting, I enjoyed the challenge DmC presented. I was only somewhat disappointed by the boss fights, but then again, this isn’t Dark Souls. I don’t know what the hardcore Devil may Cry fans think about this game but I think it is a great game for players familiar and unfamiliar with the series alike.

It deserved to fail. But it also deserved not to be saddled with the whole PR fiasco. It's not Devil May Cry and shouldn't have tried to be. It's a pretty typical beat'em all that is above average in quality. Some mild camera problems but that's really about it.
I've also come to suspect Donte was massively reworked as a character since the succubus fight (which was one of the first teasers for the game) show us a much more unlikeable character than he is for the rest of the game. Really he's a pretty normal dude who's not too great at zingers.
It's not the greatest game there is, but it's competent, has some genuinely cool moments between all the middle-school tier edgy storytelling, good art direction with an identity of its own, and is mostly fun.
But all it will ever be remembered for is Tameem Antoniades trying to make it replace one of the most revered action game franchises of all time. It's pretty sad, really.
Still, for something I got for free and enjoyed (four years after the ♥♥♥♥♥torm, mind), I can't really call it bad. It is an OK game, as long as you acknowledge it doesn't have any right to be DMC's reboot.

This game is criminally underrated in the Arkham series. Two of the major complaints is that it did nothing new and that it was an Akham City reskin, though these claims are entirely exaggerated.
Arkham Origins does a lot of new things to improve upon older gadgets and questionable game mechanics. Ziplining has been overhauled with some slight improvements, the collectables actually serve a purpose beyond serving Nygma's ego (Batman has to prevent people from being blackmailed), side missions are designed and integrated better (e.g., Mad Hatter's quest adds a 2.5D trippy mission), challenges are more fun to complete, and the boss fights feel more rewarding and original compared to the previous two games (EXCEPT Mr. Freeze from Arkham City; that fight is the best of the series). Plus, the graphics look incredible for last-gen hardware.
Not only this, but the story here is better than Arkham Asylum's or City's in several ways. It's written well, features a dynamic cast of lesser-known Batman villains in addition to the classic ones, and feels a whole lot more cohesive than Arkham City's plot. There is a predictable twist partway through, though this doesn't take away from the rest of the story.
Arkham Origins, unlike Arkham City, features a realistic city this time around that's full of life. Taking place on Christmas Eve, the city feels much more alive and colourful than it did in Arkham City and this makes exploring somewhat more fun. While the city is pretty much the same one from Arkham City, it has been drastically overhauled to look less dilapidated and this makes its map better than the one from Arkham City.
That being said, combat is a bit more glitchy than in the previous games as combos break when they shouldn't and enemies attack too quickly sometimes. It doesn't feel as polished. Also, the voice-acting is missing the amazing talent from both of Rocksteady's games.
Don't let that deter you. In many ways, Arkham Origins is the best of the first three games in the series and I wholly recommend it.
