I’ve been postponing my review for this game for some time because I was too busy enjoying it. That said, there is a lot to like about this game. From the simple game mechanic to the deep strategies involve. First off, this game is not an FPS. One can see it from the trailer but you’d be surprise how many players thought it would be. Though it’s marked as a turn base strategy game with card game elements, which it is technically, it’s not completely as such. Personally, March of War: Face Off is more akin to a table top game such as Warhammer 40k but instead of bringing models to play, you bring cards (which spawn models on the board so you see the resemblance). The game also require some thought depth, thinking two to three turns ahead akin to chess. With my description alone, you’d know that despite the simple rules this game offers a great deal of strategically and tactical thinking. If you are interested in such games, Warhammer 40k and/or Chess. This game is perfect for you.
Another thing is the active participation of the Developers in the community. They really take our, the players, concerns and suggestion seriously. They also work tirelessly to make the game better and better. I commend them for their ceaseless effort.
This game is also quite dynamic in balance, or shall I say imbalance, because a game too perfectly balance ends up stale, just look at chess. I don’t see people lining up to see the World Chess Championship. On the other hand Dota 2 is a perfectly imbalance system, allowing changes to happen often without ruining the game but just changing the meta and their world series is game breaking. So expect new things added and (im)balances created to make Face Off more enjoyable. It’s another layer of depth once can explore endlessly.
Those are the few things that crossed my mind when writing this review. Overall, I give this game an overwhelming positive review.

I caught a first glimpse of this game when one of my steam friends posted a link about it on the activity feed. I checked the game out briefly, but quickly went back to other stuff as it did not really peek my interest. The game seemed a little bit weird to me (as in: it looks boring and stupid) and I was about sure I wouldn't enjoy it. About a week later, I saw one of my favourite youtubers play it and decided to eventually give it a watch. The video was over before I knew it and I clicked on the next one. And the next. After a while it was clear to me: I want this game! NOW! There was just something about it that I can't really describe, but it drew me in. And a lot of other people got drawn in too. It's like a disease being spread, the only difference being that it's a good disease. I admit I've been a little bit too quick in my (wrongful) judging of this game, and will therefore give it a (fair) second chance in this review.
You play as Beatrix LeBeau who decides to leave earth and set out for the
; a magical and adorable planet filled with slimes! Your goal? Finding slimes to Suck up their plorts (aka slime poop) with your VAC to ... sell them! Yes, correct. Plorts come in many forms and are used for various things on earth; mainly food and products (eww!). You sell these plorts on the plort market to earn some cash, which can then be spend on upgrades (for either yourself or the ranch). When slimes are fed, they'll leave one of these treasures behind for you, or two even if you are lucky. As of now, there are 3 main categories of food: fruits, veggies and meat. Each category has different types of food for you to find and feed to your slimes. If you so desire, you can also plant your own food - you'll run out less slowly (and it's fun too!). Believe me, your slimey friends will be thankful if you do. It is especially useful to plant your friends' favourite food; they'll love you for that and will definitely return the favour via plorts! I hope it is now clear that plorts are extremely valuable and so is your task as slime rancher.
The gameplay, however a bit unoriginal (find slimes --> feed slimes --> get plorts --> get money --> get upgrades etc) is very satisfying. Finding new slimes is always exciting, especially since you can create mixed breeds that are more efficient for money making (and they are just so adorable too!). The game thus encourages you to explore the planet on your 'quest' to find more and different slimes, find food and start your own farms ... and getting upgrades will make all of that easier. Be careful though, not everything is peaceful on the
. Under certain circumstances, a Tarr slime will come out and devour all the slimes in the vicinity - even you! So be cautious and take good care of your 'pets'!
The 'thing' that makes Slime Rancher so much fun for me, is the fact that there is so much freedom as to how you play. You can approach this game in a very casual way, and just go on an adventure, enjoying the different and beautiful areas with their inhabitant slimes (I could see this game used for therapy so to speak). The total opposite would be finding the most profitable slimes, combining them, putting them in a corral and making a lot of money - a dream for people who want to create a very efficient farm (or ranch rather). Or you could go inbetween and do a little of both: enjoy the slimes in their natural surroundings, but take a few home to take care of because they're so darn cute! The game is also suited for all ages, which is great. I'm pretty sure both young and old will find a certain joy playing this game and I love it for that. I could totally see a grandfather and his grandchild play this game together having a lot of fun.
The game in its current state is already super fun and stable, with minimal bugs. I estimate about 5-10 hours of content. There is still a lot of content waiting to be added, like more slimes, more types of food, more areas ... more everything! I also hope that they will add different 'modes' besides the "do-whatever-you-want" experience. I think it would make for much more replayability, which is what I'm looking for in the long run. I want to be able to play this cute game for a long time, without it getting tedious, hence my idea for different modes. (Ofcourse, this list is totally personal, and I will still love this game if it keeps up development like this - whether there be different modes or not). I'm thinking about:
+ Unique concept
+ Relaxing and/or challenging
+ Nice, soothing soundtrack
+ Satisfying gameplay
+ Excellent tutorial
+ Gorgeous looking world
+ Cuteness overload!
+- (this is temporary): lack of content
+- (this is temporary): some may find it a little bit too expensive in its current state
- The gameplay is not very innovative (as in: get slimes -> get money -> get upgrades -- repeat)
I definitely recommend this game, but please keep in mind that it is still early access. Not all the content is in the game yet, and weird stuff (buggs) may happen. If you don't mind that, by all means, please support the devs. Otherwise, just wait a couple of months for the game to be a little bit more polished.

For the third installment of this awesome franchise, it really doesn't bring anything new to the table. I both love and hate that about this game though.
I love it in the sense that it truly is a prequel. Batman doesn't even know that someone like The Joker even exists which suggests he hasn't been doing this for too long. It wold be strange if he had better gadgets and better fighting techniques than the first two games considering the fact that the events in the games chronologically haven't even happened yet.
However, I hate it in the sense that it is the third game of the franchise and it feels like I have already played this game twice.
It's basically DLC that locks away some of your gadgets and fighting techniques.
A simple and interesting device the designers could have put into the game would be something along the lines of having to press the right keys in order to string together combos for maybe even a dynamic cinematic scene of Batman whooping some♥♥♥♥♥ They also could have made some of his gadgets a little less high end. Not quite having been perfected to the rank they are in Arkham City.
Instead, the creators assumed a suitable compromise was removing some combat techniques that the Dark Knight hadn't quite learned yet on his path to justice as well as removing some gadgets he hadn't quite researched and/or developed yet.
It's not an apporpriate mechanic and/or solution and definitely more frustrating as the game sort of devolves into a third edition of monotnous repitition that isn't nearly as expansive as the previous two games.
Those are my main cons about the game. Let's talk pros.
I enjoyed the story.
I have heard some flak from friends and the internet about The Joker being involved in the game's campaign. I personally think that The Joker's involvement was a crucial plot point not only for the content of this game, but more importantly to set up the events of Arkham Asylum, which I think the developers accomplished.
Though Troy Baker's performance pales in comparison to Mark Hamill, he was still an engaging and entertaining character if you can set your bias aside.
The plot was solid and exciting.
It's understandable that the cast and charcaters are a little lackluster considering everyone on board in Arkham Asylum and City. However, viewing the game as a stand alone, it's really not bad. Once again, I enjoyed playing through the story.
What I didn't enjoy was pursuing a larger completion percentage. This coming from someone who looks forward to trophy hunting.
All of the challenges were fun, albeit some of them being a little too easy. Challenges are supposed to be challening.
The problem is the same one I had with Arkham Asylum and City. The Riddler.
Not the character. I love the Riddler as a villain. I love his concept, his backstory, and most of all his drive. Simple but entertaining given his personality.
What I hate is this game that he plays. Shutting down the radar towers is fine, but running around the city and walking around indoors looking for all of his data packs is so frustrating. Especially when you have to go through inconvenient platforming challenges you have already accomplished on your first run through the game.
I mostly hate it because there are far too many data packs which causes the challenge to become too monotonous for it to be enjoyable. It's not challenging by any means. It's tedious and mind numbingly boring.
What would be more entertaining is having a select few in every district and having to go through one of The Riddler's deathly puzzles to find your way at a data pack at the end.
This way, you eliminate the monotony; you make it challening, engaging, and fun; it's fresh; it's no longer tedious; and it doesn't feel like a chore.
I personally enjoy seeking out a larger completion rate and trophy hunting, but I want that process to be fun.
All in all, I recommend the game for a quick playthrough but not much more than that. If you play in order of release, the game just feels like a bridge from Arkham City to Arkham Knight. The entire playthrough I found myself looking forward to Arkham Knight instead of focusing on what I was doing.

I think a good place to start is that this is the first game in the series to literally denote that Batman, ♥♥♥♥ing BATMAN, is a trademark. In the game title. I think that's a good microcosm of the B-team ambition this game had.
Origins was, without a doubt, a shallow game with very little value, but at it's very core, you could see an Arkham game. The question is... is it a good Arkham game? And at that point its at a loss for words. For the record, I played it while replaying every Arkham game as part of a personal retrospective.
In no particular order, here are a bunch of gripes:
- The bossfights are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ straight up. In Asylum, the game's bossfights were often disjointed nightmares (the plant and the final), so for Arkham City all of the bossfights play to the game's strengths. Same goes for Knight, even with its flaws. But it feels like this B team endeavor with Origins forgot all the things that the A team learned after Asylum: most of the bossfights fall into three categories: QTEs and button mashing (could be better, but inoffensive), straight combat (bad), and stealth segments (REALLY bad). And unfortunately alot of them fall into those latter two categories. There are also "bossfights" which are just the game throwing a high-HP NPC named character into the middle of a bunch of enemies, and those felt like the BIGGEST copout.
- The story is really boring. Especially because the WB writers can't seem to get away from a certain member of the rogue's gallery. Also, the tacked on... ugh... ORIGIN segment for that character... well it didn't do the game favors in the slightest, especially because the only main returning voice actor from the other Arkham games is Alfred and Riddler. You don't connect with the origins of these characters because they aren't the same voices. Oh, and the entire end-segment is a ♥♥♥♥-you to anyone who wanted an actual good original story in a game literally titled Origins.
- That said, I don't hate Smith's Batman. It is a bit phoned in, but I think its alright. But good lord Troy Baker... you were not meant for the role... And his performance isn't bad, it's just miscast. There's a noted difference between a bad actor, a badly cast actor, and a badly written character, and Baker's role is a bit of both of those last two.
- The combat was either A) cheating or B) ♥♥♥♥ing easy. That said, when I played this I was running through each Arkham game, but still. It also inherited some bad genes from Batman Arkham City Armored Edition, where "here's a cool glove! oh♥♥♥♥♥♥it makes combat way too ♥♥♥♥in easy... uh... enjoy!"
- The hubworld is uninspired, filled with garbage nothing activities, and half of it is practically a straight copy of City's map. The long♥♥♥♥♥bridge in between the areas of the open world were also really obnoxious.
- The porting job was rushed to hell. Frame drops are one thing, but snow effects causing input lag during flight is another entirely. There's also a "flaming debris" particle effect in the end of the game that brought my computer to its knees for no reason, and my computer ran this game just fine and dandy up to that point. It didn't even look that good, but it made the final area of the game lag like hell.
- The PC version is also notoriously glitchy. I counted once where I straight fell through the map, four times where low textures and models would persist into a combat encounter, and twice where enemies would clip into the wall while doing a running grab, softlocking a combat encounter.
All in all, just don't bother. The changes made to the formula from City, plus the god-awful story and phoned-in acting make it a... video game... certainly. I just think that the other entries, Knight, flaws and all, included, are worth far more of your time than the 9 hours this atrocity demanded of me. I think maybe, just maybe, if you're looking to see what Arkham looks like when it's done bad, look no further than
BATMAN(TM): ARKHAM ORIGINS

Reality is the game has a whole bunch of flaws, but it also has a lot to offer that no other game has.
In a time where arena shooters are basically all the AAA market has to offer, this game rewards you for knowing every nook and cranny to a huge, huge in game map - two of them in fact. Even before you've memorized it all it's a wonder to explore.
As a newbie you'll get absolutely pounded by good players. You'll think they're hacking probably, I used to. But the reality is that they aren't. Remember the game is third person and everyone can see arund corners. If the opponent is using skype it can seem like they're wall-hacking.
You'll think there are OP guns - and there are, but they are all available in game; ntec, pmg, hvr. All the pay guns are just reskins of guns that exist or just straight up worse. Mostly just customization is restricted by money. But if you check the forums, free premium codes are given out often enough that you can rework your character for free and not get too bored with yourself.
Just try the game with a few friends (it's very hard to play alone - this is very much a team game based on team strategy) and if you don't like it, stop playing.
And if you don't have 50~ fps, come back during the summer once the engine is done being updated and you'll likely have a better time of it.
The game is pretty unique, the team is small, and if you're willing to cope it's great. If you aren't, it's awful. Don't be afraid to have your opinion.

The Raven is a well-presented adventure game with endearing characters, intriguing and enticing story arcs. I found myself exploring every bit of dialogue just to learn more about them, without regard to progression of the story. This game does suffer from sometimes awkward character movement and pathnoding, as well as stilted facial animation, but this is easy to get past and doesn't present much of a problem.
Fans of adventure games should definitely purchase this game.

The game has fairly good graphics, and seems to have an okay plot line so far but it proceeds incredibly slowly. I find most mystery games where you have to wait for the person to walk to what you want to look at pretty annoying. If you want a game the follows the Nancy Drew style of mystery games I would not recomend this game. If you like third person view on mystery games, where the person walks slow, most everything is planned in a certain way, and enjoy the Agatha Christe style game then this is for you.

So many twists, turns, red herrings that aren't really red herrings but are... the plotline is truly captivating. The game started out a little slow, but the characters are well developed throughout the story, unravelling mysteries beyond "Who is the Raven?" and "Wait, what? So who is the Raven really?" and "SERIOUSLY, WHAT? WHO?!"
The great storyline, the well acted characters with loads of personality, and the cinematic score make it a memorable--and--very replayable experience. This ain't no "hit it and quit it (at least for 2 years until you forget the plot)." As you progress through the chapters, you step in the shoes of the other characters--which really enriches the game. Going back and playing it a second time you'll pick up on a lot that you'd missed before, and that's actually part of the excellence of it. Something I also found nice was that you aren't required to complete everything possible before you move on; you can skip some things but still continue the story. Naturally, the completeness of the story will diminish, but that's why you play it again!
The only downsides are that the graphics are somewhat dated, even on the highest quality, and the cut scenes are lower quality than the in-game graphics. Which doesn't make any sense. The controls can be a little frustrating at times; I found it difficult to move about from room to room in the train especially, but you figure it out eventually. Fortunately there aren't any glitches that make it entirely impossible to move, forcing you to restart from your last save. That's a plus. Other than that, I only wish there were a couple more puzzles throughout the game. The first chapter is really heavy on the story-telling, which you can still opt to skip through if you're not much of a story person.. but why are you playing an adventure game if you don't like a good story, anyway? Crazy.
To suffice, it's a great adventure game with a well thought out plot that'll keep you interested, and everytime you think you know who the Raven REALLY is... well... you're wrong.

For a point-and-click adventure game, the main character is endearing, the overal scenery graphics are movie quality (there are weird glitches with the character though), and while it was fairly predictable, it was still good old fashioned fun! The music really fit this game as a time piece, and the dialog was well put together, if not a little long in the tooth.
I gave the entire 3 part series of the Raven: Legacy of a Master Thief a 4.25/5.0

This is a classic old-school style point-and-click adventure with some quality graphics, superb voice acting, and a brilliant orchestral soundtrack.  It has a strong nostalgic feel of a Poirot / Pink Panther whodunnit.
My one criticism is that the puzzles are pretty simple - sometimes you feel you are just clicking things for the character to reveal the story.  However, the atmosphere and superb voice acting will keep you hooked in, and it's worth sticking with it to the end to reveal the true identity of the "The Raven" - the mysterious, shadowy character you chase through the game.
The pace is quite slow - but in a nice gentle way.  It's a perfect chillout game for the mature adventure gamer on a lazy Sunday afternoon.

I don't really remember why I bought Euro Truck Simulator 2. I have never been a fan of simulators but it just happened. Probably I want to see how it is to drive a long vechicle, while I prefer European trucks over American ones. The price and visual part of the game convinced me to buy it.
Graphically, production is not highest quality within today's standards, however it is nice, trucks are detailed and well done (tekstures, reflexes etc.) and there are many picturesque landscapes over the Europe's fields n' roads. Menu is transparent enough and eye candy, what I like in every game. Audio is just adequate. Engines sounds may be better, so do ambient sounds, but they are generally okay.
Game include 7, licensed brands: Scania, DAF, Iveco, Renault, Volvo, MAN, Mercedes, most of them deliver 2 possible models. Handling is good, you could even set such things as braking strenghth and trailer stability factor, it default settings don't meet your requirements. And the truck customization is huge. Starting from setting up your seat, FOV to equiping the car with many accesories, so interior as outise ones. You can literally build your own looking truck using custom paintjobs, accesories, wheel paints etc. but...
... more than half of it is a part of paid DLCs. But wait, I wouldn't point it as a bad thing. It is fun to do, and the prices of such DLCs are quite low (1 to 3 Euro mostly) and they introduce fun things into the game that allow you to paint truck to suit your taste. And they are not obligatory, for me just nice gadget to have and a nod for developers.
What is worth to add, there are thousands of free mods which can be downloaded from over the Internet or (limited amount but still growing up) via Steam worksop. They can modify every aspect of the game and installation is really reasy - using build-in game mod manager. Just several clicks and you are done. I can't tell much about free mods, because I have used only a couple, I prefer original content over fan-made, sometimes unstable mods.
On the other side, I have the feeling that the game has been made heavier for the PC through all those DLC and updates. It is not graphically demanding like some well looking titles, but it requires quite good computer. Mine is low-end right now, but I run for example DiRT Rally at capped 50 frames per second at medium setting and ETS2 is running much worse. In cities or in traffic I got about 20 fps, sometimes it even drop below while on really low settings. And I do not know what is the reason, beacuse while American Truck Simulator is based on the same engine it worths so much better for me.
In conclusion, it is definitely game not for everyone. For some people it may be boring, as long whole gaming joy is just about driving and delivering goods. Sometimes it is boring even for me, because game just deliver driving on straight, flat roads. There is lack of difficult, narrow mountain roads, and only experience with the Alps you will have is driving through tunels. Of course there are some up and down parts of map but there are definitely too short and in too small amount. But it is the best truck driving simulator on the market. If you are looking for one, take this and you won't be disappointed. Just sit down, brew a cup of tea, turn on ingame Internet radio and take a journey over European highways in 40 ton truck.

Overall review:
A hack and slash game in which a rich weapon system is develped and  it is all about combination and creativity after you get familiar with the commands and rules, thus giving you immense satisfaction and content if your own stylish combo works out as expected.
Pros:
1. Not system requirement demanding. I played this game on an old laptop with i3-390M and AMD 6370M early in 2014 and everything was smooth.
2. Seamless character animation. Every move and the transition between the moves are fast and look natural.
3. Great support for both mouse w/ keyboard and controller. I beat the game with m/k before and this time on steam I play with Xbox one controller (wired, in case of low power). Normally not a single problem can be found with either of them, except that the devil trigger is not very easy to activate with a controller, which can be fixed by modifying game input file.
4. Funny dialogues. Dante here is a careless badass and the humor from the gameplay never makes me feel dull.
5. Blood pumping music in fights. You might search the music after you beat the game, at least I did.
Cons:
1. The game-crashing issue happened 3 times with this steam version, Also, I encountered game freezing problems at times.
2. All SSS ranking achievement is time consuming on both dante and vergil's stories, because there is always one level that you need to try 10 times before you get an SSS.
This is a fantastic game but dont play it if you a nice person!

I have been playing since about alpha 14.  Fantastic game!  9/10
You build a prison to house inmates.  Feed them, provide work and education, family visits, chapel, showers, entertainment... but most of all keep them locked up.
Sounds easy, but soon you start to get medium security prisoners which are a bit difficult to control.  Then come the maximum security prisoners who are extremely dangerous.  Some will start fights for no reason, others will kill your prisoners and guards or try to escape by digging tunnels.  Next you will get legendary prisoners and dead men walking which add another layer to the challenge.  Now the perfectly placed cafeteria won't work well because you want to keep your max security prisoners seperate from the general population.  Further complicating the game are prisoners with special traits like Snitches and Ex-Cops, they will be instantly targeted so you need to put them in protective custody.
There are tools to help with all of this.  Security forces can get info from snitches, the chapel will calm inmates, well-placed fences will slow down tunnel digging.  Most importantly you need to create an effective prison layout to accomodate all of the prisoners and keep the number of guards to a minimum while still being ever present.
The main mechanic in the game is you get increasing amount of $$ for housing more dangerous prisoners.  So max security prisoners give you a bunch of money, but you need twice as many guards/cameras/dogs to keep them under control.  If you want to make lots of cash, go light on guards, but then you risk a riot.  I have never had a riot in the game, but it seems common from watching gameplay vids.
Pros:
The Devs are awesome!  Watch some of their alpha videos they are great, and you can really see how much the game has progressed since the early Alphas.
Lots of options for construction
Lots of options for controlling your prisoner intake and their schedules
Unique game type
Challenging, but fun gameplay
Cons:
There isn't much for music
Limitations to how big you can realistically build the prison due to how long it takes prisoners to walk around
Every patch would break damn near every mod on the workshop.  This might have settled now with less updates.

So I start the game up, set the quality to high of course and I look at a black screen for what seems like days. A series packaged in (the now common) monthly Chapters has finally reached it's conclusion. Fans of Poiret and Agatha Christie Novel style games should pick this up. Or if you simply enjoy good detective stories done well. I enjoyed the puzzles and the voice acting was strong in places but weak in others. The enviroments repeated themselves often as you played similar events from different points of view but it was done in a way that didn't feel lazy or some rehash.  Achievments for perfect scores are broken which annoyed me as I wanted to do a clean hintless run but it takes nothing from the game. Considering this was made during some downtime from The brilliant Book of Written tales you have to give it credit. Over the 3 Chapters you play as various protagonists and antagonists to unravel the mystery of "Who is The Raven?" You get bonus points for paying attention and accuising them in the game so its worth uncovering all the clues. Slow paced but understandibly so.
Yes, it is difficult.
It will make you start question your own sanity, so nothing major. Brilliant game, though. I would definitely like to plunge into my inevitable death again.
classic mistery adventure full of character, playing as Constable Zellner on the Orient Express makes me feel like a wise old man :)
Great Adventure game with Agatha Christie Influences. Full of charm and some pretty amazing twists.

Too far from Christie's work to be a directly based digital manifestation, yet too close to be inspired by it.
Too straightforward to be a true quest, yet too far from a digital novel.
It is a shame, the game had potential.
The work of artists is quite magnificent and the plot is mostly just above average if compared to an FPS for example, but it's too shallow for a thriller or detective fiction. The problem is that the gameplay is so streamlined, it is nonexistent.
It feels like unpausing a movie when you solve a puzzle, there is literally nothing to divert the attention of the player and to confuse him - what you do simply does not fail.
The large locations are wasted because there are at most two-three points of interaction that are easily found without extensive pixel hunting.
If I was to choose between recent detective adventure games would rather get myself B. Sokal's "Sinking Island" or perhaps "CSI" or even "Evil Under the Sun" or the great "L.A. Noire", but not this failed attempt at a quest.
Developers forgot that the player actually has to play.

I do recommend this game, but under certain conditions.
For starters, you can not play this if you take gaming seriously.  There is no matchmaking in this game at all.  They claim that matchmaking is done by your ranking in the game, however their ranking system is complete and total crap. I made a new character earlier, to test this. With my BRAND NEW character, I did ONE mission. On this mission, I got one kill, and died around 7 times. (Behold, pay to win aspects, will detail later). After the mission was over, I was rocketed from bronze one, to silver 3. I skipped ALL the bronze ranks because of ONE kill.
Now maybe, you'd think, they would at least make the game fair to free players. Not everyone has money they can spend, right? How about, instead, they market their microtransactions to give you game breaking advantages that allow you to dominate every player who doesnt have them. If you get matched up against a pay-to-win player, as a free player, you can reserve your cemetary plot now, because you wont stand a chance.
"But Akalron, they have to make money right?" Yes, of course a company needs a way of generating revenue, but ruining a free players experience is not a proper way to  do that. I have played FTP games where the company did just fine by selling cosmetics, not advantages.  APB COULD have easily done this, but they took a less retroactive approach to it. Granted they probably generate more revenue this way because of all the players who desire a win that bad.
Heres my favorite part however. I can deal with the pay-to-win, I can deal with the bad matchmaking, but what I can't begin to fathom is their lack of optimization. This game has been out for years, and yet it still runs like its in pre-alpha development. Textures load slower than a snail, the game constantly freezes up (usually in the middle of driving or a fire-fight. Hope you didnt want to avoid hitting a wall or dying.) The loading times are atrocious. The only thing slower than how slow the textures load is how long the game takes to actually open.
My computer is no potato, I have no problems running any of the other 150+ games I have, but when this game sits there loading the district select screen for over 5 minutes? What on earth is this? Are they so focused on adding more over-powered guns for their revenue that they dont care about optimizing performance? Or are they just banking on computer hardware advancing faster than their games requirements?
I do have some positive things to say about the game however.
I have a blast playing this game. It is fun after it finally loads.  Its a fantastic blend of GTA and Saints Row. It has a lot of (unlockable) customization, but also takes its gameplay moderately seriously. If you go in expecting to have fun, not expecting to win, you will enjoy yourself.
I recommend playing with friends, because if you do decide to do missions, being able to communicate will assist in winning even against pay-to-win players.
Steal a van, hop in with all your friends, vibe out to the ingame radio and gun down pedestrians like a boss. Enjoy yourself.
And for you developers who may or may not read this review: For the love of god, please fix your game, its too much fun to watch it slowly die off. I've worked for a game with a similar market strategy, and lets just say, they didnt do well. Take that as you will.

The game's story (or lack of one) is about Sonic arriving in the city of Station Square (which is actually more of a glorified shopping mall) because he's bored & has nothing better to do. Sonic then finds some water monster called Chaos attacking police, intervenes & saves the day. Later while catching some rays by the pool he sees Tails flying a plane & then crashes said plane on the beach but somehow survives uninjured.  Sonic rushes after him & the two group up to go on a journey of finding all the Chaos Emeralds which just so happen to be in the city you're in because why not?
Eggman shows up, farts in your face & steals them from you.  Later you collect more emeralds only to lose them because Knuckles decides to slap you around until you crap them out & Eggman snatches them up.  After all of your blunders you finally find out Eggman wants the emeralds to feed them to Chaos.  His reason for doing so is destroying the city & building a theme park called "Robotnik Land" over the ruins because again, why not?
So you go after him in an attempt to stop him from destroying the city.  Along the way you find Amy being abducted by one of Eggman's robots so you go after her & eventually wind up on the Egg Carrier (which is probably the coolest hub in the game).  As you progress through the ship you fight a Robot called E-101 Gamma & just as you're about to destroy the foul creation of evil Amy stops you.  E-101 takes a liking to Amy for some reason & decides to no longer work for Eggman.  Gamma then goes on a journey of saving his Robot Brothers from Eggman's control by murdering them one by one.  Ah, brotherly love.
Eventually you fight Chaos & Robotnik a few more times & all is well. Until Chaos destroys the city & gains his final form Perfect Chaos. You then fight him as Super Sonic in one big DBZ style rip off & then the game ends with everyone (except all the dead & homeless survivors) living happily ever after.
Until Sonic Adventure 2.
You play as Sonic, Tails, Amy, Knuckles, E-101 Gamma, and Big The Cat.  You go through world hubs to get to levels and each level plays pretty terribly.  In the fast segments (Which are supposed to be the highlight of Sonic) you hit walls, can't control yourself very well, and sometimes you'll clip straight through the ground or through walls.
You unlock the extra characters by playing through Sonic's main story, and the extra character's levels are just rehashes of the same levels so it's just there to add replay value.  If you complete all the story modes for each character you unlock Super Sonic and fight the final form of Chaos.
There's also a "Missions" menu where you go around the world up fulfilling mundane tasks that were meant to unlock Game Gear games on the GCN but are now reduced to simple Achievement farming since the GG games are not in this version.
If you played this on the DC or GCN you're not missing much.  The game is pretty much an exact port, that somehow adds new problems and makes the older issues worse.  The graphics have been improved slightly over it's DC counterpart but are not as good as the GCN version and some areas are glitchy with texture clipping and shadow flicker, especially in Big's levels.
Gameplay varies for each character that you play.
First thing you'll notice is this game has an overworld hub.  I dunno what they were thinking adding this to the game.  I guess they wanted the "Adventure" in the title to mean something, but the hubs are so small it's really a useless feature that only serves to take up space & add useless text dialog to manequin people walking around town.  In any case, you go to levels through these hubs but you usually have to solve some mundane puzzle first before you can get into each level.
Sonic's levels start as simple "run as fast as you can to the end" but later on they turn into slow platforming segments.  There's even one level where all you do is farm rings so you can buy an emerald from a casino.  This level used to have a running segment between all the ring farming but they cut that out for some reason which is kind of lame since that was one of the more fun parts in the game.  Every now and then you'll fight a boss which range from baby-mode easy to down right broken & frustrating.  Egg Viper is the worst boss in any Sonic game (or any game) ever, imo.
Tails' levels are a similar style to Sonic's except you're racing him to the finish & you have to beat him to progress.  Aside from new shortcuts everything is pretty much the same.
Knuckles' levels are all about finding gem shards of the master emerald.  You go around each level with a Radar that tracks each gem.  Knuckles probably has the best game mode since you actually feel like you're on an "Adventure" & not some linear path.  Sadly, his levels also have some of the worst fixed camera angles in the game.
Amy's Levels are comparable to Tails', except you're not racing to the finish but trying to outrun one of Eggman's robots.  Every now and then he'll jump-scare you & try to capture you.  Her levels aren't bad but they are slower compared to other characters.
E-101 Gamma is a robot who shoots things with homing missiles.  His missions are mostly blowing stuff up & reaching the end of the stage.  At the end of each stage you'll fight a miniboss with the last 2 stages being real bosses.  Gamma's storyline is probably the best out of all the characters.
Then there's, ugh. Big The Cat.  Big's levels are the worst in the game.  His pet frog ate a Chaos emerald & is now running away from Eggman's robots so you have to go after him & capture him by fishing.  Yes, they decided to put a fishing mini-game as a requirement for beating a Sonic game.  These levels aren't hard, but if you don't know the trick to catching Froggy they may take you some time.
After completing every Story Mission you unlock Super Sonic, which let's you fight Final Chaos in Super Sonic's form.  It's mostly just Run as fast as you can & hit the boss 3 times.  Then the game ends.  Nothing too impressive, really.
There are still some parts of the game that I remember being broken on Dreamcast that are still broken in this version.  One of which involves riding a stone snake through a part of the Mayan level but Sonic is constantly fidgeting and clipping through the snake, or when you need to ride an elevator with Amy she will constantly clip through the elevator and drop to her death.  You'd think after almost 20 years they'd fix these glitches.
The biggest problem this game has is its camera.  It goes everywhere and nowhere.  It clips through walls, goes behind objects to obstruct your view and has set angles in certain areas that just make the game harder because of the angle it's forced into.
Voice acting is bad but it's not the worst I've heard.  Sounds and music are decent.  The best song in this game is in the title screen.  Every character also has their own theme song which isn't too bad.
This version of DX also doesn't include the Game Gear games that the original Gamecube rendition has which is rather disappointing.
In short, there are good Sonic games, there are bad Sonic games & this one is the latter.  You may want to wait for a sale of some sort before buying unless you really wanna feel some good old Dreamcast nostalgia.  Sadly, if you only played the GCN version you'll just be disappointed.

I got a coupon for this game, and was intrigued after watching the trailer. Looking at the negative reviews, I expected the game to have choppy functions and lack of content. Although I haven't experienced any buggy gameplay mechanics (running Windows 7 x64), one of my friends has (running Windows 8.1 x64). As such, if you're using Windows 8 or 8.1, I would advise caution with this game, as it may not function properly.
The amount of content is what you'd expect after watching the trailer; you just shoot the enemies before they get to the line. The game is controlled entirely with the mouse and mouse buttons; moving the mouse moves your spaceship up or down like you'd move the mouse cursor, and left click fires a shot. As such, this game can be played entirely with one hand.
As far as I can tell, there are 2 gameplay modes; "Match 3" and "Survival". In survival mode, you have to kill the enemies before they reach the border line on the left. However, each kill makes the border move a little bit to the right, requiring you to kill enemies faster. Killing enemies in rapid succession moves the border to the left. In Match 3 mode, each kill moves the border to the right, but killing 3 of the same enemy color in a row will move the border a bit to the left, which I find to be a unique idea. In either mode, however, accuracy is a must; as the trailer said, this is an accuracy-based shooter. There are also several difficulty levels, although I've only played on normal difficulty so far.
When starting the game, you're greeted with a settings screen where you can choose the screen resolution, whether or not to play in full screen, whether to display special effects, and adjust the volume controls.  However, after this screen, there is no way to change these settings except for the volume. Fortunately, it's very easy to exit and restart the game to change the settings if need be.
A very simple game at its core, and definitely worth the $0.66 I paid for it.

I can't say enough good things about this game.  I was hoping this game would be something different from the usual, relaxing, engaging and beautiful and it is all that and more. I purchased the game in a sale bundle which for a bit less than retail for the core game also included for free the DLC's Going East, Scandinavia, High Value cargo and a couple other cosmetic dodads.   Probably the best value of any of the many games and bundles I've purchased on Steam.
I'm not a hardcore gamer and I'm running this on an older MacBook (which necessitates much lower graphics settings) but playing ET2 is simply a beautiful experience.  It's like spending hours driving through European postcards and yet it provides frequent enough decisions (gas, repairs, job choice,  occasionally difficult driving situations, managing your company, etc...) that 90 hours in I still feel engaged and excited to play more.
As for the visuals, I have to praise the designers. There's so many ways they could have done less and still had a game that was nearly as good, but it's amazing how much detail they include.  As an example, most driving games have areas with tall highway sound barriers and that's the edge of the world, but in ET2 when using the chase camera suddenly you see that on the other side of the barriers is even more of the world: forests or an industrial zone or a castle or a....  Because of this, and even though it's just s smidge more fiddly to drive, I highly recommend using the chase camera when driving during the day.  It's really ups the beauty factor.
Lastly, if you don't have a driving rig I highly recommend a PS2 style controller or other pad with 2 joysticks.  Being able to assign one joystick to the steering and the other to provide an incrmental control for the throttle (accelleration and reverse) makes the trucks much easier to control and the game even more fun to play.  If you need one the Logitech F310 (newer version of what I have) is well rated and tends to go for $15-20 on Amazon. I assure you it will be money very well spent.

Sonic Adventure is a fairly overrated game. For those of you who haven't already clicked away or tuned out from this review, I assume you'll want to hear me out. Just so no one gets me wrong, I like this game. There are a lot of cool things about it. And I even think it has aged alright.
Sonic Adventure brings the Sonic universe into 3D with five different playable characters, each with their own adventure. There's some good variety. Sonic has the most levels and has the most freedom, as he can go as fast or slow as he wants in most of the levels. Not too much pressure, but lots of possibilities. He's also the most useful character in terms of his abilities. Tails' campaign focuses more on flying through rings and beating Sonic to the end of the levels. So basically, like races or time trials. Knuckles is looking for shards of the master emerald, which has him searching around levels freely rather than in a linear fashion. I really like this campagn because it lets you really appreciate the level design. Amy is running for her life in her stages, being pursued by Eggman's robots. It's a tense run to the finish. Big the Cat has the most unique campaign by far, consisting of a bunch of fishing levels. As much as people hate the character and his levels, I think they're a nice change up and a break from the action while still being somewhat involved as far as gameplay goes. And lastly, Gamma's levels are scrambling to get as much time as possible by locking on to targets. So there's a lot of variety as each character controls in their own unique way.
It's also cool how, even though this was more or less Sega's answer to Super Mario 64, it feels like quite a different type of game. Everyone's stories intertwine at some point and every character gets boss fights, even Big the Cat suprisingly enough. There's replay value for those of you who want to try and get all the medals, and that probably isn't easy but I didn't put myself through that so I can't say for sure. The music is cool, blening band songs with game music. The visuals are also pretty neat. Lots of cutscenes where were nice for the time. Honestly, I really do have fun with this game.
Well if I like all this stuff about it... why am I calling it overrated? Because I hear how GREAT this game is, most likely by people who played it on the Dreamcast when they were kids. The game isn't great by any stretch, but it IS good. I have plenty of complaints. I know it's the director's cut but... there are too many cutscenes in this game. They aren't anything spectacular and don't add a whole lot to the game so having so many pads the playtime and breaks up the action a lot. This is also coupled with the issue that the open world aspects, as they're called, are merely just you running around mostly baren hub worlds with very little to do in them. There are some people to talk to but they are largely unintersting. There are a few things to find and a few places you can go, but most of the overworld is rather pointless. So, basically you have three sections of the game. Cutscenes, hub worlds, and actual levels. The actual levels only make up about a third of your playtme. That's a bit annoying and since going through the overworld and watching these cutscenes happen between pretty much every level... well... it kind of ruins the flow of the game. And Sonic games are kind of about flow. Speed, flow, rhythm. This is counter intuitive to what Sonic games are about.
While characters all control in their own way and have their own missions, they tend to share the same levels. I guess it makes some sense and works in some cases. It'd be tough to win the races as Tails if you never played the levels before as Sonic. Exploring the levels in depth with Knuckles lets you appreciate stuff you may have sped through before. I guess even playing as Big is different since you are fishing and therefore looking for water more than anything else. But Amy and Gamma, on top of having such short campaigns, just play the same levels as other characters. It feels a little lazy after a while and having some new levels along with replaying other ones would've been a good idea. And speaking of Gamma... boy did I hate his campaign. Yeah, I actually thought it was WORSE than Big's. Why? Well, you see, Gamma is the last character in the spinning wheel. I completed the campaigns in that order. So by the time I got to Gamma... his playstyle was a step backwards and largely out of place. He's not all that fast, can't jump very well, and hit attack is locking on to multiple enemies with homing rockets. It's just way too easy compared to the rest of the game... boring even. It feels like it should be one of the first things you do, not the last.
The Chao garden... no I didn't forget. A lot of people love it. I'm sure it's a lot cooler if you had the Dreamcast or GameCube version because... well... you could do stuff with your chao on portable devices. But with this version, you're stuck training them the hard way... the long, tedious way. I just didn't enjoy it. It was boring for me. This isn't what I signed up for when I was looking to play a 3D platformer. It just seemed like there were more important things to do. You know... stop Eggman, get the shards of the master emerald... fish for my froggy friend. ANYTHING but feeding and petting my chao so that I can put it into races and cheer from the sidelines with seems to have little to no effect on the outcome whatsoever. It's all just an overblown and underdeveloped mini game that I have no patience for nor interest in.
So there you have it. It's not a bad game, it's just nowhere near great. I like it, but it has a lot of flaws. Also, this version doesn't sound like the best because of chao garden situation, and the GameCube version has extra games on it as well. This has achievements... I guess... and some capability for modding... but... it's really nothing all that special. I guess if you don't have a Dreamcast, a GameCube, or a backwards compatible Wii, then this is a fine alternative. It's $8. Is it worth that? Well... if you're a big Sonic fan, sure. If you're just interested... wait for a sale maybe. It's not real high for a big name title like this, but I can't help feeling you could wait and get it cheaper. Sonic Adventure DX gets a 6/10.

I played this for the Gamecube before and wanted to play this game again for the PC. Odd to say I now own this copy, but the question is this: is this version of the game worth it?
Honestly, it depends. If you already own a console version, I'd stick with those since they're pretty much perfect for being Dreamcast ports. If you already own a PC version of this title (2004), you should stick with that since it is by far the best version out there for one thing: Mod support.
It is odd for a Steam version of Sonic Adventure DX to be... well, once again a port of a console version of an another console title that it originated from. By now this game should have graphical improvements and additional content, but here it's a step back from the 2004 PC version. This product seemed to have missing features that the console versions had so why a downgrade? Who knows...
And that's not all, of all the ports out there, this one is the least accurate version. People claimed to have missing textures and missing sound effects here and there. It depends on what kind of rig you have. This probably may be a sign of a rushed port just to grab some extra cash. So far this sounds like it may not be worth getting for a watered-down port that doesn't do what it should've done.
The worst part? No mod support for the Steam version. This is a deal breaker when the original PC version supported it.
That all sounds like it's not worth owning, but here in 2014, talanted dudes found a solution to restore this version to be the best version again like the original ten years back. With them, I think this game feels fresh again and honestly, it's fun. Oh and it's possible to achieve 4K here, it's beautiful. For a more interesting twist, try using multiple monitors as one ... it's pretty weird. Unless you don't care to mod the Steam version, I'd go with the console versions.
In short: On its own, Sonic Adventure DX on Steam is a not-so-great port, but one clever mod to change the game can make this one just as great like the old.

I have played a lot games in my time and this is absolutely one of my favorite games ever.  I don't know how to accurately describe it, but to me, it is sort of like a combination of chess, maybe spades, and the old Panzer General turn based games.

It is simple enough for anyone to pick up and play, but hard to master due to the various strategies and play styles that you will encounter in the PVP area. Every game will be unique and this is what keeps it fresh and addictive. You have to strategize and build decks to attack and/or defend against many types of units.  There are Advance deployment units, Bombers, Shielders, Turrets, Tanks, Annihilators, Snipers, Commandos, Rangers, Medics, Engineers, Hover Platforms, Supply drops, Napalm and many many more. Way too many to list.  Then you also have to take into account the luck of the draw during each game.
Even though I bought some gems to support the developers of this awesome game, you don't have to spend any real cash to obtain card packs. There are new campaign challenges nightly that you earn 750 gold from (almost all my cards have came from completing these challenges). You also get 70 gold every time you win a PVP game.  A new pack of cards cost 2000 gold (you keep these cards forever and you can use them across any of your custom decks). If you don't like the cards you opened or you get dupes, you can disintegrate those for tickets that you can use to buy any available card in the game.
The online community and devs have been great so far too. The devs are constantly interacting with players in the chat area and the player base is very friendly. I highly recommend checking out this game if you are fan of strategy games.

If you're a fan of the original storyline of the DMC series then I would caution you when deciding to purchase this game.
I bought this game as part of a bundle with the DMC 4 Special Edition which I don't regret at all, however if this was purchased independently then I would be incredibly upset.
If I were to rate the game on its own, separate from the original DMC franchise, then it's an alirght game to play at least once. The graphics were good, I liked the soundtrack as it matched the feel of the game, but there was some things that weren't great at all.
I've experienced far too many empty spaces while playing the game. You would turn a corner into an open area that almost always leads you into a dead end, no enemies to fight, no secrets or valuables at all just an empty space which is just unacceptable and poor level design. Not to mention that the gameplay is horrid, it wasn't even fun to play this game, I rushed to finish the story which was weak.
PROS:
-Alright graphics
-Decent soundtrack
-Nice art design
CONS:
-Poor gameplay mechanics
-Less than great level design
-"So-so" story
All in all, if you're new to the series (which I highly doubt) I'd recommend playing this game first before playing any of the others, but beware that this is an entirely different story than the main series (alternate universe, if you will). Personally I wouldn't pay full price and wait for it to go on sale, but even then that's pushing it.

So what's the deal with batarrangs?  When you get hit by one does it lacerate your skin and do all kinds of damage or is it just a minor inconvenience? In some pieces of media, a well placed batarrang will put a criminal gunman out of commission for the rest of the fight.  In others, it's just a minor nuisance.  The Arkham games fall into that latter category.
That's just one of the things that bothers me about these games.  One of those things that I wouldn't notice if the entire game hadn't felt like a cynical cash in.  "Hey, they're releasing Assassin's Creed every year.  Why not Batman?"  I'll tell you why not Batman.  You're going to run out of interesting characters to pit him against.  Batman vs. Deathstroke is probably the marquee fight of this production, and they get it out of the way pretty early.  You also get reused assets from other games and no Mark Hamill.
Positives:  They do Bane a little more justice than normal.  I hadn't heard of Copperhead before this thing, and she seems pretty cool.
TL: DR Just stick with Arkham Asylum/ Arkham City.  You can probably skip this one.

Prison Architect is a game about building and running a private for-profit prison. And it's pretty good at that. You're given quite a bit of control over nearly all aspects of your prison, from deciding what security level prisoners enter your prison, what do they do during the day, what programs are available, when and what do they eat, what happens when they fight and destroy and more. The prisoners themselves are also pretty smart, working to satisfy their various needs, sneaking tools and even working together to dig tunnels from their toilet to their freedom.
Prisoners can sometimes also have traits like volatile or tough, they may be snitches and have a hit out on them, they may be members of gangs that fight to control territory throughout your prison and the player is given tools such as the ability to hire guards, research body armor, conduct taser training, get snipers, armed guards, dogs, automatic doors, cctvs, confidential informants and more to combat this. Eventually, you can even unlock the ability to accept death row prisoners and the conduct their execution process.
Prison Architect also features a ~5 hour long campaign that both showcases different ways to run a prison and various design ideas while also acting as a kind of tutorial, explaining a couple of the mechanics. There's also an escape mode, where you can play instead as a prisoner in either your own or one of the thousands of prisons available on the workshop. And a lot can be found and downloaded from the Steam Workshop, such as the prison from Shawshank Redemption, new items, new game mechanics, reform programs, skins, themes and more.
There are a few issues I have with the game though. Some systems, such as temperature, are a total afterthought and others, such as the gang system, are a little limited on what you can really do to solve it. Sometimes the game also feels like a menu management simulator, where you have to scroll through, use a search bar, or switch through several pages to change something or spend quite a bit of time trying to manage it, such as with the scheduled patrols or wires overlay. I have also encountered quite a few bugs in the AI, and the game doesn't even have a main menu.
Overall though, I Prison Architect is one of my most played games on Steam and I've enjoyed it a lot. The freedom the game gives you in nearly every aspect of building, along with its various complex system and options given to the player of managing all your inmates is fantastic. And there's nothing better than seeing all your planning come together or fall flat in a deadly riot.
I choose to be happy .

There's a pretty basic recipe to achieve success in each mission or prison, which takes some time to learn, but there is a great degree of freedom and diversity in the layout of your prison you can take advantage of once you have the recipe down in order to keep things interesting.
The campaign doesn't explain all the game mechanics too well, I think a more comprehensive tutorial would have been a nice touch. The Wiki help option in the menu is your friend, use it often, and read up on other stuff as there are many things that don't get explained to you in the campaign.
You can also purchase surrounding land to enlarge your prison later as you become thirsty for more, which is a great feature, as I tend to fill the map with stuff before I've built enough prison cells.
I don't like the repetitive sound and background noise mechanics, as they tend to grate on my nerves after a while. It's too busy, and no one likes institutional-like background noise like scraping chairs and people talking and such. I know they did it to keep the game more realistic, but some alternative options would have been great.
There are some minor bugs in the game, but bug fixing is relatively quick.
I hate how building new foundations onto an existing series of walls (shared with a neighbouring room) wipes the walls out and also resets your guard patrols and your allocated number of prisoners working in that room. It's very frustrating having to remember to assign both again every time you build onto a common wall.
The 'planning' feature is great. I love laying down "ghost" walls to plan the whole prison layout (on pause) before I build. I only discovered this later in the game, but I recommend you use it every time.
I highly recommend this game.

RATING: 8.5 - [ Highly Addictive ]
For a Prison Simulation/Building Management game... this is by far, amazing. For a Simulation/Building Management game... this game is pretty great... but falls a bit short with some very small bugs and lack of little personal touches.
I wish the prisoners, guards and the general people that populate this little world... had personalities that affect the gameplay. I would definitely say once you pop... you can't stop... and you too will be delighted in this basic yet heavily advanced game. But for the most part... you will be constantly building, changing, tearing down and discovering what works for you... and what works for the game.

Just finished the campaign after taking my sweet time to finish it (63 hours). This game in incredible, you'll lose half your sleeping life to it and not even mind. There's a pretty basic recipe to achieve success in each mission or prison, which takes some time to learn, but there is a great degree of freedom and diversity in the layout of your prison you can take advantage of once you have the recipe down in order to keep things interesting.
The campaign doesn't explain all the game mechanics too well, I think a more comprehensive tutorial would have been a nice touch. The Wiki help option in the menu is your friend, use it often, and read up on other stuff as there are many things that don't get explained to you in the campaign.
You can also purchase surrounding land to enlarge your prison later as you become thirsty for more, which is a great feature, as I tend to fill the map with stuff before I've built enough prison cells.
I don't like the repetitive sound and background noise mechanics, as they tend to grate on my nerves after a while. It's too busy, and no one likes institutional-like background noise like scraping chairs and people talking and such. I know they did it to keep the game more realistic, but some alternative options would have been great.
There are some minor bugs in the game, but bug fixing is relatively quick.
I hate how building new foundations onto an existing series of walls (shared with a neighbouring room) wipes the walls out and also resets your guard patrols and your allocated number of prisoners working in that room. It's very frustrating having to remember to assign both again every time you build onto a common wall.
The 'planning' feature is great. I love laying down "ghost" walls to plan the whole prison layout (on pause) before I build. I only discovered this later in the game, but I recommend you use it every time.
I highly recommend this game.

Not revamped, not rejigged, not redesigned. Reloaded. APB's new suffix is apt, as this free-to-play reincarnation of 2010's deflated cops and robbers MMO is a retread of the same ground. The same drab city, the same hollow combat, the same lopsided results.
The original city of San Paro has been left standing, a monument to badly judged level design and the colour grey. The first game's devs, Realtime Worlds, intended the place to live and breathe. Instead, it spluttered a few times before its life support failed. Its resurrection is a miserable one.
Reloaded's missions usually pit two small squads of human-controlled criminals and enforcers against each other, asking them to perform a multi-stage series of mini-jobs. One team has to drive to a place, collect a thing, and deliver it somewhere else. The other team has to stop them. Occasionally this leads to the kind of scenes that flicker through the minds of non-players when you describe APB to them: high-speed chases through busy streets, lastsecond jumps into getaway cars.
These do happen more regularly than before – little adrenaline shocks to punctuate hours spent bumbling around between jobs. More often, playing Reloaded's missions is like beating your head against one of San Paro's flat, grey concrete walls.
Mission locations are invariably overlooked by high ground. The first team to occupy that ground is the de facto winner, possessing sufficient cover to pop anyone who comes close. Grenades can't flush them out. Well-versed players will simply set up camp in an unassailable location and sit out ten minutes of screaming frustration. San Paro is so full of hiding spots and high ground that it's far easier to put someone else's mission under lockdown than it is to complete your own.
Urban renewal doesn't seem to have been high on GamersFirst's list of priorities: APB had the same spatial problems, and the same tiresome missions. The new devs have instead focused on the economy. Reloaded is free to play, supported by item, modification and vehicle sales, as well as a premium semi-subscription option. Steer clear of the latter and you get obnoxious little reminders telling you what you could've won in XP and in-game currency if you'd stumped up the cash.

If you love COD or anything like it and can get down with customizing , this is the game for you.
That being said, i can't stand this game anymore.
The set up is awesome, the customization is awesome, the map lay outs are detailed and super expansive. But the matching system is broken. As a newbie you can easily find yourself up against the best of the game right from the start.
There are servers dedicated to different player ranks but it hardly matters. The gun you start out with is an ar that might as well be a airsoft. when your enemy comes at you with a bazooka. While the developers have done what they can to make this game fair for everyone they really over looked certain aspects.
Hit boxes are a joke, there are no critcal hit (headshot) areas, your just one big block. oh and even if your character is small, your hit box is still the same size as if you made the largest possible character.
the weapons in the game are exspansive, and while you can TECHNICALLY get any gun that anyone else has, it requires some serious dedication to unlock them all, let alone rent them< (yes RENT) but even then someone always seems to have a better gun than you some how, and with no way of knowing what others are using, good luck guessing what to aim for.
Speaking of aim, recoil is HEAVY in this game. sure might make it realistic but when it destorys the point of a weapon.
for instance, loads of sniper rifles in this game, problem? none of them are 1 hit kill (which is obviously an attempt to balance the game) but the recoil on them is so heavy you will never get your second killing shot off in time to get your target unless they are inexperianced (which is rare) as such SR are rarly used.
the most common gun use you will see are assult rifles, light machine guns, and anything explosive.
any other gun is a waste of your time , and of course those are some of the hardest weapons to get the best of.
my main beef with this game is the combat, simply from being completly out classed as a new player with no way to train up and become better except to be fodder for everyone else and lose match after match.
however i must also state, the driving controls are pretty wonky as well, very easy to flip over your car from taking a slightly too tight turn.
Enemies also make heavy use of the slightly broken vehical issues.
like being able to blow up your car, with you in it, to get that 1 hit kill. or hiding key items in a spawned car that you cant access and waiting for the timer to tick away. its a pretty low tactic but one that works so well, its common.

in Space is an addictive, surprisingly enjoyable space shooter with enjoyably simplistic mechanics. As a ship with what basically amounts to a peashooter strapped to it, you fire at coloured shapes to stop them from reaching past your defences. However with each shot your defensive line edges forward, making the game harder and harder. This is where the aformentioned simplistic mechanics come in. In one mode of the game you need to destroy three or more of the same coloured shape to get your defensive line to move back. In another, you have to time your shots and destroy ships in rapid succession  to get it to recede.
This mechanic is really cool and nifty and makes the game fun to play. It requires pinpoint accuracy and you only really have yourself to blame if you break your combo.
Throw in some cool Atari Esque visuals and a decent soundtrack and you've got a game that is more than worth the 79p it's sold for.

This game is beautiful. The worlds are atmospheric and vibrant to the extreme, the lighting and effects are impactful, the machinery and structures are delightful, and the characters and animations are beyond loveable. Interaction is satisfying, with particle and sound effects perfectly complementing intuitive item management and world interaction without the use of text heavy 2D menus. Progression makes sense in a familiar and attainable way. Build an elaborate array of platforms and machines based on your needs. Exploration and death is daunting but aided by various items, strategies and precautions. Astroneer features an impressive terrain deformation system which is surprisingly robust and easy to manipulate. I was able to build a simple wall around my base, and a tunnel that goes underneath to keep safe during sand storms, without the need for much practice. The music is smooth and dreamy. It's comparable to Minecraft - not revolutionary, but very pleasing.
There are many other reasons to praise the game, simple drop-in multiplayer for example, but I thought I would mention a few issues as well for the sake of balance. Some of these coincide with the fact that game is currently in early access. Everyone has their own opinion on what that means so I won't bother to advocate for or against the principle of it, just know that I recommend the game wholeheartedly as it is in its current state.
My biggest grievance as of writing this is with performance. My framerate has suffered at times, I estimate due to some combination of extended periods of planetary exploration, increased complexity of save data (base construction, terrain modification), and perhaps other contextual factors like weather effects or multiplayer synchronization. Obviously this could be hardware related, some of my components are starting to show their age. There are only a few configurations to adjust to improve performance, so don't expect much flexibility. Among the few graphics options are a slider for draw distance, a toggle for v-sync, and a few other essentials. I was able to improve my framerate by dropping the draw distance, but you can imagine this results in pretty severely delayed object population. Thankfully it seems to only affect non-critical objects. I have found that Locomotion in general is a little floaty, in part due to gravity varying from planet to planet. I occasionally lose control both while on-foot and when operating land vehicles, which can be hilariously and frustratingly fatal. I have also found the MMO-style right-click camera control to occasionally behave strangely. possibly due to playing in windowed mode. Finally, do expect to encounter some bugs, mostly related to quirky physics mixed with the above.
I highly recommend Astroneer. It is one of the most charming games I've played in a while, and a striking example of tasteful compromise.

I honestly love this game and think its definitely a 9.5/10 with only two subjective cons. First, I think they should have added a 3rd person mode to the game, not like fallout and skyrims ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones, but more of a classical option like you could choose it at the beginning would've been great. I think they redeemed themselves by making Battleborn in my opinion though. From the outside, Borderlands 2 looks like it is just your regular FPS game, and in some way it is true, but you'll be doing this game an injustice if you only thought that far.
As a FPS game goes, it's one of the best FPS games I've ever played, and that is saying a lot.
There are many reasons why I praise it, so let's begin.
The graphics are some of the most unique I've seen in a game. Whilst most FPS games try to go for realism, Borderlands 2 can't give a damn about that. Show me screenshots of al the popular FPS games right now, and Borderlands 2 will stick out like a sore thumb. This game has an identity.
The sound design is on point. Weapons made by Jakobs have a very mechanical sound, due to them being very old-school, mechanical weapons. The same can't be said for makes like Hyperion and Maliwan, which are very futuristic and differ greatly in every aspect.
The enemies are amazing in this game. Their taunts and fighting styles are very varied and unique, and sometimes I don’t kill them immediately, just so I can hear what they are going to say next. On the higher levels they can be very challenging too, so you always have to push yourself to stay ahead of the game. Challenging, but just as rewarding.
The soundtrack, oh my GOD the soundtrack! It’s awesome! Each area has such a unique atmosphere and the music simply amplifies that by a factor of 100. If I listen to each song, I know exactly where it is played. It’s one of those soundtracks that you can listen to completely on its own, and it will still be awesome.
The leveling system is very robust and adaptable. Even though you have four playable characters in the vanilla game, the amount of options you can chose from when leveling up can lead to one character having different play styles on their own, essentially increasing the amount of different ways you can play.
The story is satisfactory, but little else. It’s not horrible or the most complex, but it does get you involved and caring for each character. Job done.
In conclusion, I highly recommend you buy this game and KILL JACK!

March of War: Face Off is quite a decent game. As a newcomer to CCG's (I've dabbled a little with Infinity Wars), in it's current state it's pretty easy to understand. This is helped by there only being two factions currently but I'm assuming this will be expanded as the game progresses, and that would be a logical and sensible step. To limit the game to just two factions overall would be detrimental to it, but while in early access it's ideal. Apart from the strategy of playing various cards, there is also the requirement, once a card is placed, to manoeuver it about the board, to progress toward the base of your opponent while at the same time selecting targets to attack or avoid. Once a card reaches the third row along from your own base, it automatically begins to damage the opponent's base. This adds a whole extra level of strategy of moving various pieces around the baord so to speak.
Now there are some bugs obviously, but the great thing I've noticed so far is that even when the game stops and I have to start again, when I go to commence a new game it actually starts me from where I was in the game, so the game itself isn't lost. That is a bonus at this stage of development, alleviating a lot of frustration.
The game isn't too much of a grind either and I certainly hope the developers provide a realistic avenue for gamers to collect all cards without having to pay for it (as it appears already exixts), though that option is there is you desire to use it. Each day provides a task to complete that gives you some in-game currency (750 coins) and leveling up also gives you some currency ( up to 1000 coins) but not for every level. So just doing that means I can get a new pack of 5 cards (2000 coins) every couple of days. That seems pretty reasonable to me.
There is also a good crafting system whereby if you get repeats of a card you don't want, you can use them to craft cards you do want. It costs 5 cards to get one new card of the same tier (so 5 bronze cards to get one new bronze card for example). I doubt you'd be able to realistically use this system to craft gold cards though, since each higher tier costs a lot of the lower tier cards to craft it (You need 1000 basic cards for example to craft one gold card). That's probably fair too, since I can get gold cards in the packs, though they are rare as they should be.
Anyway, looking forward to where the game progresses and hopeful any new factions keep the war theme happening without going all undead or spiritual. Loving what you've got at the moment.
