This one turned out to be a surprise sleeper for me. A very easy to learn card game that is played out on a 3x7 game grid of squares. You get +1 Manpower (Mana for you Magic fans) per turn automatically (NO LAND SCREWS!!) and each card has a cost to play them (Cast them) and when you play a card it become a unit on the battlefield grid with its own attack power and health rating. Each unit has movement cost and firing arcs (For you fans of Starfleet Battles). The cards and abilities are very well explained. I was up and playing this game in 5 minutes flat. There is a surprising amount of strategy involved with this game for something so basic and simple to learn and play. You have different card types basically unit cards (seperated into organic units - people and mechanical units) and the Command cards (Sorceries) that have a 1-time affect and they go away. At first glance one would think this is a "Pay-to-Win" format but I have done very well in Multi-player and I havent spent a dime yet. You earn experience for playing each match and you can grind against the Bots or humans. As you level up you get coins as a reward for making certain levels. You earn coins for playing a PvP match. You earn coins on the Daily (a goal to meet like win 5 games today) ... and I have bought about 7 booster packs so far off these earned coins. You can create your own decks as well. This is one of the FEW FTP games out there that I would highly recommend you give a try. If you like card games and strategy ... this one is for you  ... AAA game IMO.

So far, so good.
As I can see, this game is very similar to RimWorld, in my opinion. So if you liked it, it may also bring you joy and satisfaction. However, Prison Architect is based mostly on how you're spending your money and building the rooms in order for your prison to survive.
First of all, you can get very creative with this game, thing that I love the most. You have plenty of game options, from campaings and "basic prison" mode, to enabling cheats and very hard challanges. I find this very useful If  you want to go through every little piece of content Prison Architect has. struggling or not. While playing, you'll find many handwritten notes from prisoners and I think from staff too hiding on the map. It can be simply an escape plan, or a tip or just some prisoner's thoughts. Also, you'll find a lot of pictures. And all of these notes and images can be accesed via menu, so you won't lose any of them.
Second, the management. You are in control of EVERYTHING; money, bussiness, prisoners and their psyhological needs, staff, investments, time, prison's policy and schedule and a lot more. Basically you need to take care of everything, and it's very challanging. Ups and downs, good or bad choices, everything has a price and you'll pay it whole. Every decision you take will affect your entire facility; rooms position, pipes position, room size, courses you prisoners  attend, food quality and diversity, etc. With this option, you can either build a very well equipped and happy prison with everything your prisoners and staff need, but you can also build a less "comfortable" one, and it will function too. All of them depend on the money you're willing to spend. Don't forget your taxes!
The security; Prisoners are divided in minimum, medium and maximum security. Based on that, they will act diffent from the others and may have different needs and punishments. They all have their unique sentences based on what they did and some of their stories are either funny or ♥♥♥♥ing creepy. For example, a minimum security prisoner just stole a jar of peanut butter and doesn't need much attention, he will mostly be peaceful if you give him what every human being needs and make him attend "How to not be a jerk" classes. But a maximum security prison is a sick psycho. It's obvious if you kill your entire family with a fork you'll be called "The FORK killer" your entire life and punished much harder in prison, even executed. You decide the punishments and how hard they are.
Long story short, there is much more to talk about. If you love to manage, to be in control and to build from scrach a facility, this game is for you. Loving it, playing it.

They are going to work on making sure the game runs well, and the features work properly, then they will work on making it shine. Also know as, FORM FOLLOWS FUNCTION. If you must have multiplayer, fancy graphics, and cannot tolerate regular bugs and the like, don't play it yet. If you're like me and possess some patience and a willingness to not only experience the bugs but try to hunt them down and let the devs know, buy and play away!

For Sonic's first true jump into the 3D world, it did a fine job to bring a great game to the table at the time, but many set backs and flaws keep it from being a great game today. I guess what I'm trying to say is that this game has aged.  It's obvious by now that the best parts about this game are the main trio's portions of the game. I'll go ahead and say this right now, the classic series are superior in quality in terms of gameplay. If you're into the nostalgic aspect, go ahead and give the game a try once again like you did with your Dreamcast, but if you're getting into the series, give it a go if you're willing to go for the whole game, because I can't guarantee you'll enjoy the entire experience.
Bad: The animation during cutscenes are sloppy and downright horrible. The voice acting is questionable as well. Amy's portions are slow and dull, Gamma is a shooting fest, and Big...... The story overall is meh. Each character has their own respected stories, but none of them are really that intriguing and the overall story focusing on Chaos is just executed poorly. Sonic gets Eggman with Tails, Knuckles finds the emerald pieces, Amy helps a bird, Gamma saves his fellow robots, and Big fishes. This all leads up to Eggman using a water creature that uses the emeralds to become huge and destroy Station Square. No, There's no need to use the /spoiler because in the end what really matters is everything else.
Good: Sonic's gameplay is chock full of exploration and contains fast paced platforming. Tails and Knuckles are basically the same, they just have less stages. I don't mind the emerald hunting much in this game because it's done pretty well.
None of the stages between these three feel like a chore or take 50k years to finish. Also, this game gives Sonic the BEST control he's ever had in 3D. The music is AMAZING. I ♥♥♥♥ING LOVE this soundtrack to death.
Because this isn't a full fledged review, I may be jumping the gun a bit here but, this game has aged. I can't guarantee that everyone will enjoy this game in the state it's in, but remember this is a decade old. The best parts are only half the game, and that can be a problem for some people. I say, if you've always been a Sonic fan like me, go for it, if you're getting into the series, go for Generations or even the Classic series, then come back to this if you want. If you're curious or just don't care, go for it, you may really enjoy it.
TL DR; It may be♥♥♥♥♥♥for some people, but for others it may be a gem, it depends on your tastes. So go play a Sonic game unanimously considered good before you come back to this.

I have always been a fan of the classic series, the 'original Devil May Cry' if you will, and it took me years to finally warm up to this game.
With that said, all in all the game itself is immensely satisfying. I managed to get over my initial hang-ups about Dante and Vergil’s drastic changes from the original series and took a good hard look at the story line and the game play.
It’s relatively easy to follow, game play is smooth and the story is well played out for a Devil May Cry audience of the 2000’s.
My only real displeasure with this game was the drastic departure from the original series which again is why it took me YEARS to actually play the game. Rather than being half demons, Dante and Vergil are Nephilim. Rather than their mother being human, she was an angel. Rather than their father Sparda being a demon knight who turned against his brethren for the sake of mankind, he was the blood brother of antagonist Mundus.
All that I feel takes away from the original feel of the series. It spoke a lot to the character of Sparda because he turned his back on his own kind for the sake of humans and even took a human wife.
The only other thing that REALLY bothers me about the game is how they pronounce the names; particularly Eva and Mundus. To grating on the ears for my taste.
In truth, this game is fantastic… If it’s not Devil May Cry. It took away too much of what made DMC what it is to be a true ‘reboot’ of such a classic series. Still recommend you give it a try though!... After you play the original series first.

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥.. this game is rough. The good reviews, well edited trailers, and neat concept fooled me. It might be a good game, but at this point it's pretty far off.
AI is hilariousy bad. Graphics are worse. The under water area on the game is indescribebly barren and the trailers make it seem MUCH more than it is. The "fight off" pirates part is a hilarious misrepresentation of what combat is all about.
Combat is as follows: Upbeat string music begins playing, you look around and spot a dingy with a driver and a man firing at you. The boat pulls up to within about 15-20 feet of you (every time) from whatever intial angle of attack they first came in on, with no variation, maneuvering, or semblence of any real AI. They cant shoot through the cabin of the boat, so you just time the shots and peak between firing, because otherwise the gunner WILL hit you as they have laser accuracy at whatever distance they can engage. Both driver and gunner take 3 shots each, if the gunner is killed first the boat immediately does a u-turn and tries to flee,  if you kill the driver the boat sinks, you get some loot. And then another one comes... And another. And another. Annnnd another. Until you destroy a beacon with 50 shots or about 300 swings of an axe. Enemies on platforms stand entirely still, no seeking cover, no running from shots, and no rection to being shot. As stated turrets and pirates can engage from a long distance and will hit you EVERY SINGLE TIME. So in the case of attacking a pirate fort... there's probably 15 people and 5 or so turrets firing at once, making it impossible to even leave your cabin.
I'm sure if the dev is worth his salt and continues to work on it, it could be a pretty cool game. But at the moment it's far too rough. $15 is even too much at this point.

Landless is the debut Steam title from indie developer, CodeBullet.
In Landless you play an unseen and unnamed woman living on a little boat in the post-apocalyptic Earth of the future. The seas have risen far beyond the most pessimistic predictions of global warming spruikers, leaving the remnants of Earth's population clinging to survival on boats, floating towns, and the few very small islands of land that remain.
You begin the game drifting along on a semi-procedurally-generated ocean-based map (some components, such as the first town and research tower, are fixed in every game). There's a brief tutorial that introduces you to some basic principles: starting, moving, and stopping your biofuel-powered boat; interacting with people; and gaining strange black boxes by destroying the increasingly well-defended "Ecotech research beacons". These you can then trade for technology points to buy new blueprints for crafting. The economy is based on "woil': whale oil, which you can use to buy most goods from traders, and also have to spend to craft items, but which seems to be strangely unobtainable from whales.
There seems to be quite an interesting back story with various factions, but currently it's only hinted at here and there, so I've not yet learned enough to know what's really going on. Unlike many survival sandbox games, though, Landless has a quest system so your tasks are a bit more goal-oriented than many other games in the genre.
Ultimately, Ecotech seems to be the enemy. Destroy Ecotech towers to unlock cool stuff, collect resources and craft other cool stuff, and try very, very hard to not run out of fuel.
Landless is played in 3D from first-person perspective. I feel a bit mean saying it, but honestly most of the graphics are not that great. The game looks like a low-budget Waterworld.
Characters are poorly modelled and animated. Most of the world models and textures don't look much better, though there are a few exceptions. When you swing your axe, little cut marks stay visible for a few seconds, like crosshatching in the air. The underwater sections (deep diving and swimming) somehow look even worse. And for a game that's set in a world almost completely inundated with oceans, the water is even disappointing sometimes.
Okay, now that's out of the way, I will say that the waves look pretty nice, as does the day-night cycle, and there are some great effects. It's lovely and peaceful just drifting along under a full moon and the starry sky, and the sunset and sunrise colouring and water reflections are quite nice to look at, if not completely realistic. Shadows aren't bad, either, and some of the models are okay.
The interface isn't that great, either. Parts of it aren't exactly obvious, and some sort of highlighting of in-game objects when you're near enough to interact would be useful. There are missing tooltips and some icons that aren't obvious as to what they mean. This all creates a steeper learning curve than necessary, but once you work out what you're doing it's not so bad. ProTip: press ALT to enter 'cursor mode' so you can select interface icons.
There are a few graphics options, but no vsync; running the game made my GPU fan go pretty wild.
I've only heard a very small number of music tracks and they get a bit repetitive. There's a simple and catchy tune that makes for good travelling music. There's also a western saloon - style ditty in towns, and a higher-tempo, dramatic combat tune. I think that might be it. All are well produced and sound pretty nice.
Sound effects are okay, but nothing special. The boat's motor sound seems a bit too loud, while gunshots seem very quiet, but it could be the weird volume controls causing me issues. I turned it up to full to start with and had hideously loud distortion even though my system volume was only set to about 20%. I eventually got it adjusted so there was no distortion, but normalisation seems off.
There are no voices, I think.
Landless's controls are pretty typical for a first-person shooter: WASD to move, mouse to aim and shoot, and a handful of keys to interact with the game. The default keys are okay (though some don't work) and are remappable, but at the moment only from the standard Unity launcher when you first launch the game. I'm hoping the developers will add some in-game control settings.
Basic gameplay involves puttering around in your boat looking for loot (randomly spawned floating boxes are common), blowing up Ecotech towers (fighting off the pirates that come out of nowhere to attack you), collecting basic materials, crafting, and taking on contracts (side quests) that come in on the radio. You can also fish, trade, and explore, as long as you have enough fuel. If you do really well, or visit a town with a deep-sea diving suit, you can also dive down to the ocean floor and look for more loot among the old rusting hulks of ocean vessels, as well as detritus from the old surface cities. It's not as grand as it sounds, though.
There's quite a lot of stuff to craft, which is pretty cool, but the crafting system is weird. Everything costs woil to craft as well as basic ingredients, which doesn't make sense. One of the most interesting things to craft is your own floating building that you can choose to tow along behind your boat like an aquatic caravan! It's a great concept, but even the most basic structure will take you quite a while to build as the raw materials can be hard to come by.
The main plot concerns downloading information on the Ecotech headquarters through a satellite link, then going there and causing havoc. It's not that well explained, though, and so far I've not got very far towards it, but I do like the idea of having an overriding goal structure to a sandbox game, to pursue if and when I feel like it.
I've encountered a few more bugs and other issues, but I expect they'll be addressed by the time the game is released out of EA:
- Wonky physics: a whale touched my boat and it flipped over, with no way of getting it back again; rough seas bounce you around and prevent interaction because the game thinks you're moving; you get stuck on geometry often; unrealistic movement: swimming is running through the water, running is like gliding really fast, and boats stop immediately when you cut the engine, like driving Automan's car; and why can't I pull myself up onto a sloped floating platform without a ramp?
- The sleep/save option saves, but doesn't sleep; to sleep you have to nap.
- Make sure you don't loot when your inventory is full; the items disappear.
- I don't understand what happens when you die; it says "game over", but then you respawn back in town.
- Poor grammar.
- Swimming controls are awful, like bobbing for apples.
- The economy is broken. There's no point crafting to make money; requiring woil to craft anything is illogical and breaks the game. It's a shame because the crafting is really good fun.
- Has no one heard of sails!?
Pros:
+ Great idea; fun crafting
+ Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Broken economy and crafting costs
- VERY rough around the edges
After a couple of hours I was getting pretty frustrated with Landless, but I think the RNG had been giving me a bad trot. After restarting again I had a much better time, even finding enough raw resources to refuel my boat and build a little floating caravan.
If you're a fan of survival-crafting games and don't mind some bodgy graphics and physics and quite a few rough edges, then by all means pick up Landless and have a play around. There's a lot to do already, and I can only assume that will increase further as the game goes through Early Access.

This is a very faithful port of Sonic Adventure DX to the PC, which is both good and bad. Good in that it'll be exactly how you remember it, but bad in that it'll be exactly how you remember it. This port brings no changes to the physics system, which can be sometimes janky depending on what you think the input should be versus what input the game wants, and the story still has the occasional odd moment that makes you wonder exactly why you are playing.
There is little issue getting this title to run on a Windows 7 machine unless you want to play full screen. The included configuration tool just doesn't work without adding a small registry key change that you can find in the Steam forums. Making matters worse, the full screen option is kind of a misnomer because the actual game play is boxed in by a border when playing on an wide screen monitor. I know the original game was meant for 4:3 displays, but it shouldn't take any effort at all to include varied resolution options on the PC (especially when the next game in the Sonic Adventure series has these options).
As for controls, a gamepad is certainly recommended, but it isn't unplayable without one. I actually found that I had an easier time lining Sonic up with lines of rings with the keyboard controls, but overall (considering this was originally a console game) it feels much more natural with a gamepad. This is the first fully 3D Sonic game, so the camera leaves something to be desired, but it doesn't impede gameplay most of the time. The camera is only a real nuisance when navigating the forest in the Mystic Ruins Adventure Field.
Like I stated before, this is a faithful port, so don't go into this expecting any kind of extra missions or features. The game's page from within Steam shows Achievements, but they actually do not work at all as of the writing of this review.
The story is hit and miss. I imagine most will play this once and never play it again. There are problems with the pacing given the way that they divided it between six playable characters. You get to experience the perspective of each character's place in the plot at large, but this means revisiting some scenes multiple times. It helps that the dialogue is slightly altered when playing as different characters, but this doesn't shake the feeling of, "Been there, done that." Occasionally, the delivery of some of the lines is particularly narmy, but the voice acting is otherwise acceptable (though Eggman's character actually benefits from the over the top performance). The most egregious example of "Been there, done that" by far is through the credits. The game ultimately has an ending that wraps everything up, but you have to sit through the same unskippable credits after finishing each character's individual arc.
The levels are extremely linear and this may seem contradictory, but the level design is actually great. There is a nice variety of enemies and obstacles, and levels don't drag on for too long. The game has an excellent soundtrack, so you won't find yourself wanting to rush through the levels anyways. The fishing levels really aren't any fun, but they are relatively painless because you can skip straight to the objective of the level.
Aside from the actual stages themselves, the Adventure Field is an interesting way of organizing the game, but it can feel tedious at times when looking for items to unlock the next level. The few boss battles in the game aren't difficult at all, but neither were the ones in the 2D Sonic games. However, the more sudden variety of boss battles are a complete joke since the AI doesn't usually even get a chance to attack.
Despite its flaws, I still recommend playing Sonic Adventure DX at least once. It may not be the greatest platforming/action game of all time, but it is a great effort by the Dreamcast-era Sonic Team. They manage to successfully capture the mood of the plot and platforming mechanics of the 2D Sonic games in this initial 3D Sonic offering.
This game brings back so many fond memories! As dated as it may be, if you have played this in the past or even if you are just a fan of the franchise, this game is a must get!

March Of War: Face Off is a Collectable Card Game with Strategy elements, unlike most card games this game put a lot of focus on movement with cards being played on 3 by 7 grid.
The game requires player to attempt to defeat the opponent by reduces their life from 20 to 0. To do this you must move characters into the damage zones which increase as you get further across the board. The game does a great job of integrating card mechanics that take advantage of this aspect of the game with each card having a different movement cost, movement per turn and attack direction for a diverse card pool.
While it isn't graphical impressive as well as me personally being a big fan of the aesthetic of the game, I found that I could move past it as the gameplay is engaging, fun and fair.
I found the animations to be a strong point of this game with them looking genuine and interesting to watch.
Music seems to consist of 3 tracks played on repeat with a 10 minute silence before repeating the loop, however this could be a bug or a personal problem I had so keep that in mind.
As a final point I want to mention that the game is free to play not pay to win. The game uses the same system as Hearthstone. Awarding playing for completing daily objectives and levelling! Unlike Hearthstone however it also has a recommendation system awarding you and the recommended player currency just for joining the game and reaching level 10 (Not payment from you or the recommended player required!).
In conclusion March of War: Face Off has an interesting basis for a card game which incorporates movement as a cornerstone of it's game design with a few kinks in needs to sort out, which is expected due to it's Early Access state! Heavily Recommended for experts and new comers of Card games a like!

Normally I am lenient towards bad games, but this may be the worst I've ever played. The only redeeming quality I can think of is the price tag, because you cannot justify charging people money to play this "game", it is only right that it's free. It occurred to me that it may be aimed at VR users, but it's not VR-enabled, and it would probably be just as terrible on VR anyway, so there's that.
The gameplay starts with you outside your crashed landing capsule on the moon, and a woman telling you via radio you have been separated from your companions, and must find them. She doesn't know where they are, but she marks 5 possible places, each several kilometres away, on your HUD and tells you to pick one and go to it. You have to rely on dumb luck and hope that you've picked the right one, because you won't have the oxygen to go to more than one or two.
Literally all you do in this game is walk across the surface of the moon. Sounds relaxing, even therapeutic, right? Wrong. You might as well go out for a walk in the park IRL, because there's nothing scenic, picturesque, or aesthetically pleasing about this game. Just barren rock as far as the eye can see, and walking. And meteorites. Lots and lots of meteorites, constantly hitting the surface, which are the only immediate threat besides running out of oxygen.
This game was built with a unity engine, so that should give a fair idea of how the grapics will look, and how abysmal the physics are. The aforementioned meteorites are probably the most comically bad assets they've used, for a multitude of reasons. They don't form craters on impact with the surface - they bounce, then disappear. If you actually get hit by one - you'll only lose about 5% of your oxygen, even though a pea-sized one would kill you IRL. After hitting the moon's surface, the meteorites will bounce right through you. I have had meteorites the size of small elephants just bounce off my character's head, which was hilarious. Furthermore, I have also run into a steep incline and been launched 50 metres in the air as a result. Terrible physics.

Batman Arkham series is held high for perfect depiction of Batman universe. Arkham City is considered the best Arkham game in the franchise and Arkham Origins is nearly ignored for being lame. But its not correct. This is as good as Arkham City.
Arkham Origins takes you through the initial years of Bruce Wayne as Batman. It is a direct prequel to Arkham Asylum. The best thing about Origins is the story/game progression. I will term it 'epic'. You may think the starting pace is little slow, but as it progresses it becomes very intriguing and at times emotional. I adore its storyline! To play this story, you get a bigger playground ....map bigger than Arkham City.
And the time.....its Christmas eve! Who doesnt love christmas time? And to go with that, you have a perfect bgm. Christopher Drake did a fantastic job in combining and serving the dark theme with sleigh bells depicting the atmosphere impeccably.
The dialogues are perfect. Voice over....perfect! But wait....there is no Kevin Conroy or Mark Hamill?! Yes, the devs chose to pick Roger Craig Smith (beloved Ezio's voice) and Troy Baker (another genius of the industry) to play young Batman and Joker. Amazingly delivered performance! Both did full justice to their respective characters. I never missed Kevin or Mark during whole game. Roger and Troy are both genius of this industry and glad i could hear their voices as Batman and Joker.
Combat stays pretty much the same if you've played previous arkham games. Every gadget is same except for few new ones. What this game really excels is in the
You will see one of the best boss fights in this game....as said by many gamers. You can't just buttonmash! Each boss is unique in its own way, each plays differently. Defeating these bosses is very satisfying experience as they can get difficult at times.
Only major downside, the side quests/collectibles. I loved finding the nicely hidden Riddler's trophies in Arkham City. It was very satisfying finding each one, as you have to
to get that trophy. In Origins, you just throw batarang, and collect data packs or something. Very uninteresting. Anarky spreads some symbols thoughout Origins map for you do discover and some other not so interesting quests/collectibles. Arkham Ciy nails it in this aspect.
I didn't encounter any kind of crash or bug or glitch in the game. And it ran pretty smooth on my potato as well. Great job WB!

A solid reimagining for the long running series. The combat remains fluid, the gameplay is faithful to the original and the game runs smoothly. The new story is rather forgettable but it’s worth it on sale or if you’re curious. Recommended with a gamepad. Playthrough lasts about 10 hours.
This is an action adventure game with a change in developer but it remains fairly faithful to the series’ gameplay. This major element is combat but there is also exploration, platforming and a more well realised story.
The combat remains the best part of the game with a mix of combos, weapons, techniques and enemies to use them on. On the starting difficulty it can feel a little like the game takes away your meal before you’re done chewing with small arenas and low numbers of enemies. It is hard to balance short stages for everyone but a few more enemy types and harder bosses would have been an improvement.
The platforming looks nice but isn’t interesting. It is very scripted and just requires you to use your grappling hook when prompted. It had occasional problems registering when I could hook onto something which I thought was in range but I wasn’t in exactly the right spot for it to work.
The major change that the new developer has brought is a more realistic tone for the story and visual design. The style is eclectic, focusing on twisting everyday scenery to a demonic netherworld, and is generally successful if a little hit and miss. The highlight for me was the giant statues and shattered masonry over the sea. The nightclub stage with strobing dancefloor demon battles was hard to look at and can go to hell (haha).
To be fair I don’t recall the original devil may cry story. Something about demon hunting maybe? It was never the focus of the original and unfortunately here it’s just not very engaging. The tone stumbles between comic book fiction and heavy handed analogies between demons and the current affairs of 2010. Granted it’s hard to tell an engaging story in an action game where every battle begins with the hero, Dante, walking up to a demon who says ‘you will die Dante, you are not strong!’ and then Dante replies ‘No, it is you who will die!’.
Technically the game runs very well and looks great, PC ports of console games are often pants, here you have fully customisable controls and full options for tweaking visual settings.
Overall I would recommend it for it’s style and combat if you can find it on sale.

When Borderlands was released back in 2009, it surprised everyone with it's unique hybrid of shooting and role playing. Borderlands was definitely unique, and personally, I thought it was the first true RPG/FPS hybrid. Sure, there were games like System Shock 2 beforehand, but SS2 isn't so much a shooter as it is an action role playing survival horror hybrid, and from a FPS standpoint, it's actually horribly repetitive and clunky. But Borderlands combined Diablo-style looting and frantic FPS combat, all the while providing for some of the most intense and satisfying gun play in a shooter. Borderlands was definitely a breath of fresh air in the FPS market, and it's a darn shame we don't have more games in the genre like it. Now, Borderlands is back with this top notch sequel, and the series is better than ever.
I won't say too much about the single player experience, but given the amount of missions available, it seems Borderlands 2 will provide a lengthy, satisfying experience. I'm not finished with the game yet, but I can tell that it isn't going to end any time soon. People who have beaten it already have said the game will take around 30 hours to complete, so single player fans will be satisfied. From what I gather, numerous reviewers are saying that you will want to play through the entire game more than once (!) as well, thanks in part to it's diverse skill classes. Even better, Borderlands 2 now let's you play the entire game with all of your stats in tow, so expect some heady replay value for single player.

An excellent game back in the 90s and even now i still consider it one of the best Sonic games and my personal favorite 3D Sonic game. Sonic Adventure DX is the remake of Dreamcast's launch title Sonic Adventure and it's still considered the very best of Sonic's 3D carrier and for very good reasons.
The game actually haves a complicated story though not as good as Sonic Adventure 2's story (That game's story was fantastic). Instead of the classic old school "saving the forest and the animals from an evil dictator" this game actually haves Sonic interacting with humans for the first time and the story involves a lethal water-like creature possessed by Dr.Eggman called "Chaos" the only guy who can stop Chaos' rampage is the one and only Sonic The Hedgehog but this time he's not alone.
In this story every Sonic character takes the spot from the little flying fox Tails to the super strong Echidna Knuckles and even the little pink hedgehog Amy Rose from Sonic CD makes a return this time with a very different make up and also two new comers E-102 Gamma and Big the Cat.
The gameplay is basically (with the exception of Amy, Gamma and Big) the classic team's transition to 3D and because of that the characters have their old abilities only with new power ups and new skills like the homing attack and the light-speed dash
The controls are the best in any 3D game, the characters control just like they should and it's very helpful because this game is everything but linear as the hubs and levels are very big and while it's still "go from point A to point B" you never have to take a specific path because there are a lot of shortcuts.
The music is awesome and i'm my opinion one of the best of Sonic, the themes, the hubs, the levels and don't forget about "Open your Heart" which was very well composed.
Unfortunately the game has problems like the voice acting and the cutscenes and the DX version includes tons of glitches that ironically weren't in the original version.
Overall it's a great game and the DX version includes various extras like Mission mode, Metal Sonic and the Game Gear games (only in the original PC version and the GC) i suggest to give it a try.

I just started playing this game today, and a dev asked me to write a review if I liked the game, so here I am, writing my first steam review. While this isn't the first game I've enjoyed on steam, this IS the first time I've spoken to a dev of a game I've liked.
This game is like chess, in the sense that you compete to control the middle of the board and you maneuver your pieces to gain an advantage over the opponent. Except everyone creates their own team of pieces, so there are many many ways to achieve that goal. As you unlock new cards new strategies and tactics are opened up, and it is very very interesting to think about how you'll go about winning a match.
Increasing your collection is not hard, you get coins and cards by just playing, and recycling unnecessary cards gives you gems to get even more cards so  there really is no need to spend a single cent unless you want to. Also, I liked how there is no way to get a truly OP deck as you are limited in how many cards of a certain level you can have in your deck (e.g. only one copy of a gold card is allowed per deck), and more powerful cards will have higher costs to play.
The community is just downright amazing. Let me tell you a story. My last match today was against this dude named MING with a marvelously appropriate character protrait of a chinese warlord. He was soundly whooping my♥♥♥♥♥while friendlily giving me great tips on how to improve. Suddenly, I realised that I had totally lost track of time and was now late for lunch. I apologized profusely while begging my leave, hoping he would not think I was giving up because he was ahead.
He did something I have never ever experienced in any other pvp game ever. He surrendered so I'd get more rewards from the game. Wow. *speechless
So to sum up March of War: Face Off
Pros:
+Great, hands-on and involved Devs
+Deep strategy and gameplay
+Awesome, friendly community
+NOT p2w
Cons:
-Made me lose track of time and be late for lunch

This was the first Arkham game I played. Needless to say I binge-played it and ended up sad when it was over.
10/10

This game had intrigued me ever since I first saw the trailer with all these assassins coming after him. After I got it I immediately began to like it and it is now one of my all time favorite games, it being the most played game I actually own.
Likes:
The unique Boss battles, not every boss has the same idea and concept behind it and each fight between bosses has a new spin and taste to it so nothing is repetitive. Deathstroke was near impossible for me to defeat but once I finally did he is one of the easiest bosses (Electrocutioner being the easiest of them all, no idea why he seemed to be such a tough talker-play the game to understand what I mean-) and the most fun to fight.
The predator and combat maps, some would say its cheating to use the custom maps but I love it. The ability to upgrade batman is one of the most fun things to do. I have the feeling of being a tough Batman. However, I also like using the de-buffs. I like a challenge and I have been surly tempted to activate every single one just to see if I can do it.
Side missions. It really gave me a feeling of being a true vigilante protecting the city when I have to solve the murder cases and stop the crimes in progress. I liked being so similar to the actual Batman I so envisioned in my mind.
The voices. It was rather surprising to find Batman’s voice to be so different than the normal Kevin Conroy, but Roger Smith’s version was a pretty cool version as well. It defiantly sounded younger and made a much better voice for interrogation. It seemed darker than Kevin Conroy’s and the coldness in the voice really gave me the feeling that Batman was in no mood for the criminals messing around.
The snow. It added a lot of mystery to me for some reason and was completely adding to the story somehow. I really liked how cool it was to be in such a weather storm.
The gadgets. I liked how they added the triple baterange. I always wonderd why they did not add this before. Batman is really talented he should be able to throw three at a time with ease. Another gadget I liked was the shock gloves. The buff it gave, though temporary till recharged, were an excellent feature. Being able to block anything and attack anyone is awesome. My favorite tool of them all, though, is the remote claw tool you take from Deathstroke. Attatching objects to people or people to gargoyals for an instant takedown is great, and I love it. I also like how I can basically make two people hug each other after targeting two people together. They fall to the ground stunned and I remain across the room laughing, but then I need to move because they will know where I shot from when they get up.
Bothers:
The walls in parts of the city. This is not Arkham City, why are there big walls around the city that do nothing but act like a castle wall? They do not bother me very much, but when they get in the way and I have to go around them it becomes a bother instead of a nice added feature. It is completely unnecessary anyways; this is a city not a fort or a city prison.
Grapnel accelerator. Do not get me wrong I like this tool; it helps get me around faster. I just dislike the idea during this time period. In Arkham City it was a prototype just being used, so it should not exist in Origins, yet here it is for you to use. I understand why it was kept, but the inconsistency is a danger to avoid, even if it is cool thing to own it is best to plan ahead so this type of issue does not come up. Bad planning is not really a good excuse to use when you are making a series. As for another incocistancy, it would be the changes in the buildings. One that I took great notice was the church. I would say this is a bother, but for some reason I am quite cool with it. As long as the church is where it should be from Arkham City, even if it looks different (not too different for those wondering), then it is okay. Besides, I like this version of the church better than the Arkham City one.
This is not really a bother or a dislike, but it is something I have no use for, the concussion detonator. All it really does is stun people for a short amount of time and it takes about three seconds to explode so not a real useful tool for escapes or takedowns. The only time it is really useful is when I fight copperhead against her hallucinations (that is all I am going to say about it). Otherwise I do not use it at all, unless it is a challenge in game.
Dislikes:
The limited repeats in game. I understand that it is a cool feature to be able to replay the game with all my upgrades, but why only once? Sure, make it more difficult than when I had to continue to level myself up but at least let me be able to replay it with all my gadgets as many times as I want. It is not much of a difference than deleting a save file only to save a new one to start over with.
Out of all of this I dare give this game a 9 out of 10, and if not I will give it 8 out of 10, but nothing lower.

I can't say enough good things about this game.  I was hoping this game would be something different from the usual, relaxing, engaging and beautiful and it is all that and more. I purchased the game in a sale bundle which for a bit less than retail for the core game also included for free the DLC's Going East, Scandinavia, High Value cargo and a couple other cosmetic dodads.   Probably the best value of any of the many games and bundles I've purchased on Steam.
I'm not a hardcore gamer and I'm running this on an older MacBook (which necessitates much lower graphics settings) but playing ET2 is simply a beautiful experience.  It's like spending hours driving through European postcards and yet it provides frequent enough decisions (gas, repairs, job choice,  occasionally difficult driving situations, managing your company, etc...) that 90 hours in I still feel engaged and excited to play more.
As for the visuals, I have to praise the designers. There's so many ways they could have done less and still had a game that was nearly as good, but it's amazing how much detail they include.  As an example, most driving games have areas with tall highway sound barriers and that's the edge of the world, but in ET2 when using the chase camera suddenly you see that on the other side of the barriers is even more of the world: forests or an industrial zone or a castle or a....  Because of this, and even though it's just s smidge more fiddly to drive, I highly recommend using the chase camera when driving during the day.  It's really ups the beauty factor.
Lastly, if you don't have a driving rig I highly recommend a PS2 style controller or other pad with 2 joysticks.  Being able to assign one joystick to the steering and the other to provide an incrmental control for the throttle (accelleration and reverse) makes the trucks much easier to control and the game even more fun to play.  If you need one the Logitech F310 (newer version of what I have) is well rated and tends to go for $15-20 on Amazon. I assure you it will be money very well spent.

Since this game dared to call itself Devil May Cry, it's inevitable that it will be compared to the "real" Devil May Cry games. And that's the one thing I hate most about DmC: it strays too far from the series. Dante and Vergil are now half-demon-half-angel instead of half-demon-half-human. Dante is now black-haired and extremely bad-boy: even the young Dante in DMC3, the most rebellious one in the series, doesn't drink or go to strip clubs or show his d*ck to guests. Vergil now leads an entire Order to battle Mundus, instead of running lone-wolf and hunting for what he wants by himself. The twins are Dante and Vergil by name, but they are not Dante and Vergil. Even almost 5 years after release I still don't accept that they are Dante and Vergil.
However, settings aside, this is a pretty awesome hack-n-slash action game.
There are 5 melee weapons in DmC, some heavy and brutal, some light and swift, some in-between, and each comes with an entire list of moves to let you juggle enemies with style. Add that to the 1-button evasion, and you get a core fighting experience that is highly fluent, stylish, satisfying, and a bit easier than the DMC games.
What DmC did much better than DMC is movement. For enemies you now have the option to pull them towards Dante, or pull Dante towards them. There's a new mid-air move that dashes forward a bit and glides down, helpful when you need to cross a large gap. And there's the forementioned evade button. These new features make the game very acrobatic, even when Dante's not in combat. While in combat these moves make it really easy to perform air combos, too.
One other thing worth mentioning is music. Believe it or not, DmC is where I heard dubstep for the first time in my life. I think this genre fits the game really well, especially during large boss fights, where the lengthy low frequencies of sound greatly enhance the heaviness of the boss.
The story is disappointingly simple. It's so naive that I don't even care to use spoiler tags: Mundus enslaves human, Dante and Vergil plan to kill Mundus, their plans succeed in every step, and finally Mundus dies. There is a minor plot twist at the end but even that feels childish for a modern game's plot. What's even more weird is that at almost every step in the plan, Dante has to repeat and confirm the plan in smaller words. Are the writers treating Dante as an idiot?
Another minor complaint is the lack of manual lock-on. Occasionally I attack an unintended target and lose my rhythm. I also have no way to tell the remaining HP of enemies to plan ahead.
+ Stylish fighting action
+ Swift movement
+ Giant boss fights
+ Epic dubstep music
- Overly simple story
- Complete overhaul of beloved DMC characters
8 out of 10, excellent.

Stylish, over-the-top, and excellently paced game. Narration is much deeper than in previous DmC instalments, and the rehashed Dante, Vergil, and Mundus are way more nuanced and interesting. Combat is fast and engrossing, but a little shallower than your usual DmC: at standard difficulty settings, the game is a walk in the park, and it is only when you unlock the hardest difficulty levels that you come close to a true challenge.

This being a port of a port of a remake (that's how they say it, right?), it's not the worst Sonic game out there.  But it's not quite the best either.
Pros:
-Gameplay-wise, this is still the same as its previous incarnations.  Six playstyles available - Sonic has high-speed Action Stages, Tails' stages involve a "race to the finish" style with lots of shortcuts, Knuckles' stages involve exploration and treasure hunting, Amy's stages require you to outrun a robot that's constantly on your hide, Big's stages involve FISHING of all things (which I'll detail in the Cons later), and Gamma's stages revolve around shooting targets and getting through before time runs out.  Plus, there's a Chao raising system (just not as advanced as Sonic Adventure 2's system), so there's plenty of variety.
-Sound is great.  The game's soundtrack is excellent, especially during the Final Boss.
-Additional sub-games also provide more variety, including shooting targets while flying the Tornado, a whack-a-mole type game, and Boss Rush mode for all characters.
-Unlike the console versions that were released, the Mission Mode and Metal Sonic are automatically included in this version, saving you a chunk of change.
Cons:
-Big the Cat's fishing levels are purely designed to raise one's blood pressure.  Now, I'm not saying this in the terms of this version - I wasn't expecting a remake - I'm saying it in terms of ALL versions, including the GameCube.  This mechanic is broken beyond belief, and it just doesn't sit in with the rest of the play styles.  You'll be wrestling with Big's portion of the game for quite a while, I'll tell you that much.
-Chao raising is fine and dandy, but the races will also raise your blood pressure.  One thing SEGA could've tweaked was the "cheering" system.  Unlike Sonic Adventure 2, which has a meter and only allows you to cheer for your Chao, this game has it  much more messed up.  You can only cheer for a Chao when it sparkles.  The catch?  9/10 times, the computer will pick an OPPOSING Chao for you to cheer for!  That's right, you barely get to cheer for your own Chao to propel it to victory.  So you'll really have to grind for small animals to jack up your Chao's stats, because you need to finish about 10 races to get five of the game's Emblems.
-Chao raising, while it is a nice and cool break, is very hard to do so with Big (who lives up to his name) and Gamma (who can't go into water).  It's much harder to take care of a Chao with these two characters than the rest of the cast (who are considerably shorter in comparison).
-Similar to Sonic CD, the controls are locked.  Unlike Sonic Adventure 2, you cannot change them (without modding anyway).
-Unless you have the configuration mod available in the community, you'll have blue borders in full screen.
In all, I would recommend this game if you would like it for nostaligic purposes, or if you've completely new to Sonic Adventure.  8/10.

Gareth Doney wasn't exactly a good man.  He'd made some mistakes.  But he was paying for them.  He had 6 years of hard time to think about the woman he hurt.  He went to church in prison a lot.  He felt good.   He became a believer.
Three years passed.  Gareth Doney was up for parole.  He felt good about it.  But his parole was denied.  He wouldn't get to get out and see his ailing grandma before she passed.  And then he didn't feel good anymore.  He felt it again... the rage that he had felt on that fateful night 3 years ago.  A prison guard came into the parole room to take him back to his cell as his lawyer and the parole officer put their papers back into their briefcases.  "Sorry Gareth" the prison guard said.
One punch.  That was all it took.  The guard was down.  The club was in Gareth's hand.  The parole officer panicked but couldn't get out the door before he brought the club crashing down on his skull.  He turned to his lawyer, staring at him wide eyed.  The club raised and came down again.  The rest was a blur.  Guards rushing at him.  He took down one, another, and then another.  Finally one managed to aim his tazer true and Gareth was down, 5,000 volts coursing through  his body.

In early access atm. But having a look through the updates. These guys are tearing their way through this game like no other. I watched a vid of it from May. Which as of this review is just 2 months ago. And it was a completely different game nearly. They have added so much to the game and are continuing. I like that they respond well in the discussions. You start off with your own little boat. And it is really awesome. It reminds me so much of the jaws boat lol. You can fish. Hunt. Have firefights with pesky raiders. Trade with weird medieval-looking folk lol. Scavenge for scrap, loot, boxes and barrels with items in them in the ocean. Recently-added deep sea diving in a awesome big daddy style armoured suit. And then on top of that, the best part is crafting.
Crafting allows all the things you are used to seeing in survival games. Weapons, tools, items & best of all base building!!
Sure you have seen it all before. But there is honestly nothing quite like building a home in the ocean where you can store all your valuables and whatnot. I played my first session for 5 hours. Couldn't tear myself away from it. :P

A 2004 classic, that everyone has at least heard of. It's an amazing game for its time, but does it hold up today?
The story has a lot more depth than you'd think for a GTA game. It's a story of grief, betrayal and revenge. It's a story of a family, and how they survive through the thick and thin. Even though some of the themes can be grim, the writing still makes you laugh.
The graphics look like they belong in a Playstation 2 game, and that's because they do. The graphics are outdated, but what did you expect? It's a 2004 game. If you're bothered by the graphics, you can search for a graphics overhaul mod.
This game made a lot of innovations in terms of gameplay. This was the first GTA game that allowed you to vault over obstacles and move while crouched. If you've played GTA IV or V, the controls might feel a bit clunky in comparison, and some things are missing entirely, like the ability to take cover behind a wall and to blind shoot.
I'd say the game still holds up today, even if you've played the later ones. At the time San Andreas was considered to be a huge game, but GTA IV and V are probably larger than it. There's still loads of things to do, even if you only stick to the story missions. If you're interested in the game, I'd say give it a shot to see if you like it.

This game is a true platformer. I came across this beauty when looking for SA2 as I heard great reviews, and ooh, the Chao Garden. However, I got the games mixed up. I was super mad and felt horrible like I wasted money but as I got farther in as Knuckles I absolutely LOVED it. All characters have good mechanics, so you arent playing the same thing (but screw big and amy anyways I actually loved E-102 Gamma.) It has an good, explained story all set out but the chronological order of all the characters stories may be mixed up. The main characters, the main trio, the main pilots, the main people, the main players, the main i dont know, Sonic, Knuckles and Tails are where the story is mainly at. These characters have longer stories and more mechanics to them. You will love playing as these 3, but the other 3 not so much as the main. However, since the game was originally for the Sega Dreamcast some of the cutscenes are strange, with weird mouth movements and slow walking. However, this should not be a problem at all unless your a whiny casual, as the gameplay is better. As Sonic the Hedgehog, you go straight-out speedy 3d platforming, in many levels. As Tails, you race Sonic (and Eggman on the last level)  to get to the end and grab the Chaos emerald before Sonic does. (for Eggman, its to a rocket.) As Knuckles, you have to locate 3 Master Emerald pieces in very large sub-overworlds. You have to use your locater which will flash and change colors as you get closer, but can cause some VERY tedious moments. As Amy, you have to escape from one of Eggman's robots to the end of a level and grab an escape, using a Piko-Piko hammer as a weapon. As Big the Cat, you..... fish. Yeah, you just fish a frog out of the pond, Literally. Just go to a pond in a level and fish Froggy out. Seriously. Thats it. As E-102 Gamma you are one of Eggman's robots. You have to go through many levels where you shoot things like a 8-year old who just drank 10 5-hour energy drinks playing COD. The more things you shoot, the more time you get, and at the end you have to face another robot in the true levels. All these characters get atleast 2 powerups which can help them power up a default move, learn a new move or give them something to help finish levels better, in which some of these powerups are needed and some are optional.
In the end, you play as Super Sonic against the main antagonist, Perfect Chaos. You use the powers of the 7 Chaos Emeralds to defeat Perfect Chaos. As you progress through the skies, your ring counter goes down. You must keep it above zero or you will fail the level. This is a balance of fun and tedious, but mostly fun.
In the end, this is a great game for Sonic fans and just about anyone, especcialy platformer fans. I would totally reccomend and play for a very long time, as the levels have great replayability since you can do Mission Mode, Trials for medals, and replay levels for new times and scores. Overall, out of 10 I would give it a 9.
Also, in the end when you collect all medals, you get a Metal Sonic skin for Sonic.

The first two Arkham games have been canonised for many a reason. True innovation married to great polish, detailed presentation and the spirit of Batman made them games everyone should try. The third entry in the series is mostly known for being not made by Rocksteady, which is both fair and unfair. It is completely accurate to say there is no real innovation to be found and the polish is left unpolished in quite a few places, but calling Origins a bad game could only be unfair.
Once again Batman has a one-night adventure with an overcrowded rogue's gallery. Old favorites bump with a couple of second-stringers and in general the bad guy - proceedings pay off. The central plot is episodic, but the boss fights are memorable and interesting, as are other episodes, particularly one with Mad Hatter, who here manages to be actually creepy and unsettling for once. Deadshot has upgraded his skills (and wardrobe, thankfully!), making for a very intense Predator Room. Listing all the villain would take too much space, but suffice to say that the antagonists were interesting enough to overcome and rejoice. Origins mostly takes it cues from the Nolan films and this realism does make for a welcome change of pace from the comic book - inspired original Arkham games.
In other places this realism is more cosmetics than actual realism and cheap lipstick at that. Riddles Collectibles in particular are just as exhausting as ever, even if he is invading privacy and not stashing question marks. Other side quests are good enough as diversions, but there is far, far too much "Do X Of Y" for my liking. Gotham City feels sterile, especially in comparison to its appearance in Arkham City.
Audiovisuals are of a high standard, the new voice actors earned their paychecks as did the boys and girls in the soundtrack department. In particular I was happy to see the new, realistic outfits. No longer must Batman suppress his giggles when meeting Bane or Deadshot.
Gameplay is largely the same as before, with a few new gadgets and enemy types. Both categories have winners and losers, with the infamous Shock Gloves being the worst of the bunch and the Glue (not ice?) Grenades not far behind. Freeflow melees and the awesome predator rooms are still fun, just a bit samey, which could be said about the game in general.
They say the great artists of old worked on commission without compromising quality. With Arkham Origins things did not pan out like they did with Rembrandt, but if Origins is taken on its own merits (and with a budget price) it is a perfect weekend waster, which is sometimes enough.

TL;DR, Great game, lots to do, highly reccomended. Frame drops and ocassional falling through the world - but that never actually killed me.
Having put just under three hours in to the game I'm not sure whether I should be reviewing yet- but from what I've seen so far, I definitely intend to play more.
Upon first opening the game everything runs smoothly, after launch - as the world loads in - it lags a bit. But other than a few framedrops every now and then, it runs extremely well. Multiplayer was decently easy to set up. I mean, how hard is it to click "add to game" from your friends list?
In game, it's absolutely beautiful. The music is amazing. The simple but bouncy art style actually adds a lot to the game. At first glance I thought it was going to be decently boring, however, when I found my first cave I was more than entranced. It was interesting how, despite going in to the cave with a friend, when we went too deep the markers disappeared. Not going to lie- I got lost fast.
When I ventured too far off from the 'base', it gave me a very isolated feeling. I assume what it was intended to do. But this shocked me, considering how lighthearted the game looked at the start.
The only real glitch I encountered was, when I died, I'd spawn running and falling in to the world. It never actually killed me, since it'd slowly bring me back up, it was just something of note.
Overall the game had me sucked in right after openning it. I'd say it's more fun with a friend, but I'm not 100% on that yet.
Great fun - hope to see many improvments with more items/resources in upcomming patches!

A quirky game with a lot of potential, but unfortunately there is a distinct lack of polish and content to set it apart from the rest of the pack. Grammar errors, shoddy character models, and humor that seems almost unintentional detract from a potentially compelling setting. There is little point to building a secondary base since your boat is perfectly serviceable; Subnautica forces you to build bases to increase your tech level, for instance. Right now there's a lot of open space with nothing to do in it but attack random animals and fight pirates with awful AI. The UI is clunky and not comfortable to look at, and is slightly buggy. I was never sure if I was crafting or driving my boat. There needs to be more feedback on what exactly your character is doing. Also, why do your arms only show up when you're holding a gun?
I would wait until much later, as I have high hopes for the game, but right now it just isn't cutting it. It looks ugly where it shouldn't (the abyssal worms are particularly odd even though shooting smaller worms is hilarious), and only mildly interesting where it should look amazing.

While I really appreciate what this game is trying to do, I cannot endorse this particular itteration of the game / demo.
For almost $10, there is not enough content to justify that price point. There are many other games that will give you more for your investment.
That aside, the technical issues are just too plentiful for what is presented to us to be enjoable.
1: The A.I. only has two modes; Potato, and wall-hack. It's a 50 / 50 shot that when you come around a corner a guard will already be shooting at your, or staring at you, oblivious to your existence.
2: The aim down sights is terribly off. The further away from someone you are, the lower you have to aim. Once you get about half a room away (20 or so yards / meters) you have to aim at their belt to get a headshot.
**update** So, the issue isn't as drastic currently, but it's still very off. The current bullets are hitscan instead of raycast, but the hitscan sensor detects AFTER the kick of the gun, instead of before, causing bullets to jump, and causing aim down sights to be off increasingly more as you get further from the enemy.
3: Enemy health seems to be based off their alert status. What would normally take one or two bullets, once an enemy sees you / is attacking you, could take half a clip. I believe this has more to do with the animations. **tentatively seems to be fixed**
4: The animations, or the ones that work, are just broken. Don't believe me? Try picking up a dead guy. The first five seconds of the gameplay where you cycle through crouch, prone, crouch, and standing is just a mess.
5: Picking up dead guys just doesn't work. Out of the 50 test runs I did attempting to pick up a dead body from all different angles, I was successful once. I was then treated to a ballet of terrible animation as the guys ragdol flailed into my shoulder.
6: Picking up stuff / interacting with stuff works about 30% of the time. You have to have a very specific angle to interact with almost everything, and even then it almost never works. You have to reload after every failed attempt to be able to interact with the monitor to set your difficulty.
7: Sound. Literally everything about it.
All in all, as stated before, this game has some serious potential, but this itteration just feels like a hastily assembled pre-alpha. Neither the stealth, or the first person shooter aspects of this work to any sufficient degree to merit looking at this. Hopefully when the game is ported over to the Unreal Engine 4 most of these issues will be fixes, but as it stands, follow the project, but don't quite put your money on it yet.

From the outside, Borderlands 2 looks like it is just your regular FPS game, and in some way it is true, but you'll be doing this game an injustice if you only thought that far.
As a FPS game goes, it's one of the best FPS games I've ever played, and that is saying a lot.
There are many reasons why I praise it, so let's begin.
The graphics are some of the most unique I've seen in a game. Whilst most FPS games try to go for realism, Borderlands 2 can't give a damn about that. Show me screenshots of al the popular FPS games right now, and Borderlands 2 will stick out like a sore thumb. This game has an identity.
The sound design is on point. Weapons made by Jakobs have a very mechanical sound, due to them being very old-school, mechanical weapons. The same can't be said for makes like Hyperion and Maliwan, which are very futuristic and differ greatly in every aspect.
The enemies are amazing in this game. Their taunts and fighting styles are very varied and unique, and sometimes I don’t kill them immediately, just so I can hear what they are going to say next. On the higher levels they can be very challenging too, so you always have to push yourself to stay ahead of the game. Challenging, but just as rewarding.
The soundtrack, oh my GOD the soundtrack! It’s awesome! Each area has such a unique atmosphere and the music simply amplifies that by a factor of 100. If I listen to each song, I know exactly where it is played. It’s one of those soundtracks that you can listen to completely on its own, and it will still be awesome.
The leveling system is very robust and adaptable. Even though you have four playable characters in the vanilla game, the amount of options you can chose from when leveling up can lead to one character having different play styles on their own, essentially increasing the amount of different ways you can play.
The story is satisfactory, but little else. It’s not horrible or the most complex, but it does get you involved and caring for each character. Job done.
In conclusion, I highly recommend you buy this game and KILL JACK!

I’ll be the first to concede that when it comes to simulation and management games, my level of ability is... Well, somewhat lacking. Faced with the tasks of effective planning and precise micro-management, I tend to have a history of not making the wisest of choices, which in turn leads to disaster more often than not. It was therefore with some trepidation that I headed into Prison Architect, hoping it was designed well enough that even I could create a facility that didn’t have so many riots and escapes that it'd never leave the national news.
Thankfully, my worries were unfounded. You see, Prison Architect kicks off in quite a unique manner via a story mode, with missions teaching you each of the game's features in turn until you've mastered the essential. As each mission unfolds, so too does a tale that is full of dark events and surprisingly heartfelt moments, and is far more engaging than a title in this genre has any right to be. It’s a really effective learning tool that goes beyond just drily telling you how to go about things via endless pop-ups, and I like it a lot.
When it comes to creating your own prisons from scratch, things do get a little more complicated, and (as you’d likely expect) your first few attempts aren’t going to result in anything stellar. Thankfully there’s another feature in place that really proves useful in making sure you’re getting the essentials down, and that’s the grants system. Put simply, each grant is an overarching objective, under which there's a list of tasks to complete. You'll be challenged with providing effective medical facilities, for instance, and given some cash to get things going. Fulfil all the criteria, and you’ll get even more cash as a reward. It’s clever because it’s a training tool, a reward system, and a goal to aim towards all rolled into one – and that’s a nice little bit of genius design to see.
Another shard of genius comes from the fact that the overall level of complexity that Prison Architect has to offer is completely open to your own personal interpretation. You can use the game’s basic tool set and never go beyond that, and you'll never be penalised for it. But there’s a great deal of complexity here for those that seek it. You can map out precise patrol routes for every guard, you can automate your doors to open and close at precise times, and much else besides - most of which my tiny little brain couldn’t possibly hope to imagine. No matter your skill level or personal tastes in the simulation genre, you’re probably going to find something that you like here.
Sadly, for all Prison Architect has many positive design elements, it also has a small collection of negative ones. None are game-breaking by any stretch of the term, but they do suck some of the fun out of things. For instance, open the menu to map out a room, and you’re immediately faced with a giant list of all those that are available to you. Yet here’s the rub; they’re not in alphabetical order, or listed by any other sort of discernible logic I could work out – they’re just jumbled about, leading to situations where it can take far too long to find what you’re actually looking for.
Roughly the same problem holds true when it comes to adding items to rooms, and even though there’s search bars and the highlighting of key items which mitigate the problem somewhat, they simply don’t feel like an effective solution. Why not put different rooms and item types in different sub-categories, allowing for quicker and more refined navigation? That’s only one method of tackling the issue, but even if you disregarded that one, it still honestly feels like there’s a better approach that could be taken than what's on offer here.
Prison Architect also isn’t very good at helping you resolve the logistical issues and other problems you’ll encounter while running your facility. In many cases, there seems to be no means you can intuitively solve them, or even turn to the game itself for some sort of guidance. To provide an example - I set up training courses for my prisoners to enrol on, but no-one seemed to express an interest, despite all of their needs essentially being met. It was only via some snooping round the internet that I found it was the presence of a mere handful of armed guards that was putting them off. It seems logical in hindsight, but as far as I could tell there was either nothing in the game to actually tell me of this feature, or it was far too obscurely hidden to be of practical use.
A few other scenarios have played out in a similar manner during my time with the game, and I’d be willing to scratch them all up to my own relative inexperience... If it wasn’t for the fact that every time I searched the web, I saw tons of other players asking the exact same questions. You’re never going to understand every mechanic a game like this has, sure, but when there’s so many of them causing people to ask such questions, there’s clearly a bigger issue at play.
Put these things aside, however, and Prison Architect is still a remarkably compelling game. It’s satisfying to start mapping out and planning your next big expansion or project, and there’s a strong sense of pride in seeing such projects come to fruition. And let’s not forget the escape mode, or the many weird and wonderful prisons you can download from the Steam Workshop – both features I haven’t dabbled in much myself yet, but can only add more length to your playtime. When it comes to whether you should be spending your cash on this game or not... Trust me when I say this really isn’t a hard cell.

Arkham Origins is probably one of the most underrated games I've ever played, and it's a shame. I guess when all the braindead "fans" decide to exile it from the franchise, it tends to give the game a bad name. I'm telling you right now, don't listen to them. This isn't even remotely close to being a bad game. Yes, it has some glitches and some minor plotholes, but that doesn't make it the worst game of the franchise. See Arkham Knight for that.
Origins gives us a new take on Batman, one that hasn't been done before. Instead of being this calm and collected superhero, he's green as grass when it comes to defending Gotham, stubborn, much more agressive, and his decisions are very impulsive. Much like in the Nolan trilogy of the Batman movies, pretty much everyone is out to get him. Even GCPD.
Like Arkham City, Origins is also open world. This game uses the same island from the previous game, but it also adds a completely new section. Due to how big the game is, you are able to fast travel to certain points on the map. To unlock them, you need to deactivate a few towers, kinda like in Far Cry 3. The open world in this game is great, but it would have been nice to be able to see some civilians outside, or maybe some cars driving around. They justify this by making the game take place during a snow storm, which isn't that bad I guess. Still would have been pretty nice to see more people other than criminals and police officers.
The combat in this game looks identical to the one in the previous games, but something feels off. I don't know what it is, but something was changed. I found myself constantly being hit by enemies a lot of times. I browsed the discussions to see if I was the only one, but I wasn't. It isn't too bad, but it does feel different compared to the one in City.
The boss fights are really well done, so no complaints there. The bosses have multiple phases, and they always keep up with the player. Playing NG+ on Hard can get pretty brutal sometimes.
Overall, Arkham Origins is a great game. The story was actually good, the boss fights were amazing, the soundtrack is incredible, and the way they did the Crime Scenes really took me by surprise. The Crime Scenes alone were the ones that made me buy the game. Aside from a few bugs and plotholes, the game is pretty good. All those people saying the game is trash don't know what they're talking about. This game is worthy enough to be part of the Arkham franchise, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. It isn't on Arkham City levels, but in my opinion is one of the best games of the series. If you have money to spend, buying it without a discount will still get you your money's worth. If you're not too sure about it, you could always just wait for a sale.  One thing is for sure - you NEED to buy this game.

I can't say enough good things about this game.  I was hoping this game would be something different from the usual, relaxing, engaging and beautiful and it is all that and more. I purchased the game in a sale bundle which for a bit less than retail for the core game also included for free the DLC's Going East, Scandinavia, High Value cargo and a couple other cosmetic dodads. I'm not a hardcore gamer and I'm running this on an older MacBook (which necessitates much lower graphics settings) but playing ET2 is simply a beautiful experience.  It's like spending hours driving through European postcards and yet it provides frequent enough decisions (gas, repairs, job choice,  occasionally difficult driving situations, managing your company, etc...) that 90 hours in I still feel engaged and excited to play more.
As for the visuals, I have to praise the designers. There's so many ways they could have done less and still had a game that was nearly as good, but it's amazing how much detail they include.  As an example, most driving games have areas with tall highway sound barriers and that's the edge of the world, but in ET2 when using the chase camera suddenly you see that on the other side of the barriers is even more of the world: forests or an industrial zone or a castle or a....  Because of this, and even though it's just s smidge more fiddly to drive, I highly recommend using the chase camera when driving during the day.  It's really ups the beauty factor.
Lastly, if you don't have a driving rig I highly recommend a PS2 style controller or other pad with 2 joysticks.  Being able to assign one joystick to the steering and the other to provide an incrmental control for the throttle (accelleration and reverse) makes the trucks much easier to control and the game even more fun to play.  If you need one the Logitech F310 (newer version of what I have) is well rated and tends to go for $15-20 on Amazon. I assure you it will be money very well spent.

Dark Storm : Ascension is a stealth-action game which was planned by Fenrir Studios but regrettably failed on kickstarter. Not a developer to be deterred, Fenrir is determined to prove commitment to the project by releasing a mini-version of Dark Storm : Ascension in the form of Dark Storm : VR Missions. There are currently 10 weapons and 10 stages to play around in, but no objectives to be seen. Is it a promising Early Access title? Partially. You can go through killing everything, or turn on a stealth mode that ends the simulation once you're caught.
The stealth aspects still need to be tightened, and the hip-fire needs to be loosened. Enemy AI is hardly consistent and they will stop chasing you to follow a thrown noise-maker even while you're still in sight. I find it hilarious to treat the enemies like a dog, who is endlessly tricked by a fake throw of a ball, but it doesn't make for very engaging gameplay.
I like the colorful design of the levels, as well as the realistic gunfire and spot-on voice-acting. Depending on the story we could be looking at the next Deus Ex, or the next Solarix. If you haven't heard of Solarix (or read my review), there is a very strong reason for that. This game is leagues ahead of Solarix in terms of the stealthing and combat, and while there are still a number of screws to tighten in the form of hip-fire, stealthing, and enemy AI but overall I experienced no crashes, had a fair bit of fun, and remain quite hopeful.
