DmC: Devil May Cry is the 2013 polarizing reboot to the classic Devil May Cry games and frankly, I think it was absolutely fantastic. I vaguely remember from when the game was initially released, but there was a lot of controversy over the game not being a proper sequel and because the main character's appearance was changed. Honestly, I had this in mind prior to starting to play the game, but I eventually forgot about this and simply enjoyed the game for the many things it had to offer, great gameplay, graphics, and a very well fitting OST. For the most part, I fully enjoyed the game and since I've only played the first DMC on PS2, none of the complaints that most fans had for this game applied to me.
For the most part, DmC could be described as a hack and slash game, but it's so much more than that. Initially, your weapons are limited to your main sword and your dual wielded pistols known as ebony & ivory, but as you progress through the game you're able to unlock abilities and discover many more weapons. What really grabbed my attention in this game is that when using these pistols, Dante does the same swaying back movement as he did in the original DMC game, I thought it along with the other weapons offered were a great reference to it.
Almost immediately as you begin this game you realize how fluid the combat is. At times it appears that Dante is almost dancing as he hacks and slashes his way from enemy to enemy. What's great about this is that in the hands of a very skilled player there's a lot of room for creativity and this is beneficial in more ways than one, seeing as how the more diverse/connected your attacks are, the higher your score will be at the end of a level. The higher your score, the better off you'll be in regards to being able to purchase useful items and abilities to further diversify Dante's attacks.
Another thing I noticed in regards to the weapons and attacks in DmC is how they're organized. The way it's done leads to good weapon selection balance whereas in most games you would have to individually select which weapons to use until you choose to switch. In this game, you're able to select them all in-game and this is done with the D-pad along with the left and right triggers plus their particular buttons. I felt that this was well done because it ensured that combat would flow smoothly, rather than having to go into a menu each and every time you wanted to switch weapons.
Up to this point I've mainly described DmC's weapon/combat system, so it would make sense to mention the enemies that you encounter in this game. Like everything else in this game, there's an abundance of enemies to deal with and that's great, combat never feels stale. Combat not only feels fresh due to the types of enemies that you encounter, but also due to the game's music. I didn't expect it, but DmC's OST is worth listening to and I even looked it up on Youtube soon after beating the game. The OST is fairly diverse, but the chunk of it is modern metal. This particular genre of music was a good choice because it fits this game's overall image and gameplay very well. I'd also like to add that as toolish as it may sound, tearing demons up as metal is playing in the background makes you feel like a badass.
The thing worth mentioning about the enemies encountered in DmC is that they're mainly demons that range from low to high level and depending on which one you're facing, you will have to change up your strategies. Some of these enemies can easily be disposed of by spamming your basic attacks, but others will also require specific weapons or even strategies due to their size or elemental specialties. The enemy types are diverse, but there's a few that are simply stronger versions of the enemies encountered earlier in the game. At times you'll also have to face various combinations of enemies so it's a constant challenge. This is best showcased when dealing with the game's few, but remarkable bosses.
Within 20-25 minutes, depending on the difficulty setting you choose and your abilities as a gamer, you will encounter a boss fight. At first I thought this meant that the boss fights would be frequent, but I was wrong. As previously stated, the boss fights are few and far between, but they're possibly the best part of this game. Like in other games, the bosses in DmC are much larger than your character, but if anything that makes things much more exciting. I didn’t mention it before, but two of your weapons have the ability to function as a hookshot, either to bring enemies to you/you to them, or simply to gain access to hard to reach areas. This function is almost always used in boss fights, but they're always done in different ways. One thing that stood out to me in one boss fight was how freely I was able to swing around the enemy thanks to this ability, it felt similar to how Spider-Man swings freely from skyscraper to skyscraper. I also have to mention that despite being few and far between, the boss fights are generally quite the interactive experience and particular.
Besides the overall entertaining gameplay, the graphics in this game are also noteworthy. Honestly, being that this game is almost five years old, I didn't expect the graphics to stand out as much as they did. Maybe it's because I'm gaming on a 1440p/60hz monitor with a gtx 1080, but I got the impression that DmC was well optimized due to not really having any sort of FPS drops or general problems. The game's great graphics were usually best displayed in its two different cutscene styles. One consisted of drawn still images, which reminded me of the first Max Payne, and the other was more conventional yet visually stunning animated scenes. Certain levels also made use of the game's great graphics due to how bright/colorful the visuals were. This is definitely a game worth playing with good hardware, you'll notice the difference.
Honestly, I enjoyed DmC more than I originally expected to, the few flaws I saw in it aren't extreme or numerous at all. I previously mentioned how stunning the graphics in this game are, and maybe I'm just nitpicking in regards to this, but shadows in cutscenes appeared to be a bit blocky/fuzzy looking, especially around faces. This isn't as awful as say facial animation problems, but it's noticeable due to how long some cutscenes will focus on the character's face.
Two other things that caught my attention could be seen more as neutral issues rather than outright negative flaws. I previously mentioned that you are able to use numerous abilities/weapons, but it can honestly be a bit overwhelming. Depending on your playstyle, you may rely more on certain abilities/weapons than others, but even then it can get problematic due to having to press a lot of particular buttons and it leads to some overlapping. This is especially problematic when facing hordes of enemies and being in the middle of a high combo, one little mistake could lead to you being hit and having your combo cut short.
In the beginning of this review I mentioned that this game was polarizing for many reasons, the appearance of Dante being one of them, but I could also see the dialogue of the game and general personality of this game's Dante being seen as sophomoric or even cringey. I can’t recall specific moments, but there were instances where Dante's response to a situation was nearly the equivalent of a 15 year old internet troll. It didn't really bother me because the gameplay was very satisfying and this game could be seen as a sort of origin story for Dante. It has occurred in other games/mediums where a character/hero wasn't fully mature right from the beginning and that feels corrected towards the end of this game, along with the controversial appearance of Dante.
To conclude, I highly enjoyed DmC and I see myself eventually playing it again. I give DmC a 4.5/5 and I highly recommend it.

I was a bit apprehensive about purchasing this game due to so much of the negativity that surrounded it in the past. From what I gather, there were fans of the old franchise that were sincerely irritated (Putting it mildy) that the new face of Dante wasn't to their liking. Seeing as I haven't played much of the old games, this wasn't an issue to me at all. In fact, maybe it was because of that lack of history with the franchise which is the reason why I enjoyed this one so immensly.  Here's a quick breakdown of certain elements of the game.
MUSIC: 9/10
While I can see not many people being into the heavy metal genre, I for one am a fan of hard rock. The perfect blend of heavy, twisted metal coiled around a hectic, fast paced combo system was truly satisfying.
GAMEPLAY: 8/10
Fun, quick combos that can be mashable and still retain their entertainment. While the combat isn't a brain teaser, it keeps it simple, yet varied. Definitely a lot of fun factor here.
OPTIMIZATION: 10/10
While I do have a mid end gaming rig, I found that 99% percent of the time my fps were in the mid 200s. I'm a simple guy to please and any game that maintains a constant 60+ fps is great my book.
PROTAGONIST: 8/10
Yes, I do know this is probably where the most critique goes as fans of the original games disliked the new spin on Dante, but honestly, for me, he seemed. . .likable. Sure, he had his immature moments. But he seemed like a guy who had it rough growing up. He has some edge. Maybe it's the fact that I don't know the old Dante that enable me to look at this new Dante and judge him on his own merits. For a main guy, he wasn't unlikable. I guess he just grows on you if you let him.
FUN FACTOR: 10/10
I haven't truly had a moment where I wasn't having fun with this game. So far, the only times I've put down the controller was to find something to eat and sleep. I've probably logged over 7 hours into this game in one day, and I've yet to bore myself of it.
CONCLUSION
Give it a try. If you're a fan of the old games, have an open mind. Think of this an alternate universe if that helps. The gameplay is fun. The story is engaging. the protagonist is likable. For the price I got it on the steam sale, I don't have a single regret. Maybe you won't either. Cheers!

I was skeptical about this game, but friends convinced me, and I must say, I haven't stopped having fun.  It's just one of those games where you can go wild, doing whatever you want.  The Earth shaping reminds me of a super-toned-down, 3rd-person Photoshop tool (add, remove, smooth).
The most appropriate description I've heard is "It's everything No Man's Sky should have been."  I even went so far as to buy this game for 3 other friends to experience the full shenanigans that can arise.
People are inevitably saying "There's no content: 0/10, or it's buggy: refunded" -  of course it is! the game was released mid-December as an early-access, pre-alpha game.  Right now, the game is a framework; a test to see how the community responds.  Since it's release about 3 weeks ago, the Devs have patched 3 times already!  If it continues, we may hit alpha before summer! (but no rush.  don't want another NMS)
As for the bugs: yes, your vehicles may go flying, or resources clip through the ground, it's a given.  is it utterly game breaking? No.  You may have to save and restart sometimes to cope with the error dump getting to large, but (for me) that was few and far between.
Content: limited, but playable -  I'm one of those people who doesnt mind grinding resources, spending hours just to build a wind turbine field.  Several buddies and I actually lost our base and had to scrap the world because we lost the base in our "epic journey"xD
It may get a bit monotonous going it alone, but it's 20$.  Grab a friend, have them test it out.  You can have a ton of fun with friends, it's all in how you approach the game.
TLD;R:  Solid 8.5/10 for the current form (pre-alpha)
Content: limited, but fun and playable
Price: AFter NMS, $20 seems more than reasonable for a game thats already much better.
Bugs: duh, it's pre-alpha. some can hurt, but usually dont

I got Nefarious and (almost) finished it on the same day. It has great characters and a story that you can't help but get invested into. That being said there is one huge issue with this game:
THE CONTROLS ARE NO WHERE NEAR TIGHT AND RESPONSIVE ENOUGH
You are very slidy as a character and your close range attacks are a joke. If you are like me you will basically go through the whole level using your projectiles as you cannot get in close without running into the enemies. Most of the levels I can go through no problem. However, there are several moments in the game where i bang my head in frustration as I fall in pitholes or die from enemy attacks I simply was not able to avoid due to the slidy controls. It is like playing an ice level in mario. So why i am not waiting until after i beat the final boss to write the review? because the final boss is one of the most frustrating moments because it relies on precision attacks while avoiding a lazer, something the controls are not capable of doing.
The game would get a strong review from me if were not for this, the levels are well made and very unique, but they are designed for tight controls, which makes completing them extreamily frustrating.
So why do I still recomend the game?
Mainly because I am a sucker for good story and characters. If you want a good story and experience and are willing to forgive the not so stellar controls, then this game is for you. If you don't care about the story and just want a solid platformer, then I would suggest to stay far away from this game.
EDIT: Wow, i never thought a single boss fight could change my whole review. However, the final boss unfortunatley has forced me to change my review to a negative one. I will try to not spoil it, it is a multi stage boss fight that requires precision attacks and you must do so all on the same life with no checkpoints. A game with tight controls can pull this off, no problem.....This game does not have tight controls. It is possible to beat it and many will boast they have one it in two to three tries. that being said, it is probably in my opinion one of the worst designed bosses in the game and really highlights the lack of understanding the designers had toward their game's controls. I have used a controller for the game and it feels awful. I really want to love it, I really do, but either the controls need to be tightened up or the final boss needs to be tweaked to make up for the slippery controls.

Nefarious gives me mixed feelings. While an enjoyable single player experience, it felt hollow at times to me.
*BEFORE I go any further, note this review will have spoilers. I want to dissect this game and why its problems stand out to me in full. So because of this, I wont have censor bars. If only because that would get annoying to see almost half or all of the review blanketed. Thank you.*
First off, the music. Its not bad, but at times during a level, the music really didn't fit the mood of the situation. It feels awkward to me and the music can potentially get annoying hearing it on repeat. Some change in music would be nice sometimes.
Gameplay is weird, and it is a MUST, I REPEAT MUST to have a controller, or you'll have trouble with this game. Its movement feels a bit sticky and slippery at the same time, as your character slides with what little momenteum he's got. This makes it troubling when in later levels you have to deal with instant death pits and surfaces. It is ESPECIALLY frustrating on the secret level, when you have to hop on small moving platforms to get to the next checkpoint. I just got frustrated at this game really. The punching is awkward as it sometimes, if not, always misses the enemies or doesn't push them back enough to not get hit. Making the ranged weapon a must use. And lobbing grinades is annoying enough as it is as you have no way of telling what the tragectory is unless you spam it, which is equally risky as your bombs can knock you around.
Topping this with platforming and enemies that can fill the screen and/or attack through surfaces like walls, then you have frustrating gameplay. And this doesn't help when the true final boss is a little more fast paced than previous fights. And this current state of the gameplay isn't equipped for that if you top THAT with bad hit detection, which is very, very frequent. Weapons that should miss you by inches hit you anyways, and being on the hearts system, thats not a good recipe. I really dont like this gameplay on later levels as it really does break my interest in the game when I have to be focused on the dumbest things. Especially on bramble path, which, by the way, has the most infuriating platforming in a game with slippery/sticky controls while enemies flood you at every orface. This is not fun, this is annoying. A bunch of badly made mechanics are clumped together to create an annoying game that is realized later down the line.
The one thing that kept me going, although, was the story and humor. The humor is gigglingly funny if only because the story lines up well with it. Being about a villian trying to break the status quo of "Hero beats baddy, wins the day". I like it then, but then the story goes into "friendship solves all problems", which was kind of a let down, but the humor was enough to make me ignore some of the stories downfalls. If you like funny and witty dialogue, come down here.
The artstyle, let me be honest, is not that great. Its trying to go for a cartoony look but it just doesn't fit. I feel it should've had more flare to it or at least some interesting theme around it, but its just plain cartoony. In all honesty, I dont like it. It doesn't have to be pixelly or anything, but I would prefer it would be more interesting to look at if anything.  Mixing that with the music and it honestly feels bland after the seventh loop of the same song. Not that great in my personal opinion.
The "Reverse-Boss Fights" are...really meh when you think about it. Really its just pressing some buttons, while doing one thing that dodges their attack. It could've been more dynamic or challenging, but it just didn't feel like so. The final boss on the normal route though, that was honestly good to play, if only because the challenge felt like it was there. The true final boss fight, again, was near impossible unless you had a stroke of luck. It practically requires a controller to play and even then good luck with the hit detection/hit boxes.
Overall, not that great. It may have good humor and an interesting story, but its just held down from being what it is, a video game. Unless its on a damn good sale or you just want to see what its like for yourself, go ahead. Just be warned as the repetitive unchanging music mixed with a featureless artstyle, frustrating gameplay and somewhat disappointing outcome of the story can make for a boring experience that might as well have been time spent on something else.
I love this game for what it set out, but the outcome just didn't meet basic standards.

Medieval playground is a sandbox game, developed in Unity engine, or at least it aims to be. And by that I mean that the game is currently in Early Access and what looks like a very early alpha build.
It has a very ambitious TODO list and if even 80% of what is there, is implemented it will be a very good game. Right now it looks kind of like an early alpha of Ark. Being not much more than a terrain editor.
Gameplay:
Like I said in the premise. This is currently not in a state that you may actually call it a game. It's more like a terrain editor currently. It is very early in its development cycle, and as such, reviewing it at this point is probably not the best thing to do.
Graphics:
Graphics-wise the engine has potential and the game doesn't look bad. But on a GTX 970 that I played it on, it looks rather unoptimized at this point and there were a few graphics glitches like shimmering textures. All these are to be expected though as it is a very early build.
Music/Sound Design:
Music sounds absolutely great. And there's also an on/off toggle. Sound effects also sound good.
Pros:
-Very ambitious project.
Neutral:
-Not much is implemented yet so you can't really form a proper opinion.
Cons:
-There's not much of a game yet.
Conclusion:
This is one of those cases where the binary options don't work. The project looks very ambitious and if it indeed implements everything planned it could become a great game. At this point I can not recommend it, unless someone wants to be actively involved in its development and support the project.
Score:
Gameplay:          3/10
Graphics:		    8/10
Music/Sound:	    9/10
Concept/Story:    6/10

While I appreciate that this game is F2P, the dev team in charge of optimising it for the PC platform have managed the process with a level of compitence that can be likened that of a chimp suffering from severe autismal spectrum disorder trying to peel a banana while wearing novelty sized Micky Mouse hand-gloves.
Even an above-average computer by 2015's standards will encounter consistent and crippling fps jitter. Cases of frame drops, FPS jitter and outright freezes have been reported far and wide by people who have played this game and despite the fact that it has been available for over 4 years now, it appears that the devs have not seen fit to create a fix.
This said, it is evident that the team behind APB Reloaded has put extensive amounts of effort to replicate the visual style of the security camera monitors at your local corner store that snap a monochrome picture every half-second. A daring and bold move by any video game developers standards, however it is nonetheless evident that they have more than achieved this goal.
FPS issues within this game can be caused by, but not limited to: Particle physics, loading objects, shadows (even when turned off), vehicles moving, moving in a vehicle, players in your party moving, other players moving, moving, colloding with other vehicles while driving, colliding with objects while driving, colliding while driving, driving, sprinting on foot, colliding with objects on foot, colliding with other players on foot, moving while on foot, and moving.
As you can imagine, having FPS issues in such crucial moments of the game (throughout the entire game) can become very frustrating for players who are using this as a substitute until the next Grand Theft Auto release in March 2015.
Overall I would liken my experience of this Citizen Kane of the video game medium to forcefully excreting a lemon juice coated broken bottle of vinegar from my rear end while simultaneously trying to power-sniff my mustache off of my upper lip.
1/10 - If an axe murderer broke into my house in the night and gave me the choice to either play this game for one hour  or watch him butcher my children I would relish in the knowledge that I will get to sleep longer each morning whereas in the past I would have had to drive my children to school.

My Story:
So like everyone else I woke up at my crashed pod, began looking around to check my surrounds. I began walking forward, got about 40 meters out when BAM, and advanced life-form that can teleport came out of no where and bashed my skull in. This life-forms name? Meteors. This brought down my O2 levels to approximately 80%. Don't ask me why getting my skull bashed in brought down my O2 levels because I don't know. (Maybe it depletes faster because of a crack and that's just how it shows it?)
After that point I took note: Dodge the rocks. Now, in theory this would be fairly simple, just predict their paths and move out the way. In this case, it's wrong. You waddle like a penguin that has a bowling ball strapped to the side of his head. After walking past a few more low-poly rocks, I came across a valley that seemed to have a marker in the middle of it. I decided to head to it.
After jumping about 17m in the air I came waddling down incline and reached the flats of the valley. Moving forward another 500m and dodging all the space rocks, I found a small device that I have no idea what it is. I tried the normal buttons to press in a game when interacting with something, (E, mouse-click, even tried middle mouse.) After failing I decided to look at the controls again in the menu, so I press my trusty Escape button and go to press "Options." I also fail in doing this because I press the Restart button. Do not ask why they have a restart button, because I don't know. The game even opens up with saying, "This game will not hold your hand. Once you die, you die."
So why would we even use the restart button?
The most likely answer to this question is they accounted for every single invisible wall you run into. If you get caught in the wrong corner, you're stuck. So once I restarted I decided to try and bash my skull into every meteor that flew by, hoping it would end my suffering and this infernal nightmare. But then I thought...
I control this.
I have the power to stop this.
I used my powerful skill "Escape Quit" and returned home; scarred for life, but living.
I'm here to share my story, and to prevent others from sharing my fate. Now quickly, run away. Go back to your families with your loved ones and cherish every moment because soon... The advanced life-forms will find a way.
They always do.

This game is a really mixed bag.  In general the game is really solidly designed with excellent gameplay.  The boss "fights" are mostly epic and memorable.  But I cannot give this game a positive review because some of the levels are (for me at least) virtually unbeatable, including some levels which you must beat to progress in the game.
I appreciate that the developers wanted to provide an immensely challenging platformer and for the most part I appreciate and applaud that desire.  However, the way some of the levels were designed is downright sadistic.  There were levels where I knew exactly what to do at exactly which time, but I would fail and fail again and watch the minutes turn to hours while I was still trying to accomplish the same task, and no matter how many times I tried, I never succeeded in beating those levels.  At that point the game ceases to be fun and becomes something more like a chore.
If the game had checkpoints, save states, or the ability to rewind time like Braid, then these moments would have been tolerable.  Instead there were a handful of parts in the game that almost had me wishing harm on the developers for including them.
I'm stuck on the last level of the chapter called "The End" before the boss fight, I know what I have to do to beat that level, and I've come to accept that there's no way I will ever beat that level without devoting more than a full day of gameplay (and maybe several days) just to complete that one task.  Maybe it's just me, but that's really not something that I should be forced to accept from any game.
I grew up with platformers since the year the NES was released, so it's not like this is my first rodeo playing these kinds of games.  I think I've read that the developers themselves compared this game to Ghouls 'n Goblins on NES, which was notorious for being the most unbeatable game on the NES platform.  Well, considering that this game will be unbeatable by many who attempt to make it all the way through, I guess I would agree with that comparison.... but (and again, maybe it's just me) I don't think making games that most people won't be able to beat no matter how many hours they spend playing them should be something modern game devs strive for.
If you want a game you can beat without spending days of gameplay just trying to beat a single level in the game, this isn't it.  Otherwise there's plenty about this game to recommend, including the soundtrack, the boss "fights", and 95% of the gameplay.  It's the other 5% that makes me unable to recommend this game.

Sonic Adventure DX is a super fun game that definitely takes the cake for "Best 3D Sonic game" in my book. I loved playing it on the Gamecube when I was younger and when I found out they were putting on Steam, I couldn't be happier.
On my old computer (that had Windows 7), this game worked like a dream. If you have Windows 7 and want to get this, do it. It'll be worth your while... So long as you can figure out how to handle Sonic and company with your keyboard (some levels made me rage so hard but that's only because I'm crap with Sonic games on the PC).
HOWEVER, if you have Windows 8, I suggest NOT getting this game. Here's why:
I don't know why this happens, but I've read it happened to a lot of other people, including myself after I got my new computer... When you boot up the game, you'll hear the sounds and you can hear yourself going through menus but the window will stay black. There will be no visual anything. Apparently some customers made patches that were meant to fix this but it doesn't work for everybody and if it does work for you, you won't be able to play it through Steam and will have other little misc. problems.
The patch doesn't work for me (I've tried making it work twice) and Sonic DX crashes upon opening. But even if it did work I'd still be minged off. Steam and SEGA are responsible for making this game work. They shouldn't put it on their customers to jerry-rig the files to force it to work. And if it doesn't work for you, it feels like they're flicking you off because they haven't been paying attention to those of us who are having the problem. Yeah so the game isn't that big, so what? We still paid for it. We expect it to work regardless of what Windows version we have. Though I do admit that Windows 8 is garbage with compatability so it's not entirely Steam and SEGA's fault... But someone in any of those companies should be doing SOMETHING if it happens to more than just a handful of people.
I don't know, it just seems really unfair to me and I wish someone was paying attention. I would be playing Sonic DX right now if it wasn't for this problem. But here I am ♥♥♥♥♥ing about it.
I really hope someone fixes this... In the mean time, again, if you have Windows 7 and under, get this game because it's great. If you have Windows 8, I say don't. Buy yourself a Gamecube, a copy of DX for it, and play that instead.

Nefarious is a VERY good game, albeit a bit short. It has loads of charm and personality all it's own and while a bit rough around the edges I would truly consider it a gem. Heck I decided to support any future plans of this series insofar as possible I loved this game so much. The artwork by Gashi-gashi was also a fantastic touch.

Nefarious sees you take on the role of Crow the villain in a 2D platformer with essentially Megaman as your main arch rival.
While the whole game is nothing amazingly new there are some pretty cool things in here which make Nefarious a definite highlight in an already jam packed 2017.
The basic levels are pretty standard platform run and gunning type games. There is a pretty cool mechanic that halfway through each level you manage ti kidnap the princess you are hunting (for your princess powered doomsday device) and she alters the controls and gives you a brand new ability that alters the rest of the level.
I am surprised that you could not the go on to replay levels with the other princesses powers to access new areas but perhaps that was what the Metroidvania game this really should have been could have done to stand out from the crowd.
A real highlight fo the game, however, is the boss fights where instead of playing the sprightly hero you play the big hulking boss complete with big death rays and easily telegraphable attacks. Most of these fights are excellent and it really is something that makes the game stand out.
Visually the game is very pretty and some of the more artistic sections (particularly and underwater level) are damn right gorgeous to loo at.
The storyline is also very interesting and I was desperate to see where it was going to end up. I must say however the standard ending was very disappointing and I was left desperate to see the true ending which sadly didn’t massively improve the outcome.
The general gameplay is a mixed bag but mostly enjoyable and I really did have a great time with Nefarious in my 4hourish playthrough.
Nefarious is not perfect by any means but it is a very enjoyable game that I would definitely recommend if you are looking for a fun action platformer with a decent twist.

Batman is a difficult character. His appeal lies in the fantasy of strength and resolve employed judiciously and sparingly, violence a necessity carried out with due restraint; the vigilante as emergency room surgeon of social ills. This makes Batman an eminently literary character: Any good Batman story will discuss what the values he represents means to the author.
Thus, Alan Moore’s Batman is insane, a stoic wall of Authority to his arch-nemesis’ Anarchy; ultimately a joke about privilege. Grant Morrison’s Batman is vulnerable, his battle against crime an externalized repression of his own criminal insanity. Frank Miller’s Batman is a gleeful embodiment of the SNAFU principle: The world is insane, and so is he.
Unfortunately, Arkham Origins is an eminently benighted game. Batman is a gadget dispenser, a smattering of brand-values assembled over time in a sandbox-metroidvania structure. There is no separation between Batman and Bruce Wayne. Instead, Alfred plays superego to Batman’s id, chiding him like an obstinate teenager while Batman sullenly batprograms his batcomputer to batprepare the batplane for a batmission.
So let’s talk about multiplayer instead, where Batman as a concept divorced from his character actually works. Archetypical Batman is a well-defined bundle of rules and affordances. He’s a toolset for solving stealth-challenges, a way of studying prey before striking. He controls vertical space where his thug opponents control the horizontal.
This novel approach to team-deathmatch demands a giant contrivance to facilitate Batman, namely a cooldown-limited visor revealing Batman to thugs. Immediately appearing inelegant, visors makes the competition interesting by turning gun battles into a positioning rather than aiming game.
Made vulnerable, Batman turns into a persistent but mostly unseen threat. He’s why you’re suddenly alone in the darkness, trying to keep an eye on every corner at the same time. Batman is never far from your mind. Batman is why you can’t have nice things.
But you do have a boss, who either turns the tide of battle, or cements a victory. Bane and Joker can plow through enemy ranks, but have no visors and needs thugs for eyes to avoid Batman. This is the game’s greatest success: A handful of simple systems that require thugs to truly cooperate, to watch each other’s backs, stay organized and find safety in numbers.
This means Batman is hunting cunning, crafty opposition rather than inevitable victims, aware of the danger they’re in, not strictly fighting Batman but conscious that he’s after them.
While plodding movement and gun feel weakens the visceral pleasure of battle, the metagame is strikingly accessible. Every tool is a means to disrupting your opponents’ rich situational awareness and encourages outmaneuvering over outgunning them.
The multiplayer succeeds by stripping away the open-world from the singleplayer, capitalizing on its strongly characterized game systems and discrete challenge-chambers. Line-of-sight from different points is carefully considered, and ensures chokepoints don’t dominate the flow of battle.
Had Arkham Origins been a pure multiplayer game, it would be a classic. Now, it’s a remarkably well-hidden gem sure to be abandoned and forgotten.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Medieval Playground is currently in Early Access.
Medieval Playground is not (yet) a game; at this point it's more of a world builder for an as-yet unimplemented game. But it's still very early in its Early Access life, and the developer has stated a number of goals that will turn it into a full game, which would be even better if it could be easily extensible by its players.
Picture a medieval world, raw and untouched by humanoids. Then picture it inhabited by a small group of people who have the ability to alter the terrain, create objects out of nothing, and even create animals and people to populate the world. And then picture becoming one of these people, fighting off invading goblinoid creatures to protect the world and people that you and your friends have created. That is the sort of grand vision that I imagine the developer has in mind, although details are as yet quite few and far between: only a few paragraphs in the Early Access description.
At the moment, however, all we have is a slightly clunky-to-use first-person-perspective terrain editor and pre-fabricated model placement tool. But if the developer can implement his plans, it will eventually be much more.
Graphics - The graphics so far implemented in Medieval Playground are a very mixed bunch. It's made with Unity, so we have the standard launch dialog box allowing selection of graphics quality and resolution, which is a good thing. There is a reasonably large selection of models, most of which look okay together, but there's no model or texture blending at all, so it's very easy to make areas that look like boxes placed on or slightly in other boxes, and quite hard to make them fit together seamlessly.
The quality of the models varies a fair bit. None are great, but most are acceptable. Most textures a blandly coloured -- lots of wood and stone, but hey, it is a medieval setting after all -- but they are reasonably nice and look okay at 1920x1080.Terrain looks nice at a distance, but not quite realistic up close. Animal model animations are quite nice looking, but not yet well blended with the world; for example, they walk horizontally up a hill, with some of their feet treading air. People look pretty awful so far, with low-poly models and poor texturing, but I expect they're mostly just placeholders at this point. The skyboxes are okay, but not great.
There are some depth and clipping problems, allowing you to see through solid objects, and the water looks nice from a distance, but not so nice up close, especially when you're in it and the surface of the water can't decide whether it should be visible or not. There are no reflections or fancy graphics features as yet, although you can place a large number of campfires (lights) without a noticeable performance degredation, which is nice. Speaking of performance, it mostly runs without any difficulty, but then occasionally, and seemingly at random, FPS will drop massively, only to recover a few seconds later. Thankfully this doesn't happen too often, though.
Sound - There are a number of thematic music tracks that play in the background while you create your areas. These are quite pleasant, ranging to good, and in the time I've played so far I've left them going the whole time. Sound effects so far are pretty limited: a growl of a bear, grunt of an ogre, or a swish of your sword.
Gameplay - Medieval Playground isn't really a game yet, so the gameplay as such involves walking around an area and creating something from the list of prefabricated models. It's familiar WASD first-person controls, with a few hotkeys for bringing up the object selection menus or editing objects that you've placed in the world. Terrain modification is very simple with the mouse, and quite fun when creating caves. Ultimately, though, I would expect this to be just part of the 'game', with those who want to building worlds for others to play in.
You place objects with the mouse, and can then edit them (position, rotation, and scale) using a simple mouse-driven menu as well. You can place some larger pre-combined assets (e.g. houses), but some of these act as multiple smaller models once they're placed, so if they're not exactly right to begin with then you have to manually adjust each part separately. You can also delete placed assets with the mouse, but again this doesn't work properly for some of the larger pre-combined assets, which you have to delete part by part and even then they leave invisible barriers behind.
So far the gameplay is quite clunky, but remember that it's only early days yet. Current menus are only limited placeholders, and I hope the same is true of the assets available for inclusion in your part of the world. There's basic combat mechanics (left click to swing your sword and right to raise your shield), but there's no point to them yet, because any enemies you create have basic AI to walk towards you and attack, but no way of actually damaging you, or you them.
Pros:
+ Nice idea; should be a fun game if the developer reaches his goals.
+ Large world with many areas, although so far there are only a handful of separate terrains
+ Pleasant music
+ Simple controls; it's easy to start creating
+ Making caves is fun
Cons:
- Not much to do yet
- Clunky interface and a large number of little niggling bugs (but it is EARLY, Early Access!)
- Limited pre-fabricated models, many with low poly count and poor textures (especially people)
- Water is terrible!
Medieval Playground is in very, very Early Access. As a game, well ... it's not, yet. As a world builder, it's a good start, but the clunkiness and small range of options available limit its utility here, too. If it sounds like your sort of thing, then definitely add it to your wishlist and follow it, and if you want to support an indie developer and maybe have some say in what you want to see, then pick up Medieval Playground and have a play around with it yourself.
I'd love to be able to wholeheartedly recommend the game, but at this stage I just can't in good faith do so. There's not enough to the game yet, and not enough information presented by the developer to know in detail where it's going to go. I'll be watching it closely and will update this review as the game develops, though, and I hope to be able to change my recommendation before too long.

Super Meat Boy is simply put a masterpiece of the indie genre. I believe it will be studied in the not so distant future as the cornerstone it is. Its very tight controls, the awesome map layout, its great variety, the optimization of its mechanics and its humor are just some of the qualities that make it unique. The music is so great that I sometimes listen to it even when I’m not playing, the different characters offer different ways of beating the same levels and the way the game is divided into light and dark world is an awesome way of providing an additional challenge for those that crave for more.
The instant respawn, the original achievements, the boss stages and seeing all your deaths at the same time once you beat a level are just signs of how awesome this game is. Yes, you’ll probably rage quit anyway a few times, but after having a go at a difficult level for 50 times, you can do half of it with your eyes closed (seriously). It becomes such a mechanical action that I sometimes just used the time to think about other stuff and put my thoughts in order. It’s almost therapeutic. At the very end of the game, beating a stage could easily take me more than 60 minutes… and the worse is, that once you beat a level, you’re automatically ready for the next one. I’m terrible at this game (more than 50 hours and haven’t even done half of the dark world) but I still had a lot of fun. I’m ready to say goodbye, at least for now, to Super Meat Boy, but it will always hold a special place in my library (and my meaty heart). *dramatic chipmunk sound*

Interesting little game. The learning curve is steep at first, but becomes a lot easier as you play. It's vital to play a few rounds against the computer first -- if you're hunting, then you need to know what the monsters do ... and if your the monster, you need to know how not to give away that you're the target. A bunch of hunters who don't know how to play won't ever find the monster except through luck. A monster that doesn't know how to play is DEAD.
As the monster, your goal is to cripple all the other players. But if you just wade in and start throwing around your monster attacks, they'll all know you're their quarry and gang up on you. Priority one is grabbing a weapon that can hurt humans. Then wait for the other players to group up, trying to figure out which one is the monster -- while you pick off any stragglers in other rooms. With any luck, the big group of hunters will self-cripple a player or two, meaning you don't have to!
There are 5 monster powers, and this is key for the hunters. You have to figure out what powers your quarry has and use the weapons that target those powers. Your dinky little Brawl skill might work in a 3-player game, but any bigger and the monster will not only out-damage you, they have more health than you do: that's a recipe for failure. With the right weapon, you'll hit on 2, 3, 4 and 6 (67% of the time) and for double damage on the 6. The monster can't withstand that kind of punishment for long!

Short version:
Besides the initial (at times very frustrating) hour or so, I have found this game extremely fun to play. It's a decent challenge, looks incredible and the developers are very responsive and diligent at tackling bugs. It is a gem of a game that has production values and mechanics on par with the elite digital card games out there, but which will cost you a fraction of the price to remain forever competitive.
Pros:
- Looks great!
- Unique location mechanics, card abilities and strategies versus other digital card games.
- Very responsive, helpful developers.
- Very stable playing as the Survivor faction (the faction that I have played to date).
- One-time purchase - no spending additional money on decks and booster packs.
- Good sense of progress.
- Fun!
Cons:
- Initial steep learning curve.
- The default Survivor decks can kind of suck.
- No save function when doing a 5 mission Supply Run (not a deal breaker for me)
- Possibly some nasty bugs remain for the Fallen faction (which I don’t play so I can’t confirm 100%)
- No multiplayer (if that is deal breaker for you).
-------------------------------------------------------
Long version:
Before I start I want to make clear that my 19 hours of play to date have all been as the Survivors faction (I want to kill zombies, not be them). As such I have not encountered the frustration or confusion that I have seen a couple of people assign to the Fallen (zombie) faction. This review is based solely on playing as Survivors. For transparency, I was also a Kickstarter backer back in 2012 which is why I did not purchase my key from Steam. I do not know the developers at all except for what I have read in Kickstarter updates.
I don’t write reviews. I don’t submit bugs to developers. I don’t actively engage in discussions on Steam. Like many, I am busy and have a family. I play games to have fun and be challenged. If a game isn’t quickly fun to me I’ll usually move on to something else, maybe coming back to try the game one more time after a few patches. So what is it about Z Year One that has me altering all of the above behaviours, including writing this review? It is because I think this is a gem of a game, with extremely passionate, helpful developers, which might easily get lost amongst the tide of low quality games, skins and DLC that flood Steam’s new releases feed every day. I enjoy this game so much that I want it to succeed so that the developers can one day expand the game even further.
Pros:
- The game looks great - the production quality of the photos on the cards is superb, the design of the different locations are solid and varied, and the leader select videos in Supply Run mode are awesome (unlike anything I have ever seen in a game).
- Diifers from othe DCGs - I love the themed location decks that differ per location. Each location doesn’t just apply a different, cosmetic skin and a global variable to the playing area. Instead each location has it’s own themed deck of people you can save (or try to avoid...), and places and equipment you can discover. Things such as stealth, scavenging, protectors, equipment, rooftops, and barricades all bring diverse, and often unique, elements to Z.
- Very responsive developers - Despite being a two person team, the developers are very active in the forum, helpful and open to feedback.
- Very stable - the game has never crashed for me and I have never encountered a game ending bug. I did encounter a number of card specific bugs at launch but after 3 quick patches I have now played 10 games in a row with zero issues encountered.
- One-time purchase - once you buy the game you receive all content. You won’t spend another cent on buying decks or booster packs. Some cards are initially locked but as you earn XP you permanently unlock these additional cards. You also earn booster packs through play which give you improved versions of the core cards that can be used for playing in Hardcore mode.
- A sense of progress - I’m constantly improving and thinking of better ways to tackle different locations or Fallen. You can’t ride a single deck to steamroll through every location and Supply Run game. Things that initially frustrated the heck out of me became manageable when I equipped the right equipment or combination of cards.
Cons:
- Z has a steep learning curve - You don’t start out playing easy to win tutorial games that teach you the mechanics. You can access a written rules overview at any time by hitting the TAB key, and the developers have created some video tutorials outside of the game, but the game differs enough from other DCGs that I didn’t fully understand many of the rules until I played quite a few games. If you persevere you will learn all of the rules and understand all of the individual card abilities. If you are someone who prefers games where you can get stuck in and start winning (or even have close, competitive games) early on, then Z might be a bit of a shock.
- The default Survivor decks kind of suck - The intent of each deck is to individually highlight three different aspects of playing the Survivors, namely Attack, Stealth and Defence. In my opinion the Firepower (Attack) deck lacks some key things that help you survive the early zombie onslaught. The Scavengers (Stealth) deck has good early survivability but a distinct lack of powerhouse units or weapons to handle the later part of a game. To be fair the Last Stand (Defence) deck is OK, it just isn’t my preferred play style. Using the default decks I lost almost all the time and I found it very frustrating. I nearly gave up on Z completely during that first hour or so because each game wasn’t even slightly competitive. Once I created my own deck blending a balance of early game stealth, defense, and scavenging, and later game offense, then I started to win more than I lost which increased the fun of the game and helped me better learn its rules and nuances. I think it might be a good idea if the developers created a fourth, balanced starter deck and put it at the front of the deck selection queue.
- No Save function when doing a Supply Run - Supply Run is a series of 5 games in a row where the win conditions change and the Fallen get cumulatively stronger each game. Supply Run games also fetch you the best rewards. After each game you can alter your deck if you so desire. In an ideal world I would be able to save between each game so I wouldn’t have to complete a five game run in a single gaming session, but this is something the developers don’t currently have the time and resources to implement. So instead, whenever I play a Supply Run game, I treat it like a tournament from other DCGs and ensure I first have enough time to get to the end of the run. To be fair, completing a Supply Run game in full is much shorter than playing a full tournament in many other DCGs, so this lack of save functionality more a nice-to-have than a great need.
- Possibly still some bugs left - Playing as the Survivors, I have not yet encountered any bugs since patch 1.3. To be transparent I have seen a couple of people say that there are still some bugs when playing as the Fallen but I cannot verify or dispute these. All I can say is that, to date, the developers have been very committed to tackling all bugs, so if there are bugs left I expect that they won’t be around for much longer.
Z isn’t perfect yet, but besides the initial, frustrating hour or so, I have found this game extremely fun to play. It's a decent challenge, looks incredible and the developers are very responsive and diligent at tackling bugs. It is a gem of a game that has production values and mechanics on par with the elite digital card games out there, but which will cost you a fraction of the price to remain forever competitive.

Counter Strike: Global Offensive is one of those games that you find yourself coming back to over and over again. I hear reviewers on websites like IGN or GamesRadar brag about putting 80 hours into a game, and I laugh. I have put almost 400 hours into CSGO, and I still haven't put in as many hours as 1/2 of the community.
Counter-Strike has a lasting appeal when compared to other games because of one main reason: consistency. Because CSGO is a competitive E-sports title, consistency is an extreemly important determining factor as to how well it will find relevance. And Counter-Strike does that very well. I know that when I pick up CS tomorrow evening, I will have roughly the same experience I did when I played it yesterday. It becomes thereputic after a while, to the point that when you've had a bad day, you come home to Counter-Strike instead of your Girlfriend.
I can confidently say that I have gotten my $15 worth out of this game, and will look forward to playing the title for years to come, as Valve further refines weapon balance and statistics. If you haven't taken a shot at CS yet, try it. You might not like it, but if you do, I can assure you that you'll have a new hobby.

note: what I said about the ammo types was incorrect, the game does in fact allow you to check what ammo your gun uses, credit to Ziggylata for pointing that out.
I know that I don't have a lot of hours in this game but hear me out as it will save you the time of downloading it and getting enraged. I'll be splitting this review into three parts, the main plot of the game, the goods and the bads.
Plot: The aim of the game is simple, you have a series of tasks to complete and in order to do so you must gather several materials items in order to proceed, these are usually placed around the map convinently, other times not so much. Usually at the end of these rounds or levels you get a point A-B run through as you would expect from the likes of games like Left 4 Dead.  Ammo is scarce and you start out with a few weapons both melee and ranged by your side and sometimes the ranged weapons can contain a few round if you're fortunate enough.
Bad: if you're expecting servers with admins on and rules then you're not going to find it here. This game is a f-ckfest when it comes to joining servers with friendly fire, players can shoot each other with no consequence what so ever and since this game is heavily relied on Teamwork although its not necessary it breaks the whole game entirely. There is a votekick/voteban system but this is only a plugin to the server so you will be lucky to join a server that has it. Players can spam leave and join to re-enter the round instead of entering spectator which means that they can kill eachother over and over and over eventually this just turns into a free for all CoD like experience which I'm sure most of you that are looking into this game do NOT want. The ammo in this game is a mess, there is no UI so unless you have any gun knowledge and what types of ammo guns usually use then you will most likely find yourself clueless as you scavange for ammo boxes and keep picking the wrong ones up, there is no indication of what ammo you're looking at except for a tiny description on the box which can be quit irritating, especially when you're in a hurry with hundreds of zombies after you. Fortunatly they aren't very fast but that's also part of the issue, there aren't a lot of runners which are the faster variaty of zombies so you will mostly be fighting the slow ones which only are an issue in big groups so levels will last quite a long time before the players actually die, furthermore there's no timer so players don't feel the need to rush through the activities making the gameplay even more sluggish. Because its hard for zombies to grab hold of you unless you are really close to them then teamwork isn't really required and watching each others back doesn't become a necessity. Players will wonder off and get killed instead of staying in a group, of course this depends on who you're playing with so experiences may vary. One thing to note is that there are children zombies so if you don't feel good killing zombie minors then this isn't the game for you. :(
Good: This game is one of the few zombie games out there that even one zombie poses a reasonable threat. Zombies can corner you and when they get hold of you your health begins to deplete. This makes players more cautious as they go through rooms and tight areas. Light is well implemented and used in the game, you will usually get a flashlight when you start the game which is useful for exploring unlit areas, this acompanied with the atmosphere provided by the game can make you feel a little on the edge when you're playing through it, more so if you're the only person alive. You can board doors up using planks that you find around the level which to me was used as last resort tool if you find yourself with no place to run and low on health with tons of zombies but its nice to know that you can board up a door and take your time collecting the various items scattered across.
Overall this game which is also a mod for the Half Life 2 game is a good time waster if you're looking for zombie games. Unfortunatly you will run across various people abusing the friendly fire feature and join/leave spamming games to continue to do so and break your experience. I personally for this reason and some of the other reasons I stated above I don't recommend it but it is definatly an interesting game and fun game and can be considered a free alternative to other zombie games out there.

So, I have a pretty strong suspicion of most early access games. Games in Alpha are often barely even games. Slime Rancher is a pleasant surprise to me.
It already has a fully functional, very smooth engine in place and a world that is actually larger and more fun than most betas. And it is in Alpha. Even if you explore the whole current world quickly, there's still a pretty decent amount to do in managing your ranch.
While it is very good for an alpha, I think what is more exciting is its potential. The alpha currently showcases the fundamentals of what the engine and game mechanics will be capable of. As more content and choices are added, I am sure the simple and intuitive mechanics will evolve to create interesting narratives and complexities in play.
One thing I do think it needs is a little more threat. Right now, Tarrs and wild slimes pose little threat to the ranch itself as long as you take proper precautions with your greed. Air nets and high walls are nearly invincible, even against many boom largos. A well funded rancher faces very little threat from internal tarr creation, and slimes in the wild don't ever encroach on the ranch itself. But these are all things that may come later, in one form or another. There's plenty of time and this is definitely an encouraging start. I'd say it was worth the 20 dollars.

Super meat boy is a fast paced platformer that should not be ignored, this game is extremely fun and is one of my favourite indie games of all time. Whilst it's very fun it's also harder than a necrophilliac in a graveyard, this game can make you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at a level but also make you happy as ♥♥♥♥ when you beat it. It also makes you care way too much about bandages.
Atleast give it a go if you're looking for a challenge. 8/10

Summary
Polished brilliant Indie game....... but has an edge of frustration that could be too much for some people (... including me!).
Gameplay
Super MeatBoy is a modern day quality platformer, it is incredibly hard to master the game but other than being a little frustrated along the way you will be enjoying every minute of trying to rescue Bandage Girl.
This is the kind of game that you will need to play in short spurts as playing for hours on end will probably age you a few years if not breaking fragile items that are placed around by your play area.
Basically, each level you need to reach his girlfriend (Bandage Girl) as quickly as possible without dying by avoiding enemies and traps. All of the levels take place in varied locations such as Caves, Volcanoes etc to bring a varied reply factor to the game and the game progress's at a nice pace to a climatic battle at the end with Dr Featus.
Graphics/Music
The graphics are extremely polished for an Indie title and look great in 1080p, each world has its own distinct art style that plays through perfectly in the game world.
The Music and Sounds are nice, as you will (almost guaranteed) be repeating some levels over and over and over.... you need to have a soundtrack that doesn't get annoying fast and I'm pleased to say that Super MeatBoy's soundtrack is good and is easy to listen to for an extended period of time.
Pros/Cons
Pros
+ Graphics/Music and Sound are great for an Indie title
+ Frustrating yet addicting in the same sentence, it has that positive  'just one more try' mentality to it.
+ Great little story cutscenes before attempting each level/hub.
Cons
- Very tough to master, starts off 'easier' not easy and ramps the difficulty up.
- Not really a 'casual' game in the respect of the hard difficulty.
Final/Personal Thoughts
I personally didn't pick up Super MeatBoy at launch and waited a while for it to appear in the great Steam Sales, overall I would not have been disappointed if I would have picked this up at full price early on as it is a title that is definitely worth it.  The amount of content that is in included is fantastic and worth the effort. Patience, please!
If you do spot this in the sale with a discount please do not glance over it... what are you waiting for.... purchase now if you haven't already!

I now wish I'd bought extra DLC while the sale was on!
I can't really explain why this game is awesome, or why after 70 hours I still feel like a noob lol. Let's be clear - it isn't a perfect game. It's core is about 5 years old, and to be honest the graphics look a bit older (the new DLC look A LOT better), It's a good "truck simulator" but a poor "road simulator" if you get my drift, and there are lots of areas it could be improved. That said... this is one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time, and the developers seem to really love what they do and favour getting it right over "feature flooding" the game.
Check out squirrel's channel on youtube to see what it's really like, but ultimately you won't really understand why driving 20 tonnes of deisel from Felixstowe to Munich perfectly and on time is so rewarding until you do it.
Oh and be prepared for a learning curve - first time out I jacknifed, got stuck in a ditch, ruined the engine and destroyed about 50% of my cargo.... but once you get through that.. what can I say? you buy a truck, deliver cargo, buy more trucks, get employees, deliver cargo, repeat. If you enjoy shouting the word "gay" into the microphone on activision server's this isn't the game for you, but if you're kind of sitting there wondering why everyone is raving about a truck driving game... just do it :D

To start things off this game isn't that bad.  It has potential but it also has it's own share of problems.
Let's start with the positives,  One of the games biggest strengths is it's character interactions.  The game does have a lot of charm to it and I do like a lot of the characters that we do meet.  The artwork is alright with the character portraits being some of the best looking bits.  The music isn't too bad and I found myself wondering which track is my favorite because as soon as I thought I had one favorite track the next level would suprise me with an even better track.  It has a decent amount of stages with secret ones that show up once certain criteria are met.
However there are a few flaws that I would like to talk about.
One of the biggest ones has to do with the music.  As nice as the songs are, they have a problem with not being able to loop seamlessly like you would see in practically every other game.  The songs have clear endpoints and start points so it's obvious when the track restarts.  Heck some of them even leave you with a few seconds of nothing before the music starts up again and it can be annoying especially on the longer stages.  Again the music isn't bad but I just wish they actually looped correctly.
The next point of contention has to be the boss battles.  They are somewhat varied as in the stages that do contain them have different fights so that the fight in one stage is not the same one you get in another.  One example would be the snow stage boss involves you in a giant robot while the lava stage boss fight is a turn based rpg battle.  However this variety comes at a cost.  No boss fight feels really complete.  They are all barebones and simplistic.  This would have been a great chance to get creative but it seems to be a wasted opportunity.  An example of this would be the snow stage.  It basically consists of you inside a giant robot with the only thing to attack with is your robo fists, by smashing them down on the hero running across the bottom of the screen.  You can see everything about the fight within the first several seconds becasue that's all the fight is.
However the biggest problem lies within the sovereign.  If you happen to leave the game and come back, you will be in your ship however all the princesses that have been kidnapped so far will have disappeared.  This will lead to a problem in three seperate occasions.  The first being that there is a part of the game where you need to talk to them for a quest and since they won't be there because you quite the game, you essentially become stuck until restart the stage because restarting the game won't fix your problem.  The other two times so far will cause you to miss cutscenes that happen when you try to select a level.  One of the cutscenes that can be missed will in fact lock you out of a secret level because the cutscene is needed to initiate the stage that unlocks the hidden stage.  It's a problem that I don't know how the developer missed it  through testing.
All said I would recommend the game because despite it's flaws it really isn't that bad.  It just needs more polish and for the boss fights to be fleshed out better and not be so barebones.
I've always wanted to be the villain, and Nefarious captures that perfectly. I kinda wish there were more reverse boss fights, though.

I really wanted to love this game.
The concept of pitting the player as a boss type villain in a platformer is original, the world is colorful thanks to the artistic talent of Gashi-Gashi, the music is serviceable with a few catchy tunes you'll no doubt be humming to and the writing is charming due to the quirkiness of the many characters present in Nefarious. However, the one component that is holding the game far back is the gameplay itself. There's a great game underneath waiting to be released from the chains of its frustrating sluggish controls, the slippery platforming, the odd lacking of sound effects in game and the questionable placement of enemies in the game. The "Boss" Sections of the game while no doubt harking back to that of classic bosses felt underwhelming in execution with said sluggish controls and lack of sound effects bringing down the feel of being this destructive "final boss" and ruining the satisfication one would normally experience in other games as the hero beating said boss.
This by no means is a horrible game but rather a game with unrealized potiential, a game that very much needs more polishing to fully realize its concept as being this platformer supervillain boss in a quirky colorful world. I would buy this game again in a heartbeat if these issues were addressed but for now it is not worth the $14.99 price tag.
EDIT: Looking back more closely, yeah Gashi-Gashi had only did the character potraits and the promotional art of the game. Not the sprites and background of the game at all, a bit disappointing but ah well.

Origins is without a doubt the worst game of the four Arkham games (excluding the Origins Blackgate, which is totally different). Unlike the three other Arkham games made by Rocksteady, WB Montreals is unpolished, unoriginal and kind of dull.
Although I don't think this game is bad, it is a dissappointment in basicly every way you look at it. The story turns into another one of those 'with a certain character in it', who is revealed about 2 hours in. For a lot of people, including me, that was really a bummer. As a side note the grey-ish environments - that seem off-scale compared to the size of Batman - is boring to look at, despite the almost omnipresent chirstmas decorations.
For others, its the large amount of errors and bugs that is inherent with this installation of the series. I experienced crashes and weird enemy behaviours (e.g. getting stuck in walls and frozen animations), but others suffered from more severe ones, like falling through the ground upon restarting from checkpoint. In that case, the player has to restart the whole campaign! I also happen to own this game for the Wii U, where the textures sometimes take forever to load in, making the world look extremely muddy and low poly.
As for the gameplay, I'd say its just alright. The combat feels great, when it works. Often times I felt like my button inputs didn't register causing me to lose that crucial combo. Another dissappointment (in the main game) is the aweful amount of combat, in contrast to the amount of stealth segments. One of the prominent things that change up the pace from the combat, are the stupidly-easy riddler trophies (or in this case datapacks), that even the most simplest animal can solve. Like: sliding under a fence and....solved!
As a completionist, this game is a chore. Not only the above mentioned datapacks are redundant, but also smaller achievements like 'listening to everything Alfred has to say' require more attention than you would want to give it. If you're aiming to get all the achievements, than you'll notice that there isn't a reason to check out the Initiation DLC, as the devs didn't even add the 2 achievements for those on Steam. Even worse, the multiplayer mode has been officially closed since july 2017, making about 10 achievements unobtainable.
Oh, some achievements are bugged for some players too.
The Cold Cold Heart DLC on the other hand is really well done and worth checking out! The main game though, despite the memorable bossfights, is lackluster.

Ingredients
2 cups sugar
1-3/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 cup HERSHEY'S Cocoa
1-1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1-1/2 teaspoons baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1 cup milk
1/2 cup vegetable oil
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
1 cup boiling water
"PERFECTLY CHOCOLATE" CHOCOLATE FROSTING (recipe follows)
Directions
1. Heat oven to 350°F. Grease and flour two 9-inch round baking pans.
2. Stir together sugar, flour, cocoa, baking powder, baking soda and salt in large bowl. Add eggs, milk, oil and vanilla; beat on medium speed of mixer 2 minutes. Stir in boiling water (batter will be thin). Pour batter into prepared pans.
3. Bake 30 to 35 minutes or until wooden pick inserted in center comes out clean. Cool 10 minutes; remove from pans to wire racks. Cool completely. Frost with "PERFECTLY CHOCOLATE" CHOCOLATE FROSTING. Makes 12 servings.
VARIATIONS:
ONE-PAN CAKE: Grease and flour 13x9x2-inch baking pan. Heat oven to 350° F. Pour batter into prepared pan. Bake 35 to 40 minutes. Cool completely. Frost.
THREE LAYER CAKE: Grease and flour three 8-inch round baking pans. Heat oven to 350°F. Pour batter into prepared pans. Bake 30 to 35 minutes. Cool 10 minutes; remove from pans to wire racks. Cool completely. Frost.
BUNDT CAKE: Grease and flour 12-cup fluted tube pan. Heat oven to 350°F. Pour batter into prepared pan. Bake 50 to 55 minutes. Cool 15 minutes; remove from pan to wire rack. Cool completely. Frost.
CUPCAKES: Line muffin cups (2-1/2 inches in diameter) with paper bake cups. Heat oven to 350°F. Fill cups 2/3 full with batter. Bake 22 to 25 minutes. Cool completely. Frost. About 30 cupcakes.
"PERFECTLY CHOCOLATE" CHOCOLATE FROSTING

2/3 cup HERSHEY'S Cocoa
3 cups powdered sugar
1/3 cup milk
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Melt butter. Stir in cocoa. Alternately add powdered sugar and milk, beating to spreading consistency.
Add small amount additional milk, if needed. Stir in vanilla. About 2 cups frosting.

So After I beat the light world I decided that I should write a review of this game. Super meat boy is a one of a kind platformer where you as meat boy, a red little guy try to save your love bandage girl from the evil doctor fertus.
The concept is quite simple you try to get to the end of a really short level (all under 1 minute) and usually getting absolutely obliterated by sawblades. The game offers 7 worlds full off levels and an extra "dark world" witch contains the same levels but much more difficult. It contains a few bosses as well which I personally found a little boring since all of them were much easier than the actual levels. There's also a few warp zones which contains levels with different styles.
The game is also insanely difficult which you most likely can tell from my review already and others too. It's not too rare you end up spending well over an hour on just completing one level which i personally like but for some it might be a big minus.
A little feature they added but which makes a huge difference in my opinion is the fact that meat boy is splashing blood all over the place and that they show all meat boys you've killed in the replay after you complete a level, it makes a nice touch and gives you perspective over how many times you've gotten ♥♥♥♥ed over.
In sum up, super meat boy is a super addicting platform game with insane difficulty, where you run around splashing blood all over the levels. It is one of the best, if not the best platform game I've played up to date and I'd really suggest you to get it if you're a fan of the genre, It's also reasonably priced considering the amount of content it offers.
