Game: Sonic Adventure DX
Genre: Adventure
Developer: Sonic Team/SEGA
System: Steam (PC)
Total Score: 84/100
Value Score: 8.4/10
• Story: 10/10
o Sonic Adventure DX's storyline takes place mostly in a area within a city named Station Square. One day a institution was being attacked by a strange blue creature who eventually was defeated by Sonic who was near by the area. One event led to another and Sonic found himself on a new journey to defeat Eggman who he finds out is responsible for the blue creature. Eggman is planning to take over the world again with the help of the blue creature who seems to be mysteriously powered up by the chaos emeralds. Sonic and friends must go through their own trials and tribulations to unravel the mystery of the blue creature and the unknown visions that each of them have been having throughout this adventure.
• Characters: 10/10
o Many new and old characters return in this new adventure. Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Eggman and Amy from Sonic CD makes a return to the series already making the game the biggest cast of Sonic characters. Not only them but some new characters have been included such as Chaos the blue creature that accompanies Eggman, Tikal who has a mysterious connection to Knuckles, E-102 Gamma a former robotic minion of eggman, and Big the Cat a new mainstay. Ironically this is also the first Sonic game to include human characters who are nothing more than NPCs but a nice addition to the otherwise barren world that would of been if there werent any. The enemies of the game are completely new with some being a replacement for this 3D adventure which is a nice touch.
• GamePlay: 8/10
o Sonic Adventure DX's gameplay is very different from the usual 2D Sonic games that people have played for years before this game came out. The type of gameplay also varies depending on who you are playing as. In the case of Sonic you have the usual running through stages just like the older games however in 3D view. Some of the other characters you play as include Tails, Knuckles, Big the Cat, Amy and E-102 Gamma who have a alternate type of playstyle such as Tails who mostly tries to catch up to Sonic, Amy who tries to get away from a captor, E-102 Gamma who tries to find a exit or pod to release animals, Big the Cat who's levels are just fishing levels, and Knuckles who looks for 3 crystal shards of the Master Emerald. The characters all have same points of areas to explore however the level design and goal for each is different. Each character has his or her own storyline with their own set of cutscenes and boss battles. By completing each and every storyline will get you the chance to unlock an additional secret story which takes you to the conclusion of the game. Throughout the game you will find powerups for characters which will assist them in their adventures. The gameplay is also similar to any other Sonic game as well such as collecting rings to keep you alive as well. However unlike previous Sonic games, exploration is key to the game and you'll be exploring a majority of the time for certain points of the game or for certain items.
• Graphics: 7/10
o Sonic Adventure DX's visuals have greatly improved from the older sonic games. It seem like Sega couldnt at first figure out how to make Sonic in 3D after a few failed attempts but it seems like they finally got it right by completely changing the usual art style they have had for the series. The series seem to be pushing more forth a teenage like audience rather than the usual child audience they have been catering too - despite that they managed to maintain the same content they have had for years but bringing a fresh new look. The visuals are quite amazing for its time with the overall world being fully detailed such as in a GTA like game. The character models are also well done and the animation is quite nicely done with a few rough edges here and there but that was mostly because this was the Sonic team's first full attempt at making a full fledged 3D sonic game. Despite that fact even though it has been years since the original game's release and technology has far improved it doesnt seem like Sega had any intention to improve the overall visuals as the game pretty much is the same as it has been since the beginning.
• Sound: 7/10
o Sonic Adventure DX uses the same sound effects from previous sonic games when breaking a pod or collecting ring but it also includes several new effects thanks to the departure from the 2D landscape to the 3D world. Along with that for the first time the Sonic series now has voice overs for characters which gives a nice touch to the overall storyline. However despite nice additions, some of the voice acting can be pretty unbearable such as Amy's voice but other than that nothing seems too forced.
• Music: 10/10
o Sonic Adventure DX uses a completely new style of music more of a rock/indie rock type themes rather than the traditional industrial type of music that the series has used for quite a while. Along with that there seems to be some pop music added and along with that several vocal tracks for boss battle and character themes. Overall it is one of the best OSTs in the Sonic series.
• Length: 7/10
o Sonic Adventure DX so far is the longest Sonic game, there are over 5 characters to play as with their own respected storyline, the exploration in the game adds more to the length and you get the additional storyline once you finish all other character's storylines. Overall a decent length for a platformer, this game should take you somewhere between 10-15 hours at the max.
• Replay Value: 7/10
o Sonic Adventure DX lets you play stages again if you want and also includes a boss battle mode where you can fight against the bosses again. Unlike the previous sonic games where you would have to play the games all over again, you can just go back to the specific area and play that level again depending on who you play as. Of course you are also free to restart a storyline from the beginning without actually having to explore around for powerups.
• Player Value: 8/10
o Sonic Adventure DX is an amazing addition to the Sonic the Hedgehog series. The game has revolutionized the series with its new look, new and expanded gameplay, groundbreaking visuals compared to older games, a decent change to the music, and a well developed storyline that revolves around each and every character with their own role in the storyline. If you can look past the problems, Sonic Adventure is a pretty damn good game. The level design is still pretty good, the music is catchy and memorable, and the core gameplay as Sonic is really fun. But sadly, it's issues and flaws have made the game unbearable for me, despite my nostalgia.
Either way, it's still the same Dreamcast classic from over 15 years ago. It's fun, but don't be surpirsed if it's not nearly as great as you remember.

Kidnap Princesses! Defeat Heroes! Be the Villian! And embrace all the tropes that come with it!
Nefarious could have been seen as another clever, fun platformer, there are a lot, but it really sets itself apart from the pack. The humor and riffing on the classic hero vs villian mentality makes even the truly evil Crow a joy to watch as he wrecks havoc, princess in tow. Most times having a princess with you will also add a new element to the platforming, like a high jump, or creating bridges with smoke. Then, after all the mooks and common do-gooders have been defeated, take part in what they call a reverse boss fight. Be the boss smacking the hero around! Get your giant robot and shoot lasers at a nimble hero, trying to take you down! These fights are fun, if only a small part of the whole, but thematically they're awesome and all the fun outweighs the feeling of it just being a different kind of boss fight.
It's not without faults, the grenades seem to sort of just... go where they will, and physics can be a bit wonky at times. I also thought we were past insta-kill traps but here we remain.
Also, the music is great, I think the animation is fantastic, and it's a lot of fun, that's all very subjective though.

"Are you ar real vilain? Have you ever caugh a good guy, like a superhero? Have you ever tried to disguise? Alright, I can see that I'll have to teach you how to be vilains"
Memes aside, Nefarious is a indie 2D platformer that was funded via kickstarter where you plays as Crow, the boss of a vilainous group, who kidnapp princess for a living and try to take over the world. The game is fully aware of the different tropes of the genre and fully play with it. Since you play as the bad guy, expect boss fight where YOU are in the giant mech.
While the game is good, it's far from perfection.
Graphically speaking, it's not very great. The differents backgrouds are nice and everything is well animated, but the rest is kinda meh (think of flash games you can find on newgrounds)
Gameplay wise, it's solid. Movement key, jump, punch, shoot and interact. Most level ask you to go and capture a princess, leave while using some power given by her then fight a good guy to end the level. Each boss fight is different and no level feel the same.  With the money you get during levels, you can upgrade Crow by expanding his life and grenade count or change how his punch and grenades works. The game is rather easy since there is a lots of checkpoints and death is only a nuisance (you lose some money, you can get it back if you go where you died).
The game isn't that long but each level has 3 crown to collect and a vinyl (used to listen to the OST between levels), each level taking from 5 min to 15. There is 2 endings and a bunch of difficult achievement.
Speaking of OST, some are great, some are meh, the only big downside is that the music doesn't loop properly, leaving a blank of 2-3 second before playing the intro again.
The story isn't that deep (which is expected for the genre but still with some surprising twist) but some of the characters are well written (saddly, most of them are meh or haven't enough interaction to have any real personnality).
The game cost 15€ but I'd recommand to wait 'till it's on sale before buying it. The dev' promised some bonus content in the futur even if they haven't met any stretch goals.
Nefarious might not be vilain numer one, but it's still a good game overall.

Here's the thing about Nefarious: Great ideas for making you feel like the villain, especially in the boss fights, but this game displays a REMARKABLE lack of polish.
For example, the first boss fight sees you piloting a small spherical ship carrying a wrecking ball on a chain that you swing around to hit the attacking hero, which is essentially the first boss fight from Sonic the Hedgehog but with you as Eggman/Robotnik. Great idea, right?
The hero raises these towers from the ground that he'll stand on to shoot at you, and you can use the ball to knock them down. But when you knock them down, they just fall over. There's no particle effects, no screen shaking, there aren't even any
to go along with it. And when you hit the hero with the ball, it just plays a small "whack" sound effect and
bounces off of
. You'd expect that he'd get flung across the stage from the force of being hit, but no. He's not affected by being struck by the ball in the slightest, except that it makes him a little dizzy. The ball, however, bounces right off his head as if he's made of concrete. This makes it feel like the ball actually weighs
than the hero does, and more like you're swinging around an oversized party balloon instead of a massive wrecking ball of solid metal.
This kinda stuff doesn't make the game BAD, but it really gives the whole experience a very ho-hum feeling because nothing you do seems to have any real impact. Any POWER! You're finally given access to all the rad weapons that every villain you've ever had to fight has used against you, and they just seem hollow and lackluster. Combine this with the fact that there's ZERO dialogue after beating any of the heroes (in stark contrast to practically every other interaction with them), and the end result is that these super cool and cleverly designed encounters just come across as unimpressive and gimmicky. Which is a real shame, because the actual gameplay is pretty fun and interesting, and you can tell that a lot of effort went into making them challenging while being faithful to the original boss fights they were inspired by AND also fun at the same time.
I
hope that this is something StarBlade can address by pushing out some updates to the game or something, because it wouldn't take a whole lot of work compared to what they've already done, and I have a feeling that it'd really improve the game's overall reception. They have a solid design, great characters, and snappy voice acting to flesh out geniunely comedic writing, but they really need to make it seem like Crow is the badass evil mastermind that he deserves to be.
With a small amount of extra attention, Nefarious could really be something special.

Nefarious explores what might happen if a video game villain got a bit of momentum behind him and got to see some of his evil plans actually come to fruition. Revived from the ashes of every 16-bit action platformer ever, Crow is a princess-capturing evil genius who manages his first triumph when the resident hero of Macro City decides he’s tired of dealing with bi-weekly kidnapping attempts and skulks off. Stolen princess in hand, Crow returns to his floating sky fortress, which is resplendent with an army of minions and a collection of war machines, desperate to keep his streak going. With only another four more princess' in tow, he’ll finally be able to power his Doom Howitzer. Then, all of those pesky governments would be forced to bow to his demands!
Only… there’s something a little off with his tyranny. Though Princess Mayapple is undoubtedly his prisoner, she seems pretty relaxed about it, asking Crow’s minions about the well-being of their families and treating the sky fortress as a second home. It becomes clear quite quickly that she’s actually quite fond of Crow and his gang of crooks, hanging out with his assistant, Becky, and (to further her parodying of Princess Peach) reminding Crow of all the times she took him to tennis matches and kart races on their down time. Successful missions add further captives, who all socialise among themselves and lead to a dynamic I never really expected out of Nefarious. We’ve all seen the roguish villain turn out not to be the black-hearted cruelster he initially seems, but rarely has an evil-doer’s sinister persona been so expertly assaulted.
It’s hard not to take an instant liking to Crow, thanks to his pseudo-Mega Man get-up and his self-admitted addiction to villain tropes and clichés. All he wants to do, after all, is rule the world, which is something he inches closer and closer to doing as the game proceeds. Each stage he undertakes is a kingdom ruled by one of those princesses he needs, the completion of which leads to another member of royalty in chains, and another populace’s defence force smashed. Mayapple’s human kingdom is awash with rookie officers and police mechs, while a nearby Insect kingdom tries to defend their ruler with wasp knights and armoured beetles. They all maintain the familiar genre groundings of hidden collectibles and scattered currency to collect, but still offer differing environments to explore and overcome.

TL;DR: Buy it, you won't regret it.
Nothing can compare to Euro Truck Simulator 2. It's not somehting specific but a concoction of many different things that peice this game together into a beautiful mix of stress and relaxation.
The joy of roaming the world at the start, working for others in their trucks is blissful. Being able to ding the truck untill it is 100% damaged with no consequences makes the later parts of the game have so much more gravity and realism.
At the moment of taking a loan out from the bank and buying your own truck is the moment it all becomes real. When 1% damage costs as much as £1000 of your own money is the moment you get serious about being a professional truck driver and not a suicidal maniac on the roads of Europe.
But all that pressure washes away as you are making your delivery bound from London to Luxemburg when listening to the volunteer run radio stadion does Barbie Girl, The Crazy Frog, Blue (Da Ba Dee) and finally Sandstorm all play in a row. In addition to that, you can make you game even harder with punishment from the community like 'More AI Traffic' which ramps ups your frustration towards other drivers and your sympathy for truckers everywere.
The fun really begins when you realise that you can turn off the speed limiter that is turned on by default and add 30+ mph to your travels. While it sounds like nothing, it doesn't feel that way when you make a poor overtake down a narrow mountain road with a blind bend and run your truck head on into an innocent oncoming vehicle.  Then you realise that 30k in repairs will bankrupt you so it's either that and make a perfect 30 minute delivery with no fines and 'dings' to pay off your mounting debts  or attempt to make deliveries with a truck that randomly has engine failures whilst bombing down the motoway at 80mph.
10/10, would scream at poor AI drivers at 3am and wake the house up again.

This may not be the best Sonic game, but it is certainly my 19th favorite video game.

IN SHORT,
This game is a SUPER fun city builder/manage game, it's probably my favorite game on steam, and even though I have nearly 400 hours of playing time, I'm still having fun playing it.
---
If you're creative and/or enjoy city builders/managment type games then, you'll enjoy this game.
Prison Architect has 3 different modes to choose from:
The first mode is the story mode. It's not too long but it's a pretty interesting story. Its main purpose is to serve as a tutorial for the sandbox mode of the game; Which it does a great job doing.
And because, the storymode is a tutorial, if you haven't played the story mode, you'll have a lot of trouble understanding Sandbox mode. Sandbox mode is where the game's really at. The idea is to play as an almost omnipresent prison owner who hires people to build a prison from the ground up, manages the income of the prison, (which is done primarily through accepting more prisoners to watch over the prison) hires prison guards/armed guards, prevent contraband from entering the prison, keep the prisoners from killing each other, and most importantly make sure they live to finish there sentences. But doing this isn't as simple as it sounds.
You have to manage the prisoners schedules; telling them where to go and when to go there, give the prisoners some rehab programs, and whatever else they need to keep them happy. All so they have a less chance of returning to prison. A happy prisoner (for the most part) is also a content prisoner. So the happier they are, the less they'll try to escape.
On this mode, you can play with or without mods or built in cheats. Steam offers tons of mods (and pre-built prisons to watch over in case your feeling lazy)
If you make a really great prison you can also put it on the steam marketplace for others to use. It's great fun!
Speaking of good prisons, the third mode, escape mode, is most fun when you have a seemingly unescapable prison. In this mode you play as a prisoner who tries to escape your own prison. Personally, I don't like it as much as sandbox mode, but it can be a good and fun challenge from time to time.
10/10, would recommend to any gamer.

Greetings!  Today we have Prison Architect; a building management tycoon style game done with a (very) simple art style that started out as early access and now appears to be fully released.  Does it hold up to other Tycoon games and can it hold on to your hard earned money in an age of triple A graphics and adaptive AI?  Uhh...Yup.
What are you in for:  The game is more or less a standard building management game where you give orders to have things built, areas watched and things crafted but have no real direct control.  The twist comes from the fact that you aren’t hosting tourists, tenants or dungeon delvers but inmates.  Inmates that not only have to be kept in line but taken care of with a careful balance of mitigating harm to prevent escapes or deaths but also encourage education and reform; at first I really only cared about the former but the later does become very important as you start optimizing your prison.  This is a very simple interface but does have a few bugs and poor quality of life decisions, not all of the options feel intuitive and some tool tips are just plainly broken.   Some of it you just have to learn as you go and from trial and error; leaving the game definitely in an unfinished feel.
Go directly to Jail:  The game has a single player campaign disguised as a tutorial.  This threw me off at first as I was actually trying to initially rush through it thinking it would be a few minutes of story and then on to a sandbox.  Well, I can tell you I was wrong…and I am very happy at that.  I won’t ruin the story as I found it enjoyable with several twists and moments that I was sure the game was trying to sell politics until it immediately turned the coin over and showed the other side.  I found this story oddly intriguing and I did find that I was rushing objectives to get to the next plot piece.  I should note that each chapter of the campaign does relate so pay attention to each chapter; they aren’t stand alone.
Meeple City:  The graphics aren’t initially something that you think would have much to talk about but I found that they conveyed the information needed while remaining charming.  This is odd because I tend to lean towards more realistic graphics, though I will openly admit the sound was very forgettable and I eventually muted it.  As I stated above the controls could use some work (would like to know what items have access points without having to build and move).  I will say that I would have liked to see some more interesting options during the sandbox, can I accept corruption?  Maybe I have a VIP who needs to be protected?  Have an inspection I need to prep for?  Dirty guards that are on the take?  I mean the options are endless, I’d love to see these added in expansions.
So, does this oddly animated kickstarter turned release hold up?  In a word, yes.  Simply put if you like tycoon or building management games you will get your money from this game.  Though many will disagree I did find myself at the cusp of being bored when I finished but the journey was well worth the crime committed (yay prison puns).  As always, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

If you're a hardcore Devil may cry fan you've probably already bought and played this game. This is my 2nd copy and i must say that it holds up really well to this day! So im just gonna get the elephant in the room out of the way, which is the direction that ninjatheory went with this game in therm of style. This game got alot of hate for not being faithful to its sourcematerial, and to some consent i agree. Dante and Virgil are some of the most beloved characters in all of gaming and here they stick out like a sour thumb. Especially Virgil which lacks all of his characteristics from the past games and does a 180 for the worse in my opinion. Note that this is a subjective matter, and should not be a decisive manner for you to buy the game.
But if you can look past the somewhat flawed characteristics you're in foor a treat.
The story takes place before the first Devil may cry game. Long story short: in a world controlled by Mundus the king of demons, you take control of Dante: the bad mouthed, "wisecracking" demon slayer and with the help of your twin brother Virgil you try to recover your past and take revenge on Mundus for the killing of your mother (Eve), and the banishing of your father (Sparda). The story isn't something groundbreaking that will make you drop your jaw to the floor, but that isn't the case for any dmc game.
Where this game really shines is in it's art direction. Ninjatheory really nailed it with the world of Dmc: Devil may cry and it is the most beutifull game in the series by far. Switching from the real world and limbo is a treat for the eye and seeing the world do everything to stop you as you progress makes for some of the best parts in the whole series.
But a devil may cry game isn't anything without its combat. All in all the combat feels great to play around with and it's something that other games in the genre should take notes from. New players will find it easy to do combos and feel like a badass, but there is enough depth for veteran players to get ssstylish. Switching around from diffirent weapons alsow feel easy and rewarding while in combat and you will find yourself using all of the buttons on your controler/keyboard.
But there are two flaws in the combat system which are holding it back from being 10/10.
The first one is not to bad which is that some weapons in your arsenal is clearly better then the others which makes the other feel pretty usless in many situations which is a shame. Note that this isn't sutch a big flaw because it's not like they are totaly usless and they are still fun to play around with.
The other flaw which is a giant facepalm is that in your weapon arsenal there is angel and demon wepons. For some reason ninjatheory thought it would be a good ide to make some enemies only take damage from angel wepons and some only from demon wepons. This seems cool at first but you'll soon realise that this is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when there is alot of enemies at the same time because it takes away all the style out of the combat when you accidentally hit a angel demon with your demon wepon and bounce of ruining your flow. This makes you go for cheap tactics just so you can focus on one enemy.  If this feuture wasn't in the game it would have been twice as good.
All in all this is a great game. It nails most of parts but at the same time falls flat when it comes to the core of devil may cry. But with great combat, a pretty neet story and amazing visuals. If you're a oldschool devil may cry or hack and slash fan there is something here for everyone and in my opinion you owe it to yourself to pick this game up for the current price!

Nefarious is a very short, sweet experience.
Let me just start by saying I love what this game set out to do. I've been wanting something like this since I first started gaming as a child. Sure there's plenty of games where you played a badguy, but never before have you felt like THE VILLAIN. Princess in tow, Hero on your heels, running a life of crime from a flying fortress. And Nefarious delivers. Its concept, design, idea, and even style is top notch. However the game is far from perfect.
Where Nefarious suffers a lot is in the gameplay standpoint. Now, its really hard to rate this because I've never felt this way about a game's gameplay before. How do I phrase this properly?
I love the gameplay, but I don't think it was perfected. The ideas are there, but it feels like there was some programming issues that were never looked at or resolved before release, possibly due to the size of the team. Jumping is floaty, and slippery, and can get stuck on things. The hit box for your punching sometimes doesn't add up. Being hit and hitting things doesn't feel right, everything just kind of rubs off eachother like two balloons.
And the sound design. WOOF. Does someone need to get fired for the sound design. Music doesn't loop properly. Sound effects for things as basic as footsteps aren't consistent. The volume is all over the place, including a boss battle in particular that has a nearly Screamer level sound byte that made me jump the first time I heard it. I had to play the fight with my headphones off, and there was no way to adjust it.
Overall, despite my gripes, the love was there. The idea was there. It just felt like the project ended up bigger and more complicated than the team had planned for, and some unfortunate things had to be rushed or cut.
I would love to see this game get a sequel, where the gameplay is trimmed up, improved, and expanded upon, and the story is pulled to a much larger perspective. I would fund the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that.
::Pros::
+ Wonderful, creative, and unique idea.
+ Charming artstyle
+ Very fun theme and engaging world
+ An extremely hard attempt was made
::Cons::
- Gameplay and programming felt rushed and buggy
- Not much replayability
- Sound Design issues (Needs to be fixed ASAP)

I just finished watching the after-credits scene, and I guess it's time to review ths bad boy.
So.
What is Nefarious?
It's a Megaman style (kinda) 2D platformer with hand drawn graphics where you play as Crow - super villian who plans to kidnap all princesses in the world and use them to power a machine that will make him the ruler of the world.
Like in Megaman you go from left to right fighting legions of enemies and have two different ways of arracking: punching people with your robotic arm and shooting grenades. When you kidnap a princess, you get a new ability for a while: for example the bee princess makes makes you glide, with the demon one you can use grenades to make platforms, artificial one gives you super jumps and unlimited ammo, but the dwarf one starts riding you like a horse and you dash through a cave filled with monsters while she throws axes everywhere. After you get to the end of the stage with the princess, you encounter the local hero and you two fight, but there's a small difference: since you are the bad guy, you get to play the role of the boss. You can fly in the Robotnik style flying machine with a huge ball on a chain, punch a dwarf hero in a mech or chase your superhero rival in a big robot through the city.
The platforming in this game works pretty well, and I like the concept of using grenades to reach areas you can't jump to. There were some parts that I got pretty frustrated with, for example the Academia: while the music in this level is really awesome, it's definitely much harder than the previous stages since you have do dodge lasers, jump on small platforms while avoiding enemies and do other tricky platforming♥♥♥♥♥♥ Turns out I was not the only one who got mad at this stage, but since everything else was pretty enjoyable, I will just blame this one on me being bad.
Story in Nefarious is actually really good. It's pretty light-hearted with several funny moments (like when Crow gets destroyed by a princess and decides to kidnap her brother instead, and the mentioned scene with the dwarf princess riding Crow like a horse is also pretty hilarious), but it also gets serious at times. It also does it's own twist on several gam tropes, for example the villian finally has a good reason for kidnapping the princess other than "He's just evil okay? Screw off, like go and find all the stars or something geez", and on the concept of "good" and "bad" guys.
The game also has two endings. In the Good Ending Crow actually starts becoming friends with the people he kidnapped and ends up standing up for them before the final phase of his plan. The good route is pretty adorable, as you can see that Crow is not that bad at all. He kinda reminds me of Gru from Despicable me (you know, before they decided to focus on these annoying yellow ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and it all went to♥♥♥♥♥♥, only a bit more evil. The princesses (and prince) are also very likeable characters and missions in which they work together with Crow are pretty adorable.
Because the Good ending is so touching, the Bad ending becomes pretty heartbreaking, since Crow backstabs people that wanted to his friends and honestly, I can't really do the evil route since I'm really satisfied with the good one.
In the end, Nefarious is a pretty solid platformer with adorable characters and great music that puts it's own twist on common videogame tropes.
I heavily recommend you to give it a shot.

Story: 10/10
The writing is witty, entertaining and in serious moments it caught me off guard more than once. The story itself is a deconstruction of villain-centered tropes, but the characters and world manage to be colorful and imaginative enough that they're memorable in their own right.
Crow is a villain protagonist, and without spoiling anything, he manages to form real connections and have genuine development with the other characters without hitting the muck of anti-heroism. He's a villain 100%, and he does it because he loves it. It's as simple as that, without it being all that simple.
The Princesses are monarchs in all but name of their respective kingdoms; true videogame princesses. And even from the position of being kidnapped and stashed on Crow's ship like a trophy collection, they all have personal agency and an active role in the story. They all have interesting personalities and defining character moments.
The game manages to avert gameplay/story segregation. During gameplay it still felt like there was a story happening around me, and strictly story moments didn't lose the sense that I was playing a game.
Gameplay: 5/10
It lacks polish. The controls are sluggish and imprecise. I found myself relying more on Crow's ability to absorb damage than reflex or skill. His basic melee attack has a delay that feels like it belongs in a slower-paced, more methodical game, and his alt-weapons made every effort to not be overpowered and feel equally stifled.
Checkpoints are frequent and you don't have a finite number of lives. This helps, but it's still subpar as platformers go.
The reverse boss fights are fun the first time, but all consist of learning one tactic that works and repeating until the fight is won. Even the true final boss is like this; the fight itself is a technical mess, but it becomes easy once you learn the winning pattern.
Sound: 7/10
If this music was in anything other than a 2D platformer it'd be solid gold, but as it stands its pacing is too relaxed and doesn't click right in the brain.
The sound effects are solid and there's nothing to complain about. I wouldn't even bring them up if not for some instances of the soundwork standing out in a positive way, such as the regular steel groaning inside Crow's airship.
Visuals: 9/10
The characters are all hand-drawn down to the faceless redshirts you blow up and they look beautiful. Crow's heavier mech hand dangling behind him when he runs is a touch you don't see just anywhere. The different regions feel visually distinct.
Overall
This kind of game is to my taste, and I found it well worth the $15 wish I'd supported its Kickstarter. This game is a gem. A semi-cut, flawed gem, but a gem.

I first heard about this game in Brawl in the Family, and ever since I've had it sticking in the back of my head as a neat-looking game. So I went ahead and bought it on launch day and played through the whole thing in one sitting, and felt... Marginally satisfied. Could have been better, but it's still quite good.
PROS
-Superb art and animation, it pops well and looks sufficiently cartoony for the theming.
-Excellent soundtrack, wonderfully catchy and atmospheric.
-Good design choices lifted from Shovel Knight (Infinite lives, pick up money after death, music pickups, etc).
-Well-written story with fun characters and witty dialogue. Has lots of good trope-skewering moments and affectionate parodies.
-Controls smoothly, maneuvering isn't an issue and the platforming is good.
-Good level variety.
CONS
-Combat is weak. The maneuvers you can do are very limited (Punch or throw grenade), and some enemies can be frustrating due to too much health, too many of them, or attacks that are too tough to dodge.
-Boss fights are kind of meh; Good concept, but often weak execution due to oversimplification or the heroes acting like predictable bosses, destroying the point of the fight. Can also be frustrating, ESPECIALLY the true final boss.
-Level design is good for the most part, but can be very obtuse/annoying in a few places (Looking at you, last level).
-Wonky sound design; Some sound effects are too loud, others are too soft or just aren't there when they should be.
-Not much replay value outside of finding the crowns (Which do nothing as far as I know).
-Short; As noted above I completed it in one sitting. However, it was a long one and it's a $15 budget title.
OVERALL
I think this game had a superb concept and some mostly-good execution but some iffy parts; The team behind it put passion and interest into it and probably put a lot of love into it and I absolutely appreciate that, but there are a few mistakes that make me think they were inexperienced. Or maybe they didn't have the resources considering the Kickstarter just barely made its goal. Regardless, as a fun little $15 game, I rather liked it. It's a little disappointing compared to what I was expecting; Honestly, with the fact that the devs clearly were invested in the project I would feel really bad giving it a negative review. It's still an all right time, though; I would rate it at about a 7/10. Maybe 6.5.

Another zombie survival game. This very broad genre has so many similar games that it makes it very difficult for a new game to stand out. Being a very succesful mod, NMRiH had a lot of high expectations as a stand alone game, perhaps to high. Although the overall gameplay and graphics are great, this game has its fair share of flaws. For example, the waves can take a rediculously long time because the zombies are slower than a sloth on tranquilizers. Because this game is only multiplayer, it can also get frustrating finding decent servers, and, sometimes you have to be a spectator for ages because the last survivor either has no clue how to complete the objectives or just loves annoying the others. Many reviews also complain about the lack of resources, weapons and ammo. I for one, love this about the game, with such limmited resources, surviving waves of zombies is quite challengeing, and that is what they are meant to be. Many modern zombie games make it way too easy to find good weapons and enough ammo to wipe out the entire planet.
Do i recommend it? Surprisingly yes. I for one will not spend a lot more time playing this game, but i can see why people would like it. There are a lot of great things about this game and the mod had great reception. Many of the flaws can be fixed and if they are, this has the potential to be a really fun game.

This game is definitely worth its money despite only being like 6 hours long for some reason (maybe Steam is tracking that wrongly?! I could have sworn it was longer, but that's the beauty of it: it doesn't FEEL short). It's a typical spectacle brawler with moves upon moves and upgrades and items and gauges, etc.
The main game comprises of 20 missions, each between 10 to 20 minutes long on average (easy and medium at least). You will be platforming, looking to find all the secrets and fighting groups of baddies with an ever increasing arsenal of skills. But enemies will also get tougher later on. I think there are 5 boss fights in the game, each one is interesting and in its own way challenging (apart from 1 really, which is just a bit annoying). The levels are each highly different and action-packed, and in order to find all secrets you will need to replay the game. In the missions you can also find keys that unlock special mission doors (kill x enemies in x seconds with x attack for example), which give additional rewards (keys carry over into other missions by the way).
The main goal, however, is to defeat enemies as stylishly as possible, in which you will be rated from D to SSS. Getting hit drops the style combo, using the same attacks over and over again will also not net you a high score, so you want to be as diverse as possible...and there are more than enough moves to do so. At the end of each mission you'll be rated by your overall performance and the results are posted to the global leaderboards. After you beat the campaign you can go at it again in some different modes that shuffle enemy groups around or make you be a 1-hit-1-death-wonder (which also applies to you, however). For people who like that kind of stuff I think they made a good effort.
The story itself, while so standard, is actually presented quite nicely. I've had fun.
Save your money on the DLCs, those are just costumes. Maybe get the brawl pack to fight against hordes of enemies if you fancy that. Other than that only Vergil's Downfall is worth your time I'd say. It adds another 1-2 hours of gameplay, in which you play as Vergil after the events of the main game. Vergil actually plays pretty nicely, but the lack of a double jump was really jarring and I still don't know why they stripped that out. The DLC also seems a lot more difficult, even on the same difficulty level, at least when it comes to achieving style points.
The camera, however, is ABSOLUTE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and whoever designed that needs to go back to class. It gets frequently "stuck" on walls, which can result in an untimely demise at worst and is a major inconvenience at best.

Greetings!  Today we have Prison Architect; a building management tycoon style game done with a (very) simple art style that started out as early access and now appears to be fully released.  Does it hold up to other Tycoon games and can it hold on to your hard earned money in an age of triple A graphics and adaptive AI?  Uhh...Yup.
What are you in for:  The game is more or less a standard building management game where you give orders to have things built, areas watched and things crafted but have no real direct control.  The twist comes from the fact that you aren’t hosting tourists, tenants or dungeon delvers but inmates.  Inmates that not only have to be kept in line but taken care of with a careful balance of mitigating harm to prevent escapes or deaths but also encourage education and reform; at first I really only cared about the former but the later does become very important as you start optimizing your prison.  This is a very simple interface but does have a few bugs and poor quality of life decisions, not all of the options feel intuitive and some tool tips are just plainly broken.   Some of it you just have to learn as you go and from trial and error; leaving the game definitely in an unfinished feel.
Go directly to Jail:  The game has a single player campaign disguised as a tutorial.  This threw me off at first as I was actually trying to initially rush through it thinking it would be a few minutes of story and then on to a sandbox.  Well, I can tell you I was wrong…and I am very happy at that.  I won’t ruin the story as I found it enjoyable with several twists and moments that I was sure the game was trying to sell politics until it immediately turned the coin over and showed the other side.  I found this story oddly intriguing and I did find that I was rushing objectives to get to the next plot piece.  I should note that each chapter of the campaign does relate so pay attention to each chapter; they aren’t stand alone.
Meeple City:  The graphics aren’t initially something that you think would have much to talk about but I found that they conveyed the information needed while remaining charming.  This is odd because I tend to lean towards more realistic graphics, though I will openly admit the sound was very forgettable and I eventually muted it.  As I stated above the controls could use some work (would like to know what items have access points without having to build and move).  I will say that I would have liked to see some more interesting options during the sandbox, can I accept corruption?  Maybe I have a VIP who needs to be protected?  Have an inspection I need to prep for?  Dirty guards that are on the take?  I mean the options are endless, I’d love to see these added in expansions.
So, does this oddly animated kickstarter turned release hold up?  In a word, yes.  Simply put if you like tycoon or building management games you will get your money from this game.  Though many will disagree I did find myself at the cusp of being bored when I finished but the journey was well worth the crime committed (yay prison puns).  As always, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

I definitely recommend checking this out if you're a fan of 2d platformers like mega man or shantae, and enjoy the subversion of videogame tropes.
The story is by far the most excellent part of the game. The dialogue is clever and fun, and the story is enjoyable while allowing the player some agency over its direction.
My only complaints were a few platforming puzzles that felt awkward and not fun to traverse. Also, the sound effects could use improvement in a few ways. Namely, some sounds are not well normalized and are too loud versus the rest of the music and sounds. Also, there are moments where, if you had the music off, there would not be enough sound effects to match the action going on. There needs to be a few more sound hooks for explosions and other events in the game, particularly during boss fights and cutscenes.
The soundtrack is very good. The vocal bits were really well done, and for the most part, everything fit very well with the game. Similar to the audio complaint above, there are some moments where, for cinematic purposes, it would be nice to have a music cue change, but the same track keeps looping. A minor complaint though, as all the tracks are good.
Overall, I'd give this game a good 80% rating. I think it would have benefitted from one more polish pass over some of the awkward platforming segments, the sound hooks, and some cinematic moments ending a bit a bruptly. If those were polished up, it'd be a 90%+ game in my opinion.
Regardless, if you skip this one, you're missing an awesome story and some really enjoyable characters. Don't miss out, buy this game and enjoy the hours of fun it provides!

This is an amazing game if you're interested in the concept.
The whole game is based around looking at the main good guy vs bad guy trope in video games, and it makes light of the idea a bunch, while tying in a more serious story.  It does that really well, and is fun to play through that.
Most of the characters are simple enough, while still be exciting.
However, what a lot of people criticize it for is the gameplay.
The gameplay isn't phenomenal, and shouldn't be why you play it.  It's simple and fun enough that you can usually breeze through and enjoy the rest of the beautiful game without too much issue, with just enough challenge that it feels like you're actually doing something.
When it does get hard, it's usually obnoxious jumping challenges or parts that just feel unfair.  That doesn't happen often, so it's not too big of a deal, but as said before, it reinforces that this isn't really the game you play to get a game with solid gameplay.
There's also a few places where the world wasn't made quite perfectly, so if a few small flaws will get to you, perhaps something else.
If you have any interest in the concept the game advertises itself as, pick it up and play it.  The gameplay won't really get in the way much, except for a few times near the end.
If the concept doesn't seem for you and you just want a game with great gameplay and tight controls, perhaps look into something else.

I really enjoy this game but unfortunately I cannot recommend it in its current state. Yes, it's in early access. Yes, the devs are good with updates and communication, and yes the game has a lot of potential. But I'm sorry, the moment you start charging money for a game, expect it to be reviewed as it is, not on hopes and promises. And unfortunately, this game is just not worth the trouble at the moment. The point of this review is not to complain. It is not to vent. It is not to bash the developers. It is simply to inform potential buyers of whether or not the game
is worth their time and money. The relative "worth" of the game has been determined by judging what the game currently brings to the table relative to other similar games of similar pricing on Steam.
This is not meant to be a comprehensive review that covers all the pros and cons of the game but rather just explanation of the main deal-breakers. If you are looking for the echo chamber of "AMAZING POTENTIAL" there is plenty of that to be found in the other reviews.
If you are consistently researching artifacts at a decent pace, you will likely unlock every piece of technology the game has to offer within the first couple hours. Within the first several hours you're likely to have constructed all of it. There are a few planet and moon types to explore but you'll find they have nothing new to offer you outside of an initial sense of wonder.
The game does offer quite a robust sculpting tool to shape the terrain. The idea that you can completely reform an entire planet is a novel one, even if the feat is nearly impossible. If the idea of sculpting land and creating large sculptures and elaborate structures is appealing to you, then you might be able to justify a $20 price tag. Maybe.
But for those of you looking for in depth features and a plethora of toys and tech to enrich your sandbox, you may find the core gameplay loop, in its current state, to be a bit sparse. Before you point out my 30+ hours logged, time played does not necessarily equate to variety and depth of gameplay. I've spent more than that playing
but that doesn't mean Solitaire has a lot to do.
So, no. Not a lot of content. Forgivable in an early access title. However, lack of content is the least of your issues as you will probably rage quit before you even see all of it because of the
I get it, the game is in pre-alpha. It's going to have bugs. But as I said earlier; if you are charging for a product, then everything included in the product is fair game for reviewing. And that includes bugs.
This is by far the
issue I have with the game. The bugs in this game are not just a minor irritation or a slight inconvenience. They are frustrating, game-breaking, experience-ruining bugs. Here are just a few examples of what you will encounter in the game on a minute-by-minute basis:
-items being unable to be picked up
-falling through the floor, dying, and losing all your stuff.
-unsecured items falling through the floor
-resources not loading in
-new respawn points not working (preventing you from setting up new home bases)
-equipment refusing to connect to your vehicles
-your vehicles (full of resources and expensive equipment) deciding to fly away into space never to be seen again.
-not connecting to working tethers and suffocating.
-Save files literally no longer working.
The majority of these bugs are not occasional and rare, but happen constantly several times an hour as reported by both myself and my girlfriend. Most of the above bugs seem to only happen in co-op play though. But considering a large selling point of the game is its co-op play, the fact that it is plagued with game breaking bugs needs to be addressed before I can give this game a recommendation.
I usually have the patience of a saint but even I'm starting to get discouraged by how far I get set back every time one of these bugs decides to rear its head and screw me over.
Its because of these reasons that I just can
recommend this game right now in its current state. If the major bugs are fixed and more content is added in, it'll easily be worth the price of entry but as it currently stands, there are too many other similar games for a similar price on steam that actually function on a playable level. If you want to throw money at the developers game and if sculpting and shaping the land amidst a sea of bugs is enough for you, then sure get the game. But If you are looking for a functioning game with longevity for you and your buddies to invest time and money in... like I said, there are better options elsewhere.
If and when the above issues are fixed, I will gladly update my review but as Steam clearly displays, this is an
so I will not give it a review based on promises and potential. Coming in, I read the warnings and I knew there would be bugs. As a regular player of early access games  I thought I could power through them but after 20 hours I'm starting to see the severity of the issues and I just hope this review will help you see it long before then.

As an aside, I do understand the concept of Early Access. The money you spend on the game is largely to support the further development of the game. That said though, I have seen far too many Early Access games left to rot as developers move on to other projects. It is not their fault, but rather the nature of Early Access. When an unfinished game rides on the hype train perpetrated by fanaticism, it can end up generating a lot of revenue. So much so, in fact, that it would be financially irresponsible of the developer to put in all the man hours and resources to actually finish the game. Developers are not gods sitting in the sky with unlimited manpower and time to develop games, they are normal people with rent and bills and obligations. If the majority of people who would buy your game at release have already done so, there is little reason left to finish the game and many reasons not to.
Because of this, Steam asks that you only buy Early Access games if you feel the game's current state is worth the price of entry. This is why I've chosen to review the game the way I have.
I have purchased two copies of Astroneer for myself and my girlfriend, so in that respect I have given more than my fair share of "support". My lack of a recommendation is the
way I choose to support the developers. If more and more people hold off on purchasing the game until it is in a more playable state, System Era will have more and more motivation to see Astroneer through to the end. And that's something I'm sure we all would like to see.

I picked this up on a whim, and I've since been pretty pleased with what I found.
The first word that comes to mind about the game is "cute." Everything from the weird plants in the environment to the character's death animations essentially screams whimsy. It's like Alice in Wonderland, if Alice wore a giant backpack and ran out of air all the time. The terrain, character, and tools the character uses are all pleasantly chunky and soft-looking, like they're made out of Play-Doh.
The learning curve is extremely attainable. There are only a few controls besides the generic WASD-space and mouse. Q pulls out the backpack and puts it away. E pulls out the terrain tool and puts it away. Alt and Ctrl add and smooth terrain, repsectively. And Tab puts your character into whatever vehicle or dwelling he (she?) is near. SUPER easy. The tutorial is all of two minutes long.
There are no other NPCs available for you to interact with. I don't know if that's just a cop-out so the developer doesn't have to code an AI, but there it is.
As far as gameplay goes, it's pretty solid, but there isn't a whole lot to do yet. You can remove terrain, place terrain, and flatten terrain. You can mine materials, make stuff with them, and then use that stuff to mine different materials. Eventually, you can make a spaceship, go to a different planet, and do that stuff again.
The music is relaxing, which is nice, but there's nothing about it that makes me sit up and go "ooh." It reminds me of the music of Minecraft. Relaxed, floaty, kinda like wind chimes. Good to just have on, but not to sit and listen to.
So, at this point, the game doesn't have a whole lot for the player to do. Yes, it's pretty. Yes, it's cute. Yes, it's fun. But games are a kind of medium that tells a story, or has a goal. Even Minecraft has a "goal" now. Astroneer, thus far, does not.

Just so we're clear, this is my lest favorite Arkham game, but that's not saying it is bad. I'm simply saying this takes last place in this fantastic franchise. Arkham Origins barely introduces anything new to the series, and why should it. It's a prequel to the whole series. The game itself is rather slow, but it does a superb job in bringing up character development. This was when Batman was still considered a fugitive to the police of Gotham so Bruce has no real allies except loyal Alfred. Here are my problems with Origins, the environment, its rather dull, colorless, and barely shows any life. Gotham has been placed in a curfew on Christmas Eve due to events that happened at Blackgate Prison. So the only people about are thugs, gangs, and even corrupted police. When compared to the other Arkham games, the open world is rather dulled out, there are not so many side missions and they are not as long or complex as Arkham City or Arkham Knight. The problem with how people reacted to this game was because Arkham City set the standard for an open-world Batman game, however, this game came out after that, so it does make sense in why fans are disappointed with this one.
Here is the plot; crime-lord Black Mask has murdered the corrupted Comissioner of GCPD and hired 8 Assassins to hunt and kill Batman on Christmas Eve. Looks like its going to be a busy night for Batman. However, a new name enters in "the Joker" and soon Batman must do whatever it takes to beat Black Mask, beat the 8 assassins, and find out who this Joker is and stop whatever he is planning.
Now, since I have covered the bad about this game. Here's the good of Arkham Origins. The game does start out slow and loose, but when the Joker is first mentioned, the game begins to pick itself up. The boss fights are entertaining and I will say a few are cooler than the ones in Arkham City. Fighting Deathstroke was fun and dealing with Copperhead was actually intense and interesting. Bane was actually a formidable foe in this game (in Arkham City, all you did was destroy TITAN canisters and lock Bane in a cell without a fight). Each assassin is unique, some hunt you down, some you have go to them, some threaten innocent people to lure you, and there is one who is such a ♥♥♥♥♥ that you literally take him out with one punch. Another pro is the character development, we are introduced to a more brutal and independent Batman, who even would argue with Alfred's advice. He goes in believing he could simply take these assassins all by himself, only to realize after too many close calls, he may need some allies and even listen to some advice.
Roger Craig Smith (Ezio from AC) plays Bruce Wanye/Batman very superbly almost sounding like Kevin Conroy's Batman. And Troy Baker (Last of Us, Brothers in Arms) plays the Joker with perfection. Sure, he is no Mark Hamill, but I would absolutely consider Mr. Baker to be Mr. Hamill's understudy for the Joker. The Joker in this game was very entertaining and this game brings forth very good development in plot and character. The relationship between Bruce and Alfred is made strong which the other Arkham games never really focused on. Alfred is shown to be a father-figure to Bruce and expresses great concern about Bruce's safety.
Now, the game is not the best of this series, but I can say that this game is far from being considered a bad game. I would recommend that you start the series somewhere else (like Arkham Asylum or Arkham City) but I will say to any Arkham fan, you can't pass this one. It's a good game, just not the best of this amazing franchise. Think of it like MW3, its really good, but it's not as popular as MW2.

Arkham Origins is the third installment in the acclaimed Batman: Arkham series, and serves as a prequel to the previous two games, depicting Batman's early years and his first encounters with some of his enemies. It wasn't made by the series' titular dev Rocksteady Studios, but internally by Warner Brothers.
+An area where Origins manages to outclass even Arkham City is definitely in characterization, that's a step forward from the nailed-but-one-dimensional we've had so far and finally explores Batman's personality, as well as some of the villains', with some degree of depth.
+The plot itself, while sometimes leaves something to be desired, is solid and cool, and won't disappoint longtime fans.
+The map is even larger than before, and features a copious amount of sidequests and, as usual, it's filled to the brim with collectibles and easter eggs for the diehard fans.
+Combat and stealth are as good as ever, with only minimal tweaks applied to the now classic formula. If it ain't broken, don't fix it, i guess. The one introduction this game made (powered gloves) is pretty overpowered anyway.
+Graphics are nice. They aren't a significant step forward from City, but they're sure as hell good.
+Investigating a crime scene now features an elaborate gizmo that reconstructs what's happened with some imput from the player. Impossible science AND still less than thrilling, but surely cooler and more active than what preceded it. It's not random that this feature was carried over to Arkham Knight, too.
-Starting with minor things, i would point out a bunch of annoying bugs, the less than stellar voice actor chosen for Batman (Kevin Conroy apparently sounded too old, even if this game isn't nearly as much Batman: Year One as they want you to think. And that's a real shame, it would have probably been amazing) and, last but not least, a few questionable design and plot choices.
-The bosses, once again with one notable (and bada*s) exception are still somewhat poor, and stealth sections can still be trivialized with some amount of boring but failsafe tactics.
-Oh, right, there's multiplayer in this game. Nobody particularly cares unfortunately: it's not horrid, it's simply very average and feels very, very forced. For these reasons, it's quite empty.
-The two main DLCs are so-so: Initiation is underwhelming, simply being some challenge maps depicting young Bruce's training as a pseudo-ninja, held together by a paper-thin plot. Cool and all, since NinjaBruce doesn't have the same moveset as BatmanBruce, but still not much, and extremely short. A Cold, Cold Heart is the first encounter between the Bat and Arkham City's resident ensemble darkhorse, Mister Freeze. It's cool enough. It features a badass Bat-Heatsink suit. The game works perfectly fine without it, too, and it's short and separated as always.
-And now to why Origins is universally, or almost, considered the weakest chapter of the saga, even while Knight has all sorts of problems: Arkham City took everything that made Asylum great, made it even better and added a billion other things. Origins took everything that made City great... and copy-pasted it with some minor additions. So while WB sure did a more than decent job in terms of plot and expanded the map a bit (in Origins, you can explore the entirety of what would be Arkham City in the eponymous game plus a few more locations), they still threw at us a game that, barring the obnoxiously overpowered gloves, plays exactly like Arkham City.
All this automatically makes Arkham Origins a good, if not above average game, but wether to buy it or not depends on how you feel about it. While City was the bigger and better kind of sequel, Origins is a prime example of "more of the same". Do you want more Arkham City in a slightly different package? I did when I bought it, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. The choice is up to you.

Its a fun, highly customizable game that is receiving an engine upgrade and console port somewhere in 2015. Buying stuff for real money off their marketplace is HIGHLY optional and I've never found the need for the guns, which by far are just better looking and sounding reskins of the existing in-game guns. There are also a significant number of community-wide contests held by Reloaded Productions giving away small items that almost convince you to go back every time. There are always OMFG moments though, as sometimes you could be facing highly co-ordinated teams that everyone accuses of hacking and are really not but you learn to roll with it. I have additional 1200 hours on this game besides the Steam count and have completed the progression thrice with different characters. The GMs have, in the past, promised a lot of things to be given a long time ago (read: a year). They have not delivered yet. This includes more content that isn't just a simple reskin, an engine upgrade and a new anti-hacking system. The last was implemented in Q4 2014.
Simply put, this game can be very enjoyable and very annoying as well. As a new player in this game, it works to your advantage if you haven't played MMOs before allowing you to keep the tolerence to learn the game instead of rage quitting. You will die a lot and you will be abused a little by other players, but if you learn, you'll love this game...

The GASP Experiment:
It’s the scenario where the practical joker stands at the street corner staring up in the sky when a passerby stops becomes curious then also looks up and then the next does the same until you have a crowd of people staring up at nothing, the joker laughs quietly to himself and leaves. You are left with a crowd of people looking at nothing in the hope that something interesting happens.  There you have social experiment of 'GASP'.

Astronauts are the best of the best.  Well in this game you are not a member of that group, you probably got to the moon by winning a charity auction.  As you will soon discover you don’t have the Right Stuff.

I got this game as part of the Sonic Hits Collection, so I went into this game without much of an idea of what it was.  It's a port of a Sega Dreamcast game starring Sonic.  That's pretty much the only good thing I can say about it.
Despite it setting my screen resolution to a 16:9 widescreen (I have a 1280x1024 5:4 screen), the game itself is 4:3, and everything is boxed inside an ugly blue border.  The game didn't recognize my controller, so I was forced to play using my keyboard.  This game, ironically, has better keyboard support than Sonic Generations; all on-screen instructions were "translated" to keyboard controls, so I didn't have any issues there.
The game itself simply isn't very good.  The voice acting feels awkward, as though the actors were shown their scripts word-by-word and had to record the whole game in a single take.  The gameplay switches between decent Sonic platforming (albeit with bad controls -- I'll get to those in a minute) and bad pseudo-adventure gameplay where you run around like a caffinated gopher trying to find the next platforming section.  These "adventure" areas are confusing, badly designed (there are invisible walls everywhere), and simply un-Sonic-like.  At one point, I was teleported onto a weird island full of "Chao" with no way out except restarting the game.
The platforming segments, on the other hand, seem decently designed, but they're soured by horrible controls and camera movements.  3D Sonic requires an analog stick to work well, and since my controller didn't work with the game, I was stuck with the keyboard equivalent of a D-Pad.  Making matters worse was the camera; it moved all over the place, hid things from me, and sometimes messed up my jumps.
All in all, Sonic Adventure DX on Steam is a bad port of a bad Dreamcast game, and I would suggest giving it a pass unless you truly feel the need to own every single Sonic game in existance.

My Vet Practice - Marine Patrol is slightly better than the first game in the series. Although that's kind of like saying that 10 fire ant bites are better than 100.
In the game you play as a vet that needs to take care of injured wildlife in Northern Canada. This boils down to completing some simple mini-games to treat the animals and set them back free in the wild.
It's about as simple and boring as you could imagine. Park Rangers bring in the same animals constantly and many of the tactics used to treat animals are very similar to eachother. Usually you end up clicking and dragging the mouse around a certain part of the animal.
The minigames are actually improved upon from the original though. In the first game you would haphazardly fiddle with different tools until you figured out what to do, while this one just gives you them to make it easier and quicker. I appreciate that aspect because I didn't smack my head on my desk quite as quickly.
The game moves at a very slow pace where after nearly an hour I was still treating gulls and puffins even though the game said I would be treating larger animals and had purchased the dock to do so.
There are quite a few spelling mistakes in the dialogue and it repeats very often.
The game also isn't accurate to the region of the world it takes place in. As I said the game is set in Canada yet there are penguins and dolphins, neither of which live in the Arctic Circle. Penguins in particular literally live on the opposite side of the world. I wouldn't have a problem with it if the game didn't specify where it was set, but it's detailed as Canada in the description which simply doesn't make sense.
At one point the game was most likely a Nintendo DS title called Pet Vet: Marine Patrol. This is evident as the title screen for the game on startup still uses that as the title. It seems like Anikids is just releasing ports of their DS games and changing their names so nobody would see the reviews for the portable versions. That's not really an okay thing to do, Anikids.
While this is probably the best Anikids developed or published game I've played (the others are truly awful), it still isn't something I would give to a child to play. It's basic to the point that there is no fun to be had by anyone of any age. You can make good kids games that are enjoyable to play, even if they have simple mechanics. This is just lazy developing under the guise of being kid-friendly.
Also, I'm still convinced that Anikids is a tax writeoff as they are owned by a German editing software company.

A quaint little game with an interesting premise. There is an always present problem with playing a villain (or just a dark side character) in any game ever - it always comes down to one of two ways: either game forces you to be a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is a jerk to anyone and everyone just for the sake of it, regardless if it is beneficial for you or not, OR while you're being called "bad guy" throughout the game, the "good guys" are actually much worse than you so the only difference from being a hero in some other game is switched labels.
Nefarious manages to gracefully dodge both of those pitfalls - the protagonist, Crow, is definitely a villain through and through (the whole point of the game is wreaking havoc, stealing coins and kidnapping royalty), yet he doesn't do anything depraved, adheres to some sort of moral code, etc. And, spoiler alert, Crow never does heel-face turn - he is the villain till the end.
So if that's the experience you were looking for - playing the villain "as seen in the NES era games", then look no further.
Game not without the cons though. Being a doujin game it has some misc graphical issues in some areas (z-fighting, incorrect layer number for textures, "shaking" sprites of static objects as you move around) but nothing game breaking or progress impeding.

This is a game that gets a surprising amount of fun and mileage out of what would be predictable tropes. It's fun being the villain, kidnapping princesses and pounding good guys in your mechanical menaces. But it also has heart to it, that goes beyond just nods toward classic gaming tropes. The artwork is really well done (bonus points for using hand-drawn art instead of going the lazy retro pixel route) and the music is really catchy.
It's not a perfect game; the difficulty curve is a bit wonky, there are bugs, and there are a few places lacking the polish you'd expect from a professional creation. But this wasn't a professional creation; it was a labour of love, and it shows. It's well worth looking into, for the platform lovers and the trope-savvy alike.

Traditionally, games about games have always been a bit divisive. Some think that they stand on the shoulders of giants, contributing little and coasting on nostalgia. Others see games trying to deconstruct what came before, using the context of the present to find new ways to tackle the past. StarBlade’s Nefarious is a bit of both, featuring callbacks to all manner of 16-bit classics while also bringing something new to the table by flipping the script. As the name would suggest, this game casts you in the role of a dastardly antagonist, and each level ends with you mounting into some overcomplicated contraption to stomp out a hero. It’s a great setup, and the game sticks the landing more often than not, leading to an experience that’s definitely worth a second look despite its shortcomings.

The point of this review is not to complain. It is not to vent. It is not to bash the developers. It is simply to inform potential buyers of whether or not the game
is worth their time and money. The relative "worth" of the game has been determined by judging what the game currently brings to the table relative to other similar games of similar pricing on Steam.
This is not meant to be a comprehensive review that covers all the pros and cons of the game but rather just explanation of the main deal-breakers. If you are looking for the echo chamber of "AMAZING POTENTIAL" there is plenty of that to be found in the other reviews.
If you are consistently researching artifacts at a decent pace, you will likely unlock every piece of technology the game has to offer within the first couple hours. Within the first several hours you're likely to have constructed all of it. There are a few planet and moon types to explore but you'll find they have nothing new to offer you outside of an initial sense of wonder.
The game does offer quite a robust sculpting tool to shape the terrain. The idea that you can completely reform an entire planet is a novel one, even if the feat is nearly impossible. If the idea of sculpting land and creating large sculptures and elaborate structures is appealing to you, then you might be able to justify a $20 price tag. Maybe.
But for those of you looking for in depth features and a plethora of toys and tech to enrich your sandbox, you may find the core gameplay loop, in its current state, to be a bit sparse. Before you point out my 30+ hours logged, time played does not necessarily equate to variety and depth of gameplay. I've spent more than that playing
but that doesn't mean Solitaire has a lot to do.
So, no. Not a lot of content. Forgivable in an early access title. However, lack of content is the least of your issues as you will probably rage quit before you even see all of it because of the
I get it, the game is in pre-alpha. It's going to have bugs. But as I said earlier; if you are charging for a product, then everything included in the product is fair game for reviewing. And that includes bugs.
This is by far the
issue I have with the game. The bugs in this game are not just a minor irritation or a slight inconvenience. They are frustrating, game-breaking, experience-ruining bugs. Here are just a few examples of what you will encounter in the game on a minute-by-minute basis:
-items being unable to be picked up
-falling through the floor, dying, and losing all your stuff.
-unsecured items falling through the floor
-resources not loading in
-new respawn points not working (preventing you from setting up new home bases)
-equipment refusing to connect to your vehicles
-your vehicles (full of resources and expensive equipment) deciding to fly away into space never to be seen again.
-not connecting to working tethers and suffocating.
-Save files literally no longer working.
The majority of these bugs are not occasional and rare, but happen constantly several times an hour as reported by both myself and my girlfriend. Most of the above bugs seem to only happen in co-op play though. But considering a large selling point of the game is its co-op play, the fact that it is plagued with game breaking bugs needs to be addressed before I can give this game a recommendation.
I usually have the patience of a saint but even I'm starting to get discouraged by how far I get set back every time one of these bugs decides to rear its head and screw me over.
Its because of these reasons that I just can
recommend this game right now in its current state. If the major bugs are fixed and more content is added in, it'll easily be worth the price of entry but as it currently stands, there are too many other similar games for a similar price on steam that actually function on a playable level. If you want to throw money at the developers game and if sculpting and shaping the land amidst a sea of bugs is enough for you, then sure get the game. But If you are looking for a functioning game with longevity for you and your buddies to invest time and money in... like I said, there are better options elsewhere.
If and when the above issues are fixed, I will gladly update my review but as Steam clearly displays, this is an
so I will not give it a review based on promises and potential. Coming in, I read the warnings and I knew there would be bugs. As a regular player of early access games  I thought I could power through them but after 20 hours I'm starting to see the severity of the issues and I just hope this review will help you see it long before then.

As an aside, I do understand the concept of Early Access. The money you spend on the game is largely to support the further development of the game. That said though, I have seen far too many Early Access games left to rot as developers move on to other projects. It is not their fault, but rather the nature of Early Access. When an unfinished game rides on the hype train perpetrated by fanaticism, it can end up generating a lot of revenue. So much so, in fact, that it would be financially irresponsible of the developer to put in all the man hours and resources to actually finish the game. Developers are not gods sitting in the sky with unlimited manpower and time to develop games, they are normal people with rent and bills and obligations. If the majority of people who would buy your game at release have already done so, there is little reason left to finish the game and many reasons not to.
Because of this, Steam asks that you only buy Early Access games if you feel the game's current state is worth the price of entry. This is why I've chosen to review the game the way I have.
I have purchased two copies of Astroneer for myself and my girlfriend, so in that respect I have given more than my fair share of "support". My lack of a recommendation is the
way I choose to support the developers. If more and more people hold off on purchasing the game until it is in a more playable state, System Era will have more and more motivation to see Astroneer through to the end. And that's something I'm sure we all would like to see.
