The Devil May Cry rebooty is very interesting in comparison to the main series. It has a lower skill barrier and skill ceiling than that of DMC 4, which is the only other DMC I have played and can use as a comparison. That being said, the game is very enjoyable. The combat is smooth and intuitive. It welcomes many players, though might alienate the hardcore crowd that grew up with the original series. I grinded many hours on the Ps4 Definitive version and now having a PC copy, I still enjoy the series as much as I did before. As a more lower level DmC player, this game can still be a challenge despite the initial comments stating the game was too easy. In all fairness, was before the Ps4 version's release.
DmC also got a ton of flack for basically bringing in a different personality for Dante, but in all honesty isn't that bad. They progressively develops as a character, making him more likeable by the end. While I personally do not like Vergil's character all too much, his role is vital to the story even if people don't realize it.
One difference I have found with the game is the lack of controller customization options in comparison to the Ps4 version. On the Ps4 version you would have multiple alternative layouts for your controller, but there is only the default controls on PC. The default layout can be quite a pain for performing optimized combos and I would recommend customizing the controls if you find yourself not feeling too comfortable.
I got this for $1 through the HumbleBundle Capcom bundle. I was honestly surprised it played as well as it did on my laptop given I run an i5 with Intel HD 520 graphics. So I was extremely happy playing this again.
I believe the beauty in Dmc: Devil May Cry is that while it may not be objectively better than the previous games, that doesn't necessarily stop it from being interesting. We're dealing a more contemporary Dante who grew up a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and a degenerate. Realistically speaking, what else could you expect from the potty mouth edgelord as he grows into a better character.
Never played the game when it was released, but heard good things. Picked it up for $1 from Humble Bundle and couldn't be more glad that I did.

The game has a crash-on-startup issue relating either to controller inputs or Nvidia hardware (or some combination of those). Patching as of 7/15/2017 does not address the issue. For me, I was eventually able to start the game by removing all USB devices, starting, then re-plugging them in. The game being for sale in its current form seems bad. The quality of the game itself is fine, but I don't recommend the Steam release unless you "budget" extra time for potentially troubleshooting something like this.

Easy to pick up.  You control the 1 big green dumb troll on the screen, kinda.  You click anywhere during a battle and the troll stumbles over (maybe).  If you clicked an enemy, the troll will only continue moving if the target is alive and will push through groups of enemies to get to said target.  Only the troll can pick up the gold left behind from fallen enemy units, so make sure to grab it before it disappears.
Between battles is building up the defense from the stick huts at the start to a stone castle after everything is maxed out.  The trick being your ability to manage how many workers are assigned between the tasks.  Construction needs builders, but they do not repair the fort and seperate little guys with hammers are assigned to do that.  Stone from the quarry, iron from the mine, wood from the trees and then the looters.  Looters clean up the area around the fort immediately after the battle and pick up the dead, taking gold and materials from them.  Good time management skills are key before the next wave assembles with stronger friends.
Overall it is an addictive little gem.  Really hope this developer does not fade away or go the pay2win route.  Enjoy, I nominated it for an award.

With One Troll Army, there aren't many features or game mechanics beyond what you see on the game's store page.  The concept of the game is simple and with that being said, it will eventually become boring, as most tower defence games do.  You kill enemies in order to make money in order to build better defences which in turn kill more enemies.
Even after reaching maximum level defences and offensive abilities for your troll, the game will eventually reach a breaking point where you can only hold out for so many more waves until you are faced with an impossible enemy horde, stifling any sense of achievement you may have gotten if you had decided to power through the game.
There were game features such as the Twitch integration which I unfortunately didn't have a chance to experiment with but sounded like impressive ideas.  With that aside, there are only two criticism which I can level against the game:  Firstly, ranged mob units are incredibly powerful in both their damage and health, as well as in the fact that their strikes often stun your troll, and for those reason I feel that they should be nerfed.  Secondly, the framerate of the game drops significantly when you reach higher levels, especially when fast forwarding through your base's down time.
All in all, speaking as of v1.03, One Troll Army is a nice free to play game which offers around half a day of entertainment without being a time sink, while it is in need of some minor balancing.

This is one amazing mod. The devs really knew what they were doing. Everything from the level design to the weapons is well made and fun. It also takes on a realistic note. Avoid close combat with zombies unless you have heavier weapons like the sledge hammer. Even with two people, maps like Night of the Living Dead (based off the original film) is really fun. Personally, i prefer the survival maps over the escape ones. In Survival, the map has 1-3 zones and you must protect these zones or you lose. Exploring the map reveals lots of secrets. Locked rooms, army drops which contain bags which repair your zones and other delights.
The shooting mechanics are brilliant. Instead of a HUD dislaying your ammo, you need to check how much you have by holding the reload button (default, R). Your character will perform an animation by pulling the clip out and checking how much ammo there is. But close combat is difficult, and I try to avoid it as much as possible. The only weapons that can one-shot zombies is the sledgehammer and fireaxe, provided you aim at the zombies' head. But smaller weapons don't deal a lot of damage and most times you find yourself losing health when trying to melee a zombie. More cool mechanics include the bleeding system, where you can bleed yourself to death unless you get bandages. Also, you can become infected. You will see yourself becoming infected when red and orange veins begin creeping across your vision. You need to find Phalanx pills you'll turn into one of them.
Great mod, and it's fully free, no micro transactions, no useless cosmetic items, and no ads.

Do not get my non-recommendation wrong, this game is excellent in its theming, and framing. The story is nice. the gameplay is good. I wanted to love this game, I really wanted to love every moment of it. It holds a ton of nostalgia for games like Megaman, and Megaman X. Which is a big plus for me.
But, I never knew it was possible, until this game, that it was even possible for me to get so irritated by the small things, that I had to abandon the game. It makes me sad. This game had so much potential, and I'm really sad I had to let it go. The audio mastering was terrible, both in the general sound effects department, and in the BGM department. the BGM had its own character, and flavor, and was unique, but didn't jive with the gameplay. Fun, action-oriented levels with passive, underwhelming music in the background, I felt like all of the music being used in the main levels should have been used in instances of dialogue, instead. It's like combining an eye-opener of a game, with music you could fall asleep to.
The music was the least of my worries, however, as the sound effects for the game just sounded cheap, REALLY cheap. Which,  when combined with the aforementioned music choices, it made for a really empty experience. It's so bizarre, that an otherwise good gaming experience, for me, was so easily dismounted, so easily undone, by the sound design alone. Any qualms I had with the game itself were minimal. I can't say any of the levels, themselves, were boring, aside from a certain level where you dive underwater to find sunken treasure.
So, that's just it. The thing that irritated me most for this game, was the fact that I didn't like it. I wanted to like it so badly, and yet, here I am, quietly requesting that the game developer step back, and remaster the audio.

Boneless Zombie has potential, but it fails to reach it, no pun intended (the game is all about a zombie reaching his arms and legs out in an effort to get around each level).
The cartoon graphics are quite nice, and the basic idea is fine, but the game is let down by its other elements.
If you play the game for a few minutes, it's fine, but as you start to level up, it just becomes annoying, due to the key mapping.
I found the controls to be terrible, especially the use of I and P as main keys; I think that it would have been better if it was designed with the two keys chosen to have been right beside each other.
In any event, that problem could have been overcome if the game allowed players to change the key configuration, but it doesn't - so it fails miserably on that score.
As a minor point, the Help screen informs players that Esc is the self-destruct key, but it actually is the Space key that is used for self-destruction. As it is one of the few controls for the game, it was a bit slipshod to have got it wrong on the Help screen. Luckily, one of the tips you receive when you first play the game tells you that you can use the Space key for self-destruct, but if you miss that or gloss over it, then the Help screen will be of no use (I only discovered it because the tip appears in a screenshot that I took).
If the controls for this game were improved, or - better yet - if players could change the configuration of the keys used, then that could make all the difference. But, as it stands, I cannot recommend this game.

So In total I guess you could say that I have only played the game for about 3 - 4 hours and I must say that I love it. Being in early acces and having my type of PC gives me a tiny bit of lag here and there but nothing to big or really noticable (or atleast that often).
The game is about the player being a Slime Rancher in an unknown World. Overall you could say that it is a mix between Harvest Moon and Rune Factory - being able to activly fight the Monsters of the world. And yes, there are Monsters besides the normal Slimes which are... SLIMES! In all seriousness: The Monsters basically are a corrupted version of the normal slimes that have combined with another slimetype. If they now eat something they shouldnt and would basically transform again because of it they corrupt and turn into an evil entity that tries to kill everything that is around, meaning that it even attacks the adorable Slimes that it was created of.
Even though there isnt much to the game it has a big area to explore, farm upgrades and upgradable areas and a wide variety of Slimes. And is up to you to capture and combine them. If you do this, Watch out. Like mentioned above the Slimes, if they eat something they shouldnt, will corrupt. And this has nothing to do with what they like to eat or what not. Because what they dont like/dont want to eat, they wont eat. But there are things they dont know as food and they might get curious as to what it tastes like. And then it is up to you to save your little slimes.
It is an early access game and I know how many people dislike this sort of stuff. But maybe it helps when I say that I bought this hours before it was released on Steam just so I could finally play it.
If you really want the game: Buy it. If the overall game looks nice but you dont know if it would be a game for you: Dont buy it. I say this is a take it or leave it kind of game because you will have to invest alot of time and thought into what you are doing on your farm.

(Add a few hours to whatever my Steam playtime says, because I played this game a lot via Humblestore download before it came to steam)
In Slime Rancher, you take on the role of a brand new... slime rancher!  Surprised?  Your home-base is a ranch with a house and several empty plots of land.  Your goal is hunt slimes, suck them up with your vaccuum pack, then take them home and take care of them.
Why?  Because slime poop is very valuable, of course!
When slimes eat, they 'poop' little crystals called Plorts.. you can trade these Plorts in for money.. then use that money to expand your ranch, transform plots of land into corrals, coops, gardens, storage units, etc, and buy upgrades to make yourself a more effective slime rancher.
You can raise chickens, grow crops, feed your slimes, and explore the world for new and exciting things, all in a physics-enabled First-Person adventure, with your trusty vaccuum pack to manipulate the world around you.  Slimes can also be bred to create new types of slimes for bigger profits.  Just be careful, because combining the wrong types of slimes can be dangerous!  I warned you!
So far, an excellent game.  Could perhaps use a little more content, but the developers are still adding new environments, more slimes and more resources, so I have confidence that my wishes will be fulfilled. You should at least wishlist this game and keep an eye on it.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics (as long as you don't hate bright, cartoony visuals)
-Fun and vairied gameplay.
-Appropriate for younger players, and still fun for older players.
-Very stable for an Early Access game.  No crashes, and no major bugs for me so far.
Cons:
-Could use more content, but that's being worked on!
-Wish I could somehow specify I want to pick up with vaccuum pack.  It can be a little frustrating to be collecting plorts, and end up picking up a lot of slimes and other stuff in the process.  This is a minor gripe.. you can always drop stuff you don't want.

The game feels
polished even in its current early access state. There is certainly a mix of farming and adventure game in here.
You risk adventure to help expand your farm. There are many different tactics and choices to make that could be successful, which adds lots of replay value (I haven't reached a final point with any of my farms yet, which is probably after ~15 hours so far). There is a nice little economy system, as well as a really awesome 'breeding' system (I use that term litely here, since its not quite that - but close!).
+Very polished.
+Great mix of farming and adventure.
+There is nothing very difficult in the game so far. It is quite relaxing and is definately casual.
+Quite addicting to learn how the whole system works, and to keep grinding to make your farm better and better.
+Lots of awesome upgrades for yourself (ie. rocket pack, health-ups, and many more), and your farm (ie. more pens, better safety and capacity, among many many others).
+The economy system can really offer a bit of strategy at the moment with prices that fluctuate with in-game days, as well as trading, etc.
+Music and graphics are very well done. Very fitting, too.
-I'm hungry for wayyy more slime varieties and wayyy more upgrades! Game has
much room for expansion!

Nefarious is a unique concept and a great throwback to old-school platformers. I give it
(play the game and you'll get it) and my strongest of recommendations. The game is a great pick-up for seasoned platform gamers and newbies alike with a difficulty curve very reminiscent of the old Sonic the Hedgehog games.
Incredible soundtrack
, great nostalgic references for seasoned platform gamers, great humor, RPG-like upgrade system, multiple endings, great replay value.
Contols are a little difficult to pick up initially. Akin to Megaman games, some of the later bosses verge on too difficult for casual gamers to enjoy.
The game's levels play like a Megaman game with the ability to power Crow up as you collect money, and a fun and interesting "bomb jump" mechanic that lets you perform a non-damaging double-jump when colliding with your own projectiles in mid air. An added bonus is most princesses you kidnap embue with some of their powers while you hold them, like higher jumps or unlimited ammo. Then come the bosses...
Ever played Sonic, gotten frustrated and said "Dr. Eggman is so cheap and has it so easy in that giant machine."?
Well, this game's signature "reverse boss fights" let you see from Eggman, Bowser and the like's perspective that the grass isn't neccessarily greener on the other side. Instead of playing Hulk Smash, the fights are a challenge akin to swatting a very intellegent fly.
There are multiple endings and enough achievements and sub-quests to sate even the thirstiest of completionists.
Make like Crow kidnapping Mayapple and pick this one up today!

I like Taranto's Brawl In The Family comics and musics, so I was a bit biased when I bought this game. I'll try to be objective by saying it's a good game, with big strengths and tolerable issues.
First, the visuals are gorgeous, a lot of effort has been put into the characters and background. The music is good, though a bit too slow-paced sometimes (and the cuts between loops have been unacceptable since the last two decades) and the sound effects lack punch. Writing is more clever than I expected from a a deliberately cliché story. The gameplay is solid, running, jumping and punching feels nice and fun. I've only done three levels so far, but I still feel like it's not difficult enough - and when it is, it's for wrong reasons, like enemies attacking from offscreen, or clunky controls during the reverse boss fights. I think the clunkiness is intended, but it still spoils what is otherwise an interesting concept.
Fun Game, would recommend if you like torturing yourself.

An extremely well-made high-standard difficult platform game.
9.5/10
Pros:
- outstanding controls (use a controller or rebind your keyboard input, the default keyboard controls are garbage)
- simple but precise and well-thought gameplay
- fair "it's your fault if you die" difficulty with an accessible difficulty curve
- an amazing game to speedrun
- references
- game length: many levels (7 chapters with a light and dark version, with many extra levels: wapzones, Super Meat World)
- the music is great
Cons
- Dark Cotton alley (last chapter) level design is a bit cheap, just spamming enemies and making the player wait (levels 7-16X and 7-18X). Level 7-19X doesn't even work for some people (Hamb, the 106% speedrun world record holder for instance)
- Cheap achievements (but fun to do for crazy people): deathless chapters aren't reasonable achieves in my opinion, considering Edmund couldn't do it himself (his 106% personal best time is 6h, which means he hasn't mastered the game to the point of being able to get all the achieves. Not that big of a deal, but hilarious)
- Super Meat World is no longer supported :(
- Cotton Alley music is isn't as good as the others, it's less hype-inducing in my opinion. It's not bad it's just that I don't like it that much.
Overall, worth the money even if you don't finish it entirely ^_^

You use pipes that originally come from your landing pod at the start of the game, these pipes transport oxygen around the base and to you, if your near them. There isnt currently a need for any food and drink, but there is a need for oxygen; i like this current system, and i dont really want it changed. Getting oxygen is always a constant worry, but if you construct mini oxygen tanks that you can stick on your backpack, the supply will last quite a while. Even if you do find yourself with a lack of oxygen while away from base, there are (usually) quite a few oxygen crystels lying about, which are extrememly useful. Though i haven't done this yet, you can go to different planets by building landers, and habitations allow you to build new bases on the planet you're on.  The addition of a buggy and a truck are incredibly useful, as you can stick a storage pad on the back, and power it via solar panels, the charge on the vehicle can also charge you, as you need power to mine(though it slowly recharges by itself). However, the driving on these vehicles are perhaps the worst controls i've ever had the misfortune of using. The sandstorms are brilliant, Im pretty sure they are dynamic, as they seem to travel in big balls around the planets. So far, im REALLY enjoying the game, and i really do hope that the devs stays commited and build the brilliant game thats already got a great foundation.

Slime Rancher! Where to even start with this game?! Let me just start by saying I tend to play only games where I can be competitive with other players in a multi-player setting. A single player game that I play "alone" has to be REALLY good to grab my attention, let alone keep it. I am not easily impressed, I'm cynical at times, and I think I am a hard judge. Slime Rancher is one of those rare games for me that just won right away. I've been playing for a while before it came out on steam - when I first downloaded it in Alpha and booted it up, and I think I played about 6 hours straight without a break, and then finally snapped out of it and realized how long I had been sitting there captivated, and that I had made more in-game currency than my character could spend on any more upgrades, gadgets, or buildings.
You know what really defines this game? It's just fun. Everything about it is fun, and enjoyable to be a part of. The graphics are fun, the sounds are fun, the music is fun, the way the controls work and how you interact with the world is fun. A game has to be fun to grab you and not let you go for hours and hours on end. I wouldn't say it will appeal to everyone, but if you're like 'Ooo, that looks like something I would probably like", then I think its fair to say you will really dig it. If you like simulation games, farming games, collecting games, adventure games, or any mix of those - this is a game you can't pass up.
I am SO excited for the future of this game - it has so much potential, it could grow and grow until it was a Massively Multiplayer Online game if it wanted to. It could be like World of Warcraft, but it would be World of Slime Rancher. I hope the Slime Rancher "world" will expand hugely if it gets the support it deserves on here. I think the Devs are really professional and have a lot of talent - this game takes concepts that you may have enjoyed before in other games, and shines them up to a perfect mix that has to be played to be understood. The sheer enjoyment you get out of simpley running around and vaccuuming up all the various resources and living things the land has to offer is mind-boggling enough - it's like an easter egg hunt on drugs. This game is drugs.
PLEASE Monomi Park, expand this drug of a game so I can stop reloading your website and twitter feed 5 times a day! We wait with baited breath, and hang on every word. We're not completely sure why, but we want MORE =)

So In total I guess you could say that I have only played the game for about 3 - 4 hours and I must say that I love it. Being in early acces and having my type of PC gives me a tiny bit of lag here and there but nothing to big or really noticable (or atleast that often).
The game is about the player being a Slime Rancher in an unknown World. Overall you could say that it is a mix between Harvest Moon and Rune Factory - being able to activly fight the Monsters of the world. And yes, there are Monsters besides the normal Slimes which are... SLIMES! In all seriousness: The Monsters basically are a corrupted version of the normal slimes that have combined with another slimetype. If they now eat something they shouldnt and would basically transform again because of it they corrupt and turn into an evil entity that tries to kill everything that is around, meaning that it even attacks the adorable Slimes that it was created of.
Even though there isnt much to the game it has a big area to explore, farm upgrades and upgradable areas and a wide variety of Slimes. And is up to you to capture and combine them. And then it is up to you to save your little slimes.
It is an early access game and I know how many people dislike this sort of stuff. But maybe it helps when I say that I bought this hours before it was released on Steam just so I could finally play it.
If you really want the game: Buy it. If the overall game looks nice but you dont know if it would be a game for you: Dont buy it. I say this is a take it or leave it kind of game because you will have to invest alot of time and thought into what you are doing on your farm.

In Slime Rancher, you take on the role of a brand new... slime rancher!  Surprised?  Your home-base is a ranch with a house and several empty plots of land.  Your goal is hunt slimes, suck them up with your vaccuum pack, then take them home and take care of them.
Why?  Because slime poop is very valuable, of course!
When slimes eat, they 'poop' little crystals called Plorts.. you can trade these Plorts in for money.. then use that money to expand your ranch, transform plots of land into corrals, coops, gardens, storage units, etc, and buy upgrades to make yourself a more effective slime rancher.
You can raise chickens, grow crops, feed your slimes, and explore the world for new and exciting things, all in a physics-enabled First-Person adventure, with your trusty vaccuum pack to manipulate the world around you.  Slimes can also be bred to create new types of slimes for bigger profits.  Just be careful, because combining the wrong types of slimes can be dangerous!  I warned you!
So far, an excellent game.  Could perhaps use a little more content, but the developers are still adding new environments, more slimes and more resources, so I have confidence that my wishes will be fulfilled. You should at least wishlist this game and keep an eye on it.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics (as long as you don't hate bright, cartoony visuals)
-Fun and vairied gameplay.
-Appropriate for younger players, and still fun for older players.
-Very stable for an Early Access game.  No crashes, and no major bugs for me so far.
Cons:
-Could use more content, but that's being worked on!
-Wish I could somehow specify I want to pick up with vaccuum pack.  It can be a little frustrating to be collecting plorts, and end up picking up a lot of slimes and other stuff in the process.  This is a minor gripe.. you can always drop stuff you don't want.

I genuinely mean it when I say I have mixed opinions about this game. It's also times like these where I wish Steam had a "mixed" option instead of just giving us "yes" or "no"
Devil May Cry is my most favorite gaming franchaise of all time. I own the HD collection, 4, and this on PS3, as well as 3 and 4's Special Editions on Steam as well, and I hold no regrets.
Now, you probably remember back when this game was announced, it was panned and memed to hell and back because of what kind of direction Capcom (or Ninja Theory depending on how you're interpreting the development process) decided to take by rebooting the series. And when it was released, it wasn't critically or comercially deemed a failure, although people still legitimately panning this game existed.
What do I think of it? Well...
Let me get the negatives out of the way first by saying that the characters and the story are complete ♥♥♥♥ing garbage. DMC game or not, political commentary is extremely "safe", it doesn't really go out there. I'm not expecting the same thing with the previous games or something crazy over-the-top, but I AM expecting something more thought and fleshed out than a dystopia/freedom fighters schtick. No joke, I would probably dig a DMC in a post-apocalyptic setting. Certainly would be more interesting than this "LUL [current president], amirite?! givbe likez pLs" bullcrap.
Characters are either morally ambigious for the wrong reasons, or are flat-out useless and solely exist as checkbook examples. Even when not compared to the previous games, Vergil in this game comes across as having forced motivations (unintentional DMC3 reference, ehehe) and his DLC campaign doesn't help matters. To quote a chat I had with a friend, "it feels more like a crappy grimdark Looney Tunes fanfiction where Daffy killed Bugs, Iron Maiden style, just because he was tired of playing second banana to him"
But in terms of pretty much everything else, it's pretty good! The combat, while nowhere near as technical or involved as the other games, is just deep enough to be a stylized hack-and-slash title. The graphics are pretty great, if a little too oversaturated in the coloring sense, and the soundtrack is surprisingly very fitting for a DMC game.
While I strongly recommend the other games because of their complexity and better stories/characters, I can't hate this game that much because, gameplay-wise, it pretty much does what it sets out to do. The control scheme may be a little too wonky for first-timers, but after getting used to it, it's not going to be that big of a deal.
If you're a hardcore classic DMC fan, just keep in mind that the Back/Select/Share button is your friend. Use that little guy to skip all those pesky cutscenes! ...no, really, do it. No one wants to hear Dante of all people say "♥♥♥♥ YOU!" again.
All jokes aside, this is not a bad game by any means. You can pick it up if you want to, I'm not your dad.

Before you read any further, please note that this game only gets a half-hearted recommendation from me. It's certainly not a terrible game or anything - it is good. But it's not really great, either. Just kind of... average good.
Like, ok, so the art looks fantastic. The game is downright gorgeous, as you can see from the screenshots. And the writing for the story is pretty top-notch as well, and the game has some very creative moments involving the story. But as for the gameplay? Well, it's not *bad* or anything, it serves its purpose. But its not super entertaining. Once you upgrade your health one or two times, the levels become very trivial (except for the final level which spikes up in difficulty so far it feels like slamming into a brick wall). And the reverse boss fights - which were easily the thing I was looking forwards to the most, mind you - were a bit of a letdown. They all controlled a bit clunkily, and the one where you punch the ground gets special mention for being incredibly frustrating to control. Not to mention the heroes you're supposed to be fighting are very, VERY predictable, and as a result not difficult at all to fight.
But, in my opinion, the game's biggest sins come from its sound design. Now, the music on its own is all fine - I love Taranto's work, usually. This time around, however, the tracks sound... lacking. I'm not quite sure how to put it other than that. They feel like they needed maybe a couple more passes to make them something truly spectacular. On top of that, most of the time the tracks are far too sweeping and slow paced to fit the fast paced, action-y feel of the game. Also they commit the unforgivable sin of improper looping - instead of seamless loops (which have clearly been composed into the tracks), they fade out after about 2 loops and then start over at the beginning. As a sound designer myself, I cannot forgive that. It's just lazy.
Overall, this game feels... unfinished. The sound design all sounds kind of work in progress, there's a lot of areas where the game feels a bit unpolished (no death animations, no flashy animations for defeating heroes (hell, not even any dialogue for that), things that clearly should have sound effects not having them, etc.).
I still reccomend the game. For what it's worth, it's a good, servicable product. Just don't expect anything great.

This is one of those games that you know from the first minute of playing, will be amazing. There are many, many issues, but the gameplay thats already present more than makes up for them. The art style is one of the most appealing things about the game, the polygonal terrain makes the terraforming really satisfying to play around with. The base building is currently limited, but you still make a pretty large base, and i love the way in which the dev has allowed the base building to happen. You use pipes that originally come from your landing pod at the start of the game, these pipes transport oxygen around the base and to you, if your near them. There isnt currently a need for any food and drink, but there is a need for oxygen; i like this current system, and i dont really want it changed. Getting oxygen is always a constant worry, but if you construct mini oxygen tanks that you can stick on your backpack, the supply will last quite a while. Even if you do find yourself with a lack of oxygen while away from base, there are (usually) quite a few oxygen crystels lying about, which are extrememly useful. Though i haven't done this yet, you can go to different planets by building landers, and habitations allow you to build new bases on the planet you're on.  The addition of a buggy and a truck are incredibly useful, as you can stick a storage pad on the back, and power it via solar panels, the charge on the vehicle can also charge you, as you need power to mine(though it slowly recharges by itself). However, the driving on these vehicles are perhaps the worst controls i've ever had the misfortune of using. The sandstorms are brilliant, Im pretty sure they are dynamic, as they seem to travel in big balls around the planets. So far, im REALLY enjoying the game, and i really do hope that the devs stays commited and build the brilliant game thats already got a great foundation.

A Choose Your Own Adventure for fans of the Gundam series. This book has a concept I love more than anything: a save feature. That's right, we can now dog-ear the beginning of a chapter so players can come back to it and see if maybe they wanted to try things differently. It's a great anti-frustration feature that's rarely utilized in these games. The customizability of your mecha isn't quite as extensive as it could be, unfortunately. On the other hand, you have the option of deciding a few different things about some of the more important characters in the story or even leaving it up to randomization, which is either unique, or generally only comes up when selecting your own character's sex and preference.
On top of that, the stats matter a great deal, but not necessarily in a way that cripples players. There are multiple paths to saving the day to account for different choices and stats. As a minor caveat, however, this is a game where you specialize in a stat and then lean heavily on it. If you're a fan of CYOA games that give you a chance to be well-rounded, or where well thought-out choices always work, or where you're allowed to adapt to the game as you find out more, this is not that sort of game.
So, good story, interesting choices that can change it, and a save feature. It's worth a few gos.

Pros:
- It's a relatively unique game, like a mix between a Real-Time Strategy and a Tower Defense, with a hero you can upgrade.
- OTA gives room for many tactical decisions; do you spend your goblin-power collecting resources, building, or repairing, and do you spend your resources upgrading, recruiting more units, or upgrading the Troll?  Do you send the Troll deep into the fray, putting him at greater risk, or do you bring him into the fight after the enemy has concentrated more on your fort's walls, putting your fort at greater risk?
- It's free to play - and the only rewards for paying are aesthetic.  (Even TF2 couldn't stick to this.)
Cons:
- Beating each level poses little to no challenge.  This is because losing rewards you with the progress you made before the last attack, but giving you back the time you spent.
- There's a pretty major exploit where each time you tell the Troll to attack, it resets the cooldown for his attack, making him a killing machine.  The devs seem to have balanced the game around this, but it feels very unpolished.
- Killing enemies makes them drop resources, but you have to tell your Goblins to pick them up.  This wouldn't be a problem, except the resources disappear (a set amount of time after the enemy is killed), and it's pretty much guaranteed that even if you immediately use all your goblins to Loot, a good percentage of the resources will disappear before they can be collected.
- The campaign is VERY short.  A couple of non-campaign game modes help alleviate this.
Overall, the game isn't great.  If you want to repeatedly click to tell a Troll to kill stuff, and tell Goblins to build stuff, and don't need a game to put up a consistent challenge, you might like this game.  Otherwise, I'd recommend putting up the money to get something of higher quality, like Defense Grid.
Full Disclosure - I played on Medium, through to nearly completing the second (of four) levels.  And I don't have Defense Grid on Steam, but I have it on Xbox 360.

I got my money's worth with this one! Hours and hours of puzzling. I like being able to toggle between a 2D and 3D views. The variety of logic gates confused me at first. I've played through this a couple times, and still have to peek at the guide for some levels.

Prelogate is one of the most underrated puzzle games I have ever played. It is a logic puzzle game similar to the programming-oriented titles such as Spacechem and Human Resource Machine. Honestly, I enjoy this game more than both of those titles. The length and difficulty are a lot higher than Human Resource Machine while the interface and mechanics of the game are more casual and simplistic than Spacechem. The best part is that unlike some other games in this genre, it is entirely graphical and very easy to learn with no programming background required.
After playing the game for eighteen hours, I have finally reached the last chapter, and I am so hooked on the gameplay that I have no desire to stop playing even when I hit a wall. Prelogate consists of ten chapters and while some chapters are quick and easy, the difficulty increases significantly about halfway through the game. The most difficult chapters I found were 4, 5, and 10. There were numerous instances in which I thought the game was a bit too easy, but Chapter 10 blew that notion out of the water. Even now, I am still stuck on the third level of the last chapter, so close to the end of the game yet so far.
Since this is a niche title and not a mainstream puzzle game like Portal 2, it really isn't for everyone so you are most likely going to either love it or hate it. The expert puzzle gamers might consider this game to be mediocre compared to games like TIS-100 and Spacechem, but as an intermediate puzzle gamer who is not a professional programmer, I found this title to be much more accessible than many of its counterparts. If you are interested in logic-based puzzle games but you don't have the coding background to enjoy the more technical programming-based games, Prelogate serves as a great starting point and makes for an enjoyable experience.
As a cassual game I guess this is ok if you are bored of picking your nose or chewing on your toenails.

The low poly art style is amazing and the colorful environments are so beautiful, even when there's nothing interesting (gameplay-wise) at all, like on arid planets. The terrain modifying mechanics are really smooth and powerful, without being overpowered by limiting use based on power. Base building is very solid with really cool and varying work stations to use, although I wish that you would be able to change the length of the conduits connecting buildings to the habitat and link multiple buildings to each other. Researching is decently rewarding by unlocking new vehicles and buildings, but there isn't a way to find out where you can find what you unlocked or a detailed description of what it does yet without finding out yourself and it honestly isn't very satisfying after dragging around a lump that takes up a ton of space on a rover instead of a more late-game truck which has more storage. Vehicles are fun and simultaneously difficult to operate, but include a crane, a rover, a shuttle, and more, and have different upgrades to them done by attaching different modules to the limited attachment points (which was a very smart way to tackle inventory/upgrade space). But I think what completes this game for me is the multiplayer. Although it's in it's very early stages, and bugs are bound to be found, it is so much fun to be able to explore caves and worlds or build a super organized and power-efficient base. All-in-all, I love this game so much and it has a unique spot in anyone's library for being one of the only space exploration games with lots of cool buildings and planets to be explored, and it's only in pre-alpha.

In short: Arkham Origins delivers the same excellent gameplay as its predecessors, without attaining any new heights. For fans of the series, AO delivers more of the same. For newcomers, Arkham City is probably the better investment, but AO is definitely still worth playing.
If you are familiar with the series, then the gameplay in AO is exactly the same. There are some helpful minor tweaks with new upgrades and a fast travel system, but nothing truly innovative. And that's fine - if it ain't broke then don't fix it. If you're looking for more of the same, then AO is worth getting.
If you're new to the series, then what is there to say? The Arkham series beautifully blends movement, combat and stealth. The mechanics of the gameplay are near flawless. There is a wonderful satisfaction in picking off isolated enemies carefully in stealth, or putting together seamless combos. Despite its sophistication, the gameplay is actually easy and fluid. Grappling and gliding come so easily. For fans of action-adventure, Batman or those looking for something new, then this whole series excels.
I would still maintain that AO is inferior to Arkham City, but probably better than Arkham Asylum (I haven't yet played Arkham Knight). But if you enjoy one, then you'll enjoy the others.
The visuals are also surprisingly good. It may not be breathtaking, but there is genuine attention to detail. The atmosphere (due in no small part to the weather effects) is excellent, even if the lifelessness of the city is disappointing. The city also felt larger than the version in Arkham City. It may not be wider, but it was certainly taller and more varied in AO.
The one major area of improvement is the boss battles, which were decidely underwhelming in the two predecessors, but are occasionally excellent in AO. Sure, some still fall into the same 'perform a trick to damage the boss, beat up goons, try not to get hit by boss's AoE attack, repeat', but others liven the process somewhat.
Most of my gripes are relatively minor. The story is confused, and borderline incoherent. I was often at a loss to tell why I was doing what I was doing. Attempting to shoehorn so many Batman villains into a single game necessarily destroys any hope of a consistent narrative. This is a theme that has plagued the entire series. Don't, therefore, expect any miracles in the narrative department.
I also felt that the achievements were poorly designed. There are several that are easy to miss, and good luck doing the multiplayer ones now. Plus, many of the rest consist of lengthy grinds. They even added a mode where you have to complete the story without dying which is a recipe for frustration. None of it is particularly fun, and a lot of the side quests only serve to bloat the game. This is nothing new for the series, but AO takes it beyond acceptability. If you slogged through all of Arkham City's achievements, then you probably won't want to bother again, with even more.
The UI also deserves criticism. The menus (in-game) were clunky, and it took me a while to become orientated. Your mileage may well vary, and I think other games in the series had similar trouble.
The DLC was ok. It almost feels like much more was planned, but got axed because of poor sales. Hence the 'season pass' barely gives you anything at all.
As for bugs, I had no real problems. Apart from a couple of very minor instances, the game ran perfectly. I also recommend using a controller to get the most out of the gameplay - a keyboard feels too clunky.
Pros:
- Excellent gameplay
- Relatively strong visuals, with a great atmosphere
- Improved boss battles
- Solid across the board
Cons:
- Weak story
- Lengthy achievements
- Too much bloat from side quests
- Poor UI
Verdict: The excellent gameplay and atmosphere easily carry this game. Despite some minor gripes, it is an enjoyable experience from start to finish. It may be more of the same, but that's more of the same high quality gameplay. Even at full price, it's great value for money, though you can probably skip the DLC.

The physics at work in
seems to play into the idea of being "hard to learn and hard to master." Reports tell of experienced
players who can accomplish marvelous things once they have the required skills. I'll grant that that would be a satisfying place to reach. But for the typical player, most of their time spent in the game will be helplessly struggling with the controls––spending five minutes trying to jump to the necessary height, or spending a Sisyphean eternity trying to move a block up a gentle slope. Am I just bad at the game? Probably.
The point remains that typical lauded platformers afford great control to the player, and then test that through varied, difficult challenges. Gish affords limited control (at first, ostensibly) and then gives really basic challenges in order to teach or, in many cases, frustrate. There may be some clement space around the 10-hour mark where you come into your own and find it has all become effortless; but for those of us not seeking
discipleship, it's a grueling road.

First a warning: this is definitely not a game for everyone. It's old (2004), and it has a very unique and complex physics system which defines the whole game. All interaction are physics-based, combat, jumping, even basic movement. This is never explained properly and can be very hard to get on your own. At first it looks like your average platformer with gimmicks, but then you gradually realise that even to do proper high and far jumps you need to utilize its physics. Learning it on your own can be quite frustrating, I recall getting to world 3 and being stuck right at the beginning of the first level. You can't progress until you learn to bounce and conserve your momentum, Which is actually a very good thing: instead of making you fail somewhere in the middle of a level , wondering what you did wrong, you are told right at the beginning "You must jump THIS TALL to enter". Nowadays with youtube I'm sure you can find good videos which explain the mechanincs, but back in 2006 it was quite a pain for me.
That said, once you understand the controls properly this becomes one of the most fun and dynamic platformers you ever see, and the whole game can be completed fairly quickly. If you like unique games and have the patience to learn, then I can't recommend this game enough.
PS: some reviews claim that a patch a couple of years ago broke the game, so that you can die simply from moving through a narrow passage. I didn't check if this is true at the moment, but I'm sure it would be easy to find a fix on the internet.

The problem is this is a 2004 physics puzzler.  No one had an idea how to do these types of games at the time, and it shows.  Yes it came out before Half Life 2 and was impressive for it's time.
Only thing is I'm writing this in 2016, there's been over 10 years of development in physics, and honestly if Gish came out today?  It'd get horrible reviews.  The controls are weak (And I know I'm supposed to use momentum, I do, and yet I can't make the motion I want to half the time, it seems luck based often. Plus you often if you lose momentum the level become painful)   The levels are interesting the first time but overused.  There's no level select so if you miss a secret or a achievement it seems you have to play the game again.
But let's talk about the game itself.  While the levels can be interesting, the game itself is just not interesting.  The story is typical (Someone stole you're girl) but the levels aren't really related to that and aren't that unique.
I feel like this is an unpolished game, maybe it was rushed, maybe the team didn't know how to "finish" a game, and released it too early, maybe it just has too many issues under the hood but it just doesn't feel "finished" it doesn't have a nice polish that it needs, and that hurts a lot.
My advice, pay the extra money, go get Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy.  Leave Gish in the past where it belongs, because it was a novel concept now, but Edmund's become a far better designer since these days, and that's a good thing.

Before I start, let me just say that this game is 100% worth the price. I bought this game several years back and despite it being a bit rough around the edges in places I've enjoyed it every time I played it. However, if my word alone isn't enough to convince you to buy this, here's the longer review, prepare for a lot of reading.
Firstly, the really compelling part of this game is the sheer amount of clomplexity of it's systems. every single system acts logically within the game world and interacts logically with the other systems. Introversion could have just let you place a "Library" room and made prisoners fulfill their education needs when they stand in it, but instead, if you want a library you have to place it, furnish it, wait for workers to place said furniture, train prisoners through school work, staff said prisoners in the library, sort through all of the books, let prisoners take those books, etc... This attention to detail permeates every mechanic in the game, and you can tell that Introversion really put their heart and soul into developing it.
Secondly, I should talk about the aspects of this game that leave a little to be desired. Most of it boils down to a simple lack of polish but it's still worth mentioning here. I've encountered numerous graphical bugs and glitches throughout my time playing, and even though the graphics themselves are passible, they still leave a lot to be desired. The UI can feel a bit clunky at times, but after a while you'll get used to it. Some of the experimental map settings like water and derelict buildings never really seem to work for me without mods, and they just tend to make the game less fun even when they generate well. Maybe that's just me but it still needs to be said. Also, escape mode in the game is really just a joke. It's kind of novel at first to try to escape from the prison's you've built, but it gets very dull very fast. However, so long as you don't see escape mode as an actual game mode, but instead as a fun little add on that you'll try once or twice and never use again, you won't be very disapointed. All in all, it seems like most of the flaws in this game just seem to stem from a lack of polish, but because of the size of the team involved and the robustness of the rest of the game I'm very quick to forgive Introversion for the few gripes I do have with the game.
Finally, I need to touch on the theme that this game represents. To say it bluntly, this game is dark. You won't notice it at first, because other than the campaign and the death row system there is nothing overtly depressing or sad in this game. However, after you've played several hours you might take a step back and realize that those little sprites on the screen represent human people that you are keeping locked up for (In game) years at a time. Introversion had two ways to go with this theme, they could've just not bothered with it or they could use their game to convey a message, and they chose the latter. In the game you can either treat your prisoners poorly or you can treat them well. Being the good samaritan I am, on my first playthrough I decided that I wanted to treat them well. I gave my prisoners all the amenities that they wanted and made sure that they were happy and healthy. However, despite this making me feel good it also left me bankrupt, and the biggest way to make money in the game is to take on more prisoners, so I did. Eventually though, this turned my nice little prison into a living hell. I overcrowded the limited space I had, and becasue of that fights broke out, not enough prisoners had access to the amenities that I provided, which sent there needs down, and both my reoffending rate and my murder rate went through the roof. Pretty soon my quaint little penitentiary had turned into one of those for-profit prisons that people see on TV or YouTube and get mad about. This game taught me about the dangers of for-profit prisons more than any statistic or documentary could, and that's because it let me see first hand how the incentives of the prison system force prisons to treat their inmates poorly and overcrowd the space that they have. This game's message and it's ability to teach  are what really turn this game from really good to great in my opinion, and I give Introversion the highest praises for tackling this issue with the respect and insight that it truly deserves.
This review is getting pretty long now, so I'll wrap it up with a quick list of pros and cons.
Pros:
- Excellent managment mechanics
- Great replay value
- Difficult yet fair
- Insightful message
- Educational (Somewhat)
Cons:
- Lack of polish
- Escape mode not very fleshed out
- Experimental map settings leave a lot to be desired
TL;DR if you like management games this is a must buy. everything you'd want in a city builder with an intriguing theme to boot. 9/10
Thank you to anyone who actually took the time to read all of this, and I hope I've been helpful in helping you make a decision.

In this interactive text-based novel by
, you can now channel your inner Gundam/mecha/robot/Pacific Rim fan and man your own robotic battlesuit in space! Is your robot quick and agile with a focus on ranged combat or are you going for the slow, undestructable powerhouse with plasma sword? And what kind of a leader are you -- a ruthless, inspiring warrior or a perceptive diplomat?
With lots of customisation options for both your robot and your personality, anything is possible. The battles you fight will decide many things, such as the possible survival or gruelling deaths of your squadron, and, more importantly, whether you will side with the space colonies fighting for independence or will join Earth's noble monarchy...
+ Customise your robot in many different ways (really fun)
+ Save points after each chapter
+ The ability to customise all NPC genders
+ Three quite different romance options
- The story lacks depth; protag still manages to feel a bit like a blank slate
- The story also relies a bit too much on Gundam story elements
- Sometimes the pacing in battle scenes can be a little bit clunky
- No skip option
If you liked the many different iterations of the Gundam phenomenon (as I do) or just love big robots in space fighting each other, then you will probably like this. The battles are exciting and keep you on the edge of your seat. However, don't expect a deep and profound story -- especially if you're already familiar with Gundam lore, you'll know where it is heading and what types of people some characters are or will turn out to be.

This game is quite the mind bender. In fact, it bends your mind so much you may swear you can hear it screaming for you to stop. Prelogate is pretty much what it says on the main page; A game that uses lasers and mirrors to solve complex problems. The game itself is pretty straight-forward in that you just have to solve the puzzles. The music selection is slow and ambient, which is nice, but felt grating at some points. There's a...sorta plot, but at the same time its not entirely a plot. While the game itself is a challenge, it gets to a point where the challenge is excessive and one relies more on solution codes than spending 3 hours on one stage. While I
recommend it, it's not something I'd recommend to just anyone.
The gameplay is, as said before, using lasers and mirrors. Cool, right? Who doesn't like using lasers for weird stuff? Unfortunately, the fun part wears off pretty quickly. The game starts with simple mirrors and lasers, relying on reflection and splitting to get to an endpoint. This lasts for a few levels before the game introduces logic gates; IF, OR, AND, XOR. Naturally, anyone with a smidge of computer science learning, or fumbling around in programming, knows what these are. So it's rather an unhappy moment when you realize these logic gates don't really...feel like they belong. Sure you know how they work because of the small text window, but that's all you get. You have to figure out how they work entirely in the levels they give it to you, because it does not get esaier after this point. It is here you realize the game is about to turn from difficulty curve into a full blown Kleiner's bottle of difficulty; no matter how hard you climb, you never really escape it. Solutions become downright maddening just to clear one step out of eight. Again, it is here you start to rely more on solution codes than actually working it out.
It's there, sure. It's pretty basic, nice space-like ambience to make you feel relaxed. Which doesn't help because this game needs you to fire all cylinders in your brain. Strange how that works.
The game has some...interesting mechanics outside of the actual game. However, these interesting mechanics are simply superficial; They're there to just sit there and look nice. You can interact with the pre-level UI in some ways, but it doesn't really do much. Can't explore who you are, why you're there, what kinda people are working with you. It's just for kicks. Part of me thinks it was going to be a part of something larger, but was scrapped for reasons unknown. While the over-arching plot is you making AI systems with lasers, I felt like there could've been a little more.
I personally just could not enjoy the game after getting halfway through it. The logic gates really made the puzzles far more mind-bending than they deserved to be and the unfortunate reality to feel like I was too stupid to figure it out for myself, let alone for the rest of the game, really gave me a terrible taste in my mouth. The game does what it sets out to do, and does it well. That said, don't be surprised if you fall short of what the puzzles ask for and end up flailing hopelessly because you just don't entirely understand it. Thankfully, the pricetag is quite an enticing factor, so even if you don't really like it, 3$ for 64 levels of puzzles is a pretty rad deal.
I'm reluctantly recommending it on the off-chance people are masochistic and love a good challenge. Don't say I didn't warn you!

I only recently found the Arkham games, although I had played arkham city for an hour or so once and not liked it much. I was out of games, and decided to give Arkham knight a try, as I was bored and could not find a single game on steam that I wanted to play. I like comic books, but given the glut of comic book movies I am pretty burnt out on comics. I used to watch the Batman animated series 20 years ago, and they were one of my favorite shows, but Batman was never my favorite superhero. I always saw him as one dimensisonal, and he had no superpowers...
I never thought I would ever find another game as good as the witcher 3, but Arkham knight was one that matched it. Despite everything, I was hooked onto the game, and finished 2 playthroughs, and looked for other arkham games. I had arkham city, so I gave it another chance. I liked the game a lot this time around. It was short, and it had some horrible frame rate issues that took a while to fix, but the game had most of the same excellent combat and excellent voice acting. It was polished, it was made with care. The riddler puzzles, which I had initially hated in Arkham Knight, grew to be  my favorite things over these two games, and Arkham city was full of them. So the next game I bought was this one, ARkham origins, expecting it to be more of the same great stuff. And it seemed that way until about five minutes in... and my opinionof this game has  been a slow downward descent since then.
It is a game that took all the excellent combat systems, animations and gameplay elements of Arkham City, and then replicated them as much as possible, with minor changes to equipment and a new crime scene thing that you do a couple times in the game that is nothing special. But where it differs from the other two games is in the level of care and effort put into the game. Those intricate puzzles hidden cleverly throughout the world? gone. The puzzles themselves? mostly gone. Even the combat has a bunch of bugs in it. Moves are jerky, your enemy bounces up and down ten feet when you finish them off sometimes, you get stuck gliding in the same spot, your remote batarang suddenly loses responsiveness in certain spots, etc... There are so many instances in this game where the difference between arkham city and this are like day and night. You can really tell that there was very little care put into this game, and that they sought to simply create a product that could ride off the success of the previous game rather than innovate. Even the graphics are not greatly improved, given the year it came out in. For some reason, your suit is now reflective, and has a permanent white sheen on it, making you look out of place. In anything but complete darkness, you glow with this dull white sheen. The city  you explore is dull, boring, and enemies will respawn even as you just grapple to the next building. It  almost seems like this game chose to be in the middle of a snowstorm to avoid having to do the work of making detailed environments. Much easier to just cover everything with snow. They badly miscalculated on this, because it makes the game world look dull and lifeless, which it is. There are thugs and evil police everywhere, which makes no sense, and there are no citizens around at all, which makes even less sense. Your grapple is really clunky and will often target something you do not want to, and its a real pain getting where you want at times. This game has some good things about it, but its much less enjoyable than the others. It is to the Arkham series what Andromeda is to the Mass effect series... Actually, that is a bit harsh... This game is to the Arkham series what peeing is to drinking a beer. It feels like the mildly satisfying task that you are left with after enjoying yourself.
There are some good things about this game. The boss battles are sometimes fun, although some of them feel like prolongued quicktime events. It is very easy and probably the best game to start if you have never played an arkham game before, since things can only get better from here. The voice acting is... tolerable. The loss of Mark Hamil as Joker is probably the worst thing about this game. As good a job as Troy Baker did, he just can't quite do this character properly. But that might be the writing, and not all his fault. The best part of the game is the story and the potrayal of Batman as a beginner. He is a lot more violent, a lot more angry, and his meeting with Joker for the first time, and relationship with Alfred are all interesting and well done. The cinematic feel you get in the cutscenes and such is excellent, and much better than the other ARkham games.

This is my first game in Devil May Cry series, so I'm not totally aware with the controversies surrounding this reboot. Still, the hack 'n slash part intrigues me. And WOW, I have to say that DmC: Devil May Cry is probably one of the best game of its genre I’ve ever played despite all of its shortcomings. Let me tell you a glimpse about the experience during my own playthrough and what it has to offer.
The story for the most part is fine as far as it goes. But some conversations are just… well, uninspiring at best but completely bearable. At least the cinematic cutscenes are stellar and movie-worthy. It’s also worth mentioning that they used motion capture for the cutscenes, and they did a great job at that.
The way the combat is handled on the other hand is great, if not excellent. It is fluid, transition between weapon modes is seamless, and its animations are superb. Combos are easy to perform yet still difficult to master nonetheless. One thing from DmC which really shines is its world design, particularly when we’re dragged into Limbo. Beautifully crafted, unconventionally artistic, and each level feels diverse and unique. The environment itself is “alive” within Limbo’s boundary. Last but not least, the graphic quality is still relevant enough today for a 2013 game (especially true on the highest settings). Simply marvelous.
I suggest to at least give it a shot before anything else. If you like the game and already have finished it, the Vergil’s Downfall DLC may be worth a try.
PROS :
+ Visually striking Limbo City and its “Limbo”.
+ A plethora of weapons and combos.
+ Slick combat mechanics and animations.
+ Some aspect of replayability (upgrades, mission ranks, secret missions and collectibles).
CONS :
- Short and linear story mode.
- The writings, mainly dialogues, could have been better. MUCH better.
- Some minor camera issues.
- Need the additional features and contents from console’s Definitive Edition.

Gish by Chronic Logic, despite the fact that some people think it’s an old Smashing Pumpkins album, is actually a platformer video game.  Pretty standard fare.  The twist is, you have no legs.  Or arms.  Or… anything except eyes, a mouth, and a body.  You’re a 12lb ball of tar.
Gish’s lady friend Brea has been kidnapped and taken into the sewers, and it’s up to you to save her.  Fight your way through five worlds and reclaim your love.  Now, to be honest, this title has not aged well aesthetically.  The graphics are mediocre at best, and the audio is not very memorable.  The five worlds are made distinct by little more than sprite-swapped square bricks with new lighting colors.  There is a charming bit when you open the game  where the loading screen shows a poster of a pop culture icon with the main star replaced by Gish.  The Gishorcist, Gishheart, Gish Fiction.  But the real draw here is the unique and simple-but-deep gameplay, which still shines through today, making this a game worth a look.
Gish can jump, but it’s a pretty ineffectual maneuver.  To reach a ledge, you’ll need to gain momentum by jumping, compressing him down, and then releasing all that energy into a jump again.  Gish can also modify his body in a few important ways.  You can slide through narrow passages, increase your weight in order to crush enemies or obstacles, or make yourself sticky to cling to objects or surfaces (even ceilings).  The whole game is based around learning these different modifiers and applying them through each (relatively short) level.  This is a deep physics-based platformer, and you’ll develop a working understanding of momentum, trajectory, and crushing things with a tar ball.  Pushing a box onto a pressure switch is a much different experience when you can’t pick it up with hands.  You’ll need to stick yourself to it and propel it, or make yourself rigid and heavy to push it along.
Some of the levels can get extremely frustrating, and a single mistake can cost you quite a bit of time spent retreading platforming sections.  Some jumps have very little margin for error, and the unique controls take a while to get used to.  This leads to situations where you know exactly what you need to do, but getting Gish to actually accomplish that in the physics engine can be difficult.  Especially frustrating is when objects like catapults or swings, which you need to use to progress, end up killing you randomly and draining you of precious lives.  A few bugs like this are irritating, but not game-breaking.
Besides the main quest, there’s also a “Collection” mode and a Versus mode.  Collection mode tasks you with collecting all the amber pieces on a level within a certain time limit, and can be a fun challenge, and a great way to learn the systems at play before diving into the main story.  Versus mode is exactly what it sounds like.  You and up to 3 other friends compete to kill each other using different tar balls.  A fun little diversion, but not much else.  For as long as the game has been out, it seems the Steam achievements haven’t worked, but it appears that recently they have been fixed!  Finally, validation from Steam of my success in this game!  They’re still really difficult to get, however.
While the game shows its age, and there are a few irritating bugs present in the systems, this is a title worth checking out for the sheer novelty of its control scheme.  Manipulating Gish’s body to take advantage of the physics at play is hugely rewarding when you finally master it, and Gish’s descent down to Hell and back is quite a fun ride.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a game that simulates being a truck driver in Europe. The game spans across a good chunk of European countries, ranging from the UK all the way to Italy. The open world is truly massive, and there are tons of roads to be driven and explored. You start of as a hired driver who takes jobs to deliver cargo from one place to another with a truck that is provided by the company offering you the job.
I can easily say that the traffic system in this game is quite well made compared to other open world driving games. For instance, I have come up to many intersections and upon a car or truck pulling up, they will sometimes notice me and stop to let me pull out. The traffic system is very well made and very complex, which helps to make the experience much more realistic. However, it seems as if no matter how fast the speed limit is on the highways, even if I travel on the exact speed limit, every other vehicle always seems to pass me. Am I going to slow or is everyone else allowed to speed?
The outer and inner workings of all the trucks you can drive in this game are made to very realistic standards too. The game isn't exactly on the pretty side in terms of graphics, but there are so many things that you have to pay attention to to ensure your truck stays moving toward its destination.
No, actually. At first glance, one could and would assume that this game only consists of driving back and forth across Europe hauling a trailer to the same destinations across the same highways. Well, the game makes sure that it isn't repetitive at all with a lot of features. One of those features is the fact that the open world availible to the player to drive around in is HUGE. To explore it all would take a long time. The second feature is how many things you have to pay attention to while driving. You will get penalized for running red lights, hitting cars in traffic, and driving over the speed limit. You have to make sure you do not run out of fuel before you reach your destination. You have to pay attention to the map to ensure you don't veer off course. All of those things make every drive different, offering a unique experience every time.
Most of all, this game is relaxing. I personally play this game with a racing wheel and pedals, so driving across Europe is both a realistic, fun, and exciting experience. This game pulls off hauling cargo across Europe like no other game could even attempt to pull off - and for that it is truly one of a kind, and incredible.

Before I start, let me just say that this game is 100% worth the price. I bought this game several years back and despite it being a bit rough around the edges in places I've enjoyed it every time I played it. However, if my word alone isn't enough to convince you to buy this, here's the longer review, prepare for a lot of reading.
Firstly, the really compelling part of this game is the sheer amount of clomplexity of it's systems. every single system acts logically within the game world and interacts logically with the other systems. Introversion could have just let you place a "Library" room and made prisoners fulfill their education needs when they stand in it, but instead, if you want a library you have to place it, furnish it, wait for workers to place said furniture, train prisoners through school work, staff said prisoners in the library, sort through all of the books, let prisoners take those books, etc... This attention to detail permeates every mechanic in the game, and you can tell that Introversion really put their heart and soul into developing it.
Secondly, I should talk about the aspects of this game that leave a little to be desired. Most of it boils down to a simple lack of polish but it's still worth mentioning here. I've encountered numerous graphical bugs and glitches throughout my time playing, and even though the graphics themselves are passible, they still leave a lot to be desired. The UI can feel a bit clunky at times, but after a while you'll get used to it. Some of the experimental map settings like water and derelict buildings never really seem to work for me without mods, and they just tend to make the game less fun even when they generate well. Maybe that's just me but it still needs to be said. Also, escape mode in the game is really just a joke. It's kind of novel at first to try to escape from the prison's you've built, but it gets very dull very fast. However, so long as you don't see escape mode as an actual game mode, but instead as a fun little add on that you'll try once or twice and never use again, you won't be very disapointed. All in all, it seems like most of the flaws in this game just seem to stem from a lack of polish, but because of the size of the team involved and the robustness of the rest of the game I'm very quick to forgive Introversion for the few gripes I do have with the game.
Finally, I need to touch on the theme that this game represents. To say it bluntly, this game is dark. You won't notice it at first, because other than the campaign and the death row system there is nothing overtly depressing or sad in this game. However, after you've played several hours you might take a step back and realize that those little sprites on the screen represent human people that you are keeping locked up for (In game) years at a time. Introversion had two ways to go with this theme, they could've just not bothered with it or they could use their game to convey a message, and they chose the latter. In the game you can either treat your prisoners poorly or you can treat them well. Being the good samaritan I am, on my first playthrough I decided that I wanted to treat them well. I gave my prisoners all the amenities that they wanted and made sure that they were happy and healthy. However, despite this making me feel good it also left me bankrupt, and the biggest way to make money in the game is to take on more prisoners, so I did. Eventually though, this turned my nice little prison into a living hell. I overcrowded the limited space I had, and becasue of that fights broke out, not enough prisoners had access to the amenities that I provided, which sent there needs down, and both my reoffending rate and my murder rate went through the roof. Pretty soon my quaint little penitentiary had turned into one of those for-profit prisons that people see on TV or YouTube and get mad about. This game taught me about the dangers of for-profit prisons more than any statistic or documentary could, and that's because it let me see first hand how the incentives of the prison system force prisons to treat their inmates poorly and overcrowd the space that they have. This game's message and it's ability to teach  are what really turn this game from really good to great in my opinion, and I give Introversion the highest praises for tackling this issue with the respect and insight that it truly deserves.
This review is getting pretty long now, so I'll wrap it up with a quick list of pros and cons.
Pros:
- Excellent managment mechanics
- Great replay value
- Difficult yet fair
- Insightful message
- Educational (Somewhat)
Cons:
- Lack of polish
- Escape mode not very fleshed out
- Experimental map settings leave a lot to be desired
TL;DR if you like management games this is a must buy. everything you'd want in a city builder with an intriguing theme to boot. 9/10
Thank you to anyone who actually took the time to read all of this, and I hope I've been helpful in helping you make a decision.

I rather like this game. Prelogate is quite what it says on the tin. "Solve puzzles by redirecting laser beams, mixing them and controlling them with logic gates." There is really no better way to put it. If that sounds like something you'd play, go ahead!
Even so, though, I only reluctantly recommend this game. While the concept is certainly sound, the level design is rather flawed. Some levels in the later parts of the game, for example, are extremely forced (in that there's only really one solution that's completely obvious) and are therefore a waste of time. Others are repeats of these "extremely forced" levels. Furthermore, said levels are often placed AFTER levels with much harder solutions.
Furthermore, there are a few gates that would REALLY help the game: for example, a "MIX ONLY IF THERE ARE TWO INPUTS" or a "LET COLOUR THROUGH IF NO INPUT" gate. It's really annoying to keep constructing these gates manually in each level that needs them.
Finally, the game allows a 2D mode, but if you're playing some of the later levels (with raised blocks), this makes the game impossible to play. Likewise, many "colourblind mode tags" are obscured by "incorrect input" tags on 2D mode.
If you can look past these problems, then at heart it is a good game flawed by implementation.

Overall: Good to Very good
Difficulty: Medium to Medium-high
Likes:
- Puzzles are divided into steps.  In each step, a different subset of lasers / receivers are active, and laser beams must not hit inactive receivers.  Your solution must be valid for all steps simultaneously.  This is an innovative take on laser puzzle games that is interesting and challenging.
- There are 10 sets of puzzles, and almost every set of puzzles is based on a different theme and plays differently
- For additional challenge, you can make your solution "clean" (laser beams don't go off the screen or hit obstacles).  You can also optimize your solution to minimize the number of devices used; the total length of the laser beams; or the number of devices plus the number of separate beams.  See comment below.
Dislikes:
- UI is clumsy.  If you click Play, you can't navigate to previous solved levels (need to click Level instead).  If you click Level, you can't proceed to the current unsolved level (need to click Play instead).  No quick puzzle reset (need to escape to menu).  Some pieces are hard to visually distinguish (e.g. mixers and diffusers).  Visually unclear in 2D view (e.g., raised walls are nearly invisible).  Always need to rotate camera when starting a puzzle.
- Every puzzle is progress locked
- For the Obstacle and Platform sets of levels, the puzzles felt a bit uninspired, and less interesting
Comments:
- The optimization aspect of the game is reminiscent of SpaceChem, but the puzzles are not as open-ended and engineering-focused as in SpaceChem
