is an old-school, turn-based medieval strategy game that has been updated from the original. The updated edition holsters new features under its belt along with some new game modes I presume. You play as one of three different medieval factions, either the French noblemen, English court or the Vikings. According to history, the Vikings and English were at war, then the French and English along with the Vikings and English. Everybody in the medieval era hated the Vikings because they were ruthless, showed no mercy and came in conquest to take land, gold, wealth and treasures as they stole and plundered from others and beseeched them earnestly. The main weapon of offensive units were marauders that would come in with incredible force infiltrating the whole offensive line. The main weakness in
for the Vikings are their long-range artillery and of course calvary that dies off quickly. The French succeeded because of their defensive stance, positions they took on the defensive line and their choice of using reinforced armor made out of better materials. The English were your primary long-distance dealers and in this game they succeed by using spears and bows.


Three current game modes exist, campaign, skirmishes and the hotseat. I stuck with the campaign through this playthrough to test out the game and take a test drive in it.
Each different faction has both their strengths and weaknesses, however what stays consistent throughout the whole game is mostly the type of buildings that are built. There are garrisons, barracks, horse stables, a blacksmith to craft your weapons; upgrading your weapons, crafting armor, upgrading armor, the church to recruit priests of the court to fight beside you giving an incredible bonus to all your adjacent units, a war school for research and new and improved weapons, a marketplace to increase gold per turn, iron gates to strengthen protection of your castle and finally the weapon store providing better supply during sieging castles.


The turn-based strategy combat makes this game very simple. Imagine that you are playing either chess or checkers with someone online or against the computer. This is exactly how the combat is stationed, you get the chance to move your units and to upgrade your units, buildings and defenses once per turn. Once you are done with your turn, you click on the hourglass on the lower right of your screen to end your turn, then the opposing faction attacks on you while you try your best to defend. There is no way to block or defend yourself against the opposing faction. You simply must rely on upgrading to better weapons, better materials those weapons are made out of and better armor for all of your defenses. It is very simple, maybe even too simple with no advanced learning curve. However, considering the original reflects the more old-school style of strategy games such as
, this is allowed and shows subordination towards it as a precursor.
Likewise, of chess, you want to keep your distance away from your enemies. I recommend using archers first after hiring a blacksmith if you are the English, however, the Vikings don't do nearly enough damage at all upon the French due to their incredible armor made of steel and higher amendable quality. Thus for Vikings, you are going to have to rely on Marauders and hope you can eventually upgrade to a unit called the battering ram in order to do some excessive damage and capture all of their buildings, their control points.

You move along a grid allowing room for your units to be facing diagonally, adjacent to one another, side-by-side, backed up from a defensive standpoint and also spread out. This works very well and is a nice addiction towards the simplicity.

The controls utilize basic double-clicking of the mouse from area to area. If you want to get closer to the castle, all you do is first double-click on your unit and then move forward which is followed by catch phrases like, " Yes my lord" and others. All in all, for the most part as long as you know what you are doing they are responsive.

While the graphics are not mind-blowing they don't need to be. The graphics remind me of another game,
which is fine and nice. The graphics are simple yet elegant with just the right colors to bring the grid battlefield system and turn-based combat to life in color. That is all that is really needed without including any special bells and whistles along the way of more modern grand-scale based strategy games such as the newer
games and one of the most renown PC title series,
. The textures and graphic scale of pixels is not meant to be as intense and heavy under load such as the Civilization series which I can appreciate due to the change of pace from a complex steep learning curve in more grand-scale strategy games to pure simplicity in turn-based ones that never make the game more complicated than a game of chess and checkers.

Advantageous Implementations
•An excellent balance between creating the right units based upon the opposing factions you face against
•An incredible array of different music that is orchestrative in bringing the Medieval era as a whole to life
•A good update to the original game
•Simplicity makes the cut, being empathetic upon the feelings, values and beliefs of people within the strategy genre
•Nice text based layout of text without overdoing it once you survive a mission and capture the opposing team's resources, buildings and castle
•I sincerely hope that this game appeals to a much wider audience of people [/h1]
•It takes time, patience and the ability to know and to recognize instantaneously the weakness and strengths of your opponents
•Lack of more graphical settings and options in which we can all deal with but it would be nice to be able to modify it some
•I would have liked it to have some tutorial, especially good for those like me that decided in the latter part of the summer to start getting into the strategy genre as a newer genre I play. Knowing nothing about strategy myself and the simplicity of this game with carefully timed attacks and chess based strategy, I am led to take careful notes upon all weaknesses of my army and use all my strengths earlier on in the beginning to my advantage.
•There is a tutorial only for game help for those that have never played. While it does educate you on the gameplay and mechanics, I still would of liked to see one match in which the computer shows you examples in different situations of unit placement and the times in which you should advance and other instances in which you should retract.

After several hours playing the original game of Medieval Battlefields (MB), the Black Edition offers pretty much what the developers describe: “…plenty of improvements and major bug fixes. Game looks and plays better overall, there are new visuals and existing artwork is improved. The units are rebalanced, single-player AI is improved and the mechanics now display added functionality. Battlefields and maps are enhanced. Multiplayer system, account creation and networking are upgraded and considerably more stable. There are added Steam achievements, Steam Cloud functionality and soon-to-be-implemented Steam trading cards.”
The product has a cozy boardgame feel to it, and most strategy gamers will have little need for the online manual, except perhaps to check some of the Siege rules in the game. Movement and combat is reminiscent of Panzer Corps (PC), with a few differences. First, there is no defensive support from adjacent units like artillery or AT in PC. What I’ve always disliked about PC is the numerical (1-15) representation of unit strengths. In MB, strength is based on a percentage of 1-100, so there is more variability in combat losses. Also, there are no combat predictions to hold your hand, as in PC.
Although the game is simple and straightforward, there are fortunately plenty of options to extend replayability. English, French and Vikings with 9 different units – although not dramatically different performance-wise. Also, each of the 9 buildings that construct units can be upgraded twice. So theoretically, one player can have 27 units with slightly different stats on the game board at one time. Swordsmen, Halberdiers, Crossbowmen, Knights, Archers, etc. must be used as historically. It is possible to compare your unit’s stats with a competitor’s to determine what bonuses will be in effect before combat.
“Fast-paced” is a good description of the gameplay, and the designers fortunately chose TBS rather than RTS. Players must decide whether to go for villages, farms and other structures which will gain them income or capture the opponent(s) castles(s) while defending their own. There are fortification bonuses available and castles can also be recaptured by their original owners.
There is no fog of war, in part because it would cause AI scripting to be infinitely more complex, if not impossible. Instead, the AI(s) zero in on enemy castles first, bonus hexes second, and vulnerable enemy units third. This simplification makes for a much tougher artificial opponent. I watched two AIs play on a tiny map for almost 10 minutes before one finally got the upper hand. I believe this illustrates that the AI rarely makes mistakes.
There are 26 maps available from 8x8 up to one 24x24 monster. The 16x16 maps are ideal, and up to 8 players or AIs can take each slot and starting location. Depending on the set-up, this “simple” game can get quite complex with numerous armies vying for position and the battle constantly swaying back and forth. Larger games are most enjoyable and present the most challenge. Multiplayer would add further complexity, although as a single-player gamer, I did not attempt to start an MP game and cannot comment on the health of the lobby, etc.
I encountered no bugs or crashes, but I never had a problem with the older version either. What I would wish for most in a patch is more 24x24 maps and/or a map generator. Fortunately, there is a good variety of 16x16, but hey, we could use a few more.
Even with the intense competition among other $10 games on Steam, I feel a price of $8 to $12 is fair for this title. A $5 sale may come one day, but for now that would simply be unfair to the developer based on what has been created in the Black Edition.

As much people say about how horrible the game is of constant bashing of how the game is and supposed to be. Don't listen to them.
It as much as a development game as to see how it would be like in space stranded with potentail hazards of falling *Space rocks * from the moon's sky.
There is potential of how this game could be worked out , its main mechanic is supposed to be a simulator. Not some high tech fancy Call of Duty Black Ops 3 Space battles you are all familier with.
It is ment to be a horror game and with specs to use a VR headset to *simulate * the feeling of being alone in space. Never knowing the dangers of being in space. Your oxygen tank takes damage to *being hit* with space debris falling at you in a constant rate. Also you may take *damage* to your oxygen otherwise as it takes time to get to place to place. So it makes you want to be wary of whats up above you and around you. And the worry of making it back with your reserve tanks becomign low and the meteores falling down at you makes it more unsettling of you making it back.
The time alone I have may show I didn't spend much but I played offline for countless hours. Trying to get to the unknown signals left stranded in the open moonscape.
The lack of choosing a option to see what to do in the world leaves me a bit unease to figure out that if hitting buttons is my first thought. No tutorial or such. Even to mapping keys. I was left with my screen showing that I had no *Primary* fire or alt fire button. And 3 other misc buttons that could be possible left in development.
The scene's are leaving my eyes a bit sore after about 30 mins into looking the moonworld. The constant wierd glossy on the below of my screen made my eyes become irritant and quickly had to take a break for 15 before diving in again. The *buttons not configured* overlap your HUD's radar of seeing your signals makes it quite harder to even look down as your radar is barely visable due to the *weird* glossy shiny moon texture. Yet it still felt to me that even looking ahead of you and trying to reach the signals and hoping you reach some goal. It lead me to keep going even with the moon looking like a shiny marble on a table.
The game however has a *Zoom* (Right Mouse Button) button and you can descend a lot slower (Holding Space bar) upon going into deep chasms or just wanting to dive into a huge crater.
The Pros
* Its a space horror simuation.
* Its Free
* Potentail hours wasted if you're into the sort of simulations
The Cons
* Lack of Options and controls.
* Still buggy as to 1.4d Patch - EXPECT BUGS - STILL NEW -
* Lack of Teaching players what to do.
Overall I give this a 6.5 out of 10.

I really enjoyed this game, being someone who frequently plays hard platforming games. One aspect to the game i really enjoy is the dark world, which offers that extra challenge to people like me who've had experience with harder platforming games, which can only be unlocked by passing the light-world levels by beating a certain time.
The soundtrack is full-on amazing, and a lot of effort was put into it considering it was for a 2d-platformer, something that (most of the time) doesn't do very well on the market.
Another thing i enjoyed were the references to indie games like I Wanna Be The Guy, and them taking it a step further and being able to unlock characters from said indie games.
Finally, the physics to me were really weird to get used to at first, with Meat Boy sliding all over the place, but if you pressed the opposite key you were moving in at the right time he'd just come to a sudden halt. Although it's annoying at first, it allows for super-fast gameplay once you master it.
My conclusion? If you enjoy platformers, or just a general challenge, definitely give this game a try... You don't have much to lose, and sometimes you can get it on sale for little over $3!

Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

I absolutely love Rust in every way possible. I have never gotten more enjoyment out of playing a video game than I have while playing this game. Rust is not for the weak though, it is rough and very frustrating. But even when things are not going well, the game is still fun. What I love most about this game is the player interactions and freedom to do as you please. I also love that the developers continue to push out weekly content, providing a stable foundation for the game to continue growing and getting better. I have been playing Rust for over two years now and the game has come a long way. Although I may not agree with all of the new things being added, I sure am happy that the devs put this much time into a game where we are only charged once at a max of 20$.
Getting started on rust can be hard, which is what I believe to be one of the main faults with Rust. Solo players tend to have a more difficult time than people who are in groups, especially if they are new to the game. If you fall into this category, I would advise you to learn a lot about Rust -- the types of servers you can join, like solo/duo/trios, and even the combat tag servers to practice your pvp skills, how to build good bases and understand the game mechanics, and lastly how to communicate or make new friends within Rust. Although the Rust community is known for being toxic, there are a lot of people out there that will take in a competent new Rust player.

This game is beautiful! in depth, crafting items and gathering resources does not feel like a chore, when in turn the game rewards you with cool stuff, making your first vehicle and exploring the terrain gathering materials for your base is the first objective, once you have spaceships, your spare oxygen and battery tanks, and a self sustaining powerhouse of a base, its time to go explore!

Not having random alien animals around gives you a peace of mind knowing you can explore unharmed, and it feels like you aren't constantly fighting for your life. all you worry about is your oxygen, and the occasional poisonous plants. My friend made it a challenge to dig a hole to the other side of the planet, ultimately defeated, we found out someone else has done this already, and it takes about 5 hours to complete.. The bugs are quite halarious, I posted a few screenshots of an 'octopus winch' that my friend broke trying to tow a crane. I wasn't angry about this, I was amused and we got a good laugh. 1st of the bugs that really bother me at the moment is when I'm hosting a game, I have about 10-5 frames per second, making it very unplayable, and now that my bases are so large, and there are so many sprites loaded into my world, I have put my world to rest because the lag is unbearable. Everyone that is connected to me is just fine - about 50-60 frames per second, so I would need to create a dedicated server if I was to enjoy my game myself. Please fix hosting asap!
2nd bug that bothers me is the random crashes and inventory errors, I'm patient though, I know these will get ironed out.
3rd is the lack of visual controls, I get extreme vertigo sometimes when I'm on a fast flying world, and motion blur makes me want to vomit. If I could disable the motion blur that would be nice.
4th and last is the terraforming tool, its god awful, I want nice flat surfaces to work with, it's hard to use and some people want to build a mud hut fort, just sayin'
Once this game gets polished some more, maybe new content, online lobbies, permanent save files, I want to boldly say this might be the minecraft killer, even in it's current state, this game has Wow'ed me dozens of times. Well worth it's asking price.

Being a fan of hard games I was excited to see there's a F2P game that focuses on cautiousness rather than a quick triggerfinger. On top of that there aren't any ingame cash transactions so there's no "pay 2 win" either. It seems that the developers keep in touch with the community, which is always nice. According to the shop site there are still lots of content to be added in the future.
The game's graphics aren't the best but being an ascended mod running on the Source engine I guess that's not too big a deal. It also has little to no impact on the gameplay and atmosphere.
The sounds on the other hand are quite nice. You get your typical shooter acustics- footsteps, gun sounds, melee smacks, zombie groans, but the soundtrack is where the game's audio really shines. There are lots of different pieces (in style of soundtracks like The Walking Dead's and State of Decay's) that play according to the current situation in the game.
The game's atmosphere is awesome. In contrast to L4D's cannon fodder zombies, the undead in NMRIH are a true menace. Even a single zed can take down an uncautious player in a few hits and bites. This level of difficulty manages to deliver a constant feeling of threat, something I missed in (the flawed but great) State of Decay, to name a current example (especially thanks to the OP cars in that game). From frantically running around, dodging zombies left and right while trying to fulfill the map's final task, to carefully sneaking around in a mansion or theater, covering each other while scrounging for ammo or medicine- the game manages to present an
atmosphere that's worthy of being called "survival horror" (something that's become rare in today's horror games).
NMRIH tries to abstain from using a HUD. There's no health and stamina meter, so the player has to keep an eye on the character's heartbeat, breathing and vision. The amounts of ammo in your gun are only shown when the player takes the time to actually check the magazine. This might seem a bit overwhelming or confusing at first but it surely adds to the atmosphere. Something that took a bit of getting used to is the handling of the melee weapons. In my first few matches I found myself constantly missing the zeds right in front of me, leaving my char open to be grappled and overwhelmed. There's no real sense of 'depth', if you will, to the melee attacks, which means that the player has to learn about the actual ranges of his weapons. A few hours later I can say that I know my favourite weapons and I know how to use them (without the game actually becoming too easy), although there are some other weapons I don't like to choose because they just suck in my opinion- but that's not an issue of the game itself.
All in all I just can say:
Grab a friend, download this gem, go out there and survive!
Seriously, even if you find yourself not liking this game, at least give it a chance. It'll cost you nothing but a bit of time.
Having a friend to play with and to actually communicate with while playing helps a lot (as always)- because someone you can depend on is always nice to have in case the world ends ;)

Awesome game :D

Story 8.5:
It's not about Arkham nor is it an origin story despite it being a prequel. But it provides an interesting twist to the already familiar Wayne tale. Black Mask placed a $50 million bounty on Batman's head and has hired 8 assassins to kill him. So Butt hole has to stop them from taking him and Gotham down. Plus, it takes place on Christmas Eve.
Visuals 8.5:
Gotham looks pretty, the animations are extremely well choreographed, and character models are detailed. The DirectX 11 Enhanced features look great (everyone leaves footprints everywhere)! But the city is lifeless and lacks the easter eggs that made exploring in the other games so rewarding. There's also some pop-in which is disappointing considering the other games hid it so well. Facial animations could also use work.
Audio 9.5:
The soundtrack sets the mood (especially the main theme!) The voice acting is outstanding as always. The stand out is Troy Baker as the Joker. He's so damn close to Mark Hamill's voice that I couldn't really tell the difference. Kevin Conroy will always be my Batass, but Roger Craig Smith does the teenage Lil Wayne voice exceptionally well.
Gameplay 8:
It almost has the same great combat of the other 3 games. Almost because it has ideas that turn bad after a while. The shock gloves (which are unlocked late in the game) basically rob you of what makes combat interesting. Riot shields and body armor are no match for Bruce Lee. I highly advise you to not use them unless you're in a huge group. Predator encounters are back and they're still great. The only real "innovation" is the evidence scanner which makes you search for clues on how an innocent civillian got killed. Using the left and right mouse buttons (LT and RT or L2 and R2) to rewind and play the crime scene looks great. But really, it's just there to be showy. I also ran into some technical issues during my playthrough. I got stuck in between two spots, some random loading spots, and I ran into a bug that set my default controls as the left mouse button.
Multiplayer 7:
This is the only game in the series to feature online multiplayer and it's a mixed bag. It's actually very clever. The twist is that it's 3 vs. 3...vs. 2. The 2 characters you play as is the dynamic duo and you have to take down the other players with a clumsy version of the single player's combat and stealth. You can strategize with the good ol' "use minor as a distraction for superior to take down the big guy". The other 2 teams are the Joker team and the Bane team and they just function as your standard third-person shooter. Overall, it's okay. But I wouldn't see myself play more than a few matches of it unless my friends really want to.
The Verdict: Batman Arkham Origins lacks the polish and attention to detail that makes Arkham Asylum, City, and Knight outstanding action games and has some trouble finding interesting ideas of its own. But it shares the same great combat, a pretty good "origin" story, and a beautiful, if lifeless, city to make it a good fit for the series.
Overall:

I see a lot of reviews giving leniency to games that are free. I will not be lenient because it is free.
One Troll Army is a wave defense game. You play as a troll defending a goblin village until they can build up their defences. That's the premise. For some reason the goblins also hand over their economical and building plans to the troll, or at least it seems like they do, because you also have to handle that. You gather resources in between waves, and fight during waves. The troll is essentially useless inbetween waves and his only use is to 'provoke' the enemies into starting a wave early.
The game feels like a mobile port, except there is no mobile version that I can find. The UI is poorly designed and the controls not very good. To attack an enemy, you must move the troll to the enemies (this part is entirely reasonable), however, if you leave the troll to attack enemies on his own, he will attack at the rate of his animations. This seems reasonable until you realise that the troll is attacking for too slowly. If you spam clicks the troll will actually attack enemies much faster, though his attack animations no longer sync. This is never really explained in the tutorial it is something you have to realise on your own.
The building and resource management UI is poorly designed at best. Before a wave starts, the enemy gathers around the edge of the map, building up a progress bar; when the bar is filled, the wave begins. When you go to the building menu, it zooms in on the village and the bar is no longer visible. Unintuitively, clicking on the village itself on the map doesn't open any menus. To tell the goblins where they should be working, you click on the worker button which then opens up a large interface where you can assign workers to different tasks with sliders. There is no reason why a smaller size of this element isn't just always visible from the normal map overview, and serves only to make the game feel clunky.
There are apparantly no consequences for losing or surrendering a wave. In fact, you keep any resources you may have gained from the battle and proceed to the NEXT wave with your base fully repaired. With this in mind, there doesn't seem to be much reason to even assign workers to repair the base inbetween waves. Also with this in mind, it seems optimal to let the base tank the enemies as you wallop them from behind.
Overall, One Troll Army is an interesting mix-up that is very poorly executed.

Prelogate is a puzzle game in which you attempt to direct a series of lasers to their designated output, while using logic design in order to be able to compensate for various combinations of inputs and expected outputs. Lasers can be one of three primary colors (red, blue, green), and outputs can be any combination of those outputs, allowing for a number of difficult scenarios.
Lasers are manipulated through the use of mirrors, "mixers" which combine lasers, "splitters" which act as mirrors but also allow the laser through, "diffusers" which take input on every side and send out on every side, "prisms" which take white lasers and split them into the three primary colors, and logical AND, OR IF and XOR gates.
In addition to the general "find a solution" challenge, there are a series of other challenges relating to number of items used, length of lasers, and whether or not you have any "dangling" lasers which don't connect to anything.
The UI can be a little cramped on lower resolutions, but there's a lot of variety in how to approach the problems (fully rotatable, can be tuned into a top-down 2D view, etc). All in all, this is an excellent puzzle game which is well worth the asking price. Think of it as a game which is to logic design the same way Spacechem is to programming. I had to crack out K-maps for the first time since college, and it was delightful.

A casual upgrade-until-you-win game where you start as the landlord (literally the devil) of four apartments, get tenants (monsters) to earn money, spend the money on furnishings to satisfy tenants (and unlock stronger tenant-types), and get tenants who are around to fend off invaders (human heroes). No real plot or story, only a few recurring enemies.
There are four 'phases' of the game, starting with one floor (of four apartments) and expanding until you end up with four floors. There's a marked increase in difficulty (enemy power) each time you expand and build another floor. There are only a certain amount of missions that you can do in each phase so you'll almost always end up grinding for gold on the single repeatable generic mission they give right before an expansion (unless you did enough grinding before for stronger tenants).
The more you spend on room furnishings, the more rent you can charge. However, it feels like most will eventually go into debt if you push it anywhere close to 50%. 'This room rocks' just has to do with their satisfaction gain/loss from furnishings and doesn't mean they can actually pay that amount regularly. The thing about debt is that they get depressed and it feels like the debt can easily snowball or lead to them running away. I couldn't be bothered with micromanaging/optimizing the rent so I kept rent pretty low (enough so I rarely had to bother with debt) and had to gain money through mission grinding and tenants that were better off.
You want your tenants to be strong enough to fight off invaders but it has a messed up (morally) stat upgrade system. Children (once grown up) have better stats than their parents. But the problem is that only 3 characters can stay in a room. There are two main approaches if you want stronger tenants (that are also achievements if you only do one approach). The first way is to keep evicting the parents so that the younger generation can raise their own children (and repeat for many generations). The second is to force the parents to lose battles and perish to open up the space.
It's hard to find an alternative while keeping the game simple. Maybe they could have had it cycle through the family and the parents retire to someplace safer and leave the apartment when the children grow up. Children grow up pretty quickly so I could see the parents age just as quickly. Of course, you do play as the devil, so...
Alternatively, you could skip all that (keeping tenants for a long time very rarely lets them see a job promotion for a little higher pay) and try to get by with unlocking stronger tenants. However, I don't think their base stats are great enough that you can completely ignore the other methods. You'd probably be giving up quality for quantity and be forced to sacrifice several tenants per strong enemy anyway (and be forced a little into the second method).
The general way to play is to get tenants, do missions (invite enemy heroes to fight) for gold, spend gold on furnishings to make tenants happy/indirectly stronger, repeat. If missions are too hard, grind/wait for gold and either wait for your reputation to go up to unlock stronger tenants or wait for tenants to fall in love, have children and do the generational stat-boost.
Worth a look if you like upgrade-until-you-win, grinding games with simple mechanics.

I will be reviewing this game in three categories:
Gameplay - How are the controls? Is the gameplay fun? How about difficulty?
Presentation - Is the sound cool? Does it look nice?
Other - Miscellaneous details
Gameplay: 10/10
The game is an old-school platformer but the twist is that it is INSANELY hard! However, the curve at which the difficulty rises is always smooth and since the controls and physics engine feel on point the whole way through the game you can only blame yourself when you die. And the game gives you infinite lives plus you respawn immediately when you die. The game motivates you to keep trying over and over. And, trust me, it is immensely satisfying when you beat a certain level after so many deaths. Add in different unlockable characters to add variety to how you play and collectables that will make you rip all your hair out and you're good to go.
Presentation: 8/10
The levels look very pretty and the music is definately worth listening to on repeat (you kinda HAVE to when you keep dying all the time...). However, the cutscenes do not have the same polish and graphical appeal the game usually has. The cutscenes definitely tells you that they were made in Flash. It isn't bad enough to make you not want to look at them but I see missed potential.
Other
- Secret characters that are unlockable in this game through warp zones are characters from OTHER games. Subtle    advertisement... I LIKE IT!! :D
- A world in the game, which is called "Teh Internets", allows you make your own levels for others around the world to play. This can only go badly...
- The story goes like this...*takes a deep breath*...Meat Boy loves Bandage Girl, Bandage Girl loves Meat Boy, Dr. Fetus (yes...Fetus...) hates everyone, Hates most notably Meat Boy, Dr. Fetus beats Meat Boy up and kidnaps Bandage Girl, Meat Boy must save her now.
Result: 18/20
If you love difficulty in video games without it ever being anyones fault but yours or love old-school platformers this is definitely for you. Just remember, with death comes knowledge, with knowledge comes courage and with courage comes success.

1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

As evidenced from my play-time (5 hrs at writing), I haven't had any really truly hardcore sessions of this game.  BUT... I heartily recommend it, and I'll explain why.
Long story short, I have a *million* games I'm either playing or would like to play... and I'm largely a RPG man.  So, I just really have never felt compelled to nor been able to put a lot of time into "Mecha Ace".  That said, this game RULES -- and the world and story have ingrained themselves on my mind from the first moment, and have kept me interested no matter what else is going on, or what my "main game" is.  "Mecha Ace" continues to pull me back in, even if only for 15 minutes at a time, and that's what's so great about it.  I could go weeks without touching the game, and I still remember every detail of all my characters, and what's going on in the world.  The writing is just that good -- rich, vivid, and descriptive.
I can safely say that, no matter how long it may take me, I *will* eventually finish this game.  Because WOLF LANCE keeps calling me back (definitely the best lance name, for the record).  Because I want to know about that prototype.  Because I want to run the impie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s off, goddammit!
It's definitely a niche game if ever there was one, with its text-intensive (if rewardingly deep) world "instead" of graphics.  But... if you've read this far into my review .... it's probably up your alley!  If you still have reservations, hell, try and catch it on sale.  Either way, if you ever loved reading sci-fi and/or "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" books as a kid, then you will NOT be disappointed in this game.

Prepare to melt your brain.
If you're not familiar with logic gates you want to make sure that you experiement and fully understand what differentiates them. Example:
IF gate will allow a beam to fire through it, if the gate is struck by a separate beam.
AND gates will fire a beam if both sides of it are hit by the same color (some exceptions with secondary colors)
OR gates will fire a beam if either side or both sides are struck by a separate beam.
XOR (exclusive or) gates will fire only if one side is being struck. So an OR will fire if both sides are being struck, an XOR will not.
Then you have to recreate these gates without them... some of those are particularly rough. Once you get past those 2-3 puzzles the difficulty drops back down to reasonably hard. Other than these quibbles with difficulty curve spike. this game is fantastic and will make your brain feel amazing when you complete puzzles.
Don't let the simplicity or low price tag fool you, this game is serious business. Definitely not for the average puzzle fan, this is some hardcore logic wiring puzzles.  Although at this price if you're even mildly interested you should buy it.

Well to start off, I wanna say some nice things about Unholy Heights.
The art and presentation is great. Very charming characters and pleasant, chirpy music make for a good first impression to the game. It's also a reasonable price point considering how many hours you can get out of it, but with that said I want to list why I'm not that impressed with Unholy Heights.
The actual gameplay is painfully repetitive, tower defense aspect of the game is VERY casual and one-dimensional and the management aspect is extremely boring after you do it for a couple hours. I like the quirkiness of the monsters but not so much that I wanna buy the same few things over and over each time I get a new tenant of that type. Maybe I'm just not that big a fan of simulation/management gameplay but I also think it feels kinda tacked on, as if it were to pad the length or give you something to do during downtime between quests.
As much as I enjoy the presentation of Unholy Heights, I don't find the gameplay engaging or fun in any meaningful way. It's very casual, so if that's all you want and you really like what you see, you'll probably love it. I know there's a fair bit more content than what I got out of it, but nothing that will change how mundane and repetitive each quest is.
I think that's another thing about the "hotel management" aspect of it, you're stuck to this one setting and battles happen almost the exact same way each time. Most great tower defense games have ever-changing levels and progression system/unlocks. Unholy Heights just has "buy this ice-cream a fridge, buy this devil a heater". It wears pretty thin after a while.

Super Meat Boy is a great choice for anyone looking for a platformer with a higher difficulty then other entries in the genre. This game is excelent for offering a fair learning curve and capping at a seriously tough difficulty. In the later stages the difficulty is high enough that a skilled player could take several dozen attempts to progress, but the respawn takes under a second and you're back at the hardest part of the stage before you know it. There are alot of times where elements of a level exist obviously just to test the patience of the player, for example there will often be a tedious section at the beginning of a challenging level forcing you to go through it often to get back to the part of the level where you keep dying, these instances are few, far between and unobtrusive in my honest opinion. The game mechanics are probably the best part, movement is so fluid it's genuinely amazing, the game hinges so heavily on execution and it's hard to blame the game if you stumble. Solid gameplay is what makes the higher difficulty to not seem cheap at any point and it's so rewarding to win. Lastly, the story at face value is cliche, (you have to rescue your girlfriend from a kidnapping villain) but there is an interesting sort of dark humor that makes it unique and then there seems to be a deaper story for those willing to look carefully, just in case that peaks your interest. All in all easily worth playing.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a game that simulates being a truck driver in Europe. The game spans across a good chunk of European countries, ranging from the UK all the way to Italy. The open world is truly massive, and there are tons of roads to be driven and explored. You start of as a hired driver who takes jobs to deliver cargo from one place to another with a truck that is provided by the company offering you the job.
I can easily say that the traffic system in this game is quite well made compared to other open world driving games. For instance, I have come up to many intersections and upon a car or truck pulling up, they will sometimes notice me and stop to let me pull out. The traffic system is very well made and very complex, which helps to make the experience much more realistic. However, it seems as if no matter how fast the speed limit is on the highways, even if I travel on the exact speed limit, every other vehicle always seems to pass me. Am I going to slow or is everyone else allowed to speed?
The outer and inner workings of all the trucks you can drive in this game are made to very realistic standards too. The game isn't exactly on the pretty side in terms of graphics, but there are so many things that you have to pay attention to to ensure your truck stays moving toward its destination.
No, actually. At first glance, one could and would assume that this game only consists of driving back and forth across Europe hauling a trailer to the same destinations across the same highways. Well, the game makes sure that it isn't repetitive at all with a lot of features. One of those features is the fact that the open world availible to the player to drive around in is HUGE. To explore it all would take a long time. The second feature is how many things you have to pay attention to while driving. You will get penalized for running red lights, hitting cars in traffic, and driving over the speed limit. You have to make sure you do not run out of fuel before you reach your destination. You have to pay attention to the map to ensure you don't veer off course. All of those things make every drive different, offering a unique experience every time.
Most of all, this game is relaxing. I personally play this game with a racing wheel and pedals, so driving across Europe is both a realistic, fun, and exciting experience. This game pulls off hauling cargo across Europe like no other game could even attempt to pull off - and for that it is truly one of a kind, and incredible.

I am writing this review primarily for those who have also reviewed it and have claimed that the controls are somehow bad.
The simple fact is that if you are finding the controls difficult, you are trying to play the game wrong. Trying to play this game like a normal platformer, staying on the ground, trying to time your jumps, and ignoring many of Gish's abilties will result in abysmal failure. Instead, your main focus needs to be on your momentum. Knowing the levels is key, so that you can plan out a route before hand which is fluid and smooth. Even a tiny change in your path can drastically change how you move across the terrain and can be the difference between leaping across a huge gap or flopping and losing all your speed. Jumping is everything. Setting yourself up properly for a good jump, even if that requires you to go out of your way or backtrack, can often lead to significantly improved times due to the extra speed you will carry out of it.
That being said, this isn't easy. Even beyond the ~15 hours I have clocked on Steam I had played the demo extensively many years ago. One of the great things you can do when you do get good at it is speedrunning it for fun, as I stated before the gameplay revolves around keeping your speed, and there are also a number of shortcuts, alternate routes, or even somewhat abusable physics bugs which you can use to your advantage.
As for other things, the Edmund McMillen style is nice, though the graphics and interface are clearly dated. There are a number of minor bugs in the physics which can be frustrating until you learn to work around them. Overall I think the uniquness of the gameplay outweighs the flaws.
I'll end with a couple tips for those who want to become better:
-tapping sticky while climbing allows you to climb much faster, it also helps while moving across the ground
-being at high speed and then pressing sticky will cause you to compress down, allowing you to get a good jump in
-holding slippery+heavy while in the tiny tubes will make you go faster through them, and sometimes you can launch out of the exit
-slippery+heavy is optimal for pushing blocks around without getting caught up on them
-while climbing, you can swing around 90 degree corners by tap-releasing sticky and using the arrow keys to shift your weight

A war story, as billed, and a good one.  It could almost as easily have been a WW2-themed tale of the travails of a Panzer Squad.
If you've read other Choice of Games, especially those on mobile, be aware that this is NOT their usual fare.  Most decisions focus on tactical squad command decisions: flank, charge or wait, attack at close or long range, delegate a task or assume command, etc.  These are well-written and implemented sensibly and thoroughly.
However... characters fall into military tropes (enemy ace, commanding officer, wide-eyed rookie) instead of the usual Choice Of soap opera.  Romance is implemented, but almost grudgingly.  The gender of romanceable characters is randomized by default (this can be over-ridden), and as far as I can tell only F/M or M/F romances are allowed.  (I mention this only because most other games by this publisher go out of their way to be inclusive of all preferences when it comes to romance.)
If you enjoy the more serious aspects of the Gundam anime, or regularly read WWII memoirs in between PBEM rounds of a Slitherine wargame, you're sure to find a lot to like this game and it's absolutely worth full price.
If you're looking for something character-driven, emotional or romantic, the company's other works of interactive fiction are probably a better choice.

Great little game!
Premise: The Devil is going to make his move on the world of Man, but first He needs to destroy Earth's champions.  So ... He buys a run-down apartment building and lets monsters move in.  Slowly, the word gets out among the humans and they send progressively stronger efforts to kill Him ... exactly His plan!  For as more humans feed The Devil's unholy tenants with their blood, their power grows and even stronger beasts are drawn to this place.  Ultimately, they will become an unstoppable army for The Devil to march against the world.
Graphics and music are cute and fun.  Lots of different adorable monster types to board in your flophouse.
Gameplay falls into two basic arenas: management and combat.
* Building management is fun.  Buy stuff for your tenants to make them happy, give them exercise equipment to increase their stats, and set the rent wherever you want.  Be warned that a yeti may want different things in his apartment than a vampire, who may want different things than a chicken king.  Also watch your tenants to see if they're going to work and what their jobs are; some may love their rooms but be unable to pay the high rent your hotel deserves.
* Combat is great.  Lots of enemy types with different attacks and defenses, and of course your monster army is the same way.  Try to match your strength to the enemy's weakness by having your tenants jump out of their rooms at the right time, and in the right configuration, to catch the humans at their most vulnerable and stop them from climbing to the Devil's penthouse.
That's pretty much it!  I spent about 11 hours training my legion of the profane, and got to know dozens of wonderful monsters, through good times and bad.  (Lots of bad.)  I enjoyed myself the whole time and look forward to another playthrough sometime soon, or maybe even whenever I want to kill 15 minutes.  This game is great for picking up to do a quest or two, or you can use it to pleasantly pass hours at a time.  Easy to pick up, easy to put down ... if you choose to.

While I wasn't really into this game, I can't in good conscience give it a negative review. Even so, it wasn't what I expected. The graphics are generally pretty engaging, but a lot of the animation feels like "tweened" stuff you might see from Aftereffects animations--which is basically just a jpeg being distorted to simulate motion. It's used in a lot of Popcap games, and it's not exactly the gold standard for animation.
There are a tremendous amount of insta-kills, and many of them are pretty poorly telegraphed. Game mechanics are introduced with no real indication as to how they work. For instance, there's a sequence about halfway through where gravity doesn't apply anymore, but there's no way for a new player to know that without dying several times (I died over 400 times before beating the game). You remember that "Bramble Scramble" level from Donkey Kong Country 2? This is basically that level extended to 10 hours. Unlike Hollow Knight or Cuphead, I felt no sense of accomplishment after beating a difficult sequence. There was only relief that I would never have to play it again.
So if you're a masochist who wants to scream obsenities in an environment with more whimsy than a Skittles commercial from the early 00's, go for it. If you don't have the patience to die hundreds of times in less than a dozen hours, maybe stick to Hollow Knight--which is tough, but far more fair.

One Troll Army is a hidden gem, and the fact it’s free to play makes the experience all the more sweet. Controlling one boss troll with a rather in-depth skill tree, it’s up to you to hold back waves of enemies swarming towards a goblin’s fort. Decimate your foes and help the goblins upgrade their fort in this incredibly addictive indie game.
I’m a bit on the fence when it comes to tower defence games, and when I first saw One Troll Army, it gave me the impression it wouldn’t provide much more than the most basic tower defence game available. How delightful it was to learn I was incredibly wrong!
One Troll Army starts you off with a story as to why this massive troll is protecting a bunch of scrawny goblins. Basically they summon this gargantuan green beast and ask for his help. The troll is then offered gold, armour and new moves in exchange for his protection. But promises of loot and riches isn’t the only reason the troll accepts their request; he also like the cut of their jib!
In One Troll Army, you control the troll with your mouse. Left-clicking makes him move or attack, right-clicking or using the ‘WASD’/arrow keys move the camera around, and middle-clicking lets you zoom in and rotate the camera view.
By clicking on or pressing the number keys at the top of your keyboard to activate abilities and attacks, you are given the upper hand when laying waste to the hordes of varying monsters.
Apart from abilities like jumping, causing massive earthquakes or taunting (which can be learned by the detailed skill tree), you can also help protect the goblin’s fort by upgrading it. Upgrades come at the cost of gold, loot, wood and other resources, which can be harvested by goblin workers.
Similar to games like Starcraft and Warcraft, workers are required to gather these resources. Unlike Warcraft/Starcraft, you cannot select your workers to command them to do different jobs. Instead they are all controlled via a workers section that provides slider bars to control how many workers are assigned to each job. For example, if you’ve just finished taking care of an invasion of buffalos and rhinos, you’ll need to assign a good amount of workers to go out and collect the loot dropped by the enemies. Workers will finish the previous job assigned to them before taking on a new job, so you don’t have to worry about checking to see who’s doing what before making a move.
Building the upgrades required to make the goblin’s fort stronger will need workers to be assigned the job of builders. Builders will head to the building they’re needed at and will take some time to make the upgrades. Progress is measured by a gauge that shows a percentage to indicate how close a job is to completion. Different upgrades come in the form of archer towers, barracks, stronger walls, storage rooms etc. Most levels require you to upgrade everything to a certain level before you can move on to the next.
The first couple of levels you can play introduce you nice and easily to how the game works via mini-missions such as assigning workers to harvest lumber, or hiring orc mercenaries from the tavern. It’s once you get past the first level that the game really starts to test your mettle.
So the entire premise of the game is to protect the goblin’s fort and help it build up to be a mighty stronghold. But all the while this is happening, you are being constantly invaded by different kinds of enemies. From puny rats to mighty buffalo bosses, you’ll find your hands full most of the time.
Enemies gather in groups and rush at the goblin’s base once they’ve finished amassing. To let you know how close to an attack the enemies are at, a bar on the right hand side of the screen slowly fills. However, you can prematurely provoke the enemy to attack by sending the troll at them. This can be a smarter option to choose when you’re still starting off and want to collect as much gold as possible before either the troll dies, or the goblin’s base is destroyed.
When the troll dies you are given the option to surrender. But if the goblin’s base is fortified enough to withstand the wave of remaining enemies, you can leave things as they are and let the goblins take care of themselves. But if you do choose to surrender, you’ll lose any gold or loot that is lying on the ground.
Among enemy waves are bosses. These monsters are stronger than the usual ones and take a lot of hits to bring down. A good tactic for these baddies is the good old hit and run method. Although the hit and run method is quite good in general when dealing with invasions.
Some levels will start you off thinking there’s no way you can take on the strength of the monsters coming at you, but if you use your abilities and hang back until your cooldowns have finished and go back in again, you might very well stand a better chance at defeating them all.
Graphically speaking, One Troll Army has some beautiful environments and character models. The troll himself looks pretty awesome, and you can purchase additional outfits to deck him out. There’s one outfit in particular that I find hilariously awesome and that’s the Donatello TMNT getup.
The background music in One Troll Army is pleasant to listen to, sound effects aren’t annoying and monster/character sounds don’t grate on your nerves.
One Troll Army is a rare find. Something this addictive usually isn’t free. And if it is, you’ll usually have to deal with a tonne of adverts or in-app purchases etc. However, the devs have been very generous in that there are no adverts and there’s only one in-app purchase.
The one qualm I have with the game is that it’s so short. There are only three scenarios to play through, but after you’re done with those, you can participate in an Endless or Survival mode. Endless is as it sounds and Survival makes it so when you die, it’s game over.
The difficulty is just right and I really hope to see more scenarios coming out in the future. Even if they cost a few dollars, it’ll be worth it after the developers lived up to their promise of making the game free if Twitch viewers could beat them at their own game.
All in all, One Troll Army is splendidly done, provides a very decent amount of gameplay and is free! Also, please fork out the $1.99USD and get the Costume Sets DLC if you pick up One Troll Army. The developers deserve it.

A fairly nice interactive fiction game set in a space mecha warfare backdrop. The game is not really about mechas, though--it's about your choices and how you interact with a small set of characters. I really liked that, because it meant you could actually care (or not) about them.
Your choices offer you some semblance of RPG character development--developing your piloting, tactics, willpower or leadership. The choices really matter in the sense that you could see totally different outcomes depending on what you've done. Some characters can die or live depending on what you do. However, the actual acts are always the same (with differences in the details).
The game is short, which I actually quite liked--it felt quite the right length, neither stretched nor cut short. I finished my first run in ~3-4 hours. The 2nd run was done in 1 hour or so, since I only had to read the different scenes where I'd taken different actions.
Overall, I recommend this game if you're a fan of fiction or interactive fiction. It's fun.

This game is amazing.
On my first game, I ended up creating an entire floor of chimerae (Wolfguys, to be exact), and I rushed through missions. However, when I expanded my hotel, and the "Legendary Hero" came rampaging through, I sent out all of my wolfmen to fight him. They died pretty quick. I got upset and restarted the game. This time, I realised Wolfguys sucked, they had a good attack stat, but horrible defense, making them extremley weak. So instead of making the same mistake, I went with Abyssals. All of my little fish dudes (And Dudets) won so much, they became my main monter for defense. However, when I came near the later quests moving towards my third expansion, they lost their power. I was losing fishies left and right, one house lost their baby, another their father. I desperately sent them on a "new monster" mission, hoping for someone to replace them. To my surprise, I found just what I needed. I had found the Boneymusha.
I had saved my fishies! I moved my remaining abyssals to the second floor, and got 5 Boneymushas for my first floor. I gave them some time to find partners and train, then I sent them on their first quest. THEY DOMINATED. With their overall balanced stats, they dealed large amounts of damage while taking only little amounts of it themselves. and so here I am right now, on the third floor, still using Boneymushas. Let's see how much longer they can last.
With my little story done, lets actually review the game.
Gameplay: The gameplay is basically like it states, a hotelmanagement and towerdefense game. You need to manage your hotel to get monsters to rent your rooms, which leads to the part where the monsters renting your rooms can also be called on to beat up some stupid adventurers attempting to steal money from the Devil (The owner of the establishment, aka the player.) This cycle continues, with you being able to recruit more monsters depending on how much they like you, which is determined by a few factors I won't explain. In retaliation to your stronger monsters, quests will become increasingly harder, with better adventurers and better bosses. I'm not quite sure when (or if) the story ends, as I haven't actually found that point yet.
Replayability: To me, this game is quite fun. From personal experience, I've replayed this game 2 times. you can see it as a tiny bit of trial and error, because if you do choose to restart the game, you most likeley know that one monster is more effective than the other, and will yield better results. This also applies to the fact if you're like me, and you restart because all of your monsters die, you know which battles you should and should not fight (Rest in peace, wolfies). However, this game can get quite repetitive quick, so taking a break before each replay helps keep the game fun.
Conclusion: This game is very unique, i've never actually seen anything else like it. I think what led me to buy it was it mixed 2 of my favorite game genres ever- TowerDefense and Management games. This game feels very nice to play, with it's calm music, and creative situations. The game can be a bit challenging at times, when you can't get your monsters to pay rent, or your main fighting force is no longer able to destroy as well as it used to, but you get through. You find new monsters, evict those pesky deadbeats for better monsters, and you kill those heroes!
9/10

I'll admit that I kind of ignored Ori for a while. It was a prominent game made by Microsoft Studios, so I expected to walk into a mostly fun - but safe - game that I would play and forget, which is generally not the kind of game I'm interested in when I'm trying new things. Part of this is because of the anchoring effect based on a few reviews I watched, but looking back a lot of those reviews complained about the game's story. Which means they completely missed the point.
The story does play it safe; it's really nothing special or unique. In fact, if Ori and the Blind Forest were a movie, it'd almost be rant-worthy. But as a video game plot, it serves its purpose. Kuro's intense hatred for the light is no worse than Bowser kidnapping a sentient hat for no reason. It leaves me with questions about the world's lore, but it also leaves me with the impression that it's not supposed to be anything other than simple.
Where Ori shines (no pun intended) is in the platforming. It's absolutely brilliant. It uses its areas which are inaccessible without particular powers as a way to put those new powers to the test. I was consistently surprised at its clever level design but more so at its nearly complete lack of hand-holding in regards to its more puzzling elements. Several areas left me scratching my head wondering "how do I get up there?" and I felt genius when I finally figured it out. At least on the game's hard mode I was provided a delightful challenge and a tight focus on these platforming elements.
There is combat, but it's light. Enemies are more obstacles (and later tools) in your momentum rather than ends unto themselves. Your primary attack initiates from Sein, who is a separate entity from Ori which floats around close to you. Because of this you can attack while moving, clinging to walls, or floating, which allows Ori to focus on positioning as Sein takes out your foe. There are "Bosses" but they function more similar to a miniboss. What would be more traditional "boss" encounters are platforming races which take what you've learned and add a pressing feeling of urgency and speed.
The focus on platforming is supported by the game's checkpoint system. You have the ability to use your energy to create a checkpoint pretty much anywhere where there isn't an active trap or enemy. Functionally this is basically a quicksave if you've played other games that have that feature - but the limitation imposed on it adds needed tension. But the freedom also adds needed relief, as the game gets hard enough to make these quicksaves a godsend. The flow is almost Super Meatboy-like at parts - since when you die you instantly respawn back where you saved. I found myself flinging Ori at the presented problems until I either obtained enough practice to progress, or I found a new solution. Frustrations were quickly mitigated by re-positioning a new savepoint and trying again.
There are some parts where these savepoints are unusable, namely in the platforming races I mentioned. I personally found those parts to be thrilling, but I can see them being jarring for some players. It took me a lot of attempts to get past them especially in the late game - but that only magnified the level of satisfaction I felt on completion.
Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition is a gem. It's a specialized Metroidvania Platformer, and its unrivaled at what it does best. Other games - like Hollow Knight - capture what it does in parts, but if challenging platforming is all you want, look no further. It's a game that deserves to be praised.

HO-LEE♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's got combat to rival even METAL GEAR RISING.
I've been running around for the last year or two trying out so many different kinds of hack and slashes, and the best combat I've found was MGR, which stayed like that for almost two years. DmC has actually beaten that at this point.
The combat feels so responsive, and every single move has a purpose. It's not like Bayonetta or Nier: Automata where you can buy a lot of really cool looking moves but they don't do anything that your regular moves don't already do. In DmC, every single move you get has a very specific purpose. It doesn't feel like I'm just varying between moves at random just to spice things up. I'm actually using them in a very specific order to get the most I can out of them.
Staggering is usually a pretty important mechanic for any hack and slash. In a game like Nier: Automata, there's almost no way to stagger most enemies. In game like MGR, you can stagger certain enemies and only at certain times. In DmC, every single enemy, bar... bar none, actually, now that I think about it, can be staggered in some way. You might have to swap to another weapon real quick or hit them with a certain move, but you can stagger everyone. That, combined with all the moves, leads to a combat system where you're actually zoning enemies around the place, moving them into advantageous positions and using the stagger system to keep them at bay long enough for you to attack another enemy.
The controls are ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥ Even on a controller. LUCKILY, you're able to rebind controllers, which is kinda weird. Not many games do that. I managed to make a pretty functional setup.
The boss battles are just meh. They don't really have much variety beyond "big enemy that hits a platform you're standing on", excluding the last guy (who, by the way, has ABSOLUTELY no reason to even be a boss battle).
Story-wise, it was pretty interesting to sit back halfway through the story and consider what'd happened so far. "Edgy demon guy attacks fake news and destroys a company that sells viagra in a can. Oh, and also demonic fetuses". That's what I LEAST expected when I started playing. All the writing is hilarious if you consider that the game's written in a really stupid and whimsical way. When you finally realize that it's meant to be serious then it makes you wonder just what the ♥♥♥♥ the devs were thinking.
The game's got some problems no doubt, but the combat system definitely isn't one of them, and the game's worth playing just for that alone.

This game has a lot of features and designs that are pretty awesome. It's simple enough that you can get into it pretty quick but complex enough that you can really setup some nice stuff by combining hour-by-hour guard schedules, prisoner regimes, and so on.
The game would probably be one of my favorites except for one problem...
It is buggy as hell and needs constant work arounds to solve problems. You'll be playing a while and all your prisoners are getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, you find out why it's because they're starving to death, you check your kitchen and your cooks have simply stopped cooking. They have the ingredients, the fridges and cookers never lost power, the trays are clean and washed, they just aren't cooking anymore. It just randomly broke at some point. But you fire all the staff and rehire them and they still won't cook, so you dismantle all the cookers, fire all the staff, then replace them both, and finally they begin working again.
Meanwhile a riot broke out from all the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off prisoners and injured some of the prisoners and your guards and they aren't getting healed. So you open up your staff tab to find out where your doctors are and why they aren't doing their jobs, and come to find out they have needles in their hand running in small circles like they can't decide who to heal or what to do and they are just stuck in this perpetual loop of doing nothing unless you click on them and move them or fire them and replace them. But it's only a temporary fix because they'll get stuck again in no time, don't you worry.
Trying to remove a tunnel at the edge of the map? Well too bad. You'll end up with 3 or 4 construction workers who just vibrate around it trying to remove it and being unable to because they're poorly programmed.
Want to stop contraband from being taken back to cells and used to tunnel out? Well, you can't. I have gotten to the point where prisoners have to pass through a literal hallway of 10 metal detectors and 5 guard dogs and they still somehow get tools and weapons through there. How? Who the hell knows. Maybe they lined their asses with lead or something to prevent detection. Worst part is, one of the game features lets you examine where that piece of contraband came from and where it has gone since it was stolen and sometimes a drill or saw or shiv will pass through around 30 metal detectors before finally being discovered. And when you do a shakedown, you find hundreds of items smuggled into the cells through metal detectors and guard dogs. Makes you wonder, what is the point to having either of those things when they barely work at all?
Speaking of tunnels, there's nothing you can do about them. There is no way to prevent them at all without modding the crap out of the game. Guard dogs can sometimes tell you a tunnel exists, though you can't actually "discover" it without successfully searching the specific toilet that it originates from, and even if you search that room there is no certainty you'll discover the tunnel so sometimes it takes multple manual searches. When they ARE discovered, tunnels have to be removed manually. So if you like to play these types of games just to setup a great system for self automation, you aren't going to be able to do that here, because if you leave this game running while you sleep you're going to come back to half your prisoners having escaped through tunnels which still exist and haven't been dealt with, the other half of your prisoners♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off because now you have more prisoners coming in than your prison can support because all those cells with tunnels won't have prisoners assigned to them so they just pile up in holding cells, numerous staff deaths due to rioting which also have to be manually replaced...
Bottom line is, the game is a buggy mess that makes it more frustrating than fun to play after a while. It could also use a bit more automation, or at least ways to automate certain aspects like a number of certain kinds of staff on the payroll at all times so even if one dies he is replaced, etc. I'd be enjoyable enough despite lack of automation if it just worked and wasn't broken, but that isn't the case.
Real shame too because the game has huge potential but I feel like the devs simply don't care about the quality of the game, they're just in it for the money grab and are now working on DLC instead of fixing core problems. These aren't new problems either, I looked up solutions to my doctors being stupid and running in circles instead of healing people problem and it's apparently been a bug in the game for years and they still haven't bothered to fix it.
Everyone should pass on this one and not pay these devs until they decide to fix their game. Then, it'll be worth playing, but right now it just isn't.

For those who enjoy Robotech, Gundam or Mecha Space Opera in general will love the flavor of this game.
In essence a 'choose your own adventure' book, you have a multitude of ways you can let your character evolve in this purely text-based adventure.
Be the honorable and dutyful melee specialist, become a chaingunning berserker who cares nothing but for the thrill of battle or turn into an idealist who would live and die just to protect the civillians. Be a tactical genius with a penchant for sniper rifles and a desire for glory that makes you consider switching sides.
Or in true Gundam fashion, opt to become a madman willing to use a superweapon for your own ideology.
Romance your wingman, your 'operator' or your techie.

The idea of mechanics in Gish are innovative and creative, but the controls and implementation are absolutely horrible. The music gets repetitive, as it remains the same for several levels without changing. Then, there is the awful pseudo metal music with wailing that is completely unbearable. The game does not fit the entire screen even if you selected full screen in the settings. There are additional bonus levels as well as fan made levels that can be downloaded, but there aren't any reasons to bother. Plus, there are the local Versus multiplayer and Collection modes, with multiplayer possibly being where Gish may shine, as two people suffering through the horrible controls, physics, concept, and design might actually be funny. Each level is short but of adequate length because of the horrible controls, mechanics, and the time it actually takes to complete many of them. The story is nearly nonexistent, and the few parts where you are given a bit of background information on the character, it cuts off prematurely, without giving you a real chance of reading it. The level design is not well done, nor is it clever. They rely on the repetition of them for longevity and game play. The more difficult levels will force you to repeat them an extreme amount of times until you are able to get the horrible controls tamed. Once you are able to pass these levels, there is no feeling of accomplishment, and you are not rewarded for any of your success. The artwork is plain and unmemorable, going along with the game's general lack of charm. There is simply nothing interesting to look at while playing. Gish is not a platformer. It is an exercise in frustration and patience. The controls, mechanics, and physics are the worst I've ever experienced in a game. Accomplishing a simple, single jump, is something synonymous with a miracle, or some kind of supernatural phenomenon, if you believe in these sorts of things. The platforming (if you can call it that) is so disastrous, it is comparable to bouncing jello/jelly off of pieces of Legos, and hoping for the best. The controls are outrageous. I have never attempted a game with controls this unreasonable. It's like playing with a severe physical handicap. Gish is nearly unplayable. In the later levels, the only reason why they are able to be completed is almost by pure luck. The skills garnered by playing this game are so unprecise, that they can not be considered actual skills at all. It is a matter of chance that the physics of this train wreck behaved a certain way in order for you to proceed through the levels. I am a veteran of old school platformers, and never have I been so frustrated at the shortcomings of games of the genre before Gish came along. It is an example of game development malpractice and poor implementation of all aspects involved. Gish is quite possibly the worst game I have ever played. There is no excuse for a game of such rotten design to come out in 2004, let alone charge people to play it. Gish is a perfect example of how not to make a game.

Q:When Dijkstra gives node v a permanent label, has it correctly found the shortest path cost from s to v? 
A: Suppose that there is a shorter path to v (shown in red). That (red) path would need to leave the region R via some edge, say, from x to y.  But the portion of the red path from s to y already costs at least as much as the temporary label of y, and the temporary label of y is at least as large as the temporary label of v (because Dijkstra chose to make v 
permanent).  So, the red path from s to v (going through x and y) must cost at least as much as the path from s to v 
through u, which Dijkstra chose.
