I'll be clear with my first paragraph. I LOVE megaman games. If i was told to pick between Megaman and eating, I'd starve playing. I like food, but MEGAMAN!!!
20XX looks like Megaman, plays like it, but I'll be overly critical for a second... It's NOT megaman. Let me explain.
See, you'd think that their sticking to a strict formula of Megaman, and you'd be correct, but there's so much more to 20XX. The creators have their own flavor mixed in, which I'd normally call "a good thing". But the promises of a online co-op (a SELLING point) we're just words, it didn't happen when i tried three times in a 20 minute span. Not to mention if you get beaten (i.e. Die) you have to restart your run from the beginning, and lose any pickups you acquired during said run. One might say "Git good, scrub" except, ill admit it, I am 28yrs old. I have played games like 20XX for a looooooooooooooooooong time. Most games like it have a working SAVE function where you can just retry from your last save point. Got killed by that boss? ok, return to save and try a different approach. Missed an item? go back to save and get it. Going over my recording, I'm ashamed I missed these at first. The run starting area is just a scaled-down redrawing of the reploid base from MegaMan Zero. Skyfortress, a level in game, comes from redesigning a level in Megaman X, where you fight a former ally for going Maverick.
I'll give credit where credit is due. I'm impressed by the art and functionality. Given I played on a keyboard, moving around is smooth, weapons can be keybound, the bosses are hilariously fun to fight. I especially like that the name is a throwback to megaman (20XX was the year in which original Megaman games were set in) I even liked that enemies were not just C&P's from a knock-off site. It felt nice to go back and think on those times, and I even wondered if playing w/ other players would be fun...
Alas, I'm left with only sadness and shame for myself. It's a nice idea, but I don't think they have it figured out yet. Perhaps in hindsight, I should have looked up reviews for this first. The devs of this game seem to have followed the formula a little TOO closely. There are good things, I'll admit. But they have a ways to go before this game stands out.

If you enjoyed the Mega Man X series, you'll feel right at home with this game. 20XX is a game that combines the fast-paced gameplay from the MMX series with roguelike elements to create something truly unique. This game doesn't have much of a plot, but all you have to do is beat all the levels to win. Only catch is, it's harder than it sounds, and you only get one life (unless you play on reverent mode).
The controls are just as crisp and responsive as Mega Man X. You have all the same moves like dashing, jumping, and wall jumping, and you even get to choose between two different characters; Nina, who uses a chargeable buster to take on enemies from a distance (so basically X), and Ace, who uses close quarters combat with a saber (so basically Zero). This offers players two different playstyles to experiment with, although Nina is a better pick for newcomers, since taking out enemies from long range is much safer. While the playstyles are different, they share the same moves to traverse the stage, and not once did I encounter errors with unresponsive or sluggish controls.
While playing, you have the choice of exploring the level, searching for upgrades to give you an upper hand in clearing stages or fighting bosses. These upgrades increase all kinds of stats, such as attack power or run speed. You can also find armor pieces by clearing challenge rooms or tought obstacles to give your character special powers for the remainder of the game, like faster attack charging, the ability to heal by killing enemies, or (my personal favorites) a hover ability or even a double jump. Each time you play, all 10 levels you play through will be randomized, as well as the items you can find in them, creating a new experience every time you start a new run. In each run you can also gather soul chips to spend on upgrades in between runs to even further up your chances of success, such as increasing starting health or giving yourself a chest to open in the beginning of the game. All of these features increase the replayability tremendously, and it help that the game itself is very fun to play each time.
However, as it harkens back to the MMX days, it also shares the difficulty. Don't expect an easy walk in the park, even on reverent, or easy mode. This game will challenge you with precise platforming constantly, requiring well aimed and/or well timed jumps to reach the end. On top of that, you'll also have to blast your way through waves of enemies as you progress, making clearing the stage all the more difficult. While this game is a very fair challenge, this isn't a game for casuals or people who are feint of heart. This, however, may be the only thing that will keep people from giving it a try.
Speaking of which, this game is definitely worth your time. The gameplay itself, mixed with vibrant and good-looking visuals and an awesome retro soundtrack make this game one that anyone I just mentioned (or anyone reading this review) should try. I didn't even mention that it also supports Co-op play so you can play through the game with a friend. If you're a fan of action platformers or the Mega Man X series, you like challenging games, or you're just curious about it, give this game a try. It's a low chance that you'll be dissapointed, as this is one of the most solid action platformers of 2017.

-
It's a Mega Man X-themed Rogue-lite.  If that concept sounds exciting for you, you'll probably like it.
-
The controls are surprisingly,
tight.  I didn't expect it to feel so precise.
-
The music is great and super catchy.  Cityfires did an awesome job capturing the Mega Man feel while not banking completely on any of its motifs.  Aside from the normal boss theme being a bit weak I'd say this is one of the biggest highlights of the game.
-
The items and upgrades are great.  Tons and tons of them, with all kinds of awesome ideas.  The armor sets are all very fun and powerful, especially when you complete a set.  The lab upgrades are great and totally change how you play.
-
Both characters and all their weapons are enjoyable and worth going through the game as.  Even if the game around them could stand to have more to it (see below), the characters themselves and how the upgrades affect them and their weapons differently are enough to make the game feel like it has good replayability.
-
By far the biggest downfall of the game currently is the fact that it sorely lacks variety.  There are only a handful of enemy types, some very rare, and an equally small number of traps and stage gimmicks.  You end up feeling like 90% of the game is made up of various colors of flappy bats and the same turrets, lasers and spinny platforms over and over again in a very finite number of layouts that you will already find overly familiar by your 5th run or so.  It also doesn't help that there are only five level types and you will necessarily run into each of them twice during any full run of the game.
-
Some major game aspects feel superfluous or oddly-handled.  The permanent upgrades are all bought out
too soon, don't feel very impactful at all and are disabled on the highest difficulty anyway.  And speaking of, the difficulty system is mostly pointless; the only difference is that you have some extra lives on easy and the option to turn on challenges on hard.  It'd be best, IMO, for these to both be unlockable perm-upgrade features you can turn on or off during any run of a version of the game with only one difficulty, with options that make the game easier or harder giving less or more of a multiplier to Soul Chips or something.
-
Aside from the main characters (who look great), the character design leaves something to be desired. There was certainly an appreciable attempt, especially for an indie game, but at the end of the day the enemies come off as ultra-generic and the bosses (with one or two exceptions) just feel very visually weak compared to anything from a real Mega Man game, even
a recent facelift.  Kur and Shatterbeak might look alright but then you got Perforator over there looking like a Fisher Price toy.
-
Some of the Achievements are absolutely ludicrous, and I don't even want to attempt them, and this is coming from a guy who got a million percent on Binding of Isaac.  Some of the 'challenge skulls' like the 150% gamespeed one make the game completely unplayable.
Definitely worth it if you think you'd like the concept but could definitely use some work to be truly great or for a potential sequel.  Even some of the cons I listed may be at least somewhat alleviated in the future as the game's still being regularly patched.  Just be ready to see all the game has to offer content-wise sooner than most rogue-lites, far sooner than it takes to unlock everything unfortunately.

After playing this game for 16 hours and finishing the main story, I can finally give my opinion on this game.
I am simply going to explain what I like and do not like about each aspect of the game.
THIS DOES CONTAIN POTENTIAL SPOILERS.
Main Story:
The main story is pretty average for a Batman: Arkham game. That means that overall the story is good just like most of the Batman: Arkham games. There are a couple things that I sort of do not like about the story. At the beginning of the game, it looks like Black Mask is the main villain for the game, but it turns out that Joker is posing as Black Mask and has actually captured the real Black Mask. People do tend to complain about this, probably because the Joker is the main villain in 3 of the Batman games with Scarecrow being the main villain in Arkham Knight. I do however see the reasoning for Joker pretending to be Black Mask. So, the game is called Batman: Arkham Origins, so it is supposed to be telling the origins of the villains, right? They used Black Mask to introduce the Joker to Batman, but I do see how they could have come up with a different way to introduce the Joker to Batman without the Joker being the main villain. I do like how Batman is introduced to different villains in the game, like Anarky for example. I also do like that in this game, you can travel to and from the Batcave. Anyway, the story is pretty average for a Batman: Arkham game and overall, I enjoyed it.
Side Missions:
I might not have much to say about this, but I do have a little bit to say. So, the side missions are actually pretty fun. The side missions I enjoy the most are the Riddlers missions. I like how they came up with their own reasoning for the Riddler to hire men to hide his Datapacks. They are very similar to the Riddler Trophies in the other games. They almost always have a puzzle that you have to complete to get the Datapacks aswell. I also do enjoy gliding around and destroying the Network Relays. The Deadshot side mission was also pretty cool. That's all I have to say about that.
Gadgets:
Most of the gadgets that Batman uses in this game are the same as other games, but they also have some things that I haven't seen before. Like the glue grenade, and the shock gloves. When in combat the shock gloves felt super nice to use when they were activated. I also liked that the shock gloves were able to break an armored thug's defense. It was also a lot of fun to glue people's arms shut with the glue grenade. It was also pretty neat that the game allowed you to use the glue grenade to create a raft in the water.
Evidence Scanner:
I really like the evidence scanner in Batman: Arkham Knight, but in this one, it seemed like they threw in the feature and didn't spend much time on it. Some of the crime scene investigations seem like they are all over the place and they don't seem to tell what exactly happened. The most confusing of all of them was the crime scene of the supposed dead Black Mask. It just seemed a little bit confusing.
Combat:
I don't know what it was, but the combat in this game felt super clunky and it didn't feel the same as the other Batman games that were made by Rocksteady. I found myself, punching at air more often than in the other Batman: Arkham games. That might just me but I felt like something was off, I don't know what it was. It was also super weird that when in combat, Batman would continuously keep his fists raised as he moved around, and he would also walk kinda weird when in combat. I don't remember the other Batman games being like that.
Gliding Mechanics:
It was the same as always. I do like the grapnel accelerator a lot though, and I was very surprised that it was in this game since it came out before Batman: Arkham Knight. I did like that I could make my grapnel accelerator faster in Batman: Arkham Knight but unfortunately that was not a feature in this game (because Arkham Origins came before Arkham Knight).
Glitches:
I have to talk about glitches, sadly, there are a ton of glitches in this game. At one point in a mission, I found 2 of Joker's men running in mid air with guns, trying to find me. I used my grappling hook on both of them, and both of them fell off of the building and they went straight through the roof of a smaller building below. Also, enemies will often be looking for you and all of a sudden freeze in place but still continue their dialogue. This happened a lot in the final fight against Bane. Also when gliding I would often kind of flop up and down like a fish. Yes, like a fish. That's the only way I can describe it. This glitch would also often cause me to glide much slower. There's also a very often and noticeable glitch with Batman's cape. It sometimes spazzes out and occasionally gets in the way of the camera view. I also don't know if this is a glitch, but if it is, it's hilarious. Often times in combat when you punch people, they will go flying up into the air and go about 10 feet above Batman's head. It's really funny but it occasionally ruins a cool fight.
Cutscenes:
The in-game cutscenes are kind of stuttery, I guess. They are sometimes very poorly put together, is what I am trying to say. The characters mouths are also very weird because when they speak their lips don't open wide enough. It bugs me. The cinematic cut scenes are cool but they are noticeably low resolution, and it's annoying. But I have no idea if that's a problem of my own.
So those are my thoughts and opinions on Batman: Arkham Origins. This took me way too long to write, but I just really wanted to get my very detailed review out. Overall, I highly recommend buying this game.

I purchased this game thinking I would get a good 2 hours out of it, and likely get a refund for it due to its early access pre-alpha state. At first glance it looks like yet another space exploration/sandbox game with no goal, and that's what it really is. But here I am over 20 hours in and somehow I just can't get enough of it despite the lack of content. There's just something about how the presentation of the candy-like visual style and core mechanics blend so well together into something addictive and rather hypnotizing. And the music just completes the entire charm and feel-good vibe that make the grind of harvesting resources something oddly satisfying and immensely relaxing. The best part is the experience can be shared with up to 3 other people.
As of this review it is pre-alpha, so don't expect optimization. There are fps issues as well as bugs galore (though sometimes entertaining). The more you build your base, the more your fps gradually decreases. I have a GTX 1080 and i7 6700K, and while a new save starts out at a nice 100fps (with Acer x34 21:9), it can go down to around 30 fps after a few hours of building. Framerate issues seem more prominent during multiplayer sessions, and there are quite a few bugs in which non-hosts can't operate base modules or interact with some objects. Again, it's pre-alpha, so you have to manage your expectations.
Despite all of this, I haven't been deterred from putting more hours into this gem. It's quite a gem with loads of potential, and I am very excited to see where the devs go with it based on community feedback.

One of the better games I've played in 2016, which is saying quite a bit considering this is an early access title with only a few bugs.
The game is very compelling. It wants you to move out into the planet, into the unknown, it pushes you out to do things you wouldn't normally do, interesting planets, vast biomes, and large cave expanses will keep you playing for hours. Alongside this, the game has a very interesting inventory system which was a pleasent surprise considering most have you open a menu and maange your inventory via that, but ASTRONEER has you with an 8 slot backpack, which doesn't seem too difficult to manage until you realize oxygen tanks, and battery packs count as objects to put on the backpack which adds a little more difficulty to your inventory management. The art style is absolutely stunning, the landscapes and planets are extremely beautiful although a seemingly flat texture with little detail can soon have you woahing at a mountain and plain next by eachother. The flora never dims, with different types of trees, cave monsters, and areas to explore on quite a few different choices of planet. This is no "No Man's Sky" though, there are not infinite planets. Sure, there are 4-5, but not billions or endless amounts. The basebuilding in this game works impeccably. I was thoroughly impressed with the interactivity of it all. And last, but certainly not least, the soundtrack. The soundtrack is possibly one of the most calming, and at the same time alarming I have ever personally heard. It's serene, and peaceful. Too peaceful. You expect a creature to come kill you at any moment, but it never comes. When you're walking around outside, looking at landscapes and flora, mountains and plains, you are soothed by the calming music. When you're in a cave, more intense, but still peaceful music plays, keeping you alert, and reminding you that danger lurks near. I've personally only encountered a few bugs, where I died and couldn't pick up my items, which wasn't gamebreaking as it fixed itself just a minute later when the body despawned. The other massive issue right now, seemingly only in multiplayer, is that with a GTX970, I'm running around 20-30 fps. Which, not too impactful on the peaceful gameplay, was a little choppy for my liking, although I've not had any problems with the FPS in singleplayer. The multiplayer, although slightly laggy at times, is fun, especially with a companion on TS or Discord.
TL;DR:
Game is good. Buy game. Support a good dev for once, they only come around once every blue moon.

APB capitalizes on customization, great built-in design tools with lots of stuff to unlock and lots of skimpy non-clothing available for your female avatar's unproportionate♥♥♥♥♥ Even though unsubscribed players are limited in how many design elements they can have on each peice of clothing or each vehicle, it still feels functional and fun. Giving myself a back tattoo that said "♥♥♥♥ASS" for all to see provided me with deep satisfaction.
Although the matchmaking and missions are fluid, innovative and fun, the sub-par combat and driving mechanics don't provide a sturdy foundation for all of this glorious and limitless customization to stand on, and it is reflected by its ever-crumbling playerbase.
Play long enough and your "threat" level increases, putting you at a different matchmaking level to keep games fair and balanced, while at the same time isolating you from an exponentially larger part of the player pool with each rise in threat level. Before long I had reached the highest threat level, and was rewarded with a whopping 2 possible opponents that were currently online to play against. Nice. The most proposed solutions to lowering your threat level to again have fun with the game are to "lose on purpose" or "create a new character"... What? Seriously?
I'd like to see customization like this in the next stab at an online GTA-style open world game. APB definitely layed the groundwork for a matchmaking method that keeps everyone in the same world while simultaneously pitting groups of players against eachother. You'll often see fights between other teams going on right next to you.
Cool game overall, although the most fun to be had is in the customization menus and not in playing the game itself.

Gish comes from 2004, a time when every single game had some physics gimmick (Half-Life 2 was released around that time, too). Gish implements a nice physics engine in a 2d game, but then DESTROYS any chance of being a good game due to one very stupid decision: limited lives. It isn't a problem in the first or second world, but then there's a LOT of instant-deaths in the third (the "fall in the lava and die again" world). You don't combine these two things, instant-deaths and limited lives. It's not "challenging"; it just turns boring to do levels 3-1, 3-2, 3-3, 3-4 and then die on 3-5 because of a tiny mistake that throws you back to 3-1. Games like VVVVVV work because, even if you die a lot, you don't have to do again previous levels - even if it is hard as balls, it never becomes boring.
And the worst thing is: since Gish is a physics based game, your movement can't be very precise (as in VVVVVV), so you are prone to more mistakes and stupid deaths.
Squishy fun!

Too bad you can't have a 'neutral' review here, as my impressions are very mixed.
This game has huge potential - but mostly poor realization. Still, it is indeed a point-and-click adventure game that can actually be fun.
* Nice characters. I really liked Aaron - his sense of humor is exceptionally witty. And the way the heroes always quarrel between themselves - well, you can tell by that the ending would be wedding-style.
* Achievements based on mostly optional actions and 1000 Sierra-style points you can get. However, I would not get them all without a walkthrough :)
* Quite good length for such a price - there are more expensive adventures in Steam that last much less.
* The story is too loose. You get a lot of 'deus ex machina' story turns without much logic or explanation. Yes, there is a good message as for the current sorry state of the humanity, but it is hidden amongst some vague aliens and conspiracy theories.
* The graphics could be much better. Most locations are too dark and simplistic.
* Puzzles sometimes lack logic. And what is more - the good idea of having two characters with different 'superpowers' under our control is poorly realized. There are maybe only two puzzles that require coordination (with the heroes just standing on two buttons) - and we never get to use their superpowers by our own (only automatically and in predefined places).
Sorry, but 'The Apotheosis Project' is not the game it could be if all its potentials were realized. Still, I would say it is a decent game that could be recommended to adventure fans.

Penelope and Aaron are secret agents of Pandora Global Corp, a CIA-like organisation. What they don't know, is that they are used as guinea pigs in an scientific experiment in which their DNA has been changed. They are send on a mission to obtain a certain relic. Everything goes wrong, they are captured and their special powers are released. Aaron is able to tranport them to another dimension. They have to get back, unravel the conspiracy and put the responsible ones to justice.
As you guessed by the above, The Apotheosis Project is a science fiction spy adventure game. The story is well told in small doses throughout the game. You can easyly identify yourself with Aaron en Penelope as they discover the harsh truth about the people they trusted and worked for. In spite of that, they never lose their sense of humor and interest in one another as is clearly shown in the well written dialogs.
The game is fully voiced and the actors do the best they can to act naturally. At first the voice of Pandorra seems strange and irritating, but in the end you fully understand why she talks the way she does. The voices of Aaron and Penelope are well performed. I don't know about the English gram (as I'm Dutch), but everything they said was clear and understandable. Background music is good and underlines the overall atmosphere of the game.
The Apotheosis Project is an indie game, made without a big budget and expensive software. Taking that in consideration, the graphics are not bad at all. The main characters move smooth and the cut scenes fit nicely. Sure, the backgrounds are dark, but then the alternative world isn't bright and shiny, so it fits to the atmosphere. And darkish or not, they are well made and full of details.
Those details are part of the fun. Yes, that means pixelhunting. After all, the agents are in a strange world and have to solve pratical problems like opening a door or convincing people to give information. So they look around for objects which could be usefull one way or another, now or in the future. They find a lot of junk, but even that will turn out to be part of the game. Try to get 1000 points and you know why.
Aaron and Penelope are both playable characters. You can switch any time from one to another. They have there own inventories, but you can always give any object personally to the other, which is even needed in a specific place.
Controls and puzzles are not complex. Just click and think logically. Use your eyes and wits in solving problems and deceiving people and you will have a great time.
The Apotheosis Project is certainly a game a would recommend!

Full Review:
INTRO:
Penelope Barker and Aaron S. Reid are agents of Pandora Global Corp., an organization that works in parallel with the CIA. What Penelope and Aaron do not know is that they are also guinea pigs in a secret experiment - the Apotheosis Project - where scientist has tampered with the human DNA. Subjects receive special powers, which are surreptitiously suppressed by antibodies, but can be activated by means of a code word.
Penelope and Aaron are sent on a mission by Pandora Parlow, the head of the organization, to get a relic. When they meet their contact person all goes wrong and they end up being captured. But, without the antibodies, their special powers beginning to awaken. Penelope discovers that she can raise hazardous energy with her hands and Aaron turns out to be able to trigger changes in time and space.
The two end up in a strange world, inhabited by aliens and robots. They discover the secrets behind the Apotheosis Project and its consequences for the entire world.
STORY & PLAYABLE CHARACTERS:
The story is told well dosed. Along with the main characters you'll discover more and more of the plot and the hidden agenda of Pandora. Aaron and Penelope remain well in their character role and handle the problems in their own way, whereby Aaron often tries to lighten up a difficult situation with some light humour. The two clearly like each other, despite their small humorous altercations.
They solve the problems they encounter during their adventure together or apart. It is important to let both Aaron and Penelope look at items and have them both to talk to other characters in the game. After all, they both have their own way of understanding, character and qualities. Moreover, you can be earning points along, up to a total of one thousand. It pays to reach that number and it also makes you more mindful of the environment and the story during the game, which benefits the fun of playing this adventure.
GAMEPLAY:
The puzzles are logically interwoven into the story. If you want you can obtain helpful information and sometimes even hints during the game. Useful items can be obtained in exchange for another object or by a service on return. While solving situations/puzzles you do need to use your ingenuity.
During your quest you will find many items you can pick up and place in your inventory and use in certain situations, but some of these items are not needed and only serve to confuse a.k.a. red herrings. While playing you're always looking for opportunities to use all of these items and that is a nice addition for the true adventurer.
You can, while playing, freely switch between Aaron and Penelope, through a portrait of both in the inventory bar. Sometimes it is even necessary, as Penelope for example encounters a problem that can only be solved by Aaron or vise versa.
Your inventory folds out if you hoover your mouse-pointer to the bottom of your screen, very pleasant and effective. Naturally, each character has its own inventory, but items are interchangeable between Penelope and Aaron. The object gets stored in the inventory of the character that receives the object.
With a mouse click, the two playable characters walk freely and smoothly through the game scene.
GRAPHICS:
The in-game environment looks nice. The backgrounds are very detailed and matches the atmosphere and story. A thrift shop is stuffed really messy with silly things and you see the flashing reflection of the neon advertisings while in a rainy street. An office is sleek equipped and on the platform of the subway you see rubbish and graffiti. When in Infraworld, the colours are sober and while in a modern residential tower, the colours are tight and bright. All together this creates a nice, convincing impression.
Many scenes contain one or two small background animations. The transitions between the game-chapters are shown as a close-up of a three-piece comic and match perfectly with the characters and surroundings.
SOUND:
The game scenes contain perfectly fitting background music and certain situations are supported with nice sound effects.
VOICE ACTING:
The voice acting is top-notch, done by professional voice actors/actresses.
STEAM ACHIEVEMENTS:
In total there are 35 steam achievements to collect, varying from easy to hard.
In total, the game offers 35 steam achievements, obtainable in a nice mix from easy to tough.
CONFIGURABILITY:
The game is configurable using winsetup.exe:
1. Right-mousebutton-click on the installed 'The Apotheosis Project'  title in your game library,
2. Select ' Properties'
3. Select ' Browse local files'
4. Right-mousebutton-click on the file winsetup.exe and select 'Run as administrator' / Double-click the file 'winsetup.exe'
5. Set/select/change whatever needed
6. Click button 'Save'
7. Run game via Steam
Some available and possible useful settings:
* Set 'full screen' or 'windowed mode',
* Select Graphics Driver (Direct Draw or Direct3D 9)
* Select Grahics Filter,
* Select Scaling,
* Select Digital sound device & MIDI device,
* Enable/disable 'Black Borders' (Side, Top & Bottom)
SUMMARY:
The Apotheosis Project is a 2D retro indie adventure that comes with hi-res graphics, full voice acting, two playable characters, innovative and varied puzzles in a compelling science fiction story.
So, should I by this game:
If you are in to retro 2D adventure games with modern graphics and a good story/plot:
Yes, this game is for sure worth playing and worth the money. Definitely recommended.

The Apotheosis Project is a classic-style point and click adventure game about people who work for some kind of spy organization maybe and sort of have superpowers. The story is overall pretty weak and nonsensical. It's never really clear what the characters' actual job is and the superpower plot is kind of pointless, and the whole thing is drawn together into an incredibly bizarre and unsatisfying ending (full disclosure I got about 840 points so maybe the 1000 points ending is better). The dialogue tries really hard to be clever and funny but usually fails.
The art is serviceable, nothing special but fine for the price range. However the backgrounds can be pretty murky and with the amount of pixel hunting that you're going to have to do that might get irritating quickly. The voice acting is so bad that I'm pretty sure that the game would have been better off un-voiced. Every actor pronounces certain words (particularly "apotheosis" but also a few others) differently from one another, or sometimes the same actor will pronounce a word differently from scene to scene. The VA for Pandora speaks like she was being paid by the hour and is trying to draw the recording session out as long as possible.
In that "modern people making a classic point & click" way, there is a LOT of pixel hunting, and some really nonsensical puzzles (this is a wee spoiler but there is a scene where you convince a character to purchase something from you that they didn't want to purchase previously because it "looks low quality" by peeling a "high quality" sticker off a stripper pole and sticking it to the item). Most of the time there is no real need for the two characters to both be present, and I think the game could have expanded a lot on puzzles that required both characters to complete. As it is, there's this weird sort of artificial division of labor so that both characters are required, so one character is too weak to open a drawer, can't follow simple instructions to operate  a machine and refuses to talk to like half of the characters because they're "too scary" and the other character is like "I am too busy to read what's written on this paper".
At this price point the game was okay (like it wasn't actively bad really) but I can't muster up the interest to replay it and try to get more points so I can't really recommend it.

I love this game but it can be a bit of a mixed bag. So this is gonna be a looong one as I break down my review. But I'll put in a TLDR at the start here for those who want a quick one.
TLDR : If you really enjoyed Megaman/Megaman X/Megaman Zero, don't mind the story and artstyle AND
, you'll be in for a good time
:
What story?
:
Admittedly, the artstyle doesn't really match up to Megaman X's (X4-X6) anime look. I can't say I like the artstyle nor dislike it. It's just decent and I'll leave it at that. I'm alright with Nina and Ace's (X and Zero) design at least. The bosses' appearance just don't feel intimidating enough for me (Rollster is a hamster riding a buzzsaw-motorcycle thing).
:
NOW THIS is where the game REALLY shines. Both Nina and Ace are basically X and Zero respectively and have very similar gameplay to them.
Nina is basically X. She has an arm cannon and can charge up like X's X-Buster. Similarly, she can't shoot diagonal nor up or down unless you get some of her alternate weapons. To be honest, unlike Ace, she's a bit of a copy paste from X. Nothing new except for having different busters. Her default weapon feels really underpowered unlike Ace's. Her alternate weapons on the other hand are really strong. But to those who mained X back in the Megaman X games, you'll feel right at home.
Ace is Megaman X series' Zero, but with a MUCH more polished gameplay and easily my favourite in this game. Unlike Nina who's just a copy paste of X, Ace is actually an improvement of Zero's gameplay from the X series. This is because
. All of his attacks have the same combo and doing any actions won't interrupt his swings. In other words, he's a very mobile Zero with his saber and feels much faster paced. He has his own alternate weapons as well, like Nina. If you mained Zero, you'll love this guy. But no more Zero's dash-slash exploit for those who are familiar with it.
Both characters share the same powers you get from the bosses. Too bad that Ace doesn't get any of those saber skills Zero can get. But to give the game credit, each of the powers feel different and have their own uses. All the powers can easily compliment your primary weapons in doing things it can't. And the ability to use up to 3 at once makes it even better. If not for the enemies, they also play a role in the environment like removing traps, stopping disappearing platforms, destroying vending machines to get free items, etc. The devs really put a lot of thought into the powers you get from the bosses and making them balanced so that that none would feel useless. This is something not even the Megaman X games fully do (Tell me who the heck uses Dual Cyclone in Megaman X4 aside from on Magma Dragoon? Or even Ground Fire in Megaman X5.). Unless we're talking about Zero's saber skills, I even personally think this game does a better job at balancing the boss powers. Only downside is you can't charge them(except for one power) like the X series. But I suppose it's left out for the sake of balance. There is an armor set you can get to boost their effects but it's not always reliable to obtain due to the RNG on each run.
As for the bosses, most of them are fairly challenging. Some even fill the whole screen with bullets for you to dodge. As the X games, this gets easier when you have the boss' weakness. Can't say much on the boss fights, but some of the bosses have the same problem as the X series which is when you have the boss' weakness, the whole fight becomes a cakewalk as you stunlock the boss. At the very least this is only for some of the bosses. Other bosses don't get staggered or only take their 'weakness damage' if you use the weapon at the right time, which is a pretty neat design. Only wished it was done for all of them.
Excluding the final 2, there are 8 main bosses like usual Megaman X games, but 2 bosses each share the same stage. Meaning there are only 4 stages and you go through each twice to reach the final 2. Due to this, the levels can easily feel repetitive with the same traps and enemies. The enemy difficulty, pickups, boss attacks, and level length increases steadily as you work your way through each randomly-generated stages. Your boss is random and at the end of each stage, you get to pick between 3 of the next bosses you want to face. Each stages have their own set enemies excluding the final 2 stages which mixes up enemies from the other 4 stages.
As the game is a roguelike, you play through the game in an arcade style from start to finish while grabbing randomly generated power ups as you go, including armor parts which are called Core Augments in this game. If you die, you start back at your base at the very beginning. There are some permanent powerups that you can unlock for the start of, or for you to find in future runs through Soul Chips, which you retain at the end of a run(which is if you die or complete the game). The roguelike element is a REALLY mixed thing as not everyone would be a fan of it. On one hand, it can get repetitive with the same enemies, environment, and traps, which is worsened by there being only 4 different stages. But at the same time it eliminates the repetitiveness of the encounter by randomising enemies, the layout, and powerups you find. Although due to this, the enemies and traps can wind up in downright annoying locations that will be really diffcult for you to deal with unless you have a weapon or power that can deal with it.
On the hardest difficulty, Defiant, you can activate skulls which are essentially diffculty modifiers. Good if you wanna do things like adding more enemies, make levels last longer, make enemies have more health, have spikes kill you in one hit, etc. This is a really neat addition. Only wished there were more skulls like having only a specific enemy type spawn or something like so. Also on this difficulty, any permanent upgrades you purchase for the start of runs are disabled, but the ones you unlock for you to find on future runs aren't. This shouldn't be a problem once you get used to the game.
Game is pretty difficult overall, but perhaps after 10+ runs of raging and tough love like Dark Souls, you'll eventually beat the game. It's harder than some of the X games I've played, but probably not as hard as the Megaman Zero series I played.

Why the chapter is not included with the Steam version or wasn't included (was removed) in the original game is beyond me. The HO scenes are well detailed, fairly difficult, but the developer thought it was a good idea to include a strong light source in "every" scene, causing lens flare, which can be difficult on the eyes, and then thought it would be a good idea to hide objects within that flare forcing you to stare at the light source to try and find them. The game is of average length for a HOG but ends abruptly with a "to be continued," and there's no sign of a sequel yet, so you don't even get a conclusion to the story.

Gameplay:...........................5 Stars
Controls:..............................5 Stars
World Map:..........................3 Stars
Character Development:......4 Stars
Level Design:.......................4 Stars
Story:...................................5 Stars
Graphics:..............................5 Stars
Sounds:................................5 Stars
---
Final Score: 8.8
Gameplay: 5 Stars.
Your true enemy is the area itself, with lots of hard obstacles. You get many skills, most of which are made for mobility. The monsters are there to deal some damage but, most importantly, to help you get to places. Every area is unique and has it's mechanics, and when you die, you immediately respawn at the last save point. No animation played, no time lost, it's all action. It doesn't breaks your focus.
Controls: 5 Stars.
They play very smoothly. Everything is precise and you don't have much difficulty doing the moves. Controling the character feels great, you won't die because you couldn't execute a move correctly or because you thought you could jump through that obstacle. I mean, sometimes you will miss a move, the game is indeed challenging.
World Map: 3 Stars.
That's very important for a metroidvania. Unfortunately, this one is a bit small. It has only three boss fights and very little enemies variety. Its pretty much the same thing except for the mechanics of each area. It doesn't give you reasons to go back to previous areas, so the only real way is forward. It also has little secrets, and nothing game changing. It still delivers a pretty good experience.
Level Design: 4 Stars.
They give you the skills and teach you a lot with each area. The game is quite challenging, and here is quite the only critique: difficulty spikes. There are weird stupid difficult things in this game, so it ends up being 90% fun and 10% frustrating. Luckily, dying makes you lose close to no time or focus at all, which mitigates most of the frustration you would get. In fact, that is one of the reasons the game is challenging yet not stupid at the 90% fun part of the game: you die a lot and almost doesn't notice, so even the fun part is in truth challenging and difficult.
Character Development: 4 Stars.
You get skills (active moves and attacks) as you progress and explore the game, you get experience for exploring and for killing monsters, which gives you ability points to progress an ability tree (passive bonuses). I should say this tree does not have branches, so it shouldn't really be called a tree in this case. You rise your maximum hp and mp by exploring, kinda like finding heart containers in Zelda. And that's it. No equipment, no consumables, no money, no attack or defense variables... It's all very simplistic, but you still feel more powerful as the game progresses.
Story: 5 Stars.
It's not the story itself, but the story telling alone that deserves those 5 Stars. The story is simple, like some sort of childhood fable. Kinda cliche, very cute and not too deep, but it's told through gameplay in a very beautiful and emotional way. You walk through the places and have glimpses of the things that happened, with no cutscenes or long dialogues interrupting your game. It's beautiful and very touching.
Graphics: 5 Stars.
This is how you use an ultra powerful graphics card and gaming rig: by making this eye-melting mind-blowing beauty. Visually, it's a piece of art. What is most incredible is that it doesn't overload the screen with unimportant stuff. You can always tell where you are (at the center of the screen) and can easily spot whatever you need to.
Sounds: 5 Stars.
It has beautiful sound effects, and even more brilliant background music. It's memorable and goes very well with the graphics. The visuals and the sounds is what makes that game stand out. You know, some metroidvanias are known for their beautiful music and scenarios, like Castlevania, Child of Light, Aquaria and others. Ori and the Blind Forest is not behind them by any means.

It's really hard to view this game as anything but derivative from it's inspirational sources, on every single level.
While derivation is never an inherent reason for criticism, the absolute refusal to iterate, and the inability to execute well makes Ori and the Blind Forest really feel like a project that "could've been" something much more.
Ori and the Blind Forest is plagued with an onslaught of minor conveyance issues ranging from obtuse puzzle solutions to difficulty comprehending basic gameplay. Everything is so difficult to see in this game. The bright colors of this game coupled with a myriad of poor choices lead to a lot of situations of "Oops I couldnt see the bright purple projectile in the bright purple background" , Bright white character getting lost amongst bright snow, and lava projectiles being wildly difficult to see amongst identical bright orange backgrounds. Combat sections in Ori are an absolute chore hugely in part to this. The damage taken unfairly in these sections also continues to hamper the platforming experience, turning decently balanced segments into cruel one-hit trials.
Mechanically, it feels that everything in Ori is an adherance to genre notions, for the worse. Very few of the learned skills have a sincere impact on the game, with the exception of the Bash, which is the absolute best feature of Ori as it creates a very fun, intuitive means of both combat and travel. Otherwise there is a "kitchen sink" methodology in which you are frequently blasted with a myriad of relatively meaningless new abilities. If you have ever played an adventure platformer before, there is nothing really of note here except for the bash.
Artistically, Ori and the Blind Forest is a pretty frustrating experience. Artistic sentiments are very surface level, with the story preying heavily on insincere notions of "wouldn't it be sad if your family members died?". While again, this alone is not a problem, the lack of sincerity in these sentiments trivializes emotional beats into boring contrivances that exist solely to forward a paper thin plot. Almost every "emotional" moment of Ori and the Blind Forest seems almost attuned to this, as it doesn't even trust it's players to remember crucial character moments. Any semblance of taste in a scene is immediately destroyed by flashbacks or character text directly explaining emotional sentiments, for fear of it's audience not understanding basic story telling. The music is no aid to these situations, as every one of these scenes is additionally plastered with stock sad music.
The music in Ori is another iteration of it's uninspired nature. No meaningful motif is ever employed, and to be quite frank I cannot recall a single song from the entire OST, despite having completed the game. The entire soundtrack is reducible to an uninspired "Ethnic" flavored cinematic sound. Not a single interesting choice of instrumentation, performance, or composition is present here.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a game that is angering at it's worst, and offensively bland at it's best. It is solely a derivative product of the greats that it tries to copy, but it only receives the failings of said greats in return. As someone hoping to love this title, I cannot feel anything but disappointment with this title.

I actually rather liked this game. The inventory and craft aspects of the game were well done. For me it's all about story.  Iplay a TON of HOGs and if it sucks me in, to the point of 'marathon'ing it, so to speak, it's a good game. This was one of those. Unfortunately it ends much sooner than I'd like, and hints at a continuation that I'm not sure is ever coming. That's the only downside of this game for me.

Based on my experience, when a HOG comes out from Gogii Games, we are to expect either a real treat, close in standard to Artifex Mundi, or a complete waste of time that would make you pull your hair out with frustration. For
, I sincerely cannot decide what to say. It is neither of our expected choices. There are good things and bad things to say about this game, but they kinda even each other out at the end.
The curtain opens up to 1930s New Orleans, Louisiana. After witnessing a séance between a Voodoo priestess named Marie Leveau and her young apprentice Lillian, it takes a brief moment for us to understand what's going on. It seems that Marie Leveau and many other residents of New Orleans fell victim to a curse, and all hope rests on Lillian's frail shoulders to solve the mystery, save residents and confront the responsible villain. So, as an apprentice Voodoo practitioner, Lillian ventures out to do all that is expected from her.
The setting and background artwork are really interesting. Anecdotes specific to New Orleans are scattered all around and Haitian Voodoo culture is a great pick to make a HOG game out of. Character animations, on the other hand, are little more than illustrated blocks, moving as broken puppets would do. There is no lip movement to match voice recording at all. Characters just stay around to look surprised and mysterious while a mediocre voice acting follows during cinematics. Game menu can only be reached from the map, and the map itself is rather unnecessary since it only shows acts of the game, rather than usable places in an act.
There is little to no puzzle sequences: 2-3 matching games, a pipe game and 2 rotation games. There is no challenge to neither of them. That's about it. HOG scenes are pretty imbalanced too - 12 or so obvious items and 3 impossible even in a million years items - , with a favoritism for British vocabulary, rather than American. There is no cookie jar, yet there is a biscuit box. So be warned. One adventure element that I've come to like is Lillian's Grimoire: we collect recipes for spells and voodoo dolls that we have to gather items for, and combine them to cast a spell to progress. The Grimoire also contains some lore about Haitian Loa spirits like Maman Brigitte, Shango, Ogoun and Legba... and it all comes to an end within 2 hours. That's it.
One fair warning: the ending is no ending at all. The game stops at a bad cliffhanger and declares "to be continued". Sadly, there has never been a sequel, and the development team parted its ways with Gogii Games. So there is little to no hope for Lillian's story to continue. There are tons of unanswered questions and irrelevant sub stories that get away without closure. As a side note, one whole act of the game is completely cut out in this version - The Hotel. The game progresses right down to the Bank after the Bar, and leaves already frustrating storyline with more holes. If you'd prefer the complete version, go to Big Fish Games to give this game a try.
These are all common perils to HOG genre, I know. But it seems I've become picky after playing Artifex Mundi games. Considering the story has huge continuation problems and the Steam version is missing a whole part of the game, I'll end up giving this game a downvote when I think of many elaborately developed HOGs with complete stories out there. Maybe I'll update my review in the future... come to think of it, maybe not.

Despite the mixed reviews, I decided to pick this one up since the story looked interesting.  I'm very glad I did!
Although the basic interface and gameplay is the same as most hidden object games, I found the Grimoire + Mortar system for recipes/potions and the magic system to be a refreshing change from the usual fare.  I only wish there had been more of it.
The game is what I consider "Artifex Mundi style" in that it's a combination of hidden object and point-and-click, although this one heavier on the hidden object scenes and lighter on minigames than some.  The non-HO gameplay generally consists of gathering ingredients for various spells and potions to save people.
Hidden object scenes (and the rest of the visuals, for that matter) are well done.  They are challenging in a good way, not a "what the hell pixel do I need to click to pick this damn thing up" way.  I did notice a sort of British leaning in the vocabulary which might throw off some U.S. players (i.e. a biscuit jar instead of a cookie jar), but the places where that might be confusing are really pretty few.
The few cutscenes with animation are a little clunky but it doesn't detract in any way from the game itself.
Sound is pretty standard for a game of this type; there is some minimal voiceover work in the beginning but the game is generally text dialogue (which is sometimes a blessing when you compare to some games!).
The game isn't terribly long, 2-3 hours for a full playthrough if you don't stumble on any of the puzzles (which you shouldn't, it's not that difficult overall).  The $4.99 price tag is about the normal price for a game of this length, and it's even better if you can get it on sale as I did recently.
My ONLY complaint is that it ends on a cliffhanger and as the original release was quite some time ago, I have no idea if the second part was ever made or ever will be made (I didn't see it on Steam).  So you have to be okay with not having story resolution.  I think the game is good enough to overcome that minor annoyance but I know it would drive some people batshit crazy.  Just something to keep in mind.

Astroneer is a very relaxing space/planet survival game.
It's in super early access (pre alpha IIRC) right now, but the base game looks very nice, and plays well (for a while, check below for more info).  The devs are frequently squashing bugs, and bringing out updates, so at the moment the game's not the typical "early access but maybe we'll release maybe not".
With the current state it's in (as of this review), you can get upwards of 10 hours out of it, before you either run out of things to do, or the game decides to drop your FPS because of lack of optimization (it's only a couple of weeks into its current stage, so I'm giving it the benefit of the doubt) and you have to start again.
Thankfully the planets are all randomly generated, so one time you might spawn near lots of resin, and no compound, then the 2nd time it'll be the opposite.
The only downside for this game (apart from the optimization) would be the price point.  I don't think I ever feel comfortable paying $20USD ($30AUD+) for an early access game.  $10USD should be the max price, depending on where it's at in development.
If you can overlook that, then you'll definitely enjoy the game, I'm excited to see where it's going to go in the future, as it's got a great concept, and a great core as-is.

I purchased this game thinking I would get a good 2 hours out of it, and likely get a refund for it due to its early access pre-alpha state. At first glance it looks like yet another space exploration/sandbox game with no goal, and that's what it really is. But here I am over 20 hours in and somehow I just can't get enough of it despite the lack of content. There's just something about how the presentation of the candy-like visual style and core mechanics blend so well together into something addictive and rather hypnotizing. And the music just completes the entire charm and feel-good vibe that make the grind of harvesting resources something oddly satisfying and immensely relaxing. The best part is the experience can be shared with up to 3 other people.
As of this review it is pre-alpha, so don't expect optimization. There are fps issues as well as bugs galore (though sometimes entertaining). The more you build your base, the more your fps gradually decreases. I have a GTX 1080 and i7 6700K, and while a new save starts out at a nice 100fps (with Acer x34 21:9), it can go down to around 30 fps after a few hours of building. Framerate issues seem more prominent during multiplayer sessions, and there are quite a few bugs in which non-hosts can't operate base modules or interact with some objects. Again, it's pre-alpha, so you have to manage your expectations.
Despite all of this, I haven't been deterred from putting more hours into this gem. It's quite a gem with loads of potential, and I am very excited to see where the devs go with it based on community feedback.

One of the better games I've played in 2016, which is saying quite a bit considering this is an early access title with only a few bugs.
The game is very compelling. It wants you to move out into the planet, into the unknown, it pushes you out to do things you wouldn't normally do, interesting planets, vast biomes, and large cave expanses will keep you playing for hours. Alongside this, the game has a very interesting inventory system which was a pleasent surprise considering most have you open a menu and maange your inventory via that, but ASTRONEER has you with an 8 slot backpack, which doesn't seem too difficult to manage until you realize oxygen tanks, and battery packs count as objects to put on the backpack which adds a little more difficulty to your inventory management. The art style is absolutely stunning, the landscapes and planets are extremely beautiful although a seemingly flat texture with little detail can soon have you woahing at a mountain and plain next by eachother. The flora never dims, with different types of trees, cave monsters, and areas to explore on quite a few different choices of planet. This is no "No Man's Sky" though, there are not infinite planets. Sure, there are 4-5, but not billions or endless amounts. The basebuilding in this game works impeccably. I was thoroughly impressed with the interactivity of it all. And last, but certainly not least, the soundtrack. The soundtrack is possibly one of the most calming, and at the same time alarming I have ever personally heard. It's serene, and peaceful. Too peaceful. You expect a creature to come kill you at any moment, but it never comes. When you're walking around outside, looking at landscapes and flora, mountains and plains, you are soothed by the calming music. When you're in a cave, more intense, but still peaceful music plays, keeping you alert, and reminding you that danger lurks near. I've personally only encountered a few bugs, where I died and couldn't pick up my items, which wasn't gamebreaking as it fixed itself just a minute later when the body despawned. The other massive issue right now, seemingly only in multiplayer, is that with a GTX970, I'm running around 20-30 fps. Which, not too impactful on the peaceful gameplay, was a little choppy for my liking, although I've not had any problems with the FPS in singleplayer. The multiplayer, although slightly laggy at times, is fun, especially with a companion on TS or Discord.
TL;DR:
Game is good. Buy game. Support a good dev for once, they only come around once every blue moon.

Forget the issues (namely the black hair, the cigarette smoking, the deep voice, and the Assassin's Creed leather hoodie) that haunted this game's protagonist since its trailers were revealed, and criticized in the early 2010s. This game attempts to divert from its original formula where in the past 4 games, the demon-hunting took place mostly on castles, towers, churches, and other grand architectures. Now, we are treated to a setting where Earth meets Hell in a city. The fact that the Limbo environment itself changes and attempts to stop Dante is what makes the lore of this game unique.
Gameplay-wise, I can say that the control mapping is much easier to understand than DMC4, as it makes a balanced use of both the keyboard and the mouse. Switching to and from the Angel, Demon, and Human "modes" is also fast and seamless. Speaking of the controls and the three modes, combat is also fluid in a sense that the player may not need to pause for a longer time to switch weapons or execute complex combos. Grinding for upgrades and abilities also takes a lesser period of time in order to be maxed out. There are minimal puzzle sections, and more focus on the combat.
Preferably get this one on a sale since the game and the DLCs are somewhat overpriced for a 6-8 hours of campaign content, it gives off an easier overall difficulty as compared to the classic DMC games, and this is not even the Definitive Version.
To me this is best in the DmC franchise.

If you like the other Batman: Arkham games, you'll certainly enjoy Origins.
For starters, my expectations weren't as high as the reviews weren't as high as either Asylum or City. But I was really impressed with how strong the story is, specifically with the bond Batman and The Joker share and how the similarities between the two are explored. The development and admiration Batman and Gordon have for each other is also explored, as it starts with Gordon having serious disdain for Batman. I think the only weak point might be some of the assassins/super villains in that are introduced from the Blagckgate Prison breakout and aren't utilized as well. They're introduced as part of the story, so you'd think they'd be part of the main story.  There's also a huge array of characters in the game.
The assassins include Killer Croc, Deathstroke, Firefly, Copperhead, Deadshot, Electrocutioner, Lady Shiva, and Bane. Of those, I would say Deathstroke, Firefly and Bane were used in the best way possible. The rest either don't add much to the story, or you rather hunt them down in various side quests. And as far as the side quests go, there are a lot. You ultimately end up taking down most of the villains in side quests after they serve their role in the main story. I can understand some of the reasoning for that, as it is an open world game. But making it optional seems like something Batman wouldn't do.
I will say that the game runs really well. The graphics are really great. The music and original score is a highlight, especially with the orchestral Christmas themes that mix in with the stylistic Batman music. Using snow was a really interesting game design choice, but I'm glad they did it, it lets the world look really interesting. The expanded Gotham City from Arkham City is also great as glding around can be rather enjoyful. The direction in the cutscenes is also something I noticed to be incredible, they're very cinematic, well animated and acted. The voice acting is amazing from Troy Baker, he does a great Joker. Overall, I really enjoyed this game.

Arkham Origins is a good game, but unfortunately doesn't compare to the first two. This specific entry was made by WB's Montreal team, and even though the gameplay is still solid, and going back to Batman's early days is a great idea, the story eventually falls apart. These games have always had a strong narrrative to hold them together, and managed to tie enemies into the plot with purposeness and exciting battles. Origins immediately finds an excuse to bring a whole handful of villains working together as one, except they never do. What starts off as a really intriguing premise quickly becomes an excuse to wheel out the next boss fight after X amount of playtime. Worse, they undermine their own premise with an unnecessary twist that felt completely out of place, and is slowly fed to you in such a pompous manner that it feels like you're watching a train wreck in slow motion. It really made me sad, because the game is otherwise well-made, and it's only fault is that it plays out too much like a fanfiction rather than an epic Bamtan comic.
Despite my critique, I think it's a good game all-around, and would only recommend you stay away if you absolutely cannot stand predictable storylines. Otherwise, check it out and have fun trying to get that Point-Counterpoint achievement in the Deathstroke fight, seriously.

Lunch Truck Tycoon  -- Recommended with some reservations.  Casual Fun --- yes, the game is engaging on the premise of the lunchtime catering truck that is struggling to establish itself and grow.  The graphics are...average for this sort of game, not bad, but not impressive enough to elicit a nod of approval at first glance.  The figures of the customers are a bit below standard actually, looking more like the inhabitants of the streets of the 'PAPERBOY' Franchise, i.e.... blocky and non-descript.    Most of the gameplay is easy to learn, I was able to grasp the basics in less than 3 minutes.  The Text Instructions that popup at the very beginning of a game make a very direct connection to each area of info on the screen.   No long explanations, but most functions become apparent very quickly.   Overall, an enjoyable title.  Kudos to the designer for a fairly clean, uncluttered game that does what its made to do.            ....now  here comes my ..HOWEVER
However  (see I told you it was coming), Lunch Truck Tycoon loses some of its allure from being perhaps "too" clingy to the idea of  providing a somewhat 'reaslistic' simulation of the Lunch Truck Catering business.   After 6 hours of playtime,  my Lunch Truck Persona is still struggling to get to the first lunch truck upgrade.   I have been able to afford three equpment upgrades, bhut the costs of those pieces of equipment keep placing me further and further away from upgrading my truck  ( and I am only putting into consideration that I am attempting to purchase the FIRST of 6 truck upgrades --- the ultimate Lunch Truck being the 'Lunchinator' at a staggering $195K).   Now... Considering that I am selling chips, slices of pizza...cans of soft drinks, and candy canes,  I am sure that you start to see the problem.  After six hours of playtime, I only have $8623.00 saved...  If Lunch Truck Tycoon suffers from a major flaw, it is certainly that it attempts to be much too economically accurate.
When I considered submitting this review, I went back to the Store page and noticed something .... interesting.  On the sample pages of In-Game visuals is a 'sample'  of the Inventory Page within the game.   This Invenotry Page is where the player can order more items to re-stock their Lunch Truck, and set prices for the items to be sold.  However on closer inspection at the upper right hand corner of that sample page, I noticed.....  the Designer has obviously been 'doctoring' his/her own game, since the screen shows that He/or She has amassed more than $249,000 before reaching Level 12.
Now, I played for 6 hours... reached level 23, and have less than $10K.    So, here is a little "Shame on You"  to the game designer for being a bit deceptive about the actual gameplay.   But, the game is entertaining, but so frustrating in not being able to advance, that its playability is extremely limited right now.  It seems very 'fixable' however, and I certainly hope that the Designer reads this and works to come up with an active solution to this dilemna.
One other negative to the game is that I am playing on a PC .. using a mouse/keyboard option, and on the MENU Inventory Screen I am unable to scroll, page down, arrow down, jump down turn around, pick a bale of cotton......  until, I got advice from a 12 year old relative that plays Android games a lot, they advised me to treat the screen as if it was a tablet or cellphone needing a 'flick'.
So by flicking upwards with my mouse I am able to finally see the lower section of higher priced menu items to purchase/resupply.  This made a lot of difference in my gameplay, so I am now editing my review to a positve.. and hoping the Designer can add some other features to spiceup the sluggish gameplay experience.  RATING:  6 out of 10 katanas !!!

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Mega Man it is not. It is an excellent attempt at putting a twist on a genre which has done a ton, thus far. I dare say that this game does deserve the accolades that it gets, though. Here's the thing, intellectual properties are like Rubiks cubes, put a couple of twists on them and you have something new. The question is, does that new combination work. Since 20XX left early access and fully released, I would say yes! The controls are tight, the homage to MM and MMX in term of level design, music, and bosses, are there without being a blatant rip off of the very idea it so clearly idolizes. In essence, there is a ton to do, and much more than what can be covered with a simple 2 hour playthrough.
Give it some time, patience, and understanding, much like any other game. You'll be rewarded with an entertaining, frustrating, challenging, and delightful experience.
Good job, devs!!

This game is a great time-waster and well worth the dirt cheap price if you like to split/dual screen a game while something else going on online.  It's not worth your full attention, but this is a fun game to have on the side while other things are going on.
The player slowly builds up a food truck, unlocking levels, which in turn unlock different foods and tools.  These upgrades are linear, but the progress is rewarding enough.  This is no idle-game, but it's pretty base.  The player preps a day of food sales, picks a location, hits go and the day progresses.  The player needs to pay attention to a virtual cell phone that alerts HOT SPOTS, where sales might be better than the cuurent spot.
Otherwise, the cell phone indicates 2 types of challenges.  A quick or slow response challenge based on a food and degrees of Rock, Paper, Scissor.  For example, if the challenge is to make the best Coffee in town over 4 days, the player manipulates Coffee,  Milk, and Sugar between 0-15.  A winning combination might be 12-3-10, or whatever.  But the player need to pay attention to passersby who offer on-screen comments like, "Too much Coffee," or "Fantastic Milk!"  Basically, it is the children's game of "Hotter or Colder."
SUMMARY: This is not a tycoon game by any means.  This is not an idle-game.  It's a weird hybrid that requires attention every 5-10 minutes.  There's nothing to do in the middle.  Only buy of you need a simple-time waster.

Well, Batman fans or technically, arkham series fans, seems to hate on this game a lot. And I can clearly see why. It's basically a rip off from the Arkham series of Rocksteady. The combat, the gameplay and everything. It does not feel like a new game from a new studio. It does not give you anything fresh or exciting. It feels just like the same from Arkham Asylum and Arkham City but worse. way way worse. Even all of this, it does not deserve all the hates it get. It's still an okay game, a mediocore batman game, not in high quality just like Asylum or City, but not neccessarily bad. If you're a hardcore batman fan and want to try it out, you'll be fairly disappointed like me. But if you really wan to play this game, just get it on sale instead of full price.
Pros
- Great boss fights, make you think more strategically than average boss fights in most games
- Great set up for the rivalry between batman and the joker. You're really immersed into their love-hate relationship and see how it all started. The devs sure handled this plot very well
- Young and arrogant batman. You can clearly see that he's still new in this business. Still filled with rage and couldn't control his feelings. This is a very fresh and interesting take on the cape crusader as in Asylum and City , he's already developed into a more calm, mature crimefighter.
- You got to play as the clown prince of crime and see the backstory of how he turned into the joker. Staight out from The Killing Joke graphic novel. Greastest sequence in the game.
- Great Bane storyline. Also almost straight out from Knightfall grahic novel. There's even an attack from Bane that's straight out from the comic when he breaks batman's back
- Great detective investigation system. You can rewind of forward the situation that's happened in the crime scene which is really cool.
Cons
- The city feels lifeless and empty. It doesn't give you the sense of wandering and exploring like Arkham City did. It's just big and It's just there. It's like you're Batman, but you're not in Gotham city
- Lack of easter eggs. This is the thing i got frustated the most. Like, com on, this is The Batman game, at least put someting in for the fan, just a little bit. But there's none in Arkham Origins and it kinda turn you off from the game. No need to explore anything or find any hidden clues.
- Muddled story, main villians that we were promised from the start of the game (and looks very promising) turned into a side quest boss that means nothing and you can choose whether to do it or not. Such a waste of good characters.
- Enigma sidequest, bland and boring. No puzzles or collectibles that's relevant to the Batman arc at all. It gives you the feelings that "why do I bother doing this♥♥♥♥♥♥" And in the end you just walk into the room, do a couple of things and that's it. Didn't even get to meet The Riddler himself. Like. wtf devs, put some more details into this.
- Batcave, you get to see the Batcave, for crying out loud. But it's just there like the city. lifeless and empty. Nothing to do. Nothing to explore. At least give us something to do besides the training simulator.

Excellent game!! Definitely my favorite side-scroller on Steam. This game combines Megaman X with the mechanics of "rogue-likes" to make a excellent experience with plenty of replay value. As someone who plays through Megaman X about once a year, this game is a godsend.
While it is clearly influenced by the Megaman X series, in differs for all the right reasons. Since it is a roguelike you do not keep boss weapons between playthroughs, you get cool stuff much quicker than MMX, it gets much harder than MMX as it progresses, etc. These are all good in my opinion since it adds a lot of challenge and replay value to the game. Unlike MMX, there is a lot of balance to weapons, and like MMX, every weapon has some use outside of dealing damage.
20XX really is well designed game, and a great title for people who enjoy anything Megaman.

Having played this game from the Alpha release, I can personally say that this is one of the best indie games I have ever played. The game scratches the itch left by the absence of megaman games in the last 7 years, with the last (actual) megaman game coming out on May the 1st 2010. It feels just like a megaman game should be, having smooth controls (which can be changed depending on your preference), an incredible soundtrack, and great character designs.
. If you have played rogue likes before, you of course know how things are with the genre. But for those who do not know, a rogue like is a genre of game where the player character is sent into a procedurely generated level and have to reach it to the end of said level, completing whatever challenge the game presents you with. You also will in fact lose whatever items you recieved during your run when you die (aside from certain acceptions). Throughout the game you will slowly unlock new items to encounter and obtain throughout your runs,  this encourages the player to keep playing and unlock all there is to obtain. Also as a final note on rogue likes, they tend to be quite difficult so you will hopefully get better as a gamer in general thanks to the challenge presented (that, or you will stop playing the game for whatever reason you might have, which is of course fine).
. 20xx has a 32-bit feel to it and it personally makes me feel nostalgic, having really gotten into platforming games because of Megaman X4. The sprites also of course have the said 32-bit feel to them, and have gone through alot of changes throughout the different patches for the game. The Bosses all have unique designs (some very reminiscent of early Megaman X bosses) that all have a borderlands style intro slide.
But that is all I will say so as to not cheapen the experience of the game for those who don't really want any kind of spoiler whatsoever, so here are my ending thoughts. 20xx is a great game to hold over megaman fans until the recently announced
is released. The game is very unique and has a ton of personality. And while the game does have it's flaws, the overall experience you get from this game is great and will surely keep you coming back if you like platformers.
So take it from a long time platforming veteran, if you like platforming games, you will like this game. So please give it a shot, and if you don't like it go ahead and refund it. It's ultimately your choice on what you want to try, buy, or whatever. But if you have the time I highly suggest that you try playing this game.
Have a good day.

20XX is an interesting specimen when it comes to games. It's basically Mega Man X with randomly-generated layouts, various challenge modes, and actual co-op, whether it's with someone next to you or someone halfway across this planet that we call Earth. The graphics are great, the online is spectacular, and the humor for when you die or exit the game is spot-on. The gameplay itself is tight, although an XBOX 360 controller would be much better than a keyboard. This is the first review I've written on steam in 7 years. I have 120 hours in this game. Let me tell you how much of a gem this game is.
It has the control tightness of Super Meat Boy with the insane power-ups of a game like Prototype, couched in Megaman-style game mechanics and aesthetics. In a word, it's addicting.
Prior to it's 1.0 release, the game had *weekly* updates. To me, that tells me the devs 1) care about the game 2) care about the player base 3) rock and deserve free beer. When you launched the game, the game literally had a countdown indicating how long until the next update. No one playing post-1.0 will know that, no one who wasn't a beta player will know that, but it should be underscored and remembered. Every week, when my 20XX update started auto-downloading, I would always play because I would wonder what new powers they put into the game this week.
If you're reading this you probably already have a sense of what the gameplay is like, so instead of telling you about the gameplay let me tell you about the game design. The devs included Halo-style "skulls" which modify some aspect of the game. These skulls can be turned on/off, in any combination.
In the beta, dying meant losing all of the upgrades you've picked up on your current run. This is still true, but now you get the chance to re-buy some of the upgrades before starting your run. If you don't want to, you don't have to, but this gives players who don't want to start from zero the option to start their next run with a bit of a buff.
Another optional tweak the devs give you: the power-up drops in this game are random, but suppose you really hate some particular power-up. The devs added a neat "de-program" mechanic, which lets you eliminate some power-ups from randomly dropping in your upcoming run. This, like the "re-buy" mechanic feature I discussed above, costs "soul chips", which you pick up during a run. So these features are balanced in the sense that you can only re-buy and de-program according to how well you did on a previous run.
The key with both of these features is they are optional. The devs give you so many options it's mind-boggling to me how big name game companies don't invite these devs as consultants for their projects. You have the option to use skulls, the option to start runs with upgrades, or to start with just your normal weapon, and you have the option de-program power-ups.
TLDR: buy this game. It's easily worth 29.99CAD, but it's 16.99CAD regular price. If it's on sale, buy it for yourself and send the devs some love by buying it for a friend.
