The bigger complaint for me was that the (very) few puzzles that were not HOPs were all the exact same--either a spinning lock kind of deal, or a matching game. More variety--and for that matter, difficulty--in those puzzles would have improved the game for me.
I still ultimately enjoyed it, though. I am upset at the ending, especially considering there isn't any word as yet on a sequel, but this game isn't any worse than any other point-and-click, hidden object adventure game I have played. It's certainly not any better by any means, but it's not worse.

I have often dreamed of having my own lunch truck from which I could sell delicious lunches to happy people attending fairs, or on their lunch break, or relaxing in the sun at the beach. My friend Ian and I discussed it for several months at one point, even planning out our ideal lunch routes and giving our theoretical burger bus the title "Well I'll Be Burgered", a name both cheeky and fun and redolent of the hot, delicious foods within. Sadly, his wife vetoed this idea, and I went on to get a job making computer games, and our dream of a food truck selling the most delicious of take-out meals was not to be.
Happily, there is Lunch Truck Tycoon. My girlfriend purchased this for me with the belief that I would be a good 'Burger Man' and I hope that I will not fail her. I like the colourful graphics, the range of locations and the way that different areas change popularity depending on which day of the week it is. I have a carefully calculated chart in my notebook detailing which food items sell best in which areas of the city, to take advantage of the special opportunities, and I have big dreams of upgrading to 'The Lunchinator', the largest lunch truck available to me, at some point, should my lunches prove popular enough with the fine citizens of this town.
I must say, though, that the competitions are quite difficult, and I'm not quite good at them yet. Yes, my more efficient storage system was purchased with funds gleaned from the winnings of one of these competitions, but I also feel that more feedback would have been much more helpful, as I've purchased the sign that attracts more customer feedback and still do not feel I am given adequate amounts in order to competently tackle these challenges.
Besides, lunch should not be a contest. It should be a celebration; of food, of life, of flavour and culture and the joy of eating a tomato, cheddar, salt and pepper sandwich on toasted wheat bread in the sun with someone you care about. With an iced tea on the side, perhaps.
In summary, this is a fine food van simulation. I find it more engaging than the likes of Ice Cream Tycoon Deluxe, and will keep selling my tasty, nourishing wares to the proud, noble people who visit my truck in the hopes that one day, I too shall be able to call The Lunchinator my own, and in doing so, will rest easy in the knowledge that I am the greatest lunch truck entrepeneur I can be.

I bought 20XX while searching for a game similar to Mega Man X. What a great surprise! I'm really amazed with this game. I've got much more than I was looking for.
Here is a "short" description of the features of the game:
Characters:
Nina and Ace. Both are similar to Mega Man X and Zero. Nina has a buser, that shots forward, and Ace has a Saber that slashes enemies close to him. Both can charge their attacks, doubling the damage output.
Weapons:
You can find other weapons while progressing the game to replace the default one. For example, Nina has a weapon that can fire four shots in the cardinal directions, and Ace has a Spear that can extend the range of his attacks.
Special Powers:
When you defeat a boss you have a choice to get his power, or another items. Each poer is unique and you can equip three special powers at a time, on different buttons. You can manage your active special powes on the pause menu.
Bosses:
There are 8 bosses (excluding the final ones). Each boss has a unique power, and is weak to another boss power. Much like Mega Man series. The difficulty of each boss increase as you progress through the stages.
Armors:
There are 4 sets of armor, each one has 4 pieces: chest, foot, arms and helmet. Each piece for each set has an specific effect. For example, you can dash in the air, or double jump, get an extra charge for your weapon, use less energy for you special attacks, etc. You can use different pieces from different sets, or try to collect an entire set to get an extra bonus effect.
Items:
On the Mega Man X Series, we had a few items, that could replenish or raise your health/energy. On 20XX we have many stats (movement speed, height of jump, attack power, and so on) that can be modified with items and power ups. Some items will give a minor increments, while others can give a huge boost in one stat, while decreasing other. Items can be found in shops on the stages, on special chests, or after defeating a boss.
Currency:
There are three currecies in this game:
Nuts: You receive those from chests or eneies. You can use them to buy items on shops, or exchange to HP and Energy on some machines.
Tokens: In some stages, before the boss room, you may find a slot machine, where you can use those items. You may receive a power up item, some pick-ups or, if you are unlucky, nothing.
Soul Chips: Some special enemies drops those chips, that can be used to unlock new items, to be used on future runs.
Stages:
In 20XX the stages are randomly generated, so each run is unique. There is no fixed place for power ups, armor pieces and other items. There is no guarantee you will find an specific item in you run.
You cannot choose the first boss you will fight, and after beating the first stage, you have can choose between three bosses to proceed. They are not in a specific order, and you may not find the weapon of the previous boss useful against the next.
There is usually one shop (sometimes two, one of them right before the boss). Also, you may find a Glory ZOne in the middle of the stage. When entering on this room, you have a task to perform. If you are successful, you will get a piece of armor. Those tasks involve destroying enemies, reach the end of the room without damage, disabling traps, etc.
Due to this random feature, the replayability of the game is enormous. You may have a very hard run, or you may become so powerful that you can destroy the bosses in a blink of an eye.
On normal mode, you have only one life, but there is no instant kill traps. Pits and spikes cause only damage. You can always adjust this selecting another difficulty setting.
The Ark:
This is the place where you start, and where you come back after a run. From here you can choose to play a game, select another mode (daily challenges, special runs, etc), switch characters, and unlock items or buy them to use on the next runs, with Soul Chips.
Multiplayer:
You can play with a friend! The game will zoom in and out depending on the proximity of the players. The boss door will only open when both player reach it. If a player die, the other will continue alone until he can find a capsule to ressurrect the first. Power Ups picked by one player will affect the other. Armor pieces will appear in pairs, one for each player. It is possible to use two Ninas or two Aces. Tottally fun. I just wished there was a fight mode between players :)

I've played 20xx since it was in early access and I've always considered it one of the best roguelike/lite games.
However when the game was released with the option of having permanent upgrades I have to admit that my heart sank.
In the early days there were no permanent upgrades and when you died, you lost everything and had to start again. This in my opinion is how the game should have stayed.
This was a game that I always went back to again and again to try to complete it and I had a lot of fun doing it.
You went through the game hoping for that perfect run and upgrading yourself along the way. If you died, you lost it all and had to try again.
Adding permanent upgrades means that you can basically start the game with an op weapon and a massive health bar and get to the end of the game really quickly which wasn't what the game was about when I played it.
Don't get me wrong the permanent upgrades are optional and you can leave them off if you want to but anyone new to the game isn't going to have the same experience of 20xx that I had and I feel that's a great shame.
I do highly recommend the game. It's an excellent challenging platformer with great graphics and controls. I just wish it was released without the permanent upgrade option.

DmC: Devil May Cry is a game developed by Ninja Theory and published by Capcom and is a reboot of the Devil May Cry series
This game gets more hate than I think it deserves. Yeah, the writing is pretty lacking, the combat is nowhere near as deep as previous Devil May Cry games (from what I've seen) and the aesthetic is very hit-or-miss, but is DmC a bad game?
Absolutely not!
There's still a lot of depth here. The weapon system is readily accessible, and I never had any issues holding the triggers to switch melee weapons on the fly- it's very flexible and intuitive
As for the audio, the soundtrack is actually pretty okay. The Nine Inch Nails and Deadmau5 knockoffs on this game's OST are pretty catchy, and this is coming from someone who doesn't care for dubstep and the like
All in all, DmC: Devil May Cry is an underappreciated game that is totally worth checking out regardless of your opinions on the rest of the series

By far the best platformer I have ever played.
The art style is incredible, and is accompanied by one of the best soundtracks to a video game that I have ever heard. Even in the opening moments of the game, the emotion in the music is beautiful.
The game can be a bit difficult or frustrating at times, especially in the more "scripted" areas of the game where you are experiencing the same event over and over until you finally get the perfect run and complete it. These frustrating areas are HEAVILY overshadowed by areas where your control is fluid and responsive (which is the majority of the time).
The areas and environments are varied, and the skill progression is good. The abilities that you learn over the course of the game are fresh and unique (especially bash, incredibly unique).
The story is okay, but is story really what you're looking for in a game like this?
TL;DR
Great atmosphere, music, gameplay, progression. Difficult at times, but not overly so.
This is a must play.

Too bad there is no middle ground here: it's a positive or a negative rating you have to make.  Not everything is bad in that game, yet I can't recommend it and forced to put a negative rating with the system.
I love Hidden Objects games and while I can forgive a lot of stuff, I can't really recommend this one for a reason: I don't always have enough hints to guide me into the story. The tasks are self-explanatory but you don't have any hint for where to go. And when you're sure you need a tool you've seen in a scene, you might have to wait until something else happens or worse, you collect stuff BEFORE the task was given. As a result, while the story is interesting, it can be confusing because of that. Also, when you begin the story, you don't know why your character is with a medium (are you a client? Someone with abilities?), which is sad, because having a little background wouldn't hurt.
Another negative point is in the HOG scene itself: some of the objects are barely visible (I remember the fingerless glove having the same shade of color than the ground - or a wheel padlock in a light that was so bright that you couldn't really see the object).
But otherwise, graphics are correct, soundtrack is correct and while you're in the end always doing voodoo dolls to free people, you're acquiring spells that help you to advance (and THERE, you have suddenly hints for when to use them). Too bad they're underexploited. It would have been nice to use them more than three times.
Besides, will I buy a second Voodoo game? Yes, because I want to know the end of the story. They managed to make a cliffhanger. Besides, maybe they've improved it: after all, Samantha Swift, Mystery Cases Files, Mystery P.I. or any game made by Artifex Mundi improved over time.
If you can pick this up cheap then it is worth roughly 2-3 hours of clicky click.  The find the hidden object parts are pretty easy and it has a decent story but it ends with....To Be Continued.....

The Bad:

DmC: Devil May Cry (or DmCDMC, as I like to call it) is a reboot/alternate universe of the Devil May Cry franchise, and, as someone who's never played a DMC game before (although I knew the characters and had vague idea of the general plot), I must say it does a decent job at introducing the player to the franchise, or, at the very least, to the hack and slash genre. As I mentioned already, I have no experience with previous DMC games, so I can't really compare the quality of this one to the rest of the franchise, so this review will be mostly about my opinions on this game as a single entity.
To begin with, I'd like to talk about the story. I'll admit I wasn't too fond of Dante at the beginning of the game, or the game's atmosphere in general. It seemed to try to be too edgy and dark, with Dante being somewhat of a punk who didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about anything. However, I'd say it worked pretty well in the end, since, as the game progresses, you can actually see some character development in Dante, going from his original self-centered persona to someone who cares about the world, and wants to defend it from the demons. I'd say all the characters are pretty well written in my opinion; and the story is fairly decent, if a bit predictable. I'd say that Ninja Theory managed to create an interesting world, and I'd gladly accept it as an alternate universe to the main DMC franchise, but, sadly, it seems the chances of a DmC2 are pretty much non-existant.
As for the gameplay, I really like it. I'd say it's a bit confusing at first, with the three different weapon styles (normal, demonic and angelic weapons), each with their own role in combat, not to mention the fact that certain enemies are immune to certain weapons, but after you get some practice with the combos and such, combat becomes really fun, as you try and get the highest score possible. There's also some platforming sections in the game, some of which can be a bit annoying as the game tends to mess up your commands. I do have some problems with the gameplay, though. Most notably, the lack of a lock-on system, which can sometimes mess with your combos as the game decides which enemy to target (sometimes it even makes you lose a combo by not hitting anything), not to mention that it's also impossible to cancel attacks when the animation is already playing (at least I couldn't do it), which can lead you to being hit, as some enemies have faster attack animations than some of your attacks.
The level design is something I kinda liked. Most of the gameplay takes place in Limbo, which is sort of an alternate dimension to the real world, although severely distorted, and it really feels like the world itself is trying to kill you. There's a noticeable different between the real world and Limbo, with the real world looking gray and dull, while Limbo is colourful and feels alive. While I can understand the design choice (the real world looks gray because it's under Mundus' control, while Limbo, the demon world, thrives), the real world sections feel drab compared to the rest of the game. Even then, there's not much of them, so it's not a big issue.
The soundtrack is pretty great as well. A lot of heavy metal and the like, and while it is somewhat edgy in certain portions, it fits perfectly well with the rest of the game, so I'd say they did a good job.
All things said, I really enjoyed this game. I repeat, I have no idea how it might compare to other DMC games, but, on its own, it's a pretty good game, so I recommend it.

DmC: Devil May Cry combines stunningly beautiful leveldesign and presentation, extremely fluid and fast combat and a kickass soundtrack to be one of the better games that I have played in the genre.
The game has, however, so little to do with the DMC series, that it would be an insult to the originals to call this a "reboot". It's a spin-off, made for the gamers of 2013. Much more shallow, a hell of a lot easier and more focused on flashing the player than making the player flash others.
Which means that genre newbs can pick up and enjoy this game, as opposed to other DMC games which these people may simply find too hard to get into.

So I'm not really into the hidden object point/click adventures, but I was amused by the concept and thought I would give this one a try. I liked the idea, so here we go.
Good:
The concept is actually pretty interesting. The story has a basic set up: New Orleans has fallen under some kind of curse and its up to a rookie voodoo witch to set things straight. The idea of an adventure that themes itself around 'realistic' magick and spell-craft is pretty cool in my opinion, and it seems to be done well.
There actually is a bit of homework that went into this. For example: the brick dust, or red clay dust, you get at the beginning of the game actually is a thing for voodoo practioners as a defensive item, and its not uncommon to serve up mojo in cloth bags like you see in the opening sequence and throughout the game.
You spend most of the game looking for such spell ingredients and picking up mojo to cast spells and solve problems (or give you hints). Which, is an interesting break from what I normally see in clicky-click adventures. You still have plenty of times when you need to do practical things like search for a screwdriver to unscrew a latch and other things, but there are some pretty interesting moments when you solve problems in an impractical way by using magicks or spells to achieve supernatural results.
And I can give a game credit for putting a little meaning and history behind its spellcraft, instead of just saying "Magic power!"
The story actually does a decent job at throwing a few curves into the mystery of what is going on, but only every now and then. Its otherwise straightforward, and not really noteworthy or condemnable either way.
The main meat of the gameplay is the hidden object scenes, where you have to clear out a small list of items from a messy scene, which ultimately rewards you with keys or ingredients you need. They usually aren't too hard, and are a lot more entertaining than I thought they would be; coming from an action game guy. There are some puzzles too, but they are usually very short and very easy, and the exploration is a little too straightforward to be called gameplay.
And the game's still graphics look great by the way.
Some of the hidden object scenes are really quite absurd though, and it does make me wonder how any sane person could keep some of the messes seen on the desks and tables in this game!
Which brings me to the bad...
Bad:
This game's setting is really dark and gloomy. I feel like there is some legitimate work that went into this game to make it a 'dark adventure. But, then the game happens, and there is a huge dissonance in game and setting.
The game is ridiculous and inconsistent most of the time. It expects you to do things out of order, and what you can and can't do at times isn't exactly clear.
The game has a tendency to force you to do things step by step. Anytime you go through a process, instead of being able to get the whole thing done at once, you have to do part A, go get items for part B, do part B, go get items for part C, do part C, instead of getting all the items and preparing to do the task in one go like a normal human being would do. The game will literally not let you get everything you need at once; either the protagonist will say she doesn't know what to do with this, or the game just won't even notice it and write it off as background until you need to pick it up. It just causes a lot of needless backtracking.
And sadly, all the magicks and spell crafting in this game are contextual and very limited. You only make and perform each spell once, and you only use spells every now and then. Which is a shame, as I feel like the game kind of undermines its own idea by not using the character's voodoo abilities more often. Instead, it tends to favor more traditional point/click gameplay.
The story, while decent most of the time, has a lot of bumps. Lillian is noblewoman, but can somehow pick locks with no explanation as to how she knows that. She talks as if she doesn't know her own house in the first chapter, and given that her suitcase is kept in the pantry I'm not surprised. It seems like everyone you meet is very familiar with voodoo, and nobody seems to really be interested in the fact that you are saving the town with magic. Dead people don't know they are dead until you talk to them, but can accurately recall their cause of death anyways. Villains don't fry you on the spot for no reason other than to give you time to defeat them.
Its not cringe-worthy, but certainly not good. I'm not even nitpicking either. This is THE GAME. This is pretty much what makes up the story.
But here's a nitpick: For a wealthy family that owns a maid and a gardener, the house is an absolute sty.
I would actually go as far as to say that the only real effect this 'curse' has is to make things messy, as cursed presences take the form of piles of junk that have to be magicked away.
The music is ok, if overly dramatic most of the time. The 3d animations and 3d models range from bad to horrifyingly bad. I would have prefered this game to be in all 2d and still images. The voice acting is decent during some of the cutscenes, but the dialogue is overall amatuerish, cliche, and sometimes just silly.
At one point, the game asks you to put ham in a mortar and pestle. It even says it in your magic spell book, IN THE SPELL's DESCRIPTION, to put "a smelly ham" in a ceramic mortar. Someone seriously wrote that as a spell.
That's this game's biggest problem. Its got a dark adventure setup, but the game's action is just too stupid to be taken seriously. The ridiculous actions combined with the absurd dialogue just makes this game seem foolish, and that's a huge red mark for a game with this kind of set up. The constant backtracking doesn't help either.
Finally, this game is painfully short, and has the nerve to force a "To be continued..." ending.
In summary, I would just say that this game is trying to be too serious for its genre.
Overall:
I would have liked this game to be better than it was. I would have liked a game that stuck with its concept and tried to break out of the genre it set out for. I think a puzzle game that focuses more on magicking rooms back in order and a more open adventure with a focus on collecting and testing out ingredients to find solutions to problems would have been more interesting than the hidden object games. Its pretty, but the gameplay just doesn't work with the story.
Maybe I'm expecting too much of a genre I know nothing about, but I'm just going with my opinions. There was serious game potential here, and it was wasted on a silly object find game with silly writing.
I like a game with a good concept and setting though, and there is a pretty good setup. And for what it is, it was still fun for a few hours. I just would have liked a bit more content and a bit better gameplay

A very different kind of tower defense, Unholy Heights requires quite a lot of strategy, especially on the business management end of things. If you place your monster tenants in the wrong apartments, prepare to lose not only your monsters, but your money.
The different species of tenants all have their own different likes and dislikes, including other tenants: the Demons hate Demi-Humans, and love when other tenants die; the Abyssals require air-conditioners (or heaters!) to the point that they'll get sick and die without them, and hate Elementals; the Undead hate losing battles, and the Cheepies and Chimerae just enjoy when your other tenants are happy.
If these weren't enough, each species, and each variation of the species, has different rent-paying willingness and capabilities: just because a tenant is WILLING to pay rent, doesn't mean that they are ABLE to pay rent, and vice-versa.
I enjoyed this game thoroughly for it's micro-management, and the steady difficulty curve of its battles. For how much time and enjoyment you'll get out of this game, its $3.99 price tag is more than fair, and dare I say, even a little cheap.

Gish is one of those indie gems I just keep coming back to. Originally released in 2004, it has stood the test of time boldly. Gish can best be explained as a puzzle platformer, but it's gameplay is unlike anything I've seen before. On top of that, the style and story are equally refreshing.
The main character is very likeable although he doesn't speak a word, and his unique moves make you chuckle every time. Hanging upside-down from a ceiling never gets old and neither does listening to the sound of snapping enemy necks.
Technically, this game works like a charm as well with hardly any hiccups and is still visually pleasing, not only because of its scaling resolution, but also because of its nice light effects.
Gish has a lot of charm, but not that of the cutesy type; it's really gritty, which combined with the excellent soundtrack makes for a hell of an experience that you'll remember long after first playing it... not something I'm able to say of a lot of games.

So very playable! Borderlands 2 follows up on Borderlands and improves on everything. Once again you explore the
cray-cray wild west meets sci-fi world of Pandora. You do missions, you shoot stuff, you use badass powers ,you kill stuff, you loot stuff. Fun all around You do this for tens of hours and it never gets boring ( a sign of good game design)
The main missions are fun. The side mission are better, as they range from crazy to funny and usually a combination of the two. You do often really weird stuff for both old characters from B1 as well as brand new and just as crazy new characters (meet the teenage girl explosives expert who does tea parties and talks like someone from GTA)
The gameplay is as crazy as the rest of the game. As one (or up to four) man (or woman) you take on bandits, beasts and the evil Handsome (meh) Jack. You choose from a variety of gun types and a variety of crazy powers to kick♥♥♥♥♥ And did i mention those guns have crazy powers too? Well they do - like the explosion Torque weapons which blow stuff up or the tediore guns which you can turn into grenades.
There's also in-game achievements. You get these for pretty much every thing you can do in the game. As you complete more of these you can boost your stats to be even more badass.
The playthrough should give you tens of hours. But wait, it's not over yet. You can get dlcs and kick new♥♥♥♥♥in new areas. Or you can start the game over in true vaulter mode, where you keep your level and your gear but every enemy is stronger. And then once more with ultimate vault hunter mode, where amazingly enemies are even stronger and kicking♥♥♥♥♥is even more of a challenge. Or you can start the game again with a new class which plays in a very different way.
So to sum up. Borderlands 2 is a funny game which plays well and plays for a very long time indeed. I'd recommend getting it because the gameplay is such a lot of fun, but also because this is a game where you really get your money's worth.

This game gets more hate than I think it deserves. Yeah, the writing is pretty lacking (but coming from a series that has never been known for Shakespearean writing, it's forgivable), the combat is nowhere near as deep as DMC3 or 4 and the aesthetic is very hit-or-miss, but is DmC a bad game? Absolutely not. There's still a lot of depth here, and it actually manages to do some things better than the original series, particularly platforming. The weapon system isn't nearly as deep or open-ended as 3 or 4, but on the flipside, everything is readily accessible, and I never had any issues holding the triggers to switch melee weapons on the fly- it's very flexible and intuitive.
Most of the minor gameplay flaws- the lack of lock-on, the stupid color-coded enemies, the broken style meter, and having to collect different arbitrary types of keys to unlock missions- were fixed in the Definitive Edition, but Ninja Theory never made a PC port of that, and two years removed from its release, it doesn't look like we'll be getting it any time soon, which is a damn shame. If you have a PS4 or Xbone, that version is the way to go. It is to this game what the Special Editions were to 3 and 4.
As for the audio, the soundtrack is actually pretty okay. It doesn't beat the nu-metal flavorings of 3 or 4, but the Nine Inch Nails and Deadmau5 knockoffs on this game's OST are pretty catchy, and this is coming from someone who doesn't care for dubstep and the like.
All in all, DmC is an underappreciated game that is totally worth checking out regardless of your opinions on the rest of the series.

I absolutely love Ori and the Blind Forest.
The graphics are stunningly beautiful, the story is both heartbreaking and heartwarming and you just have to love every single character in this game.
My personal opinion on the gameplay itself:
- it's a really good platformer overall with some little flaws, in the very last dungeon I had my moments where I wondered why the guy who designed THAT didn't get fired in the end
- the controls are precise and fast, I like the fact that you have auto-aim with your normal attack a lot
- everything kind of blends in, even environmental dangers like spikes or foes (sometimes they blend in a bit too well, I died while thinking: what?! what killed me?)
- you may have trouble with the enemies, some of them do ridiculously much damage but it gets better later on and much easier with certain upgrades

I recommend Batman: Arkham Origins as the storyline was enjoyable as well as having great side missions, boss battles and top notch voice acting by its cast.
However, despite being an enjoyable game it is weaker than its predecessor with a list of pros and cons below!
Pro:
Firstly, ss mentioned above is has an enjoyable story as well as variety of different great side missions.
Secondly, it improved boss battles from Batman: Arkham City and has a bigger map size than previous Arkham games.
Lastly, the game introduces new gadgets for Batman and has detective mode which allows the investigation of crimes such as rewinding the events (e.g. murder) to find out what happened and how it happened in order for Batman to capture the culprit.
Con:
Firstly, the story does however lacks cohesive narrative and has fast travel which is unnecessary as it takes away the excitement of free-roaming.
Secondly, this game has a multiplayer component which is largely unnecessary as there are poor control of movement as well as poor weapon accuracy and the heroes lack empowerment because of the more restrictive combat ability and less resistance to damage.
Lastly, does not improve alot of stuff from the previous games such as the combat.

What an incredible racing game and this is coming from someone who didn't appreciate F1.
The graphics are pretty even by 2016's standard.
At first I couldn't compete in qualifying against AI which put me in the last position consistently. Then I started to learn the tracks better and I began to improve in qualifying sessions. 19th out of 24, 18th, 7th, then eventually 1st and 2nd!! The reward feeling is incredible as you win your races.
In career mode you have to also master your race strategy which means knowing which tire set to choose and when to go to pit. Temperatures of brakes and tires are simulated so if they are cold you will find yourself sliding in corners.
As I started to do well in dry races, I encountered another challenge in the dynamic weather. When it gets from sunshine to rain, you need to time your pit wisely to change tire set. New tires are cold and take time to adjust to the rythm of racing so you can't just push your car mindlessly. I struggled bad when weather turns from dry to wet until I learned when to pull a pit stop and to watch out for the temperatures of both my brakes and tires.
Again, this is a beautiful F1 game that's pretty with immersive sound effects. You can feel the competitiveness from the AI. Whoever coded the AI deserves a medal!
Buy this even if you just have a slight interest in F1.
UPDATE July 13th 2016
After I bought F1 2013 which is deemed by many to be the best F1 title from Codemasters yet, I'm loving F1 2012 even more. While F1 2013 is a bit prettier than F1 2012, it suffers from water spray not being shown in replays. I often record my games and post the videos on Youtube as a personal album of sort and this water spray bug bugs me very much especially from an F1 title vaunted very much to be the best yet from Codemasters. F1 2013 AI is also much tougher and I simply cannot keep up with the AI. In races where I could get into podium in F1 2012, I must settle with 5th-6th place instead in F1 2013. Some people may like the tougher AI but not me. Thus, F1 2012 is very much the more accessible game. As for the vaunted handling of F1 2013, I found it to be an overstatement. Cars in F1 2013 may be more twitchy at slow speeds but that doesn't necessarily make them more realistic....only more difficult to control at slow speeds. High speed handling in F1 2013 is on par with F1 2012 if not slightly more arcade (easier to drive). I regret buying F1 2013 at full price in fact because of the marginal value it has over F1 2012 which I bought for very cheap. Aside from the lackluster DLCs F1 2013 has no obvious edge over F1 2012. Certainly nothing to justify buying it at full price considering Codemasters has maintained the F1 2013 at full price for 2 years without any discount whatsoever being offered.
Here's a little comparison between F1 games that I own:
F1 2012: Great value, great handling physics, capable but not overwhelming AI (AI is at the sweetest spot imo), a minor bug in helmet visor texture, still looks good for 2016's standard, cars have V8 engine with awesome sound and you get to race as or with Michael Schumacher (2012 is his final racing year)
F1 2013: Bad value since it's not been discounted for couple years now, at slow speeds the cars are more twitchy while at higher speeds the cars feel a tiny bit more arcade than F1 2012, rather overwhelming AI that can shock new players, bug: AI water spray isn't being shown in replay, a bit prettier than F1 2012, cars have V8 engine with awesome sound though there's no longer Michael Schumacher in the game, DLCs allow you to race in 1980s and 1990s F1 cars although the track and team lists are lacking.
F1 2014: Good value when discounted, handling is quite a bit more arcade compared to previous iterations and suffers from understeer, good AI that's not as overwhelming as F1 2013, bug: AI water spray isn't being shown in replay, prettier than F1 2013, all teams are unlocked from the start in career mode so you don't have to start in a low tier team, has unlimited replay option that alleviates any worry of you ruining a race due to short lapses of concentration, cars have new turbocharged V6 engine with underwhelming sound...

Megaman-style run-and-gun mixes surprisingly well with procedurally generated rougelite shenanigans, and fans of the classic megaman x games will probably find a lot to like here. Granted, the game experiences some pacing issues and some of the later levels can throw unneccesarily antagonistic platforming at you, but on the other side, you do on occasion get an amazing and fun combination of items, so business as usual for a rougelite.

Imperfect, but a real blast. I admit, the random-generation aspects probably don't do the level design a lot of favors - they lose that lovingly handcrafted feel you see in the game's not-at-all-concealed source material. But the randomized powerups and enhancements do lend some fun and give each run its own distinct character. My chief complaint overall would be the kinda inorganic, "paper doll"-esque animations, where characters' limbs are mostly animated by just pivoting them on their joints rather than actually hand-drawing unique animations. But the immensely replayable reasonable challenge these games pose, and the fun of two player mode, thoroughly eclipses nitpicks like that. On top of all that, the devs have done a great job with continuing to hone and tweak the game post-release, including new content!

I've played about 5 hours now, i'd say it's a lot better version of no mans sky. I've only discovered a shuttle while researching and stuff, but it's been a hell of a lot of fun.
All the bugs i've seen have been stupendous and i love them. The core gameplay (gathering recourses, discovering and researching etc.) is really nice and the items/inventory system is very smooth. I also really appreciate the art style, it fits the genre of the game well, and gives off a more chilled feeling as if we aren't meant to be playing seriously the entire time. I like the idea of procedurally generated worlds since it let's you discover new things each play through. Having no GUI blocking the screen is really good too, there are only 3D buttons that pop up above tools etc. The inventory isn't even GUI, it's just a larger view into you're back pack, which you can open while on the move.
The fact there is co-op is really awesome too. I've played most of my 5 first hours playing with friends, we've abused bugs (because they're there, may as well have fun with them.), and we've left each-other stranded on planets to die. :D
Although of course i have a few problems with the game too. I'd really like to have a more dynamic/free space exploration method. Right now it's just click and move, which is boring and isn't fun in any way. I understand that the game is less than a month old (atleast on steam) and is in early access, but it's just a suggestion. I find it a bit of a bore that i haven't found any living creatures other than simple plants that impale me. I'd like creatures and other species i can interact with. This is probably the biggest flaw in the game, there is a trading platform you can get, but who are we trading to? If i do ever discover another species in the futer i'd be very happy. I've only played for about 5 hours and haven't even left my solar system yet so i don't know too much.
ahhhh the bugs, one of the funniest parts of the game. Sometimes crashed ships that i'd find would be given life and take flight for no reason. Then they'd teleport back to where they were. Had a good laugh, but my friend couldn't see what was happening so he thought i was lying and wouldn't believe me. Another fun bug that i ABUSE to all hell, is sticking myself in the ground. I dig a small hole, then cover the hole back up over the top of my character and bam! I'm floating inside the ground, i can find resources with ease and most of the time i have control over whether my character goes up or down.Althogh things go south when i pop back up into the surface and often get flung into space or into parts of my base or something like that. Another bug that i found, which isn't really that funny but it needs to be fixed, so im listing it. Sometimes if i place a new part of my base so i can place another building or place storage, it goes threw other parts of my base. I'm lucky it didn't break anything though.
Overall i think this game is a lot of fun and has a lot of stupendous moments that i share with my friends! I reccommend this to anyone who is looking for a semi-survival semi-sandbox game to play! I'd probably gives this a 10/10 but there isn't any other species as of me playing my first 5 hours, so i'm giving it a 8/10, since it could probably go with some better optimization, but tha's to be expected of such a new game.

This game has a very special crayon drawing style, and most of the items, characters and enemies in the game are also fun. However, there are several crucial problems preventing me from recommending this game.
1. The control is very labour-intensive: you have to click for each and every movement of the hero, because there's neither even the simplest path finding nor keyboard movement control. So if you pick a wrong door, you may need to click a hundred times to go all the way back.
2. This is an old-fashioned PURE rogue-like game. You won't gain anything for subsequential plays. If you die, you have to begin a new game with empty hands (expect for a set of random starting weapons) all over again. The layout of rooms is substantially fixed, while the enemies and items in a map are generated random. So you may die in the third room after starting a new game.
3. The combat is heavily dependent on chances. As someone has mentioned in an earlier review, the hit/miss results seem to be completely random. Since you have only a dozen of HPs and you are going to face hundreds of baddies, the dice will eventually fail you.
Overall, don't be fooled by the appearance of the game. It is not a cute, easy game for children. Unless you are trying to educate them on how to handle frustration.

A rogue-like for beginners:  is a fantastic starting point for people who are uncertain if they will enjoy the rogue-like genre. It doesn’t throw you in at the deep end and expect you to be a master gamer from the first go around. The mechanics are quite simple to learn – particularly with keyboard and mouse – and this makes the game accessible to almost every player. Further increasing this accessibility is that the art design, including graphics and music, is easy on the eyes and the ears. A nice touch is that you are able to name and design your character and your in-game friends.
Easy to learn, difficult to master: Sticking with the rogue-like theme of the game is an important characteristic for this game. It wouldn’t be a rogue-like if the game was too easy.  Thankfully the difficulty ramps up and even at the lower levels can present a realistic challenge that kept me playing further and further into the game.
Child or certainly teen friendly: Although there is action in the game and you do kill things the game is in my opinion child or teen friendly.
Controller issues: I generally enjoy playing most games using my controller. However, the mechanics of the game didn’t feel nearly as tight with a controller as it did with a keyboard and mouse. I often found myself moving multiple times when I intended on moving only once or into a space that I didn’t intend on moving into. This might not sound like a huge deal and perhaps in time I could’ve learned how to use the controller more accurately – so it’s not entirely the fault of the developers – but it was a regular problem that I didn’t have time for.
Repetitive: A feature that I truly do love that many rogue-like games have is that they are procedurally generated. Crayon Chronicles is not that. What this means is that each time you die you have to beat the same areas that you’ve just beaten. This is a major downfall in the game as games can last as little as a couple of minutes. This can make you feel as though you’re the hamster on the wheel playing the same content over and over and over again.
Despite the issues that I’ve stated above I do recommend Crayon Chronicles to people as a starting point for rogue-likes. I’d also recommend it to people who appreciate simple games that look cute and artsy and a game that requires smart use of strategy the further you play into it.

On reflection it seems the innitial reaciton to this game was a little harsh. Although not without flaws; occational bugs, collision detection issues, and perhaps a little less polish than previous games it is still fun to play. However I will make two major complaints despite my possitive overall mark. Firstly, the DLC policy for this game and everything that comes with it was appauling. Some truly disheartening business practices there. Secondly this game is no Arkham city. The level design, pacing, and tone are simply not on par.
However there are many other things that this game does extremely well. Each Arkham game manages to fit into the universe yet also have it's own identity. Asylum was a haunted house, City had an decayed industrial feel, and this game plays out almost as Batman: Chrismas Carol, which given the tone and morals of this game is very appropriate. Additionally it's the only game that gives Bruce Wane himself has a main story ark. Like Arkham Kinght he is bitter, impussive and arogant... the difference being is that you really get the sense that it is intentional here. Batman is suppose to be a flawed broken man in this game, with a reasonable (but occationally cliched) ark bout him learning about responsibility and the improtance of his friends an allies. Then there is Batman's dynamic with the main villian of this game, without spoiling too much... it's near perfect. Truly memorable moments and dialougue which manage to be both terryfying and halarious at the same time with a legitimately good stroy ark. It's the only time the game outshone the other arkham games.
So overall I do give it a tentative recommendation. It is not as good as Asylum or City, but has enough going for it to still be worthwhile in it's own right.

Escape from Puzzlegate is a game designed for children. It's cute. But it has a major flaw: there are very few actual puzzles in this game, despite the title.
There are four areas to visit. In each area, there is a key that makes opening the door easier. The first has an extremely simple side-scroller level; the second has an extremely simple find-the-obvious-object section; the third has an extremely simple maze section. The kicker is that the fourth area, one of the few parts of the game that actually has a puzzle-ish feel to it, has controls that are way more complicated than it needs to be. So there's three easy non-puzzles and one annoyingly complicated "puzzle", which not what I would expect from the title, especially if it's for children.
The "puzzlegate" itself is a simple sliding blocks puzzle with a time limit. Collecting more keys increases the time limit. It is possible to beat the door without collecting a single key and without ever meeting your cute little brown Sphinx companion. However, the dialogue afterwards still assumes that you're friends with the Sphinx character.  Stuff like this shows that the developer didn't really flesh out the design enough.
The game's cute though.

Gameplay :
FPS with rpg elements. You pick one of six characters and go on a rampage on the planet of pandora, alone co-op. The characters have the same story-line but are very diverse and you should do yourself a favour and try them all out.
The main-plot isn't overly long but the optional content make this a behemoth and that's a good thing. It means if you can unlock the higher modes (3 modes in total) for better loot and nastier enemies and if you overreach, you can always go back to the easier modes.
Although you can play with up to 4 people, mostly I play solo and I'm not missing anything.
Story :
Borderlands refuses to take itself seriously and almost all characters are batshit insane. The story is secondary to all the crazy quests and that's a good thing, because humour and pure gameplay is where BL2 shines. In that respect it's old school.
Loot : Tons, although in later levels (40/50 +) I wish it was better. This is where RNG turns into a bit of a troll.
Consistently funny, easy to pick up, intuitive controls and tons of content.
Do yourself a favour and pick up the complete set during a sale.

There's a lot to like about Super Meat Boy. The gameplay is generally fun, and the perfect difficulty to make you want to keep going without completely demoralizing you. It takes a second to learn and many many hours to master. The art style and menus are very appealing too.
However, there are a bunch of frustrating aspects of this game that can make it downright maddening to play. Here's an incomplete list:
1) My computer is far above the minimum requirements to run this game, and there is a noticeable input lag in full screen mode. I have been forced to run it in windowed mode at 1024x600 resolution, and there's STILL a slight lag.
2) Meat Boy spawns about three inches above the ground, meaning that after you restart a level you can't begin sprinting until he falls. If you try to run early, you often end up skidding off an edge, into an obstacle, etc. The more times you have to retry a level, the more frustrating this becomes.
3) Whenever Meat Boy *barely* touches a flat surface (i.e. half of his body is on, half is off) he sticks to it, but cannot jump off of it. I have died this way hundreds of times, and there's no reason for it. I thought it was just the input lag at first, but after over 20 hours of play time I'm pretty sure it's just not possible.
4) When you die from a saw, the edges of the saw become red. This makes sense, but it causes them to blend into the background in some of the levels, particularly in the Hell world. One solution would be to outline the saw blades in white so they remain visible.
5) When you jump, hit a diagonal wall, and end up on a vertical wall, Meat Boy will slide straight up the wall when you hit the jump button without indicating a direction instead of jumping out from the wall as he would normally. It's as if the game thinks he's standing at the base of the wall.
6) In warp zones and glitched levels, the retry time is irritatingly long. You have to wait a few seconds every time you die while it reminds you how many lives you have. Furthermore, when you get a game over and wish to restart, it takes about 10 seconds to get back to the first level instead of giving you an option to retry from the game over screen. This also gets more and more frustrating the more times you have to retry a level.
7) In warp zones and glitched levels, some of the hit boxes inaccurate. I've been able to stand inside saw blades, and I've died from spikes I did not actually hit.
With some small changes to address issues like these, this game would be one of my favorites in the genre. As it stands, I'm going to beat it and never touch it again. In a game that requires this much precision, flaws like these make it unnecessarily rage-inducing. If you love games in this genre, buy it. If not, I'd say that it's frustrating to be worth it, especially if you're like me and tend to like to 100% games.

When I saw this browsing through steam store, I had this bizarre, weird impulse that I *should* buy this game. I think a part of me always roots for obscure underdogs and amateurs looking for big breaks -- I'm that kind of person too. I'm inclined to give those people a shot like I would want others to.
So this a puzzle adventure game for kids, it'll give an adult about an hour of enjoyment. The draw is admittedly, not the gameplay, but the cute artwork and innocent storyline. It opens up with a surprisingly well-rendered intro with some pretty good character modeling. It's a cute story about a kid who gets trapped in some magical world, and befriends a sphinx. They go on adventures in different parts of the world. The sphinx character is absolutely cute, I can't imagine any kid not being charmed by it. Much of the other character art really is very nice and clean. I like that the game has themes about assertiveness and sticking up for oneself, not just about being nice. If I was a parent I wouldn't have any issues with the themes.
The puzzles themselves unfortunately lack good implementation. A lot of the issues could be solved by using a grid, the pixel-based movement (if that's the word for it) is really more than you need and makes things feel a little janky. There are only five puzzles, and only one of them is what I'd consider a real "puzzle". It's where you rearrange centipede-like creatures to build a bridge, and it would be very interesting had the developers spent some time refining it. It is especially disappointing because I was initially reminded of puzzle adventure games my childhood, like Logical Journey of Zoombinis or Island of Dr. Quandry, and Escape from Puzzlegate isn't really even comparable. In a game for kids, things need to be a lot more user friendly.
But, this is $2, and that's important. Had Escape from Puzzlegate been $10, I would have thumbed it down without blinking. But it is very cute, $2 worth of cute in fact, so I'm happy with the time I've spent with it. A modest suggestion to the developer. If:
a) The puzzles were redone on a grid.
b) The puzzles were made more user friendly.
c) There was some level of replayability.
then Escape from Puzzlegate would be an absolute no-brainer. You clearly have the art skills, I would just love to see solid implementation.

Let me start off this review by saying that I personally know the developer of this game. She is a real sweetheart and makes amazing games with the Renpy engine!
Puzzlegate, at first glance, may not turn a lot of heads. If you take a closer look, however, you'll find that the game has more than one challenging puzzle if you don't pay close attention. The difficulty is nicely balanced, the art is colorful and cheerful, and you'll grow to love each and every character! Aside from a few overworld bugs, this game is definetely worth your time and I highly reccommend giving Escape from Puzzlegate a try!

I've spent quite a bit of time playing this game. Thus, I think it is time I finally review it.
Prison Architect, for those who don't know, and can't guess by the name of the game -- is a game where you build, and develop a Prison-like facility. When first starting, you're thrown in to the 'campaign' which for honesty's sake, we'll just call it a tutorial, which it is. There you will learn the basics of the game, building, plumbing, electrical work, etc. The 'campaign' does have a tiny bit of story, which I found to be quite enjoyable and help influence me to build prisons the way I do.
After you've finished the tutorial, you will be thrown right into making your very own prison! There are a few different methods of building. Some people like to go for the Warlord approach, throwing your Prisoners into tiny cells with the absolute bare minimum. Or, you see people who make beautiful rehabilitation centers that help their Prisoners grow into successful members of society.
All in all, I love this game. Which is why I have over 500 hours played. I would absolutely recommend this to anyone looking for a fun game.

- A very complex mechanic in which you can go very in-depth and modify punishments, schedules (example: you could make a maximum security prisoner eat lunch, shower and excerise at a different time than all the other prisoners to avoid conflict)
- An optional gang mechanic to give the game more realism.
- Each & every prisoner has a family & a personality (Prisoners who have commited the crime of murder in the past will actually be more likely to kill as someone who went to prison for burgulry.)

NEUTRAL:
- The technology tree is simple, which can be good & bad, but could use some more stuff, at the moment there's not much to it & I don't think the game developers plan on updating the game soon.
CONS:
- Early - Midgame can be boring at times.
- A.I. movement is strange at certain moments.
- Prisoners will complain about wanting to take a dump when there's a toilet 2 feet away from them.
- (Nitpicking) The patrol system is a bit over-complicated in my opinion.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall though, I'd give the game a 9.5/10, it's a very well-made game, I just htink some things could be added, such as an infection breaking out in the prison, you maybe some criminals try to bust out their friend by using sneaky tactics.

Where do I start?
A single game developer soon embarking on his second I believe. I can't say I'm that hopeful after attempting this one after several tries. Anyway he can be found here...
Graphics overall is set out to be charming and won me over. Sound and music always fitting and adds to the overall atmosphere. Light hearted humor throughout the game bringing the odd smile or two to my face. Game play consists of a turn based RPG which records your history of your numerous attempts which is always fascinating to glance over. All this revolves around a paper thin story involving your customized friends being kidnapped and needing to be rescued. The settings take you to a school yard and then a cemetery creating a very quirky style backdrop for the simple to understand story. So if all these things are a plus why do I give it a solid thumbs down?
It's ROGUE as rogue can be. (Sad face) and the developer seems adamant to keep it that way regardless of the countless throngs of customers which have already requested an easier progressive mode to be added to the game. SERIOUSLY... the game apparently takes 4 hrs which I have never seen, because after two hours in I come across an unfair room while I have nothing left to defend myself with and unable to back out, I die. No saves once your dead. No chapter reloads. No progressive leveling with your next character having slightly higher stats. No siree your back to the start to have to grind through the whole thing again just to get back to the same bleeding spot and die. After 10 hrs of game play and several psychiatric visits (self admitted) and several correspondence with the developer, your left with shrugged shoulders and the puzzling question as to why on this planet would a game developer who wants to be recognized pick a niche market (turn style rpg) and further limit its appeal by making it COMPLETELY ROGUE??? Who has time for that? Gamer's have lives! Jobs! Family! Why would you not ALSO add an easier mode???
But alas he does not believe in the golden principle of 'Customers are always right!'... So while hundreds camp outside the developers fortress brandishing pitchforks and torches, over turning cars setting them alight and shouting give us what we want or we will start storming the walls. He lies with deaf ears in the bowels of the dungeon creating another....
I think someone else said it best with their review of the game and I wholeheartedly concur with this statement that they made. It is as follows...
'If it comes across i'm bitter. I am. I wanted to enjoy this game. I cannot.'

Astroneer has a great atmosphere, wind blowing, dust flying through the air, marshmellow clouds that are enjoyable to look at and overall view of space is out-of-this-world. Astroneer developers have proven their superiority over Open World Space genres. In Early Access, Astroneer has quite the beautiful content and overall satisfaction of what I would want in another open world space game.
Read at your own risk as there's spoilers below.
Before you even start playing, the smoothness and look of the main menu is quite fantastic. I believe in first impressions and I hope Astroneer's first impression didn't fail you because it didn't fail me. Even the game save is a drop-pod you use to start playing the game. In the beginning you start by choosing a drop-pod and you launch it. As you're launched you come down from space onto your very first planet - you can look around at the scenery while you fall too!
Afterwards, you land and it goes through the basic controls - basic controls are very, well, "basic". After you understand the basics, the game will point you towards the most common resources: Resin & Compound. At first I didn't notice it showing me that I needed to mine those materials, but after I played the game and started a new save I saw that it did.
The mining tool is very neat and has many options. It mines very smoothly and you can mine down or repair the holes you dug. Generally, the mining tool terrain manipulation is the best. I fell in love with the mining system when I first used the tool.
Building a base in Astroneer is very simple but requires materials. Once you have these materials there's no limits. Expand your base however you feel. There's different types of structures you can create, but the true structures comes from research. Researching unlocks more structures or you can find items within these "unknown" objects. Unknown objects sometimes aren't hard to find; however, it could be risky at times.
Caves are rich and mysterious places to explore. Not knowing what is lurking around the corner at you, in caves there's hostiles and they will kill you when they have a chance. Luckily they are stationary hostiles, meaning they don't move towards you to deal damage, but most do have ranged attacks. These hostiles, however, hold one of the most precious items: unknown.
Rovers, trucks down to spaceships, you can make them all! Exploration is another fabulous thing about Astroneer. After farming your heart out and finally building that spaceship, it is truly amazing to go exploring. Given there's a small ship, and it doesn't go far, but the Spaceship can go anywhere. Each planet type has a different experience, but I'll let you find that out for yourself.
With each planet's experience there's also survivability. Oxygen levels, hostiles and dust storms can kill you and I have been a victim to them all. Dust storms are visually fantastic. You can even see storms make their way towards you from a distance or away from you, barely missing you.
You're probably wondering about coop. Well, that's all I played in my 12h playtime. It is very fun with friends, but also very buggy. You can join your friends by them sending you a game invitation or by you joining their game by their name. Although, here's the thing about Astroneer and friends; Anybody can join your game if they are your friend and have Astroneer. If they could add some type of password or invite only option, it would make my experience much better without randoms joining my games.
Even though I'm talking highly about Astroneer, let's not forget it is in Early Access and has its issues, issues like friends sometimes not able to join games, falling through the world, rovers, trucks and objects disappearing on other planets. There's more but I'll stop there. Hopefully some of these issues will be addressed soon so we can have an even better experience..if it can get any better than it already is!
I cannot recommend Astroneer more. Hopefully they really stick to development and add more content because I've done all I can!

Okay... I may have just logged 23 minutes of this game so far, but I might as well as talk about this...
I'll go ahead and start with an overview. This game is essentially about an astronaut who crashed his ship on the moon (or Mars) and is stranded. With five signals spread all across the surface of the moon (or Mars), and your O2 tank running low, you need to make the long and perilous treck across, and hope you can survive an onslaught of space rocks plummiting to the ground.
Well, where do I begin? There are so many good and bad things about this game. And with a story like that, you would think it would be stellar. An absolute gem. And to some extent, it is! It is a decent time waister, so if you're bored, you can boot this up for a quick go. Not to mention, it is pretty. It captures the near barren landscape of the moon rather well.
Also, lets not forget the setup. As I thought about it, it is a scary thought, getting stranded on a lunar body, millions of miles from Earth, with NO way of communicating than one out of five strange signals. It's pretty terrifying.
However, there are bugs in this game. LOTS. One that I can see that is pretty game breaking is God's invisible wall, which stops you after a certain point. You get blocked, and you can either return, or simply just return to the space craft and wait for your oxygen to run out.
Speaking of the oxygen, that is a nice feature. And it's depletion is rather slow, making for enough time to get to your objective. However, once you recah an objective, you gotta figure out what to do. I haven't found a single button on my keyboard that allows for you to interact, so that's pretty bad.
A fun feature is the meteor shower. That's pretty fun. Running across the moon (or Mars) as large meatballs of rock rain down from the sky is pretty fun. That is, if you figure how to run. There isn't a sprint mechanic, and that's understandable, space suit, duh. But, yeah, it's still nice.
People have said that they've been getting hit by invisible meteors. Not really, it's just your oxygen going down. I know, seems strange, as it's the smae thing as a damage indicator, but oh well.
Since this is in Early access, I say don't be too harsh on it, but don't be a panzy about what you think. It may (or may not) get better by the time it's fully released. As it stands now, yeah, I like it. Do I recommend it? Yeah, you can try it out, give a run through. It's free, looks decent, and runs pretty decently, even on my PC, so, it's worth a try. Just don't get Mars unless your REALLY want to, it's $3.00.

It has its issues - it becomes a glorified idler after a bit, there's nothing you can do to avoid your hand-grown generation 3 tenants skipping town after a bit, some monsters are plain awful - but it's addicting.
It's mostly an apartment simulator - you fit out your rooms with items, and monsters move in and pay you rent.
Then you've got a strategy game thing where adventurers attack you and you call upon the monsters to kill them. It's surprisingly addictive to spend time upgrading your rooms, getting happy tenants, helping them find partners and have kids, then kicking them out so their kids can take over with superior stats.
The idler part is that often it's better to let it run on speed 3 a bit and deal with occasional raids whilst people heal, pay you rent, and you upgrade their rooms...and hope that they don't run into financial issues and not have rent money.
The monster bit is a bit annoying with regards to variety. There's 6 races and each like different things, but some monsters (any Undead) are just far better than others (Cheepies, who are utter garbage). It's fun to try and organise who you have, but there's clear patterns as to what is good and what is not.

I've been an avid video-gamer for more than thirty-years, both on PC and console, and I'm a very harsh critic.
I don't generally waste my time writing reviews for games that are mediocre or just "OK". My reviews will either be very positive or very negative.
However, in the case of Lunch Truck Tycoon things are a little different. Although I anticipated I would need more time to write a fair review, I only required 30 minutes of gameplay, as shown on my record.
The game is only $0.99 USD. Sometimes we get what we pay for, but in this case, Lunch Truck Tycoon offers just a little more than $0.99 of entertainment.
I've would've gladly paid $20.00 for this game if there had been more strategy and customization options.
I hope that the developer has plans to expand on this game. I would definitely like to see some improvements via purchasable "add-on's" that increase the need for more strategy, and add more customization. Lunch Truck Tycoon should've been an "Early Access" game.
Will we see a Lunch Truck Tycoon 2 in the future? I hope so!
The development of "Food Truck" themed games has been neglected and is, in my opinion, an untapped oil well that would seriously appeal to the people who enjoy playing "simulation, management, strategy" games.
The game's artwork/graphics are of moderate quality. The animation and gameplay are smooth and moderately clean.
In closing, if you can afford $0.99 USD, buy the game and support an indie developer! In return, you'll receive a little more entertainment than what you paid for, and you can't have a legitimate complaint about that.

I like doing collectibles when they are put on the map and I don’t have to go hunting for them. I think WB Montreal should have took a leaf out of Rocksteady’s book for this also. The game also suffers from a few bad design choices I feel, for example the worst nightmare challenge tier. This does not have enough predator rooms available in my opinion to carry this out. It’s as if they want you to play new game+ which I guess I understand but I would rather be able to do it all in one playthrough. The tiers themselves should unlock as you do them not in order because that is just dragging them out and making them unnecessarily more complicated.

I have played Prison Architect since I backed it over 5 years ago. Since Alpha 2, I have seen the game evolve, features come and go, modding, and finally now were upto update 12.
I can say that I've easily had my moneys' worth with PA, and I love Introversion's other games to bits. However I cannot recommend Prison Architect for £20.
The game still feels unfinished, with many bugs and limitations still plaguing core systems such as staffing. It is too easy to encouter or create glitches by accident, and the continual addition of other complex processes on top of already complicated procedures has continued to add to the problem.
Many of the added systems also feel half-finished, and UI/menu interfaces are still at the same standard as they were through much of the alpha process. Modding has never really been able to flourish either with the same restrictions existing now, that did over 2 years ago.
I really want to recommend, but it would appear that Chris is bored with PA (and I don't blame him, its been over 7 years since the game was concieved). However the bugs and general lack of polish prevent me from saying yes.

Astroneer has a great atmosphere, wind blowing, dust flying through the air, marshmellow clouds that are enjoyable to look at and overall view of space is out-of-this-world. Astroneer developers have proven their superiority over Open World Space genres. In Early Access, Astroneer has quite the beautiful content and overall satisfaction of what I would want in another open world space game.
Read at your own risk as there's spoilers below.
Before you even start playing, the smoothness and look of the main menu is quite fantastic. I believe in first impressions and I hope Astroneer's first impression didn't fail you because it didn't fail me. Even the game save is a drop-pod you use to start playing the game. In the beginning you start by choosing a drop-pod and you launch it. As you're launched you come down from space onto your very first planet - you can look around at the scenery while you fall too!
Afterwards, you land and it goes through the basic controls - basic controls are very, well, "basic". After you understand the basics, the game will point you towards the most common resources: Resin & Compound. At first I didn't notice it showing me that I needed to mine those materials, but after I played the game and started a new save I saw that it did.
The mining tool is very neat and has many options. It mines very smoothly and you can mine down or repair the holes you dug. Generally, the mining tool terrain manipulation is the best. I fell in love with the mining system when I first used the tool.
Building a base in Astroneer is very simple but requires materials. Once you have these materials there's no limits. Expand your base however you feel. There's different types of structures you can create, but the true structures comes from research. Researching unlocks more structures or you can find items within these "unknown" objects. Unknown objects sometimes aren't hard to find; however, it could be risky at times.
Caves are rich and mysterious places to explore. Not knowing what is lurking around the corner at you, in caves there's hostiles and they will kill you when they have a chance. Luckily they are stationary hostiles, meaning they don't move towards you to deal damage, but most do have ranged attacks. These hostiles, however, hold one of the most precious items: unknown.
Rovers, trucks down to spaceships, you can make them all! Exploration is another fabulous thing about Astroneer. After farming your heart out and finally building that spaceship, it is truly amazing to go exploring. Given there's a small ship, and it doesn't go far, but the Spaceship can go anywhere. Each planet type has a different experience, but I'll let you find that out for yourself.
With each planet's experience there's also survivability. Oxygen levels, hostiles and dust storms can kill you and I have been a victim to them all. Dust storms are visually fantastic. You can even see storms make their way towards you from a distance or away from you, barely missing you.
You're probably wondering about coop. Well, that's all I played in my 12h playtime. It is very fun with friends, but also very buggy. You can join your friends by them sending you a game invitation or by you joining their game by their name. Although, here's the thing about Astroneer and friends; Anybody can join your game if they are your friend and have Astroneer. If they could add some type of password or invite only option, it would make my experience much better without randoms joining my games.
Even though I'm talking highly about Astroneer, let's not forget it is in Early Access and has its issues, issues like friends sometimes not able to join games, falling through the world, rovers, trucks and objects disappearing on other planets. There's more but I'll stop there. Hopefully some of these issues will be addressed soon so we can have an even better experience..if it can get any better than it already is!
I cannot recommend Astroneer more. Hopefully they really stick to development and add more content because I've done all I can!

The graphics and the other aspects of the presentation are good, especially the "notepaper" style UI.
As a roguelike it's a simple and fun one. It's still a lot more challenging that you'd expect given the "child-friendly" look of it. By simple I mean for example you don't have an inventory as such, you can just swap stuff you find with whatever you have in that slot, you can only fire ranged weapons in the 8 main directions rather than free targetting- things like that.
What the game badly needs in my opinion is ability to move and attack with the keyboard instead of the mouse. There's too much clicking for me. Basically if there's "danger" with nearby monsters you have to click once for every square you move. When you attack monsters you have to click once for every attack.
I have asked the devs if support would be added for movement and attacking via keyboard and they said "Because we have a cursor, keyboard controls were too clunky. You can hold down left click to move, when safe". As a roguelike developer myself I'm not happy with this answer so I can't recommend it.

Crayon Chronicles offers a relatively short (2-4 hours per play-through) but action-packed RPG experience that randomly generates the level layouts each time you play.
You are encouraged to play through the game more than once thanks to the random nature of the environment layouts, but also because we keep track of the interesting facts about each play-through (in our newfangled "Heroic Hallitorium") so you can compare your adventures to each other as well as to the adventures of your friends.
As the story goes, your friends have been kidnapped (tragic, I know), but as it so happens, you are brave enough to attempt their rescue. With help from a "stranger" you are soon set on the path to their salvation from the despicable Lord of the Swampyards, Stratolustrious Von Danderbeak the 37th (or Strato for short, his name is a mouth-full). If you succeed in rescuing your friends and bringing down the Swampyard Tyrant, then glory, satisfaction, and maybe a nap await you.  - Recommended!

7/10 game overall.
+Stages and music are extremely well designed.
+Very well optimized PC port (ran it at 144 fps with zero issues, specs are on my profile).
+Enemy/boss design is top notch.
+Difficulty levels are very well balanced.
+-Streamlined combat compared to the original DMC titles. If you're a fan of DMC3 or 4 and have sunk a good bit of time into either game, you'll feel extremely limited in this one. The combo depth of Style Switcher DMC3 Dante or DMC4SE Dante/Vergil just isn't possible in DmC with the weapons you're given.
+-Significantly easier to obtain and hold a SSS rank combo than previous titles.
-Character designs. I don't even know where to start here. Dante was never intended to be a serious character, but in the originals, he was overly sarcastic and had a lot of well placed witty one liners. This iteration of Dante, while not terrible visually, just has some of the absolute WORST voice lines in a modern video game. (see: ♥♥♥♥ YOU on YouTube) Also, Vergil unironically wears a fedora.
-Color coded enemies. This is an absolutely horrendous choice for a spectacle fighter that is combo based, because several of Dante's "new" weapons in this game have little to no combo potential or cancelling mechanic. Older DMC games featured enemies that would take less damage from certain attacks, but not outright invulnerable. Red weapons (the "heavy" weapons, if you will) in particular feel absolutely useless, and when the game spawns red-coded enemies that will NOT take any damage from any non-red weapon, it's more or less a giant middle finger to having fun.
-One of the worst, most anticlimactic final bosses I've ever fought in a video game.
-Vergil's DLC, while being a really interesting plot concept, is incredibly short and feels like it was rushed in development.
tl;dr it's a very good spectacle fighter, but it's a bad DMC game. It's a good buy on sale.
