While the idea of being a landlord is enticing the tower-defense part can get incredibly tedious & repetitious since there's not a whole lot of strategy to use here from beginning to end.
The idea of the tower-defense is just to stop humans from stealing your money and if they get away with it you only lose your highly expendable tenant should they have died defending the money taken so there's no real fail state. You try and stop the humans by knocking on the room doors of the monsters of your choosing and IF they're home (which most usually are) they'll do their tower-defense thing and help kill the intruders.
As you get further into the game you're able to invite specific higher tier monsters depending on what monster race you've been appealing to or otherwise. To get further into the game & earn faster money though you've got to go do quests from a quest board. While every quest grants you money there are quests that unlock new monsters for you to be able to have in your apartment, quests that unlock a new piece of furniture you can buy for your tenants, and main quests that finally allow you to expand your apartment one floor at a time. The downside to this though is that every quest from side to important are essentially all the same "stop the humans" only with varying wave numbers and a few human types with soon to be higher stats. Whatever strategy you had against weaker humans you can do the exact same thing against the stronger humans with stronger monsters in somewhat bigger numbers because the monsters you get aren't entirely different either aside from the stats when it comes to being useful in defending.
The landlord simulator part is at least more intriguing. The job is primarily housing interested monsters of your choosing and appealing to their tastes by adding or improving things in their apartment, sometimes specifically when needed as some monsters prefer having certain items in the room depending on their race and/or job.
It's a bit more taxing to house monsters when you have a certain race that's disliked by another race living in the same structure. You can still appeal to both but getting them to all be satisfied in their living quarters would take much longer.
There's a maximum of 3 vacancies per room where each vacancy specifically houses one tenant, that tenant's lover, and those two's child. So long as one tenant in a room is satisfied and alive they'll eventually find a lover and conceive a child who will also grow up for you to take money from. If the child dies another child will be conceived by the parents. If a parent dies the other parent will find another lover. If both parents die then the grown-up spawn will eventually find a lover of their own and eventually conceive their own child. I'm not sure what happens if both parents die while the child remains a child. As all the tenants in one room are old enough they usually find jobs of their own which is supposed to be a good incentive for raising their rent.
The room upgrading is incredibly bare & simple which leads to a few questionable things. For example upgrading a two-door fridge apparently grants the room a BBQ set and upgrading that gets it a built-in kitchen. You can buy a tenant a game console and/or a PC tower for their room but I find it a bit odd that you're not exactly buying it for
but for the room itself, and you don't even have to buy them a television for the consoles as far as I've seen.
Depending on how fancy a room is and what the current tenant's job is you can adjust rent to their's and your pleasing. Certain monsters though are less likely to even want to pay rent even if you set it to an incredible low. You can evict them for being deadbeats, wait a bit longer to see if they come up with the money, or wait for them to run away from paying you.
The game itself sounds better off as an idle-game somewhat but unfortunately alt + tabbing even when the game's a small window pauses the entire thing. It was pretty nice trying to be a landlord for monsters but with how tediously bland progress is I can't entirely like the game even for its cheap price.

This review will not be short but will be based on only the most important points. Don't be fooled by the hours on record, since I have almost a 100+ hours offline record and due to internet limitations, I mostly play in offline mode.
1. PRICE.
Buy only on discount. DLCs too.
2. PERFORMANCE.
Some areas are not very well optimized (by that I mean horribly), minor stuttering (it can get to irritating), and many FPS fluctuations. You certainly need a decent rig (a little beefier than the official specs). Other than that ,beautifull graphics, not in the area of textures but  mostly lighting effects and colour pallete. Performance will be stable, for the most part, according to your settings and system specs and the engine is decent to provide a silk smooth experience (with some exceptions, as always, and by that I mean quite enough). For reference I run this game on an HD 7790 1GB VRAM, AMD FX-8320, 8GB RAM on 1366x768 (HDMI). In game, GPU has a 100% usage score, VRAM usage almost always spikes, RAM is nothing really worth mentioning and CPU has about a 30% usage score. With most settings in ultra, with vsync and aa on, and all NVIDIA settings off, I get a... decent... experience of 60-45-30 FPS ,where in some badly optimised areas FPS drop to 15-10, minor to irritating stuttering, mostly in combat and long distance gliding, leaving me no choice but to lower my video settings on medium and finally have a butter (still makes it to the point but not like silk) smooth more than decent experience.
3. PLOT AND WORLD.
Enjoyable but without interesting plot twists. Very nice dark atmosphere though and gives you the "I am the Batman feeling". A mix of realism and fantasy. Beautifull and large areas, indoors and outoors, for a Batman game (in summary the size of a small city) and nicely tailored to the game plot. The music is dark themed and suits the game nicely, as expected, and the soundtrack team based the most distinct of the tracks on the kind of melody pattern  the "To Hard to Die" movie features.
4. COMBAT MECHANICS.
Standard, enjoyable beat them up style, quite fashionable, straightforward and inspired by realistic martial arts executions. Batman can upgrade his combat moves and also add some more complex ones. Batman is Batman though, so things get spicy too (to the point "That's impossible!?!" "Well DUUHHH he is BATMAN!!!").
5. EXECUTION.
The game is still plagued by bugs and glitches that depend on lack on how, when and if they appear. There are also one or two game progression breaking bugs that randomly appear..... The bugs also concern combat input lag, thug K.O. ability, gadgets utility, graphical glitches, getting stuck in rooms and all kind of things like that. It's uncommon for every buge to appear in a single installation, but WB Montreal stated that they are never going to fix them, so you will have to bear with them if you happen uppon them, or even restart the story from scratch.
6. MULTIPLAYER AND DLCs.
The multiplayer is a feature that never got popular and it's unlikely to find anyone playing it, since the servers have been shut down.... But it was playable. The DLC worth mentioning is the Cold Cold Heart. Skins and challenge maps are as always not really worth to buy, but if someone is a huge fan than he/she can go forward and buy them. Cold Cold Heart is a decent DLC, almost worth it's price. NVIDIA users be aware that the DLC is not optimized to provide the extra graphics candy the base game already has. But all in all is a worthy addition for it's plot and new areas.
7. SUMMARY.
I will rate this product with a 6/10 because of it's many bugs and glitches that keep me from enjoying it to it's max, the "ok but just that" plot, many small details that make it look and feel that it was rushed by an inexperienced studio and was mostly a milk attempt and finally because random dialogues have no subtitles. I am fluent in English but it still bugs me. Overall a nice game that is just that. Trying to make it Rocksteady level of polish but failing blatantly. If you are a die hard fan of Batman you will buy it anywhay, so no point arguing with you! But if you are just a humble gamer looking for a Batman game to have a good time, I kindly implore you to look for another title of the Arkham series. But I already said it's a nice game....right?!?
*I can't recommend it over the Rocksteady titles. You are better off playing those. So it's a "NO".

I played Borderlands 1 alot. And I really mean it - ALOT. Because the first one was a
extreme success for me, I had to get my hands on BL2 inc. all DLCs.
I played BL2 alot as well. But it will never break my time playing BL1.
Quickrating: 1/5
BL1 looting is 1000% better than BL2 looting.
BL1 weapons: powerful, exciting, alot decent drops
BL2 weapons: weak as ****, extremely boring, barely decent drops
BL2 is a tryhard BL1. Would rather buy BL1 5x than BL2 1x.
------------------------------------
Appearance 2/5:
In general the graphics are okay. Some map and object textures are messed up but I got used to it. Borderlands never wanted to be the highlevel graphics showoff game. The weapons' look is to 90% an odd piece of hightech or WW1 bull****. The other 10% are okay to very nice but all weapons should be at least 50% smaller. Characters are well designed. Sadly most of the maps get boring soon. There's not much structure and alot empty space in this world.
Differences in BL1: Almost only awesome looking guns, well structured map with far more action.
Bad shader effects/effects in general.
Story/Missions and NPCs 4/5:
The story is very entertaining. That was the main reason for me to play BL2 (sadly tbh.).
It's a nice idea to let the player have Echo-contact with the main antagonist. It makes me feel
less lonely and I get the impression that everything I do has a purpose and an effect. I appreciate that they actually made alot of content.The big plus are the crazy characters e.g. Claptrap, Elli, Torgue (DLC), Tina and the main antagonist. They are all funny in their own way. My favourite NPC is Torgue. A muscleman with a fitness-hardcore-manliness-style and a sometimes unfitting childish behaviour.The sidemissions' fun rating also get pushed by the NPCs who are connected with the mission.On the other side they screwed up the old characters from BL1 who were far cooler than they appear now in BL2
Differences in BL1: Less funny characters but more coolness factor. Worse storyline compared to BL2.
Equipment/Skilltrees 0/5:
Wowowow... what's that? 0/5? Yep. They messed up almost everything in this point.
There are soooo many useless skills in the skilltrees. But it doesn't end here:
The active skills have a range from extemely useless to extremely overpowered.
Look at the Soldier with 2 overpowered Sentryguns and compare it with the gunzerker with the useless dualwield active or the siren whos skill is as dangerous and useful as a broken stick of wood. The guns are extremely unbalanced. Assault Rifles suck so hard that Melee is an option.
SMGs suck so hard that I dont even pick them up. Snipers and pistols are the only usable weapons. Is that all? No. They screwed up the lootscaling aswell. You want a surprising drop with a weapon that actually does some awesome damage? Well BL2 has 12038 Zillion weapons. Almost all are useless junk. You never get the feeling that you've found something that really makes a difference.
Difference in BL1: One of the best looting system in games. useful skilltrees, actives are bad to medium.
Enemies/AI/difficulty (3/5):
You'll get enough enemy-types you can shoot to keep you entertained. Almost every area has new types of enemies. This makes the game more diverse and alive (although it still has its flaws with this point). To be honest: There are alot of enemies which are annoying like the flying repair-robots or some insects. The AI is 100% dumb as ****. But hey... I never wanted a hyperintelligent, cover searching enemy here. It's absolutely fitting for BL2. No complaints regarding the AI. The difficulty is apporpriate - there's no exciting point to tell about.
Differences in BL1: Less enemy variety, but better quality in general.
conclusion (1/5):
The game has alot of content, has funny parts and feels 'well made'. But the whole thing lacks in the most important part: The equipment and the skilltrees. This is THE reason why I bought BL2. I wanted more awesome guns. I got disappointed like never before. The differences between BL1 and BL2 in this point are extremely high. For everyone who looked for a worthy sequel of BL1: DO NOT BUY THIS - IT'S A ****ING TRAP! For everyone who never played BL1 before and likes MMORPG-like gameplay as a FPS: Buy it, you'll be happy with it.

Ori and the Blind Forest is not very good.
As a metroidvania, it has a fairly expansive map and movement based upgrades. The sheer number of abilities and the placement of the buttons is bad enough as it is, but it gets worse. Some of the mobility upgrades are virtually the same as others, but don't replace them. Other abilities use the same button.
Somehow pushing rocks was the worst part of the entire game, with little exaggeration. If you have a two-stage trigger, Ori does what she wants whenever she wants and there is nothing you can do about it. Sorry.
The combat consists of walking away from enemies and mashing the attack button. While there is a charge attack, it's pretty bad and uses the same resource that you use to create save points, so I can't imagine ever using it. You get exp for killing enemies to use on your "skill tree"; I don't know what to call a tree with three branches, other than sad. Especially considering the damage increases and the quality-of-life mobility upgrades are the only things worth considering.
Somehow, the story is both unremarkable and unlikable.
I wish I could say that the graphics are a redeeming factor, but the screen waving and shaking and glowing constantly is not for everyone. Personally, I found myself missing things because everything seems to blend into everything else. It really doesn't help that your constant companion is a glowing ball that looks like enemy projectiles.
Speaking of, your friend helpfully points out everything you pick up even though you have ten times before. Thanks.
tl;dr: skip borey and the blind snorefest and pick up hollow knight

For such a simple little game, it's remarkably fun.
Figuring out how to balance pleasing your tenants, charging rent within their budget and locating them in strategic locations depending on if they have melee, medium range or long range attacks all while trying to unlock new stronger monsters makes for a game with a fairly balanced complexity, allowing players the time they might need to figure out the best techniques, while still offering a challenge to those who want to progress faster.
You also get quite a lot of interesting stories unfolding within this game, an example being my Flowery family. Five generations they lived in one room. Occasionally a parent or child dying in the battle against the humans, only fuelling their rage in the next clash of leaf against blade. One day though, on a thundering night the youngest newborn Flowery lay cowering in the corner of his room, listening to his parents fighting outside his door. Screams, yells and finally silence, for no one returned to his room that day. His parents had fallen in battle, and left their mark on his soul.
Fast forward, and he's all grown up now, heading to get his first job and to my surprise he comes back with the title of 'Bondage Master'.
The next day he was promoted to 'Pimp'.
He's filling a void, I can tell.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

Quite enjoy this game. Its strongest point, to me, is its pinpoint controls; no wasted motion, no sliding, no committed-length jumps. Controller support is on point, too. This is a standard-bearer for platformer controls.
The aesthetic is fun and colorful, attacks are flashy and the destruction animations/sfx are crunchy and satisfying in a way that even Megaman X wasn't.
There are two comparisons being made, though, that aren't quite apt: Megaman X and the Binding of Isaac.
Compared with Isaac, the item pool feels painfully shallow. The game boasts 100+ items, but many of them fall under basic stat increases. Almost nothing in the item pool will define a run, will change the way you approach the game significantly. In Isaac, a player might start a run and find a powerup that makes every shot explode; this vastly changes how the player will engage enemies. 20XX is limited by its jump-n-shoot nature in that regard.
Additionally, powerups don't quite synergize the way they do in Isaac. Rather, they seem to just stack as the player grows into a much more powerful version of the same Nina they started with. Sure there are double jumps and such, but there aren't really alternate paths a double jump could make available. Why? Because not every run will have a double jump.
The level design has to exist, even in procedural generation, such that the player can get to everything with the basic kit. It feels like there are no secrets to find, no real rewards for exploration other than a chest containing a regular powerup. Megaman X crushes 20XX in this department.
The two comparable games also have lore. Megaman's is surface level and Isaac's is more esoteric, but 20XX has less of a story and more of a setting. The world feels hollow.
Boss battles in 20xx are nothing like the ones from Megaman X. I have about 10 hours into the game and, even with a splash screen proclaiming the boss pre-fight, I can't remember any of their names. I tend to think of them as mask-wall-thing, bat boss, fire goat thing, chill penguin (oh, actually, I just remembered it's Shatterbeak), and the sunflower guy. Oh, and the wheel. They just don't do that much. It doesn't feel like the boss is fighting the player so much as just doing what it would normally do if you turned its power on. They're completely lifeless.
The music is nice, but not memorable, with the boss battle music being particularly underwhelming. I should feel like I'm in a life or death battle. Instead, I feel like I'm gardening or something. Beating the bosses feels like housework. Oh, I just remembered; the boss weapons feel unnecessary, too.
Overall, 20XX is fun for a bit, but limited. Do not go in expecting Megaman X. If I'm completely honest, it still feels like this game is in early access. It's good, really good, but not for very long.

Incredible game. Really plays homage to Megaman in a classy way. Some people have hastily referred to it as a "Megaman Knockoff", which is incorrect. This game is very much an amazing tribute to Megaman, and all the other simple and fun games of the 80's/90's. Visuals are fantastic, and the soundtrack is one of the most perfect things I've heard in a game. I'm not joking, it rivals Gradius IIIs soundtrack on SNES. It really makes this game what it is.
The way the difficulty scales as you progress is very cool. Each boss has various difficulty settings that are triggered based on what stage you fight them on. The level generation isn't bad as some have complained about. It's just enough to keep the levels a little interesting and not the same thing over and over. I've noticed the main tough points in the levels never change, just the way you get to them. That's something I like a lot.
There is a wide array of enemies, and TONS of discoverable pickups.. After two days of owning the game I've completed the game a few times now, with many failures, and I have been able to unlock a bunch of the pick ups so far and it looks like there are many more at my disposal.
There are separate game modes from just the standard run and gun, like challenge modes and co-op, neither of which I have tested quite yet.
I needed to play the beginner mode (3 lives) about 4 or 5 times before I was prepared to jump in to normal, which I promptly cleared.
It has been a LONG time since a platformer captivated me like this. 20XX is a perfect example of all the little things AAA developers look over these days when making games. I sincerely hope we get a proper paid XPac or a sequel.

Nice of them to release their beta build for free so people could see how much balance work and finishing there is to do in the last few months of game development. Let's be clear, I love this game. Which is why it's so infuriating seeing something potentially amazing hamstrung by a swarm of bad design decisions.
Bugs, Balance issues, Missing features:
-Scavenging. Remove this mechanic, make the scavengers a completely separate unit from your Peons maybe tied to the market, or remove the despawn timer on loot. Additionally make the scavengers able to pick up the Gold Coins, which should ABSOLUTELY NOT DESPAWN.
-Health bars are a vague suggestion and completely meaningless as to how unclear they are. A green blob that gradients to red with lower health would be clearer even.
-When your Keep is destroyed and you restart, you go to the next day. You keep the gold you picked up (which is scant comfort), but all the corpses disappear instantly. Seemingly those creatures aren't present in the next attack either, so you lose those resources permanently. The attack after next will be at full strength again. OTA is seemingly balanced around having 100% loot collection, which due to the mechanics of the looting system is almost impossible (sometimes literally with bodies falling into unpathable terrain).
-Troll upgrades jump in cost excessively per level. Some upgrades are such inane power spikes that your Troll literally either steamrolls everything, or dies instantly. There's no middle ground, no sensation of a close battle, it's either your Troll does an imitation of a Silverback Gorilla on steroids fighting a Playschool Class, or a ball of playdough vs chainsaws.  This would even probably be fine if it weren't for the loot system (again). Though the upgrades also don't tell you anything about what the abilities actually do... no cooldowns, no range indicators, no damage indicators, you just get bars which are either blank or full. Presumably they're some kind of scale, but where do they start and end? I'm going to assume they use a variant of the brand new SI unit, the Kilobadinterface.
-Abilities are locked for what appears to be no reason. Please add a tooltip that says "UNLOCKED IN CHAPTER X"
-Have the Objective HUD element actually show what the objective subtext is when you hover over it.
-Microtransactions are fine, just don't put the button for them in the middle of a menu that never changes at any other time other than in one window. So then you conveniently have a button that stuns the player temporarily when you try to go from Troll Upgrades to Town Upgrades.
-The Troll handles worse than the Mars Rover, only less responsive.
-Buildings' construction is shown in % of how confused you are. Please use actual time, or time with the %. Information, not Data.
-Assignments for Peons should have Arrow buttons on either side for +1 or -1. Every time someone uses a slider with no other method of controlling the interface element, an orphaned puppy dies.
-Have a HUD readout of how many Peons you have in each task...

It's no wonder that DmC's reviews are overwhelmingly positive; this is an incredible game.
I've been a fan of the franchise ever since the first Devil May Cry on the PS2, and I've played through every game. 1 was good, 2 was meh, 3 was very good, but THIS is amazing. If you're a fan of the franchise but yet to play this reboot because of the change in Dante & Vergil's appearances and personalities, leave your prejudice behind because EVERYTHING in this game is an improvement on the old. Vergil is now a multifaceted personality with a lot of depth, which makes the relationship between him, Dante and the new female character (Kat) a lot more interesting.
Unfortunately, Devil Trigger no longer gives you wings and flight, but you won't need it due to the awesome Angel/Devil whips Dante has at his disposal. Using the Angel whip will pull you right up to your enemy or propel you through the air to different environmental areas, whilst using the Devil whip drags your enemies right up to you or get rid of obstacles in your path. The locomotion using the whips is a very fun part of the game, with you needing to react quickly to decide and alternate between the whips before you fall to your death.
The maps and environments are very cool, because a lot of the time spent is in a paralel demon version of our world in which demotivational, demonic words appear briefly, debris and pieces of buildings float around, at one point you're running upside down, and there's just generally a lot of variation in the sights from level to level.
Combat is smooth and very easy. You can switch between weapons at the touch of a button and mix up your combos really nicely.

400+ hours and I'm not finished with this game yet, not by a long shot.
Gameplay :
FPS with rpg elements. You pick one of six characters and go on a rampage on the planet of pandora, alone co-op. The characters have the same story-line but are very diverse and you should do yourself a favour and try them all out.
The main-plot isn't overly long but the optional content make this a behemoth and that's a good thing. It means if you can unlock the higher modes (3 modes in total) for better loot and nastier enemies and if you overreach, you can always go back to the easier modes.
Although you can play with up to 4 people, mostly I play solo and I'm not missing anything.
Story :
Borderlands refuses to take itself seriously and almost all characters are batshit insane. The story is secondary to all the crazy quests and that's a good thing, because humour and pure gameplay is where BL2 shines. In that respect it's old school.
Loot : Tons, although in later levels (40/50 +) I wish it was better. This is where RNG turns into a bit of a troll.
Consistently funny, easy to pick up, intuitive controls and tons of content.
Do yourself a favour and pick up the complete set during a sale.

If I recall, San Andreas was one of the first games I ever completed, due to having an older brother, I basically grew up playing the likes of GTA, Halo and some other games. This is in my opinion and will always be the greatest game of all time.
Story: Great, so great I don't want to spoil it one bit. Play through this game for story alone.
Missions: The missions are a blast (some of them literally) to go through, I think the only missions that are not enjoyable in this game would have to be the RC drone missions, because they are just frustration to control, other than that though, I can't think of a single mission that made dislike playing the game.
Gameplay: Apart from precise aiming which for some reason it is quite hard to do in San Andreas, the gameplay is well done, it is easy to switch between for example GTA V and GTA San Andreas, the gameplay is quite similar (definitely not technically) in a lot of ways.
World Design: I think the world in San Andreas is great, my favourite open-world by far. You've got Los Santos, which is everything from docks, to the hood, to downtown, Vinewood hills, tries to imitate Los Angeles. Then you have The Country (as I like to call it) which connects Los Santos to San Fierro and Las Venturas, filled with little towns, a giant mountain, rivers and a couple of forests/farms. San Fierro, mostly downtown and housing areas along with the docks, tries to imitate San Fransisco. Then finally, Las Venturas, much like its real life counter part (Las Vegas) has the city, with the strip. There is also desert surrounding it, with a military base, a quarry, a couple little towns, massive hills, airfields and all sorts to explore. Because of the variety of locations in this game I think it is great.
Mod Support: If you've played through the main game quite a few times (like me), you may find the game to get just a little bit repetitive, or maybe you just wanna spice things up a little. There is a lot of mods for this game, ranging from graphics mods, retextures and all that to mods that make you into Superman, Naruto or Goku from Dragonball Z. San Andreas' mod community is still active and massive.
Multiplayer Mods: Even if you typically don't like GTA games, San Andreas Multiplayer (SA:MP) or Multi Theft Auto (MTA) may be the mods for you! I personally believe that SA:MP is better than MTA but that is only because I've played more of it. Technically MTA is better because it allows server owners to make mods server side meaning that no one will have issues with installing map packs or anything. I feel like SA:MP is just a lot more friendly in terms of UI and it is easier to just jump in and play rather than MTA which is a lot harder to get into and a lot more time consuming. I often play SA:MP to play the roleplay server, Los Santos Roleplay (LS-RP) for short. But SA:MP and MTA both offer freeroam, DM, Cops and Robbers and other gamemodes. Between the two mods roughly 1,000,000 people play monthly. The mods were at their peak a couple of years ago but still many people play them.
Overall: I think you should get this game, it is amazing, my favourite game of all time.

It's a procedural-generated (to some degree) indie love letter to Mega Man X.
If you've played any roguelike, "bullet hell" style, random environment games, then you know what I'm talking about. Combine all THAT into a Mega Man X clone, and you have this game.
Mega Man (the series in general) gets a lot of fan service, but the X series seems neglected. 20XX is all about MMX, right down to the controls (including dash), the 4-piece suit upgrade and red-colored, sword-wielding companion.
It's also not exactly the most punishing roguelike. So if you're curious about the roguelike genre, this is a good starter one. There's IS a hard mode, but in these games even the easy/normal modes tend to be difficult. I'd rate this g ame's normal mode as extremely fair.
So, if you like Mega Man games, especially the X series, and are into or curious about the roguelike genre, this game is for you.
My only complaints are that there's no real endgame, and it's not one unique stage per boss. I would have liked if each boss had its own stage type, and some kinda Sigma-esque supervillain final boss fight (at least one the first run).

A really interesting Megaman/Megaman X/Megaman Zero inspired roguelite. With some caveats of criticism. This game isn't perfect. The procedural generation isn't fair and it takes some of the bad tropes of megaman, like the disappearing blocks, and places them everywhere in a little too much platforming and a little too little action. The enemies are interesting in some areas and generally boring in others. There really are only 4 level types to play and it was disappointing to see the bosses didn't each have their own unique area. The bosses get more HP and a few more tricks as you go through the upper levels, but only a few seem well done with this design and others seem blatantly unfair. Power Exploitation is fun for the bosses, but like some poorly designed Megaman weapons, you keep wishing they had more use than just for attacking. Some of the powers can be used to control traps in the areas, but it's lackluster due to the fact that the powers don't make the characters more accessible. 2 Shield powers, 2 Direct Shot powers, 2 Arcing mortar powers, a boomerang, and "melee crystal" that wishes it was a dash attacking power.
Megaman has some difficulty, but there is a difference between a mistake of the player and a mistake of the level. This game suffers more from the latter in it's design. Most damage taken from falls will feel more like an issue of the level design and less of a "This is a hard level" feel. I would suggest working more of the procedural generation to keep full blocks for well timed wall jumps and areas that encourage a little more fun of shooting/slashing enemies to pieces. Ride Armors were fun in the X games, and their placement could also add to the fun. While I like the core upgrades spiced around the area, the only one that feels complimentary to the level design is the hover. Furthermore, it would be interesting to have the leg parts be avaliable more frequently than the others. Maybe it's just my bad luck, but it always feels like the upgraded parts tend to come in order of Helm, Armor, Arm, Boots. The idea of the set bonuses are also pretty nice but I think the fact the Owlhawk and the Armatort share the hover feature feels a little disappointing. Maybe Owlhawk should have some sort of higher jump/slow fall instead?
If there were more powers, more bosses, more enemies, more levels, and a little less of the obviously cheap design, such as half block wall jumps, off timed lasers and platforms, and boxed in jumps that require the most perfect of bunny hops, this game would be a real masterpiece. As it is, it's an inspired concept that needs more polish. I'll continue to play it from time to time and I look forward to trying the Co-op later. I'm not 100% sure I could reccomend full price in it's current state. But it's a good buy for a sale.

After playing Unholy Heights numerous times since I've purchased it, I've decided to edit my original review to make it clearer as to why I love this game so much.
Okay, so it's not your ordinary tower defense game, but a management sim too. Basically, the devil decided to run his own apartment complex, and in order to protect himself he persuades the residents to fight for him. Each resident has varying stats, along with different fighting styles (melee, ranged, & magic), so having a variety of monsters is ideal. Simply knock on the door of the resident that you want to fight, and they'll go kill as many adventurers as they can handle without a second thought. The apartment management might be a little difficult in the beginning, due to the lack of rooms you start out with - just 4. If you want another level, you'll have to save up enough money to begin construction, and it can get pretty expensive. This is where planning what monsters you have is important because you'll need them to defend until you can afford to build another floor and house
monsters. Oh, and always remember to keep your residents happy :)
As I mentioned above, it's important to ensure the happiness of your residents. Happy monsters = increased popularity for the devil, and they won't run off because they hate you. Keeping your residents happy is simple, mainly because they'll tell you what they want and you just satisfy their request. Most of the time, they'll ask for better furniture, etc., but it might get a little tricky if you have two monster types that hate each other and they want you to give the other the boot. Definitely check out the beastiary if you're unsure of any monsters that might clash. Rent is also an important thing to consider; always give them a price that they're happy with. If, for whatever reason, they can't afford to pay rent, lower it a bit until they pay off their debt. An unhappy resident will leave if they are unsatisfied or in debt for too long.
Aside from fighting and asking you for everything under the sun, they're just regular monsters trying to live their lives. They have jobs, go to school, find love, and make babies. Oh, and of course you'll know every single thing they do throughout their day, ranging from things like 'engaging in pillowtalk' or 'reading erotic fanfiction' to normal chores. They're a lot like us ♡
I expected more. Even for the 2 or 3 euros it cost.

So the Devil quit his job as Lord Of All Evil to build an apartment building for monsters, and as its landlord you have to manage the tenants and get them to defend the building against overeager heroes. If that premise sounds Japanese as ♥♥♥♥ to you, then you're right on the money because the monsters are adorable, the heroes are Dragon Questy, and there are erotic cakes. And under all the weirdness and design quirks, there's a pretty good game.
Unholy Heights is a mash-up of management sim and tower defense that's way, way heavier on the management part. You start with four apartments that monsters can apply to live in, and you have full control over the rent and furnishings. That means you can fill it with all sorts of beds, appliances, plants, PCs, board games, exercise gear, and other junk. Your tenants will often request specific things like a desk to study on or smutty wallpaper to stare at, but you can (and should) also furnish empty apartments a specific way to attract certain monsters. From the outset only a handful will want to take a room in your building, but with a little work you can catch the eye of powerful demons, elementals, beasts, and elder beings.
Apartments start as single residences, but your tenants can meet and bring home a spouse, and have a child. You can also add second and third floors after completing certain quests, ultimately giving you 12 apartments of up to 3 monsters each. Monsters have jobs that they'll leave part of the day for (unless they work from home), hobbies they'll indulge, and all sorts of weird statuses throughout like "staring at the wall" and "having a wet dream". They can get sick, they can be evicted, they can lose their jobs and not make rent, and on and on and on. The depth of the sim component honestly approaches something like Tropico with how fleshed-out each resident is.
All of this contributes to the tower defense portion as well, but not always in good ways. Heroes will come to your building in an effort to get to the Devil's office on the roof and steal your money. This can happen randomly, but usually it's triggered by taking a quest. Quests have all sorts of justifications and reward you with money, new monsters, new furnishings, or the ability to expand the building, but they all play out roughly the same. Heroes appear from the right side of the screen and wind their way up towards the Devil's office. You can knock on the doors of your residents to get them out and fighting the good guys. Monsters can be melee, ranged, or magical, with different resistances and speeds to track. They also get bonuses from being content, favorable weather, and so on.
It's a smart and entertaining combination that's only held back by a few gripes. If the heroes reach your office, they steal a bunch of your money and you fail the quest. Quests can be several waves long, so failing on the boss can be pretty discouraging. Losing monsters in battle can be a pretty stiff setback, since you generally don't have time to replace them between waves. You also don't really know what you're getting into until you see the heroes in action, so it's really easy to screw yourself by unknowingly taking a quest you can't win yet.
The absolute worst, though, is getting attacked while your monsters are out. Remember how I said they have jobs and hobbies? Well, when they're out, they're out. And once you start a quest, you don't get to pick when the waves come. So if your key melee tank is waiting tables when the heroes show up, you're screwed. I had one building where every single monster worked the night shift, which made quests almost impossible to complete. I've learned to work around it, and now I have a group with several housewives and home-workers, but it's a big issue you have to look out for.
All that said, I've having a lot of fun with my kooky monsters. I don't even care for tower defense games that much, but the management side is engrossing and the combat doesn't get too in the way of my enjoyment. The learning curve is a little steeper than it should be thanks to some questionable design, but once you get past that it's an adorable little package.

A lot of potential, and as football fan with a big soft spot for nostalgia, I love the concept.  However, whilst there is a lot to like about the game, there are also a number of issues at the moment, and as such it is hard to recommend until these have been addressed.  Of course, this is still in early access, and I have high hopes I will be able to write a more positive review at a later date :)  But for now, this is how I see it:
Pros:
* All those seasons, so much choice :)
* Nice representation of player skills
* Simple and quick to pick up
* Nostalgia for the older CM games, but with new ideas as well
Cons:
* Interface can be very slow when switching screens
* Not much feedback in terms of what is going well/wrong in a game
* Not so many tactical options - probably a design choice, keeping it a quicker simpler game.  But would still be nice to change set piece takers, have more control over passing options, etc.
* Game has crashed for me, more than once
* Some interface glitches - for example, I once had a return button stuck on screen, blocking other buttons, and leaving me stuck with no option but to kill the process
* Lots of teams for lots of years - but player positions and stats are not always as I remember them
* Transfer / scouting options limited at this time
All in all it has potential to be a good, quick to play football manager game, and one perfect for fans who like to drift their minds back to the "good old days" (whenever they may be).  But still a bit of work to be done, particularly in terms of performance and stability.  But again, early days, so I hope it will live up to it's potential!

I was on the fence with giving this a thumbs up or down for a long time. At the end I decided it was worth a thumbs up to recommend for someone who wants more arkham style batman stories and open world combat adventures.
This game basically reuses the arkham city map but is a prequel from before it was destroyed and flooded and turned into a prison; but with the amount of criminals on the streets, and citizens curfewed, you don't really see any difference.
If you need more batman fix after arkham city, then pick this up, but be aware that this is nowhere near as polished as city and has a bunch of glaring bugs that will never be fixed. Some seem game breaking until you reload, and others may need you to google how to workaround. None are truly game breaking (anymore). The most major annoyance is that ground takedowns are even more unreliable than previous games. This leaves you with near 100% chance to drop combos if every enemy is knocked down.
There are also some animation bugs, sound bugs and interrogation bugs, Enemy snipers can also shoot you out of the sky from several city blocks away, Some boss battles change mechanics during the fight and are not intuitive. One of these lead to instant failure if you don't inexplicably run away from him in the middle of beating him up... leading to having to replay a very long predator sequence before getting to reattemp the fight. This leads to the point of several places where there are a lack of checkpoints.
The new gadgets are neat and the new tech tree takes away choice but makes it harder to turn yourself into instant badass after a few early levels. You are basically forced to take armor upgrades before combo ones.
Level design and artwork is still complex and beautiful, and the new crimes in progress and investigation systems add a lot of atmosphere.
The story is still fantastic, and the new voice actors do an admirable job of taking over major roles. The game does end kind of prematurely in my opinion, but was still a very satisfying storyline experience overall.

NMRiH brings zombie genre back to the spotlight. The game itself is distant from any mainstream zombie-FPS mixout. While they do have action in the game, your goal in NMRiH is to escape and survive. Despite this, there was more guns and ammo for action-lover to blast those zombies head. Yet the game itself indeed pointing out the "survival" more than "action", with limited First Aid to heal and limited Pills to tame the virus inside your body... IF you got caught in the massacre!
As for this, I like the ideas and design that NMRiH offers. And since it's FREE to play.... hehe why not you guys try it?
But before that, I'd also like to give my tips on the downside. NMRiH at this moment offers little maps to play, albeit community can make maps and put that on the server. Also, the animation isn't fluid and often times it's pretty much buggy or too slow. Sometimes, keys and doors could go glitcy and will ruin your game.
While I can understand the "survival" aspect of this game, it's still need more polishing stones to make NMRiH a good zombie game. Why? NMRiH lacks some sort of "survival" elements, like unique pick-up items that could only be used by certain character, or each character have different "skills or uniqueness" that will help others, in short I can give example of Resident Evil Outbreak series as prime example for NMRiH. Well, the other one, NMRiH relies HEAVILY on TEAMWORK. If you play with newbies or trolls or selfish player, you better quit and find another server. Well, newbies aren't gonna slow you down, you can tell them what they should do, but the other 2, they could pick everything for themselves and leave you and the rest of the team behind. And because of this, players that left behind or have no weapons usually dies. And since it does relies on TEAMWORK, you could easily dies if your party are not working together, and yet there's no punishments or some mechanics to reduce people from trolling or playing alone.
At least, NMRiH did bring back the old "slow zombies" from dead, in the wake of "new" running or super zombies theme that flocks in fiction today. And NMRiH did a good job to make that up into a game with at least good gameplay mechanics that's enjoyable as possible.
I do reccomend this game for you guys, if you want some "fresh air" from running-super zombies game at the moment :)

A fun little tower defence game reminiscent of flash games from a few years ago that were extremely fun and addicting, but suffered from a lack of content. As with those, One Troll Army is pretty fun to play but all of the game's content can be completed in around 3-4 hours, after which you unlock a "survival mode" that offers an endless version of the game's campaign. One cannot truly complain about the lack of content though, considering the game is completely free to play with no microtransactions that I'm aware of except for some cosmetic things for your troll.
The game itself focuses around a troll who offers to protect a fledgling goblin settlement from being raided and destroyed by invading migrant beastmen and to do this you are given direct control over both the settlement and your troll itself.
The troll is controlled in a manner similar to a real time strategy unit, or an action roleplaying game character; he can move around, be told to attack enemies and has access to several abilities as well as stat and ability upgrades.
The settlement itself is controlled through menus and sliders, with goblin workers that are assigned to perform different tasks to gather resources or upgrade buildings. It's a relatively simple progression system, with goblins gathering resources to upgrade buildings that either improve base defence and towers or allow you to upgrade your goblins so you can gather resources even faster. Each building upgrade also gives you more goblins, allowing you to do more things at once and do them more effectively.
Though this sounds a little like a more traditional real time strategy title, it is in fact a wave-based defence game. Each wave is split into two different roungs, with the first being a non-combat round during which you can control the economy and upgrades of your settlement. During this first round, enemy beastmen will begin to approach the settlement and hang around on the outskirts, waiting for enough of them to appear to begin an attack. When enough enemies arrive, the will initiate the combat round of the wave in which all goblins hide inside your settlement and you have to fight back the onslaught with the aid of hireable orc mercenaries and towers capable of firing upon the enemies. When all enemies are defeated or your settlement is raided, the combat round ends and the next wave begins.
This, unfortunately, is the worst part of the game. If your settlement is raided (I.E, you lose against an enemy wave), there are absolutely no negative repercussions for this loss. All of your resources remain and the difficulty of the next wave will be lowered to compensate for your inability to proceed. This leads to situations in which there is absolutely no reason not to purposely lose every single wave and just focus entirely on upgrading your settlement to maximum, since enemies cannot steal your gathered resources or kill your goblin workers to upset your progression (this does mean you don't gain gold from looting enemies, but since you can trade resources for gold and other resources at a very good rate, this is hardly a negative).
Once you have upgraded all of your buildings to maximum level, have fully upgraded your troll and and completed all three of the "campaign" levels in the game, you have pretty much seen all of what this game has to offer. It's a fun little game, but it ultimately has some serious design flaws that makes it unlikely that I'll play it again. I enjoyed my three or so hours time playing, but it's not worth investing more time than that. Still, the fact that the game is completely free means that there's no harm in trying it for yourself and having some fun.

If I recall, San Andreas was one of the first games I ever completed, due to having an older brother, I basically grew up playing the likes of GTA, Halo and some other games. This is in my opinion and will always be the greatest game of all time.
Story: Great, so great I don't want to spoil it one bit. Play through this game for story alone.
Missions: The missions are a blast (some of them literally) to go through, I think the only missions that are not enjoyable in this game would have to be the RC drone missions, because they are just frustration to control, other than that though, I can't think of a single mission that made dislike playing the game.
Gameplay: Apart from precise aiming which for some reason it is quite hard to do in San Andreas, the gameplay is well done, it is easy to switch between for example GTA V and GTA San Andreas, the gameplay is quite similar (definitely not technically) in a lot of ways.
World Design: I think the world in San Andreas is great, my favourite open-world by far. You've got Los Santos, which is everything from docks, to the hood, to downtown, Vinewood hills, tries to imitate Los Angeles. Then you have The Country (as I like to call it) which connects Los Santos to San Fierro and Las Venturas, filled with little towns, a giant mountain, rivers and a couple of forests/farms. San Fierro, mostly downtown and housing areas along with the docks, tries to imitate San Fransisco. Then finally, Las Venturas, much like its real life counter part (Las Vegas) has the city, with the strip. There is also desert surrounding it, with a military base, a quarry, a couple little towns, massive hills, airfields and all sorts to explore. Because of the variety of locations in this game I think it is great.
Mod Support: If you've played through the main game quite a few times (like me), you may find the game to get just a little bit repetitive, or maybe you just wanna spice things up a little. There is a lot of mods for this game, ranging from graphics mods, retextures and all that to mods that make you into Superman, Naruto or Goku from Dragonball Z. San Andreas' mod community is still active and massive.
Multiplayer Mods: Even if you typically don't like GTA games, San Andreas Multiplayer (SA:MP) or Multi Theft Auto (MTA) may be the mods for you! I personally believe that SA:MP is better than MTA but that is only because I've played more of it. Technically MTA is better because it allows server owners to make mods server side meaning that no one will have issues with installing map packs or anything. I feel like SA:MP is just a lot more friendly in terms of UI and it is easier to just jump in and play rather than MTA which is a lot harder to get into and a lot more time consuming. I often play SA:MP to play the roleplay server, Los Santos Roleplay (LS-RP) for short. But SA:MP and MTA both offer freeroam, DM, Cops and Robbers and other gamemodes. Between the two mods roughly 1,000,000 people play monthly. The mods were at their peak a couple of years ago but still many people play them.

Platformers aren't my favourite genre as I'm often far too picky about pixel-perfect jumps, unpredictable physics or issues with backtracking in far too many of them. Thankfully I was relieved to see that these weren't the case as soon as I launched Ori.
First thing you might notice from the videos and screenshots is the unique graphics. The game uses a parallax effect to give depth to its hand-drawn, animated 2D planes and such treatment compliments the game extremely well in the visual department. There is a ton of care put into both characters and environments, with graphics looking sharp even on 1080p+ screen resolutions and higher frame rates.
What'll probably stand out next for the potential player right after they jump into the game is the orchestral music composed by Gareth Coker. The whole score of the game is masterfully composed to the point that it doesn't simply fit in the mood of the game - it amplifies to the degrees that I often couldn't wait to visit a particular area of the game on a subsequent playthrough just so I could hear my favourite tracks again. I have to admit that the highly emotional story of the game made me fell in love with the soundtrack even more, which made me end up listening to it for months after completing the game, quietly reliving the most memorable moments of both the gameplay and story in my mind.
Gameplay wise Ori is very strong as well; The movement feels natural, as the whole world is driven by physics that feel predictable to interact with, without any quirkiness that often comes with less-polished Unity engine games. Ori controls feel right just minutes into the game and that allows for players to master new skills with ease. And speaking of character progression - it's often done in a way that kept me smiling with joy each time I earned a new ability - which in turn encouraged the backtracking I had initially dreaded. It turned out that I enjoyed it even more, as the hidden collectibles are actually worth pursuing. I'd even say that getting to them is often a puzzle that's a pure joy to solve.
There are a few problems with the game such as skill descriptions that could be somewhat improved or difficulty of some escape sequences that might be a problem for some players. The game itself tends to be on the tougher half of the difficulty spectrum and for that reason I'd recommend people that aren't well acquainted with platformers to start with the Easy mode.
The thing with the issues I had found is that... they're really miniscule as soon as one begins to appreciate the main values of the game. For new players it's sitting at around 8-10 hours of a standard playthrough or a 11-13 hours for getting extra collectibles. There are multiple save slots and challenge difficulties available, as well as extra footage added by the developers for the Definitive Edition.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to not only fans of the genre but also you, fellow reader, even if you aren't one. The big chances are that you'll at least enjoy it a whole bunch, maybe even tear up a bit, but ultimately smile in the process. After all this is what the video games often should be about: things that not only bring fun to our mundane lives, but also memorable experiences we get to share with others.

Does both the Megaman X element and the roguelike element at about 70% proficiency. As such, while it's not worth getting at full price, it's a good casual X-like game to try out when discounted. Do keep the following issues in mind though:
The vanilla game primarily suffers from being too easy. It tries to extend its replayability through modifiers and hard modes, similarly to Risk of Rain, but without the base difficulty to back it up. The balance is okay but not the best, with the Zero-like melee character being significantly easier and stronger than his counterpart to the point where he makes the game a cakewalk.
The level design also suffers from a lack of longevity. The procedurally generated levels are not only simply not on par with the handcrafted well-designed levels of, say, X1-X3, but you're also bound to see a lot of repetition very soon, much like in Dirt 4 (which also died out largely due to a flawed tile-based generator which generated significant repetitiveness). As such, the difficulty quickly turns into simply making sure you're not killed by the swarm of increasingly tougher enemies, though in my experiences the upgrade rate for the Zero-like character can easily eclipse the rate at which the enemies grow in strength.
The bosses are also very simple and lack the strategic beauty of those in the X games. While boss weaknesses do exist, for the most part there's no real point in using them as both the buster and the saber greatly outclass them in the vast majority of situations, especially when focusing on damage upgrades.
Having said that though, the game quickly gets fast and thrilling, which, for me, is easily the game's strongest suit. It's something I felt the SNES X games always lacked simply by virtue of being on the overly clunky and slow SNES. It's more reminiscent of the Megaman Zero games in that sense, which, barring the weird design choice of going with ranks and having them be important for getting new weapons, I always felt were significantly better than the X games. It certainly wouldn't surprise me if they took some inspiration from the Z games, seeing as the ending features a reference to Z4. The roguelike element does add some variety to the game as well and encourages different playstyles without really infringing on the main X-like gameplay. I've heard people mention that the graphics aren't its strongest suit, but while they do indeed look less visually appealing than those of the X and Z games, they definitely get the job done - the animations are fluid and sensible, the enemies and attacks are easily to discern and there are no issues with the camera or anything of the sort. I got used to it in just a couple of levels, without having watched any gameplay footage before.
All in all, it's a good game to do a quick run of every now and then. It lacks the rewarding feeling of the X and Z games and the replayability of some of the top roguelike games, but for a casual bit of fun after work, especially when discounted, it's definitely worth considering.

QUICK OVERVIEW
I got this game during the Summer sale for much, much less than $29.99. Nonetheless, this is one of the most fun games I have ever found myself playing. I haven't put this much time into a game in such a short span of time since the Sims 3 launch (50 hours in the first week I owned it!).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IS IT WORTH IT?
I honestly don't know if I would have purchased this game at the full asking point of $30 but I'm admittadly a bit stingy when it comes to game purchases and usually only buy games when they go on sale- however, if I had been overcome with impetuity and purchased this game at the full price, I don't think I would regret it. The story line (campaign mode), while admittadly a bit too short, was COMPLETELY surprising and very interesting. It is formatted into a sort of bare-bones graphic novel that you, as the player, get to fill in the blanks to.
However, after beating the campaign and making a couple of sandbox prisons, this game loses a bit of its luster. It has a very active steam workshop community for those of you who enjoy changing up the vanilla game (I am not really someone who utilizes the workshop very often because I like the game to rest on its own laurels).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ESCAPE MODE was something added to the game later on in its creation and I honestly don't like it. Maybe it's because I'm just bad at it but I really just don't find it fun at all and find myself laboriously making myself play it just to garner the steam achievements. Unlike the original campaign, the escape mode is poorly explained, confusing, and has no story line or reason to it. I think escape mode could be really interesting if you were presented with a story line and specific objectives, like the architect campaign.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ALL IN ALL, I would recommend this game to those of us that don't always like the stress of an RPG that enjoy games with sandbox capabilities and extremely interesting, yet somewhat short, campaigns. I don't know how often this title goes on sale because I found it just scrolling through the Summer sale but I would honestly wait until a sale, if possible. I find it hard to justify spending $30 on a game when there are so many others out there that cost less that are also fun. To each his own, though. If this game sounds like fun to you and you have room in your gaming budget to spend the money with no shame then by all means, do it. You won't regret it.

It's a very good game for a start. It's graphically beautiful, has some really nice mechanics, lots of diversity on how to play a mission, the challenges and unlocks add more replayablity, easter eggs are fun, and overall it's a good game to just mess about on too. I have no issues whatsoever with the base game at all.
HOWEVER
The devs are a little bit greedy. I know that from having this game on the Xbox One, you can buy all of the missions separately; albeit for a higher price than all of them bundled together, the option is still there. This is apparently not the case on Steam. In order for me to just play say one of the missions I really enjoy, I'd have to fork out between £35 - £50 to unlock them all. Maybe I don't want to unlock them all, but yet, if I am to fully enjoy this game, I have to pay the price. I liked the system on Xbox where you could just individually buy missions. It meant that I could buy them whenever I had money and play when I wanted. But with this, I feel as if I've got a gun held to my head as I'm deciding whether it is worth getting any more missions on Steam seeing as it's quite a hefty price. Yes I know, this is a triple-a game, yes I know this will obviously have a large price tag along with it because of this. However, this game had a different approach to how you accessed its content which at first confused me a bit, but now I actually quite like it. And to offer this service on one platform but remove it from another baffles me. It has obviously worked on console being able to sell the missions separately, I know this cos I bought the missions separately and it was a much easier way to go about things.
Overall, this is an excellent game, it's very enjoyable, but I am disappointed at the inability to purchase missions separately meaning currently I am not able to access the rest of its content. Therefore, I'm going to have to give this a thumbs down.

You get a chance to win that match all over again. That player that became your first real idol (who was pretty rubbish in retrospect, but who cares) - you get to lead him to glory. That striker that your club sold, who if you were in charge would have been chained up in the training ground, well, sorry buddy, you don't get your dream move I'm afraid.
The amount of work and detail that's gone into this game is incredible - it should be said that this is an early iteration, the first steps if you will, but if this is the start, I genuinely cannot wait until the bugs are ironed out and the final product is polished.
In terms of gameplay, it's simple. It's not FM16, with a myriad of different things you need to tweak or adjust. It's pure, pick up and play management. Go for the players you want, get them on the pitch, hope for the best, in the truest, classic CM93/94 style. No frills, no fancy animations, just history being corrected (if you're any good!).
It's very single player - as yet, you can only manage one club in game (so, no selling players to 'friendly' clubs for inflated fees - boo, hiss), the transfer system as regards foreign players needs (in my opinion), a bit of a revamp, and there are a few glitches here and there. I will say that, having seen the game develop from an idea into reality, I trust 1888 to get all of these things sorted in a smart time scale.
Genuinely, I've spent hours playing this during development and again since purchasing on Steam. For the price of a pub lunch, if you have any interest at all in football (proper football, jumpers for goalposts that is, not prawn sandwiches and £100m transfers), you need to have this game in your library.

A fun casual sort of tower defense game but with a unique premise. You play as the Devil who decides to become a landlord one day, when in truth, you're planning to conquer the world. How? By tricking monsters as your tenants annd turning them into your personal army of soldiers of course. It's pretty silly. And that's as far as the story goes.
There are various monster types and tiers, each with different tastes, wants and needs. Fulfill what they want and their satisfaction goes up and their stats are boosted too. Eventually your monsters grow more powerful and fight more powerful enemies. Typical game structure you'd expect.
But this isnt just a tower defense game. What makes the game special really, is the "Sims" aspect of it. After all, the monsters arent staying to fight, they need to make a living too. You can keep informed on a plethora of small things like what each monster is doing, see how they're doing, where are they, their jobs, occupation and their activities.
Monsters can also sleep, eat, play, even find partners, make love and bear babies. Don't bother thinking on how monsters like skeletons are even capable of reproducing, they just do.
On the more important aspect of gameplay, Unholy Heights does disappoint me slightly with how the game turned out. Controls are a little frustrating to deal with, such as when trying to select a specific monster. Combat isn't so refined and in fact, feels unfair given how the only control you have over the monsters is to retreat or attack.  The 2D platform also gives rise to limitations and cheap exploits, like cornering an enemy and glitching the AI to be indecisive on which direction to attack.
Many things are also based on luck and coincidence and this is where things can sometimes get a little frustrating. You could wait for countless hours and still not have some of your monsters refusing to give birth. The monsters freely entering and exiting the house whenever they like is another thing that sucks. Get into a battle but your useful monsters just happen to be away? You're deadmeat. About to get into battle but your useful monsters decide to leave the house half-way in? You're deadmeat.
Or what annoys me the mos: when some of your weaker monsters suddenly return back home during a battle. Sometimes they're stacked in a row stretching so far away, you cant even see them on the screen. If they meet a more powerful enemy head-on, you're helplessly screwed.
In Unholy Heights. everything runs down to what matters most: Money. Money is generated primarily from rent income, but this makes for easy exploiting. Get a stable income and just wait in-game without doing anything for hours and you'll find yourself rich automatically, although this will put you at odds with a few monster types.
All in all, regardless of a few problems... most of which I'm probably just nitpicking at, this game is actually pretty darn great. It doesn't exactly feel fun but like any decent casual game, it can definitely be addicting to play. Almost too addicting for me.
Perhaps it's the simplicity of the game, or how you can just lay back and do nothing while watching your monsters live their lifes, have sex everyday and make babies.

Unholy Heights is a quirky mixture of tower defense and apartment sim that I really enjoyed playing. The game lasts around 5 hours or so, but if you want to see everything it'll take a bit longer; around 2-3 playthroughs to see all the different monsters and get 100%. If you're interested in this game and got $4 to spare ($2 during sales!), then you should definitely check this game out.
► Simplistic, yet fun gameplay
► Humorous descriptions for items and characters
► Cutsey graphics
► Music is calm and catchy
► Cheap price for the amount of time you'll get out of the game (5 hours or so)

Wonderful game. Arguably the best artistic design I've seen for a game, too.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a very colorful metroidvania taking place in an enchanted forest, threatened by a dark force. Although the scenario is nothing exceptional, the story is told quite poetically, leaving you sometimes amazed, sometimes melancholic. These feelings are also conveyed by the excellent soundtracks.
Gameplay-wise, if I consider most Castlevanias to be 60% fight, 30% platform and 10% puzzles, I would say Ori is more like 50% platform, 30% puzzles and 20% fight. Platform phases are well thought and not repetitive: the developers have strived so that each platform phase/puzzle really differs from the others and pushes the player to think a bit on how to solve it. Like many Metroidvanias, the game is a bit short: it roughly took me 15~20 hours, and I was really taking my time to find every secret and visit the whole map. But there is stuff to keep you busy: some Steam achievements for hardcore gamers and speedrunners.
I want to insist once again: it is the most beautiful 2D game I know: wonderful design, colors, light effects, character models... I take my hat off to the developers.
A must-have in your Steam library.

Много у игры плюсов. Но и минус у игры есть, который, впрочем, присущ всем играм такого рода: низкая реиграбильность. Если вы - дотошный геймер, то скорее всего еще в первое прохождение откроете все и вся на 100%. Максимум, игру захочется пройти во второй раз на более высоком уровне сложности через какое-то время. Вряд ли вас потянет на третье прохождение.
Есть еще один минус: если у вас в ноуте стоит интегрированная и дискретная видеокарты, как у меня, велика вероятность того, что игра будет идти в слоу-мо из-за того, что выберет неподходящую графиук, например, Нвидиа. Впрочем, проблема решается легко: через панель управления графикой надо указать, какую использовать для Ори. Называться у каждого может по-разному. Где-то прямо указано, какая карта используется, где-то будет писаться "быстродействие" и "производительность".
В любом случае, игре - жирный плюс и всяческие мои рекомендации.

Tired of the lack of new Megaman games? Say hi to 20XX
The bosses are badass, the music is badass and you can bet it's worth every penny.

Dissenting opinion: as someone who grew up playing MMX 1-3, 20XX misses the mark. Instead of tightly designed levels, you get often-ugly procedural generation with chunks that become overly familiar after a few hours of play. Platforming never feels as tight as it could be, because your character's attributes are in constant flux. 20XX's action doesn't have the same impact/oomph/whatever as the SNES series. And I don't care much for the art style, sound and music; it's all overly bright and clownish.
That said, I like roguelikes and roguelites. I've sunk many hours into 20XX. The price is right, I don't regret my purchase. But if you go in expecting Mega Man X, you might be disappointed.

20XX is many things. It is a platformer with snappy controls and challenging stage layouts and bosses; it is a roguelike with random level generation and gear upgrading over the course of many, many runs; but first and foremost, it is a Megaman love letter and deconstruction all at once.
This review comes from someone with no experience with Megaman X, and little with the classic games, so if you're in the same boat, here's what I think independently of the obvious comparisons.
In 20XX, you play as either Nina or Ace, two robotic "contractors" created and now hired by Drs. Brighton Sharp and Arlan Flat (DEFINITELY not Light and Wily) to stop what seems to be a manner of robot invasion or takeover. To get the job done, you'll need to face down eight different bosses, each with different patterns and weaknesses and their own themed stages built at random. You're going to need all manner of upgrades, help from a friendly training robot and a very tired robotic cat, and some platforming skill to receive your "payment" for a job well done.
The game just FEELS good to play, once you get used to the dashing and walljumping mechanics. The controls are responsive and platforming is fun, if occasionally difficult. This is also a bit more fair than what Megaman games I've played, though it IS pretty difficult and I still don't have a full clear. Combat is satisfying and upgrades are interesting, even if some are underwhelming or can get you used to bad habits in terms of gameplay (leading to some "damn you muscle memory").
It's really a game you have to learn by doing. Each boss you kill drops a version of one of its attacks, which you can pick up and use for yourself (up to three active at one time) or forego for an upgrade or some money (and yes, the currency really is called Nuts, they know exactly what they did there and they run with it). Each boss, as is Megaman tradition, has a weakness to another boss's weapon, so you want to plan your route through the levels if you want to exploit them. Each boss power also has an "additional" practical use, and it can be fun to figure out synergies and how to go about using them properly.
The art style is very bright and bouncy, the soundtrack is fantastic. The game can get a bit busy visually at times, especially in the later stages, and the later bosses can be teeth-grittingly difficult (looking at you, late-level Astrals). Most of the levels don't feel like a long grind, though be warned that an overall run can take quite a bit of time, at least 30 minutes (though you can save and quit after boss fights). It genuinely does not feel that long. There are various difficulty modes so you can scale up the challenge for yourself with special conditions, a daily and weekly challenge, a seeded mode, and a boss rush.
Oh, also points for the writing. The game's quite funny. Look at the Datalore when you get a chance!
Accessibility concerns:
The game is demanding visually especially at later levels. Things are moving very fast. Most things are clearly defined, but some platforms in Agnisort (fire/factory) levels can look like background elements, or background elements can look like platforms. Text describing upgrades and text in the Datalore entries is quite small and can't be scaled, however the UI can be scaled and changed between visual and numbers for easier understanding. Color differentation is somewhat important to distinguish the various "elite" enemies from each other (elites tend to have a black and red color palette) as well as pickups (green vs blue vs gray), and there are four different "core" armor sets corresponding to the colors pink, orange, yellow, and green, though these are distinguished by name and shape. The elite enemy designs might be sufficiently different, but I'm not colorblind.
As with any platformer, the game asks a lot of you physically, lots of button combos and dash-jumping is almost required, as is some level of button mashing. Controls are remappable, but the game recommends you play with a controller for a reason as a keyboard won't let you make all the required button presses at the same time. Powers are mapped to Y, LB, and LT on an Xbox-style controller by default, with dash being RT, A being jump, and X being shoot.
The game can get overwhelming at times with a lot going on, as should be expected with a platformer. There are a lot of sound effects happening at the same time. Hearing is mildly important to distinguish traps or enemy fire, though I wouldn't say it's required. Nina and Ace's grunting happens a lot and can quickly get VERY grating, so be warned.
The game contains brief flashes of light at some points, namely bosses. These are not sustained.
All in all, definite 8/10, glad I bought it, definitely worth it, there's lots to do. Though completionists beware. The achievements look hellish for this one.
