I you love Mega Man X and think the idea of it being mixed with conventions from games like binding of isaac or risk of rain, such, you owe it to yourself to try this game.
There are some differences of course. Levels are random, so don't expect special level design, but the level generation does ensure challenging (and sometimes even merciless) platforming.
Mix this with plenty of off-paths in a level with chances for shops and items to increase your power and abilities.
There's plenty of items to get, and plenty of them can make a strong alteration to your gameplay.
The boss powers are (mostly) all useful in a number of ways. It can be worth having them onhand both for combat and utility.
The game even has sets of armor, which you can mix and match for your specific needs, or hope you get a whole set for a bonus extra effect.
There are 2 characters, and they feel pretty balanced. One being long ranged/low damage and one being close ranged/high damage. Needless to say, the parallels to x and zero are obvious. Nina feels like she can handle levels well and handle bosses safer, Ace feels like he can shred bosses quickly, but with the inherant danger of being close to enemies that can become quite projectile happy.
The controls of this game feel good, though it might take some getting used to using special abilities (you can have 3 out of 8 active at a time, set to different buttons). That aside, if you can control well in a megaman x game, you can control well here.
There's also the risk of getting too many motion enhancing items. you can begin to move so fast or jump so far you become hard to control, so don't just take every item without considering the consequences.
The main thing that might stick out as a negative to me is the art style. It looks like a new grounds type flash game, but honestly, this doesn't effect the gameplay and it's easy to get used to. Everything at least feels consistent visually.
The music feels like it fits the game. It has a megaman vibe but I wouldn't say it feels like megaman music per se. Off brand but still fitting in a megaman-environment kind of music.
The game can be as easy or hard as you want. The hard mode features extra modifiers to tune the game to your personal tastes in what would challenge you.
Lastly, the game has a fun sense of humor. It's definitely not a serious game, but there's decent background to everything in the game. Every boss, enemy, and item has unlockable information tied to it. It's a nice touch that I feel shows that love was put into making everything in this game was best the devs could.
Def look into this game if this sounds good to you. You can pour hours into this game have have plenty of fun (and maybe a little frustration) with every run

Ori and the Blind Forest is a Metroidvania at heart, with a nice balance of combat, puzzle solving and exploration.
As many other games in the genre, an array of new abilities is slowly unlocked during the course of your journey that let you overcome previously impassable obstacles and let you explore further.
The game also offers an experience and level system that rewards you with skill points, which you can then spend to buy passive bonuses from a skill tree.
These passive bonuses go from simple stat boost to power-ups for your abilities and to brand new powers, like the ability to breathe underwater or to see hidden items on the map.
This gives the game a nice sense of progression and keeps things fresh, as every time you learn how to do something new, you'll immediately be prompted to use it to
The presentation is absolutely stunning, with a great use of color and light effects that help give fresh and distinctive looks to each of the zones of the game.
Besides the titular forest-y and tree-y areas there are also mountains, ruins, volcanoes, underwater areas, swamps and caves, each with their own color palette and music accompanying them.
The music itself is another strong point of the game, with a variety of orchestral pieces good enough to be listened to on their own.
I've seen multiple people complaining about the game's difficulty or being scared from trying because of it.
I have to say it's definitely a valid concern, as I've found myself struggling multiple times because of how unforgiving some platforming sections are or due to how much damage certain enemies can quickly dish out.
Still, the controls are responsive so I've never really felt like the game was to blame whenever I died. I just needed to git gud :3
I can't really find anything to complain about, so it's definitely recommended as long as you're ok with an action platformer with some really challenging sections.

ASTRONEER is a game of exploration and adventure, also survival of some nasty plants and wind storms that occur. I've played 11 hours of it by the time this review was made. It's such a great game, you collect resources like in No Man's Sky, but here you use them to build several things to add to your base. I am aware that there came a new update to No Man's Sky in which you can build bases and what not, but we're here for ASTRONEER, so let's not get too involved with No Man's Sky. The graphics/art style of this game, is just amazing in my opinion, there is no need for realistic looking graphics for a game to be great. This game's art style is very enjoyable so to say. (Again, this is my opinion.) Not only is it a space adventure exploration survival game, it's also a multiplayer game. My recommendation is to NOT buy this game if you are expecting a clone of MegaMan X (like I did), but I did still find it very enjoyable. This game is supposed to appeal to X fans but it is a totally different game. Instead of writing a fat paragraph I have compiled a pros/cons list to give you an idea on what this game is about. Cons list may be a little long, but maybe it's because my MegaMan x nostalgia keeps kicking in since the X series were my favorite games of all time and still awaiting X9 which may never come out, but I do still recommend this game.
PROS:
-Addictive
-fluid controls
-fast-paced gameplay
-has online coop
-accumilate points to unlock power ups and bonuses
-gives you a choice when you defeat a boss to gain their weapon or pick other powerups
-when you die, you start everything over, so you have to make best of each run and choose your powerups wisely
-there are different type of helmet, buster, armor, etc. powerups that all do different things
-there are in game challenges that will grant you extra power ups
-every run you have will be different (1 run you may have a certain combo of powerups while in another run you'll have a different combination)
CONS:
-The music is not memorable (like it was in MegaMan x)
-Graphics kind of seem like you're playing a flash game (kind of)
-levels do not have much depth in them (even mighty no.9 had nice lengthy levels)
-bosses seem a bit too easy (however there are difficulties you can choose with "skulls" to add more of a challenge like the latest Halo games)
-you don't choose what level you want to enter when you begin to play like all of the MegaMan and MegaMan x series (you do choose from 3 everytime you beat a boss)
-there is only the weak buster attack and the charged up attack but no in between (like MegaMan X had)
-there are no hidden paths in the levels to find super secret power ups (like it was in X)
-not very story driven (but doesnt ruin the fun of the game)
I may have left some things out but you get the idea. Even though I recommend and enjoy this game a whole lot, it's not MegaMan x, and we may not ever get another MegaMan x. Times have changed and so has the way people play games nowadays. It's hard to let go of the past, but this game is a great way to bring you back to SOME lost memories.
PS I'm also the type of person that enjoyed mighty no. 9 despite the bad reviews - shoot me

I bought this back when it FIRST hit Early Access and played it once before letting it sit in my library until it was released officially. I saw the potential back then but it needed a lot of polish.
It got that polish and so much more.
The rogue-like elements works perfectly in the Megaman format. The gist of it is every run, you start on a random boss and upon defeating the boss you choose from a random 3 out of the remaining 7. This is a great twist on the Megaman format of always going in the order of weaknesses being obtained and I would love to see the Devs start adding to the boss roster to really add more of that randomness.
The game scales its difficulty the farther in a run you go and often times will put your platforming skills to the test. That wouldn't go great if the controls didn't feel as fluid as they do. Especially after considering how it felt in those first few days of Early Access. The game has come a long way.
Honestly, it's worth picking up for anyone to just try out, Megaman fan or not. It's just a really fun game that has plenty of things for you to work towards and unlock and is definitely worth the $15 they are currently asking for. I look forward to the coming updates from the Devs now that Full Release is out and I hope to see the game expand and become more than it already is.

This game is amazing, I notice some details that still remain in beta and the new char designs are really cool... THOUGH this is a positive review I will say that the ending of all the bosses is the most lengthy and repetitive part of the game.
I think this game recreates mega man very well and is really nice for people like me who want to be engaged with a game, it helps you focus and stratagize for every single twist and turn.
The game starts off easily enough with by picking a random boss for you to fight, at the end of the boss fight you get a choice of several bosses they also being randomized.
Soon after you gain momentum you feel overpowered and like you're gonna fly... oh don't present yourself to 20XX just yet...
After the eight boss, that was it in beta, that was the end, it was rip your run, You've one! But oh no no no... in this version you'll despise the end of your run.
Have you ever played one of the crazy over the top japanese bullet hells? Then imagine that, but on a 2D sidescroller with some potiential ♥♥♥♥ up depending on your run. If you got flight boots, You're a lucky one, Air Dash? Yeah you're lucky, now if you don't have any of those? Either restart your run, or prepare for a hell of a time.
The game will designate enemies to block your path to lower your hp, and that makes it borderline impossible to fight the 2nd final boss, he's just a mixture of boss attacks with a little protect beetle which is annoying but still easier then the actual stage.
Finally the Last stage, yes, you don't just fight the other boss right away, you have to go through yet another lovely unforgiving stage that will dwindle your HP and NRG, be sure you have the bolts necessary to buy hp and shop items cuz your NRG will be dead for the majority of these stages.
The final boss is cool at first but then becomes a repetitive mess and leaves your hands sweaty and slightly unsatisfied...
THEN have that you go though yet another segment that is even more hell then the final 2, again, horrible and unfair places and lava pits, luckily no traps, but you'll be fighting alot of enemies going through the final stage, some not hostile, some there to drain the remaining hp from your sorry sorry hp bar.
The end segment will not be like how Isaac's is, where you're either super OP or not, it will bleed you out of everything you own before giving you the conclusion.
It's such a good game. But the end game will not make you feel good and it will demoralize you, even when you beat the final boss, it just isn't satisfactory, it makes you work for that final damned cutscene...
Overall I give this game a 9.5. its so awesome, the music is amazing, the enemies telegraph nicely and you can tell what their about just by looking at them, and the graphics are bright and happy.
But that end Segment will make you bleed and make you say/regret alot of items you wished you had.

this is the kind of game that makes you happy about the indie game movement. it's a game made by gamers specifically to fill a niche of game that they (and others) have always wanted to play. it's like those people who made a metroidvania because they wanted more of those games to play. you gotta respect that. in this case it's Mega Man X fans attempting to capture a co-op experience. this would be admirable if nothing else, but a slavish devotion to recapture the general feeling of MMX ensures that from aesthetic to mechanics to physics you always feel that similarity. it's mostly appreciated, though at times overly derivative. the inspirational source would've been obvious without copying even the tiniest details like the silly boss names, while i would have personally liked to see the game twist its own identity in there a bit more.
regardless a co-op MMX experience is a great idea and this delivers. it's an easy recommendation to anyone who simply yearns for a game of that nature. i struggle somewhat with the amount of action going on in this fast-paced widescreen game, but i also have not practiced much in single player. if there is a potential for frustration it's mitigated by short play times to complete an entire run, customizable difficulty options, and instant replayability.

I am playing the GTA serie one after the other.
Finished GTA III and Vice City. (see my reviews)
What's different / new compared to Vice City (VC)
Same like VC
1) Overview map : Can be accessed via the game menu, in addition to VC you can add a marker.
Still the lack of a hotkey 'M' for direct map access.....because it is a console port.
2) Cash income : slow so you are 'forced' to do side missions. Later in the game, you have
access to race missions and can export cars at the harbor which are really helpfull in cash generation.
3) Buying properties and as such having a save point or an asset (cash generation)
4) Weaponry : +/- same, in addition knife or silenced pistol for stealth.
5) Music score : Same quality which means superb, choice for everyone....rock, hip-hop, rap, alternative, country.
6) pop-ups of cars and buildings even at high drawing distance settings
7) frame limiter needs to be set 'on' just like VC and GTAIII to avoid strange physics of cars.
Better then VC
1) Windows 10 : Unlike VC and GTA III, i didn't need to apply the Silent patch to run the game smoothly.
2) Map size : hughhhh, three cities connected with green land, mountains and local villages.
Each city has it's own typical lay-out with references to Las Vegas - San Francisco - Los Angeles
3) New vehicles : bike, truck, train, tractor, harvester, buggy, go-cart
4) Besides the story line missions, there are plenty of side missions. The classic ones like ambulance driving, be a fire fighter, playing the cop and chase criminals, find hidden collectibles, do unique stunt jumps, start illegal races but also new
ones like driving a truck, going back to school (bike - plane - car - boat), playing the burglar, driving a freight train, dance with the low rider car, ......
5) Graphics, it is not a major jump forward but people can walk (no zombie walk), Anti-liasing can be turned on and there are blur effects to mimic hot weather or fast speed during racing.
6) Like barbie or Ken, you can 'modify' CJ with tattoos, shoes, trousers, hair style for improving
his sex appeal and attract women's attention.
7) If you train or just by playing, you will get better in shooting, driving, fighting, swimming etc.
8) In-game references to previous games like pictures of Candy SUxxx and Love Fist, the appearance of characters of GTAIII and Vice City which is fun. Certainly the Britisch lads.
9) Police and passengers are more agressive.
10) In VC and GTAIII, water is deadly, in SA you can swim and dive.
11) No screen loadings
Less then VC
1) Story line : somehow pointless, neccessary to make connections between missions but that's it, VC is simply better.
2) Main character CJ : Errand boy.... dull character compared to Antonio Vercetti (VC)
3) NPC's : some SA-characters are nerve cracking and very childish -> Catalina, The Truth and OG Loc
4) Humour (characters and radio stations): less refined.
5) Flying a plane (not heli) with mouse and keyboard is horrible. For finishing the main game, one needs to finish the flight school and that is really painfull and frustating.
Overall it is a good game don't get me wrong but it has it's flaws.
The proper balance between quantity versus quaility.
Vice City is smaller (David vs Golliath) and offers less play time, but beats San Andreas when it comes to story, characters and humour.
Now, it is time to move on to GTA 4 (which has it's installation issues)

DmC is an awesome spectacle fighter with a killer soundtrack by Combichrist, amongst others. The fighting feels smooth and looks pretty darn awesome, with lots of interesting weapons and abilities, and enemies that require different approaches, especially when the waves begin to mix and match the types you face. The level design is impressive, and the boss battles are pure bliss.
But, and there is a but... that only applies for a little bit more than half the game. Just a bit after the half way point, the game suddenly grows monotonous. You've seen everything there is to see by then, and everything from then on is just more of the same with a few variations.
The most major flaw the game has is that it relies overly on stamina challenges, by which I mean long enduring fights with no breaks between stages, whereupon you will have to start from the very beginning of the challenge should you fail one stage. These fights are way too common and are there for no reason save to make you loose focus until you make a mistake and have to start over again. They are padding. They are not complicated, as they consists of waves upon waves of the same enemies that you've seen over and over again, they just task your endurance and your focus. There is nothing interesting about these fights.
The game also has a major flaw when it comes to non-interactive cutscenes; there are a lot of them and they tend to go on and on. In the beginning they are short and far enough between that they don't distract from the fights, just a breather inbetween the action, but towards the end, they are long as hell and the writing takes a turn for the dramatic rather than the cheese. The cheesy writing is the game's only saving grace when it comes to storytelling, and they cannot write dramatic nor can they deliver it.
Despite all of this, I'd recommend the game if you could pick it up cheap (and I mean really cheap), as it is cheesy fun for half the game, despite being dull as dishwater for the other half. Hell, I'd recommend picking it up for the cheese alone. But be warned, it will eventually become a drag. I had to force myself to finish the game when the game ran out of "new" and just started to repeat itself.

ASTRONEER is a game of exploration and adventure, also survival of some nasty plants and wind storms that occur. I've played 11 hours of it by the time this review was made. It's such a great game, you collect resources like in No Man's Sky, but here you use them to build several things to add to your base. I am aware that there came a new update to No Man's Sky in which you can build bases and what not, but we're here for ASTRONEER, so let's not get too involved with No Man's Sky. The graphics/art style of this game, is just amazing in my opinion, there is no need for realistic looking graphics for a game to be great. This game's art style is very enjoyable so to say. (Again, this is my opinion.) Not only is it a space adventure exploration survival game, it's also a multiplayer game. So you can have fun exploring it with your friends up to 3 of your friends can play with you, so there's a total of 4 people as of now, which isn't bad to be a pre-alpha game. You can settle new homes by making a "Habitat" in which you can take with you on the shuttle to a new planet, place it down, and voila. You got yourself a new base on a new planet. So your friends can have one planet each, if you'd like. The game is fine with some being on the main planet and others away on annother planet.

TL;DR: a technically amazing game that does some pretty unbelievable things with RNG. It gets a bit too obsessed with RNG, some things would have been much better being pre-generated, but it's an awesome platformer that any Mega Man fan should try.
Full disclosure- I'm a huge Megma Man fan, especially of the X series. So if I'm biased- that's the reason.
This has got to be one of the most inventive platformers I've ever player. And it's all RNG. Even now, I can't believe how much of it is randomly generated. And the game doesn't feel like a horrific patchwork of stage design like some other RNG-reliant games do. Stages have a great flow to them, they're just short enough that they don't overstay their welcome while still managing to show off their respective gimmicks.
But probably my favorite thing about this game is how easily you can "break" it, and how it just doesn't care. See, pretty early on in a run, you can get leg upgrades that let you do some creative platforming. And with them, you can skip huge chunks of a stage. And the game manages to dissuade you from doing that: if you skip too much of a level, you risk missing some loot or health pickups. So that's a nice risk/reward balance right there. You're encouraged to explore, but if you want to speed run the game, you can easily do that, and the game supports it.
The soundtrack is also great. I was kind of expecting some Jrock a la MMX, and they kinda went with generic "indie music". But it's good generic indie music, so I don't care.
You can also customize the game's difficulty by playing on Defiant (hard) mode and activating or deactivating certain modifiers. Some of them just make the game more frustrating or remove cool features, such as this cat that you can buy that drops chests a certain levels that just won't be there in Defiant difficulty, but others do make for an interesting challenge.
Sadly, the bosses aren't great as the stages. They're kind of a joke. Most of them can be beaten by just mashing the attack button. Since almost everytihng in the game deals only 1 damage to you, you can only die from excessive chip damage. So the only benefit bosses have versus regular enemies is large health bars. And even those can be burnt to nothing with a few damage upgrades.
But while we're on the topic of bosses, they do look pretty cool. But in a reverse of the bosses are too easy problem, bosses are the only enemies that are visually interesting. Jim Sterling said that they look like Pokemon. I agree, they do. Unfortunately, they look like 4th generation pokemon.
The game also has some pretty serious communication problems. When you pick up upgrades, they're described in al ine or two of text. And these descriptions can be either perfectly adequate (attacks deal more damage) or uninformative. Or worse- they can be decieving. The developers chose to describe a lot of items and upgrades using baby talk, probably to come off as whimsical or to try being funny. Sadly, that often comes at the cost of telling you what an upgrade actually does. One of the two playable characters can get a big axe. The game describes it as something along the lines of "deals massive damage, but very slow". "Slow" isn't the actual handicap of the weapon- it has a horrible, uniterruptible aerial attack. Would've been nice to know about that before I bought it. Or, the game has "very safe labs" that can give you powerful upgrades that come with significant downsides. One of them says "damage massively increased. For everyone." I thought that that means that only enemies deal more damage, and not environmental hazards like spikes, because it said "Everyone", not "Everything". The game lied there. Everything deals more damage.
Also, the game could really use some RNG controls. Sometimes, the RNG can actually cut whole features out of the game. For example- "Glory Zones" are mini-stages that you can find that provide with core upgrades- the game's equivalent of armor upgrades in MMX- when completed. These are awesome. They're pretty challenging, but give you worthwhile rewards for finishing them. But because whether or not they appear at all is RNG, you could (and probably will) have entire runs without them. Why? Why not give players an option to increase or decrease the likelihood of them appearing? You can later buy an upgrade that makes Glory Zones appear in every level, and it makes the game considerably more enjoyable. Why is that an upgrade and not a toggleabple menu option?
Also, let's go back to those core upgrades. They're also awesome. They give you interesting bonuses and can improve you platforming abilities by a whole bunch. And when you finish a matching armor set, you get some very, very impressive new power (such as dashing in the air three consequitve times, bye bye stages). But that also amplifies the RNG problem- the game doesn't care which armor upgrades you already have, so your chances of completing a whole set are very low. I've played the game a lot, and even so I could only complete two out of four armor sets, and even that was due to dumb luck.
But even so, it's a marvel that the game manages to be this fun when everytihng is randomly generated. It's as fun as some of the better MMX titles. Hell, it's probably better than them and I'm probably just blinded by nostalgia. And I know I've written a lot about its downsides but, well, that's only because they're very glaring in light of an otherwise awesome game.
If you're a fan of sidescrolling platformers, buy it. If you're a fan of Mega Man, you probably already have.

I played the original Borderlands on consoles, and was somewhat disappointed there. A sci-fi shooter with unlimited guns and deep RPG mechanics? It sounded awesome, but it all felt very samey.
Borderlands 2 addresses a LOT of the issues I had, the plot is better, the characters are more interesting and the world feels more alive (despite still all taking place on the desert planet of Pandora).
But... it's still not quite there. Finding a new gun is less like adding a new tool to your arsenal, and more like finding loot in an Action RPG like Diablo or Torchlight, you quickly check if your numbers go up, then put it in your inventory to sell it later. I guess this IS a staple of RPGs, but it's not something I would find to be a positive.
The game still feels balanced to work best with multiple players (which I didn't consistently have), still has obligatory vehicle sections that don't really work and still don't give you anything nice when opening a vault... that last one was a spoiler, I guess. Sorry about that.
If you enjoyed the first Borderlands and want more of that then this will definitely scratch that itch.
If you want a fun shooter romp with friends that offers some character variety and customization, also get this.
But rated as an RPG, judged by its story and the complexity of its systems... well, it's not really hitting that target.
But, I'm still recommending it. I had fun with this game, and can see myself loading it back up again every now and then to tackle a piece of its nearly unlimited DLC packages.
I'm just not rushing out to get the oddly named Pre-Sequel any time soon.

I am playing the GTA serie one after the other.
Finished GTA III and Vice City. (see my reviews)
What's different / new compared to Vice City (VC)
Same like VC
1) Overview map : Can be accessed via the game menu, in addition to VC you can add a marker.
Still the lack of a hotkey 'M' for direct map access.....because it is a console port.
2) Cash income : slow so you are 'forced' to do side missions. Later in the game, you have
access to race missions and can export cars at the harbor which are really helpfull in cash generation.
3) Buying properties and as such having a save point or an asset (cash generation)
4) Weaponry : +/- same, in addition knife or silenced pistol for stealth.
5) Music score : Same quality which means superb, choice for everyone....rock, hip-hop, rap, alternative, country.
6) pop-ups of cars and buildings even at high drawing distance settings
7) frame limiter needs to be set 'on' just like VC and GTAIII to avoid strange physics of cars.
Better then VC
1) Windows 10 : Unlike VC and GTA III, i didn't need to apply the Silent patch to run the game smoothly.
2) Map size : hughhhh, three cities connected with green land, mountains and local villages.
Each city has it's own typical lay-out with references to Las Vegas - San Francisco - Los Angeles
3) New vehicles : bike, truck, train, tractor, harvester, buggy, go-cart
4) Besides the story line missions, there are plenty of side missions. The classic ones like ambulance driving, be a fire fighter, playing the cop and chase criminals, find hidden collectibles, do unique stunt jumps, start illegal races but also new
ones like driving a truck, going back to school (bike - plane - car - boat), playing the burglar, driving a freight train, dance with the low rider car, ......
5) Graphics, it is not a major jump forward but people can walk (no zombie walk), Anti-liasing can be turned on and there are blur effects to mimic hot weather or fast speed during racing.
6) Like barbie or Ken, you can 'modify' CJ with tattoos, shoes, trousers, hair style for improving
his sex appeal and attract women's attention.
7) If you train or just by playing, you will get better in shooting, driving, fighting, swimming etc.
8) In-game references to previous games like pictures of Candy SUxxx and Love Fist, the appearance of characters of GTAIII and Vice City which is fun. Certainly the Britisch lads.
9) Police and passengers are more agressive.
10) In VC and GTAIII, water is deadly, in SA you can swim and dive.
11) No screen loadings
Less then VC
1) Story line : somehow pointless, neccessary to make connections between missions but that's it, VC is simply better.
2) Main character CJ : Errand boy.... dull character compared to Antonio Vercetti (VC)
3) NPC's : some SA-characters are nerve cracking and very childish -> Catalina, The Truth and OG Loc
4) Humour (characters and radio stations): less refined.
5) Flying a plane (not heli) with mouse and keyboard is horrible. For finishing the main game, one needs to finish the flight school and that is really painfull and frustating.
Overall it is a good game don't get me wrong but it has it's flaws.
The proper balance between quantity versus quaility.
Vice City is smaller (David vs Golliath) and offers less play time, but beats San Andreas when it comes to story, characters and humour.
Now, it is time to move on to GTA 4 (which has it's installation issues)

Prison Architect is an excellent sandbox world that presents the challenge of designing and maintaining a working system (in this case, a prison). The world also contains countless easter eggs which open new gameplay options and enrich game content. A thouroughly enjoyable, highly recommended game for any aspiring architect.

This is flat out a well made game.
A first glance at the 32 bit sprite and flat map doesn't look impressive, but the game shines under the hood where so many new games on 'powerful' engines fail.
To begin with, the learning curve is not forboding.  The complexity of the prison doesn't really show until you advance a bit through an early game where your goal is just to make sure all your inmates won't be going anywhere.  The interface is easy to understand and quick to learn.  Overall, a few hours with the game and you'll be on your way to building your Supermax.
Once you're past the learning curve, the depth of game functionality starts to show.  Inmates as well as your staff interact in interesting ways, and the 'crimes' you have on your list are, at times, hilariously written.  But overall, balancing your prison to both care for, yet punish your unwilling guests makes for an adventure that never plays the same way twice.
In terms of graphics...  As I said, it's flat and sprite-based, but is smooth and clean.  No complaints for the style.  There's no unneccessary eye-candy.  And your overlays and interfaces are easy to read.
The audio is appropriate.  There's always a general drone of busy activity and not really any kind of music going on.  It fits, though it does set up ear fatigue after a few hours.  Prison sounds like alarms, cells, time rollovers, etc are strong and distinct.  You can be in another room and you'll know the distinct sound of lights out the moment it ticks over.
As far as bugs go, haven't seen/remember anything noteworthy.  The game runs smooth for the most part.  About the only technical problem I can think of is that the construction staff jobs cue can be overloaded in a large prison, leading to tasks taking forever to get cycled out.
Other than that, excellent game.  Two thumbs WAY way up [/hades].

I jump late on this, I know. There was so much nice and good and true stuff written in various ways and languages, that I want to take it from a somewhat different point of view that I felt was not covered yet. I felt flustered by a recent review describing the game as dissapointing, not living up to its hype and boring. So this was kind of my response to this. I edited it some to fit it better for an actual review and not as an answer to someone else.
I love playing games that are not original at all, as long they present/cover it well. The movement is fluid, the savepoint mechanics make it incredibly fair, and the whole game rewards people with a good memory and punishes those that want to rush everything. I see a lot of games that reward efficiency, muscle memory (speedrunning platformers), mechanics and reaction time (Shooters, MOBA's), intelligence (puzzle games), but rarely I see games that punish people for playing the fast no-attention way and reward memory skills and/or slow play. Ori literally shouts in your ear "HEY SLOW LOOK AT IT". And while doing that you feel incredibly fast, have a fluid movement and the controlling is just so incredibly satisfying that you wanna dance because you feel so light. You never feel slow even if you are. No reload times and a seamless world are also very nice things to avoid frustration because you never leave the ingame world.
Now I found flaws in different areas: The skill tree was very dissapointing, especially the middle one with the exploration and pickup enhancements. It was kinda "just there" for the sake of adding another element to the game to make placing savepoints more important. Also I glitched out in a very weird place and had to start all over from zero because I was stupid enough to make a savepoint there before I realized I couldn't get out. I wasn't the only one experiencing this. Third I found some of the skills you gather rather useless - especially in the end game. Charge Flame was basically just used for opening these weird pumpkin-like crystals and dash (Definitive Edition) was only really useful and necessary in the new areas, same as the Light Burst. Sein or Spirit Flame was rather useless lategame, too, because stomp was by far the most effective way to kill enemies. I thought some balance would have gone a long way there. I pretty only used 4 skills (outside of the jump enhancement) lategame: Bash, Stomp, Glide and Charge Jump. That's it.
I also got the feeling that I have played something like this before with the type of standard platforming skills like double jump, but that actually was the reason I bought it in the first place. I wanted good platforming. And I am coming from Super Meat Boy, Risk of Rain, I Wanna be the Guy + Fangames (Boshy, oh god), Wings of Vi, VVVVVV and Flywrench, so I certainly know what hard (platforming) games are. Excluding the escape sequences, Ori was the first platformer that was never rushing me to do something, set no priority on speed  and did that while not feeling slow at all. It just didn't make me hurry and I am someone that embraces slow gameplay for completion and discovery while oddly enough enjoy watching other people speedrun it. It also was like the first game where i NEVER, not a single ♥♥♥♥ing time complained about any hitbox. It was NEVER the game's fault if I died, not even emotionally in the heat of the moment. Ori could have been harder in my opinion and I would have enjoyed it even more! But I wasn't exactly disappointed, because it wasn't crazily easy either and had enough playtime, so yeah...
But overall, Moon Studios - though not being overly innovative - did nothing stupid, nothing really bad, and absolutely nothing that was a thing that makes you stop playing and that is an amazing feat in itself. They barely made mistakes with this game and sometimes a good game can just be the result of an absence of bad things. And Ori is amazingly succesful at avoiding mistakes and falling into traps. Besides what I said in the second part of this comment I had no frustration AT ALL in that game. Not a single second. It didn't make me cry, and it hadn't had a very deep story (still somewhat enjoyable), so I think people are a bit overpaying reaction to the solid, but not really impressive story and characters and not enough emphasis on Soundtrack and unique art. But everything was coming together. Everything was in the right place, nothing felt wrong for a single second. The reason why I love Ori so much is because it's similar to Trance and Metal in music genres. They simply take their time. As much as needed. We don't wanna fit everything into 4 actionpacked minutes. We make it 11 with a proper setup. That's Trance, that's Metal and that's Ori. It's as polished as it needs to be. Nothing raw, unfinished.
Ori will not be my game with the most playing time (hey League of Legends). It will not be my most watched game (hey Super Meat Boy). It will not be the one I would pay the most money for (I'm not gonna name this one!). It's not the most touching game ever (Hey Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons!) and it hasn't the highest replay value in my opinion (hey Hammerwatch!). If somebody would ever ask me about what my favorite game is, I couldn't find many categories if any, where Ori is my top pick. But it is more than the sum of its parts and as a complete game the enjoyment was incredibly high. Sometimes you don't need to be able to explain things, sometimes it should be enough to sit back and just enjoy the ride as long it lasts. Ori was an amazing "once in a lifetime" experience for me. And I had goosebumps when I finished it because I knew this was something special. It's like how I do it with films. The more I enjoyed them the longer I stay to watch the credits. You can be damn sure I was quiet til the end when Ori's came.
No human is perfect, and thus what we do will never be perfect. No game was, is, or will ever be perfect, but Ori is one of the rare games that come close to it.
Ori lives up to the hype and is worth all the full price and then some. I don't know if I will ever say this again: But please don't buy this on sale, it's worth way more than the full price. So please pay the full one. Please.

Ori is a deceptive title. It
like a Metroidvania, but its true focus is platforming. It
artsy and cute, but is deviously challenging.
Gameplay is very well thought out. To balance out the game's eagerness to kill you, your main resource can either be used to save your game and drop a respawn point virtually anywhere, or be spent on unleashing very powerful attacks upon enemies. Death penalties are minimal and your character will respawn before you even finish swearing, keeping you in the action isntead of staring at loading screens. Metroidvania games can get very time intensive, so a sidekick character instructs and guides you through your quest, setting objective markers so that you are never "lost" exploring the world. There's also a fast-travel system between static locations to help you navigate major arcs in no time.
The visuals are stunning and every zone has a unique feel. Familiar environments change as you restore spiritual balance and heal the forest. Over-use of flashy particle effects can sometimes make it difficult to see enemy attacks, and the detailed environments can cause a deadly spike trap to blend in with innocuous foliage. Fortunately, with quick respawns and save-anywhere the frustration this causes is well-contained.
Sound design is masterful. The game's soundtrack is fantastic and the music shifts in tone with the gameplay, making you feel triumphant or sad, awed or terrified. Tempo changes cue you in to dangerous action sequences and prompt you to start running for your life. Every enemy makes unique noises and present vital sound cues to aid your play.
Ori is Studio Ghibli on the outside, and Donkey Kong Country/Super Meat Boy on the inside. If you like platformers, this is a must-play.

Ok let me start this off by saying I LOVE the original Devil May Cry series (except 2). Over the top action, cool weapons and ridiculousness abounded in each game, getting more crazy as the series progressed. This, unfortunately, is an exception. While the gameplay is fun, and some of the puzzles are kinda clever, the overall feel is...well hollow. One of the things that made the previous games entertaining was the way Dante acted, causal and laid back. Here? Teen angst to the max, complete lack of reason, and the version just comes off as a complete jerk. Other classic characters from the series share very little with their original counterparts, and the story felt too toned down. I get that Capcom is trying to appeal to this generation's audience, but I feel like more effort could have been put into this game.
This is not to say, however, that the game is complete mess. The new weapons and abilities feel very DMC and the idea of the environment being your enemy is a cool concept; but its execution falls disappointingly short. Overall, the game isn't complete garbage, but it feels like a half-done idea rushed into production. Better luck next time, Capcom.
Final Grade: D-

Astroneer is like No Man's Sky if it used the Minecraft formula. Like the block building game in its infancy, Astroneer is mostly empty aside from its beautiful, sprawling, and diverse worlds. At the start of the game you land on a randomly generatred planet with a planet sculpting tool and not much else. With it you can dig out land as well as create land and also smooth it out. You will mine the resources on the surface until you can start making modular systems for your base. You can make a printer that makes anything from wind turbines to rover seats. These tools will let you mine ores underground to make more advanced systems. There is also a fuel condenser for your lander, should you choose to leave your new home for a different challenge. You can find more things to craft by finding large pods, either man-made or found underground or in trees, to research. So far in its alpha state that's pretty much all you can do, but as of right now it's well worth it for exploring the beautiful planets. The style is unlike any other space game with its bright colors, squishy character designs, and happy music as you suffocate or get crushed by debris in a sandstorm. Everything you see in the trailers and screenshots above will correctly influence your decision because everything there is in the game and they do look that good.

Honestly, there's a lot to hate about this game. For one thing, and I'm sorry if the developer ends up reading this but the visual design just isn't very good. I by no means could draw anything remotely close, but visually it looks very amateurish, and reminds me of the sort of things that friends of mine would have been drawing in middle school. Charming in its own way, but a bit strange to me for a purchased product. I understand that this game isn't coming from even a small studio, but there are plenty of indie games that have a more polished look to them over all.
Next, our stand-in for Zero feels useless on most levels, with the X stand in being far superior. I won't blame the devs for this too much. The nature of the game being randomly generated just sort of makes it feel like our X would in general be the superior character because they've got a ranged ability. On the plus side, this game does not force you to play as different heros! You can both be the X-equivalent or the Zero-equivalent at the same time, one of you implying playing a pallet swap. That's a huge plus for me.
On the much more minor side, I can say that this game does and doesn't support ultrawide (21:9 aspect ratio) monitors. While I find the normal stages render to the entire screen, the daily challenges or whatever they're called render in 16:9 letterbox. I'm not sure why. I don't really mind it all that much, I expected the game to do 21:9 with 16:9 pillar-boxing, it's just strange that it works in one and not the other. I'm sure there's a reason.
Now, let's move on to positive, because now that I believe most of my gripes are out of the way, I do have a lot of positive things to say. First off, the game *feels* right in terms of how it handles. While the level design can sometimes be lacking, I feel like I'm playing a Mega Man X game, from the way you slide down walls, to the dash, or the dash-jump combo. It all feels right, and that's great. The game also runs very smooth and doesn't feel sluggish ever.  The games greatness weakness, the randomly generatedness, is also its greatest strength. There appears to be a lot to do in this game, and I doubt I'll ever become completely bored with it!
It's Mega Man X with Co-op guys! For a guy who really loves the series and only has one friend who really loves it too, this was a dream come true to me! You should have seen the look on my face when I was trying to find something that the both of us would enjoy playing with each other and I found a literal dream come true. I don't care about the negatives, this is a great find and I'll be logging a LOT more hours in the game than I currently have. (Probably sitting at around 3-4 hours at the time of writing?)
I'm sure some would say the music isn't going to win any awards, but I quite like it and I'm happy that I bought the soundtrack. It fits the game well. I might add more to this review in the future because I've just scratched the surface, but I'd say despite whatever negatives this game might have if you've got a friend and you both love Mega Man X style games, absolutely buy this. If you're alone, I'd almost definitely say buy it. This fills a void that's been filled by essentially nothing since the release of X7.
P.S.
Really a minor complaint but, for the life of me I'm not sure why you have the default dash bound to I believe one of the triggers or should button. I instantly rebound it to the b on the Xbox 360 controller, because that's what the dash button would have been in the Mega Man X1-3 games, and I'm pretty sure most of the series as well on the equivalent controller. Executing a jump-dash just doesn't feel as easy or as right with the current setup. Not a big deal though-- buttons are rebindable, and I'm sure there's a reason for it that I'm simply just not seeing yet.

I quite honestly can't say enough good things about this game. It's a perfect capsule of classic Megaman X mechanical demand and execution, both characters feel great to play and handle entirely differently without either feeling out of place, and the layer of rogue-like design is the perfect lift to this style of gameplay to freshen it up for a modern audience.
To get super nit-picky the only real issues are that the artstyle can make it a little easy to get lost for some folks in multiplayer. Would be awesome to see an option to convert it from the more Flash-ish look into 16-bit pixel art and that a couple of the full sets are borderline OP. Neither is NEARLY enough of a reaosn to not pick this game up.

While it is an entertaining Mega Man rogue-like...it relies so much on artifical difficulty. The controls are just not tight enough for all the micro precision jumps it WILL demand of you. Far to many seemingly pixel wide platforms that you not only must land, but many times chain to progress. Which in some levels will probably be lined with flames to further punish you for being even slightly off.
If you must buy a game to get your mega man fix, get it on a deep sale only.

If anything, 20XX is quite inspirational not just for standing out from the rougelike crowd as an example of Early Access done right, but as a labor of love by an indie team that's wound up more worthy of the Mega Man name than... well you know. Mega Man X fans will be right at home with the fast action and tight controls, but without the terrible design choices that plagued the later X games. Optional difficulty modifiers also keep the experience fresh long after you've mastered the basics: want longer stages? Stronger enemies? No currency or shops? All of the above? You got it! Even temporarily ban certain items from appearing to further suit your playstyle. A rock-solid title even those not into the procedural generation craze can get into and enjoy.

This is an excellent roguelite game! It is essentially Mega Man X, the roguelite. If you like the Megaman games, this is a must buy!
You get a choice of Nina (Megaman) or Ace (Zero) as playable characters and you must clear each of the bosses before advancing to the final stages. There are 4 distinct worlds (Fire, Ice, Jungle, Sky) with two bosses in each world. Killing each of the bosses presents the player with a choice to either take their weapon or gain a stat boost or money. Your play style may determine which weapons you take and which you leave behind. Each of the weapons does extra damage to a specific boss (but I'll leave that for you to find out) and has another secret use.
Some of the platforming (especially in the Sky world) can be a real pain, but it never feels unfair, as the character controls feel extremely tight and polished. Throughout the worlds, you will find challenge rooms, shops, and other areas, which grant you with pieces of armor and stat boosts. Each character also has several different main weapons which can be found throughout the stages.
The game feels challenging throughout, but is not very prone to unfair B.S.

Unholy Heights is an adorable game that is exactly as the tags state: Strategy and Tower Defense. You rent out rooms to different monsters who each have their own unique set of fighting traits and in return they protect your building (and your money). You have to keep your monsters happy by buying furniture and other things to put in their rooms to raise their satisfaction, and as the satisfaction rises you can raise the rent. You build your tower by completing missions and saving up the rent money you collect from the monsters staying in your building, and the bigger your tower gets, the more monsters you can rent to.
Pros:
- Super addicting if you're into that kinda game
- Really adorable
- Different array of monsters and each has their own attack/defense stats so you don't constantly get repeats
- Overall a fun casual game
Cons:
- The only thing I can see that would be a con is that it's really time consuming. It takes up a lot of time to save up money especially if your monsters aren't very victorious.
The con isn't really that big of a deal so I'd give this game a 9 and a half outta ten. Ten outta ten if you have a lot of spare time on your hands.

With any game, I look for three things before I can give my recommendation.
1. Does the game look good?
2. Is the game too hard for me to play?
3. When I shut the game down is that the last time?
Sadly I can't give my recommendation to this game. Though it's an original concept with cute graphics, the gameplay does ths one in.
Visually the game looks good, with a one screen premise and tons of cute 8-bit style characters. The pics on the store page give you an idea of the style, but therein lies the frustration.
Difficulty-wise, this game is too hard to be a casual management sim and lacks a controls scheme in order to be a good button masher. I've tried TWENTY different times with different strategies to get to one expansion on the apartment building and I honestly don't think at this point that it can be done, No combination of monsters will beat the first boss unless I'm just impatient and not letting it run on its own for a few days in order to build up my monsters, all of whom seem to be unemployed and missing rent payments. Very frustrating when you just want to see what the game has to offer at early levels and can't get past the first stage.
Replay value is a toss up. Like I said, I've given this one plenty of chances and I'm either too dumb to figure it out based on the instructions given or the game just isn't coded to be friendly to a new player (which is a problem a lot of games have these days). For me to go back for more, a developer has to make me feel as though I'm successful in the early part of the game so that I'll fight when it gets tough.
Nice try and worth a look in the bargain bin, but at full price give it a pass unless the developers come back with some gameplay fixes or some serious content.

I spent almost all of my time playing this game with friends, both this and Borderlands 1. I loved every minute of it as we goofed around, made fun of some of the enemies and then laughed when we got our butts handed to us, the strategy and cooperation we had, getting into the story... Just an all-around good time.
Meanwhile, I tried playing a separate playthrough on another character, trying to keep ahead of the multiplayer.
I found I very quickly grew bored, even when I shot past the story progression of where I was with my friends. I found the excess of enemies tedious, the randomness of the weapon spawns (most of which are garbage in vanilla game, unlike what I remember from the original), and found the pacing of the story not quite my speed. Which is weird for me, since story is normally my biggest interest in a game. I just found it so utterly depressing on so many levels and didn't care much for it.
Seriously, I wanted to love this game. And I ended up finding that, if I wasn't playing with friends, I couldn't have cared less about it. (The irony is, one of my friends I played this with regularly had the exact opposite view - she didn't want to like it, and ended up loving it.)
So yeah. An intricate story, looting simulator, level-up system, an RNG weapon drop system, crazy driving, all sorts of cooky enemies and villains, and bad jokes and humor coupled with super seriousness and emotional moments. And through all of it, the fact alone that I was playing it with friends made it fun for me. Hence the recommendation. It's an excellent way to spend some time dicking around with friends.

There are many things I like about the game, but when the last message you get from the devs is essentially a big "screw you," it's hard not to have a bitter taste. So I'm gonna focus on that part:
The One Life difficulty in this game is poorly designed to a ridiculous extent, just because of one new mechanic: Wisps. When playing on One Life mode, if you die, your save file remains, allowing you to immediately start over from the beginning, still on One Life mode. If you do restart this way (rather than deleting your save file), you'll find a "wisp" at the last place you died; touching it will grant a bunch of ability points.
Now, the first problem: picking up these wisps causes Ori to stop and do a pick-up animation. Considering that these wisps will be hanging out IN PLACES YOU DIED, that frequently means that if you accidentally pick them up, you'll end up getting hit in the face by a laser or something stupid because you were forced to stop at an obviously dangerous spot.
The second, even stupider problem: apparently, beating this game on One Life mode will only grant the Unhinged achievement if you beat it on a file that has never had a wisp; i.e., you never died and restarted on the same save file. There's no good reason for this; you still have to have played through the entire game on One Life, gaining only the benefit of some extra ability points from your wisp.
It's likely that this is an unintended result, but it's been known for years and the devs have apparently made no response nor fix (and an easy fix it should be).
This combination of stupid design and lack of response to a simple yet seriously fun-ruining bug gives the impression that the devs included One Life mode as a complete afterthought and did not care at all about the experience of the players attempting it. It comes off as disrespectful to the very players who are actually delving the deepest into the full experience of the game. No matter what else the devs accomplished with Ori, I can't recommend a game that disrespects the player in that way.

If you like strategy builder games you're in for a treat.
The tutorial is famously unhelpful, but once you've failed enough and read the online tricks and tips you'll be ready to have a half decent and semi-functional simulated prison.
Prisoners will always try to escape, so make sure you have no easy exit (fence the entire prison in or put it inside one massive building). Other than that, the choices are yours.
The campaign (story mode) is pretty enjoyable and flows well. Good idea to start off with that and mess around in the prisons after you complete each stage just to see how different prisons can be built and run. Looking at pre-existing structures helps the player work out how to do things so there's less of a trial and error system required.
Escape mode flips it to the prisoner's perspective so there's an entirely new layer to enjoy.
I have spent many hours designing prisons that flow well so my prisoners have easy access to all areas to fill their needs have a low re-offending rate. Alternately you could unlock permanent punishments and trap prisoners in tiny cells for the duration of their sentence. Whatever way you choose to play, it's easy to lose half a day in this game.

I guess the best way to review this game is by doing two different reviews. One for the newcomers and the other for the classical Devil May Cry players...
(I would really advise you to PLAY THIS WITH A CONTROLLER!!)
So...
If you are into hack'n slash, beat em' up, action games... Or better yet... Killing tons of enemies, you'll most likely like this game.
Gameplay wise I've seen plenty of people saying that it's similar to Bayonetta... However in my view I find it more like GoW (The control scheme is pretty similar and the so it's the pace of the game)
Combos are easy to pull off and the animations feel nice for the most of it.
The story... Well... I didn't like it much TBH. I feel it's too generic for my taste, same goes for the characters... The only character I really liked was Kat.
There are dialogs and attitudes that feel so forced sometimes... But also there are times when the game pulls that well resulting in a pretty funny scene.
The soundtrack is like some Techno/Industrial/Metal/Stuff (?) that fit well with the game, however none of the tracks is really memorable.
In the end... It's a fun game, good and easy to learn gameplay.
This is a complete reboot of the franchise.
One of the best aspects of the original was completely redone (character design)...
Donte is a complete a*****e/edgy kid by the beginning of the game but he's not as bad as people usually say.
He's trying to be cocky against his enemies in a more western style, but he does care about people in the end.
Vergil is a
.
By the end of the game I ended up sympathizing more with Mundus that with the actual protagonist.
The gameplay has been taken to a more easy-to-learn way. They kinda fused Nero's Devil arm with Dante.
There are no styles, which means... No ground dashes, no teleport.
However, most of the Swordmaster and Gunsliger styles are adapted into different weapons.
There are certain enemies which need a specific weapon to defeat them (Angelic/Demonic)
which are something like this...
Angelic: Shurikens and a Scythe (Like Nevan)
Demonic: Axe and something like Ifrit/Beowulf/Gilgamesh
Also the game has been paced-down, still you can find some mods for the turbo mode on the discussion boards.
One of the mayor let-downs was with the bosses... You don't get that feeling of actually fighting a boss, their patterns are too predictable.
Normal difficulty feels like easy difficulty from DMC 3 or maybe even easier, I've still have to check out higher difficulties of this game.
But still... If you don't compare it with the older games while playing it. It's actually a fun game worth the while!
So, my advise if you're looking to play this game is to play it as it is... Don't get into it looking for something similar to the old DMC, because DmC it's a complete different game which can be very enjoyable if you get into it with the correct approach.
So... If you want to get this game, do it. But don't expect something related to the old Devil May Cry series.
I'd advise you to do so, you'll have a good time... If you're unsure, wait until it's on sale :).

Before I get to the review; I want to say that the best way of playing this game is definitely with a controller, so before you purchase the game itself, make sure you have one.
I sort of have a love hate relationship with this game, as I keep progressing through the main campaign, its problems keeps dragging me back, yet its gameplay is just fun enough to keep me going until the end of the campaign. That doesn't mean the game itself is bad, though, lets start with the positives;
+ Gameplay feels fresh, fun, and fluid. With a little practice and some getting use to, you can pull off some flashy and spectacular combos that give you a sense of accomplishment
+ The style system is great and encourages players to mix up their combos, use different weapons, and not just mash buttons
+ Limbo sequences are beautifully designed and are absolutely brilliant to play in and traverse through
+ The music fits well with the theme of the game most of the time
However, it does have its flaws, and here are some of them;
- The main story is pretty boring and generic with a few yet predictable twists, the way its delivered is also pretty uninspired, as there is even a level specifically designed as a generic exposition filler of the campaign's story
- Characters are uninteresting and aren't very well fleshed out. Dante's dialogues are corny and his jokes are a hit and miss, Vergil barely does anything throughout most of the campaign, and Kat is just a boring and forgettable side character. The same goes for the rest of the story's forgettable cast.
- Enemy designs are recycled and imo is worse than previous Devil May Cry titles
- Apart from a few interesting ones, levels are quite linear and can be short sometimes, the same goes for the entire campaign; which is a tad bit short
- Bosses are tedious and follows the same basic formula; take out its first health bar, expose its weak point, hit said weak point, take out its second health bar, expose its weak point again, rinse and repeat until it dies
- Camera issues hinder the flow of combat and can lead to a lot of frustration, especially when moving or engaging enemies in tight corridors or next to a wall
- Certain button prompts seems unresponsive and some of them are poorly implemented
If you can put the game's many flaws aside, the game works for what it is, and is a passable addition to the franchise, but I wouldn't consider it worthy of becoming a reboot of the Devil May Cry series.

The creators kept improving week by week with communicating with the fans to make the game  FLIPPING AMAZING! [Story]
As of course, judging by the title of the game, this does take place in the 20XX. Chaos starts happening around world, it's up to Nina (Megamwoman) and Ace (Zero) to save the day or earth or... their payment debts? actually the story is nothing to carzy, very megaman, which is fine.

You could be a tank built doing 100 damage for your basic attack and have 20+ health or become SONIC THE FREAKIN HEDGEHOG with your speed over 10+ and pass the through the main course in a heartbeat. The choice is yours alone playing the game. What makes this game have more replay value is the SEED system, meaning random generated levels like "The Binding of Issac". No area is the same. This game can be really hard, if not prepared or skilled enough.

I have 26 hours on counter now and I'm no Megaman expert. I highly recommend it.
Overall I think it's a game with an amazing replayability. The game is hard but not punishing: falling makes you lose 1 HP and not your whole life for example. I have only tested the multiplayer in local at this point.
Pros:
+ Tight controls. It took me 10 hours to finally beat it the first time in normal mode. It feels much easier now. You just learn to get better every time you play.
+ Rogue like. This games reminds me of Toejam & Earl for its rogue-like elements despite being a fast action platformer. Every time you play it's different. The game takes me in average 1h to complete without rushing at all.
+ Save & Quit feature at every end of a stage. You can play for 5-10 min if you want and continue the day after. This is ideal for people who work and can't really afford to spend a lot of time.
+ Check points everywhere. If you fall you will just respawn to the nearest stable platform you have touched. You never feel like doing the same part over and over again.
+ Great modern 2D graphics
+ Catchy 8-bit music. They stick in your head like the music of Megaman.
Cons:
- Bouncing character effects. When your character is in movement and then stop you can see this bouncing effect like if every part of your character tries to resist the movement. A lot of indie games on Steam I have played have that. For some of them it adds some charm to the game but for a Megaman like I expect tight controls and pixel-perfect precision. The controls are tight but the bouncing effects makes you feel they aren't.
- Small minor bugs here in there. Very rare though. It's not breaking the gameplay but they are visible enough to be mentioned.
Warnings:
* This game is not really for casual players. It's hard and requires training before finishing it. It took me 10 failures before I finally beat the game the first time.
* It's a rogue like, you must not mind losing. As I said, I started with a Win/Lose rate of 1/10 (probably more actually). If you play a game in order to complete it in one go, that's not going to happen. Rogue-likes are more known for their replayability.
There is no denying it, this game is a Megaman rip-off. Not even a good one either. The controls are terrible, level design is random, and the tutorial is more frustrating than useful.

The good:
"Stupid funny" as in, if you like throwing things around in games, you'll like this one. It takes little time to get used to the game and then you have hours and hours of fun. Like, a whole day. But that's just it, it will last just a day. HOWEVER! The day will be full of lulz, laughing and, if you'll get the moment, funny screenshots.
And the "Ram" attack can be brought into good because even if it leads to you failing a wave, it's a no problem. You can't fail here. Like, at all. So all the more reason for laughing how troll "dances" around the enemies that he tries to ram. While trampling everyone around those enemies.
I actually laughed while typing this when remembered how this worked well. And failed horribly a few times.
Playing this game "smart" or "serious" way will take away the fun. For me, playing games by reading guides and calculating my moves is the standard. Here, I didn't want to do that. I didn't NEED to do that to have fun. It was just "bumble around, wreck havoc". "You're a big troll, just run over your enemies! SMASH!"
Graphics.
World of Warcraft style graphics. Just enough, but no more. You won't find super shaders, flares or whatever. It's just enough. But if you like things "fancy", then get a DLC with suits. Dress up your Troll.
Why I don't say it's a bad thing? Well, because for the most time it's useful to be zoomed out maximum to have control over battlefield.
Game pace.
Okay. You get something done, you look at your fortress, you look at troll upgrades, OH NEW WAVE!!! SMASHING TIME!
Now let's see, something to upgrade, maybe this, maybe that? New wave! BASHING TIME!
The pace goes as you read this text in a slow pace.
Pause is a useful button, but don't use it at first or second fortress at early stages. There isn't that much you can do, so don't try to brainstorm it. Smash, bash and trample stuff.
Balance of Fortress vs Troll.
Your fortress IS a fortress. Don't forget that. Your troll is NOT invincible. Don't forget that. Keep both in mind, never lose.
Got to arrogant and got surrounded? Ouch.
Forgot about fortress and didn't trample those who were bashing it? Restart the wave.
Ran around like an idiot through ranks of enemies till they all were on their backs while your fortress was shoting them? That might just work.
Pss... Abilities rock.
Challenge.
At the easy level it's possible just to look at how the last wave went and figure out what needs upgrading first: fortress or Troll? Both are important. If one is lacking, the other will pick up SOME slack, but not all of it.
FAILing.
You can not fail. At all. This was, somewhat, frustrating when I got to Survival. Eventually got all achievements at easy and... Um... Now what? I can go and play on medium, but I don't expect to see anything new. There are no achievements for beating game on Medium or Hard. Or some special achievements for beating bosses on those difficulties.
Paying again?
Might go for Medium or Hard some day, but not sure.

A fantastic game, for both fans of Blood Money and new people approaching the series .  It takes the best parts of Blood Money and Absolution, and makes a cohesive and fun sandbox experience.  Murder the targets in a variety of ways while taking on multiple fields of approach.  A plethora of disguises, paths, and ways to approach the situation.
While the game only features six episodes (and a smaller tutorial episode that is actually fun), the amount of options available to the player open up a lot of game time. Each map is fairly huge, with a large assortment of npcs and ways to get to your target.  Disguise as a chef and poison the main entree with expired food to poison your target, then push him off a cliff while he's vomiting his guts out.  At a fashion show, disguise as a fashion model that looks similar to you, walk the runway, and then approach your target.  The game is as hard as you want it to be, giving the player free choice to approach it however they want.
If that wasn't enough, there are two types of contracts you can play.  Escalating contracts are contracts that start off easy, but get progressively more difficult.  Player made contracts allow you to tag up to 5 npcs on the map, then set how to kill them.  You can pick an npcs that roams around in an alleyway and happens to pass by a scooter, cause that scooter to leak oil, and make his death look like an accident.  Then you can tell the people who play your contracts to kill him exactly the way you want.
The only problem I have with the game is the need to always be online.  While it's not a problem that affects me, it certainly affects how other people look at the game.  You can play the game without wifi, but you won't be able to progress.  Seems silly to me, and completely unneeded.
Overall, I'd easily recommend this game.  This game is a return to Agent 47's roots, feeling pretty much like Blood Money 2.  I liked Absolution, but it wasn't a very good Hitman game.  This feels like what I expected from Absolution.
What everyone wanted from Absolution, but never got. There is nothing more satisfying than watching some annoying prick get shoved off a four-story mansion in what everyone thought was an "accident".

Ori: Definitive - 10/10. I don't give 10s very often - hardly ever.
But as I sit here listening to Ori's spectacular soundtrack, I'm reminded of all the ways that Ori succeeds, captivates, and warms the heart.
The gameplay is 1st class. I'm discovering that Metroidvanias are among my favourite games, and this is a shining example of the genre. It manages to keep adding new, genuinely useful and interesting abilities throughout. There is honestly never a dull moment, and the game manages to always leave you wanting more.
The soundtrack... exceptional. Truly beautiful. I cried at several points. But at oether times I was pumped up, scared, excited... the power of a good soundtrack is that it pulls out emotion, and this soundtrack battered me senseless (in a good way!) But listen to it as you play the game before look it up on YouTube. Great game soundtracks deserve to be remembered alongside the gaming moments in which you discovered them.
The story is quite thin on the ground, and a little depressing, revolving as it does around concepts of loss, lonliness and isloation. There is some dialogue at various parts of the game, but this isn't MGS :) The gameplay and the soundtrack here are paramount.
Do youself a favour. Buy this game. Even if you don't think it's for you - pick it up in a Steam sale. You can thank me later.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a metroidvania game with two different identities. From the outside the game is gorgeous with dream-like visuals and wide array of palette to make the whole setting incredibly inviting to just about anyone peering into the screen. The sound is equally enticing as it really helps bring out the inhabitants and the environment to life as well as providing appropriate feedback of impending danger which is directly not in-front of the player’s vision but something they need to be aware of. Overall, the production values of this game is topnotch from top to bottom.
From the inside the game is a brilliant platformer. You start off weak with only basic abilities to deal with couple of enemies and move past a few obstacles; but overtime you get new abilities which are not only powerful in their own right, but can be stringed or combined together to create some truly amazing traversal and combat opportunities which you couldn’t wrap your head around in the first hour of the game. The game does not throw you a bunch of new abilities and expects you to master it from the get-go, instead like a good teacher, it introduces abilities one by one and then creates scenarios when you will be heavily relying on the new found ability. Then the game asks you to combine the new ability with everything you learned before. This way you get a lot of practice done and become comfortable with your powers to the point you can start combining and chaining them in a natural flow. Bring a metroidvania game, the abilities also open up new sections of the world which was previously inaccessible.
The game adds a sliver of tactfulness into saving. You can save anytime in the game as long as you have at least 1 unit of power and there are no enemies or danger around. You will be in situations when you need to figure out what is the right way to use that power: will you go with a powerful explosive attack? Or will you keep it a little while longer so you can save after a fight.
Alongside the abilities the game has two different types of upgrade system. You can either get giant green or blue orbs to fill the health and power meter respectively, or you can a giant yellow orb and get upgrade points which can place into the upgrade tree. This tree have three distinct paths to upgrade. You can focus on attack powers, traversal powers or you can make it easier to find the unlockables stashed across the map if you care about going 100%. Of course you can simply do a mix of everything which I did. This sort of adds RPG like specialization which many players might prefer by simply upgrading the things which they tend to rely on the most.
Ori relies on precision platforming. The problem is the game is very floating and the controls are not as precise to the level it wants to be. So it can be frustrating at times to make precise jumps.
One area the game falls hare are the escape sequences. There are a couple of them in the game and can be very frustrating. You have to traverse along a certain path filled with dangers against time. If you mistime one jump, you die; if you wait too long, you die. You will be dying a lot until you memorize the path ahead of you and get the timing area. With everything the game does right, I was surprised on just how poorly this part of the game is designed. Where the rest the game rests on your skills, reaction and intellect; these escape sequences feel like it was designed with a lot of trial and error from the player. Did I mention you can’t even save during these sequences? Yep, if you fail you are thrown back to the start of the sequence.
It took me about 12 hours to finish the game and I thoroughly enjoyed it from start to finish --  apart from those escape sequences. Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful game which plays with equal grace.

If you like strategy builder games you're in for a treat.
The tutorial is famously unhelpful, but once you've failed enough and read the online tricks and tips you'll be ready to have a half decent and semi-functional simulated prison.
Prisoners will always try to escape, so make sure you have no easy exit (fence the entire prison in or put it inside one massive building). Other than that, the choices are yours.
The campaign (story mode) is pretty enjoyable and flows well. Good idea to start off with that and mess around in the prisons after you complete each stage just to see how different prisons can be built and run. Looking at pre-existing structures helps the player work out how to do things so there's less of a trial and error system required.
Escape mode flips it to the prisoner's perspective so there's an entirely new layer to enjoy.
I have spent many hours designing prisons that flow well so my prisoners have easy access to all areas to fill their needs have a low re-offending rate. Alternately you could unlock permanent punishments and trap prisoners in tiny cells for the duration of their sentence. Whatever way you choose to play, it's easy to lose half a day in this game.
